Can the EU save consumers €12bn on appliance repairs?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
07:31:13 UTC
16:31:13 KST

Fewer than one in five broken household appliances is repaired in major EU economies, as high costs and hassle push consumers to buy new instead. Repairs still cost European households around €12 billion a year. Can the EU make fixing things easier and cheaper?
Europeans create 35 million tonnes of waste each year by throwing away broken appliances. France and Belgium have repair rates of 18% and 15%, respectively. Of roughly 28 million household breakdowns a year, only 5 million result in a technician fixing the device.
Some 77% of citizens would rather repair products than replace them. Yet only 5% of washing machines and 33% of vacuum cleaners are priced at a point where professional repair makes economic sense. Most fall into a “borderline” or “unviable” zone, where a new machine is cheaper than the spare parts.
“Access to repair is not the main bottleneck. The price is,” said Alex Bunodiere, a PhD researcher in KU Leuven’s Life Cycle Engineering research group.
The European Union wants to change this through new “Right to Repair” laws, forcing manufacturers to provide affordable spare parts, tools and manuals while banning software blocks. The aim is to give Europeans transparent quotes and independent local repair options, making it easier to fix rather than buy new.
Built to be replaced
When a small component fails, households often replace the entire 60–80 kg device. A €280 washing machine repair can mean buying a new one for the same price.
“When you buy a new product, you get a two-year warranty. But when you have a repair done, they typically only guarantee the part they’re replacing,” said Bunodiere. Convenience is another factor: a replacement can arrive within 24 hours, while repairs can take weeks.
The European Commission estimates these scenarios cost citizens €12 billion annually.
Data shows manufacturers restrict independent repair by locking supply chains. Up to 80% of independent technicians report being blocked by manufacturers restricting diagnostic software and parts or digitally pairing components.
Brands also structure manufacturing around cost-cutting and fast supply chains to meet demand for lower retail prices. Subtle design choices can force early disposal. Instead of modular components, manufacturers often solder cheap wear-and-tear parts onto major control boards, turning a €50 fix into a €250 replacement assembly.
“They can make money from repair, but I think they typically make more money from the sale than they do from a repair,” said Bunodiere, adding that companies are therefore incentivised to sell new products rather than repair existing ones.
A waste management crisis
According to consumer rights organisation Euroconsumers, smartphones and tablets are discarded, on average, after less than three years. Televisions are quickly replaced as software evolves and streaming apps become incompatible. Consumers also discard washing machines and dishwashers after major mechanical failures, and replace cordless vacuums after an average of just 4.5 years, largely because of their lithium batteries.
That shortened lifespan has an environmental cost. “Generally, I would say repair is almost always the more environmentally efficient option,” Bunodiere said, although replacing very old appliances can sometimes make sense when newer models consume less energy.
Discarded appliances generate 261 million tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions annually. Under the European Green Deal, the EU has legally binding targets to reach net zero and a fully circular economy by 2050.
Lawmakers recognised they could not meet these climate targets without reducing the more than 30 million tonnes of raw resources used each year to manufacture replacement products. After years of campaigning by the Right to Repair Europe coalition and rising inflation pressures, the Commission proposed the legislation in 2023. It was approved by the European Parliament and Council in early 2024 and took effect on July 1, 2026.
Everything included in the new directive
The Right to Repair Directive is a “full harmonisation” directive, meaning all EU states must align with it. It covers two main areas: pre-market design requirements and post-sale consumer rights. To improve retail transparency, the EU is also rolling out harmonised labels, including official repairability scores and digital product passports assessing durability.
The rules will be enforced nationally by market authorities and consumer protection agencies, with financial penalties for breaches set by each country.
The Directive’s new measures focus on consumer protection. If a product breaks during the seller’s legal liability period, consumers can choose repair or replacement. Choosing repair extends that period once by 12 months, while Member States may allow further extensions for repeat repairs. For certain products that fail later, consumers may still request a manufacturer repair where EU repairability rules apply.
This matters because repairs can otherwise offer less protection than replacement. Bunodiere noted that a new product comes with a two-year warranty, while a repair typically covers only the replaced part, leaving consumers exposed if something else fails soon afterwards.
The Directive also introduces a European Repair Information Form to make offers easier to compare. It can include the repairer’s identity, repair and diagnostic costs, expected duration, handover location, transport costs and whether a temporary replacement is available. If used, the quoted terms must normally remain valid for at least 30 days.
Consumers can receive a temporary replacement during repairs and remain free to use independent repairers rather than the manufacturer.
They should also receive clearer information about their repair rights. Producers must provide details of repair services and available options, while Member States must make these rights easily accessible, including through national websites.
Obligations for manufacturers
The new laws require manufacturers to provide repairs unless genuinely impossible. They cannot refuse because a repair is expensive or an independent repairer previously worked on the product. They must make spare parts, tools and repair information available so independent repairers can compete and consumers have more choice. Software locks, hardware restrictions and contract terms cannot be used to block independent repairs.
Manufacturers must allow original, used, compatible or safe and legal 3D-printed parts. They must publish indicative prices for common repairs online, helping consumers decide whether repair is financially worthwhile. Where required, information must be free, while spare parts and tools must be priced so as not to discourage repair.
Where manufacturers must provide repairs, they must do so within a reasonable timeframe and either free of charge or at a reasonable price.
But Bunodiere argues the key question is how “reasonable” is defined. Manufacturers may consider a price reasonable given storage, labour and logistics costs, while consumers may still find it too high to justify repair. “What is a reasonable time? ... What is a reasonable price? The question is, how do you determine that?” he asked.
The rollout
The directive took effect on 31 July 2026. By that date, member states had to transpose it into national law, inform Brussels of their national contact points and set penalties for infringements, yet countries lag behind. The EU Commission reports that only 10 member states have respected the deadline. These are Denmark, Germany, Ireland, Croatia, Greece, Finland, Lithuania, Hungary, Austria, and Slovakia.
Uneven implementation creates fragmentation. “Consumers will have different qualities of rights depending on which country they live in and cannot rely on the directive directly against private parties”, said MEP René Repasi of the Group of the Progressive Alliance of Socialists and Democrats and rapporteur of the file in the European Parliament.
For Repasi, the biggest issue comes with Article 5 on the manufacturer’s obligation to repair. “As long as the directive, and specifically Article 5, is not implemented, manufacturers can, under the previous laws, simply reject repairs […] and either not repair, impede it or push the consumer towards buying a new good”.
In these cases, consumers can shift the liability and the damages they have incurred onto the member state. “Consumers can claim to repair damages against the member state because of wrong or not at all implementation. So, if consumers have the right to repair but cannot repair and have to buy a new good, then the damages they have can be pushed through to the member states”, the rapporteur explained.
Implementation speed varies depending on existing national laws. Member states with strong consumer protection measures will need to make less adjustments to national rules.
“The guarantee period of a product in the Netherlands is much longer than, for example, in Germany; hence, the question of extending the guarantee period for repair doesn't pose itself in the Netherlands as compared to Germany. The same is true for Finland”, Repasi explained.
In Sweden, citizens already enjoy a tax benefit, with half of the labour cost for repairs deducted from the invoice. In France, reparability scores for products became mandatory in 2021 in webshops and physical stores.
Some key tools aren’t ready yet. The European Repair Platform will be operational only from 1 January 2028, with an EU-wide online interface ready in July 2027. It will include national sections to help consumers find, for free, local repair shops, sellers of refurbished goods, buyers of defective items, or community-led repair initiatives. Countries that prefer having their own national site must have it ready by the same deadline.

Australia records worst-ever maths and reading scores in global test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
07:30:09 UTC
16:30:09 KST

Australian students record worst-ever reading and maths results in international PISA test
In short:
Australia's reading and maths results in a major international high school test have continued a 20-year decline.
Australian 15-year-olds have sat the Programme for International Student Assessment exams every three years since 2000.
Australia's test scores have been in decline for two decades, but other OECD countries are declining faster.
Australian high school students' scores in maths and reading have hit their lowest point on record, according to a major international test.
While the latest Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) exams showed a slight improvement in science results since the last test in 2022, Australia's long-term learning decline continued overall.
The 2025 test results released today showed Australia continued to perform above the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) average, with Australian students ranking 10th in science and reading, and 16th in mathematics among the 91 countries and economies that sat the test.
"What the data shows us is that we see long-term declines in reading and in mathematics. We were able to stabilise our scores in science," Jonas Berling from the Australian Council for Educational Research (ACER), which administers the test, said.
According to the OECD, 20 points on a test score is roughly equivalent to one year of learning for the average student.
Those declines mean science students today are almost one year of learning behind students who sat the exam in 2006.
In reading, students last year were roughly two years behind where they were in 2000. In mathematics, they were a little over two years behind the 2003 results.
"What PISA shows is that we see a decline in especially reading and mathematics where we haven't caught up with the levels from 10 or 20 years ago, when Pisa started," Mr Berling said.
"While we see some declines in the long run, we're still a very strong country,"
Blaise Joseph from the Centre for Independent Studies think tank said the long-term picture was "troubling".
"We also have fewer high performers and more low performers across all three subjects," Mr Joseph said.
Australian students reported improved discipline in classrooms compared to earlier findings, but remained among the lowest countries in the world on that measure, ranking 69th out of 80.
The disciplinary climate is measured by surveying science students, and 21 per cent reported they could not work well in most or all lessons compared to the OECD average of 19 per cent.
Forty-one per cent of Australian students reported there was noise and disorder in their classrooms compared to the OECD average of 31 per cent, echoing a report released last week that found one-third of lesson time was being lost to misbehaviour.
"Disruption remains a challenge in our Australian classrooms," Mr Burling said.
"I think it's important that we see disruption in the larger context of the Australian system and see what resources are needed in the classroom to improve on this."
Mr Joseph blamed the high rates of misbehaviour for Australia's lack of learning growth.
"Students cannot learn effectively when classrooms are regularly disrupted. Schools need clear expectations, explicitly taught routines and consistent approaches to behaviour so teachers can teach and students can learn," he said.
Australian students also skipped school at almost twice the OECD average, with 44 per cent of students reporting skipping a day of school in the two weeks before testing compared to the OECD average of 24 per cent.
Federal Education Minister Jason Clare said the results showed the importance of reforms the government introduced to classroom teaching practice and increased public school funding.
He said the United Kingdom introduced similar reforms 20 years ago, and in this year's PISA testing, rose three places in reading, four places in maths and seven places in science.
"This shows why the reforms we are rolling out are so important. The UK results are impressive. It's also hard-earned. It's something almost 20 years in the making," Mr Clare said.
"In Australian schools that have been doing this for a while, we can see the same thing that has happened in the UK. But we have to keep going and roll it out everywhere."
Mr Clare said too much screen time might be a problem in Australian schools.
"This doesn't mean there is no place for tech in schools. Students need to learn digital skills. That includes how to use, and how not to use AI," Mr Clare said.
"But it does point to the need to wind back the amount of screen time in schools."
Australian students perform strongest in new domain
One big positive from the latest results was Australia's performance in the "learning in the digital world" category, designed to measure a student's ability to learn in technology-rich environments.
Australian students achieved a mean score of 532 points compared to the OECD average of 500 points, with 75 per cent of Australian students reaching the national proficient standard.
James Casey, a Year 10 student at Gymea Technology High School, a public school in Sydney's outer south, took the test last year.
"This was more simply a test of just pure logic and reason and ability to think," James said.
School principal Katherine Edwards said the learning in the digital world results would help equip students for the jobs of the future.
She said the school had a strong focus on science, technology, engineering and maths (STEM).
"It's an area that our students, as they're moving into the workforce, need more and more, and the jobs that they're moving into are relying on those STEM skills and are increasingly needing them," Ms Edwards said.

Germany challenges ICJ jurisdiction in Nicaragua’s case over Berlin's alleged ‘support for Gaza genocide’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
07:29:06 UTC
16:29:06 KST

Germany on Monday challenged the jurisdiction of the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in a case brought by Nicaragua accusing Berlin of providing political, financial, and military support for the genocide in Gaza.
Hearings in the case filed by Nicaragua against Germany began at the Peace Palace in The Hague.
During the first round of hearings, the German delegation presented its preliminary objections to the court’s judges.
Germany argued that adjudicating the case would first require a determination on the legality of Israel’s actions in Gaza. It maintained, however, that the case could not legally proceed to the merits because Israel, a third party, is neither a party to the proceedings nor has it consented to them.
Julia Monar, director-general for legal affairs and legal adviser at the German Foreign Ministry, was the first to address the court on behalf of Germany.
She said the country had received many requests and criminal complaints concerning its arms sales to Israel.
Monar said some applications had been taken under review, while others had been rejected after authorities determined there were no grounds to open an investigation.
She argued that German authorities and judicial bodies had provided complainants and applicants with detailed information about the reasons for those decisions.
Maintaining that Germany’s support for Israel could not be separated from its commitment to complying with international humanitarian law, Monar said: “Our unwavering support for the existence and security of the State of Israel forms the core of German-Israeli relations, arising from Germany’s enduring historical responsibility.”
She argued that this support did not amount to a violation of international law, citing Germany’s financial contributions to the UN agency for Palestinian refugees (UNRWA) as evidence of its support for the Palestinian people’s right to self-determination.
Monar also said Germany suspended the approval of export licenses for weapons that could be used in Gaza between Aug. 8 and Nov. 23, 2025.
She said the processing of arms export licenses resumed only toward the end of 2025, arguing that the decision was directly linked to the ceasefire agreement reached in October 2025.
After Germany lifted the export restrictions on Nov. 24, 2025, German defense manufacturers were granted licenses to supply Israel with military equipment worth a total of €800 million ($929 million) between January and June this year.
According to German magazine Der Spiegel, the information was contained in a written response by the German Economy and Energy Ministry to a parliamentary question submitted by the opposition Left Party, or Die Linke.
Antonios Tzanakopoulos, a professor of public international law at the University of Oxford and the second speaker for Germany, argued that no dispute existed between Nicaragua and Germany.
Tzanakopoulos said Germany had not been notified of a dispute warranting referral to the ICJ at the time Nicaragua filed the case.
He argued that the admissibility requirements necessary for the case to be brought before the court, namely, the existence of a dispute and its recognition by the parties, had not been met.
The case should therefore be dismissed on procedural grounds without proceeding to the merits, he added.
Christian J. Tams, a professor of international law at King’s College London and the third speaker for Germany, argued that even if a dispute were deemed to exist between the two countries and the case were found to meet the admissibility criteria, some of Nicaragua’s allegations against Germany still fell outside the ICJ’s jurisdiction.
Tams maintained that the court had no jurisdiction to adjudicate allegations concerning violations of international humanitarian law, the Geneva Conventions, or general principles of law.
Samuel Wordsworth, the final speaker on behalf of the German delegation, said the dispute between the two countries stemmed from the question of whether Israel’s attacks and actions in Gaza were lawful.
Arguing that the case could not proceed without Israel being a party to the proceedings and giving its consent, Wordsworth said: “At the heart of Nicaragua’s claim lies its objection to Israel’s entitlement to receive military assistance from Germany.”
Wordsworth said Germany was not taking a position on Israel’s actions in Gaza, but was merely stressing that the court would first have to determine whether Israel’s conduct was lawful before ruling on Nicaragua’s allegations.
He therefore maintained that the case could not legally proceed in Israel’s absence.
Germany will complete its defense on Wednesday during the second round of hearings, while Nicaragua will present its oral arguments to the court on Tuesday and Thursday.
Nicaragua filed a case against Germany at the ICJ on March 1, 2024, accusing Berlin of “facilitating the commission of genocide” by providing Israel with political, financial, and military support.
During hearings in April 2024, Nicaragua argued that Germany was Israel’s second-largest arms supplier and could not have been unaware that the munitions were being used in the genocide in Gaza.
It also pointed out that Germany had sent tank shells, drones, and warship ammunition to Israel while cutting aid to Palestinians.
Germany rejected allegations that it had supported Israel’s genocide in Gaza, arguing that its arms exports complied with international law and were subject to rigorous licensing reviews.
The ICJ ruled that there was not a sufficient degree of urgency to justify ordering provisional measures, but drew attention to the prolonged and widespread deprivation of food and other basic necessities among civilians.
The court’s ruling stressed that states supplying weapons to an area where genocide and other war crimes are being committed could potentially be held responsible for those crimes.
After lifting partial restrictions on arms exports to Israel, which stands accused of committing genocide in Gaza, the German government approved the delivery of around €800 million worth of military equipment to the country.
Following the ICJ’s rejection of Nicaragua’s request for provisional measures, proceedings will continue until a final judgment is issued on the merits of Nicaragua’s claims.

US Envoys Leave Moscow Without Breakthrough as Putin Holds Stance
Unknown

- Category

US Envoys Leave Moscow Without Breakthrough as Putin Holds Stance
A three-hour meeting in Moscow between US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and Russian leader Vladimir Putin ended without a breakthrough, leaving the Russian leader intent on continuing Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Putin remains committed to capturing the entire Donetsk region, a goal he believes his forces can achieve within the next six months, as reported by Bloomberg.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to calculations by the Institute for the Study of War, Russian forces are currently advancing at a rate of 2.36 square kilometers per day on the Donetsk front, meaning it would take until October 2032 to control the remaining 19% of the region.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov noted that Putin may hold a phone call with Donald Trump and did not rule out resuming three-party talks between Russia, the US, and Ukraine, though he stated it is premature to discuss specific dates or venues.
Following his visit to Moscow, Witkoff traveled to Kyiv to meet with Volodymyr Zelenskyy and national security advisers from the United Kingdom, France, and Germany, later reporting "substantial progress" from his discussions.
The diplomatic mission was preceded by an unannounced visit to Moscow by CIA Director John Ratcliffe, who presented Russian intelligence leadership with a grim assessment of the Russian military's battlefield situation and the state of the Russian economy.
Ratcliffe urged a return to negotiations, warning that escalation would only worsen conditions and stating that the full surrender of the Donbas requested by the Kremlin "simply won't happen."
Political analyst Tatiana Stanovaya noted that Putin is not interested in discussing such terms, as he remains convinced he is winning and believes Ukraine will break at some point, regardless of how long it takes. Experts from the Institute for the Study of War suggested Putin may be operating in a false reality due to systemic exaggeration of frontline successes by military commanders.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, following contacts with the US representatives, said Ukraine was prepared to observe a temporary halt to aerial strikes involving cities connected to the negotiations.

Popovic knocked back four-year Socceroos contract extension
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
07:19:50 UTC
16:19:50 KST

In short:
Socceroos coach Tony Popovic has revealed he turned down a four-year contract extension to take the team through to the 2030 World Cup.
Popovic signed a six-month contract in June to coach the Socceroos until the end of the 2027 Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia.
What's next?
The Socceroos play Brazil over two matches in Townsville and Brisbane later this month.
Socceroos coach Tony Popovic has revealed he turned down a four-year contract offer from Football Australia (FA) to take the team through to the 2030 World Cup.
Popovic instead signed a six-month extension during the World Cup to take the team through to the Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia, which begins in January.
"It was my choice to go until the Asian Cup. Although I was offered a four-year deal, I decided to go to the Asian Cup," Popovic told journalists on Tuesday.
"And I think that is something that I think is good.
"It gives the FA the opportunity if they want to go in a different decision they can, and I'm very comfortable with the decision that's been made."
Popovic led the Socceroos to the round of 32 knockout stage of the World Cup in the United States, where the team lost to Egypt in a penalty shoot-out heartbreaker.
His side won its opening match against Türkiye, lost to the United States and drew with Paraguay before the fateful match against Egypt ended the Socceroos' dream run.
He led the youngest side at the World Cup of all 48 nations with an average of 25 years and 155 days.
Some of the Socceroos stars of the tournament have since signed transfer contracts worth up to $33 million, including Lucas Herrington (Hull City), Nestory Irankunda (Sporting Lisbon), Alessandro Circati (Benfica), Patrick Beach (Troyes) and Paul Okon-Engstler (Köln).
When asked directly whether he wanted to continue coaching the Socceroos, Popovic declined to give a direct answer, instead elaborating on his focus on fostering young talent.
"I love coaching the Socceroos," he said.
"When we qualified there was obviously 12 months before the World Cup.
"I ended up signing [his six-month contract] the last week before the first [World Cup] match, and we started this evolution of the team for 12 months without knowing whether I'd be there or not.
"I've never shied away from the expectation of results.
"But I've always had an eye on the future, and I think that was reflected in the squad we chose, the players we played and how much the team changed in 12 months."
He said he was happy to make those decisions without the security of a long-term contract.
"I had no concerns about whether I signed or not and if I hadn't signed I would have been happy with what I had done and what I have left behind," he said.
"The same will be after the Asian Cup.
"I know the legacy that I will leave behind.
"And if it's someone else that takes it forward, that's fine; if it's me, great, if we agree to do this together," he said.
Popovic's decision to not take up the four-year contract offer gives him the option of pursuing a club contract now that he's been able to shop his talents through the World Cup window.
In his first press conference since returning from the World Cup, Popovic reflected on the decisions he made at the tournament and said there was little he would change.
He drew criticism from commentators for the goalkeeper substitution minutes before the penalty shoot-out against Egypt, which the Socceroos ultimately lost 4-2 when Harry Souttar and Lucas Herrington missed penalties.
Popovic introduced captain Matt Ryan, who hadn't played a minute in the World Cup, for Patrick Beach, who had been outstanding, conceding just three goals in four matches.
He said he would make the same decision again.
"There are many reasons why Matty came in," he said.
"Matty has experience; Matty saved two penalties for us in the qualifiers; Matty saved penalties for [his Spanish club team] Levante.
"Patrick Beach has not saved one penalty in any shoot-out, pretty much.
"In that moment it was very clear to me that Matty should come in.
"And like I said the next day I would have done the same thing."
The Socceroos play their first Asian Cup match against Singapore on January 9, where Popovic said he would continue his youth policy.
There will be a lot of young players probably at the Asian Cup, and that will be done without losing any expectation that I believe that we should be challenging for the Asian Cup," he said.
"Once you're there, you want to win it.
"I think that should happen for Australia."
The team has two friendlies later this month against the might of five-time world champions Brazil in Townsville and Brisbane.
Popovic said the team would have a chance to play another round of matches during the November friendly window, most likely in the Middle East.

Gridlock around A28 after bridge closed for emergency repairs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Gridlock around A28 after bridge closed for emergency repairs
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Traffic on one of the main east-to-west routes through the Netherlands ground to a standstill on Tuesday morning after a motorway bridge was closed for emergency repairs.
The A28 has been closed at Nijkerk since Monday afternoon, when the highways agency Rijkswaterstaat closed the Hardenbergerbrug in both directions.
The motoring organisation ANWB reported a 23km tailback on the diversionary route on the A1 at 8.30am on Monday and 4km on the A704. Traffic was also at a standstill through Nijkerk.
The bridge was due to be repaired in November, but during an inspection the agency found that large quantities of sand and gravel around the concrete supports had washed away.
“The pillars are unstable and we can’t guarantee people’s safety,” spokeswoman Marike Broos told NOS.
The cycle bridge beneath the road and the canal below have also been closed to traffic.
Rijkswaterstaat is carrying out emergency repairs to support the bridge with sand and gravel before the strengthening works start in November, but it is not known when the road will reopen.

EU preparing special observers to 'secretly monitor' State Duma elections, Lavrov says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
07:19:04 UTC
16:19:04 KST

MOSCOW, September 8. /TASS/. The European Union is preparing special observers who "will secretly monitor" the Russian State Duma elections, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said in an interview with the online project "Sama Menshova."
"We are currently receiving information that the European Union is beginning to train some special observers who will secretly monitor how our elections are conducted," the Russian top diplomat noted.
"They should look at themselves: back in 2004 in Ukraine, it was the West that forced a third round of voting. They compelled the Constitutional Court of Ukraine – which is supposed to uphold the country's fundamental law, even though it makes no provision for a third round--to make that decision," Lavrov continued. "Lo and behold, they did it, and it was Viktor Yushchenko who came to power instead of [former Ukrainian President] Viktor Yanukovych."
The Russian minister also recalled the 2025 elections in Romania. "In the first stage, everything was absolutely clean--none of the observers noticed anything amiss--and the winner was a man who advocated not for blindly following Brussels' orders, but for articulating Romania's national interests. Even though there was nothing to catch on to, he was simply 'taken out of the race,' and that was that," Lavrov said.
Elections for deputies to the ninth convocation of the State Duma will take place from September 18 to 20, 2026.

President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy notes that last night saw a complex Russian attack "which the Russians deliberately attempted to calculate for maximum harm to life: ballistics, cruise and anti-ship missiles, jet-powered 'Shaheds'."

Political leaders in New Mexico have pushed back against US President Donald Trump's social media posts suggesting the state be renamed "New America," NBC News reported Monday.
Democratic Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham said New Mexico's name "isn't up for debate," noting it predates the US itself.
"While the White House wastes time coloring on maps, Nuevo Mexico is busy doing the work," she wrote on US social media company X.
Trump posted several images on Truth Social over the weekend and Monday depicting New Mexico as "New America," including an AI-generated image showing him placing a "New America" sign over a "Welcome to New Mexico" sign.
"Many people suggested changing the name of New Mexico, one of the great vote cheating states of all time, to NEW AMERICA," Trump wrote Sunday.
Democratic gubernatorial nominee Deb Haaland also rejected the proposal, as did her Republican opponent Gregg Hull, who said the state's identity "is not up for negotiation."
Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich and Ben Ray Lujan and Rep. Melanie Stansbury similarly criticized Trump's posts.
“Three things I will always call by their actual names … The Gulf of Mexico, Lake Ontario, New Mexico,” wrote Heinrich on X.
“It’s New Mexico, always has been and always will be. Just like how you’ll always be a sinvergüenza and corrupt,” said Lujan, using the Spanish word for scoundrel.
“Our state’s name carries generations of history, culture, and family—and it belongs to us. We’re New Mexicans. Period,” Stansbury said on X.
The president cannot unilaterally rename a US state. New Mexico's name is established in its state constitution, meaning voters would have to approve a constitutional amendment to change it.
Trump has previously ordered federal agencies to use new names for geographic features, including renaming the Gulf of Mexico the "Gulf of America" and Denali as "Mount McKinley."

German exports rise 6.1% year-on-year in July
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08

16:15:18 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
Germany's exports increased by 6.1% year on year in July 2026, while imports rose 3%, official data from the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) showed on Tuesday.
On a monthly basis, exports dropped 0.8% to €138.2 billion ($160.5 billion) and imports fell 5.7% to €116.9 billion in July 2026.
The foreign trade balance recorded a surplus of €21.3 billion in July 2026, up from €15.4 billion in June 2026 and €16.8 billion in July 2025.
Germany exported goods worth €78 billion to EU member states in July 2026, down 1.6% from June 2026, while imports from EU countries fell 6.1% to €59.6 billion.
Exports to euro area countries dropped 2.8% to €53.9 billion, and imports from these countries decreased 6.5% to €39.9 billion.
Goods exported to non-euro area EU countries rose 1.1% to €24.1 billion, while imports from these countries fell 5.1% to €19.6 billion.
Exports to non-EU countries rose 0.2% to €60.2 billion, while imports from these third countries dropped 5.3% to €57.4 billion.
The US remained the largest destination for German exports in July 2026, with goods exports increasing 19.1% month on month to €14.4 billion; compared with July 2025, exports to the US soared 28.3%.
Exports to the UK fell 7.2% to €6.7 billion, while exports to China dropped 9.5% to €5.6 billion month on month.
China was the main source of German imports in July 2026, supplying goods worth €15.2 billion, down 7.5% from June 2026.
Imports from the US fell 8.2% to €7.9 billion, and imports from the UK declined 1% to €3.2 billion in the same period.

US officials discuss smaller Mideast footprint after Iran conflict: CNN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
07:15:01 UTC
16:15:01 KST

Busra Nur Cakmak
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
US military and intelligence officials have begun discussing a potential reduction in personnel and facilities permanently stationed in the Middle East if the Trump administration succeeds in ending the conflict with Iran, CNN reported, citing six sources.
The informal discussions could lead to another shift in Washington's military and intelligence posture in a region where the US dramatically expanded its presence following the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks, according to the report.
Officials are considering possible cuts even as about 50,000 US troops remain deployed across the Middle East alongside significant military assets, including two aircraft carriers and more than a dozen guided-missile destroyers.
The US military has developed several possible options for changing its force structure in the region as early as next year, two sources told CNN. No formal force posture review has been ordered, however.
Shifting defense burden to regional partners
Senior Pentagon officials have also privately indicated that they want to reduce troop levels in several Gulf countries while shifting more of the defense burden to regional partners, the report said.
At the same time, the Pentagon is examining ways to strengthen defenses for forces expected to remain in the region, including potentially moving some installations underground to protect them from Iranian missile and drone attacks.
The idea gained urgency after Iranian strikes during the conflict exposed vulnerabilities at US facilities, according to CNN.
"The vulnerabilities were always known, but the US never acted on it with urgency," a US official told the network.
Iranian attacks have caused significant damage to American facilities across the region, the report said. A CIA outpost in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, was effectively destroyed, while US military installations in Bahrain, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and Kuwait were also struck, according to CNN.
Officials are considering whether some intelligence and special operations missions could be conducted without permanent regional bases, with personnel and equipment instead deployed from the US for specific missions before returning home.
May choose not to rebuild damaged facilities
Washington may also choose not to rebuild some facilities severely damaged or destroyed in Iranian attacks because of the costs involved.
Pentagon comptroller Jules "Jay" Hurst III said in April that decisions on repairing damaged facilities would depend partly on Washington's future regional posture.
Despite discussions about a smaller footprint, the US and Iran remain far from a settlement. Tehran continues to target US forces and bases, including attacks on American installations in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates last week.
Pentagon officials broadly expect the US to retain some large permanent bases in the Middle East, though reconstruction could depend on host countries contributing to costs that could reach billions of dollars.
US forces are also expected to remain vulnerable to Iranian attacks in the near term.
Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle said last week that US Navy personnel would not return soon to Bahrain, the traditional home of the 5th Fleet.
"We're not getting back in there anytime soon," Caudle said.

Kyiv • UNN
The President announced new talks on the Freyja anti-ballistic system following the Russian night attack.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated after Russia’s overnight attack that Ukraine continues working with international partners to strengthen its missile defense, in particular on supplying interceptors and launching the Freyja antiballistic system, UNN reports.
According to him, during the overnight attack, the Russians used ballistic and cruise missiles, anti-ship missiles, and jet-powered “Shaheds.” Ukrainian forces shot down a total of 175 aerial targets overnight, but, unfortunately, not all of them.
Despite very good results against cruise missiles, ballistic missiles are particularly difficult, and every day we prove to our partners our need for interceptors. We have already discussed this with the Americans and Europeans, and there will be more meetings, including today, with representatives of states and companies that can help with supplies and with our Freyja antiballistic system. My condolences to their relatives and loved ones

In the morning, a locomotive of the Kyiv–Sumy train was attacked at a railway station in Sumy region. Fortunately, there were no casualties. The evacuation of people is ongoing. Zaporizhzhia and the Dnipro region were also attacked
What is Freyja
Freyja is a Ukraine-initiated project for a joint European antiballistic system, the first track of the Antiballistic Coalition, which includes 10 states and more than a dozen leading European defense companies. The system is intended to intercept Russian ballistic missiles.
The project is built around the Ukrainian FP-7.x interceptor missile developed by Fire Point, while other components are supplied by European manufacturers. As UNN reported, Fire Point’s General and Technical Director Iryna Terekh said that development had reached the stage of technical integration of the entire ecosystem—radars, a launcher, a data transmission channel, and a command center—and that tests are being conducted up to twice a week. The system’s first interception of a ballistic target is scheduled for 2027.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
07:08:10 UTC
16:08:10 KST

Faisal Mahmud
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
South Korea's nominal gross domestic product recorded its fastest annual growth in nearly 47 years in the second quarter of 2026, driven by robust exports and investment linked to artificial intelligence, local media reported Tuesday.
Nominal GDP surged 26.4% year-on-year in the April-June period, the strongest increase since the third quarter of 1979, when it rose 27.7%, Yonhap News Agency reported, citing preliminary data from the Bank of Korea.
Compared with the previous quarter, nominal GDP jumped 9.2%.
Real GDP, a key measure of economic growth, expanded 0.6% quarter-on-quarter and 3.7% from a year earlier, extending the economy's recovery after 3.8% annual growth in the first quarter.
Exports rose 1.3% from the previous quarter, supported by strong global demand for semiconductors, machinery and equipment.
Intellectual property investment climbed 3.4%, while facility investment increased 0.2%. 
Private consumption grew 0.4%, though construction investment declined 0.1%.
Real gross national income rose 15.6% year-on-year, its sharpest increase since late 1988.
The central bank has raised its 2026 economic growth forecast to 3.3%, citing strong exports amid the continuing semiconductor supercycle.

Russia Pounds Kyiv Hours After US Envoys Depart Ukrainian Capital
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
07:06:12 UTC
16:06:12 KST

KYIV -- Russia hammered the Ukrainian capital with ballistic missiles, killing at least two people in a major attack hours after White House envoys left Kyiv amid a renewed push for peace negotiations.
The September 8 attack followed a lull in near daily attacks that underscored Russia's intent to press forward in its nearly 4 1/2-year war on Ukraine despite astronomical casualties.
Emergency workers pulled bodies from the rubble in one district of Kyiv while firefighters battled to put out fires from the attack, which also included jet-powered drones -- a powerful weapon that Ukraine has struggled to defend against.
At least 10 people were wounded, emergency officials reported.
The Russian attack included dozens of ballistic and cruise missiles along with more than 160 drones overnight, Ukraine's military said.
Over the past week, Russia has hit Ukraine in near daily attacks. Ukraine’s ability to defend against the assaults has been severely constrained by a lack of missile interceptors, above all US-built Patriots.
The attack came hours after US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner departed Kyiv following meetings with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and other officials. Prior to Kyiv, the pair visited Moscow for talks with President Vladimir Putin.
It was the first time the White House officials had traveled to Kyiv; by contrast, Witkoff has met with Putin eight times since the beginning of 2025.
US efforts to push peace negotiations have been dormant in recent months as Washington has prioritized the war against Iran, now in its sixth month.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha called on Kyiv's allies to "to act and increase pressure on the aggressor."
Russia's Defense Ministry said the attack targeted Ukrainian defense and military logistics facilities.
The weekend marked the first time Witkoff and Kushner traveled to Kyiv for talks.
After meeting Zelenskyy, Witkoff described discussions as constructive and said Washington had heard "new ideas" from Moscow. Kushner said the United States was working on a broader "peace package."
Zelenskyy, for his part, called his discussions with the Americans "very substantial" and said Ukraine was prepared to move toward trilateral talks involving Kyiv, Washington, and Moscow.
National-security advisers from Britain, France, and Germany also joined part of the Kyiv discussions.
Ukraine has signaled it is ready to hold another meeting with Russian and US officials, something that hasn't happened since last year.
The Kremlin, however, has shown no indication it had softened his hard-line position on its war aims. In comments to reporters after the September 5 meetings with Putin, Kremlin foreign policy adviser Yury Ushakov said Russia would press forward to "eliminate" the "root causes" of the conflict.
"Root causes" is a phrase representing a grab bag of Russian grievances dating back to before the 2022 invasion, including the assertion that Zelenskyy is not a legitimate president and the Ukrainian government was oppressing native Russian speakers in Ukraine.

Oil prices continue to increase on Tuesday as re-escalating tensions between the US and Iran increase concerns over possible disruptions to oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.
Brent crude futures increased by 1.4% to $98.5 per barrel as of 0630GMT, hitting a six-week high.
West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures also increased 1.4% to $94 per barrel.
On Tuesday, Yemen’s Houthi group targeted cities and economic infrastructure in southern Saudi Arabia, causing deaths, according to the Saudi-led military coalition.
In addition, fires broke out at energy facilities in southern Saudi Arabia following attacks targeting the sites, the Saudi Energy Ministry announced.
On Monday, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said that it had targeted and destroyed a US military tethered surveillance aerostat in a drone strike near Erbil airport in northern Iraq.
Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said on Monday that Iran will declare a new “restricted” maritime zone outside the Strait of Hormuz in the coming days, warning that any vessel entering the area would be placed on a sanctions list.
Yemeni Coast Guard forces also intercepted an oil tanker on Sunday after it unloaded an “unauthorized” cargo at the Houthi-held Ras Isa port in Al-Hudaydah governorate, government media reported.
The two countries signed a memorandum of understanding in June, mediated by Pakistan and Qatar, outlining steps toward ending hostilities, reopening the Strait of Hormuz and addressing economic restrictions.
The two sides have since accused each other of failing to implement commitments under the memorandum, while military tensions have continued alongside disputes over sanctions and navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.

Trial into deadliest migrant Channel crossing begins in France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
07:05:54 UTC
16:05:54 KST

As the defendants face trial, survivors' testimony and a parallel probe into French naval response raise urgent questions about how the waters are policed.
Fourteen defendants go on trial in France on Tuesday over a 2021 Channel crossing that killed 31 people, including a seven-year-old, in the worst small-boat disaster involving migrants in those waters.
Prosecutors allege the accused, said to have ties to smuggling operations, bear responsibility for the sinking that claimed 27 confirmed lives — most of them Iraqi Kurds — when an overloaded dinghy went down in the early hours of 24 November, 2021.
Four victims have never been found, and just two men made it out alive.
That morning, a French fishing boat spotted bodies drifting in the Channel near Calais, not far from British territorial waters. The two survivors later described how the flimsy vessel started losing air and taking on water after hours at sea, with passengers being swept overboard and drowning one by one — this despite roughly a dozen frantic calls placed to both French and British rescue authorities.
Those who died ranged in age from seven to 46 and came mainly from Iraqi Kurdistan, and included Afghan, Ethiopian and Egyptian nationals among the dead.
Distress calls ignored by authorities
Given the scale of the loss of life and the involvement of 114 civil parties — among them bereaved families and roughly a dozen relatives who made the trip from Erbil in Iraqi Kurdistan — the trial has drawn considerable attention.
Most of the 14 defendants, the majority Afghan nationals, face charges of manslaughter and organised facilitation of illegal immigration. Two, including one Afghan national, will be tried in absentia under active arrest warrants.
Adding to the case's profile is a separate, still-unresolved inquiry. Since 2023, seven members of the French military — five staff at a maritime rescue coordination centre and two crew members of a patrol boat — have been investigated for failing to render assistance to someone in peril.
A UK government inquiry published in February concluded that faster action by French and British authorities could have prevented some of the deaths.
Nearly 12 hours passed between the initial distress calls and the moment a French fishing vessel finally located the boat — by then, most aboard had already drowned.
Matthieu Chirez, an attorney representing 113 of the civil parties, said accountability must extend to everyone who played a role in the tragedy.
Fellow lawyer Emmanuel Daoud voiced hope that the three-week proceedings would encourage the public to see migrants not as "statistics or commodities, but human beings in search of a better life".
Defendants claim they are also migrants
According to prosecutors, those on trial helped launch a vessel that was uncertified, poorly built, overcrowded, and lacking sufficient life jackets — unfit for any open-water voyage.
Investigators argue that responsibility also falls on those who transported, sheltered, or escorted the victims beforehand, framing these actions as links in a "chain of successive events" culminating in the disaster.
The defendants have pushed back, denying involvement in smuggling. Some claim they themselves were simply migrants attempting the crossing.
Prosecutors have been handed phone data and location records that investigators claim tie several of the defendants to the departure point and to coordinating Channel crossings — evidence that helped uncover two separate smuggling networks run by Afghans and Iraqis.

Moldovan citizen Nicolae Cochu, detained in the Astrakhan region on suspicion of an assassination attempt on a senior military officer in the Engels district of the Saratov region, agreed to the killing for $70,000, the Russian Investigative Committee Spokeswoman Svetlana Petrenko announced.

On September 3, after purchasing concealment and transportation and tracking the victim, he attempted to kill the serviceman.
During interrogation, the defendant gave detailed testimony on all circumstances of the crimes committed, later confirmed during a verification of testimony at the scene. The investigation will petition for his detention.

Israeli forces imposed a curfew on Palestinians in Shuafat refugee camp and nearby Anata, north of occupied East Jerusalem, on Monday as troops, military vehicles and bulldozers carried out a raid in the two areas.
The Jerusalem Governorate said the forces entered Shuafat and Anata amid a heavy military presence and announced the curfew over loudspeakers.
Israeli forces later described the operation as “focused,” saying it was aimed at what it called “terrorist activity” and related infrastructure, without providing evidence.
Raids and illegal settler attacks across occupied West Bank
The offensive came as illegal Israeli settlers carried out attacks and expanded activity in several parts of the occupied West Bank, according to Palestinian official news agency WAFA, Voice of Palestine radio and local eyewitnesses.
In Burqa, east of Ramallah, illegal settlers entered the village and moved through its streets. Others reportedly erected a tent on Mount Al-Qarana near Deir Abu Mashal, northwest of Ramallah.
Near Al-Mughayyir, northeast of Ramallah, illegal settlers were seen moving timber towards illegal settlement outposts, raising concerns among Palestinians over further expansion onto their land.
In Hebron, a Palestinian woman’s vehicle was attacked and its windows smashed, Voice of Palestine reported.
South of Yatta, settlers re-established an illegal outpost in Wadi al Rakhim just hours after Israeli forces had dismantled it, local activist Osama Makhamra told Anadolu.
Israeli forces also raided Khirbet Imneizil southeast of Yatta, entering a Palestinian home and damaging property inside.
Palestinian land cleared in Salfit
In the northern occupied West Bank’s Salfit governorate, Israeli forces and illegal settlers continued clearing Palestinian land northwest of Deir Ballut for an 11th consecutive day, according to WAFA.
The latest incidents add to a broader pattern of illegal settler violence and land seizures across the occupied West Bank.
The Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission said 3,488 illegal settler attacks were recorded across the occupied territory during the first half of 2026.

Report: Iran’s offshore oil stockpile could run out by October as US blockade dries up revenues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
07:03:58 UTC
16:03:58 KST

Iran’s oil revenues are rapidly drying up as a U.S. naval blockade prevents new crude shipments from leaving the Persian Gulf and the stockpile already positioned outside the blockade dwindles toward exhaustion, The Wall Street Journal reported.
No Iranian crude has crossed the blockade since the U.S. Navy reinstated it in mid-July, according to shipping-data firm Kpler. Iran is still loading limited amounts of oil onto tankers inside the Gulf, but those barrels remain trapped there.
Meanwhile, Iranian crude already aboard vessels beyond the blockade, which Tehran can still deliver and sell, has fallen from roughly 90 million barrels in mid-July to about 29 million. Kpler estimates that if deliveries continue at their current pace, mostly to China, that floating stockpile could be exhausted by mid-October. Payments for cargoes already delivered could largely dry up by mid-December.
The squeeze is hitting Iran six months into the war, as the rial weakens, inflation surges and the economy contracts. Oil typically finances about one-third of the state budget and also helps fund the military, including the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
Iran loaded about 255,000 barrels a day onto vessels inside the Gulf in August, according to Kpler, roughly 85% below the average recorded between February and April. Those newly loaded barrels have not made their way toward overseas buyers.
Tehran is still benefiting from crude moved abroad during a temporary easing of the blockade after U.S.-Iran diplomatic contacts in June. That window allowed Iran to transfer large quantities beyond the Gulf for later delivery, but those reserves are now shrinking quickly.
Chinese refiners have increasingly turned to Saudi, Iraqi and Emirati crude, Gulf energy officials told the Journal. Iranian oil has become scarce enough that in some cases it costs refiners more than competing supplies. Iraq has offered discounts approaching $30 a barrel on some grades.
The blockade also appears to be forcing Iran to reduce production. Domestic inventories have not risen significantly despite the collapse in exports, suggesting Tehran has cut output closer to what it needs for domestic consumption, according to Homayoun Falakshahi, Kpler’s head of crude-oil analysis.
Alternative routes offer little relief. Iran can move only limited volumes by truck or rail, with Falakshahi estimating that trucks could carry no more than about 40,000 barrels a day, compared with prewar exports of nearly 2 million barrels daily.
The pressure is also spreading to petrochemicals, Iran’s second-largest source of foreign-currency earnings after oil. Kpler estimates that loadings in August were about two-thirds lower than at the beginning of 2026.
For Tehran, the lost revenue is compounding an already severe economic crisis. Official inflation is running above 80% year over year, while the International Monetary Fund forecasts a 5.4% contraction this year. The rial has also lost almost 15% of its value against the dollar since President Donald Trump announced his latest economic pressure campaign in August.
Washington is betting that the mounting economic pain will force Tehran to make concessions, but Gulf officials and analysts cited by the Journal remain skeptical. Some warn that instead of backing down, Iran may choose further military escalation as the economic pressure intensifies.

Nijmegen streets sealed off over gunfire report after Overasselt
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Armed police sealed off several streets in eastern Nijmegen on Monday evening after residents reported hearing what sounded like automatic gunfire. It turned out to be a false alarm, a week after the deadly attack in nearby Overasselt.
Officers ordered people around the Hengstdalseweg to stay indoors and out of sight, a police helicopter came in and the DSI special intervention unit of heavily armed police was called in. Police later said they had found no evidence that any shots had actually been fired.
“We are extra alert to reports like this at the moment,” a spokesperson told regional broadcaster Omroep Gelderland. A spokesperson told news agency ANP that the scale of the response was linked to the attack in Overasselt, roughly 10 kilometres to the south, in which two police officers were hit.
Belgian arrest
 Police said on Sunday that a 26-year-old Belgian national had been arrested in Amsterdam on Friday in connection with the attack, bringing the total number of arrests to 35. Two people released earlier remain suspects.
Specialist teams backed by riot police are continuing to search Overasselt and the surrounding area for evidence.
Previous convictions
 Several of the men being held have previous convictions for firearms offences, kidnapping and fraud, the AD reported on Monday, citing the list of suspects brought before an examining magistrate on Friday. Police declined to comment on the report to broadcaster NOS.
One 23-year-old from Amsterdam was jailed for four years after firing on a house in Antwerp in 2022, the AD said. The intended target was a relative of kickboxer Jamal Ben Saddik, but the gunmen hit the wrong address.
A second Amsterdam man was given 15 months, six of them suspended, for kidnapping and robbing an elderly man at gunpoint in 2024. A third, aged 20, appeared in court over a shooting late that year and is suspected of firing the fatal shots in Overasselt, according to the paper. Prosecutors have not said who they believe pulled the trigger.

Trump’s Ukraine plans ‘scared Europeans to death’ – Lavrov
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
07:02:07 UTC
16:02:07 KST

Trump’s Ukraine plans ‘scared Europeans to death’ – Lavrov
European leaders were “scared to death” by US President Donald Trump’s proposals for resolving the Ukraine conflict and worked relentlessly to sabotage Washington’s compromise efforts, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has said.
In an interview published on Tuesday, Lavrov accused European NATO members of seeking to prevent Trump from returning to the ideas he had discussed with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Alaska last year. He also pointed to a phone call between the two leaders on July 4 this year.
“Europe understands that if the Americans suddenly return to their original proposals... as was the case in Anchorage, Europe was simply scared to death,” Lavrov said. According to him, European leaders “immediately rushed” to coax Trump into abandoning his own initiatives.
Lavrov recalled French President Emmanuel Macron’s remarks at a NATO summit in June, at which the French leader had effectively boasted that the Anchorage initiative had been “buried” and that Washington was once again aligned with Europe in a united front against Russia.
“If Western diplomacy comes down to restraining countries that put forward reasonable, balanced, compromise initiatives, then so be it,” Lavrov said. Moscow would then pursue its objectives “not at the negotiating table,” which he said Russia would prefer, “but on the battlefield.”
Lavrov’s remarks come as the Trump administration makes a renewed push to revive stalled diplomacy. US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner met Putin in Moscow on Saturday for more than three hours before traveling on to Kiev the following day.
The White House said the sides discussed “substantive plans for next steps” toward ending the conflict, while Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov described the meeting as “extremely frank” and said the American envoys had presented a number of ideas on possible avenues toward a settlement.
Lavrov, however, argued that most of the public talk about diplomacy coming from Kiev and its Western sponsors is intended to secure another pause in the fighting and give their Ukrainian proxies time to rearm and regroup. Despite the renewed US effort, Lavrov insisted that no constructive peace negotiations are currently under way.
“Nothing is happening on the diplomatic front,” he said, adding that developments are instead unfolding “on the real front,” where Russian forces are advancing.
The foreign minister also warned that Moscow intends to follow through on threats of retaliation for Ukrainian attacks on Russian civilian infrastructure. Russia had warned that such strikes would trigger a response “much heavier for Ukraine,” he said, adding: “This is happening now.”
The top Russian diplomat also took aim at London, which has vowed to remain with Kiev to the end. “I feel sorry for Britain,” he said, since that end “will not be a happy one.”
Addressing European preparations for a possible future conflict with Moscow, Lavrov reiterated Putin’s position that Russia has no intention of attacking Europe. If European countries were to attack Russia, however, he warned that it would be “a fundamentally different war” and “very short.”

Youth clubs, trade unions, pubs: here's how Burnham can fix Britain's social recession | Gordon Brown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
07:00:30 UTC
16:00:30 KST

Prime minister Andy Burnham has hit the ground running, tackling head-on three of the public’s burning concerns: falling standards of living, failing public services and a remote, out-of-touch, over-centralised Whitehall. Now, this autumn, a fourth challenge, reversing the decades-long decline of civic engagement, is about to move centre stage to achieve his ambition to put citizens back in control of their communities.
For while there are tens of thousands of local champions bringing towns, cities and villages together, Britain is suffering a civic recession, a hollowing out of the associations, clubs and organisations that once were the beating hearts of our communities.
It is a sobering fact that almost 50% of British adults are not members of any community organisation of any kind, neither a civic association nor church nor faith group, nor even a sports club.
Trade union membership has halved from more than 13 million in 1979 to less than 7 million in 2025. Then there is the widespread collapse in religious adherence – the fall in Church of Scotland membership from 1.3 million in the 1950s to less than 300,000 today being one of the most dramatic indicators. The long-established Women’s Institute has seen its UK membership fall from a peak of 470,000 in the 1950s to about 170,000 today. Since 2000, the UK has lost about 1,200 youth centres. Working men’s clubs – which were once at the centre of industrial communities – have fallen from a peak of 4,000 in the 1970s to about 1,800 now, their membership dwindling from 4 million to under 1 million. And the number of pubs in the UK, the heart of many communities, has dropped from 75,000 in the 1960s to about 45,000 today. For a fleeting moment, the boost in volunteering during the pandemic obscured a drop from 27% of all adults a decade ago to just 17% now.
But the breakdown is not just in formal memberships, but in informal, everyday relationships too: young people in particular are vulnerable, with soaring numbers in England reporting having no close friends at all.
If our physical infrastructure – our roads, railways and airports – broke down, there would be a public outcry and a demand for their immediate repair. If our financial infrastructure collapsed – if cash machines shut down and bank transfers failed – there would be panic. But the breakdown of our civic infrastructure is happening in plain sight and it needs urgent remedy.
This change is not unique to Britain. A survey of more than 30,000 people in 20 countries provides compelling evidence that, in tandem with economic decline, civic decline helps explain the widespread loss of trust, nostalgia for the past and lower levels of tolerance that are the surface manifestations of what is a deep and widespread dissatisfaction with the status quo. It should not be a surprise that many now talk despairingly of a broken society as well as a broken economy.
This sense of decline, combined with social isolation and a feeling that “traditional values” have been lost, encourages a zero-sum view of the world: the belief that life is an endless struggle between “us” and “them” – whether “them” is defined as immigrants, foreigners or simply “others”. In this view, our very commitment to democracy and a rules-based international order becomes tenuous: widespread dissatisfaction means that people agitate for their government to exclusively pursue the interests of a narrowly defined population. The fact is that someone who is not involved in their local community and has little contact with people of different ethnicities or religious views is much more likely to support rightwing populist nationalist parties and to oppose cooperation between countries.
So No 10’s plans to transfer power from the centre to regions are best seen as what is called a “double devolution”; extending spending and decision-making power beyond local authorities downwards to local communities to empower a new generation of active citizens. But this must be complemented by a boom in civic participation. An opt-out national community service for young people, a remodelled Pride in Place programme to put local people and not politicians in control, legislating participatory budgeting to allocate funding for local services, and designing services to be much more accessible to people should all now be under consideration as part of a nationwide consultation on rebuilding community life.
Learning from a Danish law that requires municipalities to fund voluntary associations and provide venues for their activities, a UK civic capital fund could go further and guarantee support to all those who want to form or join clubs in their neighbourhoods, with only one stipulation: they are open to all and contribute to the common good. Such a fund could assist with travel, venue hire, membership fees and anything that constitutes a “participation tax”.
Promoting civic education and introducing volunteering hours to the school curriculum have proved to be effective, from Ontario, where pupil volunteering is mandatory, to Sweden, where school councils are given real decision-making powers. An Erasmus-style exchange – this time between the nations and regions of the UK – could help young people connect across religious, ethnic and ideological divides.
Recent evidence shows areas without quality local news see the least civic activity and are more prone to online misinformation. So support should be given to local newspapers and websites, including through an expansion of the BBC local democracy reporting service. Online community groups also have a role to play: in my own home town, the Facebook page Love Kirkcaldy has nearly 60,000 members – roughly as many as the population of the wider town itself. The page acts as a community noticeboard but also now brings people together face to face in clubs. Such forums help us to better get to know our neighbours, and restore faith and trust in democracy.
Between them, measures like these can rebuild an ethic of mutuality and civic obligation. The distinctive feature of a successful community organisation is not just that we belong to it but that it belongs to us. And while governments, local and national, can create the conditions for a stronger civic society, the most effective way to build one is the simple act of one person inviting another person to join in.
It is when neighbours no longer talk of “the school”, “the hospital”, “the library” and “the community centre”, or even “my school”, “my hospital”, “my library” and “my community centre”, but instead speak of “our school”, “our hospital”, “our library” and “our community centre”, that we will know a community has been reborn and there is a renewed sense that we are all part of a shared future.
- 
  Gordon Brown was UK prime minister from 2007 to 2010

Lin said closer cooperation could help Taiwan and Japan build secure, trusted, and resilient non-red supply chains. Japan is promoting 17 strategic growth sectors, while Taiwan is expanding its artificial intelligence, semiconductor, and other high-tech industries, he added.
The Japan Innovation Party also supported Taiwan following major earthquakes in Hualien in 2018 and 2024. Lin said the delegation was the party’s first large group to visit Taiwan since it formed a governing coalition with Japan’s Liberal Democratic Party.

Bingo Bingo will offer higher prizes for three game options for 17 consecutive days from Sept. 25 through Oct. 11. The "Super Number" prize will increase to NT$1,500 per ticket, while the "Big or Small" and "Odd or Even" options will pay NT$175 per winning ticket.

Thailand has frequently been used as a transit point for people traveling to scam compounds in Cambodia and Myanmar.
The fight against transnational fraud rings has become a regional priority, Hsiao said. He cautioned Taiwanese against being lured into fraud operations by promises of high salaries, free air travel, and accommodation in Southeast Asia.

Taisun seeks NT$1 billion over Taiwan cooking oil scandal

06:56:02 UTC
15:56:02 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taisun Enterprise filed a civil lawsuit in Taipei District Court on Tuesday against four companies, seeking NT$1 billion (US$31.7 million) in damages over losses associated with contaminated cooking oil.
The defendants are Central Union Oil, Fwusow Industry, Formosa Oilseed, and Namchow Holdings. Taisun Marketing Vice President Niu An-ze (鈕安澤) said the company is seeking damages partly because abnormalities in oil were discovered three times beginning May 13 but were not reported to the relevant authorities as required, per CNA.
Niu said multiple abnormal signals appeared in the oil supply chain and the responsibilities of each company in handling the information should be clearly defined. If the information had been disclosed promptly, risk controls could have been initiated earlier, he said.
Taisun lawyer Chen Cheng-hsi (陳政熙) said a comparison of the prosecutors' indictment, Namchow's public statement, and other evidence revealed significant discrepancies in when the companies obtained information about the abnormalities, the extent of their knowledge, and their subsequent handling of it. Chen said the first key issue was whether the information was communicated promptly.
Namchow's public statement indicated that on May 13, an oil sample from a Fwusow Industry tanker tested positive for benzo(a)pyrene at 4.6 micrograms per kilogram, exceeding the legal standard. A May 22 retest also exceeded the standard, while SGS testing produced a result of 8.0 micrograms per kilogram on June 4, per UDN.
Chen said Taisun and Namchow simultaneously received soybean cooking oil from Central Union. Taisun submitted its finished product to SGS for testing on April 10 and received a passing report on April 21, leading the company to conclude that its product met safety standards.
If information about the first abnormal test results in May had been promptly disclosed and reported, Central Union and its shareholder companies could have begun source tracing, cross-testing, and risk controls earlier, Chen said.
Niu said Taisun would also have had an opportunity to re-examine its products and raw material sources. He added that Taisun had hoped the three major shareholders would jointly reform Central Union and rebuild its food safety and corporate governance systems, per CNA.
Taisun said that as additional evidence emerged, it would no longer remain silent about responsibilities it believes should be pursued.
The lawsuit comes after Taichung prosecutors indicted Central Union, Fwusow, Formosa Oilseed, and Taisun, along with 15 individuals, in August over oil containing excessive levels of benzo(a)pyrene. Prosecutors said the oil had been supplied to downstream food businesses and alleged that reporting of the problem was delayed.
