For Palestinian amputees in Gaza, an Adidas campaign featuring a former Israeli soldier who lost a leg has come to embody two starkly different realities.
Former Israeli soldier Shalev Biton appeared in a local campaign promoting Adidas’ “Single Shoe” service, designed for amputees and others who need only one shoe.
In Gaza, meanwhile, thousands of Palestinians who lost limbs in Israeli attacks continue to struggle to obtain basic prosthetics, replacement parts and rehabilitation.
The contrast has angered amputees in the enclave, who question why a former Israeli soldier was chosen for such a campaign while their own needs remain largely unmet.
‘How can Adidas do this?’
Omar Haliwa, 14, lost his leg in an Israeli strike while on his way to collect water. Several relatives who were with him were also killed.
“How can Adidas bring an Israeli soldier and put him in an advertisement while we, the wounded of the war in Gaza, are suffering so much?” Haliwa told Anadolu.
He said losing his leg changed his life completely, while attempts to obtain a suitable prosthetic repeatedly ran into shortages of raw materials at Gaza’s prosthetics centers.
For Haliwa, seeing a former Israeli soldier receive services tailored to amputees while Palestinians struggle to obtain basic prosthetic limbs was painful.
He urged Adidas to pay attention to Palestinian children and young people who have lost limbs in Israeli attacks.
‘We have nothing’
Kifah al-Fakhouri, who lost her leg in an Israeli strike on a seaside cafe in Gaza City, said she was shocked by the campaign.
“I would have liked Adidas to pay attention to the needs of the people of Gaza and Palestine, because we have thousands of amputees,” she told Anadolu.
“This soldier lost his leg in 2021 and now has a prosthetic limb and resources. We in Gaza have nothing – no treatment, no equipment, no supplies.”
Fakhouri said prosthetic limbs available in Gaza often fail to meet patients’ needs, with some too heavy or unsuitable for everyday use.
Amputees need modern joints, replacement parts and better prosthetics to regain mobility, she said, adding that losing her leg affected her work, movement and virtually every aspect of daily life.
‘Look at us with mercy’
Ahmed Jawadi al-Balawi, another Palestinian who lost a leg during the war, said his prosthetic had already worn out and needed maintenance and replacement parts.
“Look at us with mercy,” he appealed to Adidas.
“They do not need help the way we do. They have resources. We have nothing. We make something out of nothing.”
Balawi said many amputees in Gaza are forced to use old or poorly fitting prosthetics and struggle to find shoes and accessories compatible with them.
Nabil Abdullah Mahmoud Ibrahim lost his leg when an Israeli drone struck him while he was playing football with other children at a school sheltering displaced Palestinians in northern Gaza.
“Shouldn’t Adidas support Gaza, when so many people here have lost limbs?” he asked.
He said Palestinians with amputations should receive the same support and opportunities available to others living with similar injuries.
More than 8,000 amputees
Munir al-Barsh, director-general of Gaza’s Health Ministry, said estimates indicate that more than 8,000 Palestinians have lost limbs during Israel’s war on Gaza, including more than 3,000 children.
He said Gaza has trained specialists capable of producing and fitting prosthetic limbs, but restrictions on the entry of raw materials and medical supplies have prevented many patients from receiving suitable prosthetics.
“The priority should be the Palestinian child who has lost a leg or an arm and needs rehabilitation,” Barsh said.
He urged international organizations and global companies to support Palestinian amputees and help provide prosthetics and rehabilitation equipment.
Boycott calls, apology
The controversy intensified after images from the campaign spread widely online, with pro-Palestinian users contrasting Biton’s access to prosthetics and specialized services with the conditions facing thousands of amputees in Gaza.
Israel’s Channel 15 said posts about the campaign drew millions of views, while calls to boycott Adidas spread across social media.
Amid the backlash, Adidas Arabia, the sportswear company’s regional Middle East social media account, issued an apology over the campaign, saying an image used in a recent local activation had raised “concerns and strong reactions.”
“It was never our intent to cause offense and we apologize for anyone affected,” the statement said, stressing that the promotion was a local initiative rather than part of a global campaign.
Adidas Arabia also said the company would continue to “listen, learn and work” to ensure its actions reflected its stated inclusive values.
For Gaza’s amputees, however, the controversy exposed a gulf that went far beyond a single advertisement.
One campaign had put an amputee in the spotlight. Thousands of others in Gaza were still waiting for the chance to walk again.
The Israeli army has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians and injured over 174,000 in a brutal war that has destroyed or damaged much of Gaza’s civilian infrastructure.

Czech defense contractor: We warned our government against Datasel

Czech defense contractor: We warned our government against Datasel
Czech ammunition manufacturer STV Group told Delfi that Indian company Datasel, with which Estonia signed a contract, is a textbook example of a fraudulent company. STV Group has also been defrauded by Datasel and left without the goods it ordered.
STV Group representative Dominik Drda acknowledged that he is closely following the scandal in Estonia because Datasel advertises STV's products on its website and because STV itself has been defrauded by the same Indian company.
"They lie all the time and use every opportunity, however small, to avoid fulfilling their contractual obligations," Drda told Delfi.
In 2024, STV ordered ammunition from Indian company Datasel, but later discovered that it was an intermediary posing as a manufacturer. Datasel managed to deliver only 10 percent of the goods agreed upon and failed to return an advance payment worth millions of euros to STV. To resolve the situation and recover the money it is owed, STV Group is preparing to take Datasel to court. As the Czech government is procuring weapons for Ukraine as part of an international initiative, STV warned the government that Datasel was unreliable.
"We advised them not to let Datasel defraud them and not to enter into any contracts with the company. Fortunately, they listened to us," the STV Group representative said.
Estonia sought to purchase artillery shells for Ukraine and paid a total of €70 million in advance to the Indian company, which had never previously sold a single shell. Instead of complete military materiel, however, Estonia received a succession of new promises, and the dispute is now in court.
In August 2024, the Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) signed its first sales contract with Datasel and transferred the first €15 million. The money did not come from Estonia's state budget, however, but from the European Peace Facility.
RKIK's current director general, Elmar Vaher, said he would not have signed the contract and that the decision was made by a very small group of people. He said, for example, that RKIK's head of procurement at the time knew nothing about it.
Magnus-Valdemar Saar, who headed RKIK at the time, disputed this account. He acknowledged that purchasing ammunition from third countries carries risks, but said no major decisions were made without the approval of ministry leaders.

Tokyo tourist hotspot bans short-term rentals amid surge in complaints
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
05:31:26 UTC
14:31:26 KST

A neighbourhood in Tokyo popular with foreign tourists will ban visitors from using thousands of short-term rental accommodations after a slew of complaints about behaviour.
In the latest sign that Japan’s patience with mass tourism is wearing thin, Shinjuku ward – home to the notorious Kabukicho nightlife district and the world’s busiest railway station – will prevent visitors from using private lodgings in residential areas and near schools and important cultural sites, Japanese media reported this week.
The measure, to be introduced through a local ordinance, could encourage other local authorities to follow suit. Shinjuku, with a regular population of more than 350,000, is home to 3,775 private lodgings – or minpaku – the largest number anywhere in Japan.
While tourism has boosted sectors of Japan’s economy and raised the country’s profile overseas, the surge in visitor numbers has created tensions with residents in popular destinations such as Tokyo, Kyoto and Osaka.
Shinjuku ward believes the measure will affect as many as 2,000 lodgings in residential areas – almost half the total, according to the Mainichi Shimbun. The number of minpaku residences in Shinjuku has almost tripled since 2022.
Reports said officials had been forced to act after receiving more than 1,300 complaints from residents in the 12 months to March. Many cited disruption caused by visitors who did not dispose of their rubbish properly, made too much noise and smoked in areas where it is banned. There have also been reports of trespassing.
Officials said temporarily revoking the licenses of renters whose tenants misbehaved would not address residents’ concerns. “Even if we crack down on badly behaved operators, the number of complaints remains the same,” a ward official told the Japan Times. “So we decided it’s better to change the ordinance.”
Authorities did not single out particular operators for the ban. But it is likely to affect those using popular companies such as Airbnb.
An Airbnb spokesperson told the Guardian: “Shinjuku has been an important partner to us, and we take residents’ concerns seriously. Home sharing works best when residents, hosts and guests can all live well alongside each other, and that is what we want to help the ward protect.
“We would welcome the chance to work with the ward on measures that target the problem more precisely - a prohibition across residential zones would close thousands of registered homes affecting compliant and responsible hosts, while leaving untouched the unregistered operators behind much of the disruption residents describe.
“We believe there is a version of this ordinance that protects residents’ quality of life without closing responsible, licensed hosts, and we want to help find it.”
The ward will ask for members of the public to give their feedback on the proposal next month, with a view to submitting revisions to the ordinance in February. It also plans to reduce the number of days per year that minpaku in residential areas can be rented out from 180 to 120.
Authorities in Kyoto – where tourists flock to view temples and shrines, rent kimono and photograph traditional geisha entertainers – limit minpaku operations in residential areas to just 60 days a year, during the off-peak season between January and March.
“Residents are concerned that their communities could be falling apart,” Kyoto’s mayor, Koji Matsui, said earlier this year. “We have strengthened the oversight of operators, but that is not enough. We need to go further,” the Asahi Shimbun quoted him as saying.
A record 42 million people visited Japan last year, spending a combined ¥9.5tn ($62bn) – also an all-time high. The government has set a target of 60 million visitors by 2030 – a goal critics say will exacerbate “tourism pollution”.
Authorities near Mount Fuji have introduced climbing fees and imposed a daily visitor cap in an attempt to reduce overcrowding on Japan’s highest mountain. In February, the town of Fujiyoshida, a popular Fuji viewing spot, decided to cancel this spring’s cherry blossom festival, citing a rise in disruptive behaviour by tourists.
The mayor, Shigeru Horiuchi, said the decision had been taken to “protect the dignity and living environment of our citizens”.

Landmark study exposes scale of brain injury crisis in rugby league
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
05:30:16 UTC
14:30:16 KST

Study on degenerative brain disease finds CTE in 31 former rugby league players
In short:
Of 51 brains of former rugby league players examined, 31 were found to have CTE.
The disease was found in players in their 20s, 30s and 40s, from amateur to professional levels.
The findings were presented at the International Sports Concussion Conference in Melbourne on Tuesday.
A landmark study has found 31 rugby league players have been diagnosed with the degenerative brain disease chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE).
Rugby league players in their 20s, 30s and 40s have been found to have had the degenerative brain disease, which can only be diagnosed after death.
Among them were decorated league footballer and NRL coach Paul Green, 49, as well as Manly Sea Eagles player Keith Titmuss, who was just 20 when he died.
The ABC has obtained the latest statistics, which are based on the first 150 brain examinations of people who played contact sports completed at the Australian Sports Brain Bank.
Of the 51 rugby league players' brains donated to the brain bank, 31 were found to have CTE. They played at various levels of the game from amateur to professional.
The paper was presented by molecular biologist and data scientist Jennifer Cropley at the International Sports Concussion Conference in Melbourne on Tuesday.
CTE's sole cause is repetitive hits to the head and body. Symptoms can include memory loss, impulsivity, anxiety and anger.
The disease has been found in several athletes who have died by suicide, but experts say more research needs to be done to establish a "causal" link.
'I feel a massive responsibility'
Former league star Paul Green's widow Amanda Green is calling on all collision sports to do more for the next generation of players.
Experts have repeatedly called for football codes to ban contact until the age of 14.
Ms Green has appealed for more people to donate their brains to understand the disease and wants more awareness around the issue.
"Now that we know what we do about this disease I feel a massive responsibility, as we all should, to protect the brain health of the next generation of young athletes," Ms Green said.
"I owe it to my kids and their sports-loving mates. We need to ensure they don't make the same mistakes as our generation did. The key here is to pledge our brains and support the incredible and potentially lifesaving work of the Australian Sports Brain Bank."
Ms Green said she had "no idea" about what CTE was until after her husband died.
"I had been involved in the highest level of professional sport in this country and did not understand this disease we now know as CTE," she said.
"That was not OK I didn't know what CTE was, and since Paul's diagnosis, I have constantly called for more education on the issue. People needed to understand this disease so no-one else suffered in silence."
Green died by suicide in 2022.
Ms Green said that since learning about the disease, she could see her husband was showing CTE signs prior to his death.
"On receiving Paul's diagnosis from [sports brain bank director] Professor Michael Buckland, he had mentioned that Paul had one of the most severe cases of CTE that he had seen, but due to Paul's intelligence, there was a possibility that he has masked a number of his symptoms, but the symptoms I had seen were symptoms such as anxiety, impatience, he was impulsive in his decision making, he definitely had lower levels of tolerance and quite elevated emotions," she said.
"These were changes that I had seen over time that I put down to the stress of his job."
Swinburne University professor Alan Pearce, who is an author on the paper which reveals the latest rugby league statistics, said more needed to be done to protect players.
"Given rugby league is a collision-based sport, it is not surprising that we found over 60 per cent of rugby league donors had CTE, but this tells us we need to start implementing modifications," he said.
"Introducing contact limits in rugby league is a good start but rugby league and all contact and collision-based sports must also start modifying to non-contact versions for children to the age of 14 years of age.
"Keith Titmuss's result, having stage two CTE at 20, tells us that this is not an old person's disease.
"Keith passed in 2020, and his brain results typify that exposure risk for CTE starts at junior sport level.
"Keith played junior rugby league from the age of five years old, then schoolboy rugby union, and his brain results show the effect of that."
Titmuss played as a schoolboy at Newington College in Sydney and had had a substantial exposure to repeated head impacts throughout his 15 years playing junior contact sport.
Titmuss died of exertional heat stroke after a 2020 Manly Sea Eagles training session.
His CTE diagnosis was revealed in 2024 and sparked warnings the major football codes were not doing enough to protect young athletes. His parents Lafo and Paul donated his brain for research.
The latest rugby league statistics follow a Four Corners report in June which revealed 33 Australian Rules footballers have been diagnosed with CTE and exposed the scale of the AFL's brain trauma crisis.
The Four Corners report triggered enquiries by WorkSafe Victoria and WorkSafe WA into incidents related to footballer safety.
Last month a Boston University study revealed at least one in four former NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021 was found to have CTE.
The NRL has been contacted for comment.
Watch Four Corners' full investigation into the AFL's brain trauma crisis on ABC iview.

Israeli officials do not currently expect a significant expansion of Britain’s restrictions on arms exports to be a central part of Tuesday’s announcement. Their assessment is that London will not substantially broaden those restrictions at this stage, in part because the remaining British military equipment supplied to Israel is considered limited but important.
The move comes amid a sharp deterioration in relations between the two countries. For years, Britain largely confined its opposition to settlement expansion to diplomatic condemnations and guidance urging British companies to avoid economic activity in the settlements. Tuesday’s expected announcement would move that policy into direct economic action.
Jerusalem is preparing a forceful response and is expected to accuse the British government of intervening in Israeli politics at a sensitive point in the election campaign. Israeli officials are also waiting to see whether London announces personal sanctions in addition to the trade ban.

Marine Le Pen no longer needs an electoral breakthrough to reach the second round of France’s presidential election. What she needs is for the rest of the field to remain divided.
France will vote on April 18, 2027, with a runoff between the two leading candidates on May 2, according to France’s official election calendar. President Emmanuel Macron cannot seek a third consecutive term.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
A Paris appeals court has shortened Le Pen’s electoral ban, allowing her to run despite upholding her conviction for misusing European Parliament funds. She has appealed to France’s highest court, which is expected to rule before the election, Reuters reported.
The latest Elabe polling places Le Pen at roughly 35% in the first round. Her nearest rival, former Prime Minister Edouard Philippe, remains below 21%. In a runoff, she narrowly leads Philippe and defeats every other tested opponent by a wider margin.
What a Le Pen presidency can mean for Ukraine
For Ukraine, the election is not an abstract contest between French parties.
France is a nuclear power, a permanent member of the UN Security Council, and one of the EU’s two indispensable political heavyweights. The president is commander-in-chief, represents France internationally, and negotiates treaties. Parliament controls budgets and most domestic legislation, but the Elysee has exceptional influence over defense and foreign policy.
Macron has moved France well beyond general declarations of solidarity. Paris supports weapons deliveries, sanctions, Ukraine’s EU accession, and postwar security guarantees. France and Britain are also leading preparations for a multinational force that could deploy after a ceasefire, according to the Coalition of the Willing declaration.
Russia Appears to Break Its Own Three-Day Kyiv Truce Before Deadline
That makes the 2027 election central to two of Kyiv’s most important strategic objectives: maintaining military support and keeping its EU membership path open.
As Kyiv Post previously reported, France’s political position could be decisive for any attempt to move Ukraine toward membership in 2027. An accession treaty would ultimately require unanimous approval from every EU member state.
A French president would not need to abandon Ukraine publicly to damage its position. It would suffice to restrict how French weapons may be used, opposing a postwar force, weakening sanctions, or slowing EU decisions would be enough.
That is why Le Pen’s shift on Ukraine since 2022 matters, but so do the limits of that shift.
Le Pen changed her language, not her policy
Before Russia’s full-scale invasion, Le Pen openly promoted closer relations with Moscow. She treated Ukraine as part of Russia’s sphere of influence, refused to describe the annexation of Crimea as illegal, and argued that Europe should eventually build a strategic partnership with Russia.
Her party borrowed €9 million ($10.5 million) from a Russian bank in 2014. Le Pen met Putin at the Kremlin shortly before the 2017 French election. Her 2022 campaign printed 1.2 million leaflets featuring a photograph of that meeting. Russia’s invasion turned the image from proof of international stature into an electoral liability.
In a 2022 Kyiv Post interview, European policy expert Georgina Wright said Le Pen’s messaging about her closeness to Putin “died overnight.” Le Pen condemned the invasion, supported accepting Ukrainian refugees, and publicly backed Ukraine’s sovereignty and its right to political, financial, and military support.
The change was real – but it wasn’t complete either.
Le Pen still opposes sending French military personnel to Ukraine. She has said Kyiv should not be allowed to use French long-range weapons against targets inside Russia. In 2024, she said a National Rally government would block such strikes, a position that would reverse Macron’s policy.
She has also warned against sanctions that impose high costs on French households and presents negotiations, rather than Ukrainian military leverage, as the principal route to ending the war. In May 2026, she reiterated that France should leave NATO’s integrated military command while remaining a member of the alliance, Reuters reported.
Her rhetoric has occasionally moved further in Ukraine’s favor. When the Trump administration suspended US military assistance in March 2025, Le Pen called the decision “very cruel” for Ukrainian soldiers and emphasized the importance of American intelligence and technical support.
Where the other candidates stand on Ukraine
Edouard Philippe is the most electorally competitive pro-Ukraine candidate. During a May 2026 visit to Kyiv, he supported Ukraine’s accession to both the EU and NATO and backed deploying European forces after the fighting ends to deter another Russian attack. He would broadly preserve France’s current alignment with Kyiv.
Gabriel Attal offers even clearer continuity with Macron. As prime minister, he defended French deliveries of ammunition, air defenses, and long-range weapons. His presidential platform supports allowing Ukraine to use supplied weapons against military targets inside Russia. He has also advocated using frozen Russian state assets for Ukraine.
Raphael Glucksmann offers the strongest pro-Ukraine position on the left. He supports continued military aid, a harder European approach to Russia, and greater European defense capacity. His difficulty is electoral: he must unite moderate left-wing voters while attracting centrists without alienating supporters of Jean-Luc Melenchon.
Melenchon is the principal exception. He condemned the full-scale invasion but previously defended Russia’s annexation of Crimea and repeated Kremlin-aligned claims about Ukraine. He now prioritizes negotiations and French non-alignment while resisting a more NATO-centered European defense policy. His record, which Kyiv Post examined after France’s 2024 parliamentary election, makes him difficult for many pro-Ukraine Socialists, Greens, and centrists to support.
Bruno Retailleau, the candidate of the traditional conservative Republicans, has also backed Ukraine and chose Kyiv for his first foreign campaign trip. Green leader Marine Tondelier supports continued military assistance and stronger European security guarantees.
The result is a strategic imbalance. Le Pen has one consolidated party and a dominant position. The candidates most firmly committed to Ukraine are divided across the center, center-left, Greens, and traditional right.
Russian-linked disinformation networks have already targeted Glucksmann, Philippe, and Attal with fabricated stories and imitation news reports. France’s Viginum foreign-interference agency identified several operations, while Attal accused Moscow of trying to weaken Le Pen’s opponents because of the National Rally’s history of support for Russia, Le Monde reported. That political conclusion has not been independently established.
Le Pen is already through the first gate
France’s presidential election has two rounds. A committed base can secure a place in the runoff, but victory there requires a broader coalition.
Le Pen appears to have solved the first problem.
She received about 18% in 2012, 21% in 2017, and 23% in 2022. She then took more than 41% against Macron in the 2022 runoff.
She now polls at roughly 35% in the first round, close to twice the support of the best-placed alternative. A major legal, political, or personal shock would probably be required to keep her out of the runoff.
The second-round barrier has weakened as well. Macron defeated her by more than 10 million votes in 2017. Five years later, his margin fell to about 5.5 million. Current polling places Le Pen narrowly ahead even of Philippe, the opponent who performs best against her.
The 2022 gap was about 5.5 million votes. Le Pen could close it through a combination of new supporters and anti-Le Pen voters staying home.
The Le Pen name no longer produces the same reaction
Marine Le Pen’s father, the late Jean-Marie Le Pen, showed how France’s two-round system could produce a political earthquake and then contain it.
In 2002, the left split across multiple candidates. Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin missed the runoff by fewer than 200,000 votes, allowing Jean-Marie Le Pen to face incumbent President Jacques Chirac.
France mobilized against him. More than 3 million additional voters participated in the second round, and Chirac won more than four out of every five valid votes, according to the official results.
That response became known as the front republicain, or republican front: mainstream voters supporting almost any democratic opponent to block the far right.
Marine Le Pen has spent years weakening it. She expelled her father from the party, changed its name from the National Front to the National Rally, and shifted its public emphasis from its extremist origins toward purchasing power, public services, migration, and opposition to Macron.
The firewall still exists, but it is no longer automatic.
Macron received two-thirds of the runoff vote against her in 2017. In 2022, his share fell below three-fifths. Current polling suggests that no prospective opponent can count on the overwhelming cross-party support that carried Chirac or even Macron to victory.
France has already seen this erosion in parliamentary politics. After the 2022 legislative election, Kyiv Post noted that gains by both Le Pen and Melenchon would make French policy more difficult and unpredictable for Ukraine. The presidential race has now concentrated that same problem around control of the Elysee.
The electoral map has moved in her favor
Le Pen’s original strongholds were concentrated in the deindustrialized north and northeast and along the Mediterranean coast. Those regions remain important, but the National Rally is no longer confined to them.
In 2022, Le Pen finished first in more than 20,000 communes, compared with fewer than 12,000 for Macron, according to a commune-level analysis. By the 2024 European Parliament election, the National Rally led in more than nine out of every 10 French municipalities, according to Reuters.
Its support has spread through rural France and small and medium-sized towns, particularly in areas with lower incomes, less formal education, higher unemployment, and longer journeys to work.
Melenchon dominates a different France: major cities, working-class suburbs around Paris, parts of the southwest, and overseas territories. Glucksmann draws more support from educated, urban, and strongly pro-European voters. Philippe can compete across the center and traditional right.
Le Pen, however, has built the broadest geographical base of any opposition candidate. Her rivals remain stronger within narrower social and regional blocs.
Turnout could decide the election
France’s 2022 runoff showed how much of the electorate remained available but unconvinced. More than 13.6 million registered voters stayed home. Another 3 million cast blank or invalid ballots.
Those voters were not evenly distributed. In the first round, almost half of voters aged 25 to 34 abstained. Among people in their sixties, only about one in eight did, according to Ipsos.
Le Pen performed strongly among workers, employees, and voters who described themselves as disadvantaged. Macron dominated among managers, affluent voters, and people over 70, according to the Ipsos runoff study.
This creates both a weakness and an opportunity for Le Pen. Parts of her working-class and younger electorate are less reliable at the polls. But many voters who oppose her are also becoming less willing to support whichever candidate faces her.
In 2022, roughly four out of every 10 Melenchon voters did not cast a valid ballot for either runoff candidate. Current polling suggests that transfers between the left and center could be even weaker in 2027.
Le Pen therefore does not need France to become uniformly far right. She needs her opponents to remain divided into groups that increasingly refuse to vote for one another.
Melenchon, Glucksmann, and the search for another Macron
Melenchon came much closer to the 2022 runoff than is commonly remembered. He finished only 421,308 votes behind Le Pen, a gap small enough that a modest shift in urban turnout or support from other left-wing candidates could have produced a Macron-Melenchon runoff.
He remains capable of reaching the second round because the left is divided. But reaching it and winning it are separate questions. His strength among younger voters, major cities, and overseas France is offset by intense opposition from centrists, moderate social democrats, and the traditional right. Elabe’s current runoff test gives Le Pen roughly two votes for every one cast for Melenchon.
Glucksmann is more acceptable to pro-European centrists and moderate left-wing voters, but he does not yet have Macron’s 2017 opening.
Macron entered a race in which the Socialist Party had collapsed and the center-right candidate Francois Fillon was damaged by allegations that members of his family had received public money for parliamentary work. Macron occupied the vacant center, reached the runoff, and then benefited from a much stronger republican front.
No comparable lane exists today. Melenchon retains a large left-wing base. Philippe leads the center. Attal is competing for Macron’s former electorate. Tondelier represents the Greens, while other candidates draw smaller but potentially decisive shares of the vote.
Philippe is currently the strongest challenger because he can attract centrists, moderate conservatives, and some Macron voters. But Attal divides that constituency.
Glucksmann can unite parts of the center-left but must first overtake Melenchon without losing the voters he would need in a runoff.
Le Pen has already assembled the coalition she needs to reach the final round. Her rivals are still fighting over which one of them will be allowed to face her.
Just how likely is she to win?
Le Pen is more likely to become president than at any previous point in her career.
Her first-round position is dominant. Her legal path to the ballot has reopened. The National Rally’s vote is geographically broader, and the coalition prepared to stop her is weaker than it was in 2002, 2017, or even 2022.
Yet, she is still not inevitable. An eight-month campaign can erase a narrow runoff lead. Her electorate includes voters whose participation has historically been less reliable. A single mainstream challenger could still consolidate the center, moderate right, and parts of the left. Her appeal before France’s highest court also remains unresolved.
The difficulty is producing that challenger before the first round eliminates everyone else.
The most important figure is not Le Pen’s roughly 35% but the much smaller share currently divided among Philippe, Attal, Glucksmann, Melenchon, Retailleau, Tondelier, and the rest.
If that fragmentation survives until April, France’s republican firewall may not be defeated by a majority embracing Le Pen but by everyone opposing her separately.

What to Make of Witkoff and Kushner’s Return to Russia-Ukraine Peace Talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
05:24:00 UTC
14:24:00 KST

After a six-month layoff, US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have rejoined the Russia-Ukraine negotiating process. They made another trip to Russia – the eighth for Witkoff since February 2025 – as well as their first trip to Kyiv since taking on their mediation roles for the White House. The visit has generated much speculation as to potential progress and what may come next.
The White House may be keen to achieve something ahead of the November midterm elections in the United States, but Washington officials face steep challenges unless they can bring a dramatically new approach to the process. The meetings that took place over the weekend offered no indication that they were doing so, leaving a situation where the Kremlin will likely try to exploit US urgency while maintaining a maximalist approach.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Meanwhile, Kyiv will do what it can to support US overtures in hopes of securing meaningful progress in the peace process as well as material aid in the face of continued Russian aggression.
Catching up on negotiations
More than half a year has passed since the hiatus in peace talks began. The last trilateral Russia-Ukraine-US negotiation took place in February 2026. Then, there was only a brief sequence of bilateral meetings in Miami before Witkoff and Kushner detached altogether to focus on the US-Israel-Iran War and Gaza.
Much has happened since.
For the Ukraine side, the main change has been success with its long-range strikes and in holding the battle line. The ability to reach well into opposing territory has imposed significant costs upon Russia, including strikes against oil refineries and major logistics hubs. Importantly, Ukrainian forces have also slowed Russian advances, with Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha indicating that Russia has yet to maintain 20% control of the Donetsk region – the main target of Kremlin negotiating demands.
Ukraine’s Prosecutor General Kravchenko Resigns Over Corruption Accusations
Meanwhile, Russia has lashed out in response. This has meant increased drone and missile strikes against Ukrainian civilian infrastructure and residential areas. These continued despite this weekend’s negotiations, with Vladimir Putin rejecting the Ukrainian proposal for a broader three-day ceasefire.
But the Kremlin has also escalated horizontally with small-scale strikes against targets in NATO countries. The recent drone attack at Leipzig Airport has received significant international attention, but NATO has reported similar incidents in Slovakia, Poland, Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania. The Kremlin has also been intensifying its rhetoric toward other NATO countries, leading to wider concerns that Russia may seek to disrupt alliance unity as it initiates a new offensive against Ukraine this autumn.
Outcomes of the meetings
Overall, the engagements in Moscow and Kyiv represented a soft reset of the negotiating process. In both visits, Witkoff and Kushner discussed peace and economic proposals, exploring how to get the negotiations back on track. Neither set of meetings produced any real breakthroughs.
Importantly, there was only one deliverable from this round of negotiations with the Kremlin, which was meant to be a “no shoot” arrangement. In other words, the two sides were meant to honor a limited ceasefire confined to strikes against targets where the negotiations would be taking place.
While Putin acknowledged a reduction in overall attacks from Ukraine, Russian forces proceeded to strike multiple locations in Kyiv, including Kyiv and Boryspil international airports that could have been entry points for Witkoff and Kushner in what would have been the first cross-border passenger flight since the full-scale invasion began in 2022. Instead, the pair traveled by train via Poland.
One notable difference in this series of meetings was the presence of Gene Lange, the acting sanctions policy chief at the US Treasury Department. His presence was not altogether unusual considering Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s attendance in past meetings related to the Russia-Ukraine peace process, but what remains unclear is if Lange was there to offer incentives, present potential costs, or a mix of both.
The different importance of timing
While there is little indication from any party that they expect a near-term conclusion of the war, the timing of this outreach is nevertheless important for each of the governments involved.
For Russia, the talks come as the Kremlin has been making preparations for a major fall offensive. This includes a domestic mobilization effort and outreach to its military partner in North Korea for additional support. Ukraine’s long range attacks have demonstrated an ability to frustrate that mobilization process, and Moscow may seek to use the current negotiating push to offer just enough buffer to enable a future offensive.
For Ukraine, the timing of negotiations is important to try to derail Russia’s fall campaign before it happens. This means boosting partners’ support for Ukraine’s defense, maintaining military and economic pressure on Russia, and highlighting any intelligence on Russian forces’ preparations for a major offensive. Ukraine’s partners can help in these regards.
For the United States, it is highly likely that the White House wants substantive progress before the November midterms to boost election prospects for Donald Trump-backed candidates. The White House’s urgency can be a boon or a bane for the peace process, depending on whether it abandons its existing strategy of “carrots for Moscow, sticks for Kyiv.” All it would take is reversing that approach and strongly backing Ukraine while resolutely pressuring Russia. That could help disrupt Russia’s fall offensive and open a window for halting fighting at the current battle line.
What to watch going forward
President Zelensky has already indicated that the next step will be follow-on meetings with the US and European partners. These will be necessary for securing additional aid for Ukraine and potentially coming to agreement on further cost-imposing measures for Russia. It could also be a mechanism for building out a more comprehensive peace proposal that includes functional mechanisms for oversight and enforcement, as well as Coalition of the Willing participation.
Still, whatever may happen in that track of discussions, the three most important questions for the peace process are this:
First, when is the next round of trilateral engagements?
This answer offers indications of both the timeline and relative commitments to the negotiating process. If the Kremlin delays follow-on engagements, it will serve as evidence of stall tactics.
More broadly, the answer to that question is important because there are limits to shuttle diplomacy in a negotiation of this complexity. Achieving a durable agreement will require the parties to be able to engage each other during the implementation phase, so it is necessary for them to demonstrate that ability in a sustained and meaningful way during the negotiation phase.
Second, what was the proposal that the US envoys tabled in their recent meetings? More specifically, was it a recycling of the old 20-point peace proposal produced last December or something new?
Early indications suggest that it is an updated version of the last proposal, which will be based on outdated facts and assumptions.
The restart of talks offers an opportunity to pursue a more comprehensive agreement. The Kremlin will likely balk at it, but clarity, depth, and specificity are critical for mitigating bad faith behaviors in the peace process.
Finally, will the US finally adjust its negotiating strategy?
The Kremlin has demonstrated time and again that the White House’s existing approach only hardens its maximalist negotiating strategy. Rather than incentivizing peace, it is necessary to disincentivize aggression, and if Washington does not adapt based on the evidence that Putin has provided, then this negotiating effort will only turn out like the last.
Ultimately, whether this past weekend’s engagements turn out to be more ceremony than substance is not yet determined. Rather, that is contingent on the next steps; namely, the next aid package to Ukraine, the next sanctions regime on Russia, and the next round of substantive negotiations that focuses on a comprehensive draft agreement rather than a list of bullet point positions.
The views expressed in this opinion article are the author’s and not necessarily those of Kyiv Post.

Strategic Autonomy in motion as India hosts 18th BRICS Summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
05:22:03 UTC
14:22:03 KST

This would be the 18th summit of the grouping. (Photo: ANI)
India will host the annual BRICS summit on September 12-13 at Bharat Mandapam, returning to the venue where it held the G20 summit in 2023. That gathering is remembered for the inclusion of the African Union in G20, marking a major step in efforts to bridge the gap between the Western-led global order and the emerging Global South. At BRICS, India will look to leverage that momentum, working with major emerging economies to demand structural reforms of global governance institutions dominated by the West.This would be the 18th summit of the grouping that brings together 11 major emerging and developing economies – Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, Ethiopia, UAE, Indonesia, Iran, Egypt and Saudi Arabia – along with 10 other partner countries. Together, BRICS nations account for 49 percent of world population, 40 percent of global GDP and 26 percent of international trade.
The last time India hosted an in-person BRICS summit was in 2016 in Goa. This year also marks 2 decades of formalisation of the bloc for cooperation on issues related to global economic and political governance. The theme of India's 2026 chairship is Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability, drawing inspiration from PM Narendra Modi's 'humanity first' and people-centric approach to BRICS.
This will also be the first summit to see in-person participation by Russian President Vladimir Putin since the start of the Ukraine war. Chinese President Xi Jinping is also visiting India for the first time in 7 years to participate in the summit.Under its chairship, India has so far held over 350 meetings - 25 at the ministerial level including the foreign ministers and national security advisers’ engagements. The ministerial meetings have so far resulted in key outcomes and initiatives spanning agriculture, health, energy, environment, disaster management and also trade, reaffirming commitment to a fair, inclusive and transparent multilateral trading system with WTO at its core.India for BRICS Despite the political fragmentation and economic imbalances associated with the grouping, BRICS remains important for India for multiple reasons, especially in an increasingly uncertain world. For one, it lends India a platform to practice its strategic autonomy and multi-alignment policy, not allowing any one single bloc to acquire excessive leverage over it. That it can simultaneously expand its strategic and technology ties with the West and also work with Quad for a free and open Indo-Pacific reinforces an independent foreign policy. For India, as external affairs minister S Jaishankar has said, BRICS is an embodiment of a multipolar world. India is not giving up on its Western partnerships, only hedging against uncertainty whether from US unpredictability or Chinese ascendancy.BRICS also allows India to showcase its Global South leadership credentials, as it works with other major emerging markets to push for reforms of global institutions like the UNSC, IMF and World Bank that are not representative of the developing world. Support for UNSC reforms is important, although it still falls short of an explicit endorsement of India's permanent membership bid, mainly because of China's presence.India's approach to BRICS is also guided by its complex ties with China. Turning away would mean allowing China to single-handedly shape the agenda of the developing world. BRICS is consensus driven and even for Washington and other Western capitals, India's moderating influence should be of significance as it prevents the bloc from turning into an anti-West platform.There's focus as well on expanding financial architecture as no government would like its trade to be held hostage by instruments it can't control. As Jaishankar has underlined, institutions such as the New Development Bank and the Contingent Reserve Arrangement demonstrate the group's ability to create credible alternatives. For India, these are not initiatives targeted at any currency. In any case, India has officially said it's against de-dollarisation or any attempt to target the US currency. It has also ruled out any proposal for a common BRICS currency.BRICS provides India with markets, along with trade diversification, de-risking and supply-chain opportunities. According to a commerce ministry press release, intra-BRICS merchandise trade reached approximately $1.17 trillion in 2024. India exported an estimated $82 billion in goods to BRICS members in FY2025–26, alongside approximately $31.3 billion in services exports in 2024. BRICS membership deepens India’s trade relationships with Russia (energy), Brazil (agriculture/commodities), Gulf and African countries, diversifying away from overreliance on any single partner.Key Challenges for India The first of course is to forge a consensus on West Asia that would enable a joint BRICS declaration, a task complicated by the presence of the UAE and Iran in the group. India would not like the event to end with a Chair's Statement, like what happened with the foreign ministers' meeting, knowing well that no BRICS summit has concluded without a comprehensive joint declaration. Foreign secretary Vikram Misri said last week India has received cooperation from all members and the government is working to arrive eventually at a constructive outcome that benefits all BRICS stakeholders. India will focus on drafting a resolution rooted in the UN Charter, dialogue and diplomacy, freedom of navigation and civilian protection, while looking to ringfence economic agreements from contentious political issues by acknowledging respective national positions.Balancing relations with the US is another key concern for India, which is hosting the summit fresh off a tariff firestorm with Washington. US President Donald Trump sees the grouping itself as an assault on the US currency and has threatened to impose 100 percent tariffs on BRICS nations if they work to replace the US dollar. India backs legitimate local-currency settlement, while maintaining it is against any common BRICS currency or China-centered replacement mechanism. As it walks the diplomatic tightrope, India must steer initiatives like the integration of central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) but without appearing to endorse any anti-dollar bloc.Another challenge for India is to prevent China's predominance without destabilising its bilateral relations with Beijing. For all the talk about BRICS' combined power, China enjoys a vastly asymmetrical influence with its trade, investment, manufacturing and critical mineral leverage. Wary of China's efforts to advance its own economic interests, India has not endorsed SCO’s 2030 economic roadmap and it must find a way to work with China in BRICS on shared objectives but without allowing the forum to be co-opted as a Chinese economic or geopolitical platform.This also intersects with the challenge of ensuring that an expanded grouping remains governable and cohesive, especially with countries like Pakistan and Bangladesh pursuing membership with support from Beijing. True multipolarity and consensus-driven equality within the organisation are key imperatives for India.As Jaishankar said while announcing India's summit agenda, BRICS must transition now from a forum for discussions to a platform for delivery. In that spirit, India seems focused on delivering an outcome-oriented summit with key deliverables like a unanimous BRICS declaration, logistics supply-chain cooperation framework, incubator/ startup network, development finance, cross-border payment and continued support for Indian priorities like UNSC reforms and counterterrorism.
The inclusion of the African Union was not the only major takeaway from the G20 summit in 2023. Perhaps more dramatic was the last-minute consensus on Ukraine through a compromise language crafted by India, allowing a G20 declaration. India can take confidence from that diplomatic triumph, heading into another tough but potentially rewarding global summit.

A 46-year-old Jenin resident was arrested on suspicion of stealing the car of Tel Aviv District Court Judge Alaa Masarwa from northern Tel Aviv on Sunday morning.
Shortly after the vehicle was stolen, it was located traveling north on the Ayalon Highway. Police pursued the vehicle and arrested Tarek Jarrar, a Jenin resident who was staying in Israel without a permit, on suspicion of stealing it.
Officers from the Tel Aviv North police station who located the vehicle began following it, while officers from the Glilot station were called to prepare to block its path on Highway 5.
When the driver reached the police checkpoint, officers ordered him to stop. According to police suspicions, he did not comply, struck another vehicle, and continued driving.
Police continued pursuing him until they managed to stop the vehicle.
Body camera footage showed officers approaching the car. When the driver did not respond to their instructions, police smashed the driver's window and removed him from the vehicle. The driver was then identified as Jarrar.
Suspect claims he did not know car was stolen
During questioning, Jarrar claimed that he did not know the judge's vehicle had been stolen. According to his account, another person sold him the car, and he believed there was nothing suspicious about the vehicle.
Police suspect Jarrar of vehicle theft, intentionally damaging a vehicle, driving without a license, and driving without insurance.
During a hearing to extend his detention at the Tel Aviv Magistrate's Court, Jarrar's defense attorney argued that he had entered Israel to look for work due to financial difficulties faced by his family in Jenin.
According to his attorney, another person gave Jarrar the vehicle, and he did not know it had been stolen. During the hearing, the defense attorney asked the court to send him for a psychiatric examination.
Judge's vehicle returned as investigation continues
The vehicle was returned to Masarwa, while police continued investigating the circumstances surrounding the theft and subsequent chase.
Judge Ravit Peleg Bar Dayan extended Jarrar's detention until September 8, 2026.

The Saudi-led Coalition to Support Legitimacy in Yemen's spokesperson vowed to respond firmly to the latest outbreak of hostilities.
The Houthis, who control the most populous parts of Yemen and much of the north, have been launching attacks towards Saudi Arabia since they declared a naval blockade against Riyadh in July, with strikes targeting its vessels in the Red Sea.
The latest escalation was "dangerous," as the Houthis attacked civilian and economic entities in the world's largest oil exporter and de-facto OPEC leader, the spokesperson of the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said on Tuesday.

United Arab Emirates President Mohammed Bin Zayed Al Nahyan (MBZ) warned Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that Hamas was planning a major operation against Israel days before the October 7 massacre, a Haaretz investigation published Tuesday morning said.
Netanyahu reportedly dismissed the warning despite MBZ urging him to take the threat seriously, the report said, citing three senior foreign sources familiar with the contents of the conversation.
During a 45-minute conversation held some 10 days before the massacre, MBZ reportedly warned Netanyahu that then-Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar was planning a major operation against Israel. The UAE president expressed concern that an attack could lead to significant bloodshed, destabilize the region, and undermine the Abraham Accords, according to the report.
The prime minister reportedly responded that he believed Hamas intended to operate in the West Bank and reassured the UAE president that Israel was prepared for any scenario.
Netanyahu failed to mention the warning in subsequent security briefings leading up to October 7, with both former Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar and former IDF chief of staff Herzi Halevi telling Haaretz that they had not been informed of the warning delivered by the UAE president.
The Haaretz report also cited a close adviser to MBZ, who said the warning originated in contacts involving a Palestinian intermediary with ties to both Hamas and Israeli security officials.
The investigation said that in September 2023, Sinwar had warned through the intermediary that he was preparing a "zilzal," or earthquake, and later described what he was planning as "the mother of all surprises" and "a terrifying operation."
The message was ultimately relayed to the UAE leadership and, on September 15, to the Shin Bet. Bar briefed Netanyahu on Sinwar's warning, after which senior defense officials held a security assessment two days later.
Netanyahu failed to respond to Emirati, Egyptian warning before Oct. 7
At that meeting, Bar reportedly warned that Israel was "on a collision course" and recommended either a powerful offensive step or stronger defensive measures in Gaza and the West Bank ahead of the Jewish holidays, but no decisions were made at the end of the discussion.
After the UAE leadership concluded that Israel had not adequately responded to the information, MBZ decided to contact Netanyahu directly, according to the report.
The investigation also said Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel contacted Netanyahu around the same period and warned of "something unusual, a terrifying operation" being planned by Hamas. Netanyahu reportedly responded that Israel was in control of the situation in Gaza and was concentrating its attention and troop deployments on the West Bank.
Netanyahu did not mention either of the warning calls during a subsequent October 1 discussion on Gaza and Hamas, the report said. A senior Shin Bet official quoted in the investigation said knowledge of the warnings could potentially have changed how security officials interpreted Sinwar's earlier statements and withdrawal from negotiations.
Haaretz said MBZ did not respond to a request for comment.
"An absolute lie! Prime Minister Netanyahu did not speak with the president of the United Arab Emirates during the period in question and did not receive any warning from him," the Prime Minister's Office said in response.
Bennett backs report, says UAE, Egypt warnings to Netanyahu were true
Following the report, former prime minister and head of B'Yachad Naftali Bennett told 103FM he "knew for a fact the report is true."
"Mohammed bin Zayed of the Emirates warned Netanyahu that Sinwar was planning an operation. Abbas Kamel, the head of Egyptian General Intelligence, also warned Netanyahu days before the massacre that a major operation was being planned," he said. "I don't want to talk about my relationship with anyone. I'm telling you that I know this fact is true."
"Netanyahu led us blindly straight into this terrible disaster. He was so deeply immersed in his conception that Hamas was an asset, and despite receiving explicit warnings, he did nothing," the former prime minister claimed.
"Netanyahu bears direct responsibility for this disaster, not only ministerial responsibility by virtue of being prime minister, but direct responsibility because he built up Hamas for 15 years and did nothing."
Asked how he would have acted had he been in Netanyahu's position in the fall of 2023, Bennett said, "In a similar situation, if I had received a quarter of a warning when I was prime minister, I would have raced to the South. That's what I always do: meet the commanders and the observation soldiers, convene the IDF chief of staff and the Shin Bet chief, increase alertness and defenses, and prepare for offensive action if necessary. I would have done everything to protect the lives of the residents."
Eisenkot: Netanyahu led Israel blindly into the October 7 failure
Gadi Eisenkot, chairman of the Yashar party, also responded to the report, arguing that it only added to evidence that the prime minister had failed to act on warnings before the massacre.
"More and more signs indicate that Netanyahu led Israel blindly into the October 7 failure," Eisenkot said.
"According to the report this morning, he received an explicit warning, days before the massacre, from the president of the United Arab Emirates regarding Sinwar's intentions, but did not update the heads of the defense establishment. Who failed to wake whom up?"
"Those around him are echoing the pathetic conspiracy and betrayal theory, inventing the most ridiculous sentence a leader could cling to, 'They didn't wake me up,' because of two facts: He knows the truth; He is terrified of it and is trying to escape responsibility. Eisenkot said his party would seek to establish a state commission of inquiry after the formation of the next government.
"Immediately upon the formation of the next government, we will establish a state commission of inquiry that will investigate the previous decade, clarify what Netanyahu knew and did not know, get to the truth, and prevent the next disaster."

40% of cargo, millions of euros and a thousand jobs – Liepāja SEZ warns of consequences if transit ban is adopted
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
05:20:33 UTC
14:20:33 KST

If cargo traffic towards the east were completely halted, total cargo turnover at the Port of Liepāja would fall by around 40%, representatives of the Liepāja Special Economic Zone (SEZ) said.
Commenting on the proposal to ban the transit of agricultural and animal feed products of Russian and Belarusian origin through Latvia, the Liepāja SEZ said that restrictions on transit cargo would result in the Port of Liepāja losing all cargo flows to and from Central Asia.
The Liepāja SEZ stressed that considerable efforts have been made over several years to develop a transit cargo corridor to Central Asian countries.
For example, Brazilian sugar and Argentine soybeans are transported by ship to the Port of Liepāja and then carried by rail to Central Asian countries. At present, port companies also have contracts for handling cargo to and from Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan.
If grain transit to third countries were restricted, this would automatically lead to a sharp increase in global grain prices
and, consequently, food prices, contributing to higher inflation in Europe and worldwide, the Liepāja SEZ stressed.
According to Liepāja SEZ calculations, if cargo traffic towards the east were completely halted, total cargo turnover at the Port of Liepāja would decline by around 40%. Such a drop would reduce the Liepāja SEZ Authority’s revenue from port dues and related payments, creating a shortfall of approximately four to six million euros compared with planned budget revenue.
This would significantly affect the operations of the Liepāja SEZ Authority and could result in the loss of around 1,000 jobs at Port of Liepāja terminals and among Liepāja SEZ companies.
SEZ representatives also explained that stevedoring companies at the Port of Liepāja work with some of the world’s largest buyers of grain and agricultural commodities, including US-based Archer Daniels Midland and Singapore-based Olam Agri. From the perspective of Liepāja SEZ development, cooperation is therefore being built with companies that are active in markets where a large share of Latvian grain is sold, including Africa, the Middle East and Asia.
Liepāja SEZ representatives added that major agricultural companies purchase products, including grain, from Australia, Kazakhstan, Argentina, the United States, Russia, Lithuania and Latvia. Therefore, if the operations of international companies at Latvian ports were restricted, this would mean that these companies would no longer purchase grain grown by Latvian farmers and would instead work with other Baltic Sea ports, including those in Lithuania, Poland and Estonia.
A total of 6.87 million tonnes of cargo was handled at the Port of Liepāja in 2025,
down 2.5% from 2024. By cargo volume, Liepāja was Latvia’s third-largest port last year.
As reported, coalition parties will discuss at a cooperation meeting in the Saeima on Monday a proposal to ban the transit of agricultural and animal feed products of Russian and Belarusian origin through Latvia.
The National Alliance (NA) has proposed banning the transit of agricultural and animal feed products of Russian and Belarusian origin through Latvia, as well as the storage of such cargo at Latvian ports, customs warehouses and free zones.
The proposal has been supported by the Union of Greens and Farmers and New Unity, as well as the opposition Progressives party.
At the same time, amendments to Cabinet regulations prepared by the Ministry of Agriculture are being submitted to the government for consideration. The amendments would allow the Food and Veterinary Service (PVD) to take samples from grain shipments in transit and conduct laboratory tests to verify the declared country of origin.
The government plans to decide this week on granting the PVD the authority to inspect grain cargo in transit at Latvian ports.

How a disguised Shimon Peres helped pave the way for peace with Jordan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
05:19:26 UTC
14:19:26 KST

Newly released documents are shedding light on the secret 1993 meeting between Shimon Peres and Jordan’s King Hussein that produced an early blueprint for the historic peace treaty Israel and Jordan signed the following year.
The Peres Center for Peace and Innovation released the documents and previously unpublished quotations from the meeting to mark the 10th anniversary of Peres's death, who served as Israel’s eighth prime minister and ninth president. At the time of the talks, he was foreign minister.
The meeting took place at King Hussein’s palace in Amman in November 1993 under such secrecy that Peres altered his appearance before traveling there, according to the documents.
The contacts had begun about a week earlier. On October 26, 1993, a message arrived from the Jordanian royal court stating that Hussein wanted to meet Peres, whom the king regarded as a creative thinker, and that he was willing to hold a clandestine meeting as part of the tentative contacts between the two countries. Those discussions would eventually lead to the Israel-Jordan peace treaty signed in October 1994.
During the meeting, Peres presented his vision for regional economic cooperation, including modern networks of airports, seaports and roads that he believed could provide an economic foundation for a future agreement.
“We have many dreams and hopes for the future,” Hussein replied. “I share the commitment that there should be change, and that the younger generations should have an opportunity to live with a sense of security, which is peace.”
One of the most striking passages in the transcript reveals Hussein’s sense that time was running out. “In 1951 there was a tragic event, the murder of my father,” Hussein said, according to the transcript. “I want to leave for the future, for my brother Hassan and for the entire government, the best possible legacy. Maybe I have only a year or two left. I will put everything on the line.”
Peres, for his part, told Hussein that public attitudes were increasingly favorable toward ending the region’s conflicts. “There is tremendous public support today for a peace agreement,” Peres said. “Young people are sick of wars, poverty and the lack of freedom.”
That same night, Hussein and Peres initialed a memorandum of understanding that would help form the basis of the eventual peace agreement. Less than a year later, in October 1994, Israel and Jordan formally signed their peace treaty.
Hemi Peres, chairman of the Peres Center for Peace and Innovation, said, “It is difficult not to be moved when reading the documents from that historic meeting.” Efrat Duvdevani, the center’s director general, added: “It is a great privilege and a moral obligation to listen to the peace testament of great leaders,” she said.

Pensioner mistakenly pronounced dead has to go a month without income
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Pensioner mistakenly pronounced dead has to go a month without income
An elderly pensioner in Narva was mistakenly declared dead and will now have to go a month without receiving their pension.
The life of 79-year-old Narva pensioner Zinaida Jelina took a dramatic turn on August 18 when she was mistakenly declared dead and her name was removed from the Population Register. For a person, this means their bank account is immediately frozen and their identity documents and prescriptions are no longer valid.
"I don't understand anything. I feel like a fool. I'm at a loss for words. How could this happen? I'm alive, but suddenly I'm dead," Jelina told "Aktuaalne kaamera" news.
Zinaida suspects she may have been confused with someone else, but that has not been confirmed. Jelina is now making the rounds of government agencies in an effort to get her former life back. She received new identity documents on September 2, but her pension payments will not resume for another 10 days. Until then, police advised her to ask relatives for financial support.
According to the Ministry of the Interior, similar mistakes occur in Estonia two or three times a year and are generally the result of human error. It is impossible to make the Population Register completely foolproof.
"Let's be clear: If someone simply enters the wrong person's information, no machine can catch that. People are the weakest link in these systems. It cannot be completely ruled out," said Enel Pungas, head of the Ministry of the Interior's population facts department.
Jelina said representatives of city and national government agencies have inquired about how she is doing, but no one has apologized.
"I'd like to look the woman who let me down like this in the eye. How would she feel if this were done to her?" Jelina said.

Second-hand smoke: 2.7 billion exposed, 767 million of them children, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
05:09:42 UTC
14:09:42 KST

Second-hand smoke causes serious health harm, including heart disease, respiratory illness and cancer, and remains a leading cause of preventable death worldwide.
A third of the world’s population is exposed each year to second-hand smoke — also known as passive smoking — which continues to be a major source of illness and mortality among non-smokers.
An estimated 2.71 billion people around the world were exposed to second-hand smoke— a combination of two types of smoke inhaled by non-smokers — in 2023, contributing to 1.66 million deaths. This includes 767 million children under 15, who are especially vulnerable, along with 1.49 billion women.
These new findings come from the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2023 study, published in The Lancet Public Health, which estimated second-hand smoke exposure and health impacts across 204 countries and territories between 1990 and 2023.
Need for stronger regulation
Despite the scale of exposure, the study found that approximately 70% of the world’s population is not protected by comprehensive smoke-free laws.
As of 2024, only 79 countries, approximately 70% of them in the Americas, have achieved the highest protection standards of the World Health Organization framework — with all public places completely smoke-free or at least 90% of the population covered by legislation.
The proportion of the global population covered by comprehensive smoke-free legislation has increased from 3% in 2007 to 33% in 2024, now covering 2.6 billion people.
However, the authors noted that while smoke-free policies directly reduce smoke exposure, there is a need for extra measures such as tobacco taxation, marketing bans, plain packaging and cessation programmes.
Regional patterns
The researchers found that the number of people impacted by second-hand smoke exposure remained broadly the same globally, but rose sharply in sub-Saharan Africa, North Africa and the Middle East, which they attributed to population growth.
The exposure prevalence in the Central Europe, Eastern Europe and Central Asia region was 37.7% — higher than the global average of 33.9% — affecting 146 million people.
Most of the countries in Western Europe were included in the “high-income super region,” which showed some of the most significant progress in reducing passive smoking.
Denmark and Norway achieved some of the world's largest reductions since 1990, at -48,8% and -44,3%, respectively.
Broad health impacts
Beyond how many people are exposed, the report found that second-hand smoke accounted for the loss of 44.8 million years of healthy life and continues to be a major contributor to disability and premature death.
While a smoker inhales "mainstream smoke" through the cigarette's filter, non-smokers primarily breathe in sidestream smoke. This is unfiltered and contains higher per-unit concentrations of toxic and carcinogenic compounds than the smoke inhaled by the smoker.
The researchers estimated that second-hand smoke remains a substantial driver of global health loss, particularly through cardiovascular and paediatric respiratory diseases.
Exposure to tobacco smoke was associated with several health conditions, including stroke, lower respiratory infections, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, asthma, type 2 diabetes and cancers of the trachea, lung and breast.

A new low-pressure area will move over Finland on Wednesday, keeping the weather unsettled. The heaviest rain will fall across central parts of the country, while widespread showers are expected elsewhere too. Northern Lapland will be the exception, with dry and sunny conditions.
Despite the rain, temperatures will stay fairly steady over the next few days. Highs will reach just under 20 degrees in the south, while the north will see temperatures ranging roughly from 10 to 15 degrees.

Whether you’re looking for an ultra-luxurious stay or sleek new properties, here are some of the upcoming hotels in Türkiye to have on your radar.
Bulgari Resort & Mansions, Bodrum

The byelection here in Holborn and St Pancras is Labour’s to lose. But lose it might | Polly Toynbee
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
05:00:28 UTC
14:00:28 KST

You might think a byelection showdown between two progressive parties is unimportant when the deep struggle for the national heart is between the right bloc and the left – but the result in Holborn and St Pancras matters. It matters for Andy Burnham and Labour because this is a test of the Burnham bounce: he saw off the right in Makerfield – can he win over the left too? Can he show he has enthusiastic approval from voters in southern constituencies as well as those in the north?
For the Greens it matters almost existentially because failing here could send them and their leader, Zack Polanski, back to the political fringes. Holborn and St Pancras, neighbouring Westminster, was vacated (vengefully) by Keir Starmer last week. This plum forever-Labour constituency has attracted 96 Labour applications for selection day on Wednesday, though not, it seems, nationally recognised names.
This is Labour’s to lose. And it might. The constituency was comfortably won in 2024 by Starmer; in May’s local elections the Greens took extra council seats, though Labour kept control and remained ahead by 10 percentage points. But byelections are idiosyncratic beasts in which voters risk nothing, electing neither council nor government. Few bother to turn out. For those who do, a byelection offers a free hit for whimsical preferences, “sending messages” on maverick issues or an urge to biff the government of the day.
A Labour loss would dent Burnham’s bounce, letting air out of his optimistic bubble. But frankly, losing here would be no great surprise. Peter Kellner, former president of YouGov and a leading psephologist, lives in this constituency, as do I. While most early opinion makes Labour the frontrunner, Kellner thinks that underestimates the byelection effect. He expects a Green win in a close call: “This is just the kind of seat a Labour government loses,” he tells me. In a metropolitan district with disproportionately young voters, the left is liberated to protest against anything disappointing in a Labour government.
Demographics favour rebellion for a rainbow of reasons in an extraordinarily socially mixed seat. You see vox-poppers choosing its picturesquely famous spots – the pastel houses in Primrose Hill where Paddington Bear lives in the films, the bars and cafes of Camden and Kentish Town – as photogenic backdrops to their reports. But, such elegant streets may be deceptive given that only a quarter of residents are homeowners, compared with 62.5% across England and Wales.
Here 43% live in social housing: Camden has a decades-long tradition of good housebuilding, thanks to a well-run council under great social pressure. The constituency is home to both deprivation and high numbers of graduates; many ABC1 voters and 45% born abroad.
Leaflets saying only the Greens, or only Labour, can win here are arriving through letterboxes – and it’s true, no one else is likely to. That Polanski is seeking the nomination boosts the Greens. Tot up issues where they challenge Labour, and many resonate with the student population. They oppose nuclear weapons and seem divided over increased defence spending. They back rent controls that Burnham has rejected. They oppose Jackdaw and Rosebank North Sea oil and gas drilling, which may both be approved any day now. They want rapid nationalisation of utilities, where Labour hesitates. Locally they campaign on crime, mobile phone thefts and housing.
But it’s Gaza that may shift votes from Labour to Green: in the 2024 election, Starmer’s vote share was slashed and a pro-Palestinian, independent candidate came second with 18.9% of the vote. Arresting thousands for terrorism for silently holding placards supporting Palestine Action is another gift to the Greens. Labour instead points to impossible promises in the party’s £160bn tax, spend and borrowing pledges.
The Green campaign asks: “Why elect just another Labour MP, when a Green MP in parliament will challenge the government?” But this week Labour looks set to select not just “another Labour MP” but Sagal Abdi-Wali, Camden council’s leader and community organiser, popular with her party and a well-known dynamic force locally. Green criticism of Labour over Gaza comes up against a hijab-wearing Muslim woman who has spent years calming racial and religions tensions, and building relationships with many Jewish voters here, too. “If Greens stir up community antagonisms over Gaza,” she says to me, “that would be disgraceful”.
Reform has no foothold here but its attacks on her from afar may galvanise Labour people to come out and vote. Its poisonous home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf spits out Reform’s usual ethno-nativist bile, pointing out on X that Abdi-Wali “was born in Somalia. Do you understand what’s happening?” Georgia Gould MP, former Camden council leader, ripostes on X that she “has dedicated her life to public service” and is “the elected leader of Camden council, a community where she grew up and has lived for 35 years” who “embodies the best of our values … an outstanding example of British success”. Telegraph headlines similarly define her primarily as a “Somali refugee”. All this will remind Labour voters that fighting off the racist right is Labour’s great cause.
On the doorstep with Abdi-Wali, in a social housing estate, I saw how she is known and liked for her community work. She takes notes of people’s problems, from housing repairs to e-bikes blocking the road, her local campaign matching Burnham’s localism. But we also meet a college lecturer, who had a run-in with their employer over Gaza, who will “never vote Labour again”. Not for Abdi-Wali? It’s all about Palestine.
Nonetheless, Polanski takes a big risk here after sliding in the polls. For Labour, the challenge is to show how Burnham’s raft of positive policies can ward off hopeless wishes and still reach the left with his hopefulness.
- 
  Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist
