Second-hand smoke causes to nearly 1.7 million deaths globally: Study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
23:02:00 UTC
08:02:00 KST

Second-hand smoke causes nearly 1.7 million deaths globally: Study
- More than 2.7 billion people, including 767 million children, were exposed to second-hand smoke in 2023, causing nearly 1.7 million deaths worldwide.
- Second-hand smoke exposure leads to serious illnesses like ischemic heart disease and 5.2 million respiratory infections in children, with no safe level of inhalation.
- Despite declines in smoking rates, exposure remains stable due to population growth; women and children are especially vulnerable, prompting calls for stronger tobacco controls globally.
AI generated
PARIS – More than 2.7 billion people including children have been exposed to second-hand smoke globally, contributing to nearly 1.7 million deaths in 2023, according to study published on Sept 8 in The Lancet.
Tobacco remains a leading cause of disease globally, the study said, noting many “non-smokers exposed to second-hand smoke” were among the estimated total of eight million people who died in 2023 of smoking-related illnesses.
“Exposure to second-hand smoke is a globally recognised health risk, with no safe level of inhalation,” it said.
By reviewing studies published in the US National Institutes of Health database PubMed along with population surveys, the Sept 8 study sought to estimate the prevalence of exposure to second-hand smoke and quantify the burden of disease in 204 countries and territories between 1990 and 2023.
Among the approximately 2.7 billion people exposed to second-hand smoke in 2023 were 767 million children aged 0 to 14, the study found.
This exposure is estimated to have resulted in 1.66 million premature deaths and causing premature disability and illness, leading with ischemic heart disease, a heart condition caused by insufficient oxygen supply to the heart muscle.
In children, exposure to second-hand smoke is estimated to have caused 5.2 million respiratory tract infections in 2023, it said.
People in proximity to someone lighting up are exposed to both the “sidestream smoke” from the burning tobacco product and smoke exhaled by the active smoker, the study explained.
“The sidestream component, which dominates the air non-smokers breathe, is unfiltered... carrying higher per-unit concentrations of the toxic and carcinogenic compounds” than that being inhaled by the active smoker, it said.
Despite significant declines in smoking prevalence globally since 1990, the absolute number of people exposed has remained stable because of population growth and increased exposure in Africa and the Middle East.
Women are also disproportionately affected by second-hand smoke, particularly in regions where smoking prevalence among women is low, it noted.
“Despite this substantial burden, (second-hand smoke) exposure remains rarely acknowledged as a major risk factor for female health,” it said.
The study called for governments to implement stronger tobacco controls in public places and in homes in order to better protect women and children from second-hand smoke. AFP

Billions for space defence under new national strategy
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
00:01:53 BST
08:01:53 KST

The government has published a new UK Space Strategy backed by £7.8 billion until 2030, with more than £3 billion of it directed at defence capabilities in orbit, the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade stated.
The strategy brings government space investment and activity under a single plan covering growth, defence and national security, and formally replaces the National Space Strategy published in 2021.
Wes Streeting, the Defence Secretary, said: “This space strategy recognises that our national security depends on our freedom of action in space and, if necessary, the ability to protect UK and allied space assets. As threats in orbit grow more sophisticated, so must our ability to detect and respond to them, ensuring we protect the interests of the UK and allies while fuelling economic growth along the way.
“Backed by the Defence Investment Plan, we’re investing more than £3 billion to ensure our defence capabilities in space keep pace with the threats we face, supporting reindustrialisation and creating opportunities here in the UK.”
The largest single defence line is £880 million towards space control and intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance capabilities, funding technologies the department says can track military activity on the ground and potential attacks on satellites.
A further £2.8 billion goes towards connectivity, including the Connectivity in Low Earth Orbit and SKYNET defence communications programmes, which the department says play a pivotal role in keeping the armed forces connected wherever they are in the world. The same investment is expected to improve rural connectivity and reduce mobile signal dropouts on trains.
Space domain awareness, meaning the monitoring of satellites, rockets and debris in orbit, receives £149 million for the European Space Agency’s Vigil mission and £85 million for the National Space Operations Centre. According to the department, that funding will allow British technology to provide earlier warning of potential satellite collisions, hostile activity and solar storms.
Launch and industry
The strategy commits £148 million to European rocket programmes and £30 million to SaxaVord Spaceport in Shetland, which the government says will allow Britain and its partners to launch satellites without relying on countries further afield.
Douglas Alexander, the Scottish Secretary, said: “The UK Space Strategy is a huge vote of confidence in Scotland’s Space Sector. Scotland already builds more satellites than anywhere else in Europe, and with a £30 million UK Government investment boost, SaxaVord is now poised to deliver up to three-quarters of the continent’s orbital launch slots.
“This UK Space Strategy has defence, security and economic growth at its heart, creating skilled jobs right across Scotland, showing what we can achieve when government, industry and ambition come together.”
Jonathan Reynolds, the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Secretary, said: “As space becomes a new frontier of economic and military competition, this plan will help keep Britain secure by strengthening our ability to launch satellites, detect threats and protect the services people rely on every day.
“At the same time, this plan will enable our excellent UK industry to seize the boundless opportunities of this new age in space, creating skilled jobs, driving growth and improving connectivity for all of us.”
A further £40 million supports in-orbit servicing, assembly and manufacturing, which the department says will help repair and maintain satellites damaged by debris, solar storms or hostile interference, and clear dangerous objects from orbit. The strategy also allocates £163 million to space science and exploration missions including the Rosalind Franklin Mars Rover built at Stevenage, £190 million from UK Research and Innovation for astronomy and space science research, £57 million from the Department for Transport for rail connectivity and £9 million from the Met Office for space weather forecasting.
For the first time, the department says, government will take a single approach to buying and developing space technology, beginning with satellite communications, which it argues will help British firms win more work and deliver capabilities faster.
Industry response
Kevin Craven, chief executive of the ADS Group, said: “We welcome the publication of the new space strategy, and the sustained effort to bring a cross-government perspective to space capability delivery. It is important that government maintains an open, transparent and ambitious partnership with industry to realise its national security and growth goals.
“Certainty allows the sector to operate at pace and for its industrial base to make long-term strategic and commercial commitments. It is also a vital signal of intent to our international partners for trade and collaboration.”
Doug Liddle, chair of the trade association UKspace, said: “UKspace welcomes the publication of the government’s new UK Space Strategy. It sets out a constructive path towards a refreshed approach to space in the UK, which we hope will result in a stronger emphasis on open, inclusive cross-sector dialogue. The new, focussed strategy offers a valuable opportunity to create a more streamlined framework, strengthen collaboration and deliver greater impact across the UK space sector.”
Professors Anna Hogg and Mark Sims, co-chairs of the Space Academic Network, said: “SPAN welcomes the new cross-Government space strategy and its integrated delivery plan. We look forward to seeing the detail of the strategy and delivery plan, which will be critical in enabling academia and industry to plan, invest and work together to deliver the UK’s ambitions for space. Sustained investment across academia and industry is crucial to creating the cutting-edge technologies, capabilities, talent and growth of the future.”
The department puts the value of the UK space sector at £18.6 billion supporting more than 55,000 skilled jobs. Alongside the strategy, the government is reforming space regulation with the stated aim of reducing costs and rewarding responsible operators.

New space strategy will bolster UK defences against threats from space
United Kingdom

2026-09-08

New space strategy will bolster UK defences against threats from space
New UK space strategy to bring government's investment and activity under one plan to drive growth, strengthen security and back everyday technologies
- New national space strategy brings together UK’s plans for growth, defence, and national security to help reindustrialise the UK
- Government will design a resilient, integrated national satellite communications system to boost our security and defence
- Strategy also brings everyday benefits to Brits from better connectivity on trains to stronger phone signals
Safeguarding our national security and defence capabilities are the key pillars of a new strategy launched today (Tuesday 8 September) which puts the UK’s space sector to work in reindustrialising the country over the coming years.
Backed by a record £7.8 billion until 2030, the UK Space Strategy brings government’s space investment and activity under one plan to drive growth, strengthen security and back the technologies that underpin modern life.
It also recognises space as an increasingly important domain for keeping our country safe. Work to strengthen Space Domain Awareness – the study and monitoring of objects like satellites, rockets and debris orbiting our planet – is being backed by projects including £149 million for the European Space Agency’s (ESA) Vigil mission and £85 million for the National Space Operations Centre. UK funding will see British tech offer earlier warnings of potential satellite collisions, hostile activity and solar storms, helping protect the power, communications and navigation services people rely on every day.
Meanwhile £880 million will help beef up the UK’s space control and intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance capabilities, funding technologies that can track military activity on the ground and potential attacks on satellites, meaning we can act quickly and decisively to protect our way of life on Earth and our assets in space.
A further £2.8 billion meanwhile will go towards strengthening connectivity, including the Connectivity in Low Earth Orbit and SKYNET defence communications programmes, which play a pivotal role in keeping our Armed Forces connected wherever they are in the world.
These benefits will also be felt in everyday life, helping bring faster, more reliable connectivity to rural communities and reducing mobile signal dropouts on trains by using advanced satellite communications.
Together, these investments will help grow a UK space sector worth £18.6 billion and supporting over 55,000 skilled jobs – cementing Britain’s place as a global space leader from satellite services that underpin the economy to landmark missions such as the UK-built Rosalind Franklin Mars Rover.
Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said:
“As space becomes a new frontier of economic and military competition, this plan will help keep Britain secure by strengthening our ability to launch satellites, detect threats and protect the services people rely on every day.
“At the same time, this plan will enable our excellent UK industry to seize the boundless opportunities of this new age in space, creating skilled jobs, driving growth and improving connectivity for all of us.”
Defence Secretary, Wes Streeting, said:
“This space strategy recognises that our national security depends on our freedom of action in space and, if necessary, the ability to protect UK and allied space assets. As threats in orbit grow more sophisticated, so must our ability to detect and respond to them, ensuring we protect the interests of the UK and allies while fuelling economic growth along the way.
“Backed by the Defence Investment Plan, we’re investing more than £3 billion to ensure our defence capabilities in space keep pace with the threats we face, supporting reindustrialisation and creating opportunities here in the UK.”
The Strategy also offers an opportunity to deliver the jobs and companies of the future, with £40 million to support pioneering in-orbit servicing, assembly and manufacturing technologies (ISAM). These will help repair and maintain satellites damaged by space debris, solar storms or hostile interference, while helping clear dangerous objects from orbit – all while continuing to operate in space.
That support will help bring new products online that are directly developed in the unique environment of space, from new semiconductors that underpin our power grid to pharmaceuticals and drug delivery tools that could transform outcomes for patients.
Additional support for the UK’s wide-ranging space sector includes:
- £148 million for European rocket programmes and £30 million for SaxaVord Spaceport in Shetland – helping Britain and our partners to launch satellites without relying on countries further afield while creating new jobs.
- £163 million in space science and exploration missions, including the delivery of the Rosalind Franklin Mars Rover built in Stevenage. These missions power world-leading research while boosting this government’s mission to reindustrialise the UK with high-skilled jobs and new tech in areas like AI and autonomous systems.
- £57 million from the Department for Transport to improve rail connectivity, £190 million from UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) for astronomy and space science research, and £9 million from the Met Office to strengthen space weather forecasting.
For the first time, government will take a single approach to buying and developing space technology, starting with satellite communications, helping British firms win more work, strengthening UK supply chains, supporting skilled jobs and delivering capabilities faster and better value for taxpayers.
The new Strategy formally replaces the previous National Space Strategy, published in 2021, and will play a key role in the delivery of the Modern Industrial Strategy to deliver reindustrialisation and good growth in every postcode.
Alongside the Strategy, we’re reforming space regulations to reduce costs, reward responsible operators and make it easier for UK firms to invest in cutting-edge missions from satellite servicing to lunar exploration.
Supportive comments:
Doug Liddle, Chair of the trade association UKspace, said:
“UKspace welcomes the publication of the government’s new UK Space Strategy. It sets out a constructive path towards a refreshed approach to space in the UK, which we hope will result in a stronger emphasis on open, inclusive cross-sector dialogue. The new, focussed strategy offers a valuable opportunity to create a more streamlined framework, strengthen collaboration and deliver greater impact across the UK space sector.”
Kevin Craven, CEO of the ADS Group, said:
“We welcome the publication of the new space strategy, and the sustained effort to bring a cross-government perspective to space capability delivery. It is important that government maintains an open, transparent and ambitious partnership with industry to realise its national security and growth goals. 
 
“Certainty allows the sector to operate at pace and for its industrial base to make long-term strategic and commercial commitments. It is also a vital signal of intent to our international partners for trade and collaboration. ADS looks forward to supporting government on the crucial next steps for implementation.”
Professor Anna Hogg and Professor Mark Sims, Space Academic Network (SPAN) Co-Chairs said:
“SPAN welcomes the new cross-Government space strategy and its integrated delivery plan. Space technologies and services are integral to modern life, from secure communications to monitoring and responding to environmental change. We look forward to seeing the detail of the strategy and delivery plan, which will be critical in enabling academia and industry to plan, invest and work together to deliver the UK’s ambitions for space. Sustained investment across academia and industry is crucial to creating the cutting-edge technologies, capabilities, talent and growth of the future.”
Joanne Wheeler MBE, Managing Partner at Alden and Director of the Earth & Space Sustainability Initiative, said:
“In addition to enhancing UK security and defence, the UK Space Strategy brings together world-leading innovative regulation and insurance opportunities to enable and drive growth and investment, whilst encouraging responsible and sustainable operations.”
Simon Brown, Met Office Managing Director, said:
“Space based observations are critical for delivering weather forecasts and climate intelligence that people rely on every day to stay safe and grow the economy of the UK. Advancements in space observations are allowing us to improve our weather forecasts and also give us new imagery which helps us show the impacts of other hazards such as wildfires and drought which we have seen this summer.
“Delivering new and innovative space capability is important to enhance our preparedness for extreme weather and exploit the latest advances in our prediction capability using both physics and AI models. We welcome the new UK Space Strategy and its recognition of the vital role space plays in supporting weather and climate services, as well as the Met Office’s role as the UK’s space weather forecasting centre.”
Notes to editors:
The Strategy details how government will go further and faster to develop capability and deliver outcomes in our four priority subsectors:
- Satellite Communications
- In-Orbit Servicing, Assembly and Manufacturing
- Space Domain Awareness
- Assured Access to Space
The package of space regulatory financial tools contains measures which have been proposed by government, as well as those received in response to the previous consultation on orbital liabilities, insurance, charging and space sustainability. The package covers the following announcements:
- Adopting a world-first variable liability limits approach for orbital operations to incentivise uptake of government priorities of security and space sustainability, reduce cost burdens on UK companies and stimulate increased commercial investment in the UK’s space sector.
- Waiving operator liability for innovative and novel space missions launched before the end of 2030 (In-Orbit Servicing, Assembly & Manufacturing and lunar missions) to help support development of high potential technologies.
- Adoption of new world-first models for the provision of third-party liability insurance to support innovation in the City of London space insurance market.
- Abolishing decommissioning funds for operators of constellations in favour of a more proportionate approach to monitoring operators’ financial health.
- Further detail on the measures can be found in the government response to the consultation in the link above.

Le Creuset x Star Trek Collection: Prices, availability, release date
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
23:00:00 UTC
08:00:00 KST

Logic clearly dictates that the needs of the penne outweigh the needs of the stew, or the bun. While this would have been a gloriously fan-faithful reason for Le Creuset, the French-Belgian maker of colorful cookware for more than a century, to materialize its new limited-edition Star Trek collection, the range is being launched in celebration of 60 years of the cult sci-fi show.
No matter, because when you have such stellar items as Vulcan oven mitts, shuttlecraft baking dishes, and—perhaps best of all—a cheese grater in the shape of the classic Trek communicator (which has somewhat wonderfully been nicknamed the “Communi-grator” by Le Creuset's design team), there's only cause for celebration in the cosmos.
Going on sale today, to coincide with the space series' 60th anniversary, the limited-edition collection has actually been in development for years after Le Creuset approached Paramount to collaborate on the kitchen kit in time for the landmark birthday. Le Creuset is no stranger to fun mashups, with its recent 2024 Pokemon collection being snapped up almost instantly (those looking to get pieces now have to scour the likes of eBay for items way over original retail prices).
As well as the 15 cm Communi-grator for $68 (£52), foodies looking for Federation-themed gear might appreciate the $500 (£425) Enterprise round casserole pot complete with Starfleet insignia knob, or the $450 (£385) Klingon shallow casserole dish with trefoil "Heart of Virtue" knob—both in cast iron. Inside the Enterprise NCC-1701 pot is the legend “to boldly go”, while the Klingon dish offers up an encouraging “Qapla!” (“success” in Klingon), handy for experimental cooking.
Carrying culinary adventures into the unknown comes the Le Creuset x Star Trek: Galileo shuttlecraft casserole dish ($150), which has a roomy 1.6 liters of space inside. Vulcan votaries are well catered for with the $35 (£31) Spock ear mug (perfect for Vulcan spice tea), complete with gold detailing along the rim as a nod to the Starfleet uniform; the $55 (£36) Spock hand spoon rest; and the whimsical Vulcan salute “live long and prosper” oven mitt, resplendent in signature Star Trek baby blue for $40 (£36).
Not merely content with digitally launching the collection online, Le Creuset engaged Sent Into Space to boldly send its Enterprise casserole dish where no pan has gone before—more than 111,000 feet above the Earth, atop 99.5 percent of the planet’s atmosphere. While obviously a blatant (albeit fitting) marketing stunt, there's actually some considerable logistics to overcome in sending a cast-iron pot to the edge of space.
Sent Into Space co-founder Chris Rose had the task of launching the pot in the stratosphere via a space-capable balloon taller than the height of The White House, where it stayed for 1 hour, 19 minutes, and 4 seconds enduring temperatures down to -63.4°C (-82.12°F). “Because of the weight, we had to give some serious consideration to how we were going to hold things, making sure everything was very balanced,” Rose tells WIRED. Rose and his team also have to rely on simulations to take into account considerations such as where will the pot land as it's parachuted back down to Earth, as well as how to avoid bodies of water and built-up areas, for example.
“The legal authorities within the aviation community need to know. We can't have a Le Creuset casserole dish floating past the window of an airborne A380 as it makes its way off to some destination,” Rose says. “So we are in constant communication, both from a flight-clearance perspective before this ever leaves leaves the ground, to onboard systems for telemetry and communication.” Indeed, in the early stages of reentry, Rose says the Enterprise casserole dish reached speeds in excess of 300 mph before slowing and landing safely in Lincolnshire, England.
Back on terra firma, the Le Creuset x Star Trek collection should serve cadets and captains alike, provided you can secure your selections before stock vanishes like a cloaked Bird-of-Prey.

Black boxes recovered from Amazon cargo plane that overran Miami runway
NTSB investigators inspect ‘utter devastation’ at crash site where Boeing 767 struck two vehicles, killing five people on the ground
Investigators with the US National Transportation Safety Board said on Monday they had recovered the flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder from an Amazon Prime Air cargo plane that overran the runway and crashed while landing in Miami on Sunday, killing five people on the ground.
NTSB Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy said the two devices, commonly referred to as the black boxes, were being returned to the agency’s headquarters in Washington on Monday night for evaluation.
The 32-year-old Boeing 767-33A, operated by Miami-based 21 Air LLC, overran the runway by some 396 metres (1,300 feet) and crashed into two vehicles on the ground: an Econoline van on the airport grounds carrying seven people from an airline cleaning crew and a Toyota SUV that was driving on a road beyond the perimeter fence.
The two people aboard the plane, the pilot and co-pilot, survived and had yet to be interviewed, Homendy said in a press conference.
Five people were injured, three of them critically, officials said on Sunday.
Homendy, leading a team of 32 investigators at Miami International Airport, briefed reporters on the early stages of the investigation but said a probable cause of the accident would not be determined until the end of the investigation.

Nearly 1.7 million deaths linked to second-hand smoke in 2023, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
22:53:34 UTC
07:53:34 KST

Nearly 1.7 million deaths linked to second-hand smoke in 2023, study finds
More than 2.7 billion people worldwide, including 767 million children, were exposed to second-hand smoke in 2023, contributing to nearly 1.7 million deaths, a Lancet study said on Tuesday. Researchers found second-hand smoke remained a major global health risk, with no safe level of exposure.
More than 2.7 billion people including children have been exposed to second-hand smoke globally, contributing to nearly 1.7 million deaths in 2023, according to study published Tuesday in The Lancet.
Tobacco remains a leading cause of disease globally, the study said, noting many "non-smokers exposed to second-hand smoke" were among the estimate total of 8 million people who died in 2023 of smoking-related illnesses.
"Exposure to second-hand smoke is a globally recognised health risk, with no safe level of inhalation," it said.
By reviewing studies published in the US National Institutes of Health database PubMed along with population surveys, Tuesday's study sought to estimate the prevalence of exposure to second-hand smoke and quantify the burden of disease in 204 countries and territories between 1990 and 2023.
Read moreIn Indonesia, addiction to smoking starts in childhood
Among the approximately 2.7 billion people exposed to second-hand smoke in 2023 were 767 million children aged 0 to 14, the study found.
This exposure is estimated to have resulted in 1.66 million premature deaths and causing premature disability and illness, leading with ischemic heart disease, a heart condition caused by insufficient oxygen supply to the heart muscle.
In children, exposure to second-hand smoke is estimated to have caused 5.2 million respiratory tract infections in 2023, it said.
People in proximity to someone lighting up are exposed to both the "sidestream smoke" from the burning tobacco product and smoke exhaled by the active smoker, the study explained.
"The sidestream component, which dominates the air non-smokers breathe, is unfiltered ... carrying higher per-unit concentrations of the toxic and carcinogenic compounds" than that being inhaled by the active smoker, it said.
Read moreHow French attitudes to cigarettes are changing
Despite significant declines in smoking prevalence globally since 1990, the absolute number of people exposed has remained stable due to population growth and increased exposure in Africa and the Middle East.
Women are also disproportionately affected by second-hand smoke, particularly in regions where smoking prevalence among women is low, it noted.
"Despite this substantial burden, (second-hand smoke) exposure remains rarely acknowledged as a major risk factor for female health," it said.
The study called for governments to implement stronger tobacco controls in public places and in homes in order to better protect women and children from second-hand smoke.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Panama Canal considering more cuts in transits due to El Nino
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
22:50:00 UTC
07:50:00 KST

Panama Canal considering more cuts in transits due to El Nino
PANAMA CITY - The number of ships sailing through the Panama Canal could be cut further due to drought caused by the El Nino weather pattern, the new administrator of the waterway told AFP on Sept 7.
Panama has declared a nationwide emergency over El Nino, a phenomenon developing over the Pacific Ocean that is affecting worldwide weather patterns and pushing up global temperatures.
This year’s El Nino is expected to be the strongest since record-keeping began four decades ago.
Panama’s restrictions come even as use of the canal has risen: Shippers are seeking an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran has blocked in retaliation for the war launched by the United States and Israel.
The inter-oceanic Panama Canal – which handles 5 per cent of global maritime trade – has already reduced the maximum number of ships allowed through daily, from 36 last month to 32 by mid-September.
It operates using rainwater that collects in two reservoirs, whose levels have dropped due to the onset of El Nino.
Without water, the locks that lift and lower ships at the start and end of their crossing cannot function.
Ilya Espino de Marotta, who took over as head of the Panama Canal Authority on Sept 7, told AFP that further measures may be implemented if the drought does not subside.
“We do not rule out the possibility that in February or March, we may have to lower the limit – probably not to 24 slots per day, but it could be reduced to 29 or something similar,” she said.
200 million litres per ship
Each ship requires about 200 million litre of water, which is then discharged into the sea.
In 2023, El Nino forced a reduction in daily transits from 38 to 22 due to the dramatic reduction in reservoir levels.
Espino de Marotta, the first woman ever to head the US-built canal authority, stated, however, that she does not expect restrictions to reach the levels seen that year.
Apart from reducing the number of vessels, canal authorities have also reduced their maximum draft, from 15.2 metres to 14.6m.
The draft is the vertical distance between the waterline and the lowest point of a ship’s hull. It is a measure of how much water is needed for a ship to float safely without running aground.
Experts have warned that long-term restrictions on canal crossings could lead to higher shipping costs and longer waiting times for deliveries.
The United States and China are the main users of the canal, which is the fastest maritime route between the east coast of the United States and China.
The canal connecting the Atlantic and Pacific handles around 40 per cent of US container traffic.
The Iran war has pushed up traffic through the channel.
With shipping at a standstill in the Strait of Hormuz, a conduit for a fifth of the world’s oil and gas, the Panama Canal has become a fallback route for energy shipments. AFP

Rubio heads to Ecuador, Colombia, Peru after right-wing victories in region
Rightward shift in Latin America comes as Washington pledges to grow influence, take militaristic approach to cartels.
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio is travelling to three South American countries whose recently elected leaders have closely aligned with President Donald Trump’s administration.
Rubio will travel to Colombia on Tuesday to meet with newly elected President Abelardo de la Espriella. He will then visit Ecuador to meet with President Daniel Noboa before going to Peru, where he will meet with another newly elected leader, Keiko Fujimori.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3What’s behind the US deal to seize control of Venezuelan oil reserves?
- list 2 of 3Honduran court drops case against ex-President Hernandez after Trump pardon
- list 3 of 3‘Winds of change’: How Milei is stirring Falklands claim amid Trump-UK spat
The State Department has not yet released a more in-depth agenda for the trip, saying only that Rubio will discuss “US support for Colombia’s earthquake response; enhanced cooperation in the shared fight against narcoterrorism, which threatens our hemisphere; and the benefits of deeper commercial relationships between our countries”.
The trip comes amid a rightward shift in Latin America that has seen several Trump-aligned leaders take office. Beyond the three countries, Trump also backed Honduran President Nasry Asfura, who won the presidency in November, and Bolivia’s Rodrigo Paz, who won in October.
Beyond the new leaders, Trump has also closely aligned with Argentina’s Javier Milei, who took office in 2023, and El Salvador’s Nayib Bukele, who became the leader in 2019.
US influence over Western Hemisphere
Rubio’s visit comes as the Trump administration has pledged to assert more influence over the Western Hemisphere in what Trump has referred to as the “Donroe Doctrine”, a reference to the 19th-century Monroe Doctrine that opposed European interference in the Americas.
It has shifted to a militaristic approach to security in Latin American countries, while broadly reframing efforts to combat drug trafficking as a war against “narco-terrorists”.
In August, Colombia’s de la Espriella upped cooperation with the US by joining the Trump administration’s so-called “Shield of the Americas”.
The 19 members of the group have jointly pledged a “commitment to using lethal military force to destroy the sinister cartels and terrorist networks”.
Unlike his predecessor, leftist Gustavo Petro, de la Espriella has also praised US military strikes on alleged drug smugglers in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific. At least 227 people have been killed in those strikes, in what rights groups have condemned as extrajudicial killings.
Family members of those killed have charged that the targets were fishermen, not drug smugglers.
The US has proven a major supporter for de la Espriella in the wake of a devastating earthquake in Colombia last month in which at least 330 people were killed and thousands left homeless.
In March, the US military announced it was collaborating with Ecuador, under Noboa’s leadership, to target drug trafficking groups in the country.
Ecuador’s Interior Minister John Reimberg defended the US strikes on vessels allegedly carrying drugs in an interview with broadcaster Teleamazonas last week.
Peru’s Fujimori, the daughter of former leader Alberto Fujimori, who notoriously dissolved the country’s Congress and Supreme Court to consolidate power during his government from 1990 to 2000, has also pledged closer ties with the US and a military crackdown on criminal groups.
Conservative shift
Rubio’s visit comes after the US announced a controversial agreement with Venezuela’s interim leader, Delcy Rodriguez. The deal, struck in the wake of the January 3 US abduction of Venezuela’s ex-President Nicolas Maduro, grants US companies access to 65 billion barrels of crude oil reserves over the next 100 years.
It also comes as Washington has continued to up its pressure campaign against Cuba, with Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez on Monday rejecting any talks with the US despite its ongoing fuel blockade of the island.
Brazil and Mexico remain the only regional powers with leftist leaders. Rubio has called the region’s conservative lurch an “extraordinary achievement”.
The shift has accompanied the strengthening of ties between Israel and several Latin American countries since Trump took office.
Brazilians will go to the polls in October, when Flavio Bolsonaro, a son of former right-wing leader Jair Bolsonaro, seeks to unseat Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.
Trump has remained a staunch ally of the elder Bolsonaro, who has been sentenced to 27 years in prison for leading a conspiracy to hold onto power.
The US president has also shown strong support for the younger Bolsonaro, including inviting him to the White House in May.

Hawaii braces for Hurricane Lowell
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
22:37:25 UTC
07:37:25 KST

Hawaii braces for Hurricane Lowell
Threats of cyclones and deadly surf as the Category 3 storm path approaches Hawaiian islands on Monday night.
Hurricane Lowell, a major Category 3 storm in the Pacific Ocean, has crept closer to the Hawaiian islands with forecasters warning the weather systems could unleash tornadoes on the islands of Kauai and Niihau.
On Sunday, the United States National Hurricane Center issued emergency hurricane and tropical storm warnings for the island chain, advising residents and visitors to brace for severe windstorms and possible mudslides as early as Monday night local time. Lowell is predicted to skirt just west of Hawaii’s most northwest main islands, Niihau and Kauai, as well as portions of the vast Papahanaumokuakea Marine National Monument, tracking from south to north.
Mayor Derek Kawakami of Kauai issued an emergency proclamation in anticipation of the hurricane.
Kauai faces potential coastal flooding of up to 1 metre (3 feet) caused by rolling storm surges and unusually high tides.
The storm has been gradually pivoting toward the more rural islands in the Aloha state, moving north at 9 km/h (6 mph), according to the hurricane center. Lowell started as a tropical depression that formed over the Pacific Ocean on August 27. It was driven by a combination of warm ocean temperatures and an active El Nino pattern.
Lowell has seesawed between Category 3 and Category 5 intensity as its trajectory mushroomed. It first reached Category 5 intensity at 257 km/h (160 mph) on Wednesday morning local time, becoming the second Category 5 hurricane of the season. Only two other Pacific hurricanes in recorded history have regrouped to a Category 5 after losing strength mid-path: Emilia (1994) and Ioke (2006).
Ioke was the strongest ever recorded in the central Pacific, while the island of Kauai sustained billions in damage during Hurricane Inike, a 1992 Category 4 storm and the largest recorded in Hawaii’s history. Six people were killed.
Forecasters said Lowell could bring rainfall of 150mm to 250mm (6 to 10 inches), with maximum totals of 360mm (14 inches).
Lowell had maximum sustained winds of 195km/h (120 mph) and was pinpointed about 895km (about 555 miles) southwest of the state capital, Honolulu.
Local officials have been urging residents and visitors to prepare for a downpour of rain and fierce winds which could cause major flash flooding and hazardous mudslides.
According to the National Weather Service, tornadoes could accompany tropical cyclones. They typically occur in rain bands well away from the center of the storm.
Hawaii’s Big Island can expect as much as 100mm to 200mm (4 inches to 8 inches) of rain, with localized peaks reaching up to 305mm (12 inches).
Hurricane-force winds extended outward up to 85km (50 miles) from the centre while tropical storm-force winds extended outward up to 280km (175 miles).
Residents prepare for the worst
Kauai’s Emergency Management Agency urged residents to fill gas tanks, charge devices, refill prescriptions and store water and food ahead of the storm. The agency also said residents should be prepared to stay home for several days.
Swells generated from Lowell are expected to produce “life-threatening surf and rip current conditions”, according to a statement by the Kauai County government on Sunday evening. It urged visitors to stay out of the ocean and steer clear of the shoreline as coastal conditions rapidly worsen.
“Residents should not assume conditions will be limited to areas near the storm’s center,” the government said.
As panic-buying emptied supermarket shelves in Lihue on Kauai, residents of the 8,000-person airport town scrambled to stock up on food and water.
Real estate agent Lori Benkert bought an extra 4.5kg (10 pound) container of propane so that she could cook on the barbecue if power shut off. Benkert manages dozens of properties on Kauai and has boarded up two houses on the western side of the island.
“We’ll lose some power, probably have some trees, a bunch of tree limbs coming down,” Benkert told The Associated Press. “Everybody is probably going just to hunker down”.
Meanwhile, Category 1 Hurricane Marie churned 1,120km (695 miles) south-southwest of San Diego in southern California, bringing dangerous surf to the area and Mexico’s Baja coast. Packing 120km/h (75mph) sustained winds, the storm tracked northwest at 11km/h (7mph).
Even without coastal watches or warnings, updrafts from Marie will hit southwest Mexico, Baja California and Southern California over the next few days, creating pounding surf and dangerous rip currents.
The islands of Hawaii rarely experience tornadoes, averaging about one per year. Just 42 tornadoes were reported in the state between 1950 to 2018, according to Stephen Parker, a meteorologist with the weather service office in Honolulu.

Europe’s biggest nuclear power plant back to normal after weeks in emergency mode
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
22:32:21 UTC
07:32:21 KST

Europe’s biggest nuclear power plant back to normal after weeks in emergency mode
Power has been restored to the Zaporozhye Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP) after more than two weeks in emergency mode, the CEO of the Russian state nuclear energy corporation Rosatom, Aleksey Likhachev, has said.
The main external power line to the plant was cut off in March following what the Ukrainian authorities described as “damage” to transmission towers. It has never been restored, with no explanations from Kiev.
Since then, the ZNPP has had to rely solely on the backup line – until August 20, when it was shut down by automatic control systems following an unspecified “incident” in territory controlled by Ukraine. That forced the power plant to fall back on emergency diesel-powered generators.
On Monday, Likhachev told journalists that the external power supply to the ZNPP had finally been restored, and the facility was now “operating as normal.” The Rosatom chief thanked all the parties involved in establishing a temporary local truce needed for the repair work, including the Russian defense and foreign ministries. He also praised the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) for its “mediation efforts.”
The ZNPP operator also confirmed that external power had been restored. No violations of safety limits were reported, and the radiation situation at the plant and in the surrounding area remained stable and did not exceed natural background levels, it said in a statement. The operator added that the second power supply line has yet to be restored and regular fuel supplies to the station need to be facilitated.
Diesel fuel deliveries to the station were “problematic” because of Ukrainian shelling targeting the roads in the area, ZNPP communications director Evgenia Yashina told Interfax earlier.
Europe’s largest nuclear power plant and the adjacent city of Energodar have been targeted by Ukraine on multiple occasions with artillery and drones since Russia took control of the facility in March 2022.
In July, a Ukrainian drone hit a ZNPP service vehicle on the edge of the plant’s industrial site, killing its chief engineer, Aleksandr Yakovlev, and his driver. At the time, Likhachev called the strike a “deliberate terrorist act.”
According to the Rosatom CEO, more than a dozen employees of the plant have been killed and many others wounded in Ukrainian attacks over the past three months. Kiev’s actions pose the “real danger of a massive nuclear incident” affecting parts of Russia, Ukraine, and the EU, he warned.
Several months ago, the Ukrainian military also started remotely mining the area near the ZNPP and Energodar, where plant employees reside, according to the nuclear chief. In early August, four ZNPP employees were injured by Ukrainian landmines dropped by drones.
Moscow has repeatedly criticized the IAEA, which has experts deployed at the ZNPP, for acknowledging the attacks on the facility but stopping short of blaming Ukraine for them.

Israel sees 58% drop in returning citizens amid rising emigration: Knesset panel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
22:27:30 UTC
07:27:30 KST

The number of Israelis returning to the country fell by 58% in 2025 compared with 2009, an Israeli parliamentary committee revealed Monday, amid estimates that nearly 1 million Israelis are living abroad.
The figures were presented during a meeting of the Knesset’s Committee for Immigration, Absorption and Diaspora Affairs convened to examine the growing emigration of Israelis, according to the parliament’s official website.
Data from the Knesset Research and Information Center showed that 4,483 Israelis returned to the country in 2025, down from 10,903 in 2009.
Between 2005 and 2024, approximately 141,000 Israelis returned after living abroad, an annual average of roughly 7,000, the center said.
Estimates presented to the committee indicated that around 1 million Israelis currently live outside the country.
- Where are Israelis returning from?
According to the center’s analysis, 45% of returning Israelis came from the US, followed by 6% from the UK, 5% from Canada and 4% from France.
Germany, Russia, Romania and Ukraine each accounted for 3% of returnees, while Australia, Italy and Moldova each accounted for 2%.
More than a quarter of those returning were minors, while 47% were aged between 28 and 60.
Around 70% returned after living abroad for at least five years, the data showed.
- Government accused of inaction
Gilad Kariv, chairman of the Immigration, Absorption and Diaspora Affairs Committee, accused the Israeli government of failing to take steps to encourage Israelis living abroad to return.
“Since our last discussion on this issue, additional data have been published indicating a decline in the number of Israelis returning to Israel,” Kariv said.
He said the committee had called on the government to formulate a five-year plan aimed at bringing Israelis living abroad back to the country.
A similar plan was introduced in 2010 but has not been renewed since, he added.
“We presented a wide range of measures that could be taken to encourage Israelis to return to their homeland, but unfortunately, the government chose to ignore our recommendations,” Kariv said.
He added that the government had also failed to establish a roundtable to examine ways to encourage Israelis to return.
“There is no body in Israel responsible for addressing emigration,” he said, accusing the government of refusing to take responsibility for the issue.
The meeting also highlighted a growing exodus of medical professionals.
“We are seeing an increase in the number of doctors leaving Israel and a decline in the number of those choosing to return,” said Itai Ater, a professor at Tel Aviv University.
Highly experienced senior doctors account for around 20% of those leaving, he said, noting that other countries offer incentives to attract medical professionals.
The Israeli daily Haaretz reported Sunday on a study by Tel Aviv University showing that at least 1,370 doctors left Israel between 2023 and 2025.
One in five doctors who left during the period was over the age of 45, a trend the study described as “worrying.”
A previous report by the Israeli Finance Ministry found that around 24% of specialist doctors at public hospitals are expected to reach retirement age in the coming years.
Nearly 25% of doctors currently working have already passed retirement age but remain in their positions because of staff shortages, according to the report.
Another Tel Aviv University study published in early August found that 268,509 Israelis left the country for at least three months between 2023 and 2025, a figure the Israeli public broadcaster KAN described as a record.
Israeli reports have attributed the rising emigration to the repercussions of the Gaza war, soaring living costs and the political crisis surrounding the government’s efforts to weaken the judiciary.
A Kantar poll conducted for KAN and published on Aug. 9 found that nearly one-fifth of Israelis had considered emigrating during the previous two years.
Around 12% said the outcome of the upcoming general election could affect their decision to remain in or leave the country.
The Israel Hayom newspaper also reported on Aug. 7, citing an internal Tax Authority document, that the emigration rate among wealthy Israelis doubled between 2019 and 2024.
Annual tax losses resulting from their departure rose from around 500 million shekels ($166 million) to 1.2 billion shekels ($400 million) in 2023 and 2024, according to the document.
The figures come as Israel continues its genocidal war in the Gaza Strip, which has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians and injured over 174,000, most of them women and children, while destroying around 90% of the enclave’s infrastructure.
They also coincide with Israel’s continuing attacks on Lebanon and its ongoing threats against Iran.

Resolution doesn't endorse any specific map: MEA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
22:23:42 UTC
07:23:42 KST

India was among the 164 countries that voted in favour of UN General Assembly's Sept 4 resolution, "Correct the Map: Rebalancing Global Cartographic Representation and Promoting Equitable Representation of the World's Regions, Particularly Africa".MEA said the resolution's purpose is to encourage the use of equal-area map projections that preserve the relative sizes of continental landmasses, and it neither adopts nor authenticates any particular world map, nor does it address political cartography, including international boundaries, disputed territories or place names."India voted in favour of the resolution and also made an explanation, stressing the underlying principle of promoting equal-area cartographic representation. We also highlighted that the resolution does not constitute endorsement of any specific map, projection or depiction of national boundaries," said Randhir Jaiswal.The resolution received abstentions from Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, Moldova, Serbia and Ukraine, and a lone vote against it from US.
The resolution noted that the Mercator projection remains widely used in educational, media, digital and official materials, despite the considerable distortion of landmasses to the North and South, far from the equator.
It expressed concern that this distortion contributed to minimising the perceived sizes of Africa, Latin America and South Asia, and perpetuating an unbalanced view of the world. India welcomed the intention behind the resolution to promote more accurate and representative cartographic practices.

Ukraine’s Prosecutor General Kravchenko Submits Resignation

2026-09-07
22:23:40 UTC
07:23:40 KST

Ukraine’s Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko submitted his resignation on Monday, Sept. 7, calling the move a “political decision” days after anti-corruption investigators searched premises used by him and other senior officials at the Prosecutor General’s Office.
“This is a political decision. And I made it consciously,” Kravchenko said in a statement on Telegram, adding that he did not want the prosecutor general’s post to become an instrument of political confrontation.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Kravchenko said his position regarding the allegations against him had not changed. He thanked prosecutors working on criminal cases, assisting victims, documenting Russian war crimes and defending Ukraine’s interests, as well as President Volodymyr Zelensky and the Verkhovna Rada, and asked them to accept his resignation.
The announcement marked an abrupt turn from comments Kravchenko made only hours earlier.
Speaking to journalists on Monday, he said he did not intend to resign voluntarily, although he would leave if Zelensky initiated his dismissal or parliament approved such a move.
“I am not clinging to the position,” he said at the time.
Ukrainska Pravda later reported, citing political sources, that Zelensky met with Kravchenko and Davyd Arakhamia, head of the ruling Servant of the People parliamentary faction, on Sept. 7 to discuss whether Kravchenko would remain in office.
Burnham, Trump Agree to Keep Working Toward Ukraine-Russia Ceasefire
Sources told the outlet that a decision on his future was expected following the meeting. Kravchenko announced his resignation later that evening.
The resignation comes amid the fallout from a major investigation by Ukraine’s National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) and Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO) into an alleged criminal organization operating within the Prosecutor General’s Office.
As Kyiv Post previously reported, investigators launched an operation targeting a group allegedly involved in protecting fraudulent call centers and laundering illicit proceeds.
On Sept. 5, the Prosecutor General’s Office confirmed that NABU detectives had searched official premises used by Kravchenko, First Deputy Prosecutor General Mariia Vdovychenko and other staff.
The confirmation followed initial denials that Kravchenko’s home or office had been searched.
Kravchenko said Monday that security personnel initially prevented NABU detectives from entering because investigators had not shown which offices they intended to search. He said he later spoke with the heads of NABU and SAPO and ordered that investigators be given access to his office, other rooms and safes.
NABU and SAPO say their Operation Carthage investigation uncovered a criminal organization allegedly headed by an official at the Prosecutor General’s Office. Investigators accuse members of taking bribes in exchange for shielding fraudulent call centers and laundering proceeds from the scheme.
Ukrainska Pravda identified the suspected official as Serhii Kropyva, deputy head of the Prosecutor General’s Office’s International Legal Cooperation Department. Kropyva was detained and on Sept. 6 remanded in custody with bail set at Hr.120 million, about $2.7 million.
Kravchenko has denied involvement in protecting illegal call centers.
His submission does not immediately end his tenure. Under Ukraine’s Constitution, the prosecutor general is appointed and dismissed by the president with the consent of the Verkhovna Rada. Ukrainian law states that the prosecutor general’s powers end when the relevant parliamentary resolution takes effect.
Kravchenko has served as prosecutor general since June 21, 2025, after parliament approved his appointment and Zelensky formally appointed him by presidential decree.

Eiffel Tower employees strike after female staff removed
September 8, 2026
The Eiffel Tower in Paris, France, was closed on Monday after staff went on strike to protest the exclusion of female workers during a visit by a Hindu religious group.
Visitors to the tower on Monday saw a message that says its opening is "delayed for operational reasons."
The staff released a statement in which they condemned "professional instructions that led to female employees being sidelined, replaced and made invisible because of their sex" during the religious group's visit.
Around 100 men from the Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) spiritual movement were visiting the landmark.
The company that operates the Tower, SETE, said that the group had requested a visit as part of which the "interactions with women" would be limited.
Emmanuel Gregoire, Paris' Socialist mayor, called the incident "unacceptable."
"Equality between women and men will never end at the foot of our historic monuments, nor anywhere else in this city," Gregoire said.
Eiffel Tower operator regrets incident
SETE accepted that the decision was a mistake.
"These conditions should not have been accepted," SETE said.
Company head Ariel Weil told the AFP news agency that SETE will "draw the necessary conclusions" from the case. Weil himself is an elected official in Paris.
"No motive of a religious order could justify a distinction based on gender or any other discriminatory consideration in welcoming the public," Weil wrote on his X account.
The Eiffel Tower sees some seven million visitors a year. It was closed all day due to the strike, but will open again on Tuesday, a staff representative said.

North Korea slams joint drills by US, South Korea and Japan, warns of consequences
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
22:17:57 UTC
07:17:57 KST

North Korea has denounced a five-day military exercise by the US, South Korea, and Japan, warning of consequences from what it called Washington's increasingly provocative military activities on the Korean Peninsula.
The fourth iteration of the Freedom Edge exercise began with an opening ceremony at Yokota Air Base in Japan and will run through Friday, according to the US Pacific Command.
The drills are being conducted in international waters and airspace south of South Korea, as well as at military installations and command posts in Japan.
Freedom Edge focuses on interoperability across air, maritime and cyber domains, along with integrated air and missile defence.
South Korea has described the exercise as defensive and aimed at strengthening deterrence and response capabilities against North Korea's nuclear and missile threats.
'Military provocations'
North Korea, however, condemned the trilateral drills as a threat to itself and other countries in the region.
In a Defence Ministry statement carried by the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA), North Korea accused Washington of pursuing "military provocations" and vowed to take "response measures."
North Korean Defence Minister Kim Song-ji issued "a note of warning against the reckless military moves of the US and its satellite countries to create a serious military confrontation and possibility of conflict on the Korean Peninsula" in the statement.
He also "solemnly" warned of "the consequences to be entailed by them," according to KCNA.
The statements said there would be no change in Pyongyang's policy of responding to US hostility with the "toughest stand to the last."
The drills come weeks after US President Donald Trump said that he had instructed Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth to "substantially reduce" separate planned bilateral military exercises between the US and South Korea, citing their cost and his relationship with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un.
Trump said those exercises sent an "inappropriate and hostile" signal to Pyongyang.

While You Were Sleeping: 5 stories you might have missed, Sept 8, 2026
Jakarta airport and four others near Indonesia’s capital reopen after volcanic ash disruption
Indonesia’s main airport and several other air travel hubs reopened early on Sept 8 after days of closure due to ash from a volcanic eruption, the Transport Ministry said.
The ministry wrote on Instagram that the airport serving the capital Jakarta and four others near the city or around the island of Java are now operating again, as the air safety crisis that left hundreds of thousands of travellers stranded subsides.
Mount Anak Krakatau, about 150km from Jakarta, erupted on Sept 5, spewing a fountain of lava and a plume of volcanic ash.
Eight airports halted operations over the weekend after ash was detected in their airspace, disrupting nearly 3,000 flights and leaving more than 340,000 passengers stranded, the Transport Ministry reported on Sept 7.
Britain set to impose trade ban on Israeli West Bank settlements
Britain is set to announce wide-ranging economic restrictions targeting Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank as soon as Sept 8, according to seven officials briefed on the measures, in what experts say would be a significant censure of Israeli policy toward Palestinians.
The measures are expected to include a trade ban on goods produced in the settlements, the officials said, speaking on condition of anonymity. Three of the officials said the measures could also include sanctions on companies helping to build settlements.
Israel has become increasingly isolated on the world stage in the aftermath of the devastating war in the Gaza Strip, and international attention has focused on Israel’s tightening grip over the West Bank.
Paris probes claim that women were hidden from Hindu delegation at Eiffel Tower
Female employees at the Eiffel Tower were asked to step out of sight during a visit by a Hindu religious delegation at the weekend, according to union representatives, prompting a staff protest and an investigation by the Paris city authorities.

The dispute stems from a private visit on Sept 5 by a delegation of about 100 people linked to BAPS (Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha), a Hindu group whose representatives were in France for festivities related to the inauguration of a Hindu temple in the Paris suburbs.
Europe’s biggest mobile operators in talks for satellite-to-mobile venture
A group of Europe’s biggest mobile operators are in early talks to create a consortium to bid on satellite spectrum and offer direct-to-mobile service, which would rival Elon Musk’s Starlink service on the continent, people familiar with the matter said.
Deutsche Telekom, Orange, Vodafone Group and Telefonica would jointly bid for a share of airwaves that the European Union has proposed reserving for a local operator, a plan aimed at increasing sovereign satellite capabilities, the people said, asking not to be identified because the plans are private. No final decisions on the consortium or plans to bid have been made, they said.
To comply with the EU’s proposal, any satellite operator would need to be majority controlled by a European business.
Elena Rybakina tops Naomi Osaka, sets US Open quarter-final clash with China’s Zheng Qinwen
World number two Elena Rybakina swept past four-time Grand Slam champion Naomi Osaka 6-1, 6-4 on Sept 7 to line up a US Open quarter-final against China’s Zheng Qinwen.
Kazakhstan’s Rybakina, who added the French Open title to her 2022 Wimbledon crown this year, is into the US Open last eight for the first time in her career.
The meeting with 2024 Olympic gold medallist Zheng will carry extra weight. If Rybakina reaches the semi-finals she is assured of supplanting Aryna Sabalenka atop the world rankings, even if the Belarusian wins her third straight US Open title.

How Tokyo is widening regional defence ties to complicate Beijing’s Taiwan calculus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
22:00:13 UTC
07:00:13 KST

In FocusHow Tokyo is widening regional defence ties to complicate Beijing’s Taiwan calculus
Tokyo is strengthening partnerships across the Indo-Pacific and beyond, possibly bolstering its ability to withstand a prolonged armed conflict
The risk of a conflict over Taiwan is shaping Japanese defence planning, with Tokyo shoring up security at home and abroad for a potentially prolonged fight. But there are economic, demographic and political constraints on how far its military transformation can go. In the first of a three-part series, Gabriel Dominguez examines how Japan is building a network of partnerships to strengthen its strategic endurance.
The push was on display in Australia last month, where Tokyo and Canberra moved to deepen cooperation, ranging from defence planning and advanced weapons development to the construction and sustainment of Japanese-designed warships.
But the deepening relationship with Australia is only part of a much broader shift.
With Taiwan increasingly shaping its defence planning, Japan is connecting regional military ties with defence-industrial and technological partnerships across North America and Europe.
The United States is Japan’s only treaty ally and security cornerstone, and Tokyo is looking to other countries to complement that relationship: from operational and logistical cooperation with Australia and the Philippines to weapons production, intelligence and more secure supply chains farther afield.

Breast size dissatisfaction does not lower a mother’s confidence in breastfeeding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
22:00:01 UTC
07:00:01 KST

Many women experience dissatisfaction with their breast size, but these aesthetic concerns do not appear to lower their confidence in their ability to breastfeed. A study of pregnant women in Türkiye found no link between breast size dissatisfaction and prenatal breastfeeding self-efficacy. The findings were published in the Journal of Health Psychology.
Breasts are heavily scrutinized under cultural and societal beauty standards. Globally, up to 70 percent of women report wanting a different breast size than the one they have. This widespread dissatisfaction often negatively affects self-esteem and mental well-being. The pressure to conform to an idealized body shape can cause localized appearance anxiety.
Researchers wanted to understand if these appearance anxieties spill over into biological and maternal functions, specifically breastfeeding. Past research in various countries has shown that having a generally positive body image is linked to higher confidence in breastfeeding. A positive view of the body often translates to a stronger belief in the body’s physical capabilities.
However, specific anxieties about breast size are less understood. Misconceptions persist worldwide that smaller breasts cannot produce enough milk or that larger breasts are inherently better for feeding infants. These myths can erode a mother’s confidence before the baby is even born.
In psychological terms, this confidence is known as self-efficacy. Self-efficacy refers to a person’s belief in their own ability to succeed in specific situations or accomplish a task. High prenatal breastfeeding self-efficacy is a strong predictor of actual breastfeeding initiation and duration after birth.
To investigate this localized body anxiety, nursing researchers Kıymet Yeşilçiçek Çalık and Ebru Küçük Erdöl at Karadeniz Technical University, along with Hatice İkra Şan at Ankara Etlik City Hospital, evaluated maternal perceptions in Türkiye. In Turkish culture, breastfeeding is highly valued and viewed as a fundamental duty of motherhood. The researchers sought to find out whether a mother’s subjective dissatisfaction with her pre-pregnancy breast size might act as a psychological barrier to her self-efficacy.
The researchers recruited 518 pregnant women from the antenatal clinics of a university hospital. The participants were between 28 and 42 weeks of gestation. The women were experiencing uncomplicated, single-infant pregnancies. The average age of the participants was nearly 31 years old.
During private face-to-face interviews, researchers asked the women to provide demographic information and details about their pregnancy history. Just under half of the participants were experiencing their first pregnancy. The researchers also asked the participants if they believed breast size affects breastfeeding success or milk production.
To measure body dissatisfaction, the researchers used a visual rating tool consisting of 14 computer-generated images of women. These images featured progressively increasing breast sizes but lacked facial features to prevent bias. Participants selected the image that best matched their current size and the image that represented their ideal size. The numerical difference between these two selections represented their level of dissatisfaction.
Next, the researchers measured breastfeeding self-efficacy using a 20-item questionnaire. This tool asked participants to rate how confident they felt about various aspects of breastfeeding on a scale from one to five. A higher total score indicated greater confidence.
The results showed a high level of dissatisfaction among the participants. More than 65 percent of the women were dissatisfied with their breast size. The most common desire was for a smaller size, which accounted for nearly 49 percent of the total group. Only about 17 percent of the women wished for larger breasts.
Despite this widespread dissatisfaction, the women displayed high levels of confidence in their ability to breastfeed. More than 80 percent of the participants stated that they did not believe breast size affects breastfeeding success. Additionally, 86.5 percent did not associate breast size with milk production.
When the researchers analyzed the data, they found that the results were not statistically significant regarding a link between breast size dissatisfaction and breastfeeding self-efficacy. In other words, feeling unhappy with the aesthetic appearance of their breasts did not correspond to lower confidence in their functional ability to nourish a child.
This lack of association remained true even after the researchers adjusted the statistical models to account for women who had previous breastfeeding experience. The data suggest that in certain contexts, women mentally separate their feelings about how their body looks from their belief in what their body can do.
The authors propose that the transition to motherhood might prompt a cognitive shift. In societies where the maternal role is deeply revered, the functional utility of the breast as a feeding organ appears to take priority over its form. Appearance anxieties simply do not translate into a lack of health confidence for these mothers.
The study relied entirely on self-reported questionnaires, which can introduce bias if participants provide answers they feel are socially acceptable. The cross-sectional design of the study also captures only a single moment in time during pregnancy. This prevents researchers from observing how maternal confidence might shift after the baby is born.
The research was conducted at a single hospital in Türkiye, which limits how the findings might apply to other cultural settings. The specific sociocultural environment, where maternal identity is highly salient, likely plays a protective role against aesthetic anxieties.
The participants also reported very high baseline confidence in breastfeeding overall. This high overall self-efficacy might buffer the subtle effects of localized body dissatisfaction. A population with lower baseline confidence might show different results.
Future investigations will need to track women longitudinally from early pregnancy through the postpartum period. Researchers suggest that educational programs focusing on the biological utility of the body, rather than its appearance, could help dismantle lingering myths about breast size and milk production for those who still hold them.
The study, “The Association Between Pre-Pregnancy Breast size dissatisfaction and prenatal breastfeeding self-efficacy: A correlational study,” was authored by Kıymet Yeşilçiçek Çalık, Ebru Küçük Erdöl, and Hatice İkra Şan.

Company can be punished for offence carrying imprisonment, term can be replaced by fine: Supreme Court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
21:58:58 UTC
06:58:58 KST

NEW DELHI: A company having no physical body cannot be imprisoned and having no mind cannot possess mens rea (guilty mind), which is essential for conviction in a criminal case. So can a firm be convicted and punished?SC Monday answered the tricky questions by holding that a company can be convicted even when it cannot have a guilty mind of its own and can also be punished, though the punishment of a jail term can be substituted by a fine.A bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and Manoj Misra said there is a need to bring a law for corporate criminal liability but said the issue comes within the legislature's prerogative and it cannot be done by a court. It held that a company is not rendered immune to prosecution merely because the offence carries a mandatory sentence of imprisonment. Referring to a constitution bench ruling, the bench said a judicial discretion to impose a fine alone must be read into such provisions when dealing with juristic persons."The position under Indian law is thus clear that a corporation can be prosecuted for an offence notwithstanding that it carries a mandatory sentence of imprisonment or requires proof of mens rea. It appears that a corporation cannot be prosecuted only where the offence is punishable with imprisonment alone, or where the offence, by its nature, requires personal malicious intent, such that it is incapable of commission by a corporation at all," the bench said.
SC passed the order on a plea by Sanofi India Ltd which said a prosecution against a corporation like it, for an offence requiring mens rea, is maintainable only where a natural person has been identified and arraigned as an accused alongside it. It said that corporations alone cannot be convicted and pleaded that proceedings against it should be quashed. Rejecting the plea of the company, the bench said non-identification of the natural person does not, by itself, render the allegations incapable of disclosing the corporation's role in the offence.The case pertains to the supply of pharmaceutical products by Sanofi India to Bhabha Atomic Research Centre. As per CBI, a BARC officer had conspired with the company to procure medicines at inflated prices and in quantities exceeding the requirement. A case was registered against Sanofi, which challenged its prosecution on the ground that none of its employees had been made accused and a company alone cannot be prosecuted.
"... where the surrounding facts and circumstances, taken as a whole, disclose the possibility that the corporation acted with the requisite mens rea, that disclosure is not defeated merely because no particular individual has been identified as its source. Therefore, the ingredient of mens rea can still be disclosed even where no individual has been identified," the bench said while rejecting the plea of the company.

Britain set to impose trade ban on Israeli West Bank settlements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
21:55:27 UTC
06:55:27 KST

Britain set to impose trade ban on Israeli West Bank settlements
Adam Rasgon and Aaron Boxerman
LONDON - Britain is set to announce wide-ranging economic restrictions targeting Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank as soon as Sept 8, according to seven officials briefed on the measures, in what experts say would be a significant censure of Israeli policy toward Palestinians.
The measures are expected to include a trade ban on goods produced in the settlements, the officials said, speaking on condition of anonymity. Three of the officials said the measures could also include sanctions on companies helping to build settlements.
Israel has become increasingly isolated on the world stage in the aftermath of the devastating war in the Gaza Strip, and international attention has focused on Israel’s tightening grip over the West Bank.
The sanctions come at a time when Israeli extremists have been repeatedly attacking Palestinians, on occasion assailing homes with little intervention by Israeli forces.
Some analysts say Britain’s move could foreshadow decisions by other European countries to impose harder-hitting and broader sanctions.
While the details are still unclear, a British product ban would likely have a limited impact on the US$8 billion (S$10 billion) in annual trade between the countries, given that goods made in Israeli settlements are only a small fraction of that amount. But the measures go well beyond previous British sanctions related to the West Bank, which targeted some extremist Israeli settlers and two far-right ministers.
Gideon Saar, the Israeli foreign minister, said last week that “Israel will act” against any new British sanctions, without elaborating. The Israeli foreign ministry did not respond to a request for comment on Sept 7. The British Foreign Office declined to comment.
Britain, a longtime ally of Israel, has long condemned Israeli settlements in the West Bank, which are widely considered illegal under international law, saying they undermined the possibility of a future Palestinian state. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has shrugged off international criticism and promoted building more settlements at a breakneck pace.
Israel has occupied the West Bank since 1967. About 3 million Palestinians live in the territory alongside some 500,000 Israelis. Their exports include kosher wine, produce, plastics and other products.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham entered office in July pledging a tougher stance on Israel over the war in Gaza. NYTIMES
- This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

China calls for ties with Mexico free of outside influence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
21:50:29 UTC
06:50:29 KST

Faisal Mahmud
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
China’s foreign minister said Monday that relations between China and Mexico should remain free from third-party influence while urging closer political and economic cooperation with the Latin American country.
Wang Yi made the remarks during talks in Beijing with Mexican Foreign Minister Juan Ramon de la Fuente Velasco, according to the Chinese Foreign Ministry.
“China-Mexico relations do not target any third party, nor should they be affected by any third party,” Wang said.
Velasco is on his first official visit to China since becoming foreign minister in April, according to the ministry.
Wang said Beijing supports Mexico in maintaining independence, sovereignty and security and opposes external interference.
He called for stronger high-level exchanges, greater political trust and deeper cooperation across various sectors.
Velasco reaffirmed Mexico’s adherence to the one-China principle and UN General Assembly Resolution 2758, while pledging to expand practical cooperation with Beijing.
China and Mexico established diplomatic relations on Feb. 14, 1972 and upgraded their relationship to a comprehensive strategic partnership in 2013.
China is Mexico's second-largest trading partner globally, while Mexico serves as China's second-largest trading partner in Latin America, trailing only Brazil.
Bilateral trade reached $109.38 billion in 2025, including $89.16 billion in Chinese exports to Mexico, according to Chinese customs figures cited by the Foreign Ministry.
