Military
Ukraine's new top commander is pushing to unwind a Soviet-inherited command model mid-war. He wants combat-tested sergeants to have real authority. Ukraine inherited a system where officers decided everything and sergeants were senior soldiers with no ladder of their own.
Russia deploys missile brigade to Belarus as fears grow over new threat to Kyiv. The move comes as Russia steps up aerial attacks on Kyiv from the north and Belarus allows Moscow to use its territory to help guide strikes against Ukrainian targets.
Some ten robot boats. Five hundred Russian air sorties. One very lopsided hunt. Missions that once took a night now stretch to five days, and Russia keeps its fleet hidden, a naval drone unit commander says.
Ukrainian drones took Ryazan's blending unit after knocking out two of its four crude units. Satellite imagery in August showed half the plant's primary distillation capacity already out of action.
Ukraine's drone forces say they hit 58,465 Russian targets in August, nearly 1,900 a day. Three named campaigns did the strategic damage. Most of the volume is small front-line hits.
Intelligence and technology
Ukrainian AI targeting module placed third among 60-plus entries in NATO contest. NATO and Ukraine ran the challenge through their first jointly staffed body.
Ukrainian university and the Flamingo missile-maker opened an engineering course. On the first try, zero of 150 passed. Even students who scored well on the university entrance exam flunked the physics round.

China calls itself neutral—but its fiber ends up in the drones that hit Ukraine. The papers, reviewed by Western governments, trace drone-grade material straight from a Chinese state firm to a sanctioned Russian plant.

Humanitarian and social impact

"Now on the 1,657th day": Ukraine's crews restored power to over 900,000 homes last week as Russia keeps striking grid before winter. Crews brought it back to 596 settlements, most of them in Odesa and Donetsk.
Kyiv stockpiles food and water as Russia's new aerial tactics threaten a brutal winter. Russia has already targeted food storage around Kyiv, while Ukraine's limited air defenses struggle to stop ballistic missiles and faster drones.
Political and legal developments

Arab committee calls for ‘deterrent’ measures against Israeli attacks in Jerusalem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
21:42:29 UTC
06:42:29 KST

Laith Al-jnaidi and Lina Altawell
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
The Arab Ministerial Committee on Jerusalem called on Monday for "restrictive and deterrent measures" to halt Israeli attacks on holy sites and occupier terrorism.
The committee also welcomed a Qatari initiative to launch a media platform dedicated to monitoring and documenting Israeli violations in the occupied city.
The call came in a statement issued following the 11th meeting of the Arab ministerial committee, which is tasked with international action to confront Israel’s illegal policies and measures in occupied Jerusalem.
Held on the sidelines of the 166th session of the Arab League Council at the ministerial level in Cairo, the meeting was chaired by Jordanian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ayman Safadi, with the participation of committee members and Arab League Secretary-General Ahmed Aboul Gheit.
The committee agreed to “strengthen Arab efforts and diplomatic contacts with influential international parties to push for restrictive and deterrent measures to stop attacks on holy sites and occupier terrorism.”
Platform to document violations
The committee welcomed Qatar’s initiative to launch a “sustainable institutional mechanism”—including a media platform—to monitor, document, and expose Israeli violations against holy sites and worshippers while highlighting their consequences.
It tasked the Arab League General Secretariat, in coordination with member states, with implementing the mechanism, defining its operational methods, and identifying funding sources.
Additionally, the committee called for a coordinated Arab and international diplomatic and media campaign to expose Israeli violations in Jerusalem and the broader occupied Palestinian territories, mobilizing international pressure to stop them.
Arab–Islamic action
The committee agreed to intensify efforts within the international community, particularly the UN Security Council, to rally support for requiring Israel to halt its violations against Islamic and Christian holy sites and respect the historical and legal status quo.
It also emphasized the need for continued collaboration with regional and international organizations to document Israeli breaches of international law and international humanitarian law in Jerusalem and at its holy sites.
-Condemnation of the E1 settlement Plan
The committee strongly condemned Israeli authorities for issuing tenders to build 1,234 illegal settlement units under the E1 plan east of occupied Jerusalem.
It warned that the plan would sever geographic continuity between the northern and southern areas of the occupied West Bank, isolate East Jerusalem from its Palestinian surroundings, and undermine the possibility of establishing an “independent, viable, and geographically contiguous” Palestinian state.
Israeli authorities issued the tenders on August 18 as part of the broader E1 project, which encompasses roughly 3,400 settlement units in the area between East Jerusalem and the Ma’ale Adumim settlement. The plan has drawn widespread international opposition due to its severe impact on West Bank territorial continuity.
Raid on UNRWA center
The committee also condemned the raiding and evacuation of the Qalandia Training Center—affiliated with UNRWA, the UN agency for Palestinian refugees—in occupied Jerusalem by Israeli authorities.
It described the action as a “dangerous escalation and a flagrant breach of international law,” as well as a violation of the immunities and privileges granted to UN organizations. The committee firmly rejected the “systematic Israeli campaign” targeting UNRWA’s presence and operations.
On August 25, Israeli forces raided the facility and removed its staff, with Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir announcing that authorities had initiated the evacuation process. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu stated that the action was carried out to enforce domestic legislation regarding UNRWA.
The Qalandia Training Center is one of the oldest vocational training facilities operated by the agency.
Al-Aqsa Mosque and Hashemite custodianship
Regarding the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound, the committee condemned the “unprecedented escalation” of Israeli violations aimed at altering the site's historical and legal status quo.
The committee reiterated that the Al-Aqsa Mosque / Al-Haram Al-Sharif, encompassing its entire 144-dunum area, is “a place of worship exclusively for Muslims.”
It also underlined the significance of the historical Hashemite custodianship over Islamic and Christian holy sites in Jerusalem in safeguarding the locations and preserving their identity and historical status.
The Arab Ministerial Committee on Jerusalem was established in May 2021 by a decision of the Arab League Council to engage permanent members of the UN Security Council and other influential nations to counter Israeli policies in occupied Jerusalem.

Key Event
Westpac forecasts RBA rate hike in November to 4.6%
Westpac has become the last of the big four banks to change its interest rate prediction and is now forecasting a rate hike at the RBA's November meeting.
The bank had previously expected that the RBA's next move would be down, but chief economist Luci Ellis says the data is now telling a different story.
"The likelihood of an additional rate hike has risen enough to make a November rate hike (+25bp to 4.6%) the base case again," she said.
"The main reasons for the shift are the growing evidence of a more resilient household sector, and a larger-than-expected impetus from the spillovers from the data centre boom.
"Although the housing market is looking weaker than our previously published forecasts, its impact on consumer spending is more than offset by the wider boost coming from a globally-driven surge in tech-related spending.
"An unprecedented pipeline of investment in data centres and associated renewable electricity generation and distribution is expected to drive business investment and so GDP growth – but also limit the pace of disinflation."
A former assistant economic governor at the RBA, Ms Ellis added that it was unlikely the central bank would lift rates in September and would instead wait until the November meeting after more data landed.
Westpac however has not changed its forecasted timing for rate cuts, with three cuts of 0.25 percentage points beginning in August 2027.

There's a reason economics is known as the dismal science, Josh.
To paraphrase a quote from the 2001 DreamWorks classic Shrek, the economy is like an onion — it has layers.
An economy contains a lot of moving parts, and those parts change all the time, so naturally the various economic indicators change as well.
It's also worth pointing out that these are just different indicators being put out by the various big banks, so it's not unusual they say slightly different things. Different economists have different opinions and subscribe to different schools of thought, and that's perfectly normal.

In between those data points we're looking at other indicators to get a better look at how those economic layers are evolving.
It's complicated for sure — but we're here to try and help make sense of it all.

Key Event
Choosi misled consumers on insurance comparison services, court finds
Insurance comparison provider Choosi misled customers through its insurance comparison services, the Federal Court has ruled.
Last year, corporate regulator ASIC announced it was suing Choosi, alleging it had misled Australians by claiming to compare a range of funeral and life insurers.
ASIC alleged that Choosi only compared policies from insurer Hannover, which had paid Choosi about $61 million in commissions to advertise its products since 2019.
All up, ASIC alleged that 4,225 Hannover funeral insurance policies and 9,478 Hannover life insurance policies were sold through Choosi's website between July 1, 2019 and November 30, 2024.
The Federal Court found Choosi's website conveyed that it compared products from a range of funeral and life insurers.
"Through the Choosi Website, and each of the impugned advertising materials, Choosi falsely gave consumers the impression that its Comparison Service compared policies from a broader range of insurers than it in fact did," the judgment by Justice Anderson said.
ASIC boss Sarah Court said the ruling sent a strong message to businesses that they must be upfront and transparent with Australians.
"Consumers deserve clear and accurate information about how comparison services operate and the products they do, or do not, compare," she said.
"Businesses cannot create the impression that they offer consumers genuine choice from a range of products when that choice does not exist."
A spokesperson for Choosi said the company has already made changes to its website and advertising after ASIC first raised the concerns.
"Having now received the judgment, we will undertake that exercise again to ensure that it addresses any further issues identified by the Court," they said in a statement.
The case will return to court at a later date to determine potential penalties.

Key Event
NAB warns of 'slowing growth' as business conditions drop
The latest NAB monthly business survey has also been released today, with businesses seeing a drop in both confidence and conditions.
In August, business confidence fell by 2 points to -8 index points — putting it 13 points below its long-run average of +5 index points.
Business conditions fell by 5 points to -1 index points, making it the first time in six years it's been in negative territory and is well below its long-run average of +6 index points.
So what's behind the drop in business confidence? NAB says it's all to do with ongoing global uncertainty, the volatility in oil prices and continued cost pressures.
The fall in business conditions was broad-based across industries, and NAB puts it down to a 10-point fall in profitability and 5-point fall in trading conditions, putting both at new post-COVID lows.
Interestingly, the decline in profitability is at odds with the employment indicator captured in the report.
"The divergence between the employment index and the profitability index is unusual, and unlikely to be sustained," the report said.
"Should the profitability index remain at depressed levels, we would expect weaker employment outcomes to follow."
The report also noted that cost and price growth measures were broadly unchanged last month, but are still higher than their long-run averages.
"Overall, the key signals from this month's survey are slowing growth amid a backdrop of persistence in cost and price pressures."
In other words, it all makes for a pretty grim summary.

Key Event
Sharp fall in consumer sentiment on fuel prices and rate hike fears
The latest Westpac-Melbourne Institute consumer sentiment index for September has just been published, and it's confirmed what a lot of people are feeling — pretty pessimistic.
The index declined sharply by 5.2% to 84.4 points in September, down from 88.9 in August.
"The falls takes sentiment back towards the deeply pessimistic levels seen earlier in the year," notes Matthew Hassan, Westpac's head of Australian Macro-Forecasting.
He said both fuel prices and the prospect of higher interest rates appear to be driving the decline in sentiment.
"Local pump prices have lifted back above $2/litre for the first time since April, reflecting higher global energy prices and the end of the temporary halving in fuel excise tax," he said.
"Meanwhile, a stronger than expected monthly CPI read in July has stoked fears that the RBA will raise interest rates further in coming months. This has weighed on consumer expectations for finances and the economy.
"It has likely also added to unease about the continued weakening in housing markets."
Other key points from the survey include:
- Nearly two-thirds of consumers are now expecting mortgage rates to rise
- Consumers are feeling uneasy about jobs, particularly those working in construction and hospitality
- The housing market downturn is starting to weigh on the sentiment of homeowners
- Homebuyer sentiment has declined too, but expectations on prices are steady

BERLIN, September 8. /TASS/. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has stated that he does not intend to change his governing coalition’s policy toward Russia or its support for Ukraine, despite the decisive victory of the Alternative for Germany party and growing support for opposition forces in the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament election.
"I will not retreat one millimeter from my fundamental conviction that we must defend our freedom, including against Russia. I will probably have to explain this much more often and much more intensely," Merz said at a press conference in Berlin. He also pledged to continue supporting Ukraine.
The German chancellor also addressed the recent high-profile incident involving the discovery of a drone at Leipzig/Halle Airport. Responding to criticism from politicians who considered the public accusations premature, Merz stressed that he had deliberately decided to promptly inform the public about the results of the investigation. "Some may consider this tactically wrong. But I did not want to wait any longer to share this information with the public, along with the conclusions to be drawn from it. I will act in exactly the same way in the future," the German chancellor emphasized.
On September 1, the German government officially blamed Russia for the drone incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport in early August and announced the termination of operations at the Russian House, the closure of Moscow’s Consulate General in Bonn and other measures. Russian Ambassador to Germany Sergey Nechayev firmly rejected all accusations made by Berlin, calling them unfounded and absurd. The diplomat stated that Russian House employees must leave Germany within seven days.
Russian President Vladimir Putin earlier pointed out that Germany’s new anti-Russian decisions, taken under the pretext of the drone incident at Leipzig Airport, were another grave mistake by the German authorities, running counter to the interests of their people. In his view, these decisions are linked to Germany’s domestic political situation and, in particular, Merz’s difficult position.
The Saxony-Anhalt state parliament election was held on September 6. According to preliminary official results, the Alternative for Germany party won a decisive victory with 43.8% of the vote. The German chancellor’s Christian Democratic Union of Germany came in second, losing more than half of its support compared with 2021. The Christian Democrats received only 17.2% of the vote, their worst result in Saxony-Anhalt. The Social Democratic Party of Germany came third with 9.3% of the vote, followed by the Greens with 8.9% and the Left Party with 8.6%. The BSW party of Sahra Wagenknecht also entered the state parliament with 5.3%.

Israel intensifies south Lebanon strikes, killing 13 after weeks-long lull

Israel said it would continue targeting Iran-backed Hezbollah over alleged ceasefire violations. Hezbollah has not commented on the strikes.
Israel conducted a wave of airstrikes in south Lebanon, killing 13 people including women and children, the Lebanese health ministry said on Monday, in an intensification of violence after a weeks-long lull.
Israel's military vowed to continue targeting Hezbollah, accusing the Iran-backed militants of repeated violations of a ceasefire in place since June.
Hezbollah has not commented on the threat, or on the escalation in strikes seen in recent days.
Israel hit swathes of south Lebanon hard during the Middle East war that erupted with joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran, and its forces continue to occupy what it calls a "security zone".
One of the overnight strikes hit a building in the town of Kfar Rumman, killing 11 people, including two children and four women.
Another attack in the same town killed a rescuer and wounded another, according to the Lebanese health ministry.
Read moreIsrael warns of 'full-scale war' if Palestinian Authority launches Oct. 7-style attack
A later strike on Rihan, also in the south but further from the border with Israel, killed one person, while a strike on the city of Nabatieh wounded nine including two children and three women.
Israel has been intensifying strikes in the southern Nabatieh area after saying on Thursday that it had seized the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge from Hezbollah, a claim the Iran-backed group has not commented on.
The Israeli military in a statement said it had struck Hezbollah "infrastructure sites" across southern Lebanon after the launch of two explosive drones towards its troops, as well as "several terrorists" it said were transferring weapons.

In a separate statement, it said it killed a Hezbollah member in the area of the Beaufort fortress who opened fire on its troops from inside a building, and that "during the close-quarters encounter, two IDF soldiers were lightly injured".
School books in the rubble
Fighting in Lebanon, which erupted in March after Hezbollah targeted Israel in support of Iran, had decreased since a June memorandum of understanding between Washington and Tehran on the wider Middle East war and an Israel-Lebanon framework agreement later that month.
On Monday, Israel's foreign ministry accused Hezbollah of "repeated drone attacks" and "attempting to rebuild its military capabilities in southern Lebanon".
The ministry said Hezbollah had violated the ceasefire agreement between Lebanon and Israel that includes disarmament of the group.
The rescuer who was killed was just 18 years old, according to his civil defence organisation which is affiliated with the Amal movement, a political ally of Hezbollah.

Rescue teams were searching the debris on Monday morning for other victims.

German industrial output falls 1.1 pct in July, dragged down by auto sector
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08

06:31:45 KST

BERLIN, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- Germany's industrial production fell 1.1 percent in July from the previous month, official data showed Monday, marking a setback at the start of the third quarter after output had picked up earlier this year.
The decline was mainly driven by a sharp drop in the automotive industry, where production fell 9.2 percent month-on-month, according to the Federal Statistical Office.
Citing the German Association of the Automotive Industry (VDA), the office said a multi-week production shutdown during the conversion of a plant for electric vehicle manufacturing was among the main reasons for the decline.
More broadly, Germany's auto industry remains under pressure. Passenger car production in the first seven months of the year was still 15 percent below the level recorded in the same period of 2019, according to the VDA.
Germany's economy ministry said on Monday that industrial production had remained relatively resilient in the second quarter despite higher energy prices, but the effects of the ongoing conflict in the Middle East appeared to be increasingly weighing on output.
Restrictions on Rhine shipping due to low water levels since mid-June may also have dampened production during the summer months, the ministry said, adding that key industries such as automotive manufacturing and mechanical engineering remained under growing pressure.
"Overall, the prospects for a broader recovery in industrial activity over the rest of the year remain subdued," it noted.
Carsten Brzeski, global head of macro at ING Research, said in an analysis the latest data underscored the fragility of Germany's cyclical economic rebound.
Brzeski said the government still lacked key elements of the fundamental reforms needed to put Europe's largest economy back on a sustainable growth path, including a clear plan for affordable energy and tax cuts to boost domestic demand and investment. ■

BRATISLAVA, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- Economic affairs committee representatives from the parliaments of the Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland and Slovakia on Monday called for closer integration of industry, energy and emerging technologies, particularly artificial intelligence (AI), to strengthen the region's economic competitiveness.
"We see artificial intelligence as a major opportunity to boost productivity and modernize our economies. However, its use must be safe, transparent, responsible and human-centred," declared Robert Puci, who chairs the Slovak Parliament's Economic Affairs Committee.
Representatives from the four countries, members the Visegrad Four (V4), agreed at a meeting in Kosice in eastern Slovakia that their strong industrial bases should be increasingly combined with research, innovation, digitalization and AI to maintain competitiveness.
Puci, whose country is holding the presidency of V4, noted that the development of AI is also increasing demand for computing capacity, digital infrastructure and secure and resilient energy supplies. "It is also important that the technological transformation benefits not only large companies but also small- and medium-sized enterprises. At the same time, we must invest in education, digital skills and preparing people for a changing labour market," he said.
At the European level, the V4 countries aim to coordinate their positions more closely on AI and competitiveness policies, so that the needs and specific characteristics of the region are better reflected in EU policymaking, Puci said.
Ivan Adamec, chairman of the Czech Parliament's Economic Affairs Committee, said the Czech side values the Visegrad grouping and its common interests, stressing the importance of joint action at the European level. "If we manage to maintain and drive the Visegrad Four as we did at today's meeting, so that it works like a well-oiled machine, Europe cannot overlook us on the issues we discussed here," he said. ■

====================================================================================================

Letter from Mideast: Handmade memories at a Ramallah market
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
05:31:04 CST
06:31:04 KST

by Xinhua writer Zhao Weihong
RAMALLAH, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- One summer evening, I went for a stroll down Issa Ziada Street in the old city of Ramallah. The rich aroma of coffee, the herbal scent of handmade soap, and the smell of freshly baked bread filled the air.
Yet it was not those inviting aromas that stopped me, but some crimson and indigo threads -- fine as veins, dense as memory, stitched into cloth by hands that refused to forget.
Ayyam Tamimi, a 50‑year‑old embroiderer from East Jerusalem, picked up a panel of fabric and gently ran her fingers over the stitches.
"This is Tatreez," Tamimi said softly.
Tatreez, the traditional Palestinian art of cross-stitch embroidery, gained international recognition in 2021, when the UN Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization inscribed it on its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
Tamimi told me that she had spent over 20 years mastering the craft, first as a seamstress, then as a shop owner, and finally as the founder of her own brand.
"This is the heritage passed down from our ancestors," she said, her eyes tracing the patterns as if reading a landscape she could no longer return to.
"We Palestinian women stitched the landscapes of our occupied villages into cloth," she said. "The villages did not survive. The cloth did. We may not be able to inherit our ancestors' land, but every time I see Tatreez, in homes, at weddings, in shops, I remember where our roots lie."
Beyond Tamimi's stall, the street opens onto a parking lot transformed into four rows of booths. They were part of the Harjeh Market, which reopened this summer after a two-year suspension following the outbreak of the latest Israel-Hamas war in October 2023.
The seasonal market, intended to support Palestinian artisans and small businesses, ran on Fridays during summer and usually hosted about 100 stalls. Here, memory lives on -- stitched into cloth, carried by place names and carved into olive wood.
At a nearby booth, Sameh Abdullah bent down to pick up a placard reading "Jaffa" in both Arabic and English. His grandparents had been forced to flee that city to the West Bank city of al-Bireh in 1948.
Beside him, 30-year-old Mohammad Omar politely asked me not to film him, saying he wanted "to avoid unnecessary trouble."
Omar had driven more than four hours from Tulkarm in the northern West Bank, navigating multiple Israeli military checkpoints that turned what would normally be a 40-minute journey into a half-day trip.
"My goods are often detained at Israeli checkpoints," he said quietly.
For the past 10 years, Omar has sold placards bearing Palestinian place names. Whenever he travels to other cities, he sends them ahead with supply trucks.
"They are afraid," he said, lowering his voice. "Afraid that we will remember the name of every occupied city, every hill, every river."
Violence has continued to escalate across the West Bank. The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs documented more than 1,300 settler attacks causing casualties or property damage in the first seven months of the year, the highest pace on record.
Thousands of olive trees have been burned, cut down, or otherwise vandalised. For Palestinians, these trees are far more than a crop cultivated for millennia and a vital source of livelihood; they are symbols -- quiet and enduring -- of resistance and of home.
At another booth at the Harjeh Market, Aida Al‑Shawa arranged gleaming refrigerator magnets carved from olive wood in the afternoon sun.
"Israeli soldiers and settlers are cutting down and burning olive trees across the West Bank," she said. "So we hold tightly to every trunk and pour our hearts into our work. We want the world to see that this land belongs to us."
Her words echoed what an elderly Palestinian farmer once told me: bulldozers may split an olive trunk, but as long as the roots remain, the tree will grow again.
In Al-Shawa's hands, those roots were transformed into everyday reminders. She told me that she carves the names of places that she believes are being erased and turns them into objects for daily life.
"That way," she said with a smile, "every morning when people open the fridge to get some milk, they catch a glimpse of the homeland they may never return to." ■

====================================================================================================

Finland's largest Viking Age silver coin hoard discovered
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
05:30:58 CST
06:30:58 KST

HELSINKI, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- Finland's largest known Viking Age silver coin hoard has been discovered in the municipality of Sysma, southern Finland, Lahti City Museums said in a press release on Monday.
The hoard dates to the Viking Age, commonly considered to have lasted from 793 to 1066 in European history. It was discovered near the center of Sysma on Sept. 3 by metal-detecting enthusiast Kalle Lappinen, according to the press release.
The site was inspected the following day, and the hoard was recovered under the direction of Esko Tikkala, an archaeologist with Lahti City Museums.
The museum has confirmed it was the largest Viking Age coin hoard discovered in Finland to date.
In addition to silver coins, the hoard contains a fragment of silver used as payment, a silver bracelet, a silver fitting and a silver bead.
The coins and other objects had been placed in two birch-bark containers and buried about 45 centimeters underground between stones. The two containers were about 12 meters apart.
The coins weigh a total of approximately 4.5 kg. As they have yet to be cleaned, separated or counted, their exact weight and number, as well as their more precise dating, will be determined through further research. The museum said the hoard contains thousands of coins.
Previously, Finland's largest known Viking Age coin hoard was one discovered in the municipality of Nousiainen, southwestern Finland, in 1895. It contains about 1,700 coins and other objects weighing a total of approximately 2.2 kg, according to Lahti City Museums.
Lappinen, who has pursued metal detecting for years, told Finnish national broadcaster Yle that the hoard was found at one of his regular search sites, an area that had also been explored by other enthusiasts.
Lappinen said the discovery left him in disbelief, noting that most signals picked up while metal detecting turn out to be rubbish or mineral deposits. He immediately reported the find to the Finnish Heritage Agency, whose experts later excavated the entire hoard.
Lahti City Museums serves as the regional museum authority for the Paijat-Hame region in southern Finland, which includes Sysma. ■

Iran increases gasoline price for its heaviest consumers as economy struggles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
21:30:56 UTC
06:30:56 KST

Breadcrumb
Iran increases gasoline price for its heaviest consumers as economy struggles
Iran early Tuesday introduced a higher price for its heaviest users of gasoline, state media reported, in the latest economic pinch caused by months of war. It’s the second such hike since December.
Such gas price increases can be sensitive and contribute to inflation. An increase in 2019 sparked nationwide protests and a crackdown that reportedly killed over 300 people.
Without specifically mentioning the war with the United States, the government’s announcement cited the “current situation,” adding that the extra money from the price increase will be given to households.
Under the new system, people buying more than their quota of 110 liters (29 gallons) of gasoline a month now must pay 100,000 rials (about 7 cents) per liter, or twice as much as they have been paying since December.
Iran still has some of the world’s lowest gasoline prices, but the price increase adds to daily pressures for many of the country’s more than 90 million people. Already, the currency has been dropping to record lows, and purchasing power has weakened. On Monday, the U.S. dollar was trading at 2.22 million rials.
Keramat Veis Karami, the CEO of the state oil distribution company, on Monday said the new gasoline rate would affect 15% of consumers, the official IRNA news agency reported.
The CEO said consumption reached a record high at 145 million liters (38 million gallons) per day in August, while domestic production capacity was 122 million liters per day. The rest of the supply is imported.
Raising prices can help calm high consumption, which experts have blamed on aging cars and spare parts in Iran as well as insufficient public transportation.
But experts also say increases in gasoline prices will lead to higher inflation in a country that's already struggling with an annual inflation rate of about 67%, according to the country’s statistics center, a government agency.
Cheap gasoline has been viewed for generations as a birthright in Iran, sparking mass demonstrations as far back as 1964, when a price increase forced the shah to put military vehicles on the streets to replace those of striking taxi drivers.

Japan must reckon with how it views foreign workers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
21:30:07 UTC
06:30:07 KST

Japan must reckon with how it views foreign workers
As Japan raises fees for residence permits and tightens the requirements for permanent residency, the effect on long-term settlement warrants attention
Japan will substantially raise its fees for residence permits next month. Depending on the period of stay applied for, renewing or changing one’s residency status could cost as much as ¥75,000 (US$480). The application fee for permanent residency will rise to ¥200,000 from ¥10,000.
The government is also tightening the requirements for permanent residency. Applicants are already expected to be able to support themselves. New criteria proposed include an above-average household income, sufficient projected pension benefits, Japanese-language proficiency, and an understanding of Japanese institutions and rules governing daily life. The changes go beyond a simple revision of administrative fees.
Japan is becoming increasingly dependent on foreign labour. Faced with a shrinking, ageing population and labour shortages, successive governments have expanded the channels through which foreigners can enter and work, while refraining from describing Japan as an immigrant society.
Last year, the number of foreign workers hit another record high, reaching 2.57 million at end October. Although they accounted for only about 3 per cent of the labour force, the Bank of Japan estimates that foreign workers represented more than half of the labour force increase between 2023 and 2024.
Official data showed that last year, manufacturing employed 24.7 per cent of foreign workers, followed by the service sector at 15.2 per cent, wholesale and retail at 13.3 per cent, accommodation and food services at 12.4 per cent, and construction at 8 per cent.
The burden of the higher fees may not be evenly distributed. According to Japan’s 2020 population census, male foreign workers were considerably more likely than Japanese men to be in non-regular employment. Among male employees, excluding company executives, the proportion was about 15 per cent for Japanese nationals, compared with about 53 per cent for Brazilians, 45 per cent for Indonesians and around 40 per cent for Vietnamese, Nepalese and Peruvians.

Estonia strengthens protection against Russian cyberattacks — CPD
Kyiv • UNN
Starting in September, emails from Russian servers and the .ru domain will be sent to the quarantine of Estonia’s government institutions. The number of DDoS attacks on the country has increased to 756.
Estonia is strengthening the cybersecurity of the public sector and restricting incoming emails from Russian servers. This is reported by the Center for Countering Disinformation of the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine (CCD), reports UNN.
Details
It is noted that starting in September, emails from Russian servers and addresses with the ".ru" domain will not be delivered directly to Estonia’s government institutions. Such messages will be automatically redirected to quarantine for additional screening.
Estonian Minister of Justice and Digital Technologies Liisa Pakosta explained that this is necessary to protect government institutions from cyberattacks
It is indicated that Estonia’s decision is linked to the rapid increase in the scale of cyber threats. The number of DDoS attacks in the country increased from 484 in 2023 to 580 in 2024 and 756 in 2025. Pakosta noted that a significant portion of these cyberattacks is linked specifically to Russia.

Ukraine restores external power supply to Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
00:23:00 EEST
06:23:00 KST

Ukraine restores external power supply to Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant
Ukrainian power engineers reconnected the temporarily occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP) to an external power supply on 7 September.
Source: Ukraine's state-owned nuclear energy company Energoatom; Rafael Grossi, Director General of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA)
Quote from Energoatom: "The auxiliary systems of the temporarily occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant were supplied with power from the 330 kV Ferosplavna-1 overhead line on 7 September at 19:02. The plant's current consumption is 11 MW."
Details: Energoatom said that external power had been restored thanks to Ukrainian power engineers and a local ceasefire, which allowed repair work to be carried out.
The IAEA also said the connection was restored following three days of repairs by Ukrainian engineers under the protection of a ceasefire coordinated by the agency.
Grossi noted that it is "a crucial step to help prevent a nuclear accident".
Restoring the external power supply after an outage lasting almost three weeks means that the ZNPP can once again get power to cool its reactors and spent fuel pools, as well as to support other essential nuclear safety and physical protection functions.
Energoatom noted that the ZNPP had been without external power since 20 August, with all of the plant's critical systems supplied by backup diesel generators during that time. The prolonged loss of external power had placed additional strain on the plant's safety systems.
Background: Energoatom previously said that the actual condition of the temporarily occupied ZNPP pointed to a continued erosion of fundamental nuclear safety principles.

Ukraine’s new top commander is pushing to unwind a Soviet-inherited command model mid-war. He wants combat-tested sergeants to have real authority
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
21:17:52 UTC
06:17:52 KST

Ukraine's new top commander wants the army's combat-tested sergeants to have real careers, real authority, and clear paths to promotion — not just a role training recruits. Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi has met the senior sergeants of the force's branches, corps, and command bodies and set concrete steps to reform the sergeant corps, saying most had come straight from combat zones, Texty reported.
The push targets an old weakness. Ukraine inherited its rank system from the Soviet army in 1991 — a centralized model in which officers decided almost everything and sergeants were little more than senior soldiers, with no authority or career ladder of their own. A 2020 reform law began to change that by aligning the system with NATO standards, making the sergeant an independent figure.
Drapatyi, who became commander-in-chief in July 2026 with a mandate to carry that overhaul forward and a reputation for favoring decentralized command, is now pressing it directly.
Sergeants outgrow the training role
The sergeant's job long ago stopped being only about preparing troops, Drapatyi said. Sergeants now settle new arrivals into combat areas, handle supply and equipment, ready personnel for tasks, and command them directly in battle.
"A sergeant was a soldier yesterday. Today, he is a commander who is closest to the soldier and sees the real state of the unit on the ground best of all," Drapatyi said.
Drapatyi assigns the reform tasks
The meeting worked through the structure of the corps, the split of responsibility between sergeants and officers, training, appointments, and pay. For each, Drapatyi continued, he set specific tasks, defined next steps, and named the people responsible.
"We cannot build a modern, combat-capable sergeant corps on old approaches," Drapatyi said.
He believes that a sergeant's combat experience should turn into authority, professional development, responsibility, and a real say in how troops are trained and led.

Oil prices surge as US-Iran strikes intensify in Strait of Hormuz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
21:17:12 UTC
06:17:12 KST

Oil prices surge as US-Iran strikes intensify in Strait of Hormuz
Oil prices push China towards EVs and other trading partners as Americans face higher prices ahead of the US midterm elections.
Oil prices are rising to nearly a six-week high amid a wave of strikes between the United States and Iran in the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of the world’s oil supply travels during peacetime.
On Monday, Brent oil futures, the global benchmark, rose to hover around $97 a barrel — up 9 percent over the last five days and 19 percent over the last month. Monday’s market moves are approaching the highest point since July 24th, when prices topped $97.93.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Iran war: Why US midterms could be a pivotal moment
- list 2 of 4Diesel price hits all-time high in US amid Iran war woes
- list 3 of 4US imposes sanctions on Turkish bank, prompting legal threat
- list 4 of 4Iran President Pezeshkian calls for unity as US ramps up economic pressure
US West Texas Intermediate crude similarly rose to $92.27 a barrel, up 79 cents, also a near six-week high.
In recent days, strikes escalated in the Strait of Hormuz. The US hit three Iranian oil tankers on Saturday, while Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it had struck three tankers and three US-linked vessels in other areas.
“This is a reflection of continued conflict and exchange of fire. The supply deficits globally are persisting, and there is little end to these shortages,” Rachel Ziemba, an adjunct senior fellow at the Center for a New American Security (CNAS), told Al Jazeera.
On Monday, Saudi Aramco’s Jizan facilities were struck for the second time in the last month, according to reporting from the Financial Times that cited two people familiar with the matter.
“The fact that a Saudi refinery in Jizan was hit, possibly delaying its return to production, didn’t help,” Ziemba added.
Amid increased strikes, there’s less traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, with an average of 10 commodity ships crossing the vital chokepoint each day over the last 10 days, according to Kpler, a data analytics platform.
“Crude went back down to what the pre-war level was in early July. Then it increased again, and then it reduced again, and now it’s increasing again on this weekend’s exchange plus the Aramco attack,” Arif Gasilov, a partner at the Gasilov Group, an energy advisory firm, told Al Jazeera.
“I would say that you might eventually see an inflection point, depending on how long this keeps going on, where a ceasefire doesn’t move the market at all, maybe by just a dollar or two.”
US consumers pinched
US consumers are feeling the impact of heightened oil prices at the petrol pump. The average price for a gallon (3.78 litres) of petrol has jumped 7 cents over the course of a week, reaching $4.15 nationally on Monday, up from $4.08 this time a week ago, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which tracks daily petrol prices.
That’s up from $4.04 this time a month ago and $2.98 from February 28th, when the US and Israel first struck Iran, marking a 39 percent increase since the war began.
Last week, diesel prices hit all-time highs at $5.85 per gallon.
“US diesel prices have never been this high, and now the countdown starts for the trickle-down to everything consumers buy… record diesel will start funnelling down into the economy,” Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, said in a post on the social media platform X.
Prices have continued to climb since, with average prices on Monday topping $5.90 per gallon.
“Markets are pricing in longer disruptions. It continues to be in product markets where the biggest disruptions lie, though, including diesel,” Ziemba added.
Those price gains are weighing on Americans, who have spent an average of $764.59 per household on fuel since the war began. That’s $418.82 more than usual, according to Brown University’s Watson School of International and Public Affairs.
Ahead of the US’s September 5-7 Labor Day weekend, the unofficial end of summer and a popular time for US travel, AAA forecasts showed a 20 percent increase in flight costs compared to the same weekend last year.
Ahead of the midterm elections, the economy is emerging as a key issue for US voters — and a potential warning sign for Republicans. Polls show voters souring on President Donald Trump’s handling of the economy, with his economic approval rating falling to a new low in a recent Financial Times poll. Just 17 percent of Americans approve of his handling of the economy.
An Economist/YouGov poll similarly found that 39 percent of Americans believe Democrats are doing a better job handling the economy, compared with 32 percent who said Republicans are.
China pressures
Southeast and East Asian markets rely more heavily on imports travelling through the Strait of Hormuz directly than the US, but Beijing has moved to insulate itself from the disruption by turning to domestic sources, including its strategic petroleum reserve (SPR).
“China has been managing this situation successfully since the beginning of the war. We know that China has many domestic resources, despite rising oil prices,” John Gong, an economics professor at the University of International Business and Economics, told Al Jazeera.
“China has been conserving its oil and gas consumption for quite some time now. China was prepared for these challenges,” Gong said.
He also stressed that China’s close relations with Russia give Beijing another source of supply, with Moscow able to provide nearly half of China’s daily oil needs.
China has also begun tapping into its SPR while reducing its reliance on imports, as Beijing accelerates a broader shift towards alternative energy sources and vehicles that require little or no oil to operate.
“We have national strategies focused on transitioning to clean energies like solar and green power,” Gong said. “When we look at the vehicles purchased in China, more than 50 percent of cars sold on the Chinese market are electric.”

Russian Gold Imports to Hong Kong Reach Record 100 Tonnes Amid Western Sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
21:13:58 UTC
06:13:58 KST

- Category
- World
Russian Gold Imports to Hong Kong Reach Record 100 Tonnes Amid Western Sanctions
Russian gold shipments to Hong Kong reached a record high of nearly 100 tonnes during the first seven months of 2026, as Western sanctions continue to divert Russian bullion away from traditional financial centers like London and New York, the Financial Times reported on September 7.
Trade data shows that the volume of Russian gold imported by Hong Kong between January and July 2026 was nearly three times higher than during the same period in 2025.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022—when the US and UK prohibited imports of Russian bullion—Hong Kong entities have purchased Russian gold valued at approximately 276 billion Hong Kong dollars ($35 billion), according to the Financial Times. Neither Hong Kong nor mainland China has imposed restrictions on Russian gold imports.
Most of the gold entering Hong Kong eventually moves into mainland China, the world’s largest producer and consumer of bullion. Because mainland China imposes strict import quotas, Chinese buyers routinely purchase and store bullion in Hong Kong, which operates without import restrictions, according to Debajit Saha, an analyst at the London Stock Exchange Group.
The surge in gold exports provides critical financial support for Moscow, the world’s second-largest gold producer, as it relies on commodity trade with China to sustain its wartime economy.
Concurrently, Hong Kong has worked to establish itself as a primary clearing hub for global bullion, piloting a new gold clearing system in July. Recent logistical disruptions in Dubai stemming from war in the Middle East have also driven additional gold trade toward Hong Kong, the Financial Times noted.
The rising volume of Russian bullion passing through Hong Kong presents severe compliance challenges for Western financial institutions. In 2024, the US Treasury sanctioned several Hong Kong-based entities for operating within a Russian gold laundering network.
“Western banks do face a real risk of inadvertent exposure,” Tan Albayrak, a sanctions specialist at law firm Reed Smith, told the Financial Times. “If the transaction chain involves a sanctioned producer, there would be exposure for indirectly dealing with that sanctioned producer.”
The record export volumes to Hong Kong coincide with a historic liquidation of Russia’s domestic reserves. The Central Bank of Russia’s gold holdings had recently fallen to 73.2 million troy ounces—approximately 2,280 tons—by August 1, reaching their lowest level since January 2020.
The reductions totaled roughly 50 tons over the first seven months of the year, dropping the value of the country’s stored gold reserves by $33.7 billion as the central bank liquidates assets to cover escalating federal budget demands.

How did people spend their super during the pandemic?

EU committing ‘harakiri’ – Lavrov
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
21:09:16 UTC
06:09:16 KST

EU committing ‘harakiri’ – Lavrov
The EU is effectively committing “harakiri” by abandoning Russian energy in an attempt to hurt Moscow, Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has said.
Speaking on Monday to students at the Moscow State Institute of International Relations (MGIMO), Russia’s primary college for diplomats, Lavrov argued that European leaders are making their own voters bear the cost of their policies toward Russia.
The EU has committed to phasing out Russian fossil fuels completely by 2027, having drastically reduced Russian oil and gas imports since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in February 2022. Energy costs have risen across much of the bloc, with the US-Israeli war on Iran adding further pressure.
Germany, once considered the EU’s industrial powerhouse, has been particularly affected. Its economy contracted in both 2023 and 2024 – the first back-to-back annual decline in more than two decades – and is forecast to grow by just 0.5% this year.
“Europe is simply committing harakiri and proudly declaring that its people must suffer… for European values,” Lavrov said, referring to the Japanese ritual suicide also known as seppuku.
“Apparently, by ‘European values’ they mean Nazism, burying Nazi criminals with honors, and banning the Russian language, Russian-language education, Russian culture and media, as well as the canonical Ukrainian Orthodox Church,” he added.
Lavrov argued that the EU’s attempt to pressure Moscow has failed to deprive Russia of customers. “There’s no panic here whatsoever. We’ve always had plenty of buyers,” he said, adding that Russian exporters have shifted toward “those who are more reliable.”
“If Europe wants to pay $800-900 per thousand cubic meters for American liquefied natural gas, what can we do about it?” he asked.
Russia has increasingly redirected its energy exports toward Asia amid Western sanctions. Its seaborne crude shipments to China hit a record 1.86 million barrels per day in January, up 46% year-on-year. Russia has also remained India’s largest oil supplier, selling around 2.1 million bpd in August, or 45% of the country’s imports, according to maritime intelligence firm Kpler.
Lavrov said the shift should not be viewed as a sudden “pivot to the East,” arguing that Russia has long cultivated economic ties in both directions.
Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico, who survived an assassination attempt by a pro-Ukraine activist, similarly described the EU as a “suicide ship” in April, accusing Brussels of “ideological blindness and incompetence.”
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen acknowledged last month that the loss of cheap energy imports had dealt a major blow to the bloc’s economy. Lavrov argued that the policies demonstrate that European leaders “don’t think about the voters that brought them to power.”

Latvia bans books from Russia, Belarus over ‘war propaganda’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
21:05:22 UTC
06:05:22 KST

Latvia bans books from Russia, Belarus over ‘war propaganda’
RIGA - Latvia has banned the import of books, newspapers and printing products from Russia and Belarus, citing “disinformation and war propaganda”, its foreign ministry told AFP on Sept 7.
“The import ban is intended to protect Latvia’s security interests and further reduce economic ties with Russia and Belarus, which continue to wage and support (the) war of aggression against Ukraine,” the ministry said.
Latvia, a member of NATO and the European Union, is an ally of Ukraine and both share borders with Russia and Belarus.
It has faced what it describes at “hybrid attacks” from Moscow since the beginning of the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Amid cyberattacks, drone incursions and manufactured disinformation, the former Soviet-occupied republic has heavily invested in its security in recent years, believing it might be one of Moscow’s next targets.
Latvia has a significant minority of Russian speakers and about a quarter of the population are ethnic Russians, according to the most recent data from its official statistics portal.
The ban, which came into effect on Sept 1, is the first of its kind to be imposed on Russian consumer goods in Europe.
It also affects other consumer goods, including clothes, toys and sports equipment.
According to the Latvian government, the move is aimed at “strengthening the resilience of society and reducing vulnerabilities in the information space”.
Overall imports from Russia and Belarus have decreased by around 91 per cent since the start of the war in Ukraine, the foreign ministry said.
But books and printed materials still “constituted one of the largest remaining consumer goods import categories from Russia”, it added.
The Latvian transport ministry has also submitted proposals to amend the country’s transport law, which would ban regular and irregular passenger buses from Latvia to Russia and Belarus, as well as transit through Latvian territory to the two countries.
“The Ministry of Transport will continue to assess aspects of security, economic, and international obligations, seeking a coordinated solution at the Baltic and European Union levels,” it wrote in a statement.
Riga had previously removed VAT incentives for domestic Russian-language publishing and pushed to reduce Russian language in education, citing the need to counter Moscow’s interference and to better integrate Russian speakers.
In May, Russia announced plans to local media to take the Baltic states – Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia – to the International Court of Justice over alleged rights violations against Russian speakers.
The Baltic states have disputed such claims, instead accusing Moscow of using the Russian ethnic minority – which ballooned during the Soviet occupation of the three countries from the 1940s until the mid-1990s – to inflame tensions. AFP

Extreme poverty grips 94% of Cubans as food crisis deepens: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
21:02:00 UTC
06:02:00 KST

Nearly 94% of Cubans are living in extreme poverty, while eight in 10 have skipped at least one meal because they lacked food or money, according to a new report by the Madrid-based Cuban Observatory for Human Rights.
The percentage of Cubans living in extreme poverty rose from 89% in 2025 to 94% this year, according to the report, which uses the World Bank's extreme poverty threshold as a reference.
The study found that 68% of respondents reported monthly household incomes below 20,000 Cuban pesos, equivalent to about $30.
Power outages were identified as the country's most urgent social problem, followed by food shortages, the cost of living, health care, salaries, and insecurity.
The report also highlighted deteriorating housing conditions, saying nearly half of respondents live in homes requiring repairs. Some 25% said their homes need urgent repairs, while 7% reported living in housing at risk of collapse.
The deterioration of public services was another major concern. Respondents gave particularly negative assessments of the electricity system, followed by garbage collection, telephone and internet services, sewage systems, and health care.
The report said 95% of respondents view the government's management negatively or very negatively, while 84% said they did not trust the economic measures implemented by authorities to address the crisis.
Half of those surveyed said they expect a favorable and significant change for the Cuban people within the next six months.
Meanwhile, 76% said they want future changes to include both political and economic reforms, while 9% favored economic changes only.
Yaxys Cires, director of strategy at the Spanish-based group, described the findings as evidence of the "growing impoverishment of Cuban families."
The survey was conducted between June 27 and July 29 across all 15 Cuban provinces and 79 municipalities, using face-to-face interviews assisted by mobile devices.
The sample was stratified by place of residence, gender, age, and racial group, according to the group.

Russia burns occupied Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant’s last-resort generators as everyday power, Ukraine says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
20:58:41 UTC
05:58:41 KST

The Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant lost the 330-kV Ferosplavna-1 line—which the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) called the plant's only remaining off-site power line—on 20 August and has since run on emergency diesel generators, Ukraine's state nuclear operator Energoatom said on 6 September. A day earlier, the IAEA said the plant's diesel reserves were under increasing strain and warned it could lose all power within days unless external power was restored or fuel deliveries continued.
The Zaporizhzhia plant has been under Russian control since March 2022, when Russian forces seized the facility during the invasion. The plant stopped generating electricity in September 2022, and all six reactors have been in cold shutdown since April 2024, leaving the plant dependent on external or backup power for cooling and other essential safety systems. Repeated damage to the plant's external power connections has forced it onto emergency diesel generators multiple times, including during a month-long loss of off-site power in 2025.
How much diesel the Zaporizhzhia plant has left
The plant's most recent delivery to its off-site fuel farm took place in March, and the next one, set for May, is still held up by military activity, the IAEA reported on 20 August. At that point, the plant reported having more than 10 days of diesel available for its emergency generators.
By 29 August, the plant was down to about 10 days of diesel—its minimum regulatory reserve—and IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi said that was roughly how long it had left without restored power or more deliveries. Several dozen tons reached the plant on 27 and 28 August, but a week later the agency shortened the warning to within days, with the plant down to two generators and running its cooling pumps on and off to save fuel. No nuclear plant should have to throttle its essential cooling systems to conserve diesel, Grossi said.
How the plant lost its last external power line
Ferosplavna-1 is a backup line from the thermal plant next door, one of 10 the IAEA counted before the war. The main 750-kV Dniprovska line failed on 24 March. Technicians repaired it under a June ceasefire, but it has never been switched back on, because a substation more than 100 kilometers away was badly damaged. Ferosplavna-1 has carried the plant alone since. It went down on 26 April for the 15th time since 2022, by both counts, and cut out repeatedly around a June attack on the thermal plant. It went dead on 20 August—the 27th loss by Energoatom's count, the 26th by the IAEA's.
Ukrainian technicians began repairs on 5 September under a local ceasefire the IAEA brokered, with a few days' work expected. The line was still dead on 7 September, its 19th day without off-site power, the plant's Russian-installed management claimed to Russian media. Fixing it may not bring the power back anyway, Rosatom chief Aleksei Likhachev claimed the same day, blaming Ukrainian inaction for the other line still sitting repaired and unconnected—which the IAEA puts down to the wrecked substation.
Energoatom's assessment of the generator risk and Russian claims
Russian forces run the plant's emergency generators as everyday power, outside the conditions they were built for, Energoatom said on 6 September. Weeks of continuous running raise the risk of several backups failing together, and constant starts under load make the systems that start them likelier to fail. Even in cold shutdown, a blackout would threaten control of the safety systems and the spent fuel pools, and the plant is already in gross violation of its safe-operation limits, it said. Only a Russian pullout, military and civilian, and a handover back to Energoatom would guarantee safe operation, the company said, which also wants both grid lines back.
The plant has enough fuel for its generators but cannot restock while the access roads are shelled, the plant's Russian-installed management claimed to Russia's state news agency TASS on 31 August. TASS blamed Ukrainian forces for the shelling, though the quoted remarks named no one.

US President Donald Trump on Monday warned Canadian aircraft maker Bombardier that it would no longer be permitted to sell in the US unless it began manufacturing in the country, in what is the latest episode in a growing trade war between Washington and Ottawa.
In a post on his Truth Social account, Trump wrote: "No more selling Bombardier in the United States!"
"Their products aren’t good enough!" he continued, while claiming that the company lived off "American buyers, American companies, American airports, and American service."
He added: "If they want our market, they must build here, and stop treating America like a 'piggybank.'"
It's not the first time the president has had the company in his sights.
In January, he threatened to hit Canada with a 50% tariff on all aircraft sold to the US and to decertify Bombardier aircraft as he raged against what he said was Canada's refusal to certify certain US-made Gulfstream planes.
Bombardier was founded in 1942 by Joseph-Armand Bombardier to market and sell his snowmobiles and later other "snow-going vehicles." The firm moved into the aerospace sector in 1986 after purchasing Canadair, which built the "Challenger" business jet.
Trade war
It comes amid a growing trade battle between the US and Canada.
Their ongoing tit-for-tat dispute reignited last month after talks over a deal to avoid hefty duties on some Canadian goods collapsed as both sides accused each other of trying to implement last-minute changes.
Following the breakdown in negotiations, 50% US duties impacting around C$28 billion worth of Canadian goods came into effect in late August, prompting Ottawa to announce retaliatory measures on roughly C$27.6 billion in imports from the US.
The US tariffs affect products ranging from hockey sticks to wine to cement.
The Canadian government said its retaliatory levies, which are due to come into effect on Tuesday, would be concentrated in sectors such as steel and aluminium, appliances, dairy, agricultural equipment, plastics, pulp and paper and electronics.

“Now on the 1,657th day”: Ukraine’s crews restored power to over 900,000 homes last week as Russia keeps striking grid before winter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
20:51:02 UTC
05:51:02 KST

Russian strikes cut power to nearly a million Ukrainian families across four oblasts last week. Ukraine's largest private energy company, DTEK, brought it back, fully or partly restoring electricity to 596 settlements in Donetsk, Odesa, Dnipropetrovsk, and Kyiv oblasts between 31 August and 6 September, the company said.
Russia is hammering Ukraine's power grid again as the cold season nears, and the country's winter-resilience plans were less than half complete at the start of September.
Odesa and Donetsk absorb the worst
Most of the week's work was in Odesa Oblast, which Russia has been striking without pause. Ukrainian crews there returned power to more than 366,000 families, DTEK said.
Much of that damage followed a massed missile-and-drone strike on the region's main energy facilities on 2 September, after which national operator Ukrenergo imposed temporary grid limits to keep damaged equipment from overloading.
Donetsk Oblast came close behind, with power restored to nearly 360,000 homes despite what the company called an extremely difficult situation for its repair teams. In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, crews reconnected almost 172,000 homes, and in Kyiv Oblast nearly 9,000 more.
Strikes keep cutting the grid
The reconnections are happening under continued fire. Russia keeps attacking energy sites in Odesa and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts, damaging lines faster than they can be fully secured. DTEK crews can only begin repairs once the military and emergency services have cleared access to the damaged equipment.
"Russia keeps attacking our energy system. Despite everything, we keep working and restoring power — now on the 1,657th day," said Alina Bondarenko, chief executive of DTEK Grids.
Winter sharpens the threat
The timing is the danger. Ukraine has until the heating season to shore up a grid that Russia has spent the war trying to break.
This year's attacks have again concentrated on the energy system as temperatures start to fall.

The fourth iteration of the Freedom Edge exercise began with an opening ceremony at Yokota Air Base in Japan and will run through Friday, according to the US Pacific Command.

Freedom Edge focuses on interoperability across air, maritime and cyber domains, along with integrated air and missile defense.

He also “solemnly” warned of “the consequences to be entailed by them,” according to KCNA.
The statements said there would be no change in Pyongyang’s policy of responding to US hostility with the “toughest stand to the last.”
The drills come weeks after US President Donald Trump said on Aug. 17 that he had instructed Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to “substantially reduce” separate planned bilateral military exercises between the US and South Korea, citing their cost and his relationship with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
Trump said those exercises sent an “inappropriate and hostile” signal to Pyongyang.

Germany and the end of Europe’s old political order
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
20:50:05 UTC
05:50:05 KST

Germany shows where Europe is heading
September could prove decisive for Germany’s political future, with elections in Saxony-Anhalt, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin. If the ruling Christian Democratic Union suffers serious defeats across the board, which is by no means certain, the federal government itself could come under pressure and for Chancellor Friedrich Merz, the consequences may be more immediate.
A CDU defeat in Saxony-Anhalt had been expected, but the scale is nevertheless notable. Whether Alternative for Germany ultimately secures an absolute majority and can form a government on its own is almost secondary, because the message to Germany’s political establishment could hardly be clearer. The warning light is flashing red
Merz himself has become part of the problem. Judging by this campaign, he has reached the unenviable political stage at which his interventions appear to produce the opposite of their intended effect, so the more passionately he urges voters in one direction, the more determinedly some seem to move in another.
There is something almost late-Soviet about it, like when an official appeared on television to insist upon something and a significant part of the population instinctively concluded that the truth probably lay elsewhere.
Attempts in the final days of the campaign to portray the AfD as Nazis and Putin’s puppets plainly failed to stop its advance in this eastern state and they may even have helped it by irritating voters already tired of such accusations. Nor did the murky drone incident in Leipzig, which was used to heighten tensions with Russia, noticeably alter the political mood.
What happens next in Saxony-Anhalt will depend on the final distribution of seats, but almost every available option presents Germany’s establishment with difficulties of its own making.
Suppose an AfD government is formed in Magdeburg, then the temptation elsewhere in the federal system will be to obstruct it and there’s already discussion of limiting cooperation with AfD-led authorities, including in sensitive areas such as security and intelligence.
That would be an extraordinary path to take, given Germany’s federal system has traditionally functioned effectively precisely because the Länder (states) and federal government cooperate despite political differences. To start withholding information or obstructing a legitimately constituted state government would risk damaging the system in an effort to contain one political party. It would be the sanctions mentality, so familiar from international affairs, brought home and deployed against part of Germany itself.
The alternative may be an unwieldy coalition of virtually everyone else, assembled primarily to prevent the largest party from governing, which may be constitutionally possible, but repeating it indefinitely carries an obvious political cost and voters eventually notice when electoral victories don’t translate into political power.
The more intelligent approach might be to accept the result, allow the AfD to govern where it wins, and gradually draw the party into the political establishment. Government has a habit of disciplining insurgent movements and responsibility exposes contradictions that opposition can conceal, while administrative reality is often more effective than denunciation at diminishing radical parties.
But such a strategy requires political subtlety, something Germany’s federal leadership currently possesses in limited supply. At decisive moments, German politics has a tendency to substitute moral certainty for flexibility, which is why the mainstream spent years constructing a cordon sanitaire around the AfD. Having turned the party into something with which cooperation is deemed morally impossible, it’s now difficult to reverse course without admitting that the original strategy has failed.
The German problem is part of something larger as across Western Europe, political transformation appears to be entering a new phase, with the gap between what established parties offer and what substantial sections of their populations demand widening. Those who govern and those who are governed increasingly seem to inhabit parallel political worlds.
The origins of this divergence lie partly in the high period of globalization 25 or 30 years ago. As economies became more interconnected, more decisions migrated from the national to the supranational level, but this wasn’t simply an ideological project as in an integrated world, many problems genuinely could no longer be managed effectively by individual states.
For a time, the arrangement worked because it delivered tangible benefits. The increasingly cosmopolitan political and economic order could point to prosperity and rising living standards and while people might have felt that decision-making was becoming more remote, the system compensated them materially.
But that bargain has weakened as globalization no longer functions as its architects expected. Economic integration remains dense enough that governments can’t simply retreat behind national borders, yet it no longer produces the political confidence and economic dynamism that once legitimized it and as a result, established elites find themselves trapped between structures inherited from the previous era and electorates demanding greater national control.
The result is the rise of protest movements across Europe. They share certain characteristics, particularly an emphasis on sovereignty and hostility towards established institutions, but they aren’t interchangeable because French, German, and British nationalists won’t necessarily become natural allies simply to spite a Brussels which dislikes all of them. Nationalism by definition reflects different histories and interests.
What matters is that the old political system is beginning to wobble, even though its institutions remain powerful and retain many mechanisms for containing insurgent forces through coalition-building and institutional barriers. But the question is how long such methods can work if the underlying electoral trend continues.
Saxony-Anhalt therefore matters beyond Saxony-Anhalt and the treatment of the AfD after its electoral breakthrough will provide a useful indication of how far Germany’s establishment is prepared to go to preserve the existing political architecture, and what consequences follow when it does.
None of this means that the Western Europe emerging from the present transformation will necessarily be more congenial to Russia, and Moscow should harbor no illusions on that score. A Europe of resurgent nationalism and competing interests has historically been quite capable of producing instability of its own, and Russia has rarely escaped the consequences.
But political systems don’t remain fixed indefinitely and the European order created during the age of triumphant globalization is entering a period of profound adjustment. Germany may simply be where that transformation is becoming impossible to ignore.

The duke and duchess of Sussex will not be working royals, according to a letter from Buckingham Palace Monday following Prince Harry and former actress Meghan’s return to the UK.
The Sussexes will still not be able to use titles of "His and Her Royal Highness" and will remain "private citizens," the BBC reported, citing the letter sent on behalf of King Charles by the lord chamberlain, a top palace official.
The letter has been sent to Prince Harry's team, government departments, military officials, and lord lieutenants, who are the monarch's local representatives, and government staff often involved in royal visits and engagements, according to palace sources.

The message highlighted that the position agreed in 2020 when the Sussexes left the UK, the so-called Sandringham Agreement, is still in place.
This ruled out any "half-in and half-out" status, so the couple could not continue their own commercial interests while remaining to be working royals.
"It is well known that in January 2020 the Duke and Duchess stepped down from undertaking representative duties on behalf of the Sovereign, and are no longer working members of the Royal Family," said the letter.
It added: "The charitable work of the Duke and Duchess is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity."

In Russia, reservists have begun facing restrictions on leaving the country based on decisions by military enlistment offices — Russian media
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
23:41:49 EEST
05:41:49 KST

In Russia, reservists have begun facing restrictions on leaving the country based on decisions by military enlistment offices — Russian media
Kyiv • UNN
A 24-year-old reservist from the Rostov region was barred from leaving Russia because of an erroneous summons status in the electronic register. From August 18 to 31, 23 out of 73 conscripts were unable to cross the border.
For the first time in Russia, a case has been recorded in which a reservist liable for military service was unable to leave the country due to a military enlistment office decision restricting travel abroad. The Moscow Times reports this, citing the human rights project "Go by Forest," UNN informs.
Details
According to its information, a 24-year-old resident of the Rostov region, who completed urgent military service in 2024 and is in the reserves, tried to fly abroad from Krasnodar. However, at passport control, he was detained for an additional check and handed an official notice temporarily restricting his right to leave Russia.
It turned out that the decision had been made by the military enlistment office where the reservist was registered. In November 2025, he appeared there in response to a summons to clarify his military registration documents, and a mobilization order was pasted into his documents. At the same time, the summons was listed in the electronic register as having the status "Citizen failed to appear." On this basis, the military enlistment office decided to restrict his travel abroad. Before the trip, the reservist did not see a notification about the ban in the register and learned about it only at the border
It is reported that since March, following the full-scale launch of the electronic summons register, Russians have begun complaining about being blocked from traveling abroad. Thus, from August 18 to 31 alone, 73 conscripts who tried to cross the border contacted the project: 50 were able to leave, while 23 were not.
In a number of cases, the travel ban appeared directly during border control. Attempts to leave via Belarus also did not always end successfully: of the 11 conscripts who contacted the project, four managed to cross the border, while seven did not.
Reminder
According to The Economist, Russian dictator Vladimir Putin intends to send another 300,000–400,000 Russian men to fight against Ukraine. To this end, pressure from regional authorities will likely be used without announcing a new wave of mobilization.
