The U.S. embargo on Cuba resulted in a "record" loss of over $8 billion for the battered island between March last year and February this year, according to a government report presented Monday as the country is going through a severe economic crisis.
Cuba has been under a U.S. trade embargo since 1962, with President Donald Trump piling on pressure on top of the decades-old measure since early this year.
The damages set out in the report exceed last year's peak by 7%, said Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez.
The figure "does not include the damage from the energy blockade" imposed by Washington in January "nor the damage from secondary sanctions" imposed on Cuban entities in May, the minister added.
"The blockade does not punish a government; it punishes the daily life of a people in all its aspects," Rodriguez said.
Havana blames the crisis on an array of U.S.-imposed punitive measures, while Washington attributes the hardship to poor internal management.
Living conditions on the island are severe, with residents enduring regular rolling blackouts and chronic food and fuel shortages on a daily basis.
Rodriguez pointed to an increase in infant mortality, from four per 1,000 births in 2018 to 9.9 in 2025, as evidence of deteriorating standards.
He ruled out declaring a humanitarian crisis, however, and praised what he called Cuban solidarity in the face of difficulty.
The minister said Cuban authorities remain in contact with the U.S. State Department but ruled out any normalization of ties.
Cuba remains willing to continue engaging in dialogue "despite the lack of progress" and "lack of willingness" on the part of the U.S., he said.

The domestic armed threat facing Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
19:06:22 UTC
04:06:22 KST

The domestic armed threat facing Iran
External support for ethnic armed groups poses an escalating security threat to Iran, experts and state officials warn.
Iranian authorities have repeatedly publicised arrests and clashes with small armed cells inside the country, or skirmishes with armed groups along land borders, particularly in the lead-up to and during the war with Israel and the United States.
They have endeavoured to frame the war as a national security struggle while sending a message of control and deterrence to audiences inside the country and abroad.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Claimed Israeli capture of Lebanese ridge reshapes negotiation dynamics
- list 2 of 3Israel deports British activist who protected Palestinian children
- list 3 of 3Why do the Falkland Islands matter to the UK and Argentina so much?
In one of the latest instances, state media said on Sunday that members of an eight-member network allegedly affiliated with “anti-revolutionary” and “pro-monarchy” groups were arrested.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) in the southern province of Fars accused those arrested of using Molotov cocktails and burning tyres during nationwide protests in January.
The leaders of Iran’s Islamic Republic have in recent weeks also expressed concern about more potential protests as public discontent rises amid deteriorating economic conditions.
Why the focus on ‘monarchists’?
During Iran’s January protests and on social media, a number of Iranians have expressed support for the return of the country’s monarchy, which was overthrown in the 1979 Islamic revolution.
Reza Pahlavi, the foreign-based son of Iran’s last shah, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, has been a leading opponent of the country’s government, and in January called on Iranians to join nationwide strikes and protests. Thousands are believed to have been killed during the unrest.
But even though there are instances of chanting in support of Pahlavi in Iran, there are currently no major organised pro-monarchy armed groups operating inside the country.
And while multiple nationwide demonstrations have swept Iran in recent years, they have largely been rooted in protesting economic grievances and repression in the country, rather than support for the monarchy.
US President Donald Trump, as well as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, did openly discuss the goal of overthrowing the Iranian state during the opening months of the war, which began in late February. Calls for the monarchy to replace the Islamic Republic have been particularly prominent in demonstrations outside of Iran.
The Iranian government has since then announced a large number of arrests of people it says are supporters of the monarchy.
That has included 111 so-called “monarchist cells” arrested across 26 provinces, as announced on March 18 by the Intelligence Ministry.
Iranian authorities consider the January protests a “coup” orchestrated by armed agents of the US and Israel, including pro-monarchists.
The United Nations and international rights groups have condemned state forces for the “brutality” shown during the crackdown on protesters.
The judiciary has executed dozens of prisoners since the start of the war, including some of those who protested in January. Numerous students, artists, businesspeople, journalists, healthcare workers and others have also been arrested over recent months for acts perceived by the authorities to be against national security.
What are the main armed groups in Iran?
Kurdish fighters active close to Iran’s western borders with Iraq are the country’s largest non-state armed threat.
Multiple groups, designated as “terrorist” outfits by Iranian authorities, have been based in the semiautonomous Kurdish region of northern Iraq for years.
Iran’s military forces have attacked bases operated by these groups in Iraq in recent years, while also pursuing security deals with the Iraqi government to contain them.
At the start of this year’s war, the Kurdish armed groups were considered by the Trump administration to lead a limited ground operation in western Iran to complement extensive air strikes by US and Israeli fighter jets and warships.
The Reuters news agency reported in early March that roughly 5,000-8,000 Iranian Kurdish fighters from groups including the Kurdistan Free Life Party (PJAK), Democratic Party of Iranian Kurdistan (PDKI), and Kurdistan Freedom Party (PAK) were preparing for a potential cross-border operation and had held discussions with US and Israeli representatives.
But the groups said they lacked sufficient weaponry and did not receive a clear signal from Washington to initiate the operation. The plan was not set into motion, and by April the IRGC had sent more troops to the border provinces.
Trump later repeatedly claimed that he had supplied arms to Kurdish forces, but that they had kept the weapons for themselves.
Aside from the Kurdish forces, Iran’s disenfranchised and restive southeastern border areas are also home to separatist Baloch fighters.
In late August, security forces said they had broken up a cell belonging to Jaish al-Adl, the most prominent of the Baloch armed groups. One rebel fighter was reported to have been killed, six arrested, and rifles, grenade launchers and explosives seized. But sporadic attacks from the group have been ongoing, at times killing police officers and IRGC figures.
Iranian authorities have said they will continue to bolster border control in order to limit exposure to armed groups amid the war.
Alex Vatanka, a senior fellow at the Washington-based Middle East Institute, said that external support for the Kurdish and Baloch rebel groups could increase the security challenge facing the authorities.
“The Iranian state might see any signs of increased external support for ethnic militants to be of an existential kind this time around due to the war situation,” he told Al Jazeera.
“I only see ethnic militant groups as possibly decisive [in the war] if they are part of a broader externally-funded push to pressure the regime in Tehran, which the Islamic Republic is already anticipating and calls a foreign-led hybrid-war campaign,” Vatanka added.
For his part, Trita Parsi, the Quincy Institute’s co-founder, said that while separatist militias don’t pose an existential threat to the government, they “may prove tremendously problematic for Tehran if the war with the US escalates after the mid-terms and the US decides, for instance, to deploy ground troops”
“If Trump decides to accept military risks after the midterms that he earlier eschewed, such as deploying ground troops, then it is highly conceivable that the US will seek to use armed militias inside the country,” Parsi added.
Washington encourages internal pressure
During the January protests, Trump and other US officials backed Iranian protesters and said they should continue to act with the goal of overthrowing the Islamic Republic.
Similar rhetoric from Washington has been heard since the start of the war.
Last week, Trump discussed the possibility that the pressure from war, sanctions and a naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports could ultimately lead to an internal uprising, or even the fall of the establishment.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the pressure could prompt Iranians to take to the streets again, or even create divisions within the IRGC.
“Maybe the people will rise up,” he said. “There is 100 percent inflation, queues, the military isn’t getting paid, [and] the central bank governor was in a panic last week.”

“NO MORE SELLING BOMBARDIER IN THE UNITED STATES! Their products aren’t good enough!” Trump said in a post on Truth Social.
“If they want our Market, they must build here, and stop treating America like a ‘piggybank’,” he said.
Trump made the post as a trade dispute between Washington and Ottawa escalates, part of the near-global tariff wall in his second term that has drawn complaints from many US trading partners.
Canada is set to introduce a wave of counter tariffs against the United States on Sept 8.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on how Trump would enforce the action or the steps he would take to bar deliveries of Bombardier jets which have been approved by the US Federal Aviation Administration.
The planemaker’s jets also comply with the United States Mexico Canada (USMCA) trade deal that Trump helped implement.
US aerospace analyst Richard Aboulafia said he did not believe any business jet customers would cancel Bombardier orders and didn’t see how Trump could stop them from being sold.
Aboulafia, managing director of AeroDynamic Advisory, an aerospace management consulting firm, pointed out that most Bombardier private jets use US engines, which are produced by both Honeywell Aerospace and GE Aerospace.
Aerospace has largely emerged unscathed from Trump’s tariff war with the flow of parts and planes not currently impacted by duties.
According to US trade group Aerospace Industries Association, the country’s aerospace and defence sector has a US$109.2 billion (S$138 billion) trade surplus, with exports up 25 per cent on an annual basis in 2025.
Like the US auto sector, which depends on parts production by its northern neighbour, aerospace is highly integrated on a global scale.
Bombardier, the Montreal-based rival of US business jet manufacturer Gulfstream Aerospace, has an American workforce of 3,500, and a US footprint of 2,800 suppliers, along with factories and service centres in the country.
The company is now adding its sixth US service centre and produces wings for its flagship Global 8000 jet in Texas.
Bombardier said in a statement late on Sept 7 that it spends more than US$2.5 billion with US suppliers each year.
“Our plan is to continue to invest in our people, our customers and the communities in which we operate across the country,” the company said of the United States.
Bombardier also has a defence division with a US-based factory in Kansas where it prepares Canadian-manufactured planes for special mission purposes.
About half of the fleet of 5,100 aircraft operated by Bombardier customers are located in the US.
In January, Trump said the US was decertifying Bombardier Global Express business jets and threatened 50 per cent import tariffs on all aircraft made in Canada until the country’s regulator certified a number of planes produced by US rival Gulfstream.
Neither occurred, but the following month Canada certified several Gulfstream planes.
In July, Bombardier reported that its quarterly revenue grew 6 per cent compared with the same three months a year ago to US$2.15 billion (S$2.7 billion), helped by strong demand for aftermarket services. REUTERS

Syria detains Assad-era general accused of bloody crackdown on protests
Major-General Mohammed Ali Durgham is accused of links to 1982 Hama massacre and 2011 protest crackdown.
Syrian authorities have announced the detainment of an Assad-era general accused of taking part in a massacre and overseeing a bloody crackdown on protests.
The country’s Internal Security Forces said on Monday that they had arrested former Major-General Mohammed Ali Durgham, who is accused of partaking in the Hama massacre in 1982 and ordering the shooting of unarmed protesters in 2011.
The detainment is the latest in a series of arrests as Syria’s government – led by figures from the former rebel group Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) that deposed former President Bashar Al-Assad in 2024 after decades of brutality – attempts to bring to justice those that ran his regime.
The statement labelled Durgham “a prominent officer in the military establishment during the era of the former regime”.
He is accused of being involved in “issuing direct order” to fire on unarmed protestors in the Damascus countryside.
Human Rights Watch in 2011 quoted a Syrian army defector who said that Durgham was one of the generals who “ordered the troops to shoot at protesters when his unit was deployed to areas in and just outside of Damascus”.
Durgham was a field commander in the army’s feared Fourth Division, commanded by Assad’s brother Maher al-Assad, between 2009 and 2013.
Durgham started “as a squad commander in the Defence Brigades during the events in Hama Governorate in 1982,” the authorities said.
On February 2, 1982, amid an information blackout, then-Syrian president Hafez al-Assad launched a brutal crackdown in the central Syrian city of Hama.
The death toll ranges from 10,000 to 40,000 people killed over the nearly month-long siege of the city.
Durgham’s arrest is part of broader efforts to pursue former officials accused of crimes and abuses under the previous regime.
Since Bashar al-Assad’s overthrow in December 2024, Syria’s new authorities have arrested dozens of former security officials.
Former Major-General Jalal Kamel Saqr was detained last week for his involvement in war crimes and arbitrary detentions, the state-run Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA) reported.

IDF enters decisive phase in south Lebanon as Hezbollah clashes threaten ceasefire

The relative calm around the ridge has deteriorated rapidly in recent days, turning the area into a tightly contained but increasingly lethal combat zone in which Israeli defense officials fear a single incident could trigger a much broader escalation.
The latest confrontation came Monday during searches by troops from the Golani Reconnaissance Unit in the Beaufort area.
According to the IDF, a Hezbollah terrorist hiding inside a building opened fire on the troops at close range. The soldiers returned fire and killed him during a brief close-quarters battle, with artillery also used against the source of the fire.
Two Israeli soldiers were lightly wounded and evacuated to a hospital. Their families were notified.
Explosive drones followed by Israeli strikes
The Beaufort clash came after another night of exchanges around Ali Taher Ridge.
Two explosive drones were launched toward IDF forces operating in the security zone overnight, according to the military.
The Israeli Air Force subsequently struck what the IDF described as Hezbollah terrorist infrastructure, command centers and weapons storage facilities around Nabatieh and Kfar Roummane.
The military also said terrorists traveling in a vehicle while transporting weapons were targeted.
Lebanese reports said nine people were killed in one of the Israeli strikes, including civilians. The IDF said the incident was under investigation and stressed that precision munitions had been used in an effort to limit harm to civilians.
The mounting exchanges come as the military prepares to complete the dismantling of Hezbollah infrastructure around Ali Taher Ridge in the coming days before redeploying to positions farther back.
Israeli security officials assess that Hezbollah is trying to preserve military assets in the area before they can be destroyed.
They also believe the organization has an interest in drawing Israel into a wider confrontation that could undermine both the ceasefire agreement between Israel and the Lebanese government and the pilot arrangement currently being implemented along the border.
Why Ali Taher Ridge matters
The ridge has become a focal point because of its strategic terrain and the Hezbollah infrastructure built around it.
The IDF has been working above and below ground to clear positions in the area, which Israeli officials view as important for denying Hezbollah observation, firing and operational capabilities close to the border.
The coming days are expected to determine whether the military can complete that mission and move toward a more defensive deployment without being drawn into a larger round of fighting.
That calculation has become more complicated as Hezbollah continues to challenge Israeli forces with explosive drones and localized attacks.
Eyes also turn to Tehran
The military is simultaneously watching Iran.
Israeli intelligence and Air Force assessments do not currently point to concrete indications of an imminent Iranian attack, but officials are taking into account the possibility of direct fire from Iranian territory toward Israel.
The assessment comes amid growing pressure on Tehran following recent U.S. actions against Iran.
Israeli officials believe Hezbollah is seeking to bring Iran more directly into the confrontation, while Iran itself is weighing how to respond to the pressure it is facing.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz have both warned that Israel has plans for a severe response if Iran directly attacks Israel.
Such an attack could trigger several days of intense fighting or potentially a broader confrontation, Israeli officials assess.
The United States, however, is expected to play a central role in setting the limits of any such escalation, as Washington continues to push to prevent a wider regional war.
For the troops operating in southern Lebanon, the immediate challenge remains much closer.
With Hezbollah continuing to test the ceasefire and the IDF moving to complete its operation around Ali Taher Ridge, commanders are preparing for a period in which a single localized exchange could quickly become something much larger.

An Iranian-American citizen, Kamran Hekmati, has been released from Tehran's notorious Evin Prison, sources have told RFE/RL's Radio Farda, but he is unable to leave the country due to a travel ban.
The release has not yet been officially confirmed by Iranian authorities.
Hekmati, who was designated as a wrongfully detained person by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in March, is believed to have been released on September 5.
His release was also reported by The Jerusalem Post, an Israeli media outlet which cited Iranian sources.
The 71-year-old traveled to Iran to visit relatives on his Iranian passport in May 2025 and was detained by the authorities two months later. Tehran's Revolutionary Court subsequently sentenced him to four years in prison for having traveled to Israel for a religious ceremony over a decade earlier. Holders of Iranian passports are barred from traveling to Israel.
His sentence was later reduced to two years after a change in the law governing such travel.
Hekmati's family has repeatedly raised concerns over his health, saying he suffers from aggressive bladder cancer and has been denied access to proper specialized treatment in detention.
The case is one of several involving Iranian-American dual nationals caught up in Iran's use of arbitrary detention as diplomatic leverage against the West, a practice critics have called "hostage diplomacy."
Dena Karari, another Iranian-American, was briefly detained in Shiraz in 2024 and released on bail but was barred from leaving Iran for about 19 months. She faced accusations including "collaboration with a hostile government" and espionage but was eventually allowed to leave the country in July this year. Shortly after her departure, a Zahedan court convicted her in absentia and sentenced her to five years in prison.
Reza Valizadeh, a former Radio Farda correspondent, remains imprisoned at Evin.
In a recorded phone call from inside the prison this past June, he appealed to the US government to secure medical assistance for himself and other detained Americans, saying four US citizens held at Evin were suffering from various illnesses without access to real medical care.
Valizadeh resigned from RFE/RL in November 2022, returned to Iran in March 2024 to see his family, and was arrested that September. He was convicted of "collaborating with the hostile American government" and sentenced to 10 years in prison, along with a ban on residing in Tehran and neighboring provinces, a travel ban, and a two-year prohibition on joining political parties or groups. His appeal was rejected.

Burnham and Kristersson discuss Joint Expeditionary Force
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
19:59:20 BST
03:59:20 KST

Prime Minister Andy Burnham spoke to his Swedish counterpart Ulf Kristersson on the morning of Sunday 7 September, with the two leaders discussing the importance of the relationship between the two countries both bilaterally and through the Joint Expeditionary Force and NATO in order to protect shared interests, according to a readout issued by Downing Street.
The leaders agreed that Russian aggression, both in Ukraine and through hybrid attacks in Europe, emphasised the importance of that close relationship. Burnham reflected on his recent visit to Ukraine and thanked Prime Minister Kristersson for Sweden’s strong support, particularly as Russia has stepped up what the readout described as egregious attacks.
The Joint Expeditionary Force is a British-led grouping of ten northern European nations, bringing together the United Kingdom with Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden. It is designed to operate either independently or alongside NATO and other partners, with a focus on the High North, the North Atlantic and the Baltic Sea region, and it has been used in recent years to coordinate activity around the protection of undersea cables and pipelines and the monitoring of shadow fleet tanker movements.
Sweden’s participation in that grouping predates its accession to NATO, which it completed in March 2024 after abandoning a policy of military non-alignment that had held for two centuries. Swedish membership, alongside that of Finland, has substantially altered the alliance’s position in the Baltic and has drawn Stockholm into closer planning arrangements with London on questions of northern European security.
The call also covered economic matters with a defence and energy dimension. The leaders discussed opportunities to drive growth between the two countries, including through Rolls-Royce’s delivery of Swedish small modular reactors. The Prime Minister said the programme was a good example of how both countries could work together to deliver highly skilled jobs and support Sweden’s plans to deliver clean, reliable and secure power.
Rolls-Royce SMR, the company established to develop and build the British small modular reactor design, has been selected by the Swedish state-owned utility Vattenfall to supply reactors at the Ringhals site on the country’s west coast. The same design has been chosen for the British small modular reactor programme, and the company has pursued export orders on the basis of a factory-built approach intended to reduce the cost and construction time associated with conventional nuclear plants.
Turning to Europe more broadly, the leaders discussed the British ambition to move closer to the European Union. The Prime Minister said he was focused on driving a closer relationship that delivered for people in both the United Kingdom and Europe, increasing security, boosting opportunity and supporting growth. The two leaders said they looked forward to meeting soon.

3 years on, Morocco earthquake victims still wait for help
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
18:57:00 UTC
03:57:00 KST

3 years on, Morocco earthquake victims still wait for help
September 7, 2026
On September 8, 2023, a devastating earthquake struck the Al Haouz region in Morocco, killing over 2,900 people, injuring more than 5,500 and causing widespread destruction.
In the village of Ighermane in the High Atlas Mountains, about 50 kilometers (30 miles) southwest of Marrakech, Mohamed Ait Belaid, 72, feels like things are actually going pretty well for him three years later.
He had been living in a tent after the earthquake but now resides in a newly built house, even though it's smaller than the one destroyed in the earthquake.
"I benefited from partial [state] support and received 80,000 dirhams [around €7,300] for rebuilding," he told DW. "I added about 100,000 [€9,110] dirhams from my own pocket. And thanks to God, I like my new house and I'm comfortable in it. I'm at peace because my wife, my children and I are all healthy and I haven't lost any of them."
Around 40 kilometers away, in the town of Azgour, it's a different story. Larbi Ait Jelloulat, also 72, is sitting in front of a pile of rubble that was once his house.
"I want to know where my rights have gone," he said angrily. "Who took what's rightfully mine? For three years, I've been going from one department to another, from one complaint to another, from one petition to another, just looking for an answer. Why have I been excluded? Am I not a Moroccan citizen?"
Ait Jelloulat was formerly a council employee and saved for years in order to build the large home that was destroyed in the 2023 earthquake. As far as he can tell, bureaucratic issues mean he must prove he was a resident in the area.
"My only dream was to spend the rest of my life in my own home, a rest after years of service," he explained. "Now they say I'm not a resident … Where's the logic in that?"
Why such different experiences?
Reconstruction seems to be happening faster in Ighermane, the village where Ait Belaid lives. About 90% of the village is rebuilt and most residents' lives are back to normal, said Omar Saeed from the Ighermane Association for Development and Solidarity.
Of the village's around 150 families, 114 received state support of some kind, although most also had to contribute some of their own money to rebuild.
Meanwhile, in Azgour, where Ait Jelloulat lives, there's been more to do. Azgour was the village most impacted by the earthquake in the area.
There, about 76 families have had help with reconstruction, Ait Jelloulat said, while 56 others are still waiting for help. "What's more, the 76 families who rebuilt their homes in a different location are also having problems connecting to water and electricity," he added.
Rebuilding difficult in remote mountain villages
According to a March statement from the High Atlas Development Agency, or ADHA, which was established in October 2023 to bring help to affected areas, 54,425 homes have been built or rehabilitated and more than 3,000 homes are still under construction. The government has given out more than 7.2 billion dirhams (€656 million/$770 million) to affected families. The sum includes funds to help rebuild as well as monthly emergency aid payments.
In terms of the pace of construction, Marrakech-based architect Mohamed Belmejjad believes the state is actually doing fairly well. "I believe the progress so far, relative to the timeframe, to be positive," he told DW.
Given the circumstances, it would be hard for things to have gone much faster, he suggested.
Immediately after the earthquake, it was difficult to reach affected locations, especially remote mountain villages and towns. Then rubble had to be cleared before building could begin.
After that, other factors complicated reconstruction, including the distance of some villages from paved roads, the difficulty of transporting building materials in and debris out, problems with connecting water and power, and the need to relocate whole villages and construction sites to avoid dangers like landslides. There's also a need to respect local building traditions, ensuring that construction materials are solid and will last.
"We also lack the necessary expertise here, whether that's in terms of architects, design offices, contractors or even the labor required for construction," Belmejjad pointed out. Given all that has happened reconstruction could actually be considered ahead of schedule, he suggested.
'No one has remembered us'
Despite that, the National Coordination for Al Haouz Earthquake Victims reports receiving complaints from more than 3,000 families who haven't had any state help.
Montasser Itri, a member of the organization, explains that some of these families were excluded because they had moved to other parts of the country to work and their national identity cards then show them as residents of places unaffected by the 2023 earthquake.
"The government is trying to make us, the victims of the Al Haouz earthquake, into mere statistics linked to the progress of construction and the removal of tents," Itri told DW, "rather than treating us as human beings and with dignity."
That's why the coordinating committee is already demanding an independent and transparent investigation into how local authorities have handled the payouts. In the past they've organized demonstrations outside parliament buildings in the capital, Rabat, to demand compensation and rehousing solutions and to accuse local authorities of failing to honor commitments.
Other impacted locals are hoping the upcoming general election, slated for September 23, might make a difference.
"[Prime Minister Aziz] Akhannouch promised us a solution to the issue and God knows we are waiting," said Fawzia Aliban, whose home in Amizmiz was damaged in the earthquake. "We hope the problems will be resolved because I was denied benefits even though my house is on the verge of collapse."
"Three years have passed, and no one has remembered us […] but recently some political figures turned up and promised to solve the problem," added Mohamed Belkaid, who is still living in a tent in the Amizmiz area with his four children.
He hasn't received any aid to rebuild because he is listed as a tenant, not an owner, and is not optimistic things will change.
"They promised to review our files, asking us to trust them and to vote for them," he complained. "But this is exploitation. If they truly wanted to solve the problem, they would have done so before the elections. Where have they been all these years?"
This article was originally written in Arabic.

Climate is different at upcoming RNC as Israel becomes a political hot potato - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
18:55:33 UTC
03:55:33 KST

- i24NEWS
- Analysis & Opinion
- Climate is different at upcoming RNC as Israel becomes a political hot potato - analysis
Climate is different at upcoming RNC as Israel becomes a political hot potato - analysis
The party's commitment to Israel hasn't wavered, but with the timing colliding with Rosh Hashanah and polls showing economic concerns dominating, with Republicans steering toward domestic themes
The 2024 Republican National Convention in Milwaukee was an Israel lovefest. The party took pains to ensure voters understood it was the natural home for American Jews and Israel supporters in the aftermath of Hamas’ 2023 massacre and growing tensions between the Netanyahu and Biden governments.
The RNC gave prime speaking slots to Matt Brooks of the Republican Jewish Coalition and former Harvard graduate student Shabbos Kestenbaum, who sued the university for failing to tackle antisemitism.
Ronen and Orna Neutra, parents of Israeli-American Omer Neutra, who at that time was thought to be held hostage by Hamas and was later confirmed killed on Oct. 7, received a hero’s welcome, with Doug Bergum and Lee Zeldin, now both Cabinet members, heavily criticizing the Biden administration’s handling of Israel and antisemitism.
Displays of support for Israel were seen throughout the convention hall.
But this week, as the RNC hosts a scaled-down, two-day midterm convention in Dallas, expect a completely different focus.
While the core of the party still supports Israel and combating antisemitism with the same zeal, the politics have changed. Republicans are struggling mightily in poll after poll on the issue of affordability, which is far and away the top issue for voters.
Suggested articles
And in this climate, screaming about support for Israel is linked to support for the war against Iran. And supporting the war against Iran means acknowledging the higher oil and other costs that have come with it.
It’s simply a losing message for Republicans politically, even as the party at-large still feels it’s the right thing morally.
A look at the program for Dallas reveals almost an exclusive focus on domestic issues. A select few may affect American Jewry, like ties between faith and government and school choice. But the timing of the convention itself, finishing less than 24 hours before the start of Rosh Hashanah, has already made it difficult for some Orthodox Jews to attend.
Of course, President Trump could always work a mention of Israel, Iran, or pretty much anything, into one or both of the speaking slots he’ll have.
Other speakers, like Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent – who is handling economic measures against Iran – along with pro-Israel Sen. Ted Cruz and Rep. Mike Lawler, whose swing district is heavily Jewish, could bring related topics to the dais.
But while the love felt in Milwaukee hasn’t gone out, the climate is simply different. And with Israel being such a political hot potato, perhaps it might even be helpful if, for once, it were put to the side and allowed to cool down, even if for a couple of days.

Pope Leo unveils new fresco at sanctuary where he prayed after his election
Unknown

2026-09-07

Pope Leo unveils new fresco at Genazzano sanctuary where he prayed after his election
Pope Leo XIV returned Monday to a sanctuary where he prayed just after his election and revealed a permanent sign of his devotion to the place: a fresco depicting him praying that now adorns an upper cornice of the basilica.
Leo unveiled the portrait before celebrating Mass with his fellow Augustinian brothers at the Sanctuary of Our Mother of Good Counsel in the medieval village of Genazzano, south of Rome. He joins a handful of past popes whose visits to the sanctuary were commemorated with portraits that adorn its walls, going back to Pope Urban VIII in 1630.
Leo visited the sanctuary on May 10, 2025, just two days after his election and in his first outing as pope. The former Robert Prevost had been there many times before, since the place has special significance for the pope's Augustinian religious order.
The sanctuary is managed by Augustinian friars and has been a place of pilgrimage since the 15th century. Leo's namesake, Pope Leo XIII, elevated it to a minor basilica and expanded the adjacent convent in the early 1900s.
Leo referred to that 2025 outing during his homily at the basilica on Monday, which commemorates the birth of Mary. Leo recalled what he wrote then in the sanctuary's guest book.
The new pope wrote at the time that he felt the "need and profound desire" to come to the sanctuary after his election to pray before the Madonna of Good Counsel, "who has accompanied me all my life with her maternal presence, with her wisdom and example of love for her son who is always the center of my faith."
Leo and the Vatican are stepping up activities now that the summer lull is coming to a close. The Holy See's typically busy autumn conferences and audiences are taking shape, and Leo is gearing up for a trip to France at the end of the month and his much-awaited trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru in November.

'Serious pork-barrelling': Fears Labor may have misused millions last election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
18:52:57 UTC
03:52:57 KST

Labor's 'invite-only' grants scheme found to have been overwhelmingly spent in safe and marginal seats
An "invite-only" grants program was overwhelmingly directed into safe Labor seats and marginal seats the party wanted to win at the 2025 federal election, a Centre for Public Integrity investigation of the $560 million program has concluded.
While projects in safe and marginal Labor seats sometimes received grants worth tens of millions of dollars, 45 electorates were not invited to the Major and Local Community Infrastructure (MLCI) Program and received no funding.
Labor promised more than half a billion dollars in upgrades to sports facilities, parks and other community infrastructure at the election, and Infrastructure Minister Catherine King has said the MLCI was set up to pay for those promises.
The Centre for Public Integrity's chair, former justice Anthony Whealy, said it appeared the program had been used to pork-barrel seats Labor wanted to win.
"Prima facie, it looks like the misuse of public money or serious pork-barrelling, as it's sometimes called," Mr Whealy told 7.30.
"I think there's a heavy onus on the government now to justify the process it has used. If they cannot justify that process, then I think the public in Australia would be driven to the conclusion that this is the misuse of public money at a serious level."
An examination of the more than 220 programs invited to apply found 73 per cent of funds went to seats notionally held by Labor, compared to 23 per cent to Coalition-held seats, and 4 per cent to all others.
"To put this another way, for every dollar spent in a Coalition seat, $3.20 was spent in a notionally ALP-held seat," the centre's executive director, Catherine Williams, said.
When broken down by how safe or marginal a seat was, $493 million of the $560 million fund went to safe, fairly safe or competitive seats for Labor — while just $66 million went to seats where Labor was not competitive.
Dr Williams said if money had been distributed proportionally, marginal seats where Labor was competitive should have received $66 million less in total than they did, while non-Labor seats should have received approximately $116 million more.
The Centre for Public Integrity also examined whether the discrepancy could be explained by the relative wealthiness of seats using household income data, and found no link.
In fact, the poorest seats in the country received a below-average amount of grant funding.
The centre also found no link between "community connectedness", a measure of infrastructure need, and where grants were allocated.
To date the federal government has not explained what process it used to identify projects for an invitation, or why it chose to use a closed, non-competitive process.
In a statement, Ms King said the MLCI program was in line with longstanding practice and with the updated rules and principles for grants.
Ms King noted ministers do not make decisions on applications in their own electorate, with those decided by another cabinet minister.
The government says the MLCI program's guidelines make clear only those who are invited can apply for funding, and the assessment criteria they must meet to receive funding, with all funding that is awarded published on AusTender.
Applicants are required to demonstrate the social and economic benefits of the project, its viability and the organisation's capacity to carry it out.
Separately, it argues $1.7 billion in competitive and open grants was made available through the Growing Regions and Thriving Suburbs fund.
Marrickville Golf Club versus all others
Independent MP Helen Haines's seat of Indi, in north-east Victoria, was one of the 45 electorates where no projects were invited to the scheme.
Ms Haines has been pursuing details of the scheme in parliament, but she says what the Centre for Public Integrity found has surprised her.
"I was shocked by the scale of this, by the depth of this," Ms Haines told 7.30.
"I feel very, very angry actually, and deeply disappointed, that we have a government who are using a grants program such as this for what they call election commitments … but what in plain language we know is pork-barrelling."
Ms Haines said the scheme had come to her attention after a local golf club contacted her to ask how it could be given an invitation to the MLCI program.
Rutherglen Golf Club is nearly 100 years old, and in need of a refresh.
Its walls are lined with asbestos, the wood is being eaten away by white ants and the floor is sloping and needs restumping.
But Ms Haines had to tell the club, which she had worked with in the past to try to help secure a grant, that there was no way to be considered this time.
Only one golf club was invited to the MLCI program: The Marrickville Golf Club in Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's Sydney seat of Grayndler.
The club received a $6 million grant for refurbishments of its clubhouse, including for an accessibility ramp and fixes to the septic system.
Ms Haines questioned what assessment determined an invitation for Marrickville Golf Club, with which Mr Albanese has a decades-long association, and not for the Rutherglen Golf Club or many others.
"There are golf clubs, football clubs, all sorts of sporting organisations in need of infrastructure support and funding, so why the golf club in the electorate of Grayndler was any different to those is a question that really needs to be asked of the prime minister, I would say," Ms Haines said.
Rutherglen Golf Club member Ian Grimes said it was frustrating that there was no opportunity for the club to make its case.
"It just feels unfair and frustrating. We're not asking for special treatment,"
"We understand not everybody can get a grant. All we want to do is be able to put our case in front of people."
7.30 put questions to the Prime Minister's Office about the process used to identify Marrickville Golf Club for a grant, and if Mr Albanese or his department had any role in the decision to award it funding.
The Prime Minister's Office directed 7.30 to a media release given when the funding was announced, which noted the grant would be delivered in line with the Commonwealth grant rules and guidelines.
Ms Haines has previously introduced a bill to end pork-barrelling, which would require clear and public selection criteria for grants, tougher rules for reporting decisions and a parliamentary oversight committee to scrutinise grant programs, but it has not been supported by the major parties.
She says as long as the current rules continue, it will corrode trust in Australia's democratic institutions.
McKenzie takes aim at PM
In 2020 the Morrison government came under fire for its administration of a $100 million sports grants program, which Labor attacked as a pork-barrelling scheme and later dubbed "sports rorts".
The National Audit Office found the minister had bypassed Sport Australia's advice in some cases on which projects to fund, and there was evidence of "distribution bias" in how grants were awarded.
Then-sports minister Bridget McKenzie was ultimately forced to resign after she failed to declare an honorary membership to a gun club that had received a $36,000 grant under the program.
Senator McKenzie told 7.30 she chose to resign because she believed she had breached ministerial standards when it came to a perceived conflict of interest.
Now the shadow infrastructure minister, she maintains that she had run an open, competitive program where she had clear responsibility for the grants awarded — whereas it was very unclear how MLCI projects had been chosen, or who chose them.
"The difference is you have got a half-a-billion-dollar program where it's very, very opaque as to how and where the decisions were made,"
"Delivering on election promises is an important part of trust in a democracy. However, I think it is concerning that this is a closed program where there were no other invitees other than those who were selected by it seems the Labor Party.
"We learned only last Senate estimates that Catherine King's department didn't have the list of projects that were requiring funding, they had to go to Prime Minister and Cabinet to get that list. That is a very unusual state of affairs."
Senator McKenzie said it was also unclear what conflict of interest management processes were in place with the MLCI.
"There are, I would suggest, over 1,600 clubs that would have liked the opportunity to have applied for this grant program, and that opportunity was denied by the Labor Party," Senator McKenzie said.
"It's really up for the prime minister to answer what steps he took in assuring there was no conflict of interest with the awarding of a $6 million grant to a golf club in his own electorate, given his department was the one that provided the project list to minister King's department for sign-off."
Ms King said the MLCI program followed grant guidelines, including value-for-money principles, and the delivery of the program was in line with the Albanese government's commitment to transparency.
After invitation to the program, the Infrastructure Department is required to assess whether projects represent "value with relevant money", and whether it meets the objective of improving community amenity, accessibility and livability, and drives economic growth.

Cuba's foreign minister says no negotiations despite "genocidal" blockade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

03:52:00 KST

Cuba denounces ‘record’ economic damage from US embargo
HAVANA - The US embargo on Cuba incurred “record” losses of over US$8 billion (S$10 billion) on the communist island between March 2025 and February 2026, according to a government report presented on Sept 7.
Cuba has been under a US trade embargo since 1962, with President Donald Trump piling on pressure on top of the decades-old measure since early 2026.
The damages set out in the report exceed 2025’s peak by seven per cent, said Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez.
The figure “does not include the damage from the energy blockade” imposed by Washington in January “nor the damage from secondary sanctions” imposed on Cuban entities in May, the minister added.
“The blockade does not punish a government; it punishes the daily life of a people in all its aspects,” Rodriguez said.
Havana blames the crisis on an array of US-imposed punitive measures, while Washington attributes the hardship to poor internal management.
Living conditions on the island are severe, with residents enduring regular rolling blackouts and chronic food and fuel shortages on a daily basis.
Rodriguez pointed to an increase in infant mortality – from four per 1,000 births in 2018 to 9.9 in 2025 – as evidence of deteriorating standards.
He ruled out declaring a humanitarian crisis, however, and praised what he called Cuban solidarity in the face of difficulty.
The minister said Cuban authorities remain in contact with the US State Department but ruled out any normalisation of ties.
Cuba remains willing to continue engaging in dialogue “despite the lack of progress” and “lack of willingness” on the part of the US, he said. AFP

'Polarised Brazil': Lula remains a ‘strong candidate’ despite the challenges of incumbency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
18:50:52 UTC
03:50:52 KST

'Polarised Brazil': Lula remains a ‘strong candidate’ despite the challenges of incumbency
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on:
François Picard is pleased to welcome Andreza Aruska de Souza Santos, Director of King’s Brazil Institute at the School of Global Affairs, King’s College London and Associate Professor in Brazil and Latin American Studies. According to Aruska, Brazil’s approaching elections can be viewed through competing prisms: macroeconomic performance and political confidence are moving on different tracks. While headline indicators may suggest an economy performing relatively well, she argues that many Brazilians experience a much harsher reality shaped by the cost of living and a volatile job market.
That gap between statistical performance and lived experience could prove more politically consequential than the actual numbers themselves.
Just over the past month alone, a Quaest poll shows the second round of the presidential race tightening into a statistical tie: Lula has slightly dipped from 43 to 42 percent while Bolsonaro has edged upward 40 to 41 percent.
The current controversy surrounding the Supreme Court is at the heart of Brazil’s deeper crisis of institutional mistrust. In a highly polarised political environment, disputes involving judges rapidly spill over into the great Lula-Bolsonaro divide, potentially reopening the anti-establishment terrain that helped Bolsonaro rise in the first place. The electorate's trust in national institutions could play a crucial role.
Aruska cautions against assuming that pressure from Washington will necessarily strengthen Brazil’s Trump-aligned right. Foreign intervention can activate powerful narratives of sovereignty and nationalism and may therefore produce precisely the opposite political effect.
Ultimately, her argument suggests that Brazil’s election may not necessarily be decided by the strength of the economy, but by how people perceive it in their daily life experiences; Effective campaign messaging via both social and traditional media could also prove decisive in this razor-thin contest.

The Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant has been reconnected to external power supply again - Energoatom
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
21:50:34 EEST
03:50:34 KST

The Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant has been reconnected to external power supply again - Energoatom
Kyiv • UNN
Ukrainian energy workers restored the "Ferosplavna-1" line and supplied the ZNPP with 11 MW of power. The plant had been without external power since August 20.
The Zaporizhzhia NPP is once again receiving external power – Ukrainian energy workers have restored the operation of the "Ferosplavna-1" line, UNN reports, citing Energoatom.
At 19:02 on September 7, the auxiliary systems of the temporarily occupied Zaporizhzhia NPP were supplied with power from the 330 kV "Ferosplavna-1" overhead line. The plant's current consumption is 11 MW
Energoatom noted that the restoration of external power was made possible thanks to the professional work of Ukrainian energy workers and a coordinated local ceasefire, which created the necessary conditions for repair work on the damaged line.
It was Ukrainian specialists who, despite the serious threat posed by the unpredictable actions of the occupiers and constant security risks, carried out the necessary work to connect the plant to Ukraine's United Power System.
Since August 20, the Zaporizhzhia NPP had remained without external power. Throughout this time, the plant's critically important systems were supplied by diesel generators. This operating mode created additional risks to the nuclear and radiation safety of Europe's largest nuclear power plant. At the same time, a full guarantee of the Zaporizhzhia NPP's nuclear and radiation safety is possible only after its de-occupation and return to Ukraine's control and to its sole legitimate operator – Energoatom - the statement said.
We remind you
On September 5, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) reported that a local ceasefire had come into force to repair power lines serving the Zaporizhzhia NPP. This followed another prolonged outage.

Tunisians tell the story of their summer of shortages
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
18:50:16 UTC
03:50:16 KST

Tunisians tell the story of their summer of shortages
Frequent water and power cuts, long queues for bottled water, poultry farms destroyed by the heat: these have been the scenes across Tunisia this summer as millions of people were affected by shortages in electricity and water. Our Observers say this is the result of years of underinvestment in infrastructure while the Tunisian president, for his part, blames "deliberate and planned acts of sabotage”.
On Wednesday, September 2, Hedi Baccour, the president of the Trade Association of Supermarket Chains, told Tunisian media outlet Mosaïque FM that 2.3 million bottles of mineral water were now being “distributed daily in the big supermarkets in Tunis and its suburbs”. This was a relief for residents of the capital, after a summer when showering, drinking or even turning on the light became a daily challenge for millions of Tunisians across the country. With temperatures soaring to near 50°C, the country experienced frequent water and power cuts, some lasting more than ten hours.
In August, in order to relieve pressure on its electricity grid, the Tunisian Electricity and Gas Society (STEG) began temporary power cuts in certain areas. The increased stress on the system comes from both the need to run air conditioners as well as the heightened numbers of tourists in the summer months. Another factor is the need for water: Tunisia's National Company for Water Exploitation and Distribution (SONEDE) uses electric pumps in their water systems.
To display this content from Facebook, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
Long lines have been forming in front of shops and at delivery points, sometimes late at night as people try to get a few bottles of water, which has been rationed. No region has been spared the shortages. In Sfax, in Tunis and in tourist-packed coastal cities alike, people are waiting in line for water, paying inflated prices and dealing with raging black markets. All of this is contributing to a growing anger at the government and what is perceived as either its inability or lack of desire to come up with solutions.
‘Everyone’s fighting for a few bottles of water’
In light of the shortages, Tunisians are having to build their schedules around water deliveries. Yassine (not their real name) lives in Jemmal, about 20 kilometres south of Monastir.
 "During the day, it’s really hard to get potable water in any shop or supermarket. The large stores hide their stock and then distribute it once a day, often either right before sunset or very late at night, around 2 or 3 am. People know when the water will be delivered, so they wait for the trucks. It’s absolute chaos when the water gets delivered: people fight for a few bottles, and some people end up without any.
Some shopkeepers hide their water and then sell it at double the price. People who don’t have the means to buy a full six-pack of water, which costs more than six dinars [Editor’s note: around €1.78], drink water from wells, which is often poor quality."
To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
‘There are always people who take advantage of moments of crisis to sell their products for more money’
Ali (not his real name), who was vacationing in the small coastal city of Chebba when the power cuts really got bad, said that he has also seen rapidly rising prices:
 "There is basically a shortage of bottled water. If you go to the beach in Chebba in the evening, you’ll see people selling water for much higher than the state-mandated price [Editor’s note: 0.8 dinars for a litre of water, equivalent to €0.24]. In Sfax, you won’t find water in every shop and, if you do find it, then the number of bottles is limited per person. One 1.5 litre of water is supposed to be sold for around a dinar [Editor’s note: €0.30], but on the beach, it’s sold for 2 to 2.5 dinars. This water often comes from the black market. There are always people who take advantage of moments of crisis to stock products that are in demand and sell them for more money.”
To display this content from TikTok, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
Days marked by power cuts
Tunisians have also been struggling with frequent power cuts. Ali says that both people in Sfax, where he comes from, and Chebba, where he is vacationing, are constantly waiting for the next power cut:
 "We don’t have any electricity at my parents' house in Sfax right now. The last week in August was the worst, with the heatwave, with record temperatures and a lot of humidity. In Chebba, there are frequent power cuts— three or four a day— and each lasts an hour or two. The cuts often happen in the middle of the afternoon or the evening, when people are sleeping and need air conditioning. We try to turn on the air conditioning when we do have power, just to get a little bit of cool. People are essentially trapped at home. I heard about people who had such long power outages during the day that they couldn’t cool down their rooms and so they’d go out to their cars, just to have a bit of air conditioning. It isn’t great for the environment, but everyone is just trying to figure out how to get by.
Some people are really suffering: we’ve heard about people who died in prison. People who don’t have the means to air condition their homes or those who live in homes that aren’t insulated against the heat risk experiencing heat stroke or even dying. There are a few local radio stations that try to let people know how long it will be until the power is back on, but otherwise we are completely in the dark about the timing."
‘The situation is desperate, especially for farmers’
The power cuts are also having an impact on the economy. It seems to have been a catastrophe for poultry farmers, especially in the Sfax region, where 60% of the country’s poultry production is based. Wadie Abdelmalek runs a farm with 30,000 chickens:
 "Everything in the building runs on electricity: the water motors, food distribution and the ‘pad cooling’ that keeps the building cool. The power cuts are intense and happen both day and night— there are no fixed times. Thankfully, I have generators in the building— if not, I would have lost everything. The generators function on diesel: it costs me 250 dinars a day [Editor’s note: €74.15] for it to run reasonably. I have still lost around 500 chickens, which means nearly 5,000 dinars [Editor’s note: around €1,475].
Thank God, that’s not much compared to what other farmers have lost. A poultry farmer near me lost 12,000 chickens in an early stage of production. At around 18 dinars [Editor’s note: €5.3] per chicken, that is equivalent to a loss of between 220,000 and 230,000 dinars [Editor’s note: nearly €65,000]. And there are quite a few other people like him. The government is completely MIA, we haven’t seen or heard anything from them faced with these large-scale losses.
The tap water isn’t stable either. Last year, we had water cuts for about a month and a half, but we didn’t have a heatwave like that. This year, we’ve had cuts for more than three months— and I’m not exaggerating. I invested in a drill to make sure that I can get water.”
To display this content from Facebook, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
Rising anger as people blame the government
As anger against the government grows, a number of protests have taken place: one on the Day of the Republic, on July 25. Protests also took place on August 20.
In an official statement published on August 27, Tunisian President Kaïs Saïed spoke about “deliberate and planned acts of sabotage” by “enemies of this country and their allies”.
However, unions and state-owned companies have been speaking out against his words. They point to a perhaps more mundane cause: ageing infrastructure and investment that has been delayed for years, as well as a rising demand that sharply increases each summer.
Yassine says the responsibility lies with the current government:
 "It’s a problem that is getting worse and worse: Tunisia has had a failing system for more than 15 years, and each president fails to solve these problems."
‘People already took to the streets in 2011 and if that continues, then they might do it again’
Ali fears that what happened in 2011 might happen again:
 "There is widespread anger. Families saw their businesses destroyed by this crisis. The price of poultry meat and eggs rose during this period. Small businesses affected by the cuts are not reimbursed by their insurance companies. People already took to the streets in 2011 and if it goes on like this, they’ll do it again. I’m really worried— I don’t have the feeling that we are better prepared to avoid what we experienced this year, especially if it partially has to do with climate change.”
