Chinese state company secretly supplied Russia’s Rosatom with raw materials for producing Shahed-type Geran drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
17:20:41 UTC
02:20:41 KST

Chinese state-owned company Jilin Chemical Fiber Group supplied Russia with 46 metric tons of raw material for producing carbon fiber — enough to produce components for roughly 1,300 Geran-type attack drones — according to a joint investigation by Politico and The Telegraph, which based their findings on internal Russian transport and customs documents.
According to the outlets, the supplies went directly to Alabuga-Volokno, a subsidiary of UMATEX — Rosatom’s division for advanced materials and composites that operates a plant in the Alabuga special economic zone in Tatarstan supplying high-strength carbon fiber for the mass production of Russia’s long-range Geran (“geranium”) drones, which are built on the basis of the Iranian Shahed.
The raw material in question is polyacrylonitrile tow, or PAN precursor, an indispensable component for producing lightweight, high-strength carbon fiber. It is used to reinforce the drone’s wing and internal structures, including the fuel tank and engine.
According to David Albright, founder of the Washington-based Institute for Science and International Security, the volume of PAN precursor supplied is enough to produce carbon fiber for roughly 1,300 Russian-made suicide drones. “You can’t build the airframe without it,” Albright explains.
The documents also indicate that the shipment may have been deliberately disguised, as it was filed under a customs code that is used for civilian synthetic fibers like nylon and polyester. Under the correct classification, the shipment should have gone through as a dual-use good, Albright says.
Kerri Bitsoff, a former U.S. Treasury official who worked on sanctions against Russian arms procurement networks, concurred that the use of a different customs code could indicate an attempt to conceal the sensitive nature of the shipment.
Ukraine’s Center for Security and Cooperation (USCC) obtained the paperwork from Russian sources and shared it with the U.S. and UK governments. The U.S. House Select Committee on China reviewed the documents and found them to be authentic, an American official said. Their authenticity was also confirmed by the Ukrainian government.
USCC says it has identified at least eight tenders since 2022 for container shipments of PAN precursor from Jilin Chemical Fiber Group to Alabuga-Volokno.
Alabuga-Volokno and UMATEX have been under Western sanctions since 2023. Jilin Chemical Fiber Group is not currently under Western sanctions, and the company did not respond to reporters’ requests for comment. Meanwhile, Rosatom stated the parent company and its enterprises operate “in full compliance with applicable laws and regulations,” and called claims to the contrary false.
China’s embassy in Washington also rejected the accusations, saying they “smear China and turn it into a scapegoat.” The embassy stressed that Beijing “has never supplied lethal weapons to either side of the conflict” and strictly controls the export of dual-use goods.
At the same time, Dennis Wilder, former deputy assistant CIA director for East Asia and the Pacific, said supplies of this scale could not have taken place without the knowledge of Chinese authorities. According to the Kiel Institute, China supplies more than 60% of the components Russia needs in order to sustain its defense industry. Kurt Campbell, a former U.S. deputy secretary of state, previously said that the number of Chinese companies supplying dual-use goods to Russia’s defense industry is already in the dozens.

Iran to declare ‘restricted zone’ beyond Strait of Hormuz amid US military adventurism
TEHRAN — Iran’s Supreme National Security Council (SNSC) has announced plans to declare a comprehensive new “restricted zone” extending beyond the Strait of Hormuz into the Persian Gulf. The move significantly heightens the maritime standoff with the United States and asserts Tehran’s operational control over critical shipping corridors.
In a lengthy televised interview on Sunday night, Major General Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of the SNSC, detailed the strategic parameters of the upcoming security measure.
He stated that the boundary “will begin from the US Navy’s blockade line and extend into parts of the Persian Gulf,” directly enveloping access points leading toward major regional oil loading terminals. Under the incoming policy, any commercial or military vessel attempting to transit the designated sector without explicit prior authorization and tactical coordination with Iranian maritime authorities will be added to an official Iranian sanctions list.
Rezaei noted that entry into the restricted zone under these conditions will carry immediate punitive financial consequences, jeopardizing international maritime insurance policies and permanently barring non-compliant vessels from future passage through the strategic waterway.
Addressing current operational conditions, Rezaei forcefully rejected statements by US President Donald Trump claiming that the vital energy corridor remains accessible to global trade. He dismissed Washington’s account as a “big lie” and confirmed that the Strait of Hormuz is “completely closed and under the control of the armed forces”. To illustrate the severity of the closure, the SNSC chief provided sharp comparative transit metrics. Before the conflict, more than 100 ships carrying over 100 million tons of cargo navigated the strait daily. Currently, that traffic has collapsed to just seven or eight vessels per day, exclusively transporting essential supplies for Iran. “The Americans are trying to smuggle five to six vessels through at great expense, but these ships are usually struck,” Rezaei said.
He explained that while Iranian forces regularly intercept and neutralize these illegal crossings, Tehran has intentionally avoided sinking targeted oil tankers to prevent catastrophic environmental contamination across the Persian Gulf.
Missile test above US warship
Expanding on recent military developments, Rezaei revealed that Iranian forces executed a direct tactical operation against US naval assets operating in the area. He disclosed that 48 hours before his broadcast (on Sunday night), Iran successfully deployed and tested a newly developed, advanced anti-ship missile system in immediate proximity to an active American naval vessel. “For the first time, we tested our anti-ship missile above an American warship,” Rezaei stated. “This special missile created hell for the Americans, and they fled.”
According to Rezaei, the impact of the test was so severe that even US Central Command (CENTCOM) could not conceal the psychological disruption to its forces. Iranian media outlets further reported that the advanced anti-ship system forced the targeted US Navy warship to break formation, abandon its operational vector, and rapidly alter course to retreat from the sector.
Rezaei characterized the maneuver as concrete proof that Washington's naval blockade remains fundamentally vulnerable to Iranian defensive strikes.
 
 Rezaei also provided detailed context regarding the initial outbreak of the US-Israeli war on February 28.  He revealed that Trump had originally mapped out a swift, 10-day military campaign designed to neutralize Iranian defense infrastructure.  However, Washington was forced to abandon its offensive plan on the very first day following surprise retaliatory strikes by Iranian armed forces. Iran has targeted key US support hubs and troop concentrations across the region, including high-precision strikes against the American Titan base in Jordan and military positions in Erbil, Iraqi Kurdistan.  “Trump backed down from the 10-day war he had announced, and it was aborted in its infancy,” Rezaei explained, emphasizing that Iran's rapid retaliatory doctrine fundamentally disrupted Washington's strategic calculations.  The top security official also highlighted ongoing grievances, stating that Iran maintains its full sovereign right to respond to a lethal US attack that targeted a civilian wedding ceremony in Sirik. 
Israeli aggression in Lebanon
Turning to broader regional security, Rezaei evaluated the ongoing confrontation in southern Lebanon, asserting that despite localized tactical movements by Israeli forces, Hezbollah continues to maintain strategic superiority. He added that growing public hostility across the region would render any prolonged Israeli military presence unsustainable.
The current confrontation between Iran and the US follows months of volatile military and diplomatic maneuvering. Transit through the Strait of Hormuz has been heavily restricted since the start of hostilities on February 28. Following the April 8 ceasefire that paused the war, Iran and the US signed a memorandum of understanding on June 17. Crucially, Article 5 of the MoU granted Tehran full legal and administrative authority over the reopening and management of the Strait. However, the agreement deteriorated rapidly after Washington attempted to bypass Iranian sovereignty by establishing an unauthorized maritime transit corridor near Omani territorial waters, accompanied by renewed aerial operations and an illegal naval blockade.
In response, Tehran exercised its authority under the MoU to declare the Strait fully closed to unauthorized traffic. Rezaei announced that a formal memorandum regarding a newly designed, Iranian-managed transit corridor through the Strait will be signed with Omani officials in the coming days. However, he firmly reiterated that Tehran will not commit to opening the passage for US-aligned shipping until Washington completely halts its military aggression, lifts its blockade, and takes concrete steps to restore diplomatic trust.
Trump’s domestic woes
The prolonged maritime deadlock and severe disruptions to global oil flows have triggered intense domestic political pushback inside the United States. Citing severe supply chain shocks, rising domestic fuel costs, and the failure of American military power to secure the Persian Gulf, a mounting number of US lawmakers have openly argued that Washington has lost the strategic conflict. Facing a stalled military campaign, congressional leaders are increasingly pressing the White House to recognize its strategic overreach and utilize the legislative resolutions as a necessary diplomatic off-ramp to end the war.

King Charles clarifies Harry and Meghan’s status after UK return
Palace letter confirms couple will not use royal titles or receive state-funded security for private work
Britain’s King Charles has reiterated that Prince Harry and his wife, Meghan, remain non-working members of the royal family following their return to the United Kingdom.
A letter sent on behalf of the king to senior government officials said the couple will continue to refrain from using their royal titles as they have done since stepping back from official royal duties in 2020.
Any charity work the couple undertakes will be carried out in a private capacity and operational security decisions are matters for the relevant police agencies, the letter adds.
The letter was sent by the Lord Chamberlain, the most senior official in the royal household, to senior officials in the government and military, as well as lord lieutenants, the king’s personal representatives around the country.
“To help avoid doubt or confusion, The King has directed that [this] information be shared,” the letter says.
While the communication simply confirms that Harry and Meghan’s status remains unchanged, the decision to send the letter and release it publicly shows the concern among some palace observers that the couple’s status could allow them to become a sort of parallel royal court, competing with working members of the royal family.

Iran judiciary chief calls US claims on law and freedom a ‘bitter irony’
TEHRAN — Iran’s judiciary chief has sharply criticized the United States over its record on human rights, international law and freedom, describing Washington’s claims to champion those principles as a “bitter irony” considering its conduct on the world stage.
Speaking at a meeting of the Judiciary’s High Council on Monday, Gholam-Hossein Mohseni-Ejei also highlighted 'growing respect for Iran’s resilience and political standing' among officials from BRICS member states and religious leaders in India during his recent visit to the country.
Mohseni-Ejei traveled to India to attend a meeting of the heads of the judiciaries of BRICS countries. He said his meetings on the sidelines of the gathering offered a clear indication of a changing international perception of Iran’s power and its ability to withstand pressure from the United States and Israel.
According to Mohseni-Ejei, senior officials from several BRICS countries repeatedly emphasized that Iran’s resistance against the United States and Israel had influenced their own strategic thinking about dealing with major powers.
He said the experience had demonstrated that Washington and its regional allies could be challenged and defeated, portraying Iran’s confrontation with the two countries as a broader lesson for nations seeking to resist 'hegemonic powers.'
The judiciary chief also stressed the importance of preserving political and social unity inside Iran, warning that statements or actions that undermine domestic cohesion could damage the country’s international image.
Turning to US foreign policy, Mohseni-Ejei said Washington’s repeated claims to defend law, order and freedom were difficult to reconcile with its actions.
He accused the United States of being among the leading violators of human rights and international law, arguing that Washington invokes the rights of women and children while its own military actions have caused civilian casualties.
He also accused the United States and Israel of responsibility for attacks that killed civilians and children, arguing that a country involved in such actions could not credibly portray itself as a defender of children’s rights.
Mohseni-Ejei referred to several incidents in Iran, including an attack on a school in Minab, a stadium in Lamerd and a wedding ceremony on Sirik Island. He rejected the characterization of civilian deaths in such incidents as merely “collateral damage.”
“If the US military claims to possess highly precise weapons, how could it have failed to identify the civilian nature of these sites?” he asked.
The Iranian judiciary chief said such incidents should not be allowed to fade into history without accountability and argued that those responsible for violations against civilians must ultimately be held to account.
He also pointed out 'a longstanding pattern of US pressure and broken commitments,' saying Washington’s coercive approach extends even to its allies.
As an example, he cited recent remarks by US officials concerning Canada, arguing that Washington’s conduct toward its partners demonstrated that its pressure-based foreign policy was not confined to countries opposed to the United States.

Russia’s Foreign Ministry announced that it is closing the German Consulate General in St. Petersburg and the remaining branches of the Goethe-Institut on Russian territory, describing the move as a response to Germany’s earlier closure of Russian diplomatic and cultural facilities.
Germany’s Chargé d’Affaires in Moscow has been informed that the St. Petersburg consulate must cease operations no later than Sept. 18, with staff required to leave Russian territory by that date, European Pravda reported on Monday, Sept. 7.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The decisions were made in connection with the unfriendly actions of the German side,” the Foreign Ministry said.
Additionally, the Goethe-Institut’s branches must be vacated by Sept. 13. The relevant notes were reportedly handed formally to the head of the German diplomatic mission in Moscow.
Lavrov signaled the closures days earlier
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov foreshadowed the retaliation on Sept. 3, telling the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok that Moscow would be shutting Goethe-Institut branches in Moscow, St. Petersburg and Yekaterinburg.
“Of course, they will be closed after our cultural center was kicked out of Berlin,” Lavrov said, adding that “otherwise, we would not respect ourselves.”

The shuttered Russian House is formally known as the Russian Center for Science and Culture, part of a network run by Rossotrudnichestvo – an agency under Russia’s foreign ministry that says it operates 87 missions across 71 countries.
Opened in 1984 on Berlin’s Friedrichstrasse, the seven-story facility had long been considered the network’s flagship, hosting Russian-language classes, concerts, films and exhibitions for the city’s Russian-speaking community.
Bonn closure tied to intelligence concerns
Germany’s decision to shut the Bonn consulate is linked due to its alleged use as a coordination hub for Russian intelligence and hybrid operations across Western Europe, according to the German newspaper Bild on Sept 5.
Roughly 60 Russian diplomats, including Consul General Oleg Krasnitsky, were ordered to leave Germany by Sept. 18.
According to Bild’s sources, roughly one-third of the departing diplomats are affiliated with Russian intelligence services, specifically the Federal Security Service (FSB), the Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR), or the Main Intelligence Directorate (GRU).
Bild also reported that operations targeting Benelux nations, EU institutions and NATO headquarters had allegedly been supported by the Bonn institution.
Dispute traces back to hybrid attack
On Aug. 4, an explosive-laden drone was found near a Ukrainian cargo aircraft inside the Leipzig/Halle Airport’s secure zone, which serves as a key logistical hub for both NATO and Ukraine.
Two suspects were identified on Sept. 2 – a Belarusian national holding a Russian passport and a Russian-born man with Latvian citizenship, prompting both Germany and the EU to adopt new measures against Russia.
“If Russia thinks we will be divided by the threat, or if they think we will be deterred from supporting Ukraine, they are mistaken,” NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said in Brussels, following a meeting with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen that same day.
While the EU said it would introduce new sanctions, Germany responded by preparing a comprehensive package of domestic security measures to counter Russian sabotage, cyberattacks, and hybrid threats, including enhanced surveillance to detect spies and potential terrorists.
The German government blamed Russia for the hybrid attack on Sept. 1, saying it had employed “low-level agents” for the campaign.
Around the same time, the country announced the closing of the Russian consulate in Bonn, a city in western Germany, and terminated its agreement governing the Russian House cultural center in Berlin.
Moscow rejected Berlin’s accusations as “entirely fabricated.”
French Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs Jean-Noël Barrot stated that the EU and NATO will respond to hybrid infrastructure attacks on Sept. 5.
Barrot called the deployment of an explosive-laden drone against German infrastructure a severe escalation.

Iran warns South Korea against military role in Persian Gulf
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
17:09:51 UTC
02:09:51 KST

Iran warns South Korea against military role in Persian Gulf
TEHRAN — Iran has warned South Korea against any military involvement in the Persian Gulf or the Strait of Hormuz, while accusing Washington of creating disruption in regional shipping and rejecting Western efforts to revive international pressure over Tehran’s nuclear program.
The warnings, delivered by Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei on Monday, came as Tehran sought to reinforce its position on three increasingly intertwined issues: security in the Strait of Hormuz, the continuing confrontation with the United States and Israel, and international efforts to exert pressure on Iran through the International Atomic Energy Agency and the United Nations.
In a Korean-language post on X, Baqaei highlighted the long-standing relationship between Tehran and Seoul but drew a sharp distinction between economic and diplomatic ties and military cooperation with the United States.
Iran and South Korea have maintained diplomatic relations for more than six decades, he said, adding that Tehran values its traditionally friendly relations with Seoul. But under current circumstances, he warned, any operational military participation by South Korea in the Persian Gulf or the Strait of Hormuz would be viewed by Iran as direct support for an aggressor.
Baqaei argued that Iran is currently defending itself against 'US aggression and attacks on Iranian civilians.' Against that backdrop, he said, the deployment or participation of foreign military forces in the strategic waterway could carry serious consequences.
He also rejected the idea that sovereign states should respond to US pressure by joining military operations against Iran, saying that no responsible government should submit to coercion to participate in aggression.
Baqaei separately accused Washington of attempting to shift responsibility for disruptions to commercial shipping and rising energy prices onto Iran, arguing that the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz was triggered by the US and Israel.
In a post on X, he said the waterway had remained open until February 28, when the United States and Israel launched their military campaign against Iran.
Baqaei said the conflict had disrupted commercial shipping, halted tankers, and contributed to higher energy prices. He accused Washington of attempting to portray the resulting economic consequences as a cost imposed on the international community by Iran.
Iran warns against renewed nuclear pressure
Baqaei also rejected efforts by the United States and Israel to pressure IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi and advance a move to refer Iran's nuclear file to the UN Security Council.
He criticized a draft resolution based on a recent IAEA report, arguing that Western governments had repeatedly turned to nuclear watchdog when they were unable to achieve their political objectives through other means.
He also challenged the legal rationale being advanced by Western governments over the so-called snapback mechanism, under which previous UN Security Council sanctions could potentially be restored.
According to Baqaei, Western governments' current actions contradict their own interpretation of the mechanism and effectively reinforce the position previously taken by Iran, China and Russia that the mechanism is not applicable in the present circumstances.
He also accused the three European powers involved in the process of having lost credibility with Tehran and described some of their demands as unreasonable.
The spokesman placed particular responsibility on Washington for the current impasse over IAEA access to Iranian nuclear facilities. He argued that US and Israeli military actions had created the circumstances that prevented normal cooperation between Iran and the Agency.
Baqaei warned that Tehran would respond to any new action against it, describing the latest diplomatic pressure as evidence of hostile intentions and an effort to further escalate tensions.
Iran accuses US of deliberately targeting civilians
Responding to questions about attacks on civilian sites, Baqaei said Iran would continue to hold the United States accountable for violations of international humanitarian law.
He cited several incidents, including a deadly attack on a wedding ceremony on Iran's Sirik Island, as examples of a broader pattern of attacks against civilians.
Baqaei questioned how US forces, which possess highly accurate weapons, could have failed to identify civilian locations such as a school in Minab, a stadium in Lamerd or the wedding venue in Sirik.
Iran, he said, should not allow such incidents to disappear into history without accountability.
Tehran credits Oman with good faith on Hormuz talks
Against the backdrop of the confrontation over the Strait of Hormuz, Tehran also offered a comparatively positive assessment of Oman's role in recent discussions concerning maritime security.
Baqaei said Oman had acted in good faith during talks with Iran on shipping security and emphasized the importance of the interests of the two littoral states.
Oman, he noted, is a neighboring coastal country with longstanding and close relations with Iran and has played a constructive role throughout the process.
At the same time, Baqaei cautioned that the outcome of the next stages remained uncertain.
He said an understanding between Iran and Oman was necessary for securing shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz, but by itself would not be sufficient to resolve the broader security crisis.

Serbian government sets up snap vote with call to dissolve parliament
Upcoming election viewed as bid to tighten Vucic’s rule after months of mass street protests.
Serbia’s government has proposed the dissolution of parliament, paving the way for early elections.
Prime Minister Djuro Macut announced the call in Belgrade on Monday. The move to a snap election is seen as a bid to tighten the rule of President Aleksandar Vucic after nearly two years of anti-government unrest.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4A year after student protests shook Valjevo: Serbia at a crossroads
- list 2 of 4Serbia’s Red Star Belgrade honour Ratko Mladic with tifo
- list 3 of 4Protesters in Serbia doubt Vucic resignation will bring change

Parliamentary elections were not due until December next year, but Vucic on Monday announced plans to hold a vote in late October, with speculation rife that he will seek to move into the role of prime minister.
The early election will test how secure a grip on Serbian politics Vucic still enjoys. The veteran authoritarian leader has run the country as president or prime minister for 12 years.
However, massive and persistent anticorruption demonstrations, following the killing of 16 people when a concrete canopy collapsed at a railway station in 2024, have presented him with his sternest challenge yet.
The student-led protest movement has long demanded early elections.
“If we want to mitigate tensions in society there is no better way than to ask people,” Macut said as he announced the dissolution call.
“Serbia has faced protests, blockades, deep divisions, problems in education and heavy pressure on institutions,” he told ministers. “For some time, parts of the public have been calling for early parliamentary elections,” adding that “a responsible government never ignores such demands.”
Vucic is expected to set a date for elections in the coming days. According to the constitution, between 45 and 60 days must be allowed for campaigning.
The president has already said that the vote will be held on either October 18 or 25.
The election would allow Vucic, whose Serbian Progressive Party nominated on Saturday to run for prime minister, to try to reassert his authority.
The opposition and demonstrators accuse Vucic and his allies of violence against political opponents, rampant corruption, ties with organised crime and stifling media freedoms. The president and his circle have denied any wrongdoing.
Vucic’s opponents have condemned the fact that Serbia’s bid to join the European Union has stalled. The president has instead worked on maintaining close ties with Russia and China.
Vucic has faced additional EU pressure in the past week over public homage to war criminal Ratko Mladic, the former Bosnian Serb army commander, who was buried as a hero in Serbia on Monday despite his United Nations court conviction.

2026-09-07

The Russian roll-on/roll-off cargo ship Lady Mariia (IMO: 9220641), which is under U.S. and Ukrainian sanctions, was attacked by drones in the Mediterranean Sea, according to the head of Ukraine’s Institute for Black Sea Strategic Studies, Andrii Klymenko, who reported that the vessel had been heading toward Syria.
Klymenko published footage of the attack, while a longer video was posted on the Telegram channel of Russian opposition commentator Alexander Nevzorov. The footage shows drones dropping munitions onto the vessel, with a fire breaking out after one explosion. Nevzorov claimed the Lady Mariia was hit 12 times and suggested that the drones had been launched by Ukrainian forces from the territory of Libya. He added that the ship was carrying Iranian weapons and armored vehicles intended for Russia.
Klymenko also hinted that the drones had been launched from Libyan territory, writing: “And it wasn’t us. Those were some nice, unknown drones from Libyan territory. What do we have to do with it?”
Ukrainian authorities have not officially commented on the attack. The number of hits, the origin of the drones, and the nature of the cargo on board have not been independently confirmed. The Ukrainian outlet UNITED24 Media also noted that claims about Iranian weapons and a Libyan launch point were based on Nevzorov’s reporting and had not been independently verified.
According to the vessel tracking platform Starboard Maritime Intelligence, the Lady Mariia left St. Petersburg in early August. The vessel passed through the Strait of Gibraltar on Aug. 29 and then called at the Algerian port of Oran. It later headed east across the Mediterranean. On the evening of Sept. 5, the Lady Mariia stopped transmitting its AIS (Automatic Identification System) signal.
Starboard Maritime Intelligence data also shows that since the spring of 2020, the Lady Mariia has made three calls at the Syrian port of Tartus and three at the Iranian ports of Bandar Abbas and Khorramshahr. The platform also recorded two calls at the Libyan port of Al-Buraika.
Ukraine’s military intelligence agency (HUR) lists the Lady Mariia among the vessels that have been used to transport military cargo and weapons for Russia.
The ship is owned by the Russian company MG-Flot LLC, formerly known as Transmorflot. In May 2022, the U.S. imposed sanctions on Transmorflot and vessels linked to it. The Lady Mariia, which was previously named Stella-Maria, was also placed under U.S. restrictions. Ukraine imposed sanctions on the Lady Mariia on May 23, 2026.
According to HUR, MG-Flot is linked to Astrakhan businessman Dzhamaldin Pashayev, who built his business around the Port of Olya in Russia’s southern Astrakhan Region. The port is seen as one of Russia’s key logistics hubs for the International North-South Transport Corridor, which connects Russia with Iran.

Eiffel Tower reopens after Hindu group apologises for 'sidelining' female staff
The Eiffel Tower reopened Tuesday, after staff walked out over the removal of women colleagues during a visit by a Hindu religious group that later apologised. The iconic Paris monument was forced to close on Monday after staff went on strike to protest the "sidelining" female employees during a recent visit by a Hindu delegation.

The Eiffel Tower reopened Tuesday, an AFP reporter said, after staff walked out over the removal of women colleagues during a visit by a Hindu religious group that later apologised.
Shortly before 9:30 am on Tuesday, visitors were passing through security checkpoints at the foot of the tower, the AFP journalist said. On its website, the Eiffel Tower said the iconic monument was "open today".
Staff at the Eiffel Tower in Paris went on strike on Monday, "shocked" by the exclusion of female employees during a private visit by a Hindu delegation days earlier, according to staff and management.
In a statement issued by the CGT trade union, staff condemned "workplace instructions that led to female employees being sidelined, replaced and rendered invisible on the basis of their gender".
"Some were asked to leave their posts and withdraw to other areas. In some posts they were replaced by men," the statement read. "And all female employees were instructed not to go through or cross certain areas while the delegation was present."

The visit coincided with a cultural boat procession on the Seine organised by the Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) spiritual movement.
The organisation said 'To our knowledge, at no time was access to the Eiffel Tower denied to anyone. Nevertheless, we sincerely apologise for any pain or inconvenience caused.'

BAPS, which is close to Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling conservative Hindu nationalist party, consecrated its first major temple in France on Sunday, near Paris.
The operating company that runs the Eiffel Tower, SETE, said the delegation had requested that the visit be organised in such a way as to limit "interactions with women" and acknowledged that "these conditions should not have been accepted".
The conditions "were not in line with SETE's values, nor with the principles of equality between men and women," the company said, promising to accept the "consequences".
Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire expressed support for the strike in a post on X, describing the exclusion of female workers as "unacceptable" and contrary to the "values that the Eiffel Tower stands for".

The Tower, which receives nearly seven million visitors a year according to its website, was closed all day on Monday, but will open as normal on Tuesday according to a staff representative.
"We are going to shed light on what happened, and we will draw the necessary conclusions," SETE president Ariel Weil, who is also an elected official in Paris, told AFP.
French Equality Minister Aurore Bergé reacted angrily to the incident, writing on X: "In France, we do not ask women to erase themselves. No dogma, no religion is above the laws of the Republic."
Far-right leader Marine Le Pen, an early frontrunner in next year's presidential election, also weighed in, saying France would "never accept that women's presence be 'limited'."
Former PM Gabriel Attal, who is also running for the presidency, said that "in France, no culture, no belief, no religion, nothing and no one can come and dictate to women what their place should be".

Danger remains real despite Israeli wins against Iranian nukes, sources tell 'Post'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
17:08:12 UTC
02:08:12 KST

Despite Israeli wins against Iran’s nuclear program in 2025’s 12 Day War and in early 2026, its potential danger remains real, although not imminent, multiple sources have told The Jerusalem Post.
Among the positives are that Iran is currently not operating centrifuges to enrich uranium, its 60%- and 20%-enriched uranium are not yet easily accessible, and the vast majority of its nuclear facilities were rendered inoperable by the two major rounds of airstrikes, the Post has learned.
Those are no small achievements, setting back Iran’s nuclear program in many ways even more than during “pause” periods from 2003-2007 and from 2015-2018, when large portions of Tehran’s nuclear program were frozen although not dismantled, and other portions were still being clandestinely expanded.
Despite these achievements, the potential nuclear threat remains more serious than was hoped for in the periods immediately after the wars of 2025 and 2026, the Post also understands.
Therefore, while each facet of the nuclear program has been significantly improved for Israel, a gap of concern remains.
On the one hand, the vast majority of Iran’s estimated 20,000 centrifuges have been eliminated. On the other hand, a sizable number of centrifuges have survived deep underground.
Even if only a few hundred advanced IR-6 centrifuges could be salvaged and reconnected to their cascades at some medium-term point, that would be enough, at some future undefined point in time, to secretly weaponize enough uranium for a weapon, multiple sources have told the Post.
Tehran could develop clandestine digging strategy around enriched uranium, sources warn 'Post'
Separately, Tehran could develop a clandestine digging strategy to extract its 60%- and 20%-enriched uranium from underneath the rubble and deep underground in a way that circumvents US and other surveillance, multiple sources have said.
It is public knowledge from regular satellite reports from the Institute for Science and International Security and others that the Iranian regime is constantly adding structures to hide certain areas from ongoing satellite coverage.
In these reports, the Iranians are portrayed as digging in a wide number of areas, many of which are at a distance from the primary portion of any of the nuclear facilities that were attacked.
It could take months or even years of digging underground from a distance to smuggle out the 60%- or 20%-enriched uranium. But the possibility of secretly transferring as little as one-tenth of it might be a sufficient basis for an eventual nuclear bomb, according to the sources.
IAEA has been blind to Iran's nuclear program since 12-day June 2025 war, Grossi says
Keeping tabs on all of these issues is harder than ever in some ways. The International Atomic Energy Agency remains completely blind regarding Iran’s nuclear program since at least June 2025, IAEA Director-General Rafael Grossi told the agency’s Board of Governors on Monday.
“As stated in the report, [the] agency has neither received information from Iran regarding the status of its declared nuclear material or facilities nor had access to any of those facilities to conduct in-field verification activities,” he said. “Therefore, the agency was unable to discharge its safeguards responsibilities under the NPT [Non-Proliferation Treaty] Safeguards Agreement at declared nuclear facilities in Iran.”
People familiar with the matter said they did not expect Iran to outsmart Israeli and American intelligence, but they also do not want to underestimate the Iranians’ frequently shocking resourcefulness.
According to the sources, this may mean that the crux of keeping Tehran’s nuclear program “in the box” may shift again to some extent from uranium enrichment to holding back any weapons development activities.
Although not in the spotlight as much, one of the main focuses of Israeli airstrikes on Iran’s nuclear facilities was not only the enrichment sites but also those for converting enriched uranium into uranium metal, as well as for developing hemispheres to place them on a nuclear warhead.
Absent these and other assets, even a significant volume of weaponized uranium would not really help Iran because it would be unable to launch the uranium on a missile that could reach Israeli territory from a distance of 1,000 or more kilometers.
Preventing Iran from rebuilding such weapons facilities is now one of the primary missions of Israeli intelligence, people familiar with the matter have told the Post. So far, Tehran has failed to achieve any real progress in this area.
In essence, Iran’s nuclear program has been far more damaged than some critics have said. Yet there are also potential vulnerabilities for Israel regarding the surviving remainder of the program that senior Israeli defense officials and politicians have openly acknowledged immediately after each operation.
This means that Tehran’s nuclear program has been delayed by some years in some ways, along with its ability to rebuild the parts of the program that were struck. In other ways, however, Iranian ingenuity means that Israel remains threatened, even if the danger is reduced and less imminent.

====================================================================================================

A Reform UK without Nigel Farage used to be unthinkable. Not any more | Gaby Hinsliff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
17:08:06 UTC
02:08:06 KST

Nigel Farage didn’t know. He wasn’t told.
Sure, he was right there at the table when the undercover reporter he believed to be a rich American’s son spelled out very clearly how he hoped to channel his father’s money to Reform, in ways that certainly don’t sound too lawful.
But he wasn’t listening, you understand. God forbid that the man who insists his party takes compliance very seriously, and who never stops warning that the establishment is out to get him by any means possible, should actually pay attention to the details of a donation offered bang in the middle of a byelection that was fought over – of all the luck, eh? – some other questionable donations.
Farage’s defence is essentially that he was present but not involved, as Jeremy Corbyn once famously said of attending an event where someone laid a commemorative wreath for members of the terrorist group behind the 1972 Munich Olympics atrocity.
It didn’t work for Corbyn, any more than claiming to have tried cannabis but never inhaling worked an age ago for Bill Clinton, in part because some people just didn’t believe it. But mostly, perhaps, because critics found it revealing even that Corbyn would be at the kind of gathering where such things might happen. Most aspirant prime ministers take good care to avoid moving in circles where someone might end up venerating terrorists, or explaining exactly how they intend to get around the law. For good reason, it turns out.
What we are being asked to accept, in the instance caught on camera, is that at best Farage has been astonishingly sloppy; that he just turned up, tuned out, thanked the guy without even really knowing what for, and then went happily on his way. Take Farage at his own word and he is describing someone curiously semi-detached. Someone who, despite repeatedly claiming his enemies will stop at nothing to stitch him up, puzzlingly doesn’t seem to take such basic precautions against entrapment as noticing what’s actually going on around him. Someone for whom fighting a byelection in which nobody else of note is standing, bar a talking bin, is apparently so all-consuming that he can’t possibly be expected to concentrate on talking to donors as well.
If that degree of walking and chewing gum is a stretch, imagine what a shock running the country might be. No wonder some in Reform are starting to ask themselves if, deep down, that’s what he even wants.
What would Reform look like without Nigel Farage? Once upon a time that would have been a ridiculous question – without him, it would simply fall apart – but the party now is not quite what it used to be. Among the faithful, the fact he doesn’t seem to take the job too seriously is still part of his charm, and many Reform supporters will be nothing but indignant on his behalf at the undercover tactics used to catch him out.
But there are also people in Reform these days who have seen the very real possibility of seizing power to enact an agenda not seen before in Britain, just as Alternative für Deutschland is starting to do in Germany and as the National Rally’s Jordan Bardella (the star turn at Reform’s party conference this year) and Marine Le Pen threaten to do next year in France. They won’t want to let that opportunity slip through their fingers.
Having lost its lead in the polls, Reform finds itself ironically in a version of the dilemma Labour faced a few months ago: torn between those who think recovery depends on tacking left (in this case towards Tory voters who are Reform-curious but worry that it seems too extreme or sleazy) or tacking right (towards Rupert Lowe’s Restore, now consistently taking small but damaging chunks out of them, and other far-right groupings). Events like last weekend’s sinister black-shirted, paramilitary-style show of force in Dover by the previously little known Patriot Platform group – which even the government took a surprisingly long time to condemn in the decisive terms that chief secretary to the Treasury Emma Reynolds eventually did on Monday morning, after what looked like copycat demonstrations in Portsmouth – may now start to push those tensions into the open.
Are these their people, or not? Having ripped open Pandora’s box by saying what others would not on immigration, there would be a grim irony in Reform struggling to deal with the furies unleashed, if only the whole thing wasn’t so frightening for everyone else. Farage ended up calling the Dover mob “disgusting” because of their balaclavas, while suggesting he absolutely shared their anger about small boat crossings (now, of course, down to a seven-year low). But is covering your face at a protest the only line Reform won’t cross?
Some of its supporters clearly do want a leader prepared to say what Farage won’t, a niche that Zia Yusuf, Reform’s home affairs spokesperson, evidently aims to fill. Others more recently arrived from the old Conservative party might prefer a leader who treads a hard line on immigration, welfare and woke, but with some rougher edges sanded off (or so Robert Jenrick clearly hopes). Crucially, some in both camps will see the departure of close aide Dan Jukes – who along with head of policy, James Orr, has taken the rap for this latest donor scandal, though both deny wrongdoing – as an opportunity to replace Farage’s loyal and protective sidekicks with people less tied to him personally.
Historically, anyone daring to fly this close to Farage’s sun has got their wings scorched. But what if that sun doesn’t burn quite so brightly any more? What if the political judgment that always served him so well in the past is now fractionally off-key? For now, the idea that there could be an election any minute – forced, perhaps, by some future bond market crisis – is perhaps imposing a measure of discipline on the party. But what if that imaginary snap election never materialises?
For now, these are all still very much “what ifs”. Given his miraculous capacity for resurrection, it is a mistake to underestimate Farage or count him out when he is down.
But until recently, even the idea of Reform without its leader seemed ridiculous; he was Reform, to the point that without him it would cease to meaningfully exist. In the current climate, that assumption may no longer be safe. Bardella, after all, got his big break when Le Pen was brought down by a financial scandal. It’s time the other parties thought harder about the shape Reform might take without its maker, rather than assuming the battle begins and ends with him.
- 
  Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist

Ukrainian Bars jet-powered drones to be manufactured in Europe
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
20:08:00 EEST
02:08:00 KST

Ukrainian Bars jet-powered drones to be manufactured in Europe
A joint venture manufacturing Ukrainian Bars jet-powered drones will begin operating in Europe in early September.
Source: the developer of the Bars UAV in an interview with RBC-Ukraine
Details: According to the production plans, the plant's first products will be supplied to Ukrainian forces from 10 October.
The developer explained that the only constraint on scaling up drone production is the lead time for supplying the turbojet engines used in the Bars drones, which the company purchases "around the world".
"But nothing is currently preventing such scaling, especially following the state's provision of an opportunity to establish joint ventures. With the launch of official and transparent exports, we see only opportunities to increase and expand production capacity," the developer said.
The Bars jet-powered drone has a strike range of up to 1,000 km and can carry a warhead weighing up to 60 kg. The UAV can reach speeds of more than 700 km/h. The Bars operates as a modular platform that can be used for long-range strikes, mid-range strikes and short-range strikes, depending on the amount of fuel and the weight of the warhead.
According to the developer, more than 74% of the Bars drones are locally produced. The company has also completed final tests of an engine of its own manufacture. The UAV uses AI for terminal guidance towards the target.
Background: In July, Ukraine and Germany signed an agreement on the joint production of Bars drones. At the first stage of the project, the German side will finance the production of the drones, and all equipment manufactured will be handed over to the defence forces of Ukraine.

Record fuel price rise sparks protests in Portugal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
17:07:58 UTC
02:07:58 KST

A slow-drive protest and blaring car horns marked the day petrol and diesel prices rose again, with fuel costs hitting record highs across Europe.
Portugal woke up to another rise in fuel prices which, in the case of diesel, reached an all-time high. This time, the price increase, which has been occurring throughout the year, was marked by protests on the country's roads.
In the morning, drivers staged a mass horn protest on the 25 April Bridge, the crossing that links Lisbon to the city of Almada on the south bank of the Tagus river.
At the same time, further south, a go-slow march towards Galp's refinery in Sines, in the district of Setúbal, was getting under way. The protest, organised via WhatsApp and social media, was still ongoing after lunchtime and had no scheduled end time.
Images on social media showed cars with Portuguese flags on their bonnets, sounding their horns. According to the Lusa news agency, protesters were also carrying placards reading "Enough of rising fuel prices" and "families cannot take any more". The GNR (National Republican Guard) told the agency that between 60 and 100 vehicles took part.
Petrol at highest level since Ukraine invasion
According to projections by theAutomobile Club of Portugal (ACP) (source in Portuguese), diesel rose on Monday by 15 cents (to 2.169 euros per litre) and petrol increased by 12 cents (to 2.142 euros per litre).
These amounts do not take into account the reduction in the Tax on Petroleum Products (ISP), applied by the government on an exceptional basis, which set the increases at 12 cents for diesel and 9 cents for petrol.
This is the highest diesel price ever, according to calculations by Dinheiro Vivo (source in Portuguese). In the case of petrol, it is the highest level since the energy crisis triggered by Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Portugal among countries with highest prices
Fuel prices have been rising across Europe throughout the year. In Germany too, the Frankfurter Allgemeine (source in Portuguese) explains that fuel prices have hit a record high, with petrol surpassing the previous record of 2.203 euros per litre, set in March 2022.
But Portugal is among the countries with the highest fuel prices. Thefuel-prices website (source in Portuguese), which aggregates fuel prices in 21 European countries, showed on Monday that Portugal ranks 19th for the most expensive petrol. Only France and Denmark had higher prices. As for diesel, Portugal's position improves to 17th place, ahead of the United Kingdom, Italy, France and Denmark.
The Weekly Oil Prices (source in Portuguese), a weekly report from the European Union covering the bloc's 27 countries, published on Thursday, puts Portugal in 20th place for petrol prices including tax. Of the 27, petrol was most expensive in Denmark and cheapest in Malta. For diesel including tax, Portugal ranked 19th. Denmark was the country with the most expensive diesel in the bloc and Malta the cheapest.
Minister says rises are in line with Europe
At the end of the day, the Portuguese Minister for Environment and Energy, Maria da Graça Carvalho, held a press conference. Maria da Graça Carvalho said that the increase in fuel prices is in line with the rest of Europe, drawing a comparison with France and presenting Spain as an exception.
The minister listed the government's measures to soften the rise in fuel prices, namely the reduction of ISP, the extension of the solidarity gas cylinder scheme and support measures for the agricultural and social sectors. Responding to the secretary-general of the Socialist Party (PS), Maria da Graça Carvalho also said that "the government is not profiting from this fuel crisis".
Previously, the rise in prices had led the minister to request a study from the Energy Services Regulatory Authority (ERSE). But the study, published in mid-August, found "no evidence of operators taking advantage". It also said that no "rockets and feathers" phenomenon was observed, with prices that rise quickly and fall slowly.
"The results therefore do not support the view that price decreases are passed through persistently more slowly or less fully than price increases," the study says.
ERSE also explained the price difference with Spain by pointing to taxation. But it stressed that in Portugal the tax burden has remained constant, "in line with most countries in the European Union and the eurozone".
Hormuz and refining capacity
The rise in fuel prices in Europe has been linked to the conflict in the Middle East and the blockage in the Strait of Hormuz, which has had a disruptive effect on trade routes.
But experts also point to limited refining capacity, even when crude is available. This situation mainly affects diesel.
In terms of taxation, an extraordinary tax on oil companies' profits is now on the table. According to AFP, the ministers of Portugal, Germany, Italy, Austria, Poland and Spain have sent a letter to Ireland's finance minister so that the issue can be discussed at the next meeting of finance ministers. The meeting is scheduled for 18 and 19 September in Ireland, which holds the rotating presidency of the European Union.

Haiti gangs shift operations into countryside, report says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
17:07:01 UTC
02:07:01 KST

Haiti gangs shift operations into countryside, report says
Sept 7 - Haiti's armed gangs are increasingly expanding from Port-au-Prince into rural areas, adopting hit-and-run tactics including kidnappings, cattle theft and roadblocks while security and political responses remain focused on the capital, a new report said on Monday.
The analysis, published by the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime's Haiti Observatory, said the shift amounts to more than an extension of urban gang activity into the countryside.
• Gangs are using small, mobile units to carry out rapid raids, harass communities and move between areas serving as sanctuaries and targets, the report said. The approach allows armed groups to project influence and disrupt daily life without permanently occupying territory.
• The report cited the recent attack on Kenscoff, a mountainous community outside Port-au-Prince, as an example of the changing nature of gang violence. The assault killed dozens of people and involved a mass kidnapping, it said.
• It also highlighted worsening insecurity in Artibonite, one of Haiti's main agricultural regions, where gangs have targeted communities, transport routes and farmland.
• The growing violence in rural areas poses a challenge for Haitian security forces, which the report said lack the personnel, equipment and training needed to counter highly mobile armed groups across mountainous and dispersed terrain.
• The report said a security response alone would be insufficient, calling for measures to protect farmers, restore local economies and address long-running land and community disputes, alongside efforts to disarm and reintegrate gang members. REUTERS

Zelensky: FREYJA anti-ballistic program to be discussed at Staff meeting
According to Ukrinform, the Head of State announced this on Facebook.
“In the near future, there will be meetings with partners attended by states and companies involved in developing the joint FREYJA anti-ballistic program. We are also working to develop our additional deep-strike capabilities,” Zelensky said.
He said that the results of this work will be reviewed at a meeting of the Staff. The President also said that National Security and Defense Council Secretary Ihor Klymenko had reported on preparing the agenda for the Staff meeting.
“The NSDC Secretary is overseeing the implementation of decisions, and it is important that our previous decisions on countering Russian attack drones and accelerating the relevant production processes be 100 percent effective,” Zelensky stressed.
He thanked developers and manufacturers for their work. According to the President, Klymenko also briefed him on the changes in the NSDC’s work, securing the necessary resources, and personnel matters.
As reported by Ukrinform, Ukraine and its European partners have agreed to jointly develop the FREYJA anti-ballistic missile system, which is intended to combine Ukrainian missile technologies with European radars, sensors and command-and-control systems.
The project already involves Eurosam, the manufacturer of the SAMP/T system, as well as Leonardo, Thales and Saab.
Ukrainian company Fire Point, which developed the Flamingo cruise missile, has become the project’s lead industrial partner. Last month, the company announced an agreement with German defense company HENSOLDT to supply a radar for the system.

AfD victory exposes divisions in France’s far-right as National Rally stays silent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
17:03:48 UTC
02:03:48 KST

France’s far-right responded in markedly different ways to the AfD’s sweeping victory in Germany’s regional elections, with the National Rally (RN) maintaining a conspicuous silence on Monday while Éric Zemmour’s Reconquête openly celebrated the result.
France's National Rally party reacted to the victory of Germany’s far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party with a noticeable silence on Monday, a move that reflects its complicated ties to the party.
Marine Le Pen and Jordan Bardella — who are respectively campaigning to be France's next president and prime minister — made no mention of the AfD after the party took 43.8% of votes in Saxony-Anhalt’s elections, racing ahead of Christian Democratic Union, Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s party, which secured 17.2%.
Meanwhile, the Reconquête party — which is positioned further to the right than the National Rally and sits in the same group as the AfD in the European Parliament — welcomed the victory, reflecting political divergences within France's far-right.
Although the National Rally's leading figures have yet to comment publicly, other MPs from the party have weighed in. Bardella had also addressed the issue before the vote, when reporters at the Ambrosetti Forum — an annual economic and geopolitical conference held in Italy — questioned him about the prospect of the National Rally renewing ties with the AfD on Saturday.
In response, he said that this was not "planned," but underlined that "the electoral pressure exerted by the AfD in Germany has helped shift the political landscape within [Chancellor Friedrich] Merz's government, as Germany reinstated border controls a few months ago."
A campaign to recover the party's image
The silence at the top of the party is not surprising, given that Marine Le Pen has spent over a decade working to normalise the image of the National Rally (formerly known as the National Front), both at home and abroad, as part of a campaign to move away from the overt racism and antisemitism promoted by her father, Jean-Marie Le Pen, the party’s founder.
At present, her party is leading in the polls, with around 34 to 36% of respondents stating they intend to vote for her in the first round of the presidential elections scheduled for April 2027, according to a poll by IPSOS/BVA published by the French newspaper Le Parisien on Saturday.
National Rally politician and Patriots for Europe (PfE) MEP Pierre-Romain Thionnet told Euronews that the AfD's result "should not come as a surprise to anyone", arguing that its victory was vested in issues which mainstream parties have not worked to solve: "mass immigration, loss of national identity, and social and industrial decline."
According to the MEP, the result reflects "the collapse of the mainstream parties in favour of political forces that truly represent the aspirations of the European people."
Despite this, he ensured that the National Rally's decision to "no longer be an ally of the AfD" in the European Parliament would remain "unchanged."
"Several members of that political party continue to hold positions on historical and remembrance issues that we find unacceptable, and because there are very significant differences on other issues, such as foreign policy," said Thionnet.
The National Rally party and AfD were formerly part of the Identity and Democracy group, along with Italy’s League and Austria’s Freedom Party (FPÖ), among others. However, things came to a head ahead of the 2024 European Parliamentary elections, following a series of controversies involving some of the AfD's senior figures.
This included comments made by Maximilian Krah, the AfD's lead candidate in the Parliamentary elections, who stated that membership of the Nazi SS did not automatically make someone a criminal, during an interview with Italian newspaper La Repubblica.
The Identity and Democracy group voted to exclude the AfD in May 2024, just weeks before the European Parliament elections. Following the election, the AfD helped form a new far-right group, Europe of Sovereign Nations (ESN), which was formally established in July 2024.
Echoing these points, another MEP from the Patriots for Europe group told Euronews that "nothing will move before the French election," stating that "no one wants to be associated with the AfD, even though we have some points in common and cooperate on many topics."
Reconquête comes out in support of the AfD
The National Rally party may be keeping quiet, but the Reconquête party, part of the same political group as the AfD in the European Parliament (Europe of Sovereign Nations), came out in support of the election results.
In an X post shared on Sunday evening, MEP Sarah Knafo described the results as "historic," stating that "the European peoples have shown a great deal of patience. Today, they want to take their destiny back into their own hands. An entire continent is rising up."
Meanwhile, Éric Zemmour, the leader of Reconquête, who has said he will wait until December to announce whether he will run in France's 2027 presidential election, qualified the results as "the hour of truth." In the first round of France's 2022 presidential election, Marine Le Pen took 23.15% of the votes, while the hard-right secured 7.07%.
The Reconquête party aligns itself with the Alternative for Germany (AfD) on a number of points — notably on the concept of “remigration” — which the National Rally avoids endorsing explicitly, instead presenting its policy as favouring the systematic expulsion of illegal immigrants and foreign criminals.
According to Gilles Ivaldi, researcher and professor of politics at Sciences Po Paris, the political strategy adopted by Reconquête is more similar to the AfD's than the National Rally's.
"The AfD expresses itself in a more radical and openly far-right manner, if I may say so, whereas the National Rally is currently trying to tone down its platform significantly in order to win the presidential election, because they know that to do this, they need to normalise their image," Ivaldi told Euronews.
"Ahead of the last presidential elections in 2022, we saw two different political strategies emerge: Le Pen continued to try to normalise her image and de-demonise her party, whereas Zemmour pursued a much more aggressive strategy of radicalisation and reclaiming certain political themes."
"I think we need to be careful not to treat the National Rally and Reconquête as completely different, because they share many common views on migration, crime, and a whole range of issues concerning Ukraine and France's proximity to Russia."

Under the new system, people buying more than their quota of 110 liters (29 gallons) of gasoline a month now must pay 100,000 rials (about 7 cents) per liter, or twice as much as they have been paying since December.

The move appears to be part of Tehran's efforts to increase pressure on Washington in response to the US blockade, as renewed attacks on shipping have pushed oil prices higher.
But where will Iran's new restricted zone be, what could happen to ships entering it and what does the move mean for the already heavily restricted Strait of Hormuz?
The Israeli military could establish a "grey line" in southern Lebanon that would effectively see it pull back closer to the border while maintaining its freedom of movement to strike.
According to a report by Israel’s public broadcaster, Kan, the security establishment is considering a significant reduction in forces deployed in southern Lebanon and a withdrawal from some forward positions, in exchange for establishing a new security zone extending three to four kilometres inside Lebanese territory from the border.
IAEA head Rafael Grossi on Monday said giving the UN nuclear agency access to key nuclear facilities in Iran would have "positive repercussions" for the Islamic Republic, as a draft resolution seen by AFP proposes referring Tehran to the UN Security Council.
The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has not had access to key nuclear facilities in Iran since Israel, joined by the United States, launched a 12-day conflict in June 2025 that included strikes on nuclear sites.

Israel hit swathes of south Lebanon hard during the Middle East war that erupted with joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran, and its forces continue to occupy what it calls a "security zone".

Finland has fenced itself off from Russia: Helsinki has completed a large-scale 200-kilometer project
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
20:00:30 EEST
02:00:30 KST

Finland has fenced itself off from Russia: Helsinki has completed a large-scale 200-kilometer project
Kyiv • UNN
Finland has built about 200 kilometers of barriers along its border with Russia at a cost of €356 million. The system includes fences, cameras, and sensors.
Finland has completed the construction of approximately 200 kilometers of barrier structures along its border with russia. UNN reports this, citing Finnish media and government sources.
The project, implemented over several years following a sharp deterioration in the security situation and cases of instrumentalized migration by the russian federation, cost approximately €356 million.
Details
The official project completion ceremony took place on September 7 in the area of the Nuijamaa border crossing near Lappeenranta. It was attended by Finnish Minister of the Interior Mari Rantanen, Border Guard leadership, and representatives of contractor companies.
Finland's total land border with russia is approximately 1,340 km long. The fence covers approximately 200 km, or about 15% of the border. At the same time, this is not a continuous structure but dozens of separate sections in areas that the Finnish authorities consider most vulnerable to illegal or mass border crossings.
About 140 km of barriers were built in the southeast of the country and in the Kymenlaakso region, another 35 km in North Karelia, and approximately 25 km in Kainuu, Koillismaa, and Lapland. The main fence is approximately 4.5 meters high. The system also includes surveillance cameras, lighting, sensors, loudspeakers, patrol roads, and a strip cleared of vegetation along the border. The technical equipment is designed to automatically notify border guards of suspicious activity.
The project began to be prepared in autumn 2022, and construction of the first pilot section near Imatra began in spring 2023. Large-scale work got underway in 2024. According to the latest estimates, the total construction cost was approximately €356 million, about €22 million less than the initially allocated budget. Annual maintenance of the system is estimated at approximately €1.5 million.
One of the main reasons cited by the Finnish authorities for constructing the fence was the threat of so-called instrumentalized migration. In autumn 2023, citizens of third countries began arriving en masse at border crossing points from the russian side without the necessary documents.
According to Reuters, approximately 1,300 asylum seekers crossed the russian-Finnish border between August and December 2023. Helsinki accused moscow of deliberately directing migrants toward the border for the purpose of political pressure. russia denied the accusations. Following this, Finland closed the land border crossing points on its border with the russian federation. They remain closed today. In June 2026, the Finnish government decided to maintain the restrictions indefinitely due to the risk of a recurrence of instrumentalized migration.
In addition, at the beginning of September, the Finnish government proposed extending until the end of 2028 the validity of a special border security law that, under exceptional circumstances, allows the temporary restriction of the acceptance of applications for international protection in certain areas.
Minister of the Interior Mari Rantanen also did not rule out that Finland might build additional sections of fencing in the future and secure funding for them from the European Union.
Recall
A month earlier, Spain introduced border controls at all air and sea crossings with Italy due to a dispute over migrants. Italy had previously suspended the Schengen Agreement, citing an influx of migrants to Ceuta.

US now accesses more than half of Australia’s military bases: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:58:23 UTC
01:58:23 KST

Esra Tekin
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
The US military and its defense companies have access to 110 military facilities in Australia, or more than half nationwide, The Guardian reported on Monday, citing data compiled by the Nautilus Institute, a California-based think tank.
The data shows that the US military controls 17 facilities on the Australian mainland and has access to 75 military facilities operated by Australia while American defense companies have access to a further 18 facilities.
The number of military facilities in Australia that are either controlled by or accessible to the US military and American defense companies has reached 110, accounting for more than half of all military facilities in the country.
Richard Tanter, honorary professor of political and social studies at the University of Melbourne, who prepared the study, said this was not a matter of penetration but of pervasiveness, noting that more than half of the defense facilities examined had some level of American access.
Tanter argued that for more than a decade, the US has been developing the capacity to use Australia for intensive military operations in the event of a potential war with China, while Australia has fully “aligned itself with American strategic planning.”
The 92 defense facilities accessible to the US military are reportedly used for intelligence gathering, access to satellite data, interception of communications, training, deployment of military assets, and as logistics hubs storing weapons, ammunition, and fuel.
The joint US-Australian intelligence facility at Pine Gap, north-central Australia, is reported to play a critical role in identifying targets for US military strikes.
It hosts a ground control station for signals intelligence satellites, a relay ground station for early-warning missile launch systems, and a facility used to intercept foreign satellite communications.
Under a force posture agreement, US forces and contractors are granted unimpeded access to and use of agreed military facilities, provided that Australia’s sovereignty is fully respected.
The US military presence is expected to expand further next year, with as many as 1,200 US personnel set to operate from the HMAS Stirling naval base on Garden Island in Western Australia.
The Australian government, however, says the presence of American troops will constitute a “rotation” rather than a permanent base.
Former Defense Minister Christopher Pyne said the AUKUS security and defense partnership between Australia, the US, and the UK is “much more than submarine procurement.”
He said the partnership effectively creates a new base for US submarines in the Indian Ocean, providing the United States with a “huge strategic advantage.”
Current Defense Minister Richard Marles, meanwhile, said the “US presence is growing” in Australia and stressed that this is important for national security.
He said the American military presence on the continent would increase over the next several years.
 
Australians’ trust in US declines
Separately, Australians’ trust in the US has reportedly declined.
According to a Lowy Institute poll, the proportion of Australians who trust the US to act responsibly in international affairs has fallen to 31%, while only 21% trust US President Donald Trump to do the right thing in world affairs.
A survey by the Australia Institute found that 59% of Australians believe the country’s interests would be better protected through a more independent foreign policy rather than a closer alliance with the United States.
Emma Shortis, director of the Australia Institute’s international and security affairs program, argued that Australia’s increasing integration with the US military is progressively weakening the country’s capacity to make independent and sovereign decisions.
Albert Palazzo of the University of New South Wales also argued that the accelerating US military buildup poses a risk to Australia’s security, accusing the government of “waltzing” the country toward a war between the US and China.
Vince Scappatura, the author of a book on the US lobby and Australian defense policy, described US access to bases across Australia as a “second wave of colonization” and said Australia was increasingly becoming a “forward element” for the projection of US military power in the region.

IAEA urges Iran to re-engage as Western powers mull UNSC referral
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:57:58 UTC
01:57:58 KST

International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) head Rafael Grossi has said that giving the UN nuclear agency access to key nuclear facilities in Iran would have "positive repercussions" for Tehran, as a draft resolution reportedly proposes referring Tehran to the UN Security Council.
"The best, shortest way for a positive outcome is for Iran to engage with us," Grossi told a press conference on Monday after opening the quarterly meeting of the IAEA board of governors.
"If Iran engages with us in a serious dialogue, we can start getting access. I can guarantee to you that this will have very, very positive repercussions," he said.
The IAEA has not had access to key nuclear facilities in Iran since Israel, joined by the United States, launched a 12-day war in June 2025 that included strikes on nuclear sites.
Nuclear facilities have also been hit in the latest war, which erupted on February 28, and the IAEA has repeatedly urged access.
UNSC resolution
A resolution drafted by the United States, Britain, France and Germany expected to be submitted and voted on this week seeks to refer Iran to the UN Security Council for failing to comply with its nuclear reporting obligations.
The draft asks Grossi to "submit this resolution to all members of the agency and to the Security Council and the General Assembly of the United Nations," AFP reported.
Asked whether such a referral was the right course of action, Grossi said that "my job with Iran continues, irrespective of the resolution".
Before the June 2025 strikes, the IAEA calculated that Iran possessed approximately 440 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60 percent, which is close to the 90 percent needed to make a bomb and well above the 3.67 percent limit set by a 2015 now-defunct agreement with Iran.
Since June 2025, the fate of this stockpile has remained uncertain.
In a statement ahead of the meeting, Grossi called the lack of contact with Iran "regrettable".
"These issues are not going to disappear until we address them, until we have the necessary access, until we can return," he said.
Iran's mission to the UN on X called the draft resolution a "new desperate action" that would bring "no benefit".
In June, the board approved a Western resolution demanding that Iran immediately provide information and give access to its uranium stockpile and production facilities.

Ukraine Turns Russian Stronghold Into a Trap, Retakes Rybine Near Huliaipole
Ukrainian forces have retaken the village of Rybine near Huliaipole after a months-long operation that first severed Russian supply routes before troops moved in to clear the settlement, Ukraine’s 1st Separate Assault Regiment reported on September 7.
Russian forces captured Rybine on January 20 and subsequently turned the village into an important defensive position in the Huliaipole sector.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
By summer, however, Ukrainian troops had begun systematically dismantling the Russian position rather than launching an immediate frontal assault.
The first stage focused on logistics. Troops from the regiment’s 2nd Assault Battalion cut a key supply route used by Russian forces to bring ammunition, food and fuel into Rybine.
Once that artery was disrupted, the Russian units inside the village became increasingly isolated. Reinforcing the position and maintaining regular supplies became considerably more difficult, while Ukraine also restricted Russian attempts to move additional troops into the cut-off settlement.
Ukrainian forces then moved to the final stage of the operation, clearing Russian troops from Rybine itself.
On July 30, Ukrainian soldiers raised the national flag over the village, marking its return to Ukrainian control.
The 1st Assault Regiment stressed that Rybine was not retaken in a single assault. Instead, the operation relied on gradually weakening the Russian position by disrupting its logistics, limiting reinforcement routes, and only then moving to clear the settlement.
Previously, reports emerged that Russian forces would need more than six additional years to capture the remaining Ukrainian-controlled territory in the Donetsk region if their current rate of advance continues, putting the potential timeline well beyond Moscow’s stated goal of taking the entire region by the end of 2026.
