AIDC, Bombardier sign 20-year deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:40:13 UTC
01:40:13 KST

Taiwanese aircraft maker Aerospace Industrial Development Corp (AIDC, 漢翔航空) yesterday announced that it has secured a 20-year partnership agreement with Canada-based Bombardier Inc.
The two companies held a ceremony in Taipei yesterday to exchange signed copies of the agreement, launching the 20-year partnership under which AIDC would supply cockpit and forward fuselage structural components for Bombardier’s super-midsize Challenger 3500 business jets, the Taiwanese company said.
The agreement represents a new milestone in cooperation between the two companies, which dates back to 1999, with the Taiwanese supplier having provided rear fuselage structural components for more than 1,000 Challenger 3500 aircraft, it said.
Photo: CNA
The forward fuselage structural components for the Challenger 3500 require a high level of technical expertise, it said, adding that Bombardier in April completed a review of the Taiwanese supplier’s production capabilities.
AIDC said that the agreement represents the most significant development to date for its civil aviation business.
Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin (龔明鑫), who witnessed the exchange, said AIDC’s supply of fuselage structural components to international clients, including Bombardier, demonstrated international confidence in “Made in Taiwan” products.
AIDC has demonstrated its ability to produce fuselage structural components, Kung said, adding that, by expanding its technological capabilities to include forward fuselage structures and securing the long-term agreement with Bombardier, Taiwan has become one of the few countries capable of supplying fuselage structural components for large and medium-sized aircraft.
Amid restructuring of the global aerospace supply chain, many international aircraft makers are seeking partners, and AIDC has demonstrated its capabilities as a resilient supplier, he said.
Given the value of the Bombardier orders, AIDC is expected to enlist other Taiwanese suppliers to help fulfill the orders, he said, adding that the agreement is expected to benefit Taiwan’s aerospace supply chain.
The forward fuselage is the most technically demanding section of the airframe because of its complex shape and the need to meet cabin pressure and airtightness requirements, as well as its integration of the cockpit structure, passenger doors and numerous system interfaces, AIDC said.
Only about five suppliers worldwide have this capability, it said.
The company added that it expects to deliver structural components for at least 500 Challenger 3500 fuselages to Bombardier over 20 years.
Eric Filion, Bombardier’s executive vice president for programs and supply chain, said that AIDC has served as a critical supplier to the Canadian company for many years and that trust is the most important key to the cooperation.
The latest agreement with AIDC reflects the long-standing and stable relationship between the two companies, Filion said, adding that Bombardier will continue to cooperate with qualified suppliers worldwide to meet customer expectations for quality, performance and reliability.

FAA investigating cause of fatal crash in Miami
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:40:12 UTC
01:40:12 KST

US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) investigators yesterday were detailing their plans for determining what caused an Amazon.com Inc cargo jet to barrel off a runway at Miami International Airport, killing at least five people and injuring five others as it struck vehicles and was engulfed in flames.
The aircraft overran the runway at about 2pm on Sunday after arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico, and plowed across a road used by warehouse workers and other businesses that surround the airport. Five people were killed, three critically injured and two others hospitalized with less severe injuries, officials said.
It was not immediately clear if the pilots survived or those killed were all in vehicles when the plane struck.
Photo: AFP
The crash, which sent thick black smoke billowing into the sky, trapped the pilot and copilot in the cockpit and some occupants in cars, Miami-Dade Rescue Fire Chief Ray Jadallah said.
The agency said crews also had to extricate a person who was trapped under a vehicle.
The National Transportation Safety Board Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy was to hold a news conference yesterday, the agency said.
Among the factors investigators are likely to consider is whether the plane flew too far before touching down, experts said.
Typically, the landing zone is within the first 3,000 feet (914m) of a runway.
Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said if it was beyond that area, the plane should have aborted the landing and gone around for another attempt.
Mary Schiavo, who is a pilot and former inspector general of the US Department of Transportation, said video posted online shows the Amazon plane floating above the runway for an extended period without flaring the nose upward to force the main landing gear onto the ground.
It was not raining at the time, but dark storm clouds loomed and strong winds were reported. Schiavo said that if the plane had a tail wind, that could have contributed to it floating further down the runway.
“A tail wind would certainly add to your troubles if you’ve already given up a good chunk of the runway by not touching down and landing right away,” Schiavo said.
The Miami airport is not equipped with arresting systems that the FAA says have been installed at more than 120 airports nationwide to safely stop planes that do go past the end of a runway. Those beds of lightweight, crushable material at the end of a runway have been credited by the FAA with helping save at least 497 lives aboard planes that overran runways.
The crash halted flights at the busy travel hub for much of the afternoon. About 200 emergency personnel responded, finding the plane with heavy flames and smoke from a complex engine compartment fire, the department said. Firefighters used foam from specialized airport firefighting units to extinguish the fire, and crews were still dealing with a fuel leak on the plane hours later.
The Prime Air plane came to rest beside a roadway near two semitrucks, images showed. The aircraft appeared to be resting on its belly and was largely intact despite the fire.
The flight had been operated by 21 Air, a cargo carrier based in North Carolina. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was originally built to carry passengers and flew for several airlines for more than two decades before being converted to a cargo plane in 2015, according to flight-tracking site Flightradar24.
Schiavo said the NTSB will also closely examine the maintenance history of this plane — particularly since it has a history of foreign ownership in the past, including by a Russian company.
More than 160 flights were canceled and nearly 325 delayed by late Sunday, according to FlightAware, a Web site that tracks flight disruptions. Officials from Orlando International Airport, more than 320km north of Miami, said some flights were diverted there.
Amazon said in a statement that it would cooperate with any investigation.
“We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami International Airport,” the company said. “Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss.”

對話 Dialogue
清清：華華，你覺得你最好的朋友是誰？
Qīngqing: Huáhua, nǐ juéde nǐ zuìhǎo de péngyou shì shéi?
Photo: Unsplash 照片：Unsplash
華華：坦白說，以前我應該會說是你，但現在可能是AI。
Huáhua: Tǎnbái shuō, yǐqián wǒ yīnggāi huì shuō shì nǐ, dàn xiànzài kěnéng shì AI.
清清：謝謝你喔！其實我可以理解啦！你也每天都用AI嗎？
Qīngqing: Xièxie nǐ o! Qíshí wǒ kěyǐ lǐjiě la! Nǐ yě měitiān dōu yòng AI ma?
華華：對啊！我有什麼問題都會問問它的想法和意見，也會請它幫我找資料。
Huáhua: Duì a! Wǒ yǒu shénme wèntí dōu huì wènwen tā de xiǎngfǎ hé yìjiàn, yě huì qǐng tā bāng wǒ zhǎo zīliào.
清清：可是有時候我會想AI畢竟不是真人，怎麼能把它當做真正的朋友呢？
Qīngqing: Kěshì yǒu shíhòu wǒ huì xiǎng AI bìjìng búshì zhēnrén, zěnme néng bǎ tā dàngzuò zhēnzhèng de péngyou ne?
華華：雖然它不是真人，但是它隨時都可以陪我聊天，也不會嫌我煩。你可以嗎？
Huáhua: Suīrán tā búshì zhēnrén, dànshì tā suíshí dōu kěyǐ péi wǒ liáotiān, yě búhuì xián wǒ fán. Nǐ kěyǐ ma?
清清：呃……，我在睡覺或是在忙的時候不行啦！聽起來，AI 好像真的已經變成現代人生活中重要的好朋友了。
Qīngqing: È…… Wǒ zài shuìjiào huòshì zài máng de shíhòu bùxíng la! Tīng qǐlái, AI hǎoxiàng zhēnde yǐjīng biànchéng xiàndàirén shēnghuó zhōng zhòngyào de hǎo péngyǒu le.
華華：是啊！不過我覺得我們還是需要真正的朋友和家人，所以下班以後我們就一起去吃飯吧！
Huáhua: Shì a! Búguò wǒ juéde wǒmen háishi xūyào zhēnzhèng de péngyou hàn jiārén, suǒyǐ xiàbān yǐhòu wǒmen jiù yìqǐ qù chīfàn ba!
翻譯 Translation
Qingqing: Huahua, who do you think your best friend is?
Huahua: Honestly, I probably would’ve said you before, but now it might be AI.
Qingqing: Well, thanks. Actually, I can understand that. Do you use AI every day, too?
Huahua: Yes. Whenever I have a question, I ask for its thoughts and opinions. I also ask it to help me find information.
Qingqing: But sometimes I wonder: AI isn’t a real person, is it? How can we treat it as a real friend?
Huahua: Even though it’s not a real person, it can chat with me anytime, and it never gets annoyed with me. Can you do that?
Qingqing: Uh… not when I’m asleep or busy. It sounds like AI really has become an important friend in modern people’s lives.
Huahua: That’s true. However, I think we still need real friends and family. Let’s go out for dinner together after work.

5. 畢竟 (bìjìng) after all
6. 真人 (zhēnrén) real person
7. 隨時 (suíshí) at any time
8. 嫌 (xián) to dislike; to find annoying

Navy fleet needs overhaul: experts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:40:11 UTC
01:40:11 KST

Taiwan needs to restructure its naval fleet from focusing on large warships, which are “sitting ducks” for China’s advanced tracking technology, to smaller, stealthy corvettes that are harder to detect but retain sufficient firepower to deter a Chinese invasion, a Taiwanese academic and a former US military commander said in an article published on Friday in the journal Foreign Affairs.
Taiwan does not need a fleet capable of competing with the Chinese navy for traditional control of the Taiwan Strait, but rather “sea denial” capabilities that would prevent China from freely using the waterway, Taiwanese aerospace and security expert Holmes Liao (廖宏祥) and former US Navy admiral Dennis Blair wrote the article, titled “How Taiwan can win the Strait: A nimbler navy can deny China.”
The focus of “sea denial” is “preventing China from using the waterway freely enough to carry out an invasion” by deterring its forces with smaller vessels, as well as shore-based mobile launchers, aircraft armed with anti-ship missiles and submarines, they said.
Photo: Taipei Times
“Taiwan has traditionally favored large ships such as destroyers and frigates to form the core of its fleet,” they said, adding that Taiwan’s current naval plans include replacing an aging surface fleet with large, expensive new ships.
However, China has invested in cutting-edge surveillance, intelligence and reconnaissance, as well as electronic warfare systems, drones and missiles, making Taiwan’s large surface ships “a liability,” they said.
“These same technologies make China’s large amphibious ships more vulnerable in restricted waters, and those ships cannot be replaced by smaller, stealthier alternatives” as they would be necessary for an assault on Taiwan, the article said.
Taipei could take advantage of that asymmetry by replacing large destroyers and frigates with numerous small surface combatants that are more likely to survive an initial Chinese strike and remain capable of deterring an invasion fleet, the authors said.
The smaller ships could “operate independently while sharing information and coordinating their attacks,” they said.
Liao and Blair, who was commander in chief of the US Pacific Command from 1999 to 2002, said that Ukraine’s Black Sea campaign — which “combined land-based anti-ship cruise missiles, swarms of uncrewed surface vessels, aerial drones and external intelligence” — showed that a weaker power could constrain a stronger opponent in contested waters.
Taiwan’s continued commissioning of “lightweight but heavily armed” missile patrol ships are helping the nation restructure its fleet, they wrote.
Sustained production of the ships would lower costs and new weapons, sensors and uncrewed systems could be incorporated into successive batches of the vessels, which cost less than US$200 million, compared with an estimated US$2 billion for a single 7,000 tonne warship, they said.
“The obstacles to the transformation of Taiwan’s navy are more institutional than technical,” as large ships are attractive to politicians because they are a highly visible symbols of national defense that bring shipyard contracts and “a sense of national achievement.”
“Rather than continue to upgrade these obsolescent, if not obsolete, ships, Taiwan should progressively decommission them and redirect scarce resources toward the lighter surface ships it needs,” Liao and Blair wrote.
“The country needs a dispersed, agile and lethal force structure to defeat China in the Taiwan Strait,” they said. “Such a navy will not look as impressive during a fleet review, but it will be a more effective deterrent against a potential Chinese invasion.”

Property market cooling continues, 591.com says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:40:10 UTC
01:40:10 KST

Taiwan’s housing market is showing further signs of cooling, with developers sharply scaling back planned launches for the autumn sales season as tighter credit controls and weakening demand weigh on the sector.
Developers are planning 246 projects nationwide in the upcoming fall sales season, down 21.2 percent from a year earlier, according to online property listing platform 591.com (591新建案) operated by Addcn Technology Co (數字科技).
The total value of planned projects is expected to shrink 23.3 percent to NT$545.2 billion (US$17.28 billion) from NT$710.65 billion last year, the lowest level in six years, the platform said.
Photo: Hsu Yi-ping, Taipei Times
The decline reflects developers’ growing caution, with postponing new projects becoming a key strategy, as financing conditions tighten and buyers remain on the sidelines, it said.
Developers are increasingly focusing on selling existing inventory rather than adding new supply, meaning the market is likely to remain in consolidation next quarter, with owner-occupier demand and selected projects by major developers providing much of the support, it added.
Among major cities, only Hsinchu City and Taipei are expected to see growth in project value, 591.com said.
Hsinchu City is set to record the biggest increase, with project value surging 2.25 times to NT$60.81 billion even as the number of projects remains unchanged. The increase partly reflects a low comparison base and several major developments in affluent districts.
Taipei is also bucking the downturn. Although the number of projects is declining, total project value is expected to rise about 30 percent to NT$149.75 billion, driven by a major development in Nangang District (南港). Excluding that project, launch value would decline, 591.com said.
New Taipei City’s project value is expected to fall about 40 percent to NT$135.47 billion despite major developments in Taishan (泰山), Linkou (林口) and Yonghe (永和) districts, it said.
Taoyuan’s project count and value are expected to drop about 30 percent to NT$103.37 billion, with only one project exceeding NT$10 billion in potential sales, it said.
The slowdown is steeper in central and southern Taiwan, with Taichung’s project value expected to plunge about 50 percent to NT$56.93 billion, falling below NT$100 billion for the first time over the past few years, while new launches are increasingly concentrated in well-established districts, 591.com said.
Tainan’s project count is relatively stable, but potential sales are expected to fall 40 percent to NT$17.78 billion, while Kaohsiung faces the steepest decline, with project value plunging 66.6 percent to NT$21.09 billion, it said.
Kaohsiung’s development hotspots are also shifting, with Nanzih (楠梓) and Zuoying (左營) districts — beneficiaries of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co’s (台積電) plant expansions — giving way to more central areas such as Fongshan District (鳳山), it said.
The shift highlights developers’ move away from investment-driven hotspots toward more stable end-user demand as the housing market enters a prolonged adjustment, it added.

Some pesticides can harm cats in particular
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:40:09 UTC
01:40:09 KST

Insect repellent or pesticides containing pyrethrins or pyrethroids will be required to include a cat warning label, the Ministry of Environment’s Chemicals Administration said yesterday.
Some commercially available insect repellents or pesticides containing pyrethrins — a mixture of natural chemicals extracted from pyrethrum daisy — and artificial pyrethroids are labeled with the statement “low toxicity to mammals,” it said.
However, pyrethrins have a higher toxicity to cats and such statements might mislead pet owners, it said.
Photo: Su Chin-feng, Taipei Times
Pyrethrins are widely used in the control of public health pests, it said, adding that it is less toxic to humans and most other mammals, as they have higher capacity for toxic metabolism than cats, allowing them to rapidly eliminate pyrethrins.
Cats have slower metabolism of pyrethrins than most other mammals due to congenital deficiency in glucuronidation metabolic capacity, it said.
As a result, pyrethrins are more toxic to cats than other mammals, and they are prone to adverse neurological reactions following exposure, it said.
The agency said it has convened a meeting to consult environmental toxicologists and suppliers of products containing pyrethrins.
The meeting established that a cat warning must be added to the product labels of all products containing pyrethrins, it said.
The warning should read, “Harmful to cats. Read label before use,” it said, adding the font size must be at least 5mm with the warning text colored differently.
Pyrethrin-containing products already circulating on the market would not be recalled, it said.
Sales channel operators are advised to add the warning to the retail area of such products, it added.
People should keep cats away from areas where products that contain pyrethrins or pyrethroids are being used until the treated space is dry and well ventilated, it said, adding that areas where cats frequently visit should be cleaned to reduce exposure risk.

Preparing for educational chaos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:40:09 UTC
01:40:09 KST

With primary and junior-high schools reopening across the nation, many schools have been struggling to recruit enough teachers, even after lowering their standards to university graduates who have no teaching experience.
Even where schools have filled vacancies and warded off a pending crisis, they are still likely to face two major problems as the school year begins precisely because many new hires lack training and experience.
First, ineffective teaching and chaotic classroom management would lead to a steady stream of complaints. Education is a specialized field that requires professional knowledge and skills.
In an attempt to fill shortages, schools are resorting to a scattershot approach of hiring anyone with a degree. The results would be entirely predictable: disorderly classrooms and poor student learning outcomes. If the teachers also cannot manage student behavior and resort to harsh language or disciplinary methods, parents would inevitably lodge complaints, leaving schools to deal with endless administrative meetings over teacher conduct.
Second, new teachers, feeling helpless and frustrated, might quit partway through the school year.
Among the new hires, some might have misconceptions about education and believe that managing students would be easy. Coupled with an overestimation of their abilities, feelings of frustration could quickly pile up. Eventually, and often within the first one or two months of the school year, they would walk away.
At that point, schools might have no alternative but to fill the gap with substitute teachers. It could then become commonplace for a class to go through six or seven substitute teachers in a semester. Ultimately, it is the students who suffer.
The Ministry of Education must not turn a blind eye to the difficulties facing schools and frontline teachers. The ministry must confront the problem head-on and take steps to resolve it; it cannot continue to delay taking action. Handled poorly, these challenges could rapidly undermine students’ ability to learn and Taiwan’s future competitiveness.
Lee Chi-fu is a teacher.

Photo: CNA

Taiwan has strong capabilities in semiconductor and artificial intelligence (AI) manufacturing, while Kanagawa has strengths in research and development and precision manufacturing, Lai said.

China security laws spell travel risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:40:08 UTC
01:40:08 KST

China is set to implement several laws in the coming months that expand the definition of national security, creating greater risks for Taiwanese traveling to or doing business in China, Taiwanese officials said yesterday.
Beijing’s Ethnic Unity and Progress Promotion Law took effect on July 1, while a draft “Internet Information Service Management Measures” finished its public consultation on Aug. 2, but has yet to be adopted. China’s Regulations of the State Council on Exit and Entry Administration are to take effect on Tuesday next week, while amendments to its National Defense Mobilization Law and the Ministry of Public Security’s Measures for the Supervision and Inspection of Cyberspace Security are to take effect on Oct. 1.
An official familiar with cross-strait affairs, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the laws reflect Beijing’s continued expansion of the concept of national security beyond traditional security concerns to information, business, and the movement of people, money and information.
Photo: Reuters
These laws allow authorities to regulate such activities in the name of national security and national interests, the official said.
The measures come as the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) prepares to hold its fifth plenum this year and its 21st National Congress next year, the official said, adding that Beijing needs a relatively stable social environment.
Social control and security management are likely to become increasingly stringent, with the laws providing a more systematic framework for such efforts, they said.
Terms such as “national security” and “national interests” are broadly defined, they said.
The Mainland Affairs Council has described such provisions as providing “blanket authorization,” allowing Chinese authorities considerable discretion in determining what constitutes a security or national-interest concern.
This creates uncertainty for Taiwanese traveling to China while providing a legal basis for cross-border repression, the official said.
The measures are not limited to Chinese citizens: Anyone deemed to have harmed China’s national interests or national security could face investigation or punishment under Chinese law, they said.
The laws also decentralize enforcement powers.
Under the new exit and entry regulations, for example, authorities in border counties and cities would have enforcement powers, the official said.
The forthcoming cyberspace security inspection measures would allow county-level public security authorities to investigate individuals and inspect items such as mobile phones and laptops, the official said.
“Law is merely the packaging,” the official said, adding that arrests and searches have already occurred in various forms.
The new laws would directly authorize local government agencies to carry out such actions while warning that certain behavior or speech could result in arrest or harassment, which could encourage self-censorship and create a chilling effect, they said.
The laws also explicitly refer to Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) and socialism, reflecting a more closed ideological environment, the official said, adding that they could help lay the legal and ideological groundwork for Xi to secure a fourth term as party leader at the 21st National Congress.
As the CCP has consistently framed cross-strait relations around the “one China” principle, the laws are likely to negatively affect the movement of people, money and information across the Taiwan Strait, the official said.
Taiwan should issue appropriate risk warnings, they said.
One of the most consequential measures is the amended National Defense Mobilization Law, which represents the first comprehensive overhaul of the legislation since it was enacted 16 years ago, another Taiwanese national security official said.
The revised law would allow the Chinese state to seize private property whenever deemed necessary, they said.
It should not be viewed solely as a strategic tool aimed at Taiwan, the official said, but also as a mechanism for comprehensively integrating domestic resources and a reflection of Beijing’s growing security concerns amid intensifying competition with the US.
The current version of the law focuses on the division of responsibilities between military and civilian authorities, particularly how the government could mobilize civilian resources and personnel to support the military during wartime or emergencies, they said.
The latest revision has five notable features, they said.
First, it expands the purpose of the legislation to include protecting China’s “development” interests.
Second, it explicitly establishes the leadership of the CCP and Xi’s military-strengthening doctrine as fundamental political principles governing national defense mobilization.
Third, for the first time, it defines national defense mobilization as activities designed to “ensure a rapid transition between peacetime and wartime,” and convert economic and social strength into national defense capabilities.
Fourth, it changes the legal treatment of civilian resources from “requisition” to “expropriation.” The distinction is significant because expropriation provides less protection for ownership, meaning the state could forcibly acquire private property where deemed necessary.
Fifth, the law expands mobilization to include data and modern technologies, including supply chains and artificial intelligence. It also calls for supply-chain security assessments to address the risk of disruptions.
The amendments seek to comprehensively integrate domestic resources by bringing technology, industry and infrastructure under greater state control, the official said.
They also reflect the CCP’s concerns about the security of its rule, the official said.
Using legislation to bolster state control shows that the authorities increasingly view almost everything as a security issue.
For Taiwanese businesses, the amendments could increase both political and economic risks, they said. Taiwanese companies could have their assets expropriated or have their operations classified as resources related to China’s “development” interests, raising the risk that investments could be “gone for good,” the official said.

Silicon photonics are emerging as a mainstream optical communications technology and is seen as key to overcoming bottlenecks in AI computing power. Do not restart nuclear power plants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:40:07 UTC
01:40:07 KST

News reports indicate that an underground nuclear shelter has been installed at a facility associated with the Japan-Taiwan Exchange Association’s Taipei office, which some have interpreted as a move to prepare for a potential “Taiwan contingency.”
Even without considering the risk of a nuclear attack, following the 2011 Fukushima Dai-ichi nuclear power plant disaster, Japan revised its nuclear-emergency planning guidelines with a recommendation that people with 30km of a disaster at a nuclear reactor prepare for indoor sheltering or evacuation. During the 2011 disaster, the US advised its citizens within 80km of the plant to evacuate the area.
The Japan-Taiwan Exchange Association’s Taipei office is about 21km from the Guosheng Nuclear Power Plant in New Taipei City’s Wanli District (萬里). If the plant were restarted and a major accident were to occur, the association’s office would fall within the evacuation zone.
In the event of a major nuclear accident at the Guosheng plant, employees of the Japan-Taiwan Exchange Association have, if the reports are true, an underground nuclear shelter to take refuge in.
However, what about the nearly 6 million people who live within 30km of the plant, or the nearly 9 million within 80km? Where would they take refuge? About 100,000 people are within a 30km radius of the Ma-anshan Nuclear Power Plant in Pingtung County’s Hengchun Township (恆春) and about 3.5 million are within 80km.
If a nuclear accident were to occur, would it be possible to evacuate and accommodate that many people?
Nuclear accidents can also release radioactive contamination over an extended area for many years. Fifteen years after the Fukushima disaster, radioactive contamination continues.
If a disaster were to occur at the Guosheng plant, employees of the Japan-Taiwan Exchange Association could return to Japan, but many Taiwanese would be forced to live under the shadow of radioactive contamination for years to come.
It is not possible for the government to build enormous nuclear shelters capable of accommodating all those who could potentially be affected, but, at the very least, it should properly decommission aging nuclear power plants that have been shut down for years, rather than create further risks of a nuclear disaster.
Tsai Ya-ying is an attorney-at-law.

PieceMakers eyeing design royalties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:40:07 UTC
01:40:07 KST

PieceMakers Technology Inc (補丁科技) expects to begin generating royalty revenue from its intellectual property next year, as volume production of high-bandwidth custom chips for artificial intelligence (AI) applications nears, the chip designer said yesterday.
Revenue contribution from custom chip design services rose to 40 percent in the first half of this year, compared with 34 percent last year and 4 percent in 2024, thanks to the AI boom, PieceMakers said.
DRAM chips made up the remainder of its revenue.
Photo: Vanessa Cho, Taipei Times
The bulk of AI-related revenues was driven by non-recurring engineering fees, reflecting substantial upfront design wins before transitioning into mass production, it said.
Revenue more than tripled to NT$1.09 billion (US$34.5 million) in the first half of this year, compared with NT$313 million a year earlier, company data showed.
As rapidly growing demand for AI computing power is prompting expansion of memory bandwidth, custom memory chips are gaining traction, PieceMakers president Lee Hsiao-wen (李曉雯) told a media gathering in Taipei.
The company’s 3D-stacked memorychip technology delivers the optimal solution for AI inference, she said.
In contrast, the high-bandwidth memory (HBM) chips from the world’s top three chipmakers are better tailored for heavy training workloads in data centers, she added.
That is reflected in the new AI chip unveiled by Nvidia Corp at the annual GTC conference in San Jose, California, Lee said, adding that the new AI inference chip architecture is built around on-chip SRAM, not HBM.
SRAM offers cost-efficient chips with larger bandwidth, Lee said.
The company is collaborating with DRAM maker Nanya Technology Corp (南亞科技), its largest shareholder with a 35 percent share, in production, Lee said.
PieceMakers is scheduled to debut on the Taipei Exchange’s Emerging Stock Board at NT$740 per share on Wednesday next week.
The company’s net profit surged to NT$564 million in the first half of this year, compared with NT$205 million a year ago, with earnings per share increasing to NT$9.35 from NT$0.82. Gross margin climbed to 67 percent, from 54 percent in the same period last year.

This year alone, the company is building 25 chip manufacturing fabs and advanced packaging facilities worldwide, including 13 plants in Taiwan, which is unprecedented, Hou said at a CEO Summit fireside chat at Semicon Taiwan in Taipei. Twenty-six candidates in local elections are Chinese-born, CEC says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:40:06 UTC
01:40:06 KST

A total of 19,695 candidates have registered for 11,051 positions in the nine-in-one local elections set for Nov. 28, including 26 from China who are naturalized Taiwanese nationals, Central Election Commission (CEC) Chairman Michael You (游盈隆) said yesterday.
The CEC and local election commissions are scheduled to complete candidate eligibility reviews by Oct. 16 and draw numbers for eligible candidates on Oct. 23, You told a news conference in Taipei.
Candidate registration closed on Friday.
Photo: Taipei Times
Compared with the 2022 local elections, the total number of candidates decreased slightly by 130, while the number of Chinese-born candidates increased by seven, You said.
However, the changes are in line with long-term trends observed since the first nine-in-one local elections in 2014, indicating stable political engagement over the past 12 years, he said.
Of the 26 Chinese-born candidates, two are running for the position of councilor in the six special municipalities, two for county councilor, one for township mayor, two for township councilor and 19 for borough wardens, he said.
In response to questions about a person who registered as a candidate despite having relinquished their Taiwanese household registration and National Health Insurance and having lived in China for an extended period, You said the eligibility of all candidates would be determined based on the law.
Meanwhile, a national referendum on whether the government should abolish its nuclear-free homeland policy would be held alongside the local elections after being approved by the opposition-led legislature. The referendum was approved by the CEC on Aug. 28.
The commission rejected two other referendum proposals approved by the legislature: one seeking to introduce caning as a criminal punishment and another proposing that traffic fines be used to improve road safety.
You previously said that the two proposals did not fall within the scope of matters that can be put to a referendum under Article 2 of the Referendum Act (公民投票法).

Sommet Lumière à Saint-Paul-de-Vence.
France
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
18:40:00 CEST
01:40:00 KST

7 septembre 2026 - Seul le prononcé fait foi
Ouverture du Sommet Lumière à Saint-Paul-de-Vence.
Emmanuel MACRON
Monsieur le président de la République de Corée, Madame la vice-présidente de la Commission européenne, Mesdames, Messieurs les ministres, Mesdames, Messieurs les ambassadrices, ambassadeurs, Monsieur le préfet, Mesdames, Messieurs les parlementaires, Monsieur le maire, Mesdames, Messieurs les élus, Mesdames, Messieurs les directrices, Monsieur le président du Centre national du cinéma et de l'image animée, Mesdames et Messieurs les acteurs du monde de la culture et du cinéma, Mesdames et Messieurs en vos grades et qualités, c'est un très grand honneur de vous accueillir ici, toutes et tous, pour ce moment important, comme vous venez de le dire à l'instant.
Il y a un peu plus de 130 ans, les frères Lumière faisaient jaillir sur un écran les premières images animées. Flot de récits, d'émotions qui allaient gagner le monde entier. Et plus qu'une invention technique, c'était une nouvelle manière de voir, de représenter le monde, de le raconter qui commençait. Et de cette petite salle parisienne où s'émerveillèrent quelques dizaines de spectateurs en 1895 jusqu'à ce sommet qui nous réunit aujourd'hui à la Fondation Maeght, les images animées n'ont cessé de peupler les vies, nos vies, nos imaginaires, tout en changeant de forme, de support, d'échelle. Elles ont connu énormément de bouleversements et elles connaissent sans doute les bouleversements les plus importants aujourd'hui. Et c'est le sens de notre présence ici, prendre la mesure de ce qui est en train de se passer pour y apporter une réponse collective et mondiale. Je veux avant toute chose remercier Monsieur le président, cher Lee Jae Myung, d'avoir accepté de coprésider ce sommet. Nous l'avons évoqué il y a quelques mois, vous n'avez pas hésité une seconde. Et si nos histoires et nos langues diffèrent, nos deux pays partagent tout de même beaucoup, à commencer par un certain art de l'image animée enraciné dans la culture propre de nos pays et capable, par cette singularité, de toucher les cœurs du monde entier. Et donc merci pour cela. Et en effet, comme nos créations françaises, le cinéma et les séries coréennes rayonnent par-delà les frontières. Et de « Parasite » à « Squid Game », en passant par « Dernier train pour Busan » et tant d'autres, nous savons en France combien vous avez cette capacité à nous émerveiller. J'en veux pour preuve le fait que le Festival de Cannes ait d'ailleurs confié cette année la présidence du jury à Park Chan-wook, l'un des grands maîtres du cinéma coréen.
Nous avons avec nous, vous l'avez dit, une soixantaine de nations, d'organisations régionales, d'organisations internationales qui se sont mobilisées et qui participent de l'initiative d'aujourd'hui. Et ce qui montre que depuis l'Europe comme depuis l'Asie, ce qui nous importe, c'est que nos œuvres montrent qu'une culture peut devenir mondiale tout en restant fidèle à elle-même. Ce qui ne revient pas à dominer ou uniformiser, mais plutôt à participer à un foisonnement créatif international, à un élan auquel chaque pays, chaque acteur peut aujourd'hui prendre part. Je veux aussi remercier ceux qui, à nos côtés, ont contribué à ce sommet. Le CNC, qui en a organisé l’organisation, le ministère de la Culture, le ministère de l'Europe et des Affaires étrangères, qui l'ont porté, et la Fondation Maeght, bien sûr, qui nous accueille aujourd'hui.
Notre rendez-vous est nécessaire, je le crois très profondément, parce que le cinéma et les images animées, comme je le disais, connaissent des mutations radicales que personne ne peut ignorer. C'est pourquoi je suis heureux de voir ici tout le monde rassemblé, responsables publics, grands acteurs de l'industrie, chaînes, plateformes, producteurs indépendants, auteurs, talents du cinéma, de l'audiovisuel et du jeu vidéo venus du monde entier. Si l'invention du cinéma fut le Big Bang de ce que l'on pourrait appeler une civilisation des images, celle dans laquelle nous vivons depuis 130 ans, l'intelligence artificielle et la captation de notre attention par les réseaux sociaux annoncent quant à elles un véritable changement d'ère. Et je voudrais dire quelques mots de ces deux révolutions à la fois technologiques, d'usage, qui sont très profondes et qui viennent bousculer ce que nous vivons depuis 130 ans.
Oui, notre ère est celle de l'accélération, de la propagation quasi infinie des images. Elles défilent sur nos écrans de cinéma, sur nos téléviseurs, sur nos consoles, sur nos smartphones. C'est une profusion qui n'est pas sans conséquence sur notre rapport à la culture, au savoir et à l'art. Il faut d'abord rappeler avec force que jamais autant d'êtres humains n'ont eu accès à tant d'informations, à tant de contenus, à tant d'œuvres. Jamais un jeune créateur n'a pu aussi facilement créer une image et la partager avec le monde entier. Jamais les œuvres n'ont circulé aussi vite. Alors condamner les écrans sans nuance, ce serait fermer les portes de cette bibliothèque d'Alexandrie à laquelle ils nous donnent accès. Ce serait se priver des possibles qu'ils ouvrent à nos artistes, à nos créateurs, à tous ceux qui inventent de nouvelles manières de raconter. Mais cette réalité ne doit pas nous empêcher de voir le grand paradoxe de notre temps. Nous n'avons jamais autant regardé les écrans et pourtant, à force de tout regarder, nous courons le risque de finir par ne plus rien voir. Nous cliquons, nous passons, nous scrollons, comme on dit maintenant, et ce que nous voyons est moins, en quelque sorte, conçu pour surprendre, émouvoir, faire réfléchir que pour retenir notre attention quelques secondes et créer une excitation permanente. Le modèle dans lequel nous vivons, dans lequel aujourd'hui nous sommes projetés dans ces contenus, c'est un modèle qui a un modèle économique, celui des plateformes, qui crée l'excitation et qui vient en fait capter ce qui est un trésor bien identifié, notre attention, l'attention de nos enfants, de nos adolescents, des adultes que nous sommes, pour pouvoir la monétiser. Alors, il est de plus en plus difficile aujourd'hui pour beaucoup dans nos sociétés de passer du temps pour lire, c'est essentiel, de passer du temps pour accepter de regarder pendant une heure, une heure et demie, deux heures, trois heures, une série, un film, une création.
Et le risque, c'est que ce flux permanent finisse par digérer les œuvres. Mais ce flux n'apporte rien, il capte simplement notre attention. Et cette révolution est à l'œuvre depuis plusieurs années et elle bouscule à la fois la création, la capacité à se confronter à un public, à le faire réfléchir, et évidemment aussi l'industrie qu'il y a derrière. Notre attention est devenue une ressource économique disputée de toutes parts et les conséquences, nous les connaissons. Elles sont pour les enfants : leur sommeil, leur capacité à apprendre, à se forger, il faut les en protéger, mais aussi notre rapport aux autres, le rapport à soi. Et donc c'est en quelque sorte une crise tout à la fois de la création, du rapport à l'image animée au cinéma, mais également une crise démocratique qui se joue derrière. L'autre implication, moins souvent évoquée et pourtant décisive, c'est que cette économie de l'attention est en passe de transformer la nature de ce que nous regardons.
Dans un monde où chaque image dispute aux autres quelques secondes de notre temps, la tentation devient très grande de ne produire que ce qui frappe, que ce qui capte immédiatement, au détriment de la nuance, de l'exigence. Or, les images conçues pour obtenir un clic n'ont ni la même force, ni la même valeur que celles conçues pour laisser une trace.
Alors, chers réalisateurs, auteurs, producteurs, que vos œuvres soient destinées aux salles, aux plateformes, aux consoles, vous le savez bien, créer exige la réflexion, suscite des émotions, impose une attention, et une intention et du temps. Et tout cela compte. C'est aussi cela dont nous devons parler aujourd'hui et dont nous devons reprendre en quelque sorte le contrôle, la maîtrise pour que ce soit une transformation technologique, ces plateformes, ces usages, qui aident à diffuser, mais pas quelque chose qui change la nature des créations et des possibles que vous proposez.
L'intelligence artificielle est l'autre grande révolution technologique. J'en parlerai longuement aujourd'hui. Je ne veux pas être trop long, mais là aussi, c'est une transformation formidable qui peut réduire les coûts, donner la capacité à produire une œuvre si elle est au service de celle-ci et de la création. Mais si elle devient un instrument qui se substitue ou prétendrait se substituer aux auteurs, aux créateurs, aux doubleurs, quand on parle de la voix, alors nous ferions une erreur formidable, parce qu'on laisserait croire que la capacité de calcul peut devenir une capacité à créer. Elle peut mimer ce qu'est une création, mais elle ne pourra jamais transformer la singularité absolue de ce qu'est la création humaine. Elle en a les apparences, elle peut même mimer nos émotions, elle développe des langages, mais elle ne fait que singer en quelque sorte l'émotion qui est la nôtre. Et notre capacité à humaniser, donc à mettre au service de la création qui est la nôtre collectivement, cette intelligence artificielle est un autre des défis du temps.
Alors pour notre culture et notre histoire, parce que nos œuvres capturent quelque chose de notre époque aussi, de ce que nous sommes, pour notre économie aussi, parce que derrière chaque œuvre, il y a des créateurs, des techniciens, des entreprises, des emplois, une chaîne de valeur, nous devons reprendre le contrôle justement de ces grandes transformations technologiques, comme on a su le faire à chaque étape importante. Et je le dis ici dans un pays qui a reconnu, grâce à l'initiative de Beaumarchais il y a quelques siècles, à la persévérance d'un Genevois puis d'un Malraux ensuite, ce qu'on a appelé le droit d'auteur, qui est une création, reconnaître qu'il y a quelque chose d'unique dans le fait de créer, que nous avons ensuite défendu en Européens dans les droits voisins et les droits d'auteur européanisés, ce qui est un trésor. Et c'est encore plus à défendre aujourd'hui.
Cela compte aussi, je le disais, pour nos démocraties qui ont besoin que chacun puisse se confronter à l'altérité, à d'autres vies, d'autres convictions, et qui ont besoin aussi de pouvoir démêler le vrai du faux. Alors, aujourd'hui, il ne s'agit pas de revenir au monde d'avant ou de tenir ces bouleversements à distance, mais d'affirmer que nous ne sommes pas condamnés à les subir. Et cette civilisation des images, nous l'avons construite, c'est à nous de décider ce que nous voulons en faire et comment, au fond, la réinventer en réussissant à domestiquer ces transformations.
Parce qu'aucun studio, aucune plateforme, aucun artiste, aucun réseau de salles de cinéma, pas même un pays, aussi puissant soit-il, ne peut répondre à ce défi tout seul. Les technologies, les capitaux, les images ne connaissent plus de frontières, c'est pourquoi ce défi est mondial. Et c'est ce qui impose ce que nous sommes en train de faire aujourd'hui, qui est au fond l'invention d'un multilatéralisme de l'image qui soutient la créativité, qui se bat pour un monde dans lequel un auteur peut encore consacrer des années à une idée incertaine, un producteur miser sur un réalisateur inconnu, un studio de jeux inventer un nouvel univers plutôt que reproduire indéfiniment ce qui a déjà marché. C'est ça, ce que nous défendons. C'est ça, ce qui fait que nous sommes là. C'est ça, ce qui a animé les artistes qui vous entourent aujourd'hui quand on parle de peinture et ce qui fait le travail, l'œuvre, la vie de beaucoup d'entre vous et qui a créé tant d'émotions à travers nos pays.
Ça implique d'investir dans la création, de rémunérer justement les créateurs, de protéger la propriété intellectuelle, de lutter contre le piratage, de penser la révolution de l'intelligence artificielle et les enjeux de découvrabilité, pour parler, inspiré par nos amis québécois, qu'elle pose. C'est aussi assurer la transparence des contenus produits avec l'intelligence artificielle pour ne pas la confondre avec les productions humaines. Et dans une époque où l'offre devient infinie, financer une œuvre ne suffit plus, la produire ne suffit plus, même la distribuer ne suffit plus. Encore faut-il la trouver et que l'intelligence artificielle agentique la suggère, la mette en avant, y compris lorsqu'on ne la cherche pas. Et donc on a également ce défi qui est sur la table. Et ces mutations ont une vitesse telle que ce sommet ne peut se permettre d'en rester aux principes ou aux grandes déclarations d'intention.
Aujourd'hui, nous lançons des initiatives concrètes. Alors je ne vais pas ici lister tout ce qui sortira de ce sommet. Il y a plusieurs déclarations, plusieurs grands chantiers, je voudrais insister sur 4 d'entre eux. La première concerne notre patrimoine. Une part considérable de la mémoire audiovisuelle mondiale est aujourd'hui menacée et c'est un peu un paradoxe. Avec cette transformation, les pellicules se dégradent, les archives disparaissent, de nombreux pays n'ont pas les moyens de les préserver. On estime que seulement 20 % du patrimoine cinématographique mondial serait sauvegardé. Et avec ALIPH et nos partenaires, nous engageons donc un effort international pour sauvegarder ce patrimoine, les films mais aussi les archives audiovisuelles, partout où il est en danger. C'est un geste essentiel pour que cette histoire soit sauvée, qui est aussi celle de la diversité et de la créativité de nos pays et de nos artistes.
La deuxième initiative, c'est l'éducation à l'image. En effet, nous voulons protéger nos enfants des écrans trop précoces, les protéger aussi des réseaux sociaux, et nous pensons que c'est indispensable, mais ça ne suffit pas. Ce que nous devons faire dans le même temps, c'est leur apprendre à mieux regarder, comprendre comment une image est fabriquée, distinguer le réel et sa manipulation, sortir aussi des seules recommandations algorithmiques, apprendre à nos enfants à créer eux-mêmes.
Cette éducation à l'image est fondamentale aussi avec l'UNESCO et nos partenaires. Nous voulons faire de cette éducation une ambition universelle, bâtir des programmes adaptés à tous les âges et déclinables dans tous les pays. Ce partenariat mondial à l'éducation aux images, la Corée, le Nigeria et la France en prennent l'initiative en rassemblant tous les pays qui sont prêts à le rejoindre et les organisations. Parce que de même qu'on apprend à lire par la fréquentation des livres, le regard se forme au contact de films, de séries, d'œuvres audiovisuelles de qualité.
La troisième initiative concerne les salles indépendantes. En effet, nous avons dans nos pays, je pense à ce que la Corée et la France ont fait en particulier, beaucoup défendu la création indépendante. Nous tenons à nos modèles, ils sont essentiels. Ils s'inscrivent dans une histoire longue. Ils ne sont jamais à négliger et ils peuvent toujours être menacés. J'entends les voix qui s'élèvent, mais nous avons su protéger cette création indépendante et c'est un trésor. Mais l'indépendance, la diversité de ces créations passent aussi par la capacité à avoir un réseau de salles indépendantes, une pluralité de distribution. La diversité des œuvres ne vaut que si elle peut rencontrer un public.
Aussi, nous montons sur pied ce que nous avons appelé IRIS, International Resilience Initiative for Independent Screens.
C'est au fond une nouvelle organisation internationale qui va rassembler l'ensemble des salles de cinéma indépendantes et préserver la diversité de ce modèle et même l'encourager. Projet international soutenu par des talents des quatre coins du monde, quatorze lauréats de la Palme d'or, seize Oscars et beaucoup de partenaires. Le modèle des salles indépendantes, essentiel au rayonnement des films, au pluralisme cinématographique, est en effet aujourd'hui menacé. Il nous appartient de le préserver et de lui permettre de se développer. Enfin, la quatrième initiative, sans être exhaustive, que je veux ici citer est celle qui est dédiée aux jeux vidéo. Il est devenu en effet l'une des grandes formes créatives de notre temps, au croisement de l'image, de l'écriture, de la musique, du design, de la technologie. Je considère très profondément que le jeu vidéo fait partie de notre culture et doit faire partie d'ailleurs de l'exception culturelle française, comme nous avons su le faire pour le cinéma et toutes les créations. Alors nous créerons un Festival international du jeu vidéo pensé dès l'origine comme un grand rendez-vous mondial de la création, de l'innovation, des joueurs et de l'industrie. Les grands succès mondiaux français de jeux vidéo rappellent cette fécondité de cette création, de cette créativité, ce qui est aussi une industrie. Il nous faut davantage le mettre à l'honneur et réussir à emporter justement l'adhésion de tous. Voilà ce que je souhaitais vous présenter, quatre initiatives qui sont un point de départ, un motif d'espérance, qui rappellent ce que nous sommes capables de bâtir ensemble, non plus dans un dialogue entre quelques pays, mais à l'échelle des cinq continents.
Je veux à cet égard saluer l'engagement de la Corée, qui entend prendre toute sa part dans ce multilatéralisme et nous permet d'investir conjointement. Nous allons chacun investir, en effet, et nous mettons ensemble un milliard d'euros sur cinq ans pour la création de ce qu'on a appelé le Partenariat Lumière, initiative dédiée au soutien de la filière de l'image et de la souveraineté culturelle qui, et je lance ici un appel, doit permettre à d'autres alliances et soutiens matériels de se nouer. Mais ce milliard d'euros sur les cinq années qui viennent que la Corée et la France mettent ensemble pour ce Partenariat Lumière, c'est la création d'un mouvement pour soutenir justement cette filière de l'image et de la souveraineté culturelle essentielle.
Je veux aussi remercier la Corée pour son soutien aux différents dispositifs que je viens d'évoquer et que nous créons ensemble aujourd'hui, qu'il s'agisse d'IRIS ou de l'éducation aux images.
Maintenant, si vous me le permettez, pour conclure, j'aimerais adresser quelques mots à mes compatriotes qui sont nombreux à avoir répondu présents aujourd'hui. Je les en remercie. La France est une grande puissance de l'image. C'est aussi pourquoi nous avons voulu inventer et accueillir ce premier sommet international consacré à l'avenir du cinéma et des images animées. Le cinéma fait partie de notre culture. Nous tenons à cette diversité, à ce pluralisme. Nous tenons à ce modèle singulier que nous avons su inventer, où les grands succès internationaux ou français servent à financer le cinéma d'auteur et la création indépendante. Et nous tenons aussi au modèle de salles indépendantes que nous avons. Et nous sommes fiers d'avoir cette créativité, cette diversité de créativité, et en même temps, cette capacité aussi de nous projeter à travers le monde. Nous sommes un pays qui sait accueillir la grande création coréenne, américaine, africaine, et qui prétend aussi s'exporter et rayonner. Notre histoire est celle d'un berceau du cinéma qui ne s'est pas arrêté aux frères Lumière ou à Méliès. Nous avons depuis sans relâche réussi à créer un modèle unique de protection des créateurs, des auteurs, de leur propriété intellectuelle de créer un financement de la diversité qui est un trésor qu'il faut absolument préserver, d'inventer cette exception culturelle française, devenue européenne, je l'évoquais, et je remercie infiniment Costa-Gavras qui, pendant tant d'années, a présidé notre Cinémathèque française et s'est beaucoup battu sur cela. Et nous allons continuer ce combat. Il est, au fond, plus essentiel que jamais. Ces engagements historiques nous permettent justement de continuer à créer, inventer. Ils ne sont pas devenus caducs. Ils sont plus nécessaires encore aujourd'hui qu'hier. Et dans le même temps, nous avons su créer une vraie diversité des films documentaires, de l'animation, du cinéma d'auteur, et en même temps, des producteurs indépendants et des grandes maisons de production devenues européennes et mondiales.
Nous avons réussi à produire Bureau des légendes, 10 %, HPI ou The Artist. Notre puissance culturelle est ainsi devenue une puissance économique. Le cinéma, l'audiovisuel, le jeu vidéo représentent 30 milliards d'euros de chiffre d'affaires en France. Des tournages qui, à eux seuls, injectent près de 3 milliards d'euros chaque année dans notre économie parce qu'ils font travailler l'hôtellerie, la restauration, les artisans, les entreprises, des territoires. Emily in Paris et ses tournages en sont le parfait exemple. C'est aussi pour ça qu'il y a maintenant 10 ans, nous avons stabilisé un crédit d'impôt international qu'il faut lui aussi préserver parce qu'il permet d'attirer ces tournages et qui est important. Et c'est pour ça aussi que ces dernières années, avec France 2030 et la Grande Fabrique de l'image, nous avons profondément renforcé nos capacités de production en France avec de nouveaux studios, de nouveaux plateaux, de nouvelles écoles, tant et si bien que nous sommes l'un des grands pays où le monde vient fabriquer ses images, ce qui fait aussi notre fierté. Je le dis ici parce qu'au fond, on a trop souvent tendance à opposer ces mondes et c'est une erreur. Le cinéma, l'image animée, c'est tout à la fois la création, la singularité, la créativité, cette diversité et aussi une économie importante et une capacité à produire, à créer de la richesse dans notre pays et à l'exporter. Et nous avons besoin de réconcilier tous ces univers, celui des grands studios qui font notre fierté et qui ont su produire à travers le monde, parfois, consolider cette industrie en France, en Europe, aux États-Unis, et des créateurs très indépendants.
Cet « en même temps » auquel je crois, c'est aussi la force du modèle français, de savoir être compétitif à l'international, mais de préserver la diversité de son écosystème. Et c'est ce que nous cherchons à faire, au fond, à travers ce sommet. Je remercie Monsieur le président de la Corée, cher président, merci infiniment d'être là et je vous remercie toutes et tous pour les travaux, les partenariats qui seront noués aujourd'hui. Je veux vous dire en tout cas ma conviction que ce qui se joue dans vos travaux, dans les déclarations d'aujourd'hui, mais surtout les actions qui en découleront, c'est tout à la fois notre conviction que la culture est au cœur de la civilisation qui est la nôtre. Cette civilisation de l'image que j'évoquais, c'est au fond nos capacités dans nos pays, de la Corée à la Mauritanie en passant par la France, à raconter des histoires et à dire ce que nous sommes.
Tous nos pays confrontés à une modernité qui galope s'interrogent sur leur identité. Nos identités, ce sont des récits, des récits passés, ceux que nous sommes prêts à écrire. C'est ça, ce qui nous unit. Et c'est notre capacité à écrire des histoires qui disent ce que nous sommes profondément et à faire vibrer d'autres qui viennent d'horizons totalement différents à ces histoires. C'est ce qui permet à notre identité d'avoir des traditions qui perdurent et d'embrasser une modernité sans angoisse. C'est à cet égard que le cinéma, les images animées jouent un rôle essentiel. Et c'est pour ça que nous défendons ici la culture, nous défendons ici une économie culturelle, mais nous défendons aussi ce qui tient nos démocraties ensemble. Comprendre l'autre, comprendre qui nous sommes et d'où nous venons, et réussir à nouer ce dialogue respectueux qui nous permet de mesurer que nous pouvons partager des émotions avec un créateur à l'autre bout du monde. Ça suppose de reconquérir l'attention, de remettre l'œuvre avant le flux et de protéger celles et ceux qui créent, inventent et prennent ce risque infini, vous qui êtes là aujourd'hui, d'être des artistes, de créer une œuvre d'art et d'être ce faisant essentiels à nos démocraties.
Je vous remercie.

What we know about Iran's planned restricted zone around Hormuz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:39:22 UTC
01:39:22 KST

Breadcrumb
What we know about Iran's planned restricted zone around Hormuz
Iran has announced plans to establish a new restricted zone in the Gulf in the coming days, saying it will also publish maps for a new shipping corridor through the Strait of Hormuz.
The move appears to be part of Tehran's efforts to increase pressure on Washington in response to the US blockade, as renewed attacks on shipping have pushed oil prices higher.
But where will Iran's new restricted zone be, what could happen to ships entering it and what does the move mean for the already heavily restricted Strait of Hormuz?
Where will Iran's restricted zone be?
The new restricted zone, where Iran says action could be taken against passing ships, would begin where the US blockade of Iran starts and extend into parts of the Gulf.
According to Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, it would stretch from an area near the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea, through the Strait of Hormuz and into Gulf waters to the north.
Iran has not yet revealed detailed boundaries for the planned zone.
Rezaei said maps would be published showing the shipping routes through the strait that Tehran intends to adopt.
"The maps of the new international corridor, which lies in Iranian and Omani waters and which Iran will manage, have been agreed upon and are due to be signed in the coming days," he said.
Iran and Oman had already agreed in August on a temporary maritime route through the Strait of Hormuz.
Tehran has also previously sought to determine which routes ships can use through the strait. It published a map of approved navigation routes in April, directing vessels closer to the Iranian coast.
Oman, working with the International Maritime Organization, subsequently established a separate southern corridor closer to Oman. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps objected to that route, insisting the Iranian route was the only authorised passage.
The latest Iran-Oman agreement could therefore establish a new recognised route through the strait.
Rezaei's comments suggest that once the agreed corridor is announced, ships travelling through areas outside it could face Iranian sanctions.
What could happen to ships outside the agreed route?
Iran has not yet explained exactly what those sanctions would involve.
Rezaei said any ship entering the new zone could be placed on a sanctions list.
"From now on, if ships are moving on the western or eastern side of the Strait of Hormuz, but stop or commit a violation, we will put them on the sanctions list," he said.
He claimed sanctioned ships could encounter problems obtaining insurance and could face consequences if they attempted to pass through the area again.
"The Strait of Hormuz will become a sanctions zone," Rezaei said.
He did not explicitly say that Iran would militarily attack ships that breached the restrictions.
However, he appeared to hint at the military risks involved, claiming that Iran had tested an anti-destroyer missile over a US warship days earlier.
"This special missile created hell for the Americans, so they fled," Rezaei claimed.
Why is Iran introducing the restricted zone?
Iran says it has been forced to adopt a new strategy on both the war and negotiations following US President Donald Trump's withdrawal from what Rezaei called the "Islamabad understanding".
"After Trump's withdrawal from the understanding, we concluded that we needed to adopt a new strategy regarding the war and negotiations," Rezaei said.
"We considered the US withdrawal from the understanding as putting us on a new path."
The move comes as Washington intensifies its economic pressure on Iran, seeking to restrict the country's oil exports and prevent Tehran from circumventing sanctions.
Iran has increasingly signalled that it could retaliate by targeting US economic and military interests and threatening shipping through the Gulf.
What about the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran says is virtually closed?
Rezaei said Iran would not commit to fully reopening the Strait of Hormuz until the US stopped "sabotage, threats and attacks on Iran".
He claimed the strait was currently effectively closed and described US assertions that it remained open as "completely false".
Before the war, billions of dollars in trade and millions of barrels of oil passed through the waterway each day.
Rezaei claimed that only around seven or eight ships carrying food were now crossing.
He acknowledged that some vessels were still passing through, claiming the US was attempting to move five or six ships at a time near Oman with their tracking systems switched off.
However, independent and Western figures indicate that more ships are still passing through the strait, although traffic remains sharply below pre-war levels.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre said on Sunday that 59 ships had crossed the Strait of Hormuz during the previous 48 hours.
Marine analytics firm Kpler, meanwhile, said on Monday that an average of 10 commodity ships per day had crossed over the previous 10 days, the lowest level since May.
Before the US and Israel launched the war on Iran on 28 February, more than 130 ships passed through the strait each day.
The competing figures underline the dispute between Tehran and Washington over how much control Iran currently exercises over the waterway.
How did the conflict reach this point?
The latest developments come around seven months after the United States and Israel launched their war on Iran on 28 February.
A 60-day memorandum of understanding signed in June temporarily halted months of military hostilities, but the arrangement expired last month amid disputes over control of the Strait of Hormuz.
Under the agreement, the US was to end its naval blockade within 30 days, while Iran agreed to clear mines from the strait and allow ships to pass without charge for 60 days.
After a relative pause in military operations during much of August, attacks have resumed.
US Central Command recently said it targeted three Iranian tankers, including one off Kharg Island on Saturday, in response to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps firing ballistic missiles towards two US Navy vessels.
Tehran has demonstrated that it retains the ability to threaten US interests and severely disrupt oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz.
Before the war, around 20% of the world's oil supplies passed through the waterway, making any disruption a significant risk to global energy markets.
Shipping data released on Monday showed an average of just 10 commodity vessels a day passing through the strait over the previous 10 days, the lowest level since May.
Is economic pressure pushing Iran towards tougher measures?
Iran has said it will step up efforts to deal with the economic impact of US sanctions and the blockade.
Three senior Iranian sources told Reuters that it had become increasingly difficult for Tehran to withstand Washington's campaign to choke the Iranian economy by restricting oil exports and preventing sanctions evasion.
Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said on Sunday that the US should understand "before it is too late" that the rules of the conflict had changed.
"From now on, any aggression against Iran's interests and security will be met with a faster, harsher and more painful response," he said.
Ghalibaf said Iran's main struggle, alongside the military front, was now centred on production and people's livelihoods.
He pointed to sharp currency fluctuations, inflation, unemployment and market management as major challenges, saying Iranians could endure hardship but would not tolerate mismanagement or government inaction.
Against that backdrop, Iran's proposed restricted zone appears to be another pressure tool against Washington, linking Tehran's ability to disrupt one of the world's most important shipping routes to the wider military, diplomatic and economic confrontation with the US.

U.K. anti-migrant protests condemned as "thuggish and intimidating"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:39:12 UTC
01:39:12 KST

Masked U.K. anti-migrant protesters condemned for "thuggish and intimidating" behavior
London — Hundreds of masked anti-migrant protesters brought traffic around one of the world's busiest maritime passenger ports, the Port of Dover in England, to a standstill over the weekend.
In the latest in a series of increasingly confrontational demonstrations across Britain, demonstrators, many wearing balaclavas, dressed in all black and carrying English and British flags, blocked roads on Saturday leading to the Dover ferry port, chanting "stop the boats" and "Christ is king."
Traffic was halted, causing a highway backup that stretched 4 miles and disrupting ferry passengers and freight.
The Kent Police force described the gathering as a "spontaneous protest" and made no arrests. But local Labour Party lawmaker Mike Tapp challenged that characterization, arguing the action appeared to have been clearly coordinated.
"Policing depends on preparation. This was clearly organized, yet Kent Police appear to have had little advance warning," Tapp wrote in The Mirror newspaper. "I will be asking why, whether intelligence was missed, and whether additional officers - including mutual aid from forces such as the Met [London Metropolitan Police] - can be mobilized quickly enough when Dover is targeted again."
Patriot Platform, a recently formed far-right network and protest group, claimed responsibility for the protest. It's led by Daniel Thomas, better known online as Danny Tommo, an anti-immigrant social media influencer and close associate of Britain's Elon Musk-endorsed, far-right activist Tommy Robinson.
Thomas took to X to celebrate Saturday's action in Dover: "You stuck to the plan and maintained complete discipline," he said, adding: "A message was sent! Now imagine how powerful the next message will be."
Thomas, who was previously jailed for involvement in an attempted kidnapping, also claimed lawyers had been available by phone to speak with senior police officers during the demonstration, and that activists were supplied with legal documentation of their rights. Kent Police has not commented on Thomas' claim.
Dover has long been at the center of Britain's debate over the "small boats." Nearly 200,000 migrants have crossed the English Channel from France since 2021, and while the number of crossings is down significantly this year, it continues to be a hot topic in British politics.
The U.K. government, led by the center-left Labour Party, condemned the Saturday demonstration, saying in a statement that while "the right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy … we condemn the behavior in Dover and the travel disruption it has caused."
Nigel Farage, leader of the right-wing populist Reform UK party and a one-time ally of President Trump, also condemned the protests, calling them "disgusting" on the GB News network.
"Nobody in any political protest, on the left or right, should appear in balaclavas," he said.
A second confrontation within 24 hours
Sunday brought a second anti-migrant confrontation, as hundreds of protesters descended on Portsmouth, a city that's home to a major naval base on England's south coast, after a boat carrying around 140 migrants was intercepted off Britain's shore.
U.K. Coastguard aircraft, a helicopter and lifeboats were involved in the operation to bring the people from the inflatable "mega-dinghy" to shore in Portsmouth.
Thomas livestreamed from the city, urging supporters to travel to Portsmouth. Videos posted online show protesters confronting police as authorities attempted to bring the migrants onto land and then transport them by bus to an initial processing facility.
Some protesters attempted to obstruct the buses, while police officers formed lines to keep them away from the arrivals.
Emma Reynolds, a lawmaker and current member of the cabinet, condemned the protests as "thuggish and intimidating behavior" in an interview with CBS News' partner network BBC News.
Migration as a political flashpoint
Anti-migrant demonstrations have become increasingly common across Britain over the last two years.
Hotels accommodating asylum seekers became regular protest sites last year, while disorder and violence linked to anti-migrant demonstrations has erupted in several cities, including Glasgow in Scotland and Belfast in Northern Ireland.
Tommy Robinson has drawn large crowds to demonstrations in central London. At one 2025 rally, Elon Musk addressed Robinson's supporters remotely, telling them: "Whether you choose violence or not, violence is coming to you, you either fight back or you die."
Robinson has continued staging demonstrations in 2026, although some have drawn smaller crowds.
During 14 previous years of Conservative Party rule, and since the Labour Party came back to power two years ago, successive British governments had pledged and largely failed to stem the flow of undocumented migrants arriving by small boats from France.
More than 40,000 people made the journey in 2025, according to government data. Around 17,000 migrants had crossed between Jan. 1 and Sept. 1 of this year, which the government likes to note is approximately 43% fewer than during the same period last year.
The events in Dover and Portsmouth over the weekend appear to show that falling arrival numbers alone won't shield the government from anger over migration, especially as it is encouraged by high-profile activists determined to keep the topic front and center.

from refuge to prototype: why cabins keep redefining how we live
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:38:45 UTC
01:38:45 KST

The cabin has always promised something larger than its diminutive footprint. Reduced to shelter, enclosure and a relationship with its surroundings, it seems to return architecture to its most elementary question: what do we actually need in order to inhabit a place? Yet its contemporary appeal extends well beyond construction. At a moment defined by permanent connectivity, speed and availability, the image of a small structure removed from the city has become a shorthand for another rhythm of life — quieter, slower and apparently more autonomous. The cabin is therefore both an architectural experiment and a cultural fantasy: a place onto which we project everything we feel ordinary life no longer gives us.
Spanish journalist and curator Eva Morell explores precisely this tension in ‘Refugio, una historia de cabañas’, published by Debate in 2025. Moving from prehistoric shelters to Thoreau’s Walden, Le Corbusier’s Cabanon and cabins embedded in popular culture, the book examines shelter as both physical structure and recurring human desire. ‘For me, a cabin is an ideal, a philosophy, almost a religion: a space where you feel comfortable, calm and safe,’Morell explains. ‘The cabin is more a feeling than an architecture, because it goes beyond architecture itself.’
That desire has acquired a peculiar form in the digital age. Cabins circulate endlessly through Instagram feeds, Pinterest boards and travel accounts: isolated timber structures glowing against forests, lakes or snow-covered landscapes. They offer visual access to a world imagined as the opposite of the one through which we encounter them. Morell’s own fascination developed through Tumblr and early social media before eventually becoming El Club de la cabaña, the newsletter she launched in 2021. The contradiction is central to her reading of the phenomenon. ‘We are using the internet, which is exactly what we want to escape from, as the tool to search for the offline,’she says.‘Looking at cabins on a screen is a way of disconnecting without leaving the sofa.’
For Morell, this digital obsession is less a contradiction to resolve than a symptom to examine. The imaginary cabin offers withdrawal even when no physical journey takes place. Scrolling past these images becomes a small act of projection: picturing another house also means picturing another routine, another relationship with work, technology, possessions or time. ‘It seems to me the most honest symptom of how tired we are in this hyper-technological and productivity-driven era,’she observes. The cabin’s contemporary relevance, then, may lie precisely in this distance between image and reality. We do not necessarily want the building itself; we want the conditions of life that we believe it contains.
Architecture nevertheless remains fundamental to that promise. By reducing the domestic environment to a constrained footprint, the cabin forces decisions that larger houses can postpone or conceal. What deserves space? Which elements are indispensable? How much comfort is enough? How should a dwelling meet the landscape rather than merely occupy it? From primitive shelters to modernist experiments, the cabin has repeatedly allowed architects to rehearse ideas at a scale where every material, opening and function becomes consequential. Morell’s history places Le Corbusier’s famously compact Cabanon alongside much older and more vernacular forms of refuge, suggesting that the impulse to reduce habitation is neither new nor attached to a single architectural language.
This is also where the cabin begins to look less nostalgic than experimental. Its limitations can become useful constraints for testing self-sufficiency, material economy and a more immediate relationship between building and environment. The apparent regression toward something primitive can therefore point forward. Morell describes the first refuges as the beginnings of collective human life and argues that our relationship with them has never disappeared: ‘Before we are born we already inhabit one, our mother’s body, and after coming into life we spend the rest of our time searching for places that give us that embrace again.’ For her, ‘Refugio’ is consequently not a book ‘about little wooden houses,’ but about the much older impulse to construct spaces of protection and belonging.
Yet the cabin’s promise of simplicity becomes more complicated once it enters the contemporary market. Since the pandemic, nature tourism and remote accommodation have expanded dramatically, turning isolation, silence and disconnection into desirable — and often expensive — commodities. Morell calls this process ‘cabañificación’, comparing it to the transformation of historic neighborhoods and traditional markets through gentrification. ‘Modern world has achieved something astonishing: taking the most basic things that exist — going into the countryside, being quiet, breathing — and turning them into an elite activity you have to pay for,’she says.‘We are paying for something that should be free: not being available.’
The cabin therefore occupies an uncomfortable position between resistance and consumption. It can test how little architecture we need while simultaneously becoming a highly designed symbol of privilege; it can promise proximity to nature while helping transform that landscape into a tourism product. Morell asks the question directly: ‘When we go to a cabin, are we really looking to disconnect, or are we simply replacing urban overload with a decorated version of the rural?’ Perhaps this contradiction is exactly what makes the cabin useful to contemporary architecture. Rather than proposing that everyone retreat into the woods, its renewed popularity exposes what many people increasingly miss in ordinary habitation: silence, autonomy, reduced consumption, contact with nature and the possibility of being temporarily unavailable. The real experiment may therefore not be how to build more cabins, but how to bring some of what they promise back into everyday life.
This article is part of designboom’s MODES OF HABITATION chapter, exploring how the spaces we inhabit can reshape the ways we live together. Discover more stories rethinking domesticity, shared living, and the many forms a home can take here.

‘Rhetoric differs’: How the UK’s relationship with Israel took a downturn

‘Rhetoric differs’: How the UK’s relationship with Israel took a downturn
The UK is planning to take new steps against illegal Israeli settlements as Palestinians suffer more violence.
The United Kingdom is expected to announce trade restrictions on illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, the latest sign, some analysts say, that UK-Israeli relations have taken another downturn.
Britain is one of Israel’s strongest allies in the West, but since the Labour Party came back to power after more than a decade in opposition, some of the government’s policies and rhetoric have shifted.
