India’s new ambassador to Iran seeks to deepen ties amid shifting geopolitical dynamics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
15:59:31 UTC
00:59:31 KST

India’s new ambassador to Iran seeks to deepen ties amid shifting geopolitical dynamics
TEHRAN — India’s Ambassador-designate to Iran, Vishwesh Negi, met with a senior Iranian Foreign Ministry official on Sunday to explore avenues for boosting relations between New Delhi and Tehran.
“H.E. Shri Vishwesh Negi, Ambassador-designate of India to Iran, met H.E. Mr. Mohammad Reza Bahrami Taqanaki, Director General, South Asia Division, Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Iran,” the official X (formerly Twitter) account of the Embassy of India in Iran posted. “The meeting provided an opportunity to discuss India-Iran relations and further strengthen bilateral cooperation.”
Earlier, Negi presented a copy of his credentials to Ali Akbar Nazari, Director General of Protocols at the Iranian Foreign Ministry.
Negi is a veteran diplomat with extensive experience in political, security, and multilateral affairs. His career includes postings at Indian diplomatic missions in Tehran, Rome, and London, as well as senior positions at India’s Ministry of External Affairs (MEA), where he handled portfolios covering Pakistan, Afghanistan, Iran, the United Nations, and the Indo-Pacific. He also served as Joint Secretary for International Cooperation at India’s Ministry of Defense.
Navigating regional turbulence
Given Negi’s extensive security and diplomatic background, his appointment comes at a crucial juncture for India-Iran strategic and economic ties amid ongoing instability in West Asia, in the wake of the US military adventurism.
Amid heightened regional hostilities, New Delhi has consistently advocated for dialogue and de-escalation, reiterating its principled stance against armed conflict. This position was underscored by Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi during his recent bilateral meeting with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on the sidelines of the 26th Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Summit and the SCO Plus meeting in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, on August 31.
“We must redouble our efforts to establish peace. I firmly believe that, ultimately, peace and security will prevail,” Prime Minister Modi told his Iranian counterpart during the discussions.
President Pezeshkian welcomed Modi’s stance, expressing appreciation for India’s engagement and support for diplomatic pathways to resolve regional crises. Emphasizing the need to intensify multilateral efforts to restore stability, the Iranian president urged New Delhi to continue leveraging its diplomatic capital for peace.
Highlighting the deep civilizational, cultural, and historical links between the two countries, both leaders reaffirmed their commitment to expanding cooperation across trade, energy, connectivity, and cultural exchange.
India’s constructive engagement was also reflected at the multilateral level: Prime Minister Modi joined other SCO leaders in endorsing the “Bishkek Declaration” on September 1, 2026, which condemned the US and Israel’s war on Iran that began on February 28. Modi also endorsed the adoption of the Tianjin Declaration a year prior, on September 1, 2025, which reiterated the imperative of upholding international law and the principles of the UN Charter following the US-Israeli aggression against Iran in June that year.
From a strategic perspective, New Delhi’s dual endorsements in Bishkek and Tianjin reflect an evolving posture within non-Western multilateral architectures. By aligning with joint statements that defend sovereignty and international law, India reinforces its traditional commitment to strategic autonomy. Tehran, on the other hand, views India’s diplomatic weight not only as an essential balancer in Eurasian geopolitics, but also as an indispensable partner in pushing back against unilateral coercive measures and militarism in West Asia.
The BRICS summit and strategic connectivity
Against this backdrop, Negi’s appointment serves as a pivotal bridge between New Delhi’s top-level political commitments and their practical implementation on the ground. By dispatching an envoy with deep expertise in defense diplomacy and regional security, India is positioning its mission in Tehran to actively operationalize directives on maritime security, trade corridors, and regional stabilization.
This diplomatic engagement carries immediate significance as India prepares to host the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi on September 12–13. As full BRICS partners, India and Iran share strategic interests in strengthening South-South economic cooperation and accelerating key connectivity initiatives—most notably the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC).
At the heart of this bilateral convergence lies the strategic port of Chabahar, India’s gateway to landlocked Central Asia and Afghanistan, and a cornerstone of the INSTC framework. For New Delhi, securing long-term operational resilience at Chabahar and de-risking regional maritime supply lines in the Sea of Oman and the Persian Gulf require seasoned defense-diplomatic coordination—a capability central to Negi’s institutional background.
Furthermore, with both nations actively exploring local-currency settlement mechanisms to circumvent unilateral Western sanctions, Negi’s tenure will be critical in translating shared political will into sustainable economic channels. Negi’s appointment also provides the vital diplomatic momentum needed to translate the consensus reached between Modi and Pezeshkian into tangible outcomes at the upcoming summit in the Indian capital, reinforcing India’s role as an active partner in West Asian stability and Eurasian integration.

Supporters of Alternative for Germany are seen during the final campaign rally on the eve of state elections in Saxony-Anhalt on Sept. 5, 2026. | Jens Schlueter/Getty Images
Berlin’s political establishment is staggering after the far-right Alternative for Germany scored a historic victory in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday night, forcing mainstream parties to confront how to keep it from power — and explain its stunning rise.
The AfD won 43.8 percent of Sunday’s vote, more than doubling its 2021 result. Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s center-right Christian Democratic Union crashed to 17.2 percent, its worst-ever showing in the eastern state.
Thorsten Frei, leader of the CDU/CSU group in the Bundestag, called the result a “turning point for our country” and said conservatives must ask why they were no longer reaching voters. CDU Secretary-General Franziska Hoppermann rejected any debate over Merz’s future and again ruled out cooperation with either the AfD or The Left.
Advertisement
Saxony-Anhalt’s incumbent premier Sven Schulze, from the CDU, struck a more sober note on Sunday night. “Some say this is a dark day for Saxony-Anhalt. I say: That’s democracy,” he told ARD. “The people went to the polls today.”
The rout piles pressure on Merz, who once vowed to cut the AfD in half but has been chancellor while the far-right party has boomed in the polls.
Social Democratic Party co-leader Lars Klingbeil called the vote a “signal to Berlin” and said the result should prompt the federal government to reflect on its policies. Co-leader Bärbel Bas said the result was “frightening many people,” while Green co-chair Felix Banaszak described the AfD surge as “dramatic.”
The Left’s Heidi Reichinnek branded the result “catastrophic,” blaming federal government policies for creating fertile ground for the far right. But the CDU’s refusal to cooperate with The Left makes constructing an anti-AfD majority harder.
Left-populist BSW founder Sahra Wagenknecht declared the “firewall policy” a failure in a post on X, warning another coalition built purely to exclude the AfD would be an “affront” to voters.
The AfD, meanwhile, claimed a mandate to govern. Co-leader Alice Weidel hailed a “historic result,” while fellow co-leader Tino Chrupalla declared: “Ulrich Siegmund will be our new minister-president,” referring to the party’s lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt.
Advertisement
Chrupalla then turned Merz’s own rhetoric back on him: “We’ve cut the CDU in half.”
Yet the AfD won just 39 of 83 seats in Saxony-Anhalt, leaving it just short of a majority. The far right’s rivals now face a scramble to find a government capable of surviving without it.
Chrupalla, meanwhile, said the party would send invitations for talks to all other parties. “Then we’ll see who slaps away our hand,” he told public broadcaster ARD on Monday. Asked whether the AfD could push for fresh elections if no workable majority emerges, Chrupalla said the party was “prepared for all scenarios.”

Qatar builds case seeking damages over Iranian attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
15:58:53 UTC
00:58:53 KST

Breadcrumb
Qatar builds case seeking damages over Iranian attacks
Qatar has begun building a comprehensive legal case over Iranian attacks on its territory and is preparing to receive claims from those affected as Doha considers seeking compensation for billions of dollars in damage and losses, The New Arab has learned.
The move marks a significant step in Qatar's response to the Iranian attacks, shifting its focus from condemnation towards documenting damage and establishing potential claims for compensation.
Qatari authorities are preparing to receive claims from people and businesses affected by the attacks, which have injured around 20 people and damaged residential, industrial and commercial facilities, vehicles and critical energy infrastructure.
The legal file will document damage and losses resulting from the Iranian attacks, using information provided by those affected to enable Qatari authorities and other relevant bodies to pursue compensation at a later stage.
The development comes as Doha steps up diplomatic and legal action over the attacks, arguing they had no legal basis and maintaining that Qatar retains its right to defend itself and seek full compensation for its losses.
On 4 September, Qatar sent identical letters to UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres and the president of the UN Security Council for September, Jerome Bonafont, responding to a letter from the acting head of Iran's permanent mission to the United Nations.
Doha said Iranian claims could not, regardless of how often they were repeated, provide a legal basis for attacks targeting Qatar since 28 February.
Qatar has sought to address the dispute through international institutions, framing the Iranian attacks as an issue of international law and the UN Charter rather than solely as a bilateral political dispute.
It argued that the attacks violated the prohibition on the use of force against the territorial integrity and political independence of states under Article 2 of the UN Charter.
Qatar also cited UN Security Council Resolution 2817 of 2026, which condemned the Iranian attacks and called on Tehran to refrain immediately from acts or threats that violate international law.
Doha rejected Iran's attempt to justify the attacks as self-defence, arguing that the requirements for invoking Article 51 of the UN Charter had not been met.
Qatar said letters submitted to the Security Council in recent months documented attacks on civilian targets, including energy facilities, tankers and commercial vessels.
Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed Al Ansari on 4 September also rejected what he described as Iranian "selective quotation" from a document prepared for security and operational purposes.
He said Qatar's official record submitted to the UN documented Iranian missiles being launched at civilian, commercial and residential areas.
A Qatari letter to the UN in March documented 16 people injured in attacks, while another letter in July recorded three injuries, including a child.
Doha has also stressed that the attack on gas facilities at Ras Laffan was officially documented in UN records and was not merely an "alleged attack".
Billions in energy losses
The damage to Ras Laffan could form one of the most significant elements of any future compensation claim because of its importance to Qatar's gas industry and global energy supplies.
The Qatari Defence Ministry said Ras Laffan Industrial City and Mesaieed Industrial Area were attacked by Iranian drones on 2 March.
The attacks hit facilities linked to the gas sector, including two of Qatar's 14 liquefaction trains and a gas liquids facility.
Around 17% of Qatar's liquefied natural gas export capacity, equivalent to approximately 12.8 million tonnes annually, was disrupted.
QatarEnergy subsequently declared force majeure on contracts with buyers and suspended production operations for natural gas and related products.
The company said Ras Laffan was hit again by an Iranian missile on 18 March, causing large fires and significant material damage but no deaths.
QatarEnergy estimated infrastructure damage at around $26 billion, while Minister of State for Energy Affairs and QatarEnergy chief executive Saad Al Kaabi said lost gas revenues could reach $20 billion annually.
The company has said the affected capacity could take between three and five years to restore fully.
Record of attacks
Qatar has documented a series of Iranian missile and drone attacks since 28 February.
Sixteen people were injured by shrapnel on 28 February as Qatari air defences intercepted a barrage of Iranian missiles. The Interior Ministry said 66 missiles were launched and authorities received more than 100 reports of falling shrapnel.
Hamad International Airport was also disrupted after Qatari airspace was closed, resulting in flight cancellations.
Qatar was subjected to two further missile attacks on 8 April, hours after a ceasefire was announced, with falling shrapnel causing four injuries and damaging a home.
On 1 April, the Qatari Defence Ministry said Iran launched three cruise missiles towards Qatar. Two were intercepted, while a third struck an oil tanker chartered by QatarEnergy off the country's northern coast.
The tanker's structure was damaged, although its crew were safely evacuated and no injuries were reported.
Qatar also reported a drone attack on 4 April targeting infrastructure, while during the ceasefire a drone struck a commercial cargo ship in Qatari territorial waters near Mesaieed port, causing a limited fire but no injuries.
In July, three people, including a child, were injured by falling shrapnel after Iranian missiles were intercepted.
How could Qatar seek compensation?
Qatari lawyer Hawas Al Shammari told The New Arab that the strength of any compensation case would depend not simply on the amount Qatar sought but on its ability to document damage, establish its value and demonstrate a causal link to the attacks.
He pointed to the Democratic Republic of the Congo's case against Uganda before the International Court of Justice (ICJ). Congo sought more than $11 billion, but the court ultimately awarded $325 million in compensation in 2022 after assessing the evidence, causation and value of the damage.
Al Shammari said UN Security Council Resolution 2817 was significant because it found that the Iranian attacks constituted a breach of international law and condemned attacks on civilians and civilian objects.
However, the resolution did not establish a compensation mechanism.
He pointed to Human Rights Council Resolution 61/1, adopted on 25 March 2026, as another important development because it explicitly called on Iran to provide full, effective and prompt reparation to victims for damage and injuries resulting from the attacks.
Al Shammari said Qatar's repeated correspondence with the UN also created a dated international record of the attacks and demonstrated Doha's continued assertion of its rights, potentially strengthening a future compensation case.
There is no single clear legal route through which Qatar could compel Iran to pay compensation, however.
Al Shammari said the ICJ could be an option if a legal basis for its jurisdiction could be established through an applicable treaty between Qatar and Iran or a subsequent special agreement between the two countries.
Iran's 2023 declaration accepting the ICJ's compulsory jurisdiction is limited and does not appear to cover a dispute of this kind, he said.
Another possibility would be the creation of a dedicated international claims mechanism. Al Shammari cited the compensation commission established following Iraq's invasion of Kuwait and the Ukraine Damage Register as potential models.
Claims involving ships, tankers and commercial facilities could also proceed through insurance, reinsurance, arbitration, domestic courts or negotiated settlements.
For now, Al Shammari said Qatar's priority should be to build a comprehensive evidentiary record detailing what was damaged, when it was damaged, its value, who caused the damage and the evidence establishing that link.
The decision over whether to pursue the claims through a court, compensation commission or negotiations could come later.
Evidence not collected now may be difficult to recover in the future, he said, making documentation the foundation of any eventual claim for compensation.

Kyivstar completes transition from mass 3G use, redirects freed-up resources to LTE network development
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
18:58:37 EEST
00:58:37 KST

Kyivstar, Ukraine's largest telecom operator, announced the cessation of its third-generation (3G) network, resulting in more than 1 million subscribers migrating to 4G. The freed-up spectrum resource has been redirected to LTE network development, according to a company statement published Monday.
Kyivstar explained that by phasing out 3G technology, the available 4G bandwidth has increased by 25%, improving the speed and stability of mobile services.
The mobile operator also noted that the phased 3G phase-out began in 2023, covering all regions of the country. Among other results of the project, 20 MHz of the 2100 MHz band was redistributed in favor of 4G.
Overall, according to the mobile operator, thanks to this redistribution, data transfer speeds on the company's network increased by 20-40% depending on location, and Kyivstar recorded a more than doubling of average mobile internet speeds between 2022 and 2026.
It is noted that as of August of this year, the average download speed on the network was almost 100 Mbps, and in major cities, this figure exceeded this figure.
At the same time, the company emphasized that 3G technology will be temporarily retained locally for a certain number of B2B clients due to the specific location of their equipment, but their transition to 4G is planned to be completed in the near future.
Kyivstar previously announced that, starting August 18 of this year, it will disable 3G technology in a number of populated areas in some regions of Ukraine and redistribute its frequencies in favor of 4G. It was noted that 4G should completely replace 3G in Dnipropetrovsk region (Kryvyi Rih and Kryvyi Rih district), Ivano-Frankivsk (Horodenka, Dolyna, Sniatyn, Verkhovyna, Ivano-Frankivsk, and Kalush districts), and Khmelnytsky (Dunayivtsi, Krasyliv, Netishyn, Polonne, Starokostiantyniv, Khmelnytsky, Kamyanets-Podilsky, and Shepetivka districts).
In turn, the mobile operator Lifecell LLC (TM lifecell), part of the DVL group of companies (Datagroup-Volia-lifecell), will shut down its third-generation (3G) network in a number of settlements in 17 regions of Ukraine on September 3 and transition the corresponding regions to 4G/LTE technology.
According to the National Commission for Regulation of Electronic Communications and Postal Services, the top three leaders in terms of revenue from telecommunications services for January-March 2026 in Ukraine were mobile operators by a significant margin: Kyivstar PJSC – UAH 12.08 billion, VF Ukraine PJSC (Vodafone Ukraine TM) – UAH 6.69 billion, and Lifecell LLC (Lifecell TM) from the DVL Group – UAH 4.2 billion.

School headscarf ban in Austria challenged in Constitutional Court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
15:55:00 UTC
00:55:00 KST

A mother and her two daughters have filed an application before Austria's Constitutional Court to challenge a school headscarf ban for girls under 14 years of age, a court spokesperson confirmed to Deutsche Presse-Agentur (dpa) on Monday.
The application was lodged on the first day that the new regulation took effect at the start of the school year.
The Austrian news agency, APA, had previously reported on the legal challenge.
The ban applies to a "headscarf that covers the head according to Islamic traditions." In cases where the ban is ignored, school administrators must initially hold a meeting with the girl concerned and her parents.
If the child continues to wear a headscarf, the parents must meet with the responsible school authority. As a last resort, fines of between 150 euros ($175) and 800 euros can be imposed.
The regulation was passed by the governing coalition of the conservative Austrian People's Party (ÖVP), the Social Democratic Party (SPÖ), and the liberal Neos.
The Constitutional Court struck down a similar measure introduced in 2019 that applied only to primary schools.
At the time, the judges criticized, among other things, the fact that the law specifically targeted Muslim girls and did not apply to all religious head coverings.
The Islamic Religious Community in Austria (IGGÖ) has criticized the ban and said it would advise and support the families affected.
The IGGÖ is preparing its own legal action against the law.

British military personnel, along with their Norwegian and American counterparts, deployed troops to the remote Norwegian island of Jan Mayen as part of a NATO operation.
The UK Ministry of Defence reported this.
The exercise, dubbed Operation Atlantic City, took place from August 26 to September 4 as part of the Alliance’s Operation Arctic Sentry.
Marines, Royal Navy forces, and units of the Royal Air Force participated in the exercise, alongside the Norwegian Navy, the Norwegian National Guard, and the U.S. Marine Corps.
Jan Mayen Island lies in the Norwegian Sea north of the Greenland–Iceland–United Kingdom line and is strategically important for the defense of Northern Europe.
During the operation, the allies practiced naval operations, reconnaissance, survival in extreme Arctic conditions, and the integration of sensors and communications systems.
The United Kingdom suspended exercises involving 90 or more military personnel because of a lack of funding at the Ministry of Defense.

Punjab govt de-addiction centre admissions rise 164% in a year
Sep 07, 2026, 21:20 IST
Comments

Small

Health and family welfare minister Balbir Singh
CHANDIGARH: Admissions to Punjab government-run de-addiction centres rose by more than 164 percent in a year, with 25,290 people admitted in 2025 compared with 9,577 in 2024, according to data released by the state government on Monday.The Punjab government said the figures indicate growing public confidence in its treatment and rehabilitation network under its anti-drug campaign, ‘Yudh Nashean Virudh’, launched in March 2025. More than 14,000 people had already been admitted to government de-addiction centres by July 2026.The government said the increase in admissions suggested that more individuals and families were approaching formal treatment instead of allowing stigma around addiction to prevent them from seeking help.Admissions to government rehabilitation centres also recorded a sharp increase, rising from 2,644 in 2024 to 8,574 in 2025 — a jump of more than 224 percent. By July 2026, over 5,800 people had been admitted, nearly 68 percent of the total admissions recorded in 2025.The state’s outpatient opioid-assisted treatment (OOAT) network has also seen an increase in registrations. New registrations rose from 13,033 in 2024 to 17,702 in 2025, while more than 12,500 new patients had registered by August 2026, the government said.
Punjab has also invoked provisions under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act to facilitate treatment. As of August 27, more than 11,000 individuals had been granted immunity under Section 64A of the Act, which provides legal immunity to people suffering from drug addiction who are charged with consumption or possession, subject to its conditions.
Health and family welfare minister Balbir Singh said the rise in admissions was among the most encouraging indicators of the anti-drug campaign, as more people were seeking institutional support and entering the formal treatment system.“Yudh Nashean Virudh stands on three pillars: strict enforcement against smugglers, treatment and rehabilitation for the affected, and prevention to protect our children before drugs ever reach them,” Singh said.He added that the government’s focus was to help people recover from addiction, restore families and provide those struggling with substance abuse a pathway to recovery.

Ukraine&apos;s international reserves continue to &quot;melt away&quot; — in August, they fell to $48.7 billion
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
18:47:31 EEST
00:47:31 KST

Ukraine's international reserves continue to "melt away" — in August, they fell to $48.7 billion
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine's international reserves stood at $48.66 billion as of September 1, down 5% over the month. The decline was caused by foreign exchange interventions and lower aid inflows.
Ukraine’s international reserves as of September 1, 2026, according to preliminary data, amounted to 48,662.2 million dollars. In August, they decreased by 5.0%. The NBU reported that this dynamic was driven by a reduction in the volume of international financial assistance while foreign exchange interventions remained close to the July level, UNN reports.
The National Bank noted that the current volume of international reserves is sufficient to maintain the stability of the foreign exchange market.
Overall, the dynamics of international reserves in August 2026 were determined by a number of factors:
-  first, the National Bank’s operations in Ukraine’s foreign exchange market; 
According to the NBU’s balance sheet data, in August it sold 4,850.7 million US dollars and purchased 0.5 million US dollars in the foreign exchange market. Net foreign currency sales amounted to 4,850.2 million US dollars.
-  second, receipts in favor of the government and payments for servicing and repaying public debt; 
In August, 927.3 million US dollars were credited to the government’s foreign currency accounts at the National Bank, including:
-  894.0 million US dollars – through World Bank accounts; 
-  33.3 million US dollars – from other investors. 
In addition, international reserves increased by 1.63 billion US dollars because the government converted into hryvnias the corresponding amount from funds that Ukraine had previously received from the European Union as part of the defense tranche under the Ukraine Support Loan program. Upon receipt, these funds are not included in Ukraine’s international reserves due to their limited (targeted) purpose of use. At the same time, if the government sells them to the National Bank in exchange for hryvnias for subsequent use as intended, international reserves increase by the corresponding amount.
A total of 721.8 million US dollars was paid for servicing and repaying public debt in foreign currency, including:
-  357.9 million US dollars – servicing and repayment of debt to the World Bank; 
-  288.7 million US dollars – servicing domestic government loan bonds; 
-  16.9 million US dollars – servicing foreign currency domestic government loan bonds; 
-  58.3 million US dollars – payments to other creditors. 
In addition, Ukraine paid 285.2 million US dollars to the International Monetary Fund.
-  third, the revaluation of financial instruments (as a result of changes in market values and exchange rates) and the impact of other factors. 
In August, the revaluation of financial instruments and the impact of other factors increased international reserves by 752.0 million US dollars.

President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan has outlined Türkiye’s preparations for the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, along with new measures on social housing and urban renewal, following a cabinet meeting in Ankara.
Speaking after the meeting at the Presidential Complex on Sept. 7, Erdoğan said more than 100,000 visitors from over 190 countries were expected to attend the conference, which will take place from Nov. 9 to 20.
The event will be held at the 1.1 million-square-meter Antalya EXPO site, where renovation work is underway.
A total of 38 kilometers of roads serving the conference venue and hotels in the Belek tourism district have been completed, Erdoğan said.

Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change Minister Murat Kurum said preparations included work on four main routes and 12 roads connecting hotels in Belek. Around 160,000 square meters of indoor exhibition space is also being built.
Turning to the economy, Erdoğan said Türkiye’s goods exports reached a record $23.5 billion in August, while annualized exports rose to $280.3 billion. The country is now $1.7 billion short of its year-end target of $282 billion.
He said the government’s three-year Medium-Term Program would focus on increasing production and exports, strengthening the services sector and advancing structural reforms.
Despite the effects of regional conflicts and higher global energy prices, Türkiye would remain on its growth and development path, Erdoğan said.
“We will do whatever is necessary to make Türkiye’s economy stronger, more competitive and more resilient in every field,” he said.
Erdoğan also provided details of the government’s 500,000-home social housing program covering all 81 provinces.
The first homes are due to be delivered from March 2027.
Applications for 15,000 rental social homes in Istanbul will open on Sept. 14, with a draw for the first 1,000 homes scheduled for October.
The president also announced that the “Half of Us” urban renewal campaign would be extended until Dec. 31, 2027.
Work has begun on 435,683 independent units under the government’s urban renewal programs, Erdoğan said, adding that the figure was expected to exceed 500,000 by the end of the year.

The Italian-born independent expert has faced harsh criticism from Israel and some of its allies over her long-standing accusations that Israel is committing genocide and other war crimes against Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
Albanese, who was appointed by the UN Human Rights Council in 2022 but who does not speak on behalf of the United Nations, said she had received credible information from multiple sources last month of “deliberate and widespread removal, crushing and transport of rubble”.

‘I have no other country, by choice’: Lone soldier wounded on Oct. 7 to perform Israeli classic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
15:44:36 UTC
00:44:36 KST

The song “I Have No Other Country” has long since become part of the Israeli cultural canon. What began as a protest song written by Ehud Manor against the First Lebanon War has since taken on several incarnations, most recently during protests against the judicial overhaul.
It may take on yet another meaning Monday when it opens an appreciation event for volunteers of “Brothers and Sisters for Israel — Civilian Operations Center,” which will feature personal stories from the war.
Performing the song will be singer Hadar Strauss and combat soldier Moshe Marwick, who was seriously wounded on October 7, 2023.
“The choice of the song was made by the organization,” says Marwick, a U.S.-born immigrant to Israel who became a lone soldier. “I know its political aspects, but as someone who chose Israel as my home, the words touch me in the purest place. In a certain sense, it tells my story — that I have no other country, by choice. I was even privileged to fight for it and be wounded.”
'Only when it was all over did I realize I had been wounded'
Marwick, 24, of Bat Yam, grew up in Baltimore, Maryland, in a Haredi family. At 16, he came to Israel on a youth program and decided to stay.
“When my friends began enlisting, I felt I needed to do the same, so I made aliyah and enlisted in the Nahal Brigade. My parents were very supportive and were happy that I was doing what was right for me.”
“We immediately headed out in an Achzarit armored personnel carrier toward Holit, but we encountered a group of terrorists near the kibbutz. They fired two RPGs at us, and then we fought a gunbattle for hours.”
Marwick was wounded in the shoulder and hip within the first minutes of the fighting, but continued battling alongside his comrades. Together with reinforcement forces, they prevented the terrorists from infiltrating the base.
“Only when it was all over did I begin to realize that I had been wounded,” he says.
He was airlifted to Soroka Medical Center, where he underwent complicated surgery, and later transferred to rehabilitation at Sheba Medical Center at Tel Hashomer. Representatives of “Brothers and Sisters for Israel,” who came to visit him, noticed a guitar on his bed and suggested that he join the “Song for the Road” project they created with the Rimon School of Music, in which students work with wounded soldiers on songs.
“Because music is such a big part of my life, I jumped at the opportunity,” Marwick says. “Since I’ve been in Israel, I’ve learned to fall in love with local music.”
Part of the healing
Singer, musician and Rimon student Hadar Strauss, 25, who will perform the song with him, is taking part in the project alongside three wounded soldiers.
“At first I was worried that I had nothing to contribute to them, but the moment I met them, and especially Moshe, I realized it was going to be an enjoyable process,” she says.
At their weekly meetings, they learn about Israeli music and, sometimes, as in Marwick’s case, also perform original songs.
“I already have a second single on the way and a show at Zappa,” he says. “I think Hadar is part of my healing.”
The event organized by “Brothers and Sisters for Israel” will present on stage at Zappa the stories of the organization’s members and volunteers, from the morning of October 7 through today. It will review their civilian work during the war, from the first days, when volunteers focused on helping the wounded, to the present, as they assist communities in rebuilding.

Spain's top criminal court launches criminal investigation into Ceuta migrant influx
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
15:43:10 UTC
00:43:10 KST

A Spanish police report highlighting "total permissiveness" by Moroccan security forces formed the basis for the decision by the country's top criminal court to open the probe.
Spain's Audiencia Nacional court has ordered a criminal investigation into the arrival of tens of thousands of migrants in Ceuta in July.
In her ruling, investigating judge María Tardón said there were grounds to believe that "criminal conduct allegedly committed abroad had seriously undermined Spain's territorial integrity, using the mass entry into the country to do so."
The decision comes after the judge ruled that the National Court had jurisdiction to investigate alleged crimes against territorial integrity, negligent homicide, and criminal organisation, in line with the criteria set out by the Public Prosecutor's Office.
Tardón said the migrant flow "constitutes one of the characteristic methods of 'hybrid warfare' or the 'grey zone,' with the aim of altering the life and rights of Spanish citizens" in Ceuta.
A Spanish police report highlighting "total permissiveness" by Moroccan security forces formed the basis for the judge's decision to open the probe.
"A clear and undeniable facilitation of the process" came from the north African nation, notably "through the verified and visually documented behaviour of Morocco's security forces," Tardón said.
Uniformed Moroccan security forces made "no serious attempt" to halt the influx, with some also offering "active guidance" on how to make the crossing, the judge continued.
The Spanish government has said there is "no conclusive evidence" that Rabat was responsible for the mass entry in late July, which saw more than 70,000 migrants cross into the Spanish exclave from Morocco.
Moroccan authorities have not commented on the Spanish police report, although Moroccan media outlets have branded it a "botched" document that they say lacks material evidence.
Most of the migrants who made the crossing into Ceuta have been returned, but thousands have remained amid mounting political tensions.

AfD is rising, but it can still be stopped
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
15:42:36 UTC
00:42:36 KST

AfD is rising, but it can still be stopped
The German mainstream still has a window of opportunity to act and reverse a dangerous trend to the far right.
The victory of far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in the elections of the East German state Saxony-Anhalt is a dramatic moment for Germany. The party won 44 percent of the vote, securing 39 seats in the 83-seat local legislature.
Although this result falls short of a majority, it is close enough. The small, populist BSW party has indicated that it may enable the election of an AfD head of government in the state. This would give executive power to an extreme-right party in a German state for the first time since World War 2.
The election has already deeply disturbed Germany. It is the culmination of a decade-long process that saw the AfD move from a marginal protest party to a major political power.
Although this election has been a tough blow for the other mainstream German parties, they still have an opportunity to reverse this dangerous trend. That would depend on whether those in power are prepared to take decisive action.
When considering what strategy must be adopted in response to AfD’s surge, it is important to explore the attitudes of its electorate and the socioeconomic conditions affecting them.
In recent surveys, conducted by the think thank I co-lead, d|part, people in Saxony-Anhalt were much more likely than the national average to report job prospects, education, health care and the social environment worsening where they live.
The mismatch between public demands for better economic opportunities and social services and what the government has delivered has resulted in the anger that the AfD has been able to exploit.
While AfD’s proposed policies in Saxony-Anhalt could worsen socioeconomic problems, many voters do not see an alternative. Their trust in the parties in power has eroded too much.
According to our surveys, roughly three quarters of AfD voters do not consider any other party as a viable option at all. Among supporters of other parties, more than half could name at least one other political option they would also consider. In short, most AfD voters are firmly and distinctively committed to the party.
Among those committed AfD voters, there are many who firmly agree with the extreme right and racist positions of the party. Over the last 10 years, the support base of the AfD has shifted from a majority, saying they vote for the party despite their positions to saying they vote for it because of them.
In the short term, those hardline voters of the AfD are not reachable. But the quarter of current AfD supporters who are open to other parties could be swayed. Most of them do not think the AfD is the best on areas like the economy or cost of living.
In the immediate aftermath of the Saxony-Anhalt election, this group should be the focus of mainstream parties. How they approach these voters could make a difference in the upcoming elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern state later this month.
In the longer term, there should be a major overhaul of political strategies across the mainstream.
Our surveys show that across the country and the political spectrum, voters are deeply discontent with the status quo. Germans have a very low opinion of the current government. Chancellor Friedrich Merz has the worst approval rating of any German government head since polling began – currently at 13 percent. The disapproval of the work his government is doing is near unanimous across German society.
But dissatisfaction in the government does not mean people do not want strong state action. To the contrary, across the political spectrum decisive and transformative action is desired.
Our research shows that most people, including AfD voters open to other parties, fundamentally trust state institutions and want a government that takes actions to improve people’s living conditions. They do not just care about the money in their own pocket but rather want to see the areas they live in improve in terms of economic and job opportunities but also in terms of social, educational and cultural services.
There are many reasons why the current government – like its predecessors – is failing to deliver. But a major one is that the traditionally large parties, the Christian- and Social-Democrats, have made a huge mistake in recent years of letting the AfD set the agenda.
Hoping to gain more votes, they have picked up AfD’s focus on immigration, placing it at the centre of their agendas and rhetoric. While that has fed anti-immigrant sentiments in the country, it has not made immigration the German people’s main priority.
Our surveys show that the overwhelming majority – 80 percent – of the public think that economic policy should be prioritised over immigration policy.
This means that the German mainstream should stop trying to “steal” AfD’s votes by adopting its agenda and rhetoric. It should not accommodate AfD because accommodation leads to normalisation, and that would only fuel its ascendance.
Instead, mainstream parties should regain the initiative by setting the political agenda, pursing a credible shift in policies, and demonstrating a capacity for decisive action.
The mainstream has to offer a clear plan of action to significantly improve people’s lives. The emphasis of policy making must shift from abstract macroeconomic indicators to tangible changes that affect directly ordinary Germans. Local authorities must be empowered and financially enabled to improve the socio-economic conditions at the local level.
Most Germans want a government that takes strong action and cooperates with businesses to improve life in urban and rural places. If the AfD is to be stopped from progressing, the confidence in the government at all levels must be restored.
In the 20th century, Germany saw the dangers of underestimating a rising extreme-right party during times of economic upheaval. The consequences of that mistake devastated Europe. We must learn from history and do better now.

Far-right triumph in eastern Germany leaves migrants questioning their future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
15:42:03 UTC
00:42:03 KST

Far-right triumph in eastern Germany leaves migrants questioning their future
BERLIN, Sept 7 - Mamad Mohamad watched with mixed emotions as the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) swept to a historic victory on Sunday evening in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.
A member of the Greens, the 46-year-old is set to become one of the first lawmakers with an immigrant background to enter the state parliament, alongside Mustafa Groener of the Left (Die Linke) party.
For Mohamad, who arrived in Germany from Syria as a 16-year-old Yazidi Kurd in 1996, it was a milestone that should have been a moment of celebration. Instead, he described it as a "poisoned victory".
"My heart was split," Mohamad said, recalling the first projections that showed the AfD outperforming expectations while Chancellor Friedrich Merz's governing conservatives slumped to a historic low.
'CULTURALLY ALIEN'
The AfD has long campaigned for tighter immigration and asylum policies, arguing that Germany has lost control of its borders and that migration is putting heavy pressure on public services, security and social cohesion.
According to its election manifesto, an AfD-led Saxony-Anhalt would launch a state-level campaign to deport rejected asylum seekers.
The party also proposes encouraging businesses to adopt artificial intelligence and automation rather than rely on skilled migration from what it describes as "culturally alien" backgrounds.
The AfD rejects accusations that its rhetoric contributes to a hostile climate for migrants, insisting it opposes only illegal and uncontrolled migration.
"Everyone is warmly welcome who contributes positively to our society, who wants to work here, who is qualified, who pays taxes, and who abides by the law," AfD co-leader Alice Weidel said on Monday.
PACKED BAGS
The mood in Mohamad's family was sombre on Monday.
His daughter, he said, was reluctant to attend school, one of several criticised by the AfD over projects that examine threats to democracy.
Though anxiety is running high in many immigrant communities, the result has prompted unease rather than surprise, said Undra Dressler, managing director of the State Network of Migrant Organisations in Saxony-Anhalt.
People with migrant backgrounds have long faced discrimination and structural barriers in access to work, education, healthcare and public services, Dressler said.
"All of this is our reality," she told Reuters.
Sunday's result nevertheless marks a turning point, she said. "There are many people in our communities who say: 'We've already packed our bags and have concrete plans, and we'll be leaving soon,' or, in some cases, have already left."
Pascal Begrich, managing director of democracy advocacy group Miteinander, said he did not expect a large-scale exodus, partly because of economic realities, but agreed that many migrants but also employers were reassessing their future in Saxony-Anhalt.
"There are companies asking themselves whether they really want to locate here and whether they can ensure their workers will be safe," Begrich told Reuters.
CONSTITUTIONAL LIMITS
Mohamad said he feared the political shift could make it harder to attract newcomers to a state already grappling with demographic decline.
"Skilled workers and families will look elsewhere," he said.
Despite concerns about the state's political direction, both Dressler and Begrich stressed that any future government would remain bound by Germany's constitutional order and protections for minorities.
"Every government is bound by this," Dressler said. "And the 15 other federal states have a duty to monitor this and, if necessary, to intervene." REUTERS

IAEA chief Grossi told the Board of Governors that Tehran had provided no information on declared nuclear materials and inspectors had no on-site access, as Iran's parliament speaker threatened US energy assets with retaliatory strikes and the IRGC warned vessels off the southern Hormuz corridor.

IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi told the agency's Board of Governors that Iran was not meeting its Non-Proliferation Treaty safeguards obligations and called for constructive engagement to restore full oversight.

He attributed restrictions on IAEA inspectors to US and Israeli strikes on Iranian enrichment infrastructure.

"We can now say that talks between Iran and Oman have reached their final stage," he said.
However, the IRGC Navy's political deputy said safe passage through the US-designated southern corridor was practically impossible.
"Any vessel entering this corridor will no longer be safe from strikes once it reaches the area of Khasab, Oman," the official, identified as Mohammadi, said.

Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, announced the establishment of an "exclusion zone" outside the Strait of Hormuz, extending from the US naval blockade line into the Persian Gulf.
"Any ship entering this area without Iran's permission and coordination will have its details — along with the names of its owner and charterer — registered and placed on Iran's sanctions list," he said.
Parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf separately warned on social media that US oil and gas assets across regional waters were exposed to retaliatory strikes.
South Korea warned
Baghaei warned South Korea that any military presence in Gulf operations would be treated as direct support for US aggression.
He framed the warning in diplomatic terms, noting that Iran-South Korea relations spanned more than 64 years and were based on mutual respect.
"The military presence of any other country or its participation in operations in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz will be regarded as direct support for the perpetrators of this aggression and will have serious consequences," Baghaei said.
South Korea's foreign ministry said Seoul was in close contact with the international community over the situation in the Middle East and was working to help restore stability and ensure free passage through the strait for all vessels including its own.

Addressing the 166th session of the Arab League Council at the foreign ministers level in Cairo, Rajji said Lebanon was at a “decisive moment” to extend the state’s authority across its entire territory and compel Israel to withdraw behind the international border.

Lebanon and Israel have held seven rounds of direct negotiations under US sponsorship. The first five rounds were held in Washington, culminating in a 14-point framework agreement signed on June 26, while the sixth and seventh took place in Rome.
The latest round concluded on Aug. 6 after three days of talks covering military, political, legal and border issues, as well as prisoners.
The framework provides for a phased Israeli withdrawal from occupied Lebanese territory alongside the deployment of the Lebanese army and the disarmament of non-state armed groups.
Israel has continued its attacks on Lebanon despite the framework agreement. According to figures released by the Lebanese Health Ministry in late August, Israeli attacks since early March have killed more than 4,000 people and injured over 12,000.

EXPLAINER – How the Champions League’s 36-team league phase works
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
15:37:37 UTC
00:37:37 KST

Efe Özkan
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
- Europe’s top club competition enters third season under expanded format that replaced traditional group stage
- All clubs compete in one table, but each team faces only eight opponents before knockout places are decided
- Top eight advance directly to Round of 16, while teams ranked ninth to 24th enter playoff round
  The UEFA Champions League returns this week with its 36-team league phase, the expanded format that has reshaped Europe’s top club competition by replacing the traditional four-team group stage with one large standings table. 
The league phase, now in its third season, begins on Sept. 8 and runs until Jan. 27, when all remaining final-round fixtures will be played simultaneously. 
Under the format, each club plays eight matches against eight different opponents – four at home and four away. Teams receive three points for a win and one for a draw, as in a domestic league, but they do not play every other team in the table. 
That makes the system a hybrid: one overall league table, but with different fixtures for every club. 
The change was introduced to increase the number of high-profile matches, reduce the number of low-stakes group-stage games and keep more clubs involved in the qualification race deeper into the winter.  
How does qualification work? 
The final league table determines every club’s path. 
Teams finishing first to eighth qualify directly for the Round of 16. Clubs ranked ninth to 24th enter a two-legged knockout phase playoff, with the winners advancing to the last 16. 
Those finishing from 25th to 36th are eliminated from European competition altogether.  
Unlike the old format, there is no drop into the UEFA Europa League for clubs knocked out after the Champions League league phase. 
The playoff round also creates an important advantage for clubs finishing higher in the table. Teams placed ninth to 16th are seeded and, in principle, play the second leg at home against teams placed 17th to 24th.  
What changes tactically? 
The old group stage allowed clubs to measure themselves directly against three opponents. Head-to-head results often shaped qualification, and the same teams met home and away. 
The league phase removes that rhythm, as there is no fixed mini-group, no return fixture against the same opponent and no direct rival whose results can be tracked in isolation.  
That changes the calculation for coaches.  
A draw away to a major contender can be valuable, but smaller clubs may have to be more aggressive in home matches against teams closer to their level. 
Goal difference also matters more because many clubs can finish level on points.  
Heavy defeats against Europe’s strongest sides can damage a campaign even if a team later recovers with wins elsewhere. 
Squad depth is another factor. The league phase stretches from September to January, crossing domestic league fixtures, cup matches and international breaks. Clubs competing on several fronts must manage injuries, rotation and travel while maintaining European results.  
Turkish clubs’ route 
Galatasaray and Fenerbahce enter the league phase with demanding schedules that combine marquee home fixtures with difficult away trips across Europe. 
Galatasaray face Sporting CP, Barcelona, Lille, Stuttgart, Aston Villa, AEK Athens, Feyenoord and current champions Paris Saint-Germain. Their campaign begins on Sept. 9 with a trip to Lisbon to face Sporting CP, before Barcelona visit Istanbul on Oct. 13. The Turkish champions then travel to France to meet Lille on Oct. 21. 
November gives Galatasaray two home matches, against Stuttgart on Nov. 3 and Aston Villa on Nov. 24. They then travel to Athens to face AEK on Dec. 8, host Feyenoord on Jan. 19, and close the league phase on Jan. 27 away to PSG. 
Fenerbahce will face Roma, Aston Villa, Slavia Prague, Liverpool, Shakhtar Donetsk, LASK, Villarreal and Atletico Madrid.  
The Yellow Canaries open at home against Roma on Sept. 10 before traveling to England to face Aston Villa on Oct. 14. Slavia Prague visit Istanbul on Oct. 20, followed by another major home fixture against Liverpool on Nov. 4. 
Fenerbahce then face two away matches, against Shakhtar Donetsk in London on Nov. 25 and LASK in Austria on Dec. 9. They return home to host Villarreal on Jan. 20 before ending the league phase away to Atletico Madrid on Jan. 27.

Champagne production halves as scorching summer dents French wine grape harvest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
15:37:25 UTC
00:37:25 KST

France’s wine production is expected to fall below 3.4 billion liters this year as drought and repeated heat waves battered vineyards across the country, with the Champagne region worst affected, according to French government estimates published Monday.
The brutal summer weather pulled harvests dramatically forward. Most French vineyards began picking in August after exceptionally high temperatures accelerated ripening.
“Soil drought intensified across the entire country,” the Agriculture Ministry's statistics service Agreste said, while heat waves caused “sunscald, burns, defoliation and grape shriveling” in some vineyards.
Advertisement
In Champagne, growers reaped their earliest harvest on record, racing to pick grapes before rising sugar levels pushed potential alcohol too high. Output there is expected to be roughly halved, with grape bunch weights at their lowest in 20 years.
In southern France’s Languedoc-Roussillon wine region, by contrast, production is forecast to rebound 5 percent from last year’s weak harvest, which was about 13 percent below the five-year average. Even with that recovery, output this year remains 8 percent below average.
Conditions had initially looked promising, with good grape development and low disease pressure. But “the hot and dry conditions of the summer degraded this potential,” Agreste said.
If confirmed, the sub-3.4 billion-liter crop would be France’s smallest since 1957 — a nearly 70-year low.
And wine is only one casualty of Europe’s brutal summer. Farmer group Copa-Cogeca estimated in a report published last week that maize losses reached 50 to 70 percent in Slovenia, 40 percent in France and 20 to 25 percent in Italy, reaching 70 percent in some unirrigated areas. Croatia expects fruit and grape output to fall around 30 percent.
French Environment Minister Monique Barbut has put the summer’s economic damage at €10 billion to €15 billion, or as much as 0.5 percent of GDP.
Paris unveiled more than €1 billion in emergency farm aid Friday, though agricultural groups say the package falls short.

Ellen Burstyn said receiving the
Venice Film Festival's second Golden Lion for Career Achievement
Monday after George Clooney on opening night last week that she
hoped the United States would soon find the right direction.
                                    
                                       
				Burstyn, 93, one of the greatest actresses of American cinema,
couldn't hold back her emotion when faced with the standing
ovation she received on the stage of the Sala Grande at the
Lido.
                                    
                                       
				"You make me cry," said the great actress, born in December
1932, elegant in a long sunflower-yellow dress with a matching
jacket.
                                    
                                       
				"I realized that a lifetime achievement award isn't just a
testament to what you've actually accomplished, but also to what
you've learned."
Burstyn, who won an Oscar for Martin Scorsese's Alice Doesn't
Live Here Anymore, then gave a brief speech retracing some of
her career paths.
                                    
                                       
				"I didn't just want success. I wanted to learn to be the kind of
actress I knew and admired," she explained, emphasizing the
fundamental role of her encounter with Lee Strasberg and the
Actor's Studio (of which she is now president, ed.) "which
changed my life."
She also shared an anecdote related to the filming of Alice
Doesn't Live Here Anymore.
                                    
                                       
				"I was shooting a car scene and there was a big cliff on the
right side of the car. The problem was that I had Martin
Scorsese, the director of photography, the camera operator and
the lighting technician on the hood and I couldn't see the side
of the road, I could have skidded and killed us all.
                                    
                                       
				"Then I realized that all I had to do was follow the white line
in the middle of the road. And that's how I managed not to kill
Scorsese," she added, smiling.
                                    
                                       
				"I understood that identifying that 'white line' on the road is
a good exercise to do whenever you're in trouble, to get
yourself out of trouble, so I did it for the rest of my life.
                                    
                                       
				"I hope, indeed, I pray that my country will find its white line
very soon and that you can find it too."
At the beginning of the ceremony, there was a eulogy for Burstyn
from the president of the jury of this year's international
competition, Maggie Gyllenhaal, who directed her, making her
play an ideal centenarian Marilyn Monroe, in Flesh Impact, the
short film with Dakota Johnson screened after the awards
ceremony.
                                    
                                       
				"Ellen Burstyn is our queen," the actress and director
emphasized, recalling many of her colleague's great roles, from
The Exorcist to Requiem for a Dream.
                                    
                                       
				"Ellen is present in all those characters. With her body, of
course, but also with her brain, her heart, her mind, her life.
                                    
                                       
				It's a gesture of great courage and affection to share all this
with us."
Burstyn, who is also at the Lido as the star of Place to Be,
Kornel Mundruczo's film screening out of competition, also dwelt
at the morning press conference on the emotions involved in
playing the divine Marilyn.
                                    
                                       
				"I once ran into her, in a nightclub. She was sitting not far
from me, and naturally I was enchanted by her gaze. She was a
magical creature.
                                    
                                       
				"Then she met my gaze and nodded. Something that moved me
deeply; it seemed impossible she was speaking to me. It's a
moment that I've cherished in my heart ever since."
As for developments over her career as an actress, the situation
for women in Hollywood "has changed enormously," she explained.
                                    
                                       
				"When I started, there were no women on set, behind the camera,
or in the crew, just us actresses.
                                    
                                       
				"Then slowly, thanks also to the commitment of people like
Gloria Steinem, who recently passed away, the mentality began to
change.
                                    
                                       
				"At first, the woman was typically a script supervisor. Then a
camera assistant. And slowly, women have become more integrated.
                                    
                                       
				We're not at 50/50 yet, but we're getting closer."
As an actor, "it gives me great satisfaction to continue to stay
in touch with the younger generation. I've discovered that
talented directors are at their most creative at the beginning
of their careers, but after making a few films and going through
what I call the Hollywood hamburger factory," she concluded,
"they lose some of their innocence, their spontaneous
creativity."
Finally, when asked what stories are worth telling today, she
replied with a smile: "My country is offering many stories to
explore from an artistic and political point of view... I would
start with that."

The Hind Rajab Foundation (HRF) said on Monday it filed a criminal complaint in Slovenia against Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar over alleged war crimes, acts of genocide and torture in Gaza ahead of his expected visit to Ljubljana this week.
The complaint was filed with the Ljubljana District Prosecutor’s Office and police.
Sa’ar is expected to attend the opening of a new Israeli embassy in Ljubljana this week, the HRF said, citing information provided by the Movement for the Rights of Palestinians, a Slovenian social initiative and solidarity group.
The complaint alleges that Sa’ar bears criminal responsibility for several actions during Israel’s war in Gaza, including the attack on Kamal Adwan Hospital in northern Gaza between Oct. 8 and Dec. 27, 2024, and the arrest and continued detention of the hospital’s director, Dr. Hossam Abu Safiyeh.
The HRF also alleges that Sa’ar was involved in the destruction and occupation of Gaza, the mass displacement of civilians and the restriction of food, water, fuel and medical supplies.
The organization said the complaint invokes Slovenian law and international legal instruments, including the Fourth Geneva Convention, the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court and the UN Convention against Torture.
The filing follows earlier action by HRF concerning Sa’ar, including a communication to the ICC ahead of his visit to Brussels in February 2025 and legal action linked to his visit to London in April 2025.
The non-profit called on Slovenian authorities to investigate the allegations and take steps to ensure Sa’ar cannot use diplomatic status to avoid accountability.
“No official, no matter how senior, stands above the law,” HRF Director General Dyab Abou Jahjah said in the statement. He added that the organization was calling on Slovenian authorities to investigate those responsible for what he described as crimes against Palestinians.
Slovenia recently vetoed a joint statement by the EU and its 27 member states condemning Israel's decision to build new illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank.

L’UE veut sévir contre les locations de courte durée pour rendre le logement plus abordable
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
15:34:53 UTC
00:34:53 KST

L’UE veut sévir contre les locations de courte durée pour rendre le logement plus abordable
La future loi européenne sur le logement abordable prévoit de donner aux autorités locales une base juridique pour limiter les appartements destinés aux touristes.
Bruxelles cherche à faire baisser les coûts du logement dans les villes les plus prisées d’Europe en donnant aux autorités locales les moyens de réguler Airbnb et les autres opérateurs de location de courte durée.
Dans le cadre du Affordable Housing Act de la Commission européenne, qui doit être approuvé par le collège des commissaires mercredi, de nouvelles règles applicables au sein de l’UE permettront de déterminer si un territoire est en zone tendue (quand l’offre de logements est insuffisante face à la demande), et les autorités nationales, régionales et locales disposeront d’une base juridique pour mettre en œuvre des mesures ciblées face à la pénurie de logements.
“Les locations de courte durée ne sont pas à l’origine de la crise du logement en Europe”, affirme auprès de POLITICO Dan Jørgensen, commissaire européen chargé de l’Energie et du Logement. “Mais il est très clair que dans certaines régions d’Europe, notamment dans certaines de nos plus grandes villes, elles aggravent le problème.”
Advertisement
Les locations de courte durée enregistrées ne représentent officiellement qu’environ 1,2% du parc immobilier total de l’UE, mais elles peuvent atteindre jusqu’à 20% des logements dans les destinations touristiques très prisées, telles que Porto et les grandes villes européennes.
Selon le cabinet de conseil AirDNA, Paris comptait l’année dernière environ 60 000 annonces de location de courte durée actives, quand ces annonces représentaient près de 40% du parc locatif disponible dans le centre de Porto, et jusqu’à 56% du parc locatif de longue durée dans certains quartiers de Madrid.
“Lorsque des milliers de logements sont retirés du marché résidentiel dans une ville déjà en zone tendue, nous ne pouvons pas faire comme si cela n’avait aucun effet sur la capacité financière des personnes à accéder au logement et sur l’offre disponible”, estime Dan Jørgensen. “Les gens devraient pouvoir se loger et rester dans les quartiers où ils se sentent chez eux.”
Les gens avant les profits
De nombreuses villes tentent déjà de s’attaquer aux locations de courte durée.
Mais ces initiatives ont souvent donné lieu à de longues batailles judiciaires. Des propriétaires et des professionnels du tourisme ont poursuivi Florence en justice pour ses restrictions, et Airbnb a contesté une amende de 64 millions d’euros infligée par l’Espagne pour avoir proposé des annonces illégales. Bien que ces deux tentatives aient échoué, elles ont entraîné les autorités locales dans des batailles judiciaires coûteuses et interminables.
Advertisement
Dan Jørgensen met en avant que la nouvelle législation “donner[ait] aux autorités locales qui souhaitent prendre des mesures, la possibilité de le faire de manière efficace et sans s’exposer à des risques de litige”. Le commissaire conteste les arguments du secteur, qui affirme que ces restrictions pourraient nuire aux économies dépendantes du tourisme et aux propriétaires qui comptent sur leurs revenus locatifs. Il a souligné que “le logement est un droit, pas seulement une marchandise”, et que “les gens doivent passer avant les profits”.
Il balaye également l’objection avancée par le secteur selon laquelle la Commission outrepasserait ses compétences en légiférant sur le logement, un domaine dans lequel l’UE ne dispose que de compétences directes limitées. Dan Jørgensen souligne que, dans le cadre de la future législation, ce sont les autorités nationales, régionales et locales qui détermineront quelles zones seront considérées comme tendues et qui décideront s’il convient d’intervenir et, le cas échéant, de quelle manière.
“L’objectif n’est pas d’imposer des restrictions depuis Bruxelles”, assure-t-il. “Mais l’accès au logement est l’un des défis les plus urgents de l’Europe, et les institutions européennes ne peuvent fermer les yeux sur les problèmes quotidiens très concrets auxquels nos citoyens sont confrontés.”
“Si nous ne parvenons pas à faire face à cette crise, nous risquons de perdre la confiance de nos concitoyens dans les institutions démocratiques, poursuit-il. Et cela conduirait à la montée en puissance des forces politiques extrémistes.”
Pour Dan Jørgensen, cette nouvelle loi constitue “une étape décisive pour soutenir les villes, les régions et les pays qui souhaitent apporter des solutions immédiates aux zones et aux populations les plus touchées”, tout en soulignant que ce n’est pas la panacée.
“La crise du logement est un problème complexe”, complète-t-il, et l’UE doit encore “prendre des mesures en matière d’investissement, de simplification des règles, d’offre et de pressions sur le parc immobilier existant”.
Cet article a d’abord été publié par POLITICO en anglais, puis a été édité en français par Jean-Christophe Catalon.

Why the world needs a mechanism to regulate space debris
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
15:34:51 UTC
00:34:51 KST

Among thousands of man-made objects drifting through space is Elon Musk’s personal cherry-red Tesla, which the world’s first trillionaire launched on February 6, 2018.
With a space-suited mannequin nicknamed "Starman" strapped to the driver's seat, and the stereo set on a loop playing David Bowie's "Space Oddity" and "Life on Mars?”, Musk sent his personal car into space as a publicity test payload for the maiden flight of SpaceX’s Falcon Heavy rocket.
Scientists say the car is likely to keep drifting in space for “tens of millions of years” before crashing into the Earth or Venus.
Musk’s car is one of the tens of thousands of man-made objects – called “space debris” consisting mostly of spent rocket bodies and metal pieces – that now share the once-empty space with a rapidly growing fleet of satellites.
The resulting congestion has created operational problems that put space infrastructure at risk of collision.
Space debris travels at a high speed of up to eight kilometres a second. After splitting from a satellite or rocket, it keeps cruising at the same speed without losing momentum in the absence of any air resistance.
The problem is becoming more serious by the day as companies like SpaceX plan to deploy a million more spacecraft, including sunlight-powered data centres, in the coming years.
Experts say the risk of serious space collisions is no longer theoretical.
The reason is not a lack of awareness. It’s actually the absence of a binding international mechanism – with powers to set rules and ensure enforcement – that’s making the threat of catastrophic collisions real, they say.
John L Crassidis, a professor at the University at Buffalo School of Engineering and Applied Sciences who works with NASA and other agencies to monitor space debris, tells TRT World that the risk of catastrophic collisions is rising rapidly as mega-constellations expand.
“The more objects we put in space, the greater the chance of catastrophic collisions,” he says.
A catastrophic collision between space debris and a satellite will not only decimate the satellite, but also create thousands of pieces of fast-moving shrapnel, each capable of destroying other operational satellites or spacecraft.
Jonathan C McDowell, a space sustainability analyst who worked at the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics for 38 years, says the constellation designers work hard to ensure collision avoidance.
“Nevertheless, the risk is real, and I expect collisions to start happening in the coming decade,” he tells TRT World.
Dedicated science and space publications have documented a sharp rise in last-minute dodges as mega-constellations fill the most useful altitudes in outer space.
SpaceX’s Starlink network of satellites alone has performed more than 355,000 collision-avoidance manoeuvres in a single year.
It means each satellite had to dodge debris and other spacecraft on an “almost weekly basis” during the year-long period.
Experts have warned that proposed mega-constellations can lead to the Kessler syndrome, a hypothetical scenario in which repeated collisions generate so much space debris that entire orbital regions become unusable.
Crassidis describes how the present warning system works.
“Currently, we track about 54,000 objects that are 10cm or greater in size,” he says. Operators compute a probability of collision “between all two-object pairs”.
“If the chance is greater than one in 10,000, then we will call one of the satellite companies and tell them they should move to avoid a possible collision.
“(SpaceX founder Elon) Musk reduced that down to one in 1,000, and that information is uploaded directly to the Starlink satellites, which automatically move,” he says.
“They actually move a lot every day to avoid debris,” Crassidis adds.
“If things are done smartly, then the risk of issues with mega-constellations can be reduced,” he notes.
But that “if” is quite expensive.
Satellite operators already spend $2 billion a year on just avoiding “very improbable” collisions.
What can go wrong if a million data-centre satellites carry out a billion avoidance manoeuvres every year – an extreme scenario that looks increasingly possible given the scale of planned expansion for new constellations?
Crassidis points to the fuel-related challenges.
“There is only a limited amount of fuel on each satellite,” he says.
Operators will need to either supply satellites with more fuel, which will be costly, or face the possibility of more collisions, he says.
According to McDowell, space could become the scene of the Kessler chain reaction, where collisions become more and more common.
“Eventually, the space services, which are now an integral part of our economy, start to degrade,” he says.
No single regulatory body
Even a single high-speed collision in space can create a massive cloud of debris consisting of thousands of fragments detrimental to space infrastructure.
For example, the 2009 collision between the active Iridium-33 satellite and the defunct Kosmos-2251 produced more than 1,800 pieces of debris measuring 10cm or larger.
Scientists, however, did not just wake up to the urgent threat posed by potential space collisions. After all, humans have been sending satellites into space for decades now.
Yet, there is no single international authority for orbital traffic and debris control.
Crassidis blames a lack of international cooperation.
“The problem is that we currently don’t have any modern-day treaties between nations,” he says.
The US and its allies have created rules governing space traffic and debris, “but not all countries in the world follow them”.
The UN also put out guidelines in 2010, which were updated in 2024. Those documents matter, but they are not enough.
“We need leaders to get together to make these guidelines into an international treaty that all countries will follow,” he says.
McDowell says the bottleneck exists in the existing legal architecture under the UN umbrella.
The Outer Space Treaty governs space activities under the UN Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space (COPUOS), he notes.
“But COPUOS works by consensus, and it’s hard to get anything done, especially in the current era where certain countries are resistant to international agreements,” he says.
The Outer Space Treaty remains the cornerstone of space law, while COPUOS debris-mitigation guidelines are voluntary. So are the 2021 Guidelines for the Long-term Sustainability of Outer Space Activities.
National regulators can fine their own licensees. But they cannot easily force a foreign operator, or a state that never adopted the same standard, to follow these guidelines.
Crassidis gave the example of what enforcement looks like when national regulators choose to take action against domestic companies.
On October 2, 2023, the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) fined Dish Network $150,000 after its EchoStar-7 satellite “ran out of fuel unexpectedly, which left it 160km short of the agreed graveyard orbit”.
“We need an international body to enforce rules and impose penalties for those who break the rules,” he says.
The FCC itself described the settlement as its first space-debris enforcement action.
McDowell says a world body must have the operational powers needed to fix what's broken in space law enforcement.
“We’d need them to be able to define rules of the road: who moves when, how much separation you need from other traffic, and so on – just like air traffic control today,” he says.

Russia and North Korea open first cross-border road bridge (VIDEO)

Russia and North Korea open first cross-border road bridge (VIDEO)
Russia and North Korea have opened the first road bridge across the Tumen River, linking Russia’s Primorye region directly with the neighboring country, Primorye Governor Oleg Kozhemyako has announced.
The new crossing over the river dividing the countries is expected to boost mutual trade and provide year-round transport.
Construction of the new bridge began in April 2025 under an agreement signed by Moscow and Pyongyang in 2024. Until now, the neighboring countries’ only direct land transport connection had been the Friendship railway bridge across the Tumen River.
Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin and his North Korean counterpart Pak Thae Song launched traffic across the bridge by video link.
“The new route will ensure reliable and stable supplies of various products and will help expand trade and economic cooperation between our countries,” Kozhemyako wrote on Telegram on Monday.
The entire crossing, including access roads, stretches about 4.7 km, while the bridge itself is roughly 1 km long and carries two lanes of traffic. The Russian section measures 424 meters and the North Korean section 581 meters.
Leading the first Russian convoy across the bridge was a piece of Soviet history – a restored red ZAZ-968M Zaporozhets once owned by Soviet officer Yakov Novichenko, after whom the crossing is named. His grandson Nikolay Shcherbitsky drove the 1980 car, which he had restored himself.
During a mass rally in Pyongyang in 1946, Novichenko shielded Kim Il Sung from a grenade thrown toward the platform where the Korean leader was standing. He survived despite severe injuries and the loss of his right hand, and was later awarded North Korea’s highest labor title.
A new Khasan road checkpoint has also been built next to the bridge. It has ten traffic lanes and is designed to process up to 300 vehicles and 2,850 people per day once it operates at full capacity, according to the Russian Transport Ministry. Russian officials say the new road link should cut transport costs and increase bilateral trade.
