Thousands attend Bosnian Serb war criminal's funeral in Belgrade despite EU warnings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
15:19:31 UTC
00:19:31 KST

Serbian ministers attended despite earlier assurances no serving officials would be present, with Mladić's coffin arriving draped in the national flag and his medals on display. The EU said any glorification of convicted war criminals "has no place in the EU or in EU candidate countries".
Ratko Mladić, the Bosnian Serb commander convicted by a UN court of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity, was buried in Belgrade on Monday before a crowd of thousands, despite renewed warnings from Brussels against glorifying him — warnings Serbia's government continues to reject.
Prior to the funeral, Mladić's body lay in state since Monday morning at the Serb Orthodox Church of St Luke in Belgrade, where thousands arrived early to honour him, despite being found guilty of the worst bloodbath on European soil since World War II.
His military officer's cap and sabre rested on the coffin, which was flanked by men in fatigues, with his medals also on display.
The crowd gathered included his former soldiers in military garb and young men carrying banners with his image and flags of Serbia and the Bosnian Serb-majority entity of the Republika Srpska, as hundreds of football fans joined the procession to the Košutnjak graveyard.
The crowd clapped as soldiers carried Mladić's coffin, a gun salute rang out and a military orchestra played.
The head of the Serb Orthodox Church Patriarch Porfirije, who led the funeral service, said Mladić's name would "remain deeply etched in the memory and prayers" of Serb Orthodox people who "feel and nurture a deep sense of gratitude towards him."
Although it was earlier announced that no serving officials would be in attendance, Serbian justice, culture, defence and public investments ministers came to pay their respects, along with Russian ambassador to Serbia Alexander Botsan-Kharchenko and President Aleksandar Vučić's son Danilo. Political representatives of Bosnian Serbs were also present.
While the funeral arrangements were formally made by Mladić's family, the Serbian government sent a plane last week to bring his remains to Belgrade, accompanied by Justice Minister Nenad Vujić — who initially announced that Serbia would give Mladić "all the military and state honours," a decision Vučić later tempered.
Soldiers carried Mladić's coffin wrapped in the national flag on arrival to an unmarked maroon van, which was then given a police escort down Belgrade’s main motorway.
A military commemoration was held Saturday at an official Serbian army venue, which the government said was organised by an association of retired generals.
Honours or no honours?
Authorities earlier said Mladić would not be buried with military or state honours. There would be no artillery salutes or ceremonial military presence, and he would not be buried in the Alley of the Greats or the Alley of Distinguished Citizens despite requests to that effect.
Yet according to head of research and advocacy at the Youth Initiative for Human Rights (YIHR Serbia) Marko Milosavljević, while Mladić's funeral as such is private and organised by the family, the pomp around it and the involvement of state institutions and representatives amounts to state honours — which Milosavljević points out are contrary to Serbian law.
"After he was found guilty, he lost his rank in the army, and with that he lost the right to any state or military honours," Milosavljević told Euronews. "But as we can see in practice, in Serbia the same rules don’t always apply."
Milosavljević pointed out that one of the organisers of Mladić's funeral is Svetozar Andrić, Mladić's wartime associate suspected of war crimes who is wanted on several criminal indictments, including for ordering the expulsion of Bosniaks from eastern Bosnia in 1992.
"This wave of celebration of Ratko Mladić absolutely encourages people like him who are still at large that they will never be held accountable for war crimes despite existing evidence," he explained.
Milosavljević believes that by de facto honouring Mladić, Belgrade has opened itself up to a potential lawsuit over breaking the UN Convention on Human Rights — which was successfully litigated in the past elsewhere.
“Survivors and families of victims of crimes Mladić was convicted for could sue Serbia in front of the European Court of Human Rights on non-discrimination grounds, and there are several cases of family members of victims in Vukovar and in Kosovo who sued for reparations in front of domestic courts in Serbia," he said.
'Emotional outpouring'
Serbia, a candidate country for European Union membership, has faced strong criticism for honouring Mladić after his death.
EU's Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos cancelled an upcoming visit to Serbia in protest, arguing that "the glorification surrounding his death is incompatible with the values on which the EU path is built."
"Any glorification of war criminals, genocide denial and revisionism contradict the most fundamental European values and have no place in the EU or in EU candidate countries," a European Commission spokesperson said in a statement on Monday.
"Reconciliation and good neighbourly relations in Western Balkans remain central to building a shared future," the statement added.
Vučić, who did not attend the funeral, described it as an "emotional outpouring" that "has nothing to do with whether Vučić allowed something or not."
Belgrade, which backed Bosnian Serb forces during the war in the neighbouring country, has remained defiant over its wartime role and has repeatedly accused the West of anti-Serb bias.
"We have been persecuted and harassed for 30, 40 years ... always guilty whatever happens," Vučić said. "People just won't take it any more."
According to YIHR's Milosavljević, the emotional outpouring Vučić described had not happened by accident.
“Over the past decades, especially while he was at large, a myth was forged of Mladić as a great military commander, but also as someone who embodies resistance against the hypocritical West which has also committed its own war crimes," Milosavljević said.
“So Mladić became an exponent against NATO, against the EU … a useful symbol to represent the collective traumas.”
Vigils, murals and flares
The nearly four-year-long war in Bosnia, which broke out in 1992 after the former Yugoslav republic declared independence, left more than 100,000 people dead and some 2 million displaced and seeking refuge before it ended in 1995 in a US-brokered peace agreement.
Mladić was sentenced for orchestrating the genocide of more than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys in Srebrenica in July 1995, and the years-long siege of Sarajevo, where his troops on the surrounding hills conducted a daily campaign of shelling and sniping at the Bosnian capital's residents.
Since the announcement of his death in The Hague on 27 August, his admirers have held vigils, painted fresh murals of him in Belgrade and lit flares in his honour.
On Sunday evening, Red Star Belgrade fans displayed a large image of Mladić and a line referencing the summary execution of thousands in Srebrenica, and chanted his name at a football match in the Serbian capital.
Serbia has refused to recognise that genocide was committed in Srebrenica, calling the summary execution of thousands a "horrific crime" instead.
Last year, Belgrade buried another convicted war criminal, the former army chief of staff Nebojša Pavković, with full military honours at a cemetery for distinguished individuals.
The ICTY sentenced Pavković to 22 years in prison for war crimes and crimes against humanity during the war in Kosovo in 1998-1999.

Small German leftist party emerges as potential far-right kingmaker

Unknown Publisher

Small German leftist party emerges as potential far-right kingmaker
MAGDEBURG, Germany - The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) could end up forming its first state government with the help of a small leftist party that shares its hostility both to mass immigration and to the mainstream parties’ efforts to exclude more radical parties from power.
The AfD surged into first place in the state election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on Sept 6 but fell just short of an absolute majority, with 39 of 83 seats in the regional legislature.
While mainstream parties, including Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s CDU conservatives, have long refused to work with the AfD, in a policy known as the “firewall”, the far-left BSW reaffirmed its readiness to play kingmaker after it cleared the 5 per cent threshold to enter Saxony-Anhalt’s state Parliament.
“We’ve made no secret from the beginning that we’ll talk with all parties. The AfD is part of that,” Thomas Schulze, the BSW party’s lead candidate in the Saxony-Anhalt state election, told Reuters on Sept 7.
Schulze said the mainstream parties’ refusal to work with the AfD was “undemocratic”. Germany’s domestic intelligence agency has branded the AfD as “extremist”.
Upending Germany’s consensus
As well as their hostility to Germany’s political establishment and their social conservatism, the two parties share a number of priorities, including a hostility to mass migration - which the BSW says harms local workers’ rights - suspicion of the mainstream media and a desire to end financial and military support for Ukraine and restore ties with Russia.
“Hopefully, there are now majorities in the Magdeburg state Parliament in favour of a change of course in energy policy, an end to sanctions against Russia, better education and a fundamental reform of public service broadcasting,” party founder Sahra Wagenknecht said in a statement.
“The BSW intends to use these majorities to improve people’s lives.”
The BSW was founded in 2024 by Wagenknecht and nine others who had broken away from Die Linke (the Left), the main far-left party in Germany and heir to the old East German Communist Party.
Despite its ideological hostility, the BSW in late 2024 joined a coalition with Merz’s conservatives and the Social Democrats in the neighbouring eastern German state of Thuringia.
But the situation there has become complicated after a row over working with the CDU prompted local members to break away from the main party and form their own group. Wagenknecht herself has favoured working instead with the AfD.
The AfD came first in Thuringia’s state election, too, but fell well short of a majority and was unable to persuade other parties there to join it in a coalition government.
In Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD’s Siegmund said on Sunday evening that the BSW was “not part of the solution but part of the problem”.
For now, however, Schulze remains supportive of the far-right in Saxony-Anhalt.
“The AfD won the election, Mr Siegmund is the winner. It’s his job to form a government,” he said. REUTERS

Museum to return remains of 39 people taken during colonial rule in India
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
15:16:16 UTC
00:16:16 KST

Oxford University museum to return remains of 39 people taken during British colonial rule in India
An Oxford University museum has agreed to return the remains of 39 people who were taken during Britain's colonial rule in India.
The university's Pitt Rivers Museum told Agence France-Presse on Monday that it is preparing to repatriate the remains of 39 people taken from the Naga community in northeast India. The decision came after the university approved a restitution request by the Forum for Naga Reconciliation (FNR) and other groups.
The remains "have been away from their homeland for far too long," museum director Laura Van Broekhoven told AFP in a statement.
CBS News reached out to the university for further comment.
"Repatriation, for the Nagas, is not simply about bones and ancestral remains finding their way back to the land but importantly about memory returning to where it belongs," the FNR and other Naga organizations said in a statement sent to AFP.
According to the museum, the group's request covered 40 sets of human remains; however, the university approved the return of 39 of them in July because one "does not have a clear provenance as Naga."
The museum said it was "working closely" with the Naga community to agree on a date for a handover ceremony, which has not yet been set.
The Pitt Rivers Museum, one of the world's leading institutions for anthropology, ethnology and archaeology, holds over 6,000 Naga artifacts.
Dr. Ellen Konyak Jamir, an FNR member and coordinator for Recover Restore and Decolonise, a research initiative led by two Naga academics, told MorungExpress that recovering the artifacts involves a complex process and is not their current focus.
In the past, the museum has faced charges of racism and cultural insensitivity because it displayed its famous collection of shrunken heads and other human remains. In 2020, it removed the collection as part of a broader effort to "decolonize" its collections.
"Our audience research has shown that visitors often saw the museum's displays of human remains as a testament to other cultures being 'savage', 'primitive' or 'gruesome','' Van Broekhoven said in a statement at the time. "Rather than enabling our visitors to reach a deeper understanding of each other's ways of being, the displays reinforced racist and stereotypical thinking that goes against the museum's values today.''
The museum ultimately decided to remove 120 human remains, including the tsantsas, Naga trophy heads and an Egyptian mummy of a child.
The agreement between the university and the FNR forms part of a wider international movement to repatriate artifacts and human remains acquired by Western institutions during the colonial era.
Earlier this year, the University of Edinburgh returned the skulls of six people from the Muscogee Nation in the United States. The Muscogee (Creek) Nation, now based in Oklahoma, were the people of the Southeastern territory on the Mississippi River. The nation has about 103,000 people and is the fourth largest federally recognized tribal nation in the U.S.
In 2022, London's Horniman Museum returned 72 artifacts to Nigeria, including 12 Benin bronze artifacts. Meanwhile, Greece has for decades demanded the return from Britain of the Parthenon Marbles, saying they were looted in the early 19th century by Lord Elgin, British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire.
London insists they were legally acquired and successive British governments have noted that the decision rests with the British Museum, where they are kept.

Assad's Syrian reactor was configured for nuclear weapons: IAEA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
15:11:20 UTC
00:11:20 KST

Breadcrumb
Assad-era Syrian reactor was configured for nuclear weapons, IAEA chief says
The Assad-era government in Syria was constructing a nuclear reactor that was configured to produce fissile material for possible use in nuclear weapons, the head of the International Atomic Energy Agency said on Monday.
The “configuration” and the “technical features” of the nuclear reactor under construction in Syria during the leadership of ousted former President Bashar Assad were “very efficient in the production of fissile material that could be directly used for the fabrication of nuclear weapons,” IAEA director general Rafael Grossi said.
“Of course, that was never declared, that was always denied, so, and again, intentions cannot be judged, but that was a very serious proliferation concern that we had, and this has been difficult work,” he told reporters on the first day of a regular meeting of the IAEA Board of Governors, in Vienna.
Syria was believed to have operated an extensive undeclared nuclear program under Assad that included a nuclear reactor built by North Korea in eastern Deir el-Zour province.
Following Assad’s ouster, the new government agreed to give IAEA inspectors access to suspected former nuclear sites.
During a visit to Syria in August, IAEA inspectors confirmed that “the cooling infrastructure which has now been uncovered is consistent with that of a nuclear reactor.” Grossi and a team of senior inspectors also visited a previously undeclared site in the country.
Inspectors had to ‘tear down walls’ to find hidden material  
Syria notified the agency of the site’s existence in a July 17 letter and invited the IAEA “to cooperate with the Syrian authorities in the inspection and verification of the site and of any nuclear material to be potentially found.”
The IAEA said in its confidential report circulated to member states last Tuesday and seen by The Associated Press that this new site contained “natural uranium metal in the form of fuel rods with cladding.” The agency verified the material and confirmed “the presence of around 73 tonnes of natural uranium metal.”
Grossi said when the inspectors visited the site in August they had to “tear down walls” and go through “very difficult and narrow passages” to reach the nuclear material that had been hidden. The site had “boxes scattered all over the place,” he said.
Grossi said that “the important thing is that this material now is under safeguards” of the IAEA, adding that agency inspectors had managed to install cameras at the location.
Syria to decide what happens next 
Asked if the nuclear material will remain in Syria or be removed, Grossi said that this is “a matter that the Syrian government will have to decide.” He added: “We are not requesting them to do this or to do that. For us what’s important is that we know all the time where this (material) is until the last gram.”
Logan Mintz, a director for nuclear materials security at the Washington-based Nuclear Threat Initiative, said that natural uranium metal is not directly usable for a nuclear weapon but it could be “diverted to a covert weapons program that further processes it into plutonium for a nuclear weapon.”
She said that once deemed safe to move, the material could be “transported in certified containers” to a third country that can “safely and securely disposition it into a more chemically stable and more widely used form” for possible use in nuclear power plants.
“As with any transport of nuclear material, this movement would require robust security from theft or sabotage,” she said.

Ukraine’s 700 km/h BARS Jet Drone Enters Production in Europe With 1,000-km Range
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
15:11:03 UTC
00:11:03 KST

- Category
- World
Ukraine’s 700 km/h BARS Jet Drone Enters Production in Europe With 1,000-km Range
A European joint venture has been established to manufacture Ukraine’s BARS jet-powered drone, with production beginning in early September and the first systems expected to reach Ukraine’s Defense Forces starting October 10, the drone’s developer told RBC-Ukraine on September 7.
The move gives the Ukrainian-designed system a production base outside the country as its developers work to scale output and expand the BARS family for missions ranging from frontline operations to long-range strikes.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“With a move to official and transparent exports, we see opportunities only to increase and expand production capacity,” the developer said.
The main obstacle to faster production is no longer the airframe itself but the availability of turbojet engines, with delivery lead times currently limiting how quickly additional BARS drones can be manufactured.
Meanwhile, the platform continues to evolve rapidly.
The newest BARS configuration can reportedly fly up to 1,000 kilometers, or roughly 620 miles, while carrying a warhead weighing as much as 60 kilograms. Earlier versions were rated for approximately 700 kilometers of range with a 22.5-kilogram payload.
The jet-powered drone can exceed 700 kilometers per hour, or about 435 mph.
BARS was designed from the outset as a modular platform rather than a single fixed configuration. Developers can alter the balance between fuel capacity and payload depending on the mission, allowing the same basic architecture to serve at different ranges.
The system is divided into three principal mission categories: DeepStrike, MiddleStrike, and FrontStrike.
A longer-range configuration can dedicate more internal volume to fuel, while shorter-range versions can trade that endurance for a heavier payload.
That flexibility has been refined continuously. According to the developer, BARS has already undergone more than 40 upgrades and design iterations since the original prototype.
Artificial intelligence is also being incorporated throughout the development process, from engineering work to terminal guidance.
“We use the tools that AI technologies provide us today, and we do not shy away from them at any level—from development and solving engineering problems to implementing machine vision in our target-guidance systems,” the developer said.
During the final stage of flight, the operator can choose to retain manual control or hand the engagement over to an optical terminal-guidance system.
Earlier, Ukraine and Germany signed an implementation agreement to jointly produce Ukrainian-designed BARS jet-powered strike drones, with Germany financing the initial production phase and all completed systems destined for Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
The agreement was signed on July 8 by Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha and German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius on the sidelines of the NATO Summit in Ankara as part of the “Build with Ukraine ” initiative, according to Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry and statements published by Sybiha.

"We will not watch from the sidelines hostile steps aimed at encircling our country in our region. Türkiye is against no country, society, faith, or culture. It is not possible for it to be otherwise. But Türkiye is against every illegality, every injustice, every act of tyranny and every form of banditry, regardless of where it comes from, and will continue to be so," he said.
"We want to continue our path as an independent, stable and prosperous state in this difficult geography. We will never allow this path to be blocked. Those who are disturbed by our country becoming stronger and by our efforts to establish peace and stability in our region cannot turn us back from our path," Erdogan added.
"No one should doubt that no one has the power to change the course of history. Türkiye will shake hands with its friends, embrace its relatives and reconnect with its brothers. Those who are friends with Türkiye will win, while those who harbor hostility will lose," he said.
"We are determined to work to ensure that unity and solidarity take root throughout our broader region in line with our policy of alliance and unity. We will not show the slightest hesitation in this."
Erdogan recalled that Türkiye marked Victory Day on Aug. 30 under the shadow of news of an accident in the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC).
"In the tragic accident caused by the capsizing of a passenger ship traveling from Girne to Tasucu in TRNC, 239 of our brothers and sisters were rescued, while unfortunately 14 lost their lives. Fourteen of our brothers and sisters remain missing. In cooperation with the TRNC, we are currently supporting search efforts with nine ships and 11 aircraft," he said.
"Following the accident, the authorities in the TRNC launched an investigation, and eight crew members, including the captain, were detained. The judicial process is being closely followed by our official institutions," Erdogan added.
He added search and rescue efforts were also continuing for the 10 crew members of a dry cargo ship that sank off Silivri on Sept. 2 following a collision that appeared to have been caused by human error.
Erdogan said Türkiye would continue developing its ties with the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO), which he described as complementary to the UN.
"Türkiye is a country whose star is increasingly rising in the world with its historical and cultural heritage and its great economic and human potential. As a nation, we are heirs to a great empire that spread across three continents. We have historical ties and kinship relations with a very broad geography," he said.
"We are making efforts to advance our cooperation with all countries through an approach that places Türkiye and Türkiye's interests at the center of our foreign policy."
He said the SCO was among the leading regional organizations with which Türkiye's relations had intensified in recent years.
Erdogan said the organization represents a population of nearly 4 billion and an economy approaching $35 trillion, describing it as having significant potential. Türkiye's annual trade volume with member countries is approaching $150 billion, he said, adding that Ankara wants to increase the figure in a more balanced structure.
Erdogan said he attended the organization's leaders' summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, on Sept. 1 as an honorary guest, where Türkiye's importance to the organization was highlighted, particularly on energy security and connectivity. He said he also held talks with several heads of state and government, including Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"We will continue to develop our relations with the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, which we regard as complementary to the United Nations," the president said.
Turning to regional conflicts, Erdogan blamed Israel for the current Mideast war and its wider consequences.
"The bill for the war that began with Israel’s schemes and provocations is being paid not only by the Iranian people, not only by our brotherly Gulf countries, but by everyone, whether involved or not," he said.
He also accused Israel of undermining June's framework agreement for ending the war.
"Once again, it is Israel’s lies and sabotage that have rendered ineffective the Islamabad accord, which brought relief to our entire region," Erdogan said. "The storm of crises in our region will not subside until this radical mindset, which sees even the slightest possibility of peace as a threat, changes."
Erdogan said Türkiye was also feeling the effects of the global crisis centered on Iran, noting that important economic data had been released over the past week.
"We are very pleased that the momentum we have achieved in exports continues. Our goods exports in August rose 8.1% from the same month last year to $23.5 billion. With this figure, we broke a record for August exports," he said.
The Turkish president said exports rose 4% in the first eight months of 2026 to $185 billion, while annualized exports reached $280.3 billion, up 4.2%. He said this left a gap of $1.7 billion to Türkiye's year-end export target of $282 billion.
"On the inflation front, like the rest of the world, we are feeling the effects of the Iran-centered global crisis. Oil prices have reached historic levels in many countries around the world, including the US. Particularly in diesel prices, unprecedented increases are being experienced," Erdogan said.
He said increases in oil prices would continue to put pressure on everyone unless the deadlock in the Strait of Hormuz was resolved.
Despite regional tensions, Erdogan said Türkiye would maintain its economic course. "Although we are making some adjustments to our targets, we continue to keep the Turkish economy on the path of development and growth," he said.
He pointed to the Medium-Term Program announced the previous day as the latest example of that approach.
Erdogan said the Medium-Term Program sets out Türkiye's economic road map for the next three years, including measures to strengthen agriculture, industry and services, particularly tourism, increase high-technology and value-added production, expand export capacity and further improve the economy's competitiveness.
"Despite the difficulties arising from geopolitical risks and uncertainties, there is no change whatsoever in our policies prioritizing investment, employment, production and exports. Likewise, our determined stance in the fight against inflation will continue," he said.
"We will continue taking steps that will increase the welfare of our nation and provide permanent solutions to the structural problems of our economy," Erdogan said.
"From economic security to the business and investment environment, from manufacturing industry to price stability, from public finances to trade, employment and human capital, we will do whatever is necessary to make the Turkish economy stronger, more competitive and more resilient in every area," he added.
The president congratulated those who contributed to preparing the Medium-Term Program.
Erdogan said the Cabinet meeting also addressed the COP31 summit, which will be held in Antalya on Nov. 9-20.
He said preparations were continuing to ensure Türkiye successfully hosts the climate change conference, describing it as one of the world's largest platforms for climate diplomacy. The event will be held at the Antalya EXPO site, covering 1.1 million square meters.
"We are renovating this area and making all preparations, from infrastructure to transportation, security, and accommodation. In this context, we have taken a step that will also greatly ease traffic in Antalya, and our TOKI has completed 38 kilometers of road construction," Erdogan said.
He said the investments would remain after the summit ends, and benefit Antalya and the wider country.
"Our guests will leave, and the summit will end, but these roads and investments, as in Ankara, will remain for our nation and be used by our people for many years. The EXPO area, in its renovated form, will become a new attraction point for Antalya. Therefore, our tourism professionals, tradespeople, citizens, Antalya, and in other words, our entire country will benefit," he said.
Erdogan said more than 190 countries are expected to participate in the climate summit, with more than 100,000 visitors expected. Türkiye, he added, would host it in a manner befitting the country, just like July's NATO summit.
Erdogan also congratulated Türkiye's women's volleyball team, known as the "Sultans of the Net," for defeating Italy 3-2 in the final of the 2026 CEV Women's European Championship on Sunday, and winning the European title for the second consecutive time.

Career Lion Burstyn says hopes US finds right direction
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
17:08:23 CEST
00:08:23 KST

Ellen Burstyn said receiving the
Venice Film Festival's second Golden Lion for Career Achievement
Monday after George Clooney on opening night last week that she
hoped the United States would soon find the right direction.
                                    
                                       
				Burstyn, 93, one of the greatest actresses of American cinema,
couldn't hold back her emotion when faced with the standing
ovation she received on the stage of the Sala Grande at the
Lido.
                                    
                                       
				"You make me cry," said the great actress, born in December
1932, elegant in a long sunflower-yellow dress with a matching
jacket.
                                    
                                       
				"I realized that a lifetime achievement award isn't just a
testament to what you've actually accomplished, but also to what
you've learned."
Burstyn, who won an Oscar for Martin Scorsese's Alice Doesn't
Live Here Anymore, then gave a brief speech retracing some of
her career paths.
                                    
                                       
				"I didn't just want success. I wanted to learn to be the kind of
actress I knew and admired," she explained, emphasizing the
fundamental role of her encounter with Lee Strasberg and the
Actor's Studio (of which she is now president, ed.) "which
changed my life."
She also shared an anecdote related to the filming of Alice
Doesn't Live Here Anymore.
                                    
                                       
				"I was shooting a car scene and there was a big cliff on the
right side of the car. The problem was that I had Martin
Scorsese, the director of photography, the camera operator and
the lighting technician on the hood and I couldn't see the side
of the road, I could have skidded and killed us all.
                                    
                                       
				"Then I realized that all I had to do was follow the white line
in the middle of the road. And that's how I managed not to kill
Scorsese," she added, smiling.
                                    
                                       
				"I understood that identifying that 'white line' on the road is
a good exercise to do whenever you're in trouble, to get
yourself out of trouble, so I did it for the rest of my life.
                                    
                                       
				"I hope, indeed, I pray that my country will find its white line
very soon and that you can find it too."
At the beginning of the ceremony, there was a eulogy for Burstyn
from the president of the jury of this year's international
competition, Maggie Gyllenhaal, who directed her, making her
play an ideal centenarian Marilyn Monroe, in Flesh Impact, the
short film with Dakota Johnson screened after the awards
ceremony.
                                    
                                       
				"Ellen Burstyn is our queen," the actress and director
emphasized, recalling many of her colleague's great roles, from
The Exorcist to Requiem for a Dream.
                                    
                                       
				"Ellen is present in all those characters. With her body, of
course, but also with her brain, her heart, her mind, her life.
                                    
                                       
				It's a gesture of great courage and affection to share all this
with us."
Burstyn, who is also at the Lido as the star of Place to Be,
Kornel Mundruczo's film screening out of competition, also dwelt
at the morning press conference on the emotions involved in
playing the divine Marilyn.
                                    
                                       
				"I once ran into her, in a nightclub. She was sitting not far
from me, and naturally I was enchanted by her gaze. She was a
magical creature.
                                    
                                       
				"Then she met my gaze and nodded. Something that moved me
deeply; it seemed impossible she was speaking to me. It's a
moment that I've cherished in my heart ever since."
As for developments over her career as an actress, the situation
for women in Hollywood "has changed enormously," she explained.
                                    
                                       
				"When I started, there were no women on set, behind the camera,
or in the crew, just us actresses.
                                    
                                       
				"Then slowly, thanks also to the commitment of people like
Gloria Steinem, who recently passed away, the mentality began to
change.
                                    
                                       
				"At first, the woman was typically a script supervisor. Then a
camera assistant. And slowly, women have become more integrated.
                                    
                                       
				We're not at 50/50 yet, but we're getting closer."
As an actor, "it gives me great satisfaction to continue to stay
in touch with the younger generation. I've discovered that
talented directors are at their most creative at the beginning
of their careers, but after making a few films and going through
what I call the Hollywood hamburger factory," she concluded,
"they lose some of their innocence, their spontaneous
creativity."
Finally, when asked what stories are worth telling today, she
replied with a smile: "My country is offering many stories to
explore from an artistic and political point of view... I would
start with that."

Passengers crowd the halls and counters at Soekarno-Hatta Airport in Tangerang as monitors show cancelled flights after the Anak Krakatau eruption.
Indonesia kept several airports closed and shifted schools to remote learning on Monday as volcanic ash coated parts of Java and Sumatra. The eruption has halted about 2,300 flights and affected more than 268,000 passengers.
Authorities say the volcano remains active with intermittent eruptions and ash emissions. The Geological Agency said the 25-hour eruption ended on Sunday but warned that more activity is likely in the coming days.
Volcanic ash in the airspace around Jakarta and other cities prompted the closure of eight airports. Schools in affected areas moved to online learning to reduce exposure.
Indonesia sits on the Pacific 'Ring of Fire' and has more than 120 active volcanoes.

War criminal Mladic buried with military honors in Belgrade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
15:03:00 UTC
00:03:00 KST

War criminal Mladic buried with military honors in Belgrade
September 7, 2026
Several thousand people lined the streets of Belgrade on Monday to follow the funeral service and burial of former Bosnian Serb army commander Ratko Mladic.
Earlier in the day, Serbian Patriarch Porfirije personally officiated at the funeral service for the former general, who died while serving a life sentence in The Hague for genocide in Srebrenica and other war crimes committed during the violent breakup of Yugoslavia in the 1990s.
In accordance with his wishes, Mladic was laid to rest at Topcider Cemetery beside his daughter, who died by suicide in 1994.
Informer TV, a staunchly pro-government broadcaster, carried live coverage of what it described as a "magnificent farewell," without mentioning the roughly 8,000 Bosniak civilians and prisoners massacred by Mladic's Bosnian Serb forces in Srebrenica in July 1995.
President Vucic not in attendance
President Aleksandar Vucic did not attend the funeral, citing a previously scheduled visit by his counterpart from Uzbekistan.
Observers say that the president has tried to chart a middle course on the issue of Mladic's funeral.
Mladic was not buried with state honors, but with military honors, with Vucic insisting that the state was merely respecting the wishes of the family and ensuring a dignified burial.
"Were we supposed to forbid people from attending, forbid the funeral itself and create dog cemeteries?" he said in response to criticism from the EU.
The phrase "dog cemeteries" refers in Serbia to the unmarked graves of so-called "enemies of the people" who were executed by Yugoslav partisans during and immediately after World War II.
Vucic was equally dismissive of the decision by EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos to cancel a planned visit to Belgrade, calling her reaction "stupid." He has brushed aside other criticism of the public glorification of Mladic in much the same way.
An EU spokesman said in a statement that "Any glorification of war criminals, genocide denial and revisionism contradict the most fundamental European values and have no place in the EU or in EU candidate countries."
Politically tricky time for Vucic
For Vucic, who has long sought to balance Serbia between the European Union and Russia, the situation is politically delicate.
He is expected to call a snap parliamentary election as early as this week. The poll is likely to take place on October 25.
For the first time in years, there is a credible possibility that his ruling bloc could be defeated by the student movement, which has led anti-government protests in Serbia for nearly two years now.
Vucic is expected to head the list of his Serbian Progressive Party as its candidate for prime minister.
Elections also in Bosnia and Hercegovina
According to Dejan Bursac, a political scientist at the Institute for Philosophy and Social Theory in Belgrade, all signs point to a president increasingly anxious about the upcoming vote.
"Vucic is grasping at every available lifeline," Bursac told DW. "One of those lifelines is Mladic's funeral and the nationalism it can help generate, allowing Vucic to present himself as a patriot while portraying his political opponents as traitors."
Many Serbs, Bursac said, still feel deep resentment over the outcome of the Yugoslav wars and claim that crimes committed against Serbs during these wars largely went unpunished. "That sentiment is now being deliberately inflamed and politically exploited," said Bursac.
Tanja Topic, a political analyst from Banja Luka in the predominantly Serb entity of Republika Srpska in Bosnia and Herzegovina, where Srebrenica is located, sees a similar dynamic.
"Politics here rests heavily on emotion," she told DW. "This is an issue around which citizens are mobilized. They forget how difficult their lives are because patriotic fervor takes over."
Bosnia and Herzegovina will go to the polls before Serbia, with elections there scheduled for October 4.
Students have a different focus
In Serbia, the student movement — a coalition of faculty assemblies and protest groups operating without formal leaders or public representatives — has largely avoided commenting on Mladic, the funeral or wartime crimes on its social media channels.
Analysts note that both Vucic's party and the student-backed electoral list, which is expected to include respected professors, activists and other public figures, are attempting to function as broad "catch-all" political platforms.
In Serbia, that means neither side can afford to alienate nationalistically minded voters. "Especially because the election will most likely be decided by a very narrow margin," said Dejan Bursac.
The students, he argued, have recognized that for many citizens, it is enough to campaign for the rule of law, democracy and against systemic corruption.
The protest movement began with university blockades after the collapse of a canopy at the newly renovated railway station in Novi Sad, Serbia's second-largest city, in November 2024. Sixteen people were killed.
Although prosecutors have opened several investigations, including into possible corruption linked to construction contracts, no trial has yet begun.
The power of media control
Few people in Serbia place much faith in opinion polls. Nevertheless, it is widely assumed that both the ruling party and the student movement command roughly 40% support each.
The government directly or indirectly controls most television stations and major news outlets, many of which frequently publish identical content.
In recent days, pro-Vucic tabloid Informer has targeted anyone who describes Mladic as a war criminal, branding such critics as "professional haters of Serbs" and "traitors."
Yet political narratives in Serbia shift quickly. Vucic alone appeared on television roughly 400 times last year. By the time voters head to the polls in late October, he will almost certainly need a new issue to rally supporters around.
Mladic's funeral is unlikely to carry him all the way to election day.
Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

War criminal Mladic buried with military honors in Belgrade
September 7, 2026
Several thousand people lined the streets of Belgrade on Monday to follow the funeral service and burial of former Bosnian Serb army commander Ratko Mladic.
Earlier in the day, Serbian Patriarch Porfirije personally officiated at the funeral service for the former general, who died while serving a life sentence in The Hague for genocide in Srebrenica and other war crimes committed during the violent breakup of Yugoslavia in the 1990s.
In accordance with his wishes, Mladic was laid to rest at Topcider Cemetery beside his daughter, who died by suicide in 1994.
Informer TV, a staunchly pro-government broadcaster, carried live coverage of what it described as a "magnificent farewell," without mentioning the roughly 8,000 Bosniak civilians and prisoners massacred by Mladic's Bosnian Serb forces in Srebrenica in July 1995.
President Vucic not in attendance
President Aleksandar Vucic did not attend the funeral, citing a previously scheduled visit by his counterpart from Uzbekistan.
Observers say that the president has tried to chart a middle course on the issue of Mladic's funeral.
Mladic was not buried with state honors, but with military honors, with Vucic insisting that the state was merely respecting the wishes of the family and ensuring a dignified burial.
"Were we supposed to forbid people from attending, forbid the funeral itself and create dog cemeteries?" he said in response to criticism from the EU.
The phrase "dog cemeteries" refers in Serbia to the unmarked graves of so-called "enemies of the people" who were executed by Yugoslav partisans during and immediately after World War II.
Vucic was equally dismissive of the decision by EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos to cancel a planned visit to Belgrade, calling her reaction "stupid." He has brushed aside other criticism of the public glorification of Mladic in much the same way.
An EU spokesman said in a statement that "Any glorification of war criminals, genocide denial and revisionism contradict the most fundamental European values and have no place in the EU or in EU candidate countries."
Politically tricky time for Vucic
For Vucic, who has long sought to balance Serbia between the European Union and Russia, the situation is politically delicate.
He is expected to call a snap parliamentary election as early as this week. The poll is likely to take place on October 25.
For the first time in years, there is a credible possibility that his ruling bloc could be defeated by the student movement, which has led anti-government protests in Serbia for nearly two years now.
Vucic is expected to head the list of his Serbian Progressive Party as its candidate for prime minister.
Elections also in Bosnia and Hercegovina
According to Dejan Bursac, a political scientist at the Institute for Philosophy and Social Theory in Belgrade, all signs point to a president increasingly anxious about the upcoming vote.
"Vucic is grasping at every available lifeline," Bursac told DW. "One of those lifelines is Mladic's funeral and the nationalism it can help generate, allowing Vucic to present himself as a patriot while portraying his political opponents as traitors."
Many Serbs, Bursac said, still feel deep resentment over the outcome of the Yugoslav wars and claim that crimes committed against Serbs during these wars largely went unpunished. "That sentiment is now being deliberately inflamed and politically exploited," said Bursac.
Tanja Topic, a political analyst from Banja Luka in the predominantly Serb entity of Republika Srpska in Bosnia and Herzegovina, where Srebrenica is located, sees a similar dynamic.
"Politics here rests heavily on emotion," she told DW. "This is an issue around which citizens are mobilized. They forget how difficult their lives are because patriotic fervor takes over."
Bosnia and Herzegovina will go to the polls before Serbia, with elections there scheduled for October 4.
Students have a different focus
In Serbia, the student movement — a coalition of faculty assemblies and protest groups operating without formal leaders or public representatives — has largely avoided commenting on Mladic, the funeral or wartime crimes on its social media channels.
Analysts note that both Vucic's party and the student-backed electoral list, which is expected to include respected professors, activists and other public figures, are attempting to function as broad "catch-all" political platforms.
In Serbia, that means neither side can afford to alienate nationalistically minded voters. "Especially because the election will most likely be decided by a very narrow margin," said Dejan Bursac.
The students, he argued, have recognized that for many citizens, it is enough to campaign for the rule of law, democracy and against systemic corruption.
The protest movement began with university blockades after the collapse of a canopy at the newly renovated railway station in Novi Sad, Serbia's second-largest city, in November 2024. Sixteen people were killed.
Although prosecutors have opened several investigations, including into possible corruption linked to construction contracts, no trial has yet begun.
The power of media control
Few people in Serbia place much faith in opinion polls. Nevertheless, it is widely assumed that both the ruling party and the student movement command roughly 40% support each.
The government directly or indirectly controls most television stations and major news outlets, many of which frequently publish identical content.
In recent days, pro-Vucic tabloid Informer has targeted anyone who describes Mladic as a war criminal, branding such critics as "professional haters of Serbs" and "traitors."
Yet political narratives in Serbia shift quickly. Vucic alone appeared on television roughly 400 times last year. By the time voters head to the polls in late October, he will almost certainly need a new issue to rally supporters around.
Mladic's funeral is unlikely to carry him all the way to election day.

Russia Orders Closures of German Consulate and Cultural Centers in Tit-for-Tat Move
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
15:02:23 UTC
00:02:23 KST

Russia’s Foreign Ministry said Monday it was shuttering the German consulate in St. Petersburg and German cultural centers across the country.
The closures were announced in retaliation for Germany’s decision last week to close the Russian consulate in Bonn and a Russian cultural center in Berlin after its government blamed Moscow for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month.
Moscow gave diplomats and employees at the German Consulate General in St. Petersburg until Sept. 18 to cease operations and leave Russia.
Staff at Germany’s Goethe-Institut cultural center branches in Moscow, St. Petersburg and Yekaterinburg were given until this Sunday.
The Russian Foreign Ministry said it summoned Germany’s ambassador in Moscow to inform him about the retaliatory decisions.
“It was the German authorities who once again provoked a new spiral of escalation in bilateral relations. Full responsibility for the consequences lies entirely with the German government,” the Russian ministry said in a statement.
President Vladimir Putin accused Germany of planting evidence in order to blame Moscow for the early August incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport.
On Sunday, Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov claimed Berlin’s accusations against Moscow amounted to “an effective declaration of war against us.”
Lavrov said last week that Moscow would respond to the closure of its cultural center in Berlin by closing the Goethe-Institut cultural centers across Russia.
Russia’s first Goethe-Institut opened in Moscow in 1992, soon after the collapse of the Soviet Union.
Reuters contributed reporting.

Swiss Post plans 110 redundancies
Swiss Post has announced plans to cut costs by the end of 2027, which could result in up to 110 redundancies.
The post office justifies says the cost-cutting measures are necessary to ensure its long-term financial independence.
Swiss Post attributes these measures to the fall in the volume of letters and over-the-counter transactions. Growth in new business sectors and pricing measures have not yet managed to offset the decline in revenue.
The state-owned company plans to reduce staff costs in management and support roles. This could lead to up to 110 redundancies in “traditional administrative roles”.
However, operational staff – for example, those involved in mail delivery or working in subsidiaries – are not affected.

Chancellor Merz says AfD result 'changes all of Germany'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
15:01:00 UTC
00:01:00 KST

Chancellor Merz says AfD result 'changes all of Germany'
September 7, 2026
There are situations in which politicians who have little left to say to each other still appear together before the press. This was certainly the case when Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) and his party colleague, Sven Schulze, the state premier of Saxony-Anhalt, discussed the results of Sunday's state election. They described the results as a catastrophe for the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) — an earthquake, a disaster. Merz appeared shaken and devastated, to put it mildly.
He thanked Schulze for his work during the campaign. Then Merz added: "Not only did something change in Saxony-Anhalt yesterday but throughout all of Germany. It will have repercussions, including on the international stage."
This is because the victors in the state election, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), oppose supporting Ukraine in the face of Russia's war of aggression, and many AfD politicians maintain close ties with Russian President Vladimir Putin's government, Merz explained.
No regard for the rule of law?
Speaking about the AfD, Merz adopted an almost confrontational tone. Majorities can change, he said, and democrats must always be aware of that and accept it.
But, Merz said, it is shocking that 60% of voters in Saxony-Anhalt chose parties that disregard the rule of law in Germany. Merz was talking about not only the AfD but also the socialist Left Party and the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), which split off from the Left Party over issues that align the BSW with the AfD.
In contrast, the chancellor said his government will always defend the values of the German constitution: "In our country, these values are not up for debate. Power is granted, not seized. And the minority is not the enemy of the majority."
Historians have long described the Nazis' rise to power in the German Reich as a "seizure of power," which is why Merz's statement is sure to be the subject of much discussion.
Seeking to reassure Germany's international partners in the EU and NATO, he said, "We know that Germany bears a special responsibility because of its history. We will always defend our political order and our firm anchoring in Europe."
Could CDU politicians in Saxony-Anhalt help the AfD come to power?
Standing next to him, Schulze remained silent. On election night the previous evening, long after his defeat had become clear, Schulze repeatedly emphasized in numerous statements that the public's widespread dissatisfaction with the Merz government in Berlin had dealt him a massive blow.
As for now, the worst-case scenario has narrowly been averted: the AfD does not have an absolute majority in the Magdeburg state parliament — but only by the narrowest of margins.
And this is a problem for Friedrich Merz: Dissatisfaction is growing, even within his own ranks. Can he prevent individual CDU lawmakers in Saxony-Anhalt from voting — against the official party line — to elect Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD election winner, as head of government?
If not, then both of Merz's seats of power would be in serious jeopardy: his position as chairman of the party and his seat in the Chancellery.
Merz defends his controversial reforms
However, as of today, Merz is still defending the difficult reforms his government has undertaken. One such reform is the overhaul of the chronically deficit-ridden pension system, which will bring great hardship to many people in Germany and faced fierce opposition during the election campaign.
On election night, Vice Chancellor and center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) leader Lars Klingbeil suggested reassessing the reforms following the defeat of the coalition government in Berlin. However, Merz has not mentioned such a change in course.
AfD displays confidence
Hours before the chancellor's appearance at the CDU headquarters, the AfD took to the stage at the Federal Press Conference. The top candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, Ulrich Siegmund, sarcastically thanked the media, which had largely portrayed him during the campaign as a threat to democracy and the rule of law.
"It was also thanks to you that we made it," Siegmund said, adding, "Thank you very much for the great coverage during this election campaign."
For example, the influential news magazine Der Spiegel had recently labeled the AfD politician "Germany's most dangerous man" in a widely circulated cover story.
Siegmund then looked out triumphantly at the packed hall and declared, "Never before has there been such a wide gap between those members of the media who seek to dictate to us here in Saxony-Anhalt how we should live and the reality of life for the people in this state."
But Siegmund avoided the question about whether the election result is a clear mandate for his party to form a government — even one without a majority of its own, if necessary, or possibly with the tacit support of the economically left, populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW).
Siegmund, however, has said he does not want to be a partner in a coalition — he wants absolute power, and he doesn't have it. The situation in Saxony-Anhalt will surely be the subject of much discussion for many days, perhaps even weeks, to come.

Dover and Portsmouth showed us a new kind of far right – and the authorities were caught out | Joe Mulhall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
15:00:23 UTC
00:00:23 KST

Sadly, we’ve become used to far-right protests in recent years. Whether it’s the vast demonstrations led by Stephen Yaxley-Lennon (AKA Tommy Robinson) in central London, or the hundreds of local protests outside hotels and HMOs housing asylum seekers, the sight of far-right activists chanting anti-migrant slogans has become all too common.
What we saw in Dover and Portsmouth over the weekend feels different. At roughly 7am on Saturday morning, hundreds of balaclava-clad men, dressed all in black, began piling out of the backs of vans and blocked roads around Dover port. Shockingly, the police appear to have known nothing about it in advance.
Then, on Sunday evening, a group of men gathered near a Portsmouth beach to “block” the arrival of asylum seekers on a boat. The group had been monitoring maritime apps and tracking the progress of boats towards Britain. They put out a call for people to join them and dozens answered, including well-known activists from the neo-Nazi movement.
What we have seen over the past three days marks a dangerous new development in the far right. While previous protests – many of which descended into ugly racist violence – have been worrying enough, we are now faced with a new, more clandestine and confrontational threat.
Hope Not Hate was the first to identify that the Dover disturbance was organised by a far-right group called Patriot Platform. The balaclava-clad men blocking roads were part of a new network founded by Tommy Robinson’s right-hand man Daniel Thomas (AKA Danny Tommo).
Launched in June, the group unites a web of smaller localised anti-migrant groups into a single body. Current members hail from the Kent Patriots, Watford Patriots, South London Patriots, South-East Patriots, North-West Patriots, Surrey Patriots and Chertsey Patriots, to name just a few.
Patriot Platform is a self-professed Christian “army of patriots” formed to, in Thomas’s words, “reclaim our borders, restore order and send a clear message: Britain belongs to the British people”. The group functions as a vigilante unit to combat immigration and revive what it says are Christian values, ready to spring into action across the country at Thomas’s word.
Worryingly, there is an unusual degree of discipline to Patriot Platform’s organising. Rather than being a single entity, it operates as a network for the local groups. These groups utilise various social media platforms, most commonly Instagram, X, Facebook and TikTok, for their promotional output.
However, unlike organisers of previous public anti-migrant protests, Patriot Platform operates clandestinely, with event planning happening via closed groups and direct personal communication. Its means of operation have more in common with football hooligan gangs than with traditional anti-migrant protest groups. This is how its supporters managed to arrive in their hundreds in Dover unnoticed.
Rather than being met with the usual mealy-mouthed condemnations and talk of “legitimate concerns”, these “protests” need to be called what they are: far-right vigilantism. These aren’t fearful locals, they are organised far-right activists led by Thomas, a man who pleaded guilty to attempted kidnapping and was sentenced to two years in prison after taking part in an armed attempt to abduct a man during a drugs-related dispute.
Since the riots of 2024, Thomas has repeatedly spoken about the need to take to the streets and take direct action. He has been upfront about his intention to create a “patriotic army that is able to take control of the United Kingdom”.
Despite warnings from Hope Not Hate, the authorities have failed to act. They have allowed Thomas to agitate, organise and mobilise large groups around the country. Last weekend was the consequence of police inaction, and I fear that without decisive action things will only get worse.
Clearly, the government needs to be far more robust in dealing with far-right vigilantism. The Home Office is so preoccupied with being seen to be tough on immigration that it has neglected the safety of the very migrants and asylum seekers being targeted.
And the police response exposes serious failings in the authorities’ approach to far-right anti-immigrant violence more broadly. Time and again, they appear unaware of the strength of protests and unprepared for the violence that sometimes results.
The events in Dover and Portsmouth should be a wake-up call for anyone who believes that far-right extremism can be managed through inaction. This is no longer simply about angry protests or offensive rhetoric. We are seeing organised groups willing to mobilise quickly, operate covertly and confront those they see as enemies. The longer authorities fail to recognise the seriousness of this threat, the bolder these groups will become.
The government must act now, before vigilantism becomes normalised and far-right activists feel they can operate with impunity on Britain’s streets.
- 
  Joe Mulhall is director of research at the anti-fascism organisation Hope not Hate

Cravings ‘like heroin withdrawal’: what happens when weight-loss drugs don’t work?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
15:00:21 UTC
00:00:21 KST

When Mercedes was told by her doctor that she could be prescribed GLP-1 weight loss jabs in 2024, she broke down. “[When] she said yes, I cried in her office. And I didn’t really stop crying for a week,” she said.
“Finally, after being overweight my entire life, this was going to save me. My struggle, my burden, my shame was finally going to come to an end.”
But as time went on it was hope, not weight, that fell away.
“I was on [Ozempic] for nine months. And then I went on Wegovy for four months, then Contrave [an oral, non-GLP-1 medication], and then Mounjaro, and that was for a few months, and then nine months ago I started on Zepbound,” said Mercedes. “Nothing has worked.”
A recently retired teacher in her 50s, Mercedes is among a small proportion of people for whom the powerful new weight-loss drugs, championed by celebrities for their transformative effects, do not work.
Ozempic, a type 2 diabetes medication, and Wegovy, which is licensed for weight loss, both contain a drug called semaglutide that mimics a hormone that occurs naturally in our bodies: GLP-1. These medications reduce the rate at which food is emptied from the stomach, suppress appetite and increase the production of insulin – meaning many people lose weight.
Mounjaro and Zepbound, also now household names, have an even greater weight-loss effect. They both contain the drug tirzepatide which mimics both GLP-1 and another hormone.
The excitement around such “GLP-1s” has been hard to miss: the medications have grabbed headlines, with clinical trials suggesting they can help participants lose an average of 15% to 20% of their body weight. Studies suggest they could help with conditions ranging from heart problems and addictions to fatty liver disease. In some cases experts say the effects may not be entirely related to weight loss.
But not everyone experiences the benefits. Between 9% and a third of participants in clinical trials lose less than 5% of their body weight – depending on the type of drug and dose used.
Now researchers are trying to work out why – something they say could help doctors tailor the use of the drugs, maximise cost-effectiveness and reduce side-effects.
For Mercedes, the impact of non-response has been profound.
“Aside from the fact that it’s not working and that it’s so expensive, to say it’s hard on the self-esteem is a humongous understatement,” said Mercedes, who lives in Canada. “It’s been a real struggle, with shame and regret and big bills and disappointment that my own body is not working the way it should.”
Prof Alexander Miras, an obesity expert at Ulster University, said the efficacy of the drugs could not be blamed on patients. “If the drug does not reduce hunger and food intake for someone, it is just not going to work,” he said.
Mercedes said she has tried hard to stick to lifestyle changes alongside the medications but, for her, the jabs did not suppress constant, intrusive thoughts about food.
“I just thought: ‘No, I’ve got to get somewhere … I’m going to die of obesity’,” she said. “I was really strict with myself for a month – but the cravings, which I can only call like heroin withdrawal … it’s just overwhelming. And the food talk never ended.”
The extreme effort paid off, to an extent. “I can honestly say I lost 20 pounds in that month, but not because of the medication,” she said.
Mercedes is certainly not alone: the Guardian has heard from dozens of people for whom GLP-1 medications have had little effect.
Yury K, 57, also from Canada, said he tried a number of weight loss programmes before starting Wegovy for obesity. He exercises about five days a week, mainly with kettlebells, and does not eat junk food or fast food.
While Yury said he saw some improvements in his blood sugar levels and cholesterol while using the medication, as well as a reduction in food noise and appetite, he found his weight barely changed.
“I started Wegovy at about 242lb and, after six months, I was still about 242lb. My weight can fluctuate a little because of water, but essentially there was no meaningful weight loss,” he said. He also experienced unpleasant side effects, including constipation and sensitive skin.
“There is so much discussion about GLP-1 medications as if they work for everyone, and that was not my experience. When you put in the effort with diet and exercise, take the medication exactly as prescribed, and still see little benefit, it is difficult not to feel disappointed,” he said.
Lucille*, 53, who is based in Luxembourg, told the Guardian she has been taking GLP-1 medications for four years – initially to help with insulin resistance – starting on a daily injection of a GLP-1 medication called Saxenda, before switching to Ozempic.
Yet despite being effective at first, Lucille says the medications no longer help her lose weight – even after switching to Mounjaro and taking the highest dose. “It’s as if nothing is having an effect any more,” she says. “The Mounjaro 5mg [dose] is outrageously expensive and so far none of these medications have been approved by my health insurance,” she adds.
At present, the reason for such variations in response remains unclear. “The short answer to why some people don’t respond is we don’t really know,” said Miras.
He said research had suggested factors such as motivation, intelligence, education and socioeconomics did not predict how patients would respond to GLP-1 medications.
But other characteristics might do. “We know, for example, that age plays a role – so older people lose less weight. Sex plays a role – men lose less than women,” said Miras. “[And] people with type 2 diabetes lose less weight compared to people without.”
Studies have also suggested ancestry might have an impact, with the medications most effective in people of European ancestry, and least effective in people of African American ancestry.
Dr Mahesh Umapathysivam, an endocrinologist and clinical researcher at Adelaide University in Australia, said it was plausible that hormones could have an effect too.
“There is growing evidence that oestrogen alters GLP-1 response. We see that with the difference between male response and female response. Also, we know from some of the physiological studies that time of menstrual cycle also alters GLP-1 response,” he said.
“Finally, the use of menopausal hormone replacement therapy – which contains oestrogen – is associated with greater weight loss in semaglutide users.”
Then there is the matter of genetics. A recent study highlighted the potential role of a genetic variant that affects receptors in the brain upon which the drugs work.
“People carrying the genetic variant, we found lose about an extra 0.76kg (1.6 lbs) on average, and people who carry two copies of the variant double that,” said Adam Auton, vice-president of human genetics at the 23andMe Research Institute, and the senior author of the study.
“For people with two copies, this accounts for about 10% of the weight people might expect to lose on these medications.”
Umapathysivam and colleagues have recently published a study into two genetic variants that affect the production of an enzyme, known as PAM, that modifies many hormones including GLP-1. The team found people with such variants appear to show resistance to GLP-1.
“GLP-1 resistance simply means a given amount of GLP-1 has less effect on the body,” Umapathysivam said. “The implication for treatment is that a certain dose of GLP-1 in someone with resistance might mean less weight loss, less glucose lowering, less insulin secretion or less slowing to the gastric emptying.”
Despite emerging research, it is not yet possible to accurately predict who will respond to weight loss jabs and who won’t.
But there are reasons for people like Mercedes to be hopeful. A series of promising new drugs are in development. “Another option is to change patients to a non-GLP-1 based drug called Mysimba [the UK brand name for Contrave]. It works in the same parts of the brain, but just slightly differently and therefore may be worth trying,” said Miras. “It is not available in the NHS, just privately.”
For some who struggle to lose weight with GLP-1 medications, weight-loss surgery may be the only option left. And, Miras says, “[A] lack of response to GLP-1 based drugs does not predict lack of response to [bariatric] surgery.”
And for those who lose little to no weight on GLP-1 medications, the message is clear. “It’s not your fault and it’s not the drug’s fault either, this is purely luck,” said Miras. “I’ve seen it before, it’s not very common, but it does happen.”
Mercedes began GLP-1 medications with huge amounts of hope and expectation. “There was just so much publicity around it. So many people [using the drugs said]: ‘Oh, I forgot to eat lunch,’ that I suppose subconsciously I just sort of ignored the prospect that … the drugs didn’t work,” she said.
“I wish I knew if there were other people out there, like me, for whom [GLP-1s] are just not effective at all.”
*Some names have been changed

North Korea, Russia open first road bridge in ‘new symbol of friendship’
Unknown

North Korea, Russia open first road bridge in ‘new symbol of friendship’
The bridge can allow up to 300 vehicles to cross every day and will be linked to Russia’s federal road network, says PM Mikhail Mishustin
North Korea and Russia opened their first road bridge on Monday in a carefully choreographed display of friendship.
The structure, which crosses the Tumen river, has been cast by both sides as an important milestone in their deepening strategic partnership.
The first flag-adorned trucks trundled across the 1km (0.6-mile) long two-lane bridge as Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin and North Korea’s Premier Pak Thae Song tuned in by video link to address workers and government officials from both countries.
Construction of the new bridge, which had been under discussion for years, began in April last year after the project was agreed during a visit by President Vladimir Putin to North Korea in 2024.
There are already direct air and rail links between Moscow and Pyongyang, but until Monday there had not been a proper road link.
Instead, since 1959 and by special arrangement, planks had been placed on the nearby rail bridge – for decades the sole border crossing point – in order to move vehicles across the border between the two countries.

His summit with US President Donald Trump is just over two weeks away, but already this month Xi Jinping has had one of his busiest stretches of diplomatic travel in recent years.
First he wrapped up the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, and then he made a state visit to Egypt.
Xi is expected to head off again later this week to visit New Delhi for the Brics summit before he travels to Washington. Beijing has not yet confirmed those two trips, in line with its practice of making official travel announcements at the last minute.
Observers say the flurry of diplomatic activity is not only about making progress on bilateral ties but also an effort to strengthen China’s negotiating hand with the United States.
Sun Chenghao, a fellow at Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy, said the summit with Trump was important but Xi’s diplomatic sequencing emphasised that China’s foreign relations did not “revolve around a single axis centred on Washington”.

NABU and SAPO did not want to show the search warrants, so they were not allowed into the Prosecutor General’s Office — Kravchenko
Kyiv • UNN
Kravchenko stated that employees of the State Protection Department did not allow NABU detectives into the Prosecutor General’s Office because they did not want to show the search warrants and say which offices exactly they were heading to.
Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko said that the State Guard Department did not allow NABU and SAPO detectives into the Prosecutor General's Office building because the latter did not want to show the search warrants or say which offices they were heading to. Kravchenko made the statement while speaking to journalists, reports UNN.
Details
As Kravchenko noted, State Guard Department officers did not allow NABU detectives into the PGO because they did not want to show the search warrants or say which offices they were heading to.
I don't understand why there was no phone call. They could have said that we had a warrant for such-and-such offices. If they had shown them to the guards, they would have been allowed in. At first, they did not want to show the warrant indicating which offices
He added that he had spoken with the heads of both NABU and SAPO on the day of the searches.
Our colleagues had search warrants for my office and the deputy's office, but at first they refused to show them because they did not want us to understand where they had come. At about midnight, I spoke with the heads of both NABU and SAPO. I called and asked what was happening. They said that we had authorization to conduct searches in your office and that we would be carrying them out. I said: "Okay, everything will be opened for you—the office, the rooms, and the safes." I gave the order, the investigators were let in, and they conducted all the searches
He also said that he asked the heads of the anti-corruption agencies whether he should expect a search at his place of residence.
I was told: "You will find out everything." Then I learned that there was also a search at my place of residence. I asked... my wife was on her way with the owner. They initially climbed over the fence into the house and opened the gate. Then the locks were... they stopped and waited for my wife, who opened it and showed them everything
According to Kravchenko, during the search detectives seized empty envelopes and four gift certificates worth UAH 50,000 each from the Canali store in his office. They also seized his identification code and other data from his personal file relating to him in the reception area.

Nearly 80% of residential buildings in Ukraine ready for heating season
The Ministry for Restoration, Infrastructure and Transport announced this in a Telegram post, according to Ukrinform.
"Ukraine continues preparing its housing and utilities infrastructure and social sector for winter. Despite the risks posed by the war, work is underway in all regions. As of early September, more than 114,000 residential buildings had been prepared for the heating season, accounting for 79.2% of the planned total," the ministry said.
In addition, 14,194 boiler houses and more than 13,300 km of heating networks have been prepared, along with 2,900 water-supply pumping stations and more than 8,300 wells.
Some 20,600 social infrastructure facilities, including schools, kindergartens and healthcare institutions, are also ready.
Road services have prepared 4,124 pieces of specialized equipment, repaired 8.6 million square meters of roads, and stockpiled more than 1.3 million tonnes of road-gritting materials and reagents.
Particular attention is being paid to frontline regions, where critical infrastructure operates under the constant threat of attacks. There, it is important not only to complete repairs but also to ensure adequate reserves and readiness to promptly restore services in the event of damage.
President Volodymyr Zelensky earlier enacted a decision of the National Security and Defense Council concerning the implementation of comprehensive resilience plans for individual regions and preparations for the 2026/2027 heating season in Kyiv.
