How Three Small Baltic States Ended Up Running Europe's Crypto Plumbing  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:53:53 UTC
23:53:53 KST

When MiCA came into force, the smart money picked its winners early, and the shortlist always read like a roll call of old money, with Frankfurt, Paris, Dublin, Amsterdam, and Luxembourg turning up in every version of it. Those places have incumbent banks, supervisory headcount and lobbying muscle, so the assumption was fair enough.
The transitional window slammed shut, the raw tallies appear to confirm it. Germany sits at the top of the CASP authorisation table, ahead of France and the Netherlands, out of 322 records across the EEA.
Open that German column, though, and hardly any of the names are crypto companies. It is Commerzbank, DZ BANK, DekaBank and a scattering of regional Volksbanks, a lead built almost entirely on incumbent banks that sit well outside what MiCA was written to govern.
Of the 322 authorisations, 206 went to crypto-native businesses and 116 to traditional institutions adding crypto to an existing book. Only 17 firms on the whole register are licensed to run a live trading platform. Germany’s column is the most bank-heavy of all, which is why its headline lead is misleading.
Counting licences tells you where applications got processed. It reveals close to nothing about where Europe's crypto plumbing is being welded together, and on that question I’d point 1,500 kilometres northeast, to three countries whose combined population would fit inside metropolitan Paris.
Regulators that chose subtraction
Estonia carried 1,234 licensed crypto firms at the end of 2019 and, by 2021, an estimated 55% of the world's registered virtual asset service providers (VASPs) — a widely cited figure that is difficult to independently verify. A licence back then cost only €300 and came with light scrutiny. The country’s Financial Intelligence Unit spent three years dismantling that, and by 1 May 2023 exactly 100 authorisations were left standing.
Lithuania ran the same operation on a slower clock. Around 850 crypto companies sat on its register in late 2022; across 2025 the Bank of Lithuania received 102 MiCA applications from just 55 firms, and had granted three CASP licences by early January 2026.
Latvia never had the volume to lose and has authorised ten CASPs since the regulation took effect (a count that shifts as the register updates), a stablecoin payments firm tenth in July.
Three governments installed a filter, and it did precisely what filters do.
Riga offers consultations — at €2,500
Bank of Latvia does something unusual for a financial supervisor, which is to give its own time away. Prospective applicants get unlimited free consultations (roughly 100 a year, conducted in English) before the company in question legally exists.
Application fees run to €2,500, among the lowest in the EU, with ongoing supervision pegged at 0.6% of gross revenue and a €3,000 floor. Latvia can afford to charge that little because the consultations catch hopeless applications early. If the regulator thinks a structure won't pass, it says so in the meeting, and that's usually the end of it.
Compare this with the jurisdictions where dialogue begins only after you have paid a law firm six figures to guess what the regulator wants. Those markets end up selecting for firms skilled at navigating bureaucracy, which is a different competence from building products people can actually use.
Dual licences are the tell
Four of Latvia's ten licensed CASPs have now paired their MiCA authorisation with a payment or e-money licence from the very same regulator, several of them within weeks of each other.
Stacking MiCA on top of PSD2 is what a company does when its product is a rail. Custody and exchange permissions cover the crypto leg; the payment institution licence covers euros arriving and leaving, along with consumer protections a CASP authorisation by itself does not carry.
Talent compounds where it lands
Vilnius holds the deepest bench in the region. Lithuania's 248 active fintechs employ close to 7,800 people and serve around 40 million customers, and its payment and e-money institutions moved €163 billion last year, up 57% since the end of 2022.
Average team size there climbed from 21 to 31 over five years even as the company count fell from 282 to 248. Fewer firms, bigger firms, more experienced teams.
Tallinn contributes something harder to tabulate, in a country of 1.3 million that has produced ten unicorns and attracted over 130,000 e-residents from 180-odd countries who, between them, registered more than 37,000 Estonian companies. Skype's alumni are still seeding new ventures two decades after the exit.
Riga adds roughly 40,000 ICT specialists, about 4.4% of everyone employed in Latvia, with the country ranking third in Europe for ICT students per million inhabitants. Together, the three produce engineers who can read and handle both regulatory compliance and blockchain infrastructure.
Hiring a compliance officer who has already survived a supervisory review is an ordinary Tuesday in Vilnius. Try that in a city where the crypto industry showed up last year.
The big centres are reading it wrong
Set the compliance bar high enough to screen out the weak and what remains is a smaller, sturdier field. Passporting then carries those survivors across all 27 member states from a single regulator.
With roughly 83% of legacy-registered firms never converting to a full MiCA licence, each early licence looks more valuable by the month. Most of the 322 authorisations Europe is busy counting will never move serious volume, and a Baltic handful will end up moving most of it. Redraw Europe's crypto map around the licences that cover real rails, and its centre of gravity settles a long way north of Frankfurt.
Author:
Innokenty Isers is the founder and CEO of Paybis, a trusted crypto exchange and wallet. With over 20 years of experience in online business and technology, Innokenty has been at the forefront of driving innovation in the crypto space. Under his leadership, Paybis has grown into a global hub offering secure and compliant solutions for buying, selling, and managing digital assets, serving customers in over 180 countries. His vision is centered on bridging the gap between traditional finance and the rapidly evolving digital economy, empowering individuals and businesses to participate in the decentralized financial ecosystem.

Capalo AI and Future Energy Partner to Optimize 56 MW / 168 MWh Lithuanian Battery Storage Project  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:53:52 UTC
23:53:52 KST

Capalo AI, a sustainable technology company specializing in optimization and trading of renewable and hybrid energy assets, has entered into a partnership with Future Energy, a Lithuanian renewable energy developer, to manage and optimize a 56 MW / 168 MWh standalone battery energy storage system (BESS) in Raseiniai, Lithuania.
The project brings together infrastructure investment, EPC delivery and AI-driven optimization in one of Lithuania’s most significant new battery storage developments.
The BESS is planned to be completed by the end of 2026 and is expected to reach commercial operation in Q1 2027. Under the partnership, Capalo AI will provide route-to-market services for the asset, including Day-Ahead, Intraday and balancing market trading, as well as Balance Responsible Party (BRP) services, delivered through the Capalo Zeus VPP™.
With a storage capacity of 168 MWh, the Raseiniai BESS will be one of the largest facilities of its kind in Lithuania and among the country’s first commercial battery storage projects capable of storing and supplying energy for up to three hours. The longer storage duration enables more efficient participation across balancing and wholesale electricity markets while providing a broader range of services supporting the electricity system.
The facility is being delivered by MT Group, a European EPC contractor specializing in energy infrastructure. MT Group is responsible for the engineering, procurement and construction of the BESS infrastructure and its integration into Lithuania’s high-voltage electricity system. The battery park will be connected to the Litgrid 110 kV transmission network through the expanded Raseiniai transformer substation.
Together, Future Energy, MT Group and Capalo AI combine energy infrastructure investment, EPC delivery and advanced market optimization, connecting the physical infrastructure required for the energy transition with the digital capabilities needed to operate it efficiently.
The project has also been welcomed by the Raseiniai District Municipality as a significant investment in the region and a contribution to Lithuania’s ongoing energy transformation.
“Lithuania’s storage market is scaling quickly, with grid operators fast-tracking new battery connections to keep pace with the country’s growing renewable capacity. We already manage a substantial number of assets in the market, and this partnership with Future Energy extends that footprint and reflects the confidence Baltic developers continue to place in our trading and optimization approach” said Dainius Velykis, Regional Manager Baltics, Capalo AI.
Rimvydas Štilinis, CEO, Future Energy, said: “Energy storage is becoming an essential part of Lithuania’s energy system. As renewable generation continues to grow, the ability to store electricity, provide flexibility and respond efficiently to market and grid needs becomes increasingly important. The Raseiniai project is a significant long-term investment in this infrastructure. By combining MT Group’s EPC capabilities with Capalo AI’s route-to-market access and AI-driven optimization, we are building an asset designed not only to store energy, but to operate efficiently across Lithuania’s evolving electricity markets.”
“Battery storage is becoming a fundamental part of Europe’s energy infrastructure. The Gambling Rulebook Is Changing... Here’s What It Means for Digital Gaming  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:53:50 UTC
23:53:50 KST

Identity checks, spending limits and clearer promotional conditions are now appearing directly inside the digital gaming journey. What once sat mainly in licensing documents or terms and conditions is becoming visible in the product itself. For players, that can mean more prompts, more information and occasionally an extra step before play begins. For developers, it means the rules increasingly influence how a gambling platform is built.
The Rulebook Is Moving Onto the Screen
The European standard EN 18144, published in May 2026, identifies nine behavioural markers that may help operators recognise potentially risky patterns. They include changes in stake frequency, speed of play, deposits, withdrawals, session length, losses and the use of safety tools. It is a voluntary standard rather than legislation, an important distinction. A longer session or a larger deposit is not automatically treated as a problem. Several changes can be considered together instead, placing more emphasis on how behaviour develops over time. That requires more than a warning page hidden in an account menu. The system itself needs to be capable of noticing those changes and deciding when a response may be appropriate.
Mobile Play Has Made the Boundaries Less Obvious
In 2024, mobile devices generated 58% of online gambling revenue, according to figures published by the European Gaming and Betting Association with H2 Gambling Capital. The same dataset put total European gambling revenue at €123.4 billion, with €47.9 billion coming online. That represented 39% of the overall market, compared with 37% a year earlier.
A gambling session now sits beside banking apps, messages, streaming platforms and online shopping. Deposits, verification and account controls have to work within an interface designed for a small screen and quick interactions. Space is limited, so even a short warning or extra confirmation has to compete with menus, balances and game controls. Most mobile products try to remove every unnecessary pause. Regulated gaming sometimes needs to introduce one.
Sometimes the Extra Friction Is Deliberate
A request to confirm an identity or review a spending limit may look like another barrier between the user and the game. In some cases, that barrier is intentional. A short pause can force an active decision where a frictionless interface would normally encourage another tap. Clearer promotional conditions can do something similar by putting information in front of the user before an offer is accepted rather than expecting it to be found later.
Similar design questions already appear elsewhere online. Similar design questions already appear elsewhere online, particularly as age-verification requirements for digital products become more closely tied to how platforms are built rather than relying on simple self-declaration.
What the Licence Changes for the Player
Licensing may sound like background administration, but its effects are often practical. It can influence registration checks, payment information, account controls and the way responsible-gambling tools are presented. For readers comparing those features, a Casino.org guide brings together information on licensing, payments, games and account protections in one place. Casino.org is an independent gambling information and review site that assesses online platforms and publishes guidance on matters including licensing, payment methods, withdrawals and responsible-gambling features. Those details affect the experience from the moment an account is opened, even if the user never thinks of them as part of regulation.
Designers Now Have More Than Usability to Think About
Imagine a routine session. Someone creates an account, verifies their details, deposits money, chooses a game and later adjusts a personal limit. None of those actions looks particularly unusual. Yet each can involve requirements that affect what appears on the screen and when. Under EN 18144, a change in session duration might be considered alongside faster play, larger deposits or different withdrawal behaviour. One action does not produce an automatic judgement, but a digital system may need to recognise patterns across several actions.
The shortest journey is not automatically the best one. A prompt that asks someone to review a setting may serve a purpose precisely because it interrupts the flow. Developers also have to decide where information appears, how easy account controls are to find and which actions should require another confirmation. That includes small decisions such as whether a limit setting sits beside payments or deeper inside the account menu. None of that is as visible as the game graphics or animation, but it affects the experience just as directly. Good app design usually tries to make the machinery disappear. Regulated gaming sometimes needs part of that machinery to stay visible.
What the Player Actually Notices
Most users will never read the standards behind a platform or follow every regulatory update. They will notice the result instead: an extra verification screen, clearer conditions beside an offer, a limit setting that is easier to find or a prompt appearing at a particular point in a session. Those details may look like ordinary interface choices. They are also where the changing gambling rulebook becomes visible.

TALLINN - Estonian Minister of Energy and Environment Andres Sutt hosted the first Nordic-Baltic (NB8) energy ministers' meeting in Tallinn from September 3-4, bringing together energy ministers and senior representatives from the Nordic and Baltic countries.
The meeting, which included a Ukrainian delegation in its initial discussions, focused on supporting Ukraine's energy supply for the upcoming winter, the resilience of critical energy infrastructure, and the development of a competitive Nordic-Baltic energy market.
Sutt stressed that the closely interconnected energy systems of the Nordic-Baltic countries require stronger cooperation than ever. "Energy security in our region today is not just about having enough electricity, but also about whether our infrastructure can withstand potential threats and how quickly we can restore energy supply in the event of disruptions. Our energy systems are increasingly linked, and therefore we must view our preparedness and cooperation from a regional perspective," he said.
Discussions on Ukraine's energy supply centered on the upcoming winter. Russia's ongoing attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure are expected to make the winter extremely difficult, and the ministers explored ways to support the continuity of Ukraine's energy supply and coordinate aid from their respective countries. They also discussed the long-term recovery of Ukraine's energy sector and energy-related preparations for the Ukraine Recovery Conference, scheduled to be held in Tallinn in January 2027.
"While providing aid to Ukraine, we must not forget its invaluable experience. The ongoing war has taught Ukraine how to protect its energy infrastructure, ensure its operational continuity, and restore energy supply to residents and critical facilities as quickly as possible. We must learn these priceless lessons from the Ukrainians and use them to protect our own countries' infrastructure from potential threats," said Lithuanian Minister of Energy Lukas Savickas.
In addition to regional energy security, the meeting focused on protecting Baltic Sea energy infrastructure and ensuring the resilience of energy systems. The region's energy infrastructure is increasingly interconnected, and recent incidents in the Baltic Sea area have highlighted the need to bolster preparedness against physical, cyber, and hybrid threats. The ministers shared experiences and explored opportunities to enhance the resilience of the region's energy infrastructure and strengthen international cooperation.
"Today's discussion highlighted the importance of Nordic-Baltic cooperation in strengthening regional preparedness and resilience. Together, we form one of Europe's most integrated energy regions," added Finnish Minister of Climate and the Environment Sari Multala.
Regarding the development of a competitive Baltic Sea energy market, discussions centered on investment and financing opportunities and the creation of long-term certainty. The participants also talked about the evolution of electricity demand and production, grid development, and the need to improve the transparency and predictability of the regional energy market.
The meeting reaffirmed the shared commitment of the Nordic-Baltic countries to strengthen energy cooperation and find regional solutions to challenges related to energy security, resilience, and competitiveness. A joint Nordic-Baltic statement on energy cooperation was also issued in conjunction with the meeting.
Estonia holds the presidency of the Nordic-Baltic cooperation in 2026. The NB8 cooperation format brings together Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Finland, Sweden, Denmark, Norway, and Iceland.

The prime minister did not specify what kind of assistance had been offered.
Kulbergs said that there is currently a glimmer of hope for finding the Latvian travelers missing after devastating floods in Nepal, but the search is seriously hampered by the rainy season there.
Kulbergs also underlined that the government will do everything it can to help and support the relatives of these travelers. A representative from the Consular Department of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs has now arrived in Nepal to assist the Latvian side on the ground in maintaining contact with the Nepalese authorities. This representative will also assist in the event the remains of a Latvian citizen are found and need to be repatriated to Latvia. Relatives will also be informed about the next steps in such a case.
According to Kulbergs, several foreign tourists are known to have reached Chinese territory during the flood disaster, but Latvia has not yet received a response regarding these people.
For his part, Rinkevics acknowledged that the situation in Nepal is dire, and rescue efforts there are not as straightforward as they might be in Europe or Latvia. Nevertheless, Latvian authorities are working to provide the relatives who remain in Latvia with the maximum possible emotional and informational support.
This week, the State Police reported that it had received information about instances where scammers have attempted to defraud the relatives of Latvians who have gone missing in Nepal.
The president expressed his hope that these scammers will be apprehended and receive the harshest penalties possible, both to send a clear message that such behavior will not be tolerated and to deter others.
Kulbergs acknowledged that scammers exploit any misfortune to line their pockets, and that people must always be vigilant so as not to fall into the traps set by these criminals.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs informed LETA that a representative of the Consular Department has already started work in Nepal. Meanwhile, the honorary consul continues to maintain active communication with local authorities.
To date, 31 closest relatives of missing Latvians have submitted DNA samples.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs continues to assist and coordinate practical matters that may arise for the relatives of those missing in Nepal, with the aim of providing information on where and what kind of assistance they can receive.
Edite Medne, Director of the Foreign Ministry’s Consular Department, reveals in a video posted on X that the last communication with the guide of the largest Latvian group on the day of the tragedy took place at 8:38 a.m. He spoke with his brother in Kathmandu by phone, and this took place at a border crossing on the Chinese side.
Meanwhile, European Union (EU) authorities report that the information available to them indicates the last communication took place at 8:41 a.m. "In any case, we are talking about a fairly short period of time during which this communication has been lost," Medne said.
As reported, on August 26, a glacier collapsed, triggering a flow of ice debris and resulting in a flood of water and mud from a glacial lake, causing widespread damage in Nepal and China. By the morning of August 31, at least 900 people had been confirmed dead in the natural disaster, while approximately 4,200 were missing.
A large group of Latvian tourists, organized by yoga enthusiasts from the company Yantra, was also near the epicenter of the disaster, while a smaller number of Latvian tourists were in the disaster zone as part of a group organized by the local company Mighty Himalayan Trek. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs has information that three Latvian citizens who were in the region at the time were not affected by the flood-induced mudslide in Nepal, but 33 are currently considered missing.

Latvia is taking action in several areas to reduce inflow of Russian and Belarusian goods into market - Braze  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:53:45 UTC
23:53:45 KST

RIGA - Latvia is taking targeted action in three mutually complementary areas to reduce the inflow of Russian and Belarusian goods into the market and, consequently, economic support for the aggressor states, Foreign Minister Baiba Braze (New Unity) told LETA.
The minister noted that Latvia is already utilizing its national capacity to take action, namely, the law and the government regulations developed on its basis provide for a ban on the import of certain goods originating in Russia and Belarus into Latvia.
She emphasized that the purpose of this regulation is to limit the entry of such goods into the Latvian market. Consequently, responsible local traders are also expected to act in accordance with the nature and purpose of the restrictions, rather than seeking ways to circumvent them by organizing shipments through other countries.
Likewise, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs works on a daily basis to ensure that an increasing number of Russian and Belarusian goods are included in future rounds of European Union (EU) sanctions. At the same time, the adoption of EU sanctions requires the involvement of all member states and can be time-consuming, which is why national restrictions allow countries to act more quickly, the minister said.
Latvia also advocates for a more flexible EU approach, namely, that alongside major rounds of sanctions, more frequent and precisely targeted sanctions are needed. Braze gave the following example: if it is determined that restricting specific goods or components could directly hinder Russia’s military production, such a decision should be implemented as quickly as possible, without waiting for the next major round of sanctions.
At the same time, Braze acknowledged that technology is advancing very rapidly, so frequent and targeted sanctions would be more effective in achieving the goal.
The minister also emphasized that the Ministry of Foreign Affairs is working to ensure that Latvia’s neighboring countries and other EU partners adopt a similar approach. In her view, the more countries that impose equivalent restrictions, the fewer opportunities there are to circumvent them by rerouting the shipments through another member state.
Commenting on publicly reported information that Latvian traders are using Estonia to circumvent the ban on book imports from Russia, Braze said that the Ministry of Foreign Affairs will investigate the reports regarding the use of Estonia to circumvent the ban. If the reports are confirmed, Latvia will ask Estonia to take the necessary measures to put an end to such practices.
At the same time, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs will call on the Ministry of Economics to ensure that the circulation of goods in the Latvian market complies with Latvian legislation and established restrictions. She emphasizes that Latvia’s national action thus serves not only as a practical market restriction but also as an impetus for broader and more united action in the region.
As LETA reported, as of September 1, 2026, the import of several industrial goods from Russia and Belarus into Latvia is prohibited, according to regulations drafted by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
The ban covers printed books, newspapers, and other printed materials; clothing; other finished textile products; footwear; headwear; as well as toys, games, and sports equipment.
According to information provided by the State Revenue Service (VID), the ban applies to printed books, newspapers, pictures, and other printed materials, as well as handwritten documents, typewritten documents, and plans.
The ban also applies to knitted or crocheted clothing and clothing accessories, as well as clothing items and clothing accessories that are not knitted or crocheted, ready-made textile products, sets, used clothing and used textile products, rags, footwear, gaiters, and similar products or parts thereof, headgear and parts thereof, as well as toys, games, and sports equipment, their parts, and accessories.
The ban is in effect until June 30, 2027, according to VID.

CleanR Industry sorts well over 30 thousand tons of various types of packaging per year, recycles 10 thousand tons of polymer waste into pellets, and produces more than 25 thousand tons of fuel derived from waste (RFDF).
The works are scheduled to be completed in mid-2027. At the same time, the center will continue to operate.
Azortum, which specializes in integrating independent technological solutions and selecting the most suitable equipment and technologies for a specific project, emphasizes that such projects are based not only on installing new equipment but also on a comprehensive solution tailored to a company's operational processes and goals.
“In cooperation with CleanR Industry, our task is to create a technological solution that ensures more efficient sorting, a higher level of material recovery, and, in the long term, greater economic benefits,” says Azortum representative Taavi Põri.
CleanR Industry’s investments in modernizing the packaging sorting center are part of CleanR Group’s move to implement and strengthen circular economy principles.

RIX Riga Airport Launches the Next Stage of Its Major Passenger Terminal Expansion Project  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:53:44 UTC
23:53:44 KST

RIX Riga Airport today marked the start of the next stage of its passenger terminal expansion project with a ceremonial event at the Airport. The project will deliver a new, spacious and energy-efficient passenger terminal extension equipped with state-of-the-art technologies, significantly increasing terminal capacity, enhancing the passenger experience and providing the infrastructure necessary for the Airport's future growth.
The planning and development stage of the project has now been completed, and preparatory works for construction will begin later this month. The project includes the expansion of the existing terminal through the construction of new check-in facilities, passenger waiting areas, a security screening zone, and a baggage reclaim hall. External areas surrounding the terminal building, including access roads and parking facilities, will also be redeveloped and upgraded. The introduction of new passenger service and security technologies will further improve comfort, efficiency, and the overall travel experience at the Airport.
The terminal expansion will add approximately 20,000 square metres of new building space. In addition, 29,500 square metres of roads, pavements, public spaces, and landscaped green areas will be developed. The new facilities will provide the capacity required to accommodate future passenger growth, addressing the limitations of the current terminal, which already exceeds its originally designed capacity.
The construction cost of the terminal expansion is estimated at EUR 98 million. Financing will be provided equally by three lenders: two international financial institutions, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) and the Nordic Investment Bank (NIB), as well as OP Corporate Bank plc Latvian Branch, selected through a tender process. The financing was granted following a comprehensive assessment of Riga Airport's development plans, business strategy, and creditworthiness. Independent due diligence was conducted both by the lenders and by international advisors engaged by the lenders.
In addition to financing the construction works, the funding package will support the installation of next-generation passenger service and aviation security technologies compliant with European Union standards. These investments will enable RIX Riga Airport to provide a new level of passenger experience while meeting the highest requirements for aviation security and accessibility. The total financing available to the Airport under the lending arrangements amounts to up to EUR 150 million.
"The passenger terminal expansion is a long-term and carefully developed strategic project for Riga Airport. Its scale and complexity make it one of the most significant infrastructure projects in Latvia's aviation sector. Together with our partners, we are implementing the project in a balanced and efficient manner. The expansion is already needed today, and its scope has been carefully designed to address passenger demand while taking into account regional economic development prospects and the current geopolitical environment. Our goal is to create infrastructure that meets future needs and provides Riga Airport with the flexibility to continue growing," said Laila Odiņa, Chairperson of the Board of RIX Riga Airport.
"Riga Airport is Latvia’s main gateway to the world and a vital part of the country’s transport infrastructure. Its development is important not only for providing passengers with a more convenient and high-quality travel experience, but also for Latvia’s competitiveness in the Baltic region, its business environment, and its connectivity with Europe and the rest of the world. The passenger terminal expansion project demonstrates that Latvia is continuing to make targeted investments in its infrastructure and is preparing for future growth. It is particularly important that the project is being adapted to realistic passenger traffic forecasts and Latvia’s actual needs, ensuring a responsible and well-considered investment in the country’s future," said Andulis Židkovs, State Secretary, Ministry of Transport of the Republic of Latvia.
The terminal expansion will be delivered by the RIXLA consortium, whose bid was selected as the most economically advantageous in an international construction tender. The consortium consists of LNK Industries and Arčers. The international procurement process was conducted in accordance with the procurement procedures established by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development. A total of 17 construction companies and consortia from nine countries applied for prequalification. Five candidates submitted technical proposals, four were invited to submit financial bids, and final financial bids were received from two participants. The bid submitted by RIXLA was ultimately selected as the most economically advantageous proposal.
The contract has been concluded under the FIDIC Yellow Book framework. The project is targeting a BREEAM Very Good sustainability certification rating.
Legal support for the project was provided by law firm Sorainen.
Construction will be carried out in four consecutive stages under a design-and-build delivery model. Works on site are scheduled to begin in the second half of September 2026, initially focusing on site preparation and the development of temporary infrastructure while the original design is being adapted to meet the Airport’s updated development needs. The second stage will include reconstruction of external infrastructure and utility networks, construction of new roads and public areas, and site landscaping. The third stage will involve construction of the terminal expansion itself, while the fourth stage will complete the permanent external infrastructure and remove temporary facilities.
The project is scheduled for completion within 42 months.
Throughout the construction period, RIX Riga Airport will continue operating at full capacity. However, passengers and visitors should expect temporary traffic and access restrictions within the Airport area. Information about any operational changes will be communicated in advance through the Airport's website, social media channels and media announcements.

====================================================================================================

Vilnius, Riga, Tallinn by Train: A 7-Day Baltic Route  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:53:43 UTC
23:53:43 KST

For most of the past two decades, travelling overland between the three Baltic capitals meant one thing: a long-distance coach. The rail network inherited from the Soviet era ran east to west rather than north to south, and the direct Vilnius-Riga passenger service disappeared in 2004. Anyone wanting to see all three capitals in a single trip either booked a bus, hired a car, or flew, which on routes of a few hundred kilometres made little sense for either cost or carbon. The accommodation side was just as fragmented: three cities, three national markets, and no single place to compare them. That gap is narrowing, and platforms such as trip1 now list hotels across all three countries under one roof, which for a trip of this shape matters more than it might sound.
The transport picture has changed too. Since December 2023, Lithuanian operator LTG Link has run a daily direct train between Vilnius and Riga, restoring a link dormant for nearly twenty years. In January 2025, the Lithuanian, Latvian and Estonian railways coordinated their timetables to create a through Vilnius-Riga-Tallinn service with a single cross-platform change at Valga on the Estonian-Latvian border, sold under one ticket. Demand has run ahead of forecasts, and from January 2026 an additional daily Riga-Tallinn service was added.
What follows is a route, and rather more detail than usual on where to sleep at each end of it, because on a three-country itinerary the hotels are the part most people get wrong.
Why seven days, and how the three hotel markets differ
Three capitals in seven days sounds ambitious but is comfortable in practice. Vilnius to Riga is 348 kilometres, Riga to Tallinn 441, and the full Vilnius-Tallinn run 789. That is less than the length of Great Britain.
Two nights in each city, with the seventh day absorbed by travel or a stopover, is the sensible allocation. Travel south to north: Tallinn has the best onward connections, with ferries to Helsinki and Stockholm and a busy airport, which makes it the natural place to finish.
The three accommodation markets behave quite differently, and knowing how before you book saves money and walking.
Vilnius is the cheapest of the three and has an unusually deep boutique segment for a city of half a million, largely because the old town is full of restored palaces and merchant houses that convert well. Five-star rates here undercut four-star rates in Tallinn.
Riga has the widest range and the sharpest price gradient. Old town rates drop noticeably once you cross into the Quiet Centre, a ten-minute walk that also puts you closer to the Art Nouveau district.
Tallinn is the most expensive, has the smallest luxury segment, and sells out earliest. The medieval core is compact, genuinely worth staying inside, and priced accordingly. Book this one first.
Vilnius: two nights
Vilnius makes the strongest case for being the first stop, partly because it is the least familiar to most visitors and partly because it holds the largest baroque old town in Northern Europe, a UNESCO World Heritage site that is still a working residential district rather than a preserved museum quarter.
Two days covers the old town, the Gediminas Tower viewpoint, Užupis across the river, and the National Museum. The contemporary city deserves an afternoon too: Vilnius has become a serious European fintech hub, and the effect on the restaurant and café scene in Naujamiestis is visible.
Where to stay in Vilnius
The old town is the obvious base, and the top end punches well above the city's size.
Hotel Pacai on Didžioji street is the standout. It occupies a baroque palace built in 1677 for the Pac family, once the grandest private residence in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, and reopened in 2018 after a restoration by local architects as a 104-room Design Hotels property with a spa, restaurant and bar. The historic shell has been kept and the interiors are deliberately contemporary.
Relais & Châteaux Stikliai, on Stiklių street among the galleries and artisan workshops, is the older kind of luxury. Its restaurant has been the benchmark for fine dining in Vilnius for more than thirty years, served under a glass-roofed atrium, and the wellness area includes a pool and Roman-style baths.
Narutis, a Small Luxury Hotels of the World member on Pilies street, sits in a building first documented in 1581, which makes it one of the oldest hotel buildings in the city. It is directly on the old town's main artery, with a quiet inner courtyard and its own spa.
Radisson Collection Astorija occupies a classical 1901 building roughly thirteen minutes' walk from the railway station and includes an indoor pool. It is the reliable full-service choice, and the closest thing Vilnius has to a grand hotel in the traditional sense. Grand Hotel Vilnius, Curio Collection by Hilton covers similar ground.
In the mid-range, the Shakespeare Boutique Hotel sits in a renovated 17th-century palace fifty metres from Cathedral Square, and the Grotthuss Boutique Hotel occupies a historic building on a medieval street about eleven minutes from the station, with a small wine bar off reception. Artagonist Art Hotel, Imperial Hotel & Restaurant and Mabre Residence are all inside the old town and consistently well reviewed. For predictable business-standard rooms, Hilton Garden Inn Vilnius City Centre, AC Hotel Vilnius and Novotel Vilnius Centre are all central.
Vilnius railway station is around fifteen minutes on foot from the southern edge of the old town, so anywhere inside the walls keeps the onward journey simple. The Lithuania travel guides on trip1 break the city down by district if you are weighing the old town against Užupis or Naujamiestis.
Vilnius to Riga
The train leaves Vilnius in the morning and reaches Riga Central Station in just over four hours, comparable to driving and considerably more pleasant. Second-class fares vary between roughly 10 and 24 euros; first class is fixed at around 34 euros and includes an assigned seat and complimentary refreshments. The rolling stock is a modern Pesa diesel unit with air conditioning, Wi-Fi, power sockets and at-seat catering.
Booking opens up to sixty days ahead on this sector, and the advice is consistent: book early. The service runs full and sells out days or weeks in advance. Interrail and Eurail holders need a seat reservation.
The coach alternative is perfectly good. Lux Express and Ecolines run frequent services, journey times are broadly similar and fares often lower. The difference is comfort and the ability to move around, which on a four-hour leg matters more than it sounds.
Riga: two nights
Riga is the largest of the three cities and has the widest spread of things to see: the old town, the Art Nouveau quarter on Alberta iela with the densest concentration of Jugendstil architecture anywhere in Europe, and the Central Market housed in former Zeppelin hangars. Two nights is a minimum rather than a comfortable allocation.
Where to stay in Riga
Riga Central Station is a seven-minute walk from the edge of the old town, which makes arrival easy regardless of where you have booked.
Neiburgs is probably the definitive Riga boutique stay. It occupies a carefully restored 1903 Art Nouveau building on Jauniela, directly beside Riga Cathedral on Dome Square, and its rooms are effectively apartments, with kitchenettes, high ceilings and original plasterwork. Each room has a different footprint because the heritage building dictated it. The hotel restaurant has held a Michelin Guide listing three years running and cooks seasonal Latvian produce sourced from the Central Market.
Grand Hotel Kempinski Riga, on Aspazijas bulvāris opposite the canal gardens, is the city's flagship five-star: 141 rooms, three bars, a spa widely rated among the best in the Baltics, and a rooftop restaurant looking across the old town spires. It is about 350 metres from Town Hall Square.
Pullman Riga Old Town on Jēkaba street, renovated in 2025, is the contemporary alternative, with a spa, indoor pool, rooftop bar and large, light rooms just inside the old city gates. Grand Palace Hotel on Pils iela, a Small Luxury Hotels member five minutes from Riga Cathedral, is the more traditional five-star.
At the value end, the Eurostars Metropole on Aspazijas is Riga's oldest continuously operating hotel, open since 1871 and a seven-minute walk from the station, and remains remarkably inexpensive for the space and location. Rixwell Old Riga Palace, Hotel Gutenbergs, Konventa Sēta and Hotel Monte Kristo are all solid old town options at moderate rates.
If you would rather be near the Art Nouveau district than the medieval core, Hotel Bergs sits inside the Bergs Bazaar, an elegant 19th-century courtyard complex in the Quiet Centre, and deals almost entirely in suites. Grand Poet by Semarah and Radisson Blu Latvija are nearby and cheaper. Art Hotel Roma, in a converted early 20th-century building near the National Opera, is the most characterful mid-range choice in the centre.
The Latvia travel guides on trip1 are useful for settling the old town versus Quiet Centre question before you commit, since the two produce quite different trips.
Riga to Tallinn, via Valga and Tartu
This is the leg where train and bus genuinely diverge. The coach is faster, around four and a half hours on a good run. The train takes longer, requires a change at Valga, and costs about 30.50 euros in second class.
It is still worth taking. The route runs through the Latvian countryside and southern Estonia rather than along a motorway. And there is Valga.
Valga in Estonia and Valka in Latvia were a single town until the border was drawn in 1920. They now function as twin municipalities inside the Schengen area, with no border controls and a pedestrian bridge over which, in one of the more charming pieces of municipal design in Europe, an international swing has been installed, letting you swing between two countries. The station has free luggage lockers requiring only a small coin deposit, so a few hours here is easily arranged.
The stronger case for breaking the journey, though, is Tartu. Estonia's second city and home to its oldest university, it has a compact old town, a river, an unusually beautiful wooden railway station and an atmosphere owing more to Scandinavia than to the Baltic coast. It was a European Capital of Culture in 2024 and the investment shows.
If you stay, Antonius Boutique Hotel is the pick, a small luxury property directly opposite the main university building and about 170 metres from the Town Hall. Lydia Hotel, a contemporary building set within the historic old town, has a spa lounge with several saunas and a pool. Dorpat Hotel is the large, good-value option, 197 rooms on the Emajõgi riverfront with its own Herb Spa, near the AHHAA science centre. V Spa & Conference Hotel is the wellness-led choice, and Hotel Soho sits beside Town Hall Square.
Tallinn: two nights
Tallinn Balti Jaam is roughly eight minutes on foot from Town Hall Square, a considerably better arrival than the bus station, which needs a tram ride into the centre. On a rail itinerary this is worth factoring into where you book.
Where to stay in Tallinn
Stay inside the medieval walls. The old town is small, the alternative districts are not appreciably cheaper, and the walls are the reason you came.
Schlössle Hotel is the heritage benchmark: a restored 13th-century merchant's house in a quiet corner of the old town with just 23 rooms, a member of Small Luxury Hotels of the World, a sauna and spa, and a basement cigar lounge built around an open hearth. Queen Elizabeth II stayed here in 2006.
Hotel Telegraaf, Autograph Collection is the most complete full-service option, occupying a converted 19th-century telegraph building with a courtyard, the substantial Telegraaf Spa, and the Michelin-listed Tchaikovsky restaurant on site. If you want a polished city stay rather than a historic curiosity, this is it.
The Three Sisters spreads 23 rooms across three connected medieval merchant houses and is the design-forward choice. Hotel St. Petersbourg is the heritage option at a lower rate.
Nunne Boutique Hotel deserves particular mention on a rail trip: 74 rooms built into the city walls, about five minutes from Balti Jaam and four from Town Hall Square, with a restaurant and spa. It is hard to beat for a short stay with luggage. Go Hotel Shnelli sits directly beside the station and is the budget version of the same logic.
For views over cobbles, Swissôtel Tallinn occupies the tallest building in the city. At the value end inside or beside the old town, Meriton Old Town Garden, Merchants House Hotel, My City Hotel and Bern Boutique Hotel all review well. Kalev Spa & Waterpark is the family choice.
Tallinn sells out earliest of the three capitals, particularly across summer and the December market period. The Estonia travel guides on trip1 cover Tartu alongside Tallinn, which helps if you are still deciding whether to build in the stopover.
Booking and paying: hotels with crypto
One development worth flagging, particularly for a regional audience.
Both Lithuania and Estonia have positioned themselves as regulated hubs for digital assets under the EU's MiCA framework, and travel has been among the earlier consumer categories to reflect that. trip1 now lets travellers book hotels with crypto, paying for a room in Bitcoin, USDT or other major assets while the property is settled in euros and never has to handle digital currency at all. From the hotel's side nothing changes. From the traveller's side, it removes the conversion step.
On a single-city trip that is a marginal convenience. On a three-country itinerary it is more useful than it first appears. You are making three bookings across three markets, and a payment method that works identically for all of them, without card foreign-transaction fees and without moving funds into a bank account first, takes one variable out of the planning. For visitors arriving from outside the euro area, or for anyone holding crypto who would rather spend it than convert it, the ability to pay in trip1 for hotels with crypto is a practical advantage rather than a novelty.
It also fits the region. The Baltic states have spent a decade building a reputation for digital-first public and financial infrastructure, from e-Residency in Estonia to a dense fintech licensing environment in Lithuania. A traveller booking a Riga hotel in crypto from a Vilnius café is, in a modest way, an expression of that.
What comes next
The current rail service is a stopgap in the best sense. Rail Baltica, the 900-kilometre standard-gauge line that will eventually connect Tallinn to the Polish border via Riga and Kaunas, passed the point of no return some time ago. As of mid-2026, 267 kilometres of main line are construction-ready, around 43 percent of the first phase, with track laying underway in Lithuania and terminal works advancing at Riga Central Station and Tallinn's Ülemiste. The first phase targets 2030.
When it opens, journey times between the capitals will roughly halve and the trip described here will compress into something closer to a long weekend. Until then, the slower version has its own argument. Eleven hours from Vilnius to Tallinn, with a change at a border town where you can swing between two countries, is not the fastest way to see the Baltics. It may well be the best one.

On 6 and 7 September, the Latvian Dual-Use Export Forum will take place in Rēzekne, bringing together more than 180 participants from Latvia and abroad. The two-day programme will begin with the National Armed Forces Industry Day, featuring demonstrations of defence and dual-use technologies on land, water and in the air, as well as company visits. On 7 September, the GORS Concert Hall will host discussions with international experts, technology presentations, an EXPO and one-to-one business meetings. At the heart of the Forum is a practical question: how can Latvian companies use their technologies and manufacturing capabilities to become part of international defence industry supply chains?
Representatives from more than 15 countries are expected to attend the Forum, including more than 45 international companies and up to 120 Latvian companies. International participants include TensorOne, AJB Subsea, HISDESAT, NEST AI, Fischer Panda and Sine Engineering, while representatives of BAE Systems, Dedrone by Axon, Wolfram Europe, SAF Tehnika, Silmor, Pērkons Energy, Redwire, RAW and Origin Robotics will also take part in the programme.
More than 150 pre-arranged business meetings are planned during the Forum, giving Latvian companies an opportunity to meet potential customers, cooperation partners, investors, suppliers and representatives of the international defence industry.
“Latvian companies have technologies and manufacturing capabilities that enable them to compete internationally. The key challenge now is to turn this potential into concrete cooperation opportunities and export deals. This is why the Forum places a strong emphasis on practical cooperation, creating direct connections between Latvian companies, international industry representatives, potential customers and partners,” says Līva Stūrmane, Chair of the Board of the Latvian Exporters Association “The Red Jackets”.
6 September: technologies in action on land, water and in the air
The Forum will begin on Sunday, 6 September, with the Industry Day “Technologies in Action”. From 10:00 to 15:00, demonstrations organised by the Ministry of Defence will showcase defence and dual-use technologies operating on land, water and in the air. The programme will also include a tactical briefing and industry presentations.
The demonstrations will take place at the former Rēzekne I railway station site and in the area near Lake Kovšu, offering participants an opportunity to experience the capabilities and innovation potential of Latvia’s defence industry in practice and to establish contacts with representatives of the industry and the military. Following the demonstrations, from 15:00 to 17:30, the Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA) will organise visits to LEAX Rēzekne, Bee Tactics and VEREMS, where international participants will have an opportunity to learn more about the companies’ operations, manufacturing capabilities and solutions.
From 17:30, participant registration and the official opening will continue at the Latgale Embassy GORS.
“Strengthening Latvia’s defence capabilities and developing the domestic defence industry are closely interconnected. Every company capable of developing technologies, systems or components for defence needs strengthens both national security and its own export potential. It is equally important to provide the industry with opportunities to demonstrate its solutions in real-life environments while receiving direct feedback from soldiers and international partners,” emphasises Raivis Melnis, Minister of Defence of the Republic of Latvia.
7 September: from technology to international markets
On Monday, 7 September, at the GORS Concert Hall, the Forum will continue with the programme “From Technology to International Markets”, focusing on the growth of Latvia’s defence industry and opportunities to integrate into international supply chains.
The day will begin with Uģis Norītis, representing the Ministry of Defence, who will present on the development of a globally competitive Latvian defence industry. Laura Štrovalde, Diāna Baranova, Magnus-Valdemar Saar, Head of Wolfram Europa, and Mārtiņš Tiknuss, Head of Gateway&Partners, will discuss the development of the Baltic defence industry and regional cooperation.
International defence strategy consultant Thibault Normand will address opportunities for Latvian companies to enter international defence supply chains, while representatives of Silmor, Pērkons Energy, Redwire and UniLAB Defence will discuss financing, scaling up production and entering export markets.
Later in the programme, Normunds Bergs, CEO of SAF Tehnika, will speak about critical communications, spectrum analysers and electronic warfare.
Niklas Edelsvärd, Sales Director at BAE Systems Land Systems, Edgars Šadris, Deputy State Secretary at the Ministry of Economics, Reinis Purvēns, Head of RAW, and Christian Emaus, Regional Director for the Nordics, Baltics and NATO at Dedrone by Axon, will discuss the journey of dual-use technologies from development to integration into international value chains and cooperation with major system integrators.
Māris Ķuda, Head of Government Relations at Origin Robotics, will address the role of precision technologies on the modern battlefield.
The Forum will conclude with Christian Emaus, Regional Director for the Nordics, Baltics and NATO at Dedrone by Axon, sharing how interconnected data, a common operational picture and rapid decision-making can help regain control of the airspace. Following the conference programme, the EXPO and business meetings will continue until 15:00.
Growth of the defence industry creates new export opportunities
As European countries increase defence investment and strengthen supply chains, new opportunities are emerging not only for defence industry companies but also for civilian manufacturers and technology companies.
The Forum’s priority sectors include artificial intelligence, cybersecurity and ICT, drones and unmanned systems, smart energy and advanced materials, electronics and engineering, as well as the chemical and metalworking industries. The Forum programme will continue on 8 September in Riga with company visits, giving international participants an opportunity to learn more about companies’ technologies and manufacturing capabilities and to continue the discussions initiated in Rēzekne.
The Latvian Dual-Use Export Forum is organised by the Latvian Exporters Association “The Red Jackets” in cooperation with the Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA), the Ministry of Economics and the Ministry of Defence. Further information about the Forum, its programme and participants is available on the Latvian Dual-Use Export Forum website.

TALLINN - The Nordic and Baltic countries called on Russia to immediately fulfill its obligations under international law and demanded the complete and unconditional withdrawal of all Russian forces from the territory of Ukraine, Ukrinform reported.
Finland's Deputy Permanent Representative to the UN, Heli Lehto, made a statement on behalf of eight countries at a UN General Assembly session addressing the situation in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine.
"We, the Nordic and Baltic countries, call on Russia to immediately and fully fulfill its obligations under international law. We demand the immediate, complete, and unconditional withdrawal of all Russian forces from the territory of Ukraine within its internationally recognized borders," the diplomat said.
Lehto emphasized that respect for Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity is a prerequisite for a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace.
She pointed to the sharp increase in Russian attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure in 2026. According to her, the number of civilian deaths and injuries is at its highest level since March 2022, while residents of the temporarily occupied territories continue to face constant and systematic repression.
"UN independent investigators continue to report mass arbitrary detentions and the widespread use of torture against civilians, detainees, and prisoners of war," she said.
Lehto also referred to reports of systematic sexual violence against Ukrainians in Russian custody and the abuse of women and children in the occupied territories.
"Human rights organizations have documented the large-scale forced displacement and illegal deportation of Ukrainian children. Ukrainian authorities report deliberate efforts to destroy Ukrainian national identity in the occupied areas, including through militarization, indoctrination, and the illegal adoption of children," the Finnish representative said.
Lehto recalled that the occupying authorities have an obligation to ensure the humane treatment of the local population, meet their basic needs, and facilitate the delivery of humanitarian aid.
"It is clear that Russia is unwilling to fulfill these obligations," she said.
The diplomat also affirmed the eight countries' commitment to holding Russia accountable for the international crimes it has committed.
"We remain firmly committed to the creation of a special tribunal for the crime of aggression against Ukraine and continue to steadfastly support the work of the International Criminal Court," Lehto concluded.
The diplomat presented the joint statement on behalf of Denmark, Estonia, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, Norway, Sweden, and Finland.

Lithuania’s Luna Robotics puts 24/7 drone vision at heart of Baltic security  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:53:33 UTC
23:53:33 KST

Lithuanian defence technology company Luna Robotics is turning battlefield lessons from Ukraine into scalable technologies for unmanned systems, developing China-free imaging solutions that allow drones to operate around the clock. CEO Elvinas Kukys believes Lithuania can become a major European defence-tech hub if it succeeds in scaling production, investment and international market access.
“Luna Robotics was created to solve an operational gap: unmanned systems lose effectiveness in darkness and poor visibility,” Kukys emphasised to The Baltic Times.
Drawing on military experience and direct contact with Ukrainian users, the company builds compact, low-latency imaging systems for FPV drones, interceptor drones and other unmanned platforms.
The war in Ukraine has fundamentally changed the pace at which defence technology is developed and deployed.
“Ukraine has shown that defence innovation is now measured in weeks, not years. Technology must be affordable, scalable and continuously improved through operator feedback,” Kukys said.
Battlefield success, he argues, increasingly depends not on creating a theoretically perfect product but on rapid integration, dependable supplies and the ability to update software as tactics and threats evolve.
Maintaining drone capabilities after dark is one of Luna Robotics' principal areas of focus.
“Night vision is essential because modern operations do not pause after sunset,” Kukys said.
Effective low-light imaging allows operators to maintain reconnaissance, navigation, target identification and interception capabilities when conventional cameras become ineffective.
“It is becoming a baseline requirement, not a premium feature,” the CEO said.
The company's LunaCam provides low-latency, 24/7 imaging in a lightweight format, with colour and monochrome configurations and optional infrared illumination. Its onboard processing can support software including object recognition and last-mile targeting, while radar-data integration can guide operators towards aerial targets.
Luna Robotics develops and manufactures its technology in Lithuania, which Kukys sees as an important contribution to Baltic security and resilience.
“We develop and manufacture our technology in Lithuania, creating local engineering know-how, production capacity and a resilient allied supply base,” he said.
Its technology can be integrated into FPV drones, interceptors, unmanned ground vehicles, or UGVs, and other platforms. Local capabilities can help Baltic defence partners deploy systems faster while reducing dependence on geopolitically risky suppliers.
“In defence, supply chains are a security issue, not merely a purchasing decision,” Kukys said.
Luna Robotics says its hardware and software are China-free. Kukys points to availability, export restrictions, cybersecurity, traceability and long-term maintenance among the potential risks associated with reliance on Chinese components.
Kukys believes Lithuania possesses many of the ingredients needed to become a significant European defence technology hub, including engineering talent, military understanding, rapid decision-making and direct access to lessons from Ukraine.
“Its small size can be an advantage: developers, users and institutions can work closely and iterate quickly,” he said.
However, Lithuania, he says, now needs to scale procurement and manufacturing capacity, develop specialist talent, attract patient capital and improve international market access.
Luna Robotics has similarly ambitious plans for its own expansion.
“In five years, I see Luna Robotics as a leading European provider of vision and autonomy technology for unmanned systems,” Kukys said.
The company aims to serve FPV and interceptor drones, UGVs and potentially unmanned surface vehicles, or USVs, while expanding manufacturing and R&D in Lithuania and deepening partnerships with European and US manufacturers.

Archaeology sheds new light on Suleyman the Magnificent’s final campaign in Hungary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:52:14 UTC
23:52:14 KST

- Archaeologists identify remains of mosque, dervish lodge, guesthouse, guard barracks, wooden palisade and civilian buildings
 
Archaeological research near Szigetvar Castle in Hungary, where Ottoman Sultan Suleyman the Magnificent led his final military campaign, has revealed that the settlement established around his presumed place of death was considerably larger than previously thought.
The findings have provided new insights into the size, structure and daily life of the Ottoman settlement known as Turbek, which developed around a tomb built in Suleyman’s honor.
Research conducted by Hungary’s University of Pecs in 2024 and 2025 found Ottoman-era artifacts scattered across an area of approximately 80 hectares, with their concentration varying across different parts of the site.
The evidence indicates that the settlement was not only more extensive than earlier estimates suggested but also relatively prosperous.
The findings have drawn renewed attention to Suleyman’s last campaign and the Ottoman remains near Szigetvar on the 460th anniversary of his death during the siege of the castle on the night of Sept. 6-7, 1566.
 
Suleyman’s final campaign and death
Suleyman, the longest-reigning sultan in Ottoman history, who ruled for nearly 46 years, left Istanbul on May 1, 1566, to lead his 13th and final military campaign.
Despite his advanced age and declining health, he traveled at the head of the army. His imperial tent was erected on a hill overlooking Szigetvar Castle, at what is now believed to be the site of the tomb complex.
Suleyman died in his tent during the night of Sept. 6-7. The fortress fell to Ottoman forces shortly afterward.
Historical sources say the sultan’s death was concealed from the army to prevent a breakdown in morale and discipline and to ensure the peaceful accession of his son, Selim II.
According to historical accounts, Suleyman’s internal organs were removed to preserve his body, which was treated with amber and musk before being temporarily buried beneath the throne inside his tent.
Some historical sources and widely accepted accounts maintain that his internal organs were buried at the encampment.
His body was reportedly exhumed about 42 days later and placed in a carriage for the return journey, during which officials continued to act as if the sultan were alive. His death was formally announced after Selim II arrived in Belgrade.
 
Ottoman settlement developed around tomb
On Selim II’s orders, a tomb was built at the site where Suleyman was believed to have died and where his internal organs were thought to have been buried.
As the tomb developed into an important pilgrimage site, a mosque, dervish lodge, guesthouse and guard barracks were constructed nearby.
The complex was protected by a wooden palisade and other defensive structures, while a civilian settlement gradually emerged around it.
Known as Turbek, the settlement was destroyed as Ottoman rule in the region ended. Its exact location was eventually forgotten after the buildings disappeared and the land was converted into vineyards and gardens.
Scientific research locates long-lost tomb
Modern efforts to locate Suleyman’s tomb began after the Turkish Cooperation and Coordination Agency and the Municipality of Szigetvar signed an agreement in 2012.
An interdisciplinary team led by Professor Norbert Pap of the University of Pecs studied historical documents, maps and land records, as well as a plan of the tomb complex drawn in 1664.
The researchers concluded that the original tomb complex stood on Vineyard Hill in the Turbek-Zsibot area, about 4.2 kilometers northeast of Szigetvar Castle.
Excavations launched in 2015 uncovered a square building that researchers identified as the tomb constructed in Suleyman’s honor.
Subsequent work revealed traces of a mosque, dervish lodge, guesthouse, guard barracks, wooden palisade and civilian buildings.
 
Discoveries offer glimpse of daily life
During the 2024-2025 research period, Turkish and Hungarian researchers led by the University of Pecs used modern surveying equipment to conduct surface studies and geophysical surveys across the wider area surrounding the tomb complex.
Everyday objects, ceramics, coins, jewelry and examples of Ottoman metalwork were discovered around buildings, some of which were constructed of brick and covered with roof tiles.
Archaeologists also uncovered a well and large storage pits containing traces of grain, terracotta pieces from heating systems, footed bowls, fragments of porcelain cups and pieces of painted glass vessels.
Other finds included a rare 16th-century gold coin, a silver coin from the Crimean Khanate, pieces of Ottoman tableware, rings, decorated buckles and horse-harness ornaments.
Researchers said the findings point to the existence of an extensive Ottoman settlement beyond the central tomb complex and suggest that some of its residents and visitors were affluent by the standards of the period.

U.S. contacts with Ukraine and the Russian Federation have thawed the negotiation process, but there has been no breakthrough so far, says a political scientist
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
17:51:46 EEST
23:51:46 KST

U.S. contacts with Ukraine and the Russian Federation have thawed the negotiation process, but there has been no breakthrough so far, says a political scientist
Kyiv • UNN
According to the expert, it was important for Washington to receive positive signals from both sides, and in his assessment, this became the main result of the visits.
American negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Russia and Ukraine on September 5 and 6. A journalist from UNN spoke with Oleksii Buriachenko, president of the International Institute for Security Studies, about what to expect after the negotiation process and whether it produced any real results.
Details
Oleksii Buriachenko noted that the very emergence of a new contact between the parties is already a certain result. However, one should not expect these meetings to bring a swift end to the war for now, because, according to him, the main participants in the process have different interests.
I would not call what happened full-fledged negotiations. It was more an attempt to "revive" the negotiation process, which had been blocked by the Russian Federation, because for six months no meetings had taken place in any format. Thawing the negotiation process is better than a complete absence of such dialogue. This is probably a certain positive development that should be noted following the communications between the two special representatives of the President of the United States of America—Witkoff and Kushner
The expert also believes that the resumption of negotiations was particularly important for the Donald Trump administration. The US president promised to end the Russian-Ukrainian war during the election campaign, and now, in the political analyst's view, this issue also has domestic political significance for the White House.
Trump had already promised to end the Russian-Ukrainian war during the election campaign. This is the only foreign policy issue that was incorporated into his inaugural address, meaning it was, to a certain extent, legally recorded. Now, ahead of the midterm elections, the Democrats are actively attacking Trump and the Republican Party specifically over this issue. Therefore, this story, which is disadvantageous for Trump, had to be somehow rebooted
That is why, according to the political analyst, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were primarily carrying out a tactical task—namely, establishing contacts with both Kyiv and Moscow. Oleksii Buriachenko notes that it was important for Washington to receive positive signals from both sides, and in his assessment, this became the main result of the visits.
The goal of Witkoff and Kushner was simply to hold positive negotiations with both Zelenskyy and Putin. An additional bonus would have been to say that the parties respected the peacemaking position of the President of the United States and had agreed to a three-day ceasefire while these negotiations were taking place. At this stage, they achieved the so-called "minimum plan"—at least they attempted to stop Trump's approval ratings from falling because of the absence of any result regarding the Russian-Ukrainian war
At the same time, the political analyst sees a long-term goal of the US administration as well. It involves an attempt to achieve a result that could be presented as fulfilling Trump's promise, although under the current conditions, according to the expert's assessment, this remains a difficult task.
There is a maximum plan—to achieve, by the midterm elections, at least a first approximation of what Trump promised, and then a second approximation approximately six months later, as Kushner said. That is, ultimately, to end the Russian-Ukrainian war. But it seems to me that they may also remain with the minimum plan and continue consultations if they realize that, for a whole range of reasons, it will not be possible to move toward quick results. This is the degree of flexibility that suits the American side as of today
The expert also believes that the current situation does not indicate Russia's readiness to quickly agree to peace. He points to the lack of sufficient pressure from the United States and Europe. Meanwhile, Ukraine's long-range strikes remain one of the few factors that genuinely influence Russia.
We had a good conversation — Zelenskyy on Witkoff and Kushner's visit06.09.26, 22:40 • 12506 views
With a high degree of probability, Ukraine will enter the winter in a state of war. At least judging by the public rhetoric we have heard, the United States does not currently plan to put sufficient pressure on Putin and the Russian Federation. Without additional pressure—both European and American—it is certainly not worth hoping that Putin will simply agree to conditions unfavorable to him
Separately, the political scientist explains the presence of European representatives in Kyiv during the American visit. According to him, European states are also interested in being involved in the negotiation process, at least at the level of consultations, because they are particularly concerned that potential agreements should not create new security risks for the EU itself.
It is extremely important for Europeans now to be aware of the context of these negotiations, to be integrated both into the process itself and, most importantly, into the agreements that could hypothetically be reached through the mediation of the United States. It is important for Europeans that Ukraine does not accidentally agree to the terms brought by the Americans, because if Europe's interests are not integrated into such an agreement, Russia could then turn its attention to threats against Europe itself
In the expert's opinion, Ukraine, the United States, Russia, and the European states are currently pursuing different goals. For example, according to him, fulfilling Trump's political promises is important for Washington, ending the war on its own terms is important for Moscow, while Europe seeks to reduce the future threat from Russia. Ukraine, by contrast, is primarily interested in ending the war and obtaining security.
Each of the actors in this negotiation process has come to implement its specific priorities and goals. The achievement of peace is only the superficial goal. The United States needs to strengthen Trump's position and, accordingly, that of the Republican Party ahead of the elections. Europeans need Russia not to attack them after an agreement is reached. Russia needs the war to end on its terms, while in essence the only country that simply needs peace is Ukraine
Oleksii Buriachenko also does not expect Western pressure on Russia to intensify quickly. According to him, the American bill on new sanctions may not be adopted before the midterm elections, and it will also be difficult for Europe to quickly approve a new package of restrictions. In such a situation, Ukraine itself remains the main factor of pressure.
This leads to the conclusion that there is insufficient pressure on Russia from both the United States and Europe. The only pressure being exerted on Russia is by Ukraine itself, with the help of long-range strikes. But whether this is enough to make Putin take a constructive approach in the negotiations is difficult to say
At the same time, the expert calls the current intensification of diplomatic contacts useful for Ukraine, because Kyiv has indeed received an opportunity to restore dialogue, show its partners Russia's position, and once again emphasize the need for support ahead of the winter period.
Ukraine has received an opportunity for dialogue, an opportunity for consolidation, and an opportunity to demonstrate the full inadequacy of the Russian Federation and its unpreparedness for realistic peace. Consequently, it has an opportunity for deeper communication with American and European partners so that they truly understand: they should not hope for something to happen before winter; Ukraine needs to be strengthened now. If Ukraine stands, this is the best guarantee for Europe
The political scientist also separately emphasizes that Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are not the main architects of the negotiation process. According to him, their task is primarily to carry out the instructions of the U.S. president and maintain contacts with Kyiv and Moscow, while the formation of the further strategy, in his assessment, depends more on the leadership of the Trump administration itself.
Witkoff and Kushner are not the architects of the negotiating process. They are representatives of Donald Trump who are carrying out his instructions. They came, delivered messages, listened, made certain statements, and engaged in communication. The architect of the negotiating process is Marco Rubio, and it is this person, in coordination with Trump, who will determine the further negotiating strategies
Thus, according to the political analyst's assessment, the current contacts did not provide the parties with a ready-made agreement to end the war. At the same time, each participant obtained what they had joined the process for. For Ukraine, the main result was the restoration of diplomatic contact and the opportunity to continue working with partners.
Witkoff and Kushner departed Kyiv by the "Peace Express" train07.09.26, 01:05 • 22940 views
