The United Arab Emirates is building alternative routes for its energy exports and trade to ensure they are not "held hostage" by the ongoing US-Iran war, UAE presidential adviser Anwar Gargash said, adding that the partnership with the US is essential, but the current conflict underscored the importance of national security capabilities.
The conflict has had a significant impact on Gulf Arab states, including the UAE, after Tehran fired missiles at the country and attacked its oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz in retaliation for US-Israeli attacks.
"Our energy exports will not be held hostage, nor will our trade and economic activity," Gargash told the Hili Forum in Abu Dhabi on Monday.
The UAE has been expanding port capacity along its eastern coast, as well as developing pipelines, railways and trade routes for alternative corridors, he said.
While acknowledging that relations with Iran could eventually recover, Gargash warned that rebuilding trust after the attacks could take decades.
‘Unified strategy’ 
He also criticised Gulf Arab states for failing to mount a coordinated response to Iran, saying they had been unable to translate shared concerns into a unified strategy.
Earlier, Qatar's foreign ministry spokesperson echoed similar concerns at the policymakers' forum, saying Gulf Arab countries should not rely solely on their strategic partnership with the US for security.
Gargash argued that while the partnership with the US is essential, the current conflict has exposed the importance of national capabilities.
"Our security is our priority. When we depend entirely on others, we cannot always assume it will be their priority," he said.
Hormuz remains a central obstacle in negotiations between Washington and Tehran, mediated by Qatar and Pakistan, with Iran claiming the strait belongs to Iran and Oman, a position Gulf states broadly reject.
"Freedom of navigation is not a concession to be granted, nor a principle to be renegotiated under pressure," Gargash said, adding that any long-term resolution must include credible guarantees against further Iranian attacks on Gulf Arab states.
The conflict, sparked by US and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28, remains deadlocked. A preliminary ceasefire reached in June has unravelled, and little progress has been made in efforts to revive the peace process.

"It was the German authorities who, once again, provoked a new round of escalation in bilateral relations," the Foreign Ministry said, adding Berlin "bears full and complete responsibility" for the consequences.
Russia also earlier ordered the closure of all Goethe-Institut branches on Russian territory, with Goethe-Institut staff having to leave the country by September 13.
Goethe-Institut is a center that promotes German language and culture. Goethe-Institut is largely financed by the German government.
Germany, Russia trade barbs over Leipzig drone attack
The moves are a direct response to Germany's decision to close the Russian consulate in Bonn and Russia's cultural center in Berlin, a decision Russia labeled "unfriendly."
Germany recently announced those measures after it said Russia was responsible for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig Airport.
The EU, too, said the incident had all the signs of "state sponsored terrorism."
The Leipzig airport is an important international freight hub, also used for providing support to Ukraine.
Russia Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov rejected Germany's allegations, calling them "the beginning of a real war."

Merz warns of 'consequences' after state election defeat in Saxony-Anhalt

Speaking in Berlin on Monday, the German chancellor said he saw a society "longing for disruption" and "fundamental change."
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has expressed his shock after the far-right AfD party stormed to victory in the Saxony-Anhalt state election over the weekend.
Merz appeared before the press in Berlin on Monday, together with the CDU's lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, Sven Schulze, to address the outcome of the vote.
"Yesterday's result has changed not only Saxony-Anhalt, but Germany as a whole," Merz said following Sunday's state election results. "We are all profoundly shocked. We did not expect it to turn out like this."
The anti-immigration AfD party won the election by a landslide, taking 43.8% of the vote. The CDU came in a distant second with 17.2%.
Compared with the 2021 state election, the AfD more than doubled its vote share, while the CDU saw its share halved.
Almost 60% of voters had chosen parties that call democracy into question, the chancellor said, adding that it was "the most severe electoral defeat" the CDU has suffered in years.
"There will have to be consequences," he added.
'Longing for disruption'
For months, Merz has been sliding from one polling low to the next.
Most recently, 78% of respondents felt he was doing a worse job as chancellor than they had expected.
That is according to the "trendbarometer" survey by RTL and n-tv. The poll also showed that 59% of CDU/CSU voters were disappointed with Merz's performance as chancellor. The survey was carried out by the polling institute Forsa.
Despite his poor approval ratings and the electoral defeat in Saxony-Anhalt, Merz is sticking to his course "without wavering."
"Our country needs fundamental reforms," he said.
Merz sees one of the reasons for the public's dissatisfaction as the government's failure to communicate policies in a sufficiently emotive and compelling way.
In future, the CDU, together with the SPD, wants to create a better "narrative" to achieve this.
Merz said he also wanted to "personally do justice" to the election result in the coming weeks and that he saw a society "longing for disruption" and "fundamental change."
The need for compromise must, he argued, be emphasised more strongly.
Little room for AfD on migration policy
The chancellor also sought to reassure the public following the election defeat.
In general, the AfD would in many areas have to follow the line set by the federal government. That also applies to policy on foreign nationals and migration. There is a principle of "federal loyalty".
Schulze, the CDU's lead candidate, minister-president of Saxony-Anhalt and chair of the CDU in the state, also wants to draw lessons from the election result, although he did not provide specifics.
It comes as calls for Schulze to step down have grown louder. The Young Union (JU) in Saxony-Anhalt has demanded that the entire CDU leadership in the state resign, as the magazine "Stern" reported, quoting a resolution adopted by the JU Saxony-Anhalt.
It reportedly stated: "The CDU in Saxony-Anhalt needs a comprehensive fresh start. We therefore call for the resignation and the prompt re-election of the entire state leadership - from the state chair to the full executive board."
Schulze: No defections from the CDU to the AfD
Schulze again stressed that the mandate to form a government now lies with the AfD.
"Overall, this is a day that has shaken us deeply, not only in Saxony-Anhalt," he said.
In his own constituency, he added, his result was twice as good as the CDU's statewide performance.
As the AfD announced in a press release on Monday, it is now seeking to form a government despite lacking an absolute majority.
Previously, the AfD's lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund had ruled that out. To achieve this, the AfD wants to win over parliamentary groups or individual MPs. Only then would Siegmund seek to be elected minister-president.
Asked about this, Schulze said there would be no defections from the CDU, adding that he was sure that members of the BSW would try to help Siegmund become minister-president.

Von der Leyen tries to counter Trump with €200 million investment in Greenland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:26:46 UTC
23:26:46 KST

Ursula von der Leyen backed Greenland's territorial integrity as she unveiled a €200 million investment package to counter pressure from Donald Trump, who has repeatedly threatened to annex the mineral-rich island.
The European Union will invest an additional €200 million in Greenland over the next two years to deepen economic ties and extract raw materials, Ursula von der Leyen announced on Monday during an official visit to the vast Arctic island.
"We know that the Arctic has become one of the places where the tectonic plates of geopolitics collide, so we have a direct stake in what happens here," the president of the European Commission said in Nuuk.
The financial package aims to expand the bloc's presence in the semi-autonomous territory, which has long been in US President Donald Trump's sights.
Trump has rattled the transatlantic alliance with his push to seize Greenland from the Kingdom of Denmark. Tensions peaked in January, when he threatened to impose steep tariffs to pressure Denmark into relinquishing the territory. He later backed down amid backlash.
But in July, Trump suddenly revived his ambition to annex the island, indicating the subject was still top of his mind. On Monday, he posted a map of the world that showed Greenland under American control.
Von der Leyen used her trip to Nuuk to underline European support amid what she called "enormous pressure", though she did not mention Trump by name.
"The European Union stands in full solidarity with the Kingdom of Denmark and the people of Greenland. We will continue to do so. And we want to be very clear and repeat again here that Greenland's future is for the people of Greenland and Denmark to decide. No one else," she said in remarks to the press.
"Territorial integrity, sovereignty, the inviolability of borders. These are fundamental principles of international law."
Standing by her side, Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen and Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen thanked von der Leyen for her words.
"Greenland needs the European Union, and the European Union needs Greenland," Nielsen said. "I firmly believe this to be true. We need each other."
"Your voice has been very clear the last couple of years. We needed that, and we need it now, so thank you for that," Frederiksen told von der Leyen.
Frederiksen said Denmark was open to working "closer" with both the US and Europe on security and defence matters related to the Arctic, a region that climate change is making increasingly attractive to world powers.
The €200 million investment package will spread across three key areas: digital connectivity, including subsea cables and satellite infrastructure; clean energy, with a particular focus on hydropower; and sustainable mining of critical raw materials.
Greenland holds 25 of the 34 minerals that Brussels considers crucial for the homegrown development of renewable energy systems and cutting-edge technology. The sector is monopolised by China, leaving the EU at the mercy of Beijing's export controls.
Mining on the island, however, remains well below its potential due to harsh glacial conditions that discourage investors from undertaking expensive projects.
Minerals were among the reasons Trump cited to justify his threat to take over Greenland, though he told the New York Times it was ultimately a question of ownership. He has also complained that allies have failed to invest enough in the region.
Europeans have since tried to counter Trump's narrative by doubling down on their commitments to Greenland. Over the next two weeks, soldiers from 10 countries will take part in NATO's Arctic Shield exercise.
Meanwhile, the Commission is working to update its Arctic strategy and has earmarked €530 million specifically for Greenland in its proposal for the next EU budget.

US Navy certifies Rolls-Royce engines for autonomous ships
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
15:26:29 BST
23:26:29 KST

The US Navy has certified Rolls-Royce mtu Series 4000 and Series 2000 marine engines for use aboard autonomous naval vessels following reliability testing designed to demonstrate that they can operate for extended periods without human maintenance, Rolls-Royce has announced.
The certification allows Series 4000 engines to be used in autonomous applications providing up to 4,300kW of propulsion power and 3,000kWe of electrical generation. The engine is available in V8, V12, V16 and V20 configurations.
Rolls-Royce said the Series 4000 passed two 720-hour durability tests before receiving approval. The Series 2000 was certified following component testing and thousands of hours of operational experience, with the platform capable of providing up to 1,939kW for propulsion in V10, V12 and V16 configurations.
The testing is intended to demonstrate that propulsion systems can support an unmanned vessel during a 30-day deployment without preventive or corrective maintenance to its main propulsion, fuel or oil systems.
Scott Hanson, Vice President of Governmental Sales at Rolls-Royce Power Systems in North America, said: “The certification of our engines for unmanned operations further demonstrates the reliability and advanced technology of our mtu Series 4000 and 2000 marine propulsion systems. For decades, mtu engines have been trusted to provide reliable, mission-ready power for our crews at sea.”
He added: “As autonomous missions become increasingly important to naval strategy, we are proving that we can deliver the power systems, long-endurance capability and technology required for the new operational demands of unmanned vessels.”
The certification comes as the US Navy expands its use of unmanned surface vessels as part of efforts to increase fleet capacity and operate platforms for longer periods without putting sailors aboard them.
One of the Navy’s best-known autonomous vessels, Sea Hunter, is already powered by two mtu 12V 2000 engines. Rolls-Royce said the vessel has accumulated tens of thousands of operational hours since its christening in 2016.
Sea Hunter and the related Seahawk were operationally deployed earlier this year as part of the US Navy’s first division of unmanned surface vessels, according to the company.
Certification of propulsion systems is one element of the wider process required before autonomous vessels can be routinely deployed. Rolls-Royce said US Navy requirements also place emphasis on control systems, cybersecurity and safety-critical functions as unmanned systems become more prominent across maritime operations.

2026-09-07

Plans for a large reorganisation of local government have been put on hold after the government received new legal advice that suggested they might not comply with the law.
The Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) said the review was to ensure the process was robust and aligned with the new government’s aim to “rewire the state”, and followed “updated and privileged legal advice”.
The reorganisation plans, announced in December 2024, proposed the abolition of the current two-tier system of districts and counties in favour of a smaller number of unitary authorities – or “mega-councils” – covering large areas.
At least eight councils had launched legal challenges or were considering doing so owing to opposition to the government’s choice of boundaries for new councils.
Reform UK-led Kent county council is to consider a judicial review at a meeting on Tuesday after it did not receive a response from the government to a letter setting out concerns.
Plans for reorganisation in Essex, Hampshire, Norfolk and Suffolk have been withdrawn in the light of new legal advice.
Councils in Essex launched legal action in June after it emerged that its own preferred option to create three unitary councils in the county was backed by senior government officials but rejected by the then communities secretary, Steve Reed.
There has been little appetite for the proposals within local government, with many councils regarding the changes as expensive and time-consuming, and offering little in the way of cost savings that would ease local authorities’ dire financial crisis.
Decisions on 14 further areas will be reviewed and paused alongside the cases of Cambridgeshire-Peterborough and West Sussex, which are yet to have a decision confirmed.
The government will also confirm that local elections in May 2027 will go ahead on existing council boundaries, saying it remains committed to effective and sustainable local government and simplifying these structures.
The communities secretary, Angela Rayner, told parliament on Monday: “As we are now more determined than ever to devolve power closer to the people we represent, it’s only right that as a new secretary of state I make sure that everything we do is working towards that plan to change Britain, without delay.
“The prime minister told the house last week he was ‘prepared to look at local government reorganisation’ and he asked me as his communities secretary to ‘do that’.
“In that context, in light of legal advice, I want to satisfy myself firstly that the right process is in place, that it is robust, and of course complies with the law.
“And, secondly, I want to fully test whether our proposals for local government reorganisation meet the priorities of a new administration and a new prime minister, and any additional considerations.
“I do not take this lightly. I recognise the huge amount of work that has already gone into progressing reorganisation in each of these areas and I am very grateful for it.”
MHCLG said reorganisation in Surrey would not be affected by the review and the two new unitary authorities, East and West Surrey, would go live in April 2027.
Cllr Sean Matthews, chair-elect of the County Councils Network, said: “Many of our members will be relieved that the decisions they viewed as damaging to local services and financially unsustainable have been withdrawn or are being reviewed. For our councils that do want to proceed with reorganisation in their area, we will support them in their next steps and we will be seeking further clarity from government in the coming days.
“With the government clearly listening to our concerns, we now stand ready to work with ministers. Where reorganisation is desired, this review must ensure a robust, legally compliant process in line with the original criteria. This should include establishing realistic implementation timescales and ensuring that any further decisions only create sustainable new unitary councils capable of improving local services.”
Jonathan Carr-West, chief executive of the Local Government Information Unit (LGIU), said: “What began as the most ambitious change to local government in a generation now looks in danger of becoming a colossal white elephant – a huge drain on time, resources and goodwill. Those councils undergoing local government reorganisation have been trying to implement a massively complex project, under intense pressure and to very challenging timescales. Our overriding concern is that local government leaders, staff and councillors have strained every sinew to meet the deadlines set by MHCLG. Today’s announcement – whatever the reasons behind it – rides roughshod over 1,000s of hours of work.
“If the prime minister is serious about his ambitions to rewire the state, then lessons must be learned from this debacle and learned fast.”

Germany Makes Naval History With First Warship-Launched Ballistic Missile in Signal to Russia
Germany has successfully launched an Israeli-made LORA ballistic missile from a German Navy warship during a live-fire test in the North Atlantic, demonstrating a new long-range strike capability for its fleet.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the UK Defence Journal on September 6, two German frigates deployed to waters between Ireland and Iceland for the trial, which had not been publicly disclosed before its completion. A containerized LORA launcher was installed on the deck of one of the vessels.
The outlet described the previously undisclosed test as a direct signal to Moscow, pointing to European efforts to develop longer-range strike capabilities. NATO also presented the launch as part of a broader shift toward greater European responsibility for deterrence.
NATO Allied Joint Force Command Brunssum subsequently confirmed the test, saying the launch had been conducted secretly before being publicly revealed.
“Kept secret. Now revealed. The German Navy just tested the Israeli LORA ballistic missile from a German frigate in the North Atlantic—quietly, deliberately and with a range of 500+ km,” the command said.
Vice Admiral Jan Christian Kaack, Inspector of the German Navy, described the launch as a milestone for Germany’s naval forces. “With the successful launch of a ballistic missile last night in the North Atlantic, we made naval history. I am extremely satisfied with this achievement,” Kaack said.
He added that the weapon “can be successfully deployed from our units, and the potential range exceeds anything we have known before.”
The missile used in the trial was the LORA, or Long-Range Artillery Weapon System, developed by Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI). The company lists the missile with a range of approximately 400 kilometers and an accuracy of within 10 meters, while NATO described the weapon tested by Germany as having a range exceeding 500 kilometers.
According to IAI, the LORA was fired from an operational German vessel equipped with a command trailer and launcher. The missile completed its planned flight path and successfully struck its designated target, with the company saying the system met the objectives established for the trial.
The launch was conducted under the German Navy’s OPEX initiative, which allows new weapons, technologies, and operational concepts to be tested rapidly under conditions designed to approximate operational deployment. The program forms part of Germany’s broader Marine 2035 and Beyond modernization effort.

A Russian military intelligence special forces soldier voluntarily surrendered to Ukraine after an assault in which he says roughly 70% of his company was killed, an experience that convinced him his supposedly elite unit had simply been sent to die.
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) released the serviceman’s account through the state-run I Want to Live project, which facilitates voluntary surrenders by Russian troops on September 7.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to HUR, the prisoner served in a special operations unit subordinate to the Main Directorate of the Russian General Staff, commonly known by its former acronym GRU. Ukrainian intelligence described his surrender as unusual, saying personnel connected to Russian intelligence services are rarely taken prisoner voluntarily.
The serviceman said he joined the unit after signing a military contract and received training in weapons, tactics, engineering, explosives, topography, communications, and other disciplines.
But he said the reputation surrounding Russian special forces no longer matches their reality.
“The training there is better than in ordinary units, but expectations of these special forces are greatly exaggerated. Now they take many people in and filter them out afterward,” he said.
The prisoner also said he initially believed Russian state propaganda and regarded the war as a legitimate cause.
“I thought I was taking part in something big. Now I understand that the propaganda simply worked very well. If the state does something, you get used to thinking that it must be right,” he said.
The turning point, according to his account, came during an assault on a Ukrainian village.
His company was ordered forward and ultimately completed its assigned objective, he said, but most of the unit was killed in the process.
“We completed the task, but at the cost of terrible losses. About 70% of the company died. When I saw the settlement for which so many people had been sacrificed, I realized it made absolutely no sense. It looked more like some kind of hidden genocide of Russia’s male population,” the prisoner said.
What he found inside the village further changed his perception of the war, he said.
“We entered houses, and family photographs were still hanging there. This was someone’s home, where people had created a comfortable life. And now the Russian army leaves only ruins behind. I didn’t see anything there that needed to be ‘liberated,’” he stated.
After the operation, the serviceman began searching for a way to avoid returning to combat.
He described his options as increasingly narrow: being killed, being transferred into another assault formation, or surrendering.
The solution eventually appeared on TikTok. While watching videos from Ukrainian soldiers and interviews with Russian prisoners, he came across information about the I Want to Live project.
“I saw a link to the I Want to Live chatbot and wrote to them. Then the coordinator and I discussed the extraction plan in detail. I explained that I no longer wanted to participate in the occupation and that I understood I was taking away someone else’s home,” he said.
He ultimately surrendered voluntarily through the program. The prisoner said the project offers an alternative for Russian soldiers who no longer want to participate in the invasion.
“It is very good that such an opportunity exists. For people who have regained sound judgment, it is a chance to stop taking part in this lawlessness, lay down their weapons, and stay alive,” he said.
Earlier, reports emerged that twenty Russian soldiers are currently held in Ukrainian captivity after surrendering to the Ukrainian Defense Forces for a second time following prisoner exchanges.
Russian commanders sent these servicemen back to active duty after they returned home in swaps, leading them to surrender again when sent back to the front line.

Macron hosts summit to urge support for cinema amid impact of AI, streaming
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:23:25 UTC
23:23:25 KST

Macron hosts summit to urge support for cinema amid impact of AI, streaming
French President Emmanuel Macron on Monday called for stronger international efforts to protect cinema from the disruptive impact of artificial intelligence and streaming platforms while hosting more than 200 industry figures at the Lumière Summit in southern France.
French President Emmanuel Macron on Monday called for cinema to be protected in the age of artificial intelligence and streaming platforms, as he hosted a summit with global entertainment chiefs including major US studio bosses.
Hollywood favourite George Clooney brought some of his star power to the event, which brought together more than 200 guests from dozens of countries, including top executives from US studios such as Sony Pictures and Disney.
Called the Lumière Summit, in a nod to Auguste and Louis Lumière, the French brothers considered the inventors of the motion picture, the event took place in the medieval village of Saint-Paul-de-Vence near Nice and was co-chaired by South Korean President Lee Jae Myung.
South Korea is home to some of the world's most celebrated filmmakers, including Park Chan-wook, who chaired the Cannes film festival jury this year, and Bong Joon-ho, the Oscar-winning director of "Parasite".
Read more'Parasite' director says new film highlights strength of ordinary people
The organisers hope the event at the Maeght Foundation for contemporary art will help spur action to support the film industry, which has been weakened by falling cinema attendance and competition from streaming platforms.
Both Macron and Lee warned about the advance of AI.
"We would be making a tremendous mistake if this technology became a tool that replaces, or claims to replace, creators," Macron said.
Lee said that artificial intelligence should develop in "a more responsible and human-centred way".
"The film and audiovisual industry must be rooted in human creativity and must resonate with human emotions," he said.
'Elephant in the room'
The leaders of France and South Korea also said their countries would invest €1 billion ($1.15 billion) to support independent filmmaking.
"May this partnership transcend our bilateral relationship and reach across the globe," Lee said.
An informed source said half the money would come from France's state investment bank Bpifrance, and the rest from South Korea.
Macron also announced the creation of an organisation, with a budget of 30 million euros, aimed at supporting independent cinema.
Film stars including Pedro Almodovar and Juliette Binoche joined remotely for the launch.
Executives from streaming giant Netflix and social media platform TikTok attended the event.
But key players such as YouTube and Meta, the parent company of Instagram, declined invitations.
"The elephant in the room is really YouTube," TF1 chief executive Rodolphe Belmer said.
Leading generative AI companies were also absent.
They have been accused by rights holders of using film and audiovisual works to train their models without permission.
Gaetan Bruel, head of France's National Cinema Centre (CNC), which helped organise the gathering, said it was time for "concrete measures", even if it was impossible "to solve every problem in a single day".
He called for "a new multilateralism" in the industry, saying "that means tackling these issues using the same approach that was applied to climate change".
The director of the Cannes Film Festival, Thierry Fremaux, praised the event.
"The value of this summit lies in creating that meeting place, where the format itself helps drive the discussion," he said.
Fremaux sounded upbeat, saying cinema has been experiencing one of the strongest years since Covid.
"During the pandemic, people got used to watching films at home and wondered whether cinemas were still necessary," he said. "But audiences have come back, and younger viewers are returning to the cinema."
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Swiss labour market remains strong
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:23:09 UTC
23:23:09 KST

Swiss labour market remains strong
The Swiss labour market continues to show signs of strength against a backdrop of geopolitical and economic uncertainties.
This was stated by Jérôme Cosandey, head of the labour division at the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO), while commenting via teleconference on the unemployment figures (3% in August).
The only significant increase was among young people aged between 15 and 24, with the unemployment rate rising to 3.4% in the eighth month of the year. This was an increase of 0.6 percentage points compared with July, with 2,400 more people out of work (bringing the total to 14,700).
More
Why unemployment in Switzerland is increasing more than elsewhere in Europe
According to Cosandey, however, this is a perfectly normal seasonal phenomenon as every summer, thousands of young people who have finished school, vocational training or university enter the labour market and have not yet found a job.
Unemployment in this age group usually peaks in August. The number of unemployed under-20s then falls rapidly as autumn approaches, while for 20–25-year-olds the situation improves significantly at the start of the following year. “It should happen this time too,” he said.
The figure also confirms a structural difference: young people are more at risk of being unemployed, but find new jobs much more quickly than older age groups.
On average, it takes just over three months for those under 25 to come off the unemployment register, while for the over-55s it takes more than nine months.
There are also positive signs from short-time working: this scheme, which allows companies to temporarily reduce working hours without making redundancies, is being used less and less, confirming the resilience of Switzerland’s manufacturing sector, concludes Cosandey.

Will Trump succeed in restarting Russia-Ukraine peace talks?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:22:58 UTC
23:22:58 KST

Will Trump succeed in restarting Russia-Ukraine peace talks?
The Witkoff-Kushner visit to Moscow and Kyiv did not produce a breakthrough, but can help begin a new process.
The visit by White House envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to Moscow and Kyiv has left more questions than answers. Details of what was discussed in both meetings are scant, but all participants seem to describe them as “positive”.
It is indeed a positive development that US President Donald Trump is trying to jump start negotiations at this point. The biggest problem he faces is that Russia’s position has only hardened.
Russia wants Ukraine to be genuinely neutral, with no Western military presence, open or clandestine. It wants to keep previously occupied territories and it insists that Ukraine withdraw from the small part of Donbas that remains in its hands.
Moscow demands a cap on the size of the Ukrainian army and on the types of weapons it may possess. It also wants far-right units and paramilitary groups disbanded and outlawed, the legislation limiting the use of the Russian language cancelled and elections to be held in which Russia-friendly parties could compete freely with the pro-Western ones.
For Ukraine and its European backers, this would be a hard pill to swallow, all the more so after spending the summer trying to convince the European public and Trump that the “tide is turning” in the war.
As evidence, Ukrainian and Western officials have repeatedly pointed to the Russian offensive slowing down and Ukraine intensifying strikes deep within Russian territory, targeting oil facilities and causing fuel shortages across the country.
The campaign against Russian energy infrastructure was meant to coerce Russian President Vladimir Putin into accepting peace on conditions more favourable to Ukraine.
But the opposite has happened. Russia’s negotiating position is now even less open to compromise. The land swap, once eyed as a way to compensate Ukraine for its withdrawal from the Donbas region, is now out of the question.
Meanwhile, the Kremlin has launched its own devastating campaign of strikes aimed at collapsing Ukraine’s economy. In addition to shutting down exports of Ukraine’s main commodities, grain and ore, through Odesa ports, Russia is also methodically destroying logistical hubs and warehouses owned by large retailers as well as large-scale industry, from metallurgical plants to beverage factories.
This is the point when Trump’s peacemaking duo resurfaced on the Russo-Ukrainian front after a protracted absence. The very fact that Kushner and Witkoff embarked on this trip and were received by Putin personally signals a change of tack in Washington.
A week before their arrival, CIA director John Ratcliffe mysteriously appeared in Moscow. Ratcliffe was effectively snubbed by Putin, who refused an audience when the CIA chief’s convoy reached the Kremlin. Instead, Ratcliffe had meetings with the heads of Russian security agencies, FSB and SVR, before heading home.
Nothing emerged from this meeting, apart from media speculation based on dubious sourcing. Hawkish media outlets claimed that Ratcliffe arrived with a stern warning against Russia attacking East European NATO members.
Others claimed Ratcliffe was trying to convey the “tide is turning” narrative to Putin and push for new negotiations based on that. The Atlantic magazine claimed last month that it was the CIA director who planted the idea that Russia was beginning to lose into Trump’s head during golf games.
Russian emigre outlet Agentstvo confirmed, quoting a Kremlin source, that Putin cancelled the meeting after hearing what Ratcliffe had been telling his subordinates and concluding that he was delusional.
Whether that is true or not, it is quite telling that Ratcliffe, who is a more senior US official than Kushner and Witkoff, was turned away, while they received a warm welcome in Moscow and spent a considerable time with Putin. Clearly, Trump’s envoys did not make the long trip to repeat what the Russian president sees as Western propaganda.
Whether Kushner and Witkoff’s mission has added anything substantial to the peace process is another question. They expressed cautious optimism regarding their progress. They said that no immediate breakthrough was foreseen but were eyeing direct trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US.
What is remarkable about the Witkoff-Kushner mission is the sheer number of commentators who were all too keen to claim that it was doomed from the outset. This is a reflection of the power pro-war circles continue to wield, despite growing war fatigue in Western societies.
The pro-war party simply wants any talks with Russia to be doomed, like they wanted the Istanbul talks to be doomed in the spring of 2022 and Minsk agreements to be ditched before that.
In trying to jump-start the peace talks, Trump will also have to face off with this party, which includes, European governments, NATO leadership and parts of the political establishment in his own country.
He would be keen to achieve some progress in peace talks prior to midterm elections and pressure Putin into limiting his military cooperation with Iran, but that’s impossible to achieve while the US plays a crucial role in helping Ukraine target infrastructure in Russia’s own territory.
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s resilience is increasingly under question amid continuing brutal bombardment by the Russian army. As winter approaches, the targeting of energy and water infrastructure could severely worsen living conditions in the country.
Kyiv is already shaken by a political crisis, aggravated by corruption scandals involving top officials close to Zelenskyy, as well as a turf war between security agencies. There is also a $26bn gap in the Ukrainian defence budget, which needs to be covered by Western aid that’s not necessarily forthcoming.
There is no limit to warmongers pressuring Ukraine into fighting a suicidal war with a far stronger rival, but there is a limit to how long Ukrainians would be willing to die for an agenda that’s increasingly at odds with their national and personal interests.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

EU unveils $232M investment package for Greenland as Brussels deepens strategic partnership
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:22:48 UTC
23:22:48 KST

Melike Pala
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
The European Union announced a €200 million ($232 million) investment package for Greenland on Monday, targeting digital connectivity, clean energy, critical raw materials, and projects aimed at improving local living standards as Brussels seeks to deepen its economic and strategic engagement in the Arctic.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced the package during a visit to Nuuk, where she joined Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen and Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen for the signing of a new joint declaration on EU–Greenland relations.
The package will finance investments in Greenland over the next two years, with the EU identifying digital connectivity, clean energy, and critical raw materials as its primary strategic priorities. Von der Leyen noted that these investments are intended not only to strengthen Europe’s presence in Greenland, but also to drive local job creation, economic growth, and opportunity.
As part of the initiative, the EU is providing approximately €9.1 million over five years—co-financed by Denmark—to support satellite-based internet services in East and North Greenland. The project is expected to improve the speed, reliability, and resilience of internet access in remote settlements, schools, and businesses.
Additionally, the EU and Greenland plan to advance sustainable mining projects linked to European industry. EU support will include technical analysis and investor matchmaking to help build more resilient supply chains. Von der Leyen specifically highlighted the Malmbjerg molybdenum mining project, noting it could become one of Greenland’s largest ventures and generate up to €90 million a year in added value for the country if successfully developed.
This investment push comes as Greenland's strategic importance grows amid escalating geopolitical tension in the Arctic. Von der Leyen stated that the EU aims to be "more present and more engaged" in the region, adding that Brussels is preparing a new EU Arctic strategy to be presented in the autumn.
She also reiterated the EU's support for Denmark and Greenland, emphasizing that Greenland's future should be determined solely by its people. An autonomous territory within the Kingdom of Denmark, Greenland holds immense strategic value due to its Arctic location and vast mineral and energy resources.
Former U.S. President Donald Trump repeatedly called for U.S. control of Greenland during his presidency, calling it a historical and strategic necessity. However, both Danish and Greenlandic leaders firmly rejected the proposal, maintaining that Greenland "is not for sale."

Syrian nuclear reactor could have been useful for weapons, IAEA chief says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:21:58 UTC
23:21:58 KST

Syrian nuclear reactor could have been useful for weapons, IAEA chief says
VIENNA - The nuclear reactor Syria had nearly completed in 2007 - when Israeli jets destroyed it - was of a type that could quickly produce fissile material usable in nuclear weapons, UN nuclear watchdog chief Rafael Grossi said on Sept 7.
The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has described its recent investigation into secret nuclear activities under the Assad family’s rule as a “historic breakthrough”. 
The investigation uncovered around 73 metric tons of natural uranium metal, mainly in the form of reactor fuel.
In a report to member states seen by Reuters, the IAEA confirmed its previous finding that the bombed site in Syria’s eastern province of Deir al-Zor was a nuclear reactor under construction, and that fuel for it had been made in Syria, all of which should have been declared at the time to the agency.
“This is a reactor that is very efficient in the production of fissile material that could be used directly for the fabrication of nuclear weapons,” Grossi told a press conference, adding that it was “almost completed”.
“That was a very serious proliferation concern,” he said, while cautioning that the then-authorities’ intentions “cannot be judged”.
Since the ouster of President Bashar al-Assad in late 2024, Syria’s new authorities have committed to working with the IAEA to answer questions relating to so-called nuclear safeguards - the process of accounting for and monitoring nuclear material.
“Having received the necessary access and information from Syria, ... the agency has been able to clarify and resolve the agency’s questions concerning the outstanding safeguards issues related to Syria’s past nuclear activities,” Grossi said in a speech to the IAEA’s 35-nation board.
“I welcome Syria’s transparency and cooperation with the agency which facilitates the resolution of the outstanding safeguards issues related to Syria’s past nuclear activities,” he added. REUTERS

U.S. Army Awarded Its First Contract for the Production of Laser Weapons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:20:50 UTC
23:20:50 KST

The U.S. Army has awarded AeroVironment a contract to produce high-energy laser weapons as part of the Enduring-High Energy Laser (E-HEL) program. This is the U.S. Army’s first production contract for such a weapon system.
The official U.S. Army publication announced this.
AeroVironment revealed that the contract is worth $464.8 million and calls for the procurement of LOCUST systems to counter UAVs.
“This first-of-its-kind directed-energy program will enable our forces to neutralize unmanned systems and dominate from the outset. The combination of human ingenuity and cutting-edge technology ensures that our Army will continue to stay ahead of America’s adversaries,” General Christopher LaNeve, Deputy Chief of Staff of the U.S. Army, stated.
Under the agreement, the company will deliver “dozens” of LOCUST X3 laser systems over the next few years to support long-term deployment plans.
The systems are intended to strengthen the U.S. Army’s multi-layered air defense against Group 1–3 unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and to establish directed-energy weapons as a key component of future combat operations.
The LOCUST X3 is a 30-kW system. It can be integrated onto various platforms depending on requirements. Specifically, in September 2025, AeroVironment delivered prototypes to the U.S. Army mounted on the chassis of the M1301 Infantry Squad Vehicle.
Subsequently, as part of the second phase of LOCUST’s development, on December 18 of the same year, the company delivered two more systems mounted on the wheeled chassis of the JLTV armored vehicle. The system can also be used as a standalone container.
The E-HEL program is based on the results of testing the Army Multi-Purpose High Energy Laser (AMP-HEL) prototypes, which are already in service with the U.S. Army.
It was reported that during testing, the system demonstrated safe and effective countermeasures against drones in U.S. airspace. The company emphasized that these tests directly contributed to the conclusion of an agreement between the U.S. Department of Defense and the Federal Aviation Administration regarding the safe use of the system within the country.
It is reported that in February 2026, an incident involving LOCUST occurred while the system was being tested near the Mexican border, prompting the Federal Aviation Administration to close the airspace over El Paso, Texas.
During the tests, the device locked onto and shot down a drone operated by U.S. Customs and Border Protection agents at the Mexican border.

It’s unbelievable, but Mediazona is celebrating its 12th birthday. For over a decade, we have fought to report the truth about Russia. Our editor-in-chief, Sergey Smirnov, is known for his catchphrase: “It will get worse”. Unfortunately, he has always been right. Over the years, things have taken a turn for the worse many times—both for the people we report on and for ourselves.
When Mediazona was founded 12 years ago, Russia was already jailing people for political reasons and violently dispersing protests. New repressive laws have constantly been passed ever since. Then came the invasion of Ukraine—and a massive wave of criminal cases against those who refused to support this criminal war.
As the number of political prisoners grew, reporting on the reality inside Russia became increasingly dangerous. We have weathered multiple crises—surviving them all thanks to you:
In February 2021, when Smirnov was arrested in front of his son and sent to a detention centre, our readers’ support helped us pull together and work twice as hard;

These donations are vital. They are the only way we can keep paying our journalists and editors—including those bravely working from inside Russia. They fund the our work in English and other languages, our complex data-driven investigations, and everything that makes Mediazona what it is today.
If you value our reporting and are in a position to support independent journalism, please become a subscriber today. And please share our work with your friends and colleagues.
Thank you for standing with us since 2022. Let us wish each other the continued strength to face whatever comes next.
It will get worse, but that does not mean we won’t get through it together.

Nepal held a national day of mourning with candlelight vigils on Monday for victims of devastating glacial floods, as families of missing hydropower workers feared trapped in tunnels prayed rescuers might yet find them alive.
The August 26 glacial and mountain collapse on the China-Nepal border killed at least 1,399 people, with more than 5,500 missing, including around 800 foreigners.
Flags flew at half-mast and hundreds of people gathered for the vigils in the Nepali capital Kathmandu, as the nation marked the 13th day after death in line with Hindu mourning rituals.
Hundreds of hydropower workers are among the missing, but the rescue of three of them from deep inside tunnels – two Nepalis on Friday and a Chinese man on Saturday – have buoyed hopes that more could still be alive.
Nepal Army spokesman Raja Ram Basnet said rescue efforts were continuing at "the same tempo" to make sure "that no one is still stranded".
Entire communities have been swept away, with roads destroyed and homes demolished.
But families of some of the missing workers who gathered in Kathmandu said the government must move faster.
"We have a lot of hope," said Reena Amatya Shrestha, whose brother is among the missing.
"They say they are doing rescue. If the rescue is there, where's the result? We need the result."
Australian tunnel rescue expert Arnold Dix, who is advising Nepali teams, said the operation presented an unprecedented challenge.
"We are facing something I have never faced before," said Dix, president of the International Tunnelling and Underground Space Association, in a post on social media.
"Not one rescue, but multiple potential rescues, unfolding at the same time, in different places, each with its own dangers, uncertainties, and lives that may still be saved."
Foreign experts, including from China, India and South Korea, are aiding Nepali teams in rescue efforts.
"We are measured not only by the lives we save, but by the lives we refuse to abandon," said Dix.
Nepal President Ram Chandra Paudel visited relief camps in Nuwakot, speaking to those left homeless by the disaster.
"Today the entire nation is mourning this horrific disaster," he said in a statement.
"To everyone waiting for news of family members and friends, I want to assure you that search and rescue operations will continue."
With mortuaries overflowing, Nepal has buried hundreds of bodies in mass graves after taking DNA samples for future identification, according to police.
Despite the gloom, there have been remarkable tales of survival.
Chandika Shrestha, a 64-year-old Nepali woman, was pulled out alive from her mud-covered home in Bidur on Saturday.
Her family had already held a symbolic funeral ceremony, believing her dead.
"Chandika has got a new life," her neighbour Buddhi Lal Dongol told AFP. "It would be so good if the others who are missing also came back."
Several families held last-rite ceremonies in Nuwakot to mark the 13th day of mourning, while Buddhist monks held prayers for the dead.
"I have had to hold myself together a lot," 63-year-old Kula Priya Nepal, whose son was killed at a hydroelectric project, told AFP.
Rescuers have retrieved 1,356 bodies in Nepal, while around 4,994 people are missing, according to the disaster agency.
The toll in China stands at 43 dead and 519 missing. (AFP)

Trump administration attacks UK plans to boost traditional media on social platforms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:20:12 UTC
23:20:12 KST

The Trump administration has raised “serious concerns” over Downing Street’s plan to force YouTube and other digital platforms to hand more prominence to established broadcasters, warning the move risks “facilitating censorship”.
In a pointed intervention, the US government said the proposals to boost traditional media outlets in social media algorithms could “establish a template that authoritarian regimes could invoke to justify more control over online content”.
It also warned it could undermine “independent journalists” and amount to “extraterritorial censorship of protected speech by Americans online”.
The statement, made via the US embassy in London, raises the stakes in the plans to give the likes of the BBC, ITV and other established media more visibility on increasingly dominant digital platforms.
Ministers, regulators and public service broadcasters have suggested new rules are needed to counter growing misinformation online as people increasingly turn to less regulated online platforms such as X, YouTube and TikTok.
In a consultation this year, the UK government said it would consider legislating should the platforms not act to prioritise trustworthy content. However, Washington claimed such a plan risked effectively removing the content of “independent journalists” over established outlets.
“Preserving a free, open internet and protecting freedom of expression online are top priorities for the Trump administration,” it said. “A framework that empowers governments to influence which sources receive preferential visibility risks becoming a mechanism for viewpoint-based censorship.
“If the UK compels platforms to boost government-preferred media in algorithmic feeds, the effect on a government-disfavoured speaker or media source’s reach is not meaningfully different than outright removal. The US government would likely consider such a measure as facilitating censorship.”
The administration has asked what safeguards will be in place to ensure “any biases and preferences of UK government officials and third-party organisations” do not influence the plan in ways that disadvantage “independent or minority-viewpoint journalism”.
A spokesperson for the Department for Culture, Media and Sport said: “We welcome engagement and responses to our media green paper. We believe strongly in free expression and fair competition, and any action we take will ensure these are protected.”
Insiders say any measures would only affect the UK. The US complaint highlights its readiness to fight for the largely US-based tech companies that run the world’s largest digital platforms.
Donald Trump also has a long record of attacking and bypassing the established media, regularly accusing major outlets of “fake news” and biased coverage. He often tries to reach supporters online.
The US president is still engaged in his lawsuit with the BBC over an episode of Panorama in which it spliced together one of his speeches. The BBC has apologised for the edit, but stated the show did not defame Trump.
Social media companies have previously been sceptical about artificially boosting the prominence of traditional media, arguing that it goes against the principle of creator content.
Online content creators have compared the proposals to state control and fear their content would be pushed down the rankings as a result.
Simon Squibb, a UK YouTube creator, said he was encouraged that his concerns were shared by an “entity that I think politicians will listen to”.
“This is a very dangerous potential direction for the UK to go in,” he said. “I’m happy that the USA has stepped in.”
Supporters of the enforced prominence plans have couched them as a way of dealing with misinformation and preserving culturally British content.
However, the government has also been clear that it wants to help public service broadcasters survive the economic turmoil created by the rise of digital platforms, which all media companies are confronting.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher

23:17:59 KST

Ursula von der Leyen, Jens-Frederik Nielsen and Mette Frederiksen hold a press conference in Nuuk, Greenland on Sept. 7, 2026. | Mads Claus Rasmussen/Ritzau Scanpix/AFP via Getty Images
Greenland is making a “clear choice” to strengthen ties with the EU, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Monday, as Brussels unveiled a €200 million investment package and moved to deepen its political, economic and security footprint in the Arctic.
Speaking in Nuuk alongside Greenlandic Premier Jens-Frederik Nielsen and Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, von der Leyen cast the relationship as a two-way partnership.
The renewed EU-Greenland declaration, she said, “reflects a clear choice expressed by Greenland to strengthen ties with the European Union,” while also demonstrating Europe’s own decision “to be more present” and more engaged in Greenland and across the Arctic.
Advertisement
U.S. President Donald Trump has made repeated threats to take over Greenland. In July, he said that “Greenland … should be controlled by the United States, not by Denmark” at the outset of a NATO summit in Turkey.
The Arctic has rapidly climbed up Brussels’ geopolitical agenda. Von der Leyen said the region had become a place “where the tectonic plates of geopolitics collide,” adding that the EU has a direct stake in developments there and is preparing a new Arctic strategy for presentation this fall.
The Arctic is also expected to feature prominently in von der Leyen’s State of the Union speech next week, as Brussels prepares the revamped strategy.
She also reiterated that Greenland’s future is for the people of Greenland and Denmark to decide.
The two-day visit, which began Sunday, was aimed at turning the political message into concrete projects. A Commission official said the trip had been months in the making but was postponed at Frederiksen’s request due to Danish elections in March.
Von der Leyen signed a renewed joint declaration with Greenland and Denmark and unveiled a €200 million EU partnership package for this year and next.
Advertisement
At Greenlandic telecom operator Tusass, she launched a satellite connectivity project designed to improve internet access in remote communities. Brussels will also support hydropower development and work with Greenland on mining projects intended to more closely link the island’s raw materials to European industry.
The broader declaration expands cooperation into education, infrastructure, fisheries, tourism, housing, research, climate action, civil protection, cybersecurity and Arctic resilience.
Von der Leyen also pointed to the longer-term relationship, saying the Commission has proposed more than doubling EU funding for Greenland to €530 million through 2034.

Search continues for hundreds trapped in hydro-plant after Nepal floods
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:16:31 UTC
23:16:31 KST

In short :
More than 100 hydropower workers are feared trapped in tunnels almost two weeks after floods ripped through the Himalayan site.
A total of 900 people are still missing from the hydro-electric tunnels in Nepal.
What's next?
Rescuers are working with specialised equipment to free people they believe may have air pockets inside the vast tunnel systems.
Nepali rescuers have searched for more than 100 hydropower workers feared trapped in tunnels days after four miracle rescues from the wreckage of catastrophic floods that laid waste to towns and villages on the Himalayan border with China.
The rescues on Monday offered a glimmer of hope as Nepal marked the 13th day after the disaster, traditionally the final day of mourning in Hindu rites, for the hundreds killed in the floods.
About 121 of a total 900 people missing from the hydro-electric projects could have been trapped in these tunnels, army rescuers said.
Others may have been working elsewhere at the power plants but not inside the vast network of tunnels.
Among those rescuers were trying to find on Monday were four out of six people missing at the Chilime hydropower project in the hard-hit Rasuwa district who could still be alive, Shri Ram Neupane, a member of parliament involved in rescue efforts, told Reuters.
Authorities had obtained specialised equipment and identified techniques needed for the Chilime operation, Mr Neupane said.
Rescuers believe that there could be survivors trapped inside tunnels because many had air pockets, as well as spaces and rooms for people to stay, they said last week.
In recent days, search teams in Nepal have rescued four people, including a Chinese national who was pulled from a tunnel on Saturday.
The others were two hydropower workers rescued from another tunnel on Friday and a Nepali woman pulled out from her buried house on Saturday.
Government offices in the Hindu majority country and at missions abroad would fly the national flag at half-mast to mark the 13th day after death, the home ministry said in a statement.
The day is considered the final day of mourning by the faithful, who commemorate it with rituals and food offerings.
The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade said in a statement last week, the Australian government would deploy a team of specialist drone operators to contribute to Nepal's search-and-rescue efforts.
"The team, including members of Fire and Rescue New South Wales and the Queensland Fire Department, will depart in the coming days as part of a 15-person Disaster Assistance Response Team," the statement read.
"They will use advanced drone technology to provide rapid mapping and imaging to support Nepali authorities' search operations."
At least 1,380 people have been killed by the mudslide. More than 5,500 are missing in Nepal and Tibet, among them 35 Australians.
The disaster was triggered on August 26 when a huge mass of mud and rock, following the collapse of part of a glacier, crashed into a river along the border between Nepal and China's Tibet region.
The resulting floods washed away towns and villages and buried roads and highways under mud and debris.
Chinese officials said on Sunday that workers had recovered 12 more bodies as the search continued for hundreds still missing in Tibet.
"The Chinese side will continue to make every effort to conduct search-and-rescue operations and handle post-disaster matters," foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said at a press briefing.
China has faced pressure from some families of foreign visitors missing in Tibet, who say they have struggled to obtain information on missing relatives.
Mr Mao said Beijing would promptly release "updated information on the disaster situation and rescue activities."
On Sunday, China for the first time invited journalists from eight foreign media outlets, including Reuters, to visit the core affected areas.
With search teams still looking for survivors, Nepal's government has not planned any wider events for the final day of mourning.
"There are no government programs organised as the rescue and search operation is still going on in the flood-hit areas," Phanindra Paudel of the National Emergency Operation Centre (NEOC) told Reuters.
President Ram Chandra Paudel, the ceremonial head of state, was touring flood-hit areas on Monday and would survey damage caused by the disaster, his aide said.
Security personnel at the district jail in Nuwakot, one of the two worst-affected districts, saved 923 prisoners by shifting them to a building in a higher location before floodwater entered their low-lying building on August 26, Prime Minister Balendra Shah said in a social media post.
Authorities also captured 50 prisoners who had broken the prison wall and gates as flooding began, and had fled barely 100 metres, Shah said on Monday.

white stainless-steel cylinders form coral-like swing installation on chinese coast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:15:41 UTC
23:15:41 KST

Twelve Cylinders Form a Coral-Inspired Coastal Installation
Composed of twelve oversized white cylinders, Coral is a swing installation that transforms the coastline of Yantai, China, into an inhabitable underwater world. The work, created by XBTW Office, stands at the northwest corner of West Park at Longfor Puti peninsula. Facing tidal flats and the sea, the site is shaped by the daily rhythm of tides, sea breeze, and sunsets, which together form its most distinctive landscape. Visitors wander between shifting frames of sea and sky or swing toward the sunset, experiencing the tides and sea breeze through movement. The form of the installation is inspired by the repetition and aggregation of similar units found in coral colonies. The design uses twelve white stainless-steel cylinders as basic units, arranged into two groups above and below. A thin horizontal roof plane passes through the composition, with two west-facing swings suspended beneath it. The cylinders, positioned at different heights and orientations, overlap and shift against one another, creating an inhabitable space for people to enter, move through, and pause.
all images by Zhu Yumeng, DONG Image
Perforated Cylinders Frame the Coast and Shift with the Light
Viewed from a distance, the white forms emerge along the open coastline as an unfamiliar presence, resembling a group of marine organisms. As visitors approach, the spaces between the cylinders gradually reveal fragments of tidal flats, sea, and sky, transforming the continuous landscape into a series of constantly changing frames. Upon entering the installation, the relationship between body and scale begins to shift. The oversized cylinders surround the body, making the familiar coastline temporarily feel unfamiliar, as if entering an underwater world. Visitors can move through the structure or sit on the west-facing swings, experiencing the sea breeze, tides, and sunset through gentle movement.
The perforated patterns on the cylinders are inspired by variations in the density of deep-sea fish schools. Each cylinder contains approximately 2,000 to 4,000 perforations of different sizes, ranging from 4 to 25 millimeters in diameter. Variations in the density and scale of the openings create a gradient texture on the white stainless-steel surfaces, evoking the gathering and dispersal of fish schools. Among these openings, a small number of larger perforations take the forms of marine creatures, including starfish, octopuses, and seashells, adding another layer of detail to the surface. After sunset, light emerges through the perforations, transforming the previously quiet white forms into another state. The installation by creative practice XBTW Office gradually appears like a group of slowly breathing marine organisms.
XBTW Office positions the installation on Yantai’s open coastline

Estonia has 5th-highest obesity rate in Europe, data shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:14:00 UTC
23:14:00 KST

Estonia has 5th-highest obesity rate in Europe, data shows
Estonia has the fifth‑highest share of obese adults in Europe, with 22.0 percent of the population aged 18 and over classified as obese, according to 2025 Eurostat data.
The EU average stood at 16.3 percent, with the highest rates posted in Malta (26.6 percent), followed by Estonia's immediate neighbors to the south and north: Latvia (which saw 24.6 percent of the population classified as obese) and Finland (at 23.2 percent). Ireland at (22.1 percent was fractionally ahead of Estonia. The lowest proportions were seen in Romania (12.9 percent), Greece (12.8 percent) and Italy (7.0 percent).
In addition, 35.4 percent of Europe's population was classified as overweight, or pre‑obese, with a Body Mass Index (BMI) between 25 and 30. Overall, more than half of Europe's population was either obese or pre‑obese/overweight.
Men were more likely to be overweight than women, on the whole. The obesity rate among men was 17.4 percent, compared with 15.3 percent among women EU-wide. Meanwhile, 41.9 percent of men were pre‑obese, compared with 29.3 percent of women. Also, rates of being underweight were nearly three times higher among women (at 2.9 percent) compared with men (at 1.0 percent).
According to Eurostat, 46.4 percent of European adults were at a normal and healthy weight: 39.8 percent of men and 52.5 percent of women.
In Estonia alone, the situation is even more pronounced. ERR's science portal Novaator reported in July, citing a study by the National Institute for Health Development (TAI), which found more than 60 percent of Estonian adults were overweight as of last year, and with 26 percent classified as obese.
The TAI study also found that excess weight imposes significant additional costs on society, affecting healthcare, productivity and overall economic well‑being.
The obesity rate is calculated using body mass index (BMI), which is determined by dividing body weight in kilograms by the square of height in meters. A BMI of 30 or higher is classified as obese, while a BMI between 25 and 30 is considered pre‑obese.

Türkiye aims to reach single-digit inflation with 3-year economic plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:12:31 UTC
23:12:31 KST

Serhat Tutak and Emir Yildirim
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
Türkiye’s new Medium-Term Program (MTP) aims to resolve persistently high inflation and reach single-digit levels through the disinflation process.
The economic plan covering 2027-2029 aims to break inflationary inertia and achieve price stability by reducing the inflation rate to single-digit levels through the uninterrupted continuation of the disinflation process.
Türkiye’s annual consumer inflation rate is at 31.51% as of August, prompting Ankara to prioritize the disinflation process driven by coordination of monetary, fiscal, and revenue policies to be maintained throughout the three-year period.
The economic roadmap projects annual consumer inflation to end this year at 28.4% before falling to 21% in 2027, 13.5% in 2028, and 9% by the end of 2029.
Türkiye’s Central Bank (CBRT) will maintain its framework targeting inflation and a floating exchange rate regime to allow free market supply and demand to dictate currency values.
The plan is to utilize all monetary tools to cool domestic demand while strengthening supply policies to promote broader market competition.
The program aims to change how businesses set their prices by urging them to base their expectations on future government targets instead of adjusting prices to match past inflation, in an attempt to break the cycle of continuous retail hikes.
The plan also outlines that state purchase prices for crops will be determined by their impact on public finances and market dynamics to prevent indexation to past inflation rates, while specially tailoring agricultural production to seize regional potential to ensure long-term food security.
Communication channels will be strengthened to anchor inflation expectations within targets, while public awareness of a website for viewing prices at supermarket chains will be raised to increase transparency.

The Ministry of Defense explained what representatives of the Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers can and cannot do during an air raid alert
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
17:12:24 EEST
23:12:24 KST

The Ministry of Defense explained what representatives of the Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers can and cannot do during an air raid alert
Kyiv • UNN
Representatives of the Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers have no right to stop or detain people heading to a shelter. Document checks in the shelter are not separately prohibited.
Representatives of the territorial recruitment and social support centers (TCCs and SСs) are not authorized to stop, hold or detain citizens in public places or prevent them from proceeding to a shelter during an air raid. This is stated in the response of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine to Oleksii Honcharenko, Head of the Verkhovna Rada's Temporary Investigative Commission, which UNN has reviewed.
At the same time, the legislation does not separately require TCC personnel to immediately stop notification efforts or the verification of military registration documents once inside shelters.
Details
The Ministry of Defense noted that the procedure for actions by TCC and SS notification groups during the "Air Raid Alert" signal is regulated by legislation in the areas of civil protection, military service and the performance of service duties by military personnel. At the same time, there are no separate regulatory acts of the Ministry of Defense, orders or directives of the Ministry of Defense or the General Staff that would establish a special algorithm for the conduct of TCC notification groups in public places directly during an air raid.
The ministry reminded that, in accordance with the Code of Civil Protection of Ukraine, ensuring citizens' safety and protecting people from the consequences of emergencies, military actions or an air attack is a priority duty.
"The implementation of protective measures in response to civil protection signals is mandatory for all persons located on the territory of Ukraine," the Defense Ministry's response states.
The ministry separately emphasized that military personnel who are members of TCC and SS notification groups are not authorized to prevent people from proceeding to a safe place.
"The legislation does not grant military personnel who are members of TCC and SS notification groups the authority to stop, hold or detain citizens in public places or prevent them from proceeding to a shelter while the \"Air Raid Alert\" signal is in effect," the relevant ministry stated.
At the same time, the ministry drew attention to another legal detail: the current legislation contains no special provision requiring TCC and SS representatives, after an alert is announced, to immediately stop notifying citizens or checking military registration documents if such actions are already taking place inside a shelter or another protective structure.
It follows that the work of notification groups during an air raid must be carried out in compliance with the requirements of legislation in the areas of civil protection, military service and mobilization, while the protection of people's lives and health and compliance with established safety rules must remain the priority.
We remind you
As UNN reported, due to Russian strikes on TCCs and SSs, their work will be reformatted to ensure the safety of personnel and visitors. Possible options include dispersing recruitment office personnel, remote services and expanded digitalization.
