Germany on its way to getting Israel's Iron Dome missile defense system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
13:13:53 UTC
22:13:53 KST

Germany is on its way to getting Israel’s Iron Dome missile defense system, Defense & Tech by The Jerusalem Post understands.
D&T has confirmed that the letter of intent signed by the German state of Lower Saxony, Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, and Aurelius Capital is the first step toward the European nation acquiring the Iron Dome.
The agreement, signed at the factory on Monday, will see the Volkswagen site in Osnabruck developed into a center of excellence for innovative security and defense solutions. It will combine German engineering expertise, industrial capital and quality standards.
Though it is not a signed agreement, sources who have spoken to D&T have said that the plan later down the road is for Germany to procure the famous interceptor. Germany, a key ally of Israel, currently has the Arrow 3 missile defense system that is manufactured by Israel Aerospace Industries. Berlin, like most of Europe has been bolstering its defenses as Russia continues it's war against Ukraine.
Rafael has been active in Germany for over 20 years and has established a strong presence in the country with various subsidiaries including Dynamit Nobel Defence, EuroSpike and EuroTrophy GmbH.
Yoav Tourgeman, president and CEO of Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, said that the partnership with Germany is part of a long-term relationship with the country “with the idea that the technology will be fully produced in Germany, to protect Germany and Europe.”
“The technology at the heart of this partnership is built for the defense of today, tomorrow, and well beyond. Our outstanding combat-proven technology evolves constantly in order to be ahead of the threats, so that highly reliable defense will always be provided,” he added.
Integral part of Israel’s missile defense array
Initially designed to shoot down short-range rockets, the Iron Dome has, over the past 15 years, become an integral component of Israel's multi-layered defense array.
The system’s modular architecture enables seamless integration with additional defense layers, and it can operate independently or as part of Israel’s broader air defense network that includes the the Arrow (Arrow 2 and Arrow 3) system, which intercepts ballistic missiles outside of the Earth’s atmosphere, and the David’s Sling missile defense system which is designed to intercept tactical ballistic missiles, medium- to long-range rockets, as well as cruise missiles fired at ranges between 40 to 300 km. Rafael has also manufactured the Iron Beam laser defense system, which has been operational along Israel’s northern border.
The system’s early years were defined by rapid operational learning. Iron Dome took part in a long series of conflicts and operations, from Operation Protective Edge, Operation Guardian of the Walls, Operation Breaking Dawn, Operation Shield and Arrow, Operation Swords of Iron, and Operations Rising and Roaring Lion, where it served alongside the Arrow and David’s Sling as a central pillar in the protection of Israel’s home front.
Each round of fighting was followed by a new wave of software updates, radar refinements, and interceptor improvements.
It quickly became evident that the system was a flexible defensive layer capable of handling dense salvos, more complex trajectories, and a wider range of threats. The system’s radar was upgraded to track more targets simultaneously, its algorithms became faster and more selective, and its interceptors were refined to handle longer ranges and more demanding engagement profiles.
Yet, despite its successes, the Iron Dome is not infallible.
Israeli officials have consistently noted that no air‑defense system can guarantee complete protection. Some rockets inevitably penetrate the system’s defenses, underscoring the importance of measures such as early warning sirens and reinforced shelters.
Nevertheless, the system’s high interception rate has significantly reduced casualties and property damage during periods of conflict, altering both military calculations and civilian life in Israel.
An Israeli shield over Europe
Europe has increasingly turned to Israeli air defense technology over the past decade, especially after Russia invaded Ukraine and the growing demand for rapid, combat‑proven systems.
The news comes just one week after Israel and Greece have formalized one of the largest defense export agreements in Israel’s history, a €3 billion government‑to‑government deal that will see Israel design and deliver a complete, multi‑layered national air defense architecture for the Hellenic Republic’s Achilles Shield project.
Though the Iron Dome is not part of it, the project will integrate several Israeli‑made systems into a unified national network. At its core are David’s Sling, BARAK MX, and SPYDER missile defense systems developed by the Israeli defense companies and already deployed operationally within Israel’s own air defense array.
The package also includes MMR radars produced by IAI subsidiary ELTA for air surveillance coverage and a new national command‑and‑control system developed by Rafael to integrate all layers into a single operational picture.
The agreement represents the first time Israel will supply a complete, end‑to‑end air‑defense array to another country. According to a statement released by the Defense Ministry, the architecture is based entirely on Israeli systems and incorporates operational lessons drawn from Israel’s recent wars wherein these systems played central roles in intercepting thousands of hostile aerial targets, including drones and ballistic missiles launched by Iran, Hezbollah, and the Houthis in Yemen.
Central European states have also moved toward Israeli systems, with the Czech Republic receiving the Spyder medium‑range system, Slovakia selecting the Barak MX, and Estonia contemplating purchasing the David Sling missile defense system as it bolsters its long-range air defenses and plans to invest over €1b. in a new long-range ground-based air defense system to protect strategic sites.
Germany has also purchased Israel’s Arrow 3 as a response to Russia’s war against Ukraine and the growing proliferation of advanced missile systems. Germany signed the $3.5b.Arrow 3 contract in November 2023, the largest defense deal in Israel’s history at the time. In December, the two countries signed a $3.1b. follow-up contract to expand interceptor and launcher stocks.
Arrow 3, developed by Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI), is a highly maneuverable system designed to provide ultimate air defense by intercepting ballistic missiles when they are still outside the Earth’s atmosphere.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Monday announced a fresh funding boost for Greenland, seeking to shore up Arctic ties with the self-governing Danish territory amid U.S. President Donald Trump's annexation drive.
Speaking alongside Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen and Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, the EU chief said the 200-million-euro ($232.3 million) funding package reflects "a clear choice" by Greenland to strengthen ties with the 27-nation bloc.
"This partnership package focuses mainly on three domains, or strategic priorities. We call them the big Cs: connectivity, clean energy [and] critical raw materials," Von der Leyen told reporters at a news conference.
The funds, which is to be invested this year and in 2027, is designed to bolster ties between the EU and the Arctic, with Von der Leyen describing Greenland as "a strategic ally and a trusted friend."
It comes shortly after Icelanders voted to reject restarting EU membership negotiations and as Trump renews his push to acquire Greenland on national security grounds.
"The European Union continues to be, not only an important partner for Greenland, but also a loyal and trusted friend," Greenland's Nielsen said.
"Through these challenging times, your support to us is unfailing. You have stood by us and continue to stand by us. We feel it and are deeply grateful. Thank you," he added.
Asked whether they had any concerns about how Trump may react to the funding package and what message he should take from the announcement, Denmark's Frederiksen said: "We have been under pressure and it has been very clear, and we are very thankful for the great support that we have received from our European partners — but, by the way, also globally."
Frederiksen insisted that Denmark would like to work closely together with the U.S. on issues such as security and defense, "but we, of course, would also like to work even closer together with our European allies and that is exactly what we are doing in the Arctic region now."
The EU's Von der Leyen said Greenland "stood firm and stands firm under enormous pressure," in an apparent reference to Trump's pursuit of U.S. control of the territory. "Europe is firmly united with you too. This is the basic message," she added.
Trump has long advocated for control of Greenland, a vast, sparsely populated and largely frozen island, but the U.S. president's fixation on the territory became a major trans-Atlantic issue at the start of the year.
Trump, who had refused to rule out the use of military force to annex Greenland, abruptly announced in late January, however, that he and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte had formed a "framework of a future deal" with respect to the territory.
A working group of representatives from the U.S., Denmark and Greenland have since been meeting to discuss the way forward.

ASI collects samples from well discovered after mosque demolition in Saharanpur
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
13:07:54 UTC
22:07:54 KST

ASI examines 20-foot well found at demolished mosque site in Saharanpur (Picture credit: ANI)
NEW DELHI: An Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) team on Monday examined a nearly 20-foot-deep well discovered during debris removal at the site of a mosque demolished inside the Saharanpur Collectorate premises, officials said.The inspection was aimed at determining the age, nature and historical relevance of the structure, which was found beneath the rubble on Sunday.Heavy police security was deployed around the site and the well was barricaded to prevent access.
ASI examines well’s structure and construction
Manoj Kumar Yadav of the Uttar Pradesh State Archaeology Department said the inspection was intended to establish the antiquity of the structure and understand its possible historical context."Our primary objective in visiting here was to determine the antiquity of the structure found there. Secondly, we wanted to understand the nature of the structure itself. We also aimed to correlate it with history to understand what it relates to," Yadav told news agency ANI.According to Yadav, the structure appeared to be a well filled with debris that had fallen inside. It was around 20 feet in height from the surface level and had a diameter of nearly three feet.
"The structure is made using Lakhori bricks. The binding mortar used is a lime-surkhi mixture, and at a depth of three feet from the top surface, there is a thin layer of lime plaster," he said.Yadav added that structures made using similar techniques are commonly found in the Upper and Middle Ganga Valley regions and are generally associated with the later mediaeval period.Three ASI officials reached the site on Monday afternoon and examined the well in the presence of local administration officials. The officials measured its depth after placing a ladder inside and carried out photography and videography.Soil and brick-remnant samples were also collected from inside the well, sadar sub-divisional magistrate Subodh Kumar said.The discovery was made during debris-removal work on Sunday, when workers came across a concrete slab beneath the rubble.The slab was unusually strong. A Pokland machine failed to make a significant impact, after which workers used a cutter and found the brick-lined well.The well was approximately 20 feet deep and around 1.5 metres wide. Its exact age, purpose and historical background were not immediately established.
Mosque demolition followed court proceedings
The well was discovered a day after the demolition of a mosque located inside the Saharanpur Collectorate premises.The district administration demolished the structure in the early hours of September 5 after the mosque committee's appeal against the demolition order was rejected by the district judge's court.The City Magistrate's court had on July 17 declared the structure an illegal encroachment on government land and ordered its demolition. It also imposed compensation of approximately Rs 6.41 crore in connection with the alleged encroachment and misuse of government land.The mosque management committee had challenged the City Magistrate's order in the district court, which rejected its appeal on September 2. Authorities subsequently proceeded with the demolition amid heavy police deployment.Authorities have maintained that the demolition was carried out in accordance with court directions and legal procedures.
Claims emerge over well's historical significance
The discovery has led to differing claims about the possible history of the site.
Vikas Tyagi, the complainant in the matter and a former Bajrang Dal convenor, claimed that a temple might have existed at the site before the mosque was built.Saharanpur Congress MP Imran Masood, however, said the well was part of the mosque and had been used in earlier times to meet the requirement for water for wuzu, or ablution before prayers.The ASI examination is expected to help establish the well's antiquity and historical background. Officials have not announced any conclusion about its origin or earlier use.

The opposition right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD) party could join forces with the left-wing Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) after its landslide election win in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt, RT contributor Rachel Marsden has said.
The AfD won 43.8% of the vote in Sunday’s regional election, leaving German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) far behind in second place at 17.5%. However, the right-wing party claimed 39 out of 97 seats in the local legislature, falling short of a governing majority.

“The AFD winning here was fully expected and now the party has to work out what to actually do with all those votes... Now, the anti-establishment left BSW party is hovering around 5%, potentially making the coalition arithmetic rather uncomfortable for the [establishment] parties that have spent years insisting that there would be no cooperation with the AfD,” she said.
The AfD and BWS might sit on the different sides of the political spectrum, but their positions overlap in many areas, especially when it comes to urging dialogue with Russia and resisting the growing influence of EU bureaucrats in Brussels, Marsden stressed.
“There’s also the possibility that the AfD would refuse to work with anybody in favor of just kind of rolling the dice and hoping that nobody can form a coalition government,” which would lead to a new election, giving the right-wing party another chance of calming enough votes to govern Saxony-Anhalt alone, she added.

British Aircraft Carrier HMS Queen Elizabeth Became a NATO Flagship Following a Two-Year Refit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
13:05:18 UTC
22:05:18 KST

On September 5, the Royal Navy HMS Queen Elizabeth aircraft carrier departed the Portsmouth naval base and began a three-month deployment in the waters off the United Kingdom and Northern Europe.
Navy Lookout reported on this.
During this new deployment, a NATO command post will be established on the ship. In July, HMS Queen Elizabeth was designated as the floating command post for the maritime component of NATO’s Allied Response Force (Maritime).
This is the first time that one of the two British Queen Elizabeth-class aircraft carriers has been assigned this role.
A command center has been established on board the aircraft carrier to direct NATO’s multinational naval forces and coordinate the interaction of ships and aircraft from various Alliance countries during crisis situations.
HMS Queen Elizabeth sails from Portsmouth this evening as she returns to operations today after her first major refit.
She will be away for 3 months operating in the Euro-Atlantic region. First up – further training and certification by @FOSThttps://t.co/o1EMekv2q5
Via… pic.twitter.com/IoPYpaEuJ8
— Navy Lookout (@NavyLookout) September 5, 2026
HMS Queen Elizabeth underwent its first major overhaul since joining the Royal Navy in 2017. The multi-phase maintenance program began in November 2024.
One of the key stages was the ship’s eight-month stay in dry dock at Rosyth. During the overhaul, specialists modernized its propulsion system and carried out a number of other engineering tasks.
Before the aircraft carrier is deployed for operations and exercises, an intensive training program will be organized under the guidance of the Fleet Operational Standards and Training (FOST) organization.
This program will cover aviation operations, the combat use of the aircraft carrier, and the fundamentals of naval warfare. Along with HMS Queen Elizabeth, the Type 45 destroyer HMS Dauntless departed from Portsmouth on September 4.
Both ships may participate in the Atlantic Thunder 2026 exercises, which involve joint training with the U.S. Navy to destroy a target ship off the coast of Scotland. The exercises are scheduled for September 17–21.
HMS Queen Elizabeth’s training will continue through 2027 and will include large-scale NATO exercises.
By the end of 2027, the aircraft carrier is set to replace HMS Prince of Wales as the Royal Navy’s flagship and primary strike vessel with high combat readiness.
This fall, HMS Prince of Wales will embark on the second phase of Operation FIRECREST, which will also take place in the North Atlantic.
The return of HMS Queen Elizabeth to active service comes as the United Kingdom prepares to establish a hybrid carrier air wing.
The Defense Investment Plan allocates £240 million to develop new unmanned aerial vehicles, including jet-powered UAVs, which are intended to operate alongside F-35B Lightning fighter jets.

Rats plague pedestrian zone in the City of Brussels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
13:04:32 UTC
22:04:32 KST

The pedestrian zone on the Anspachlaan in the City of Brussels is plagued by a new rat infestation. Discarded fast-food scraps and bread are a real treat for these critters.
On Saturday evening, passers-by in the pedestrian zone at the heart of Brussels were surprised to see several rats running fearlessly back and forth in a building site near Le Grand Café. Such activity points to a severe rat infestation.
The pedestrian zone has been struggling with a rat problem for some time, but during the exceptionally hot summer, the creatures seemed to have largely disappeared from the surface. They were presumably seeking relief from the heat in the sewers. Now that temperatures are bearable again and there are regular showers, the rats are reappearing.
Digital rat traps
Anas Ben Abdelmoumen, Alderman for Public Cleanliness in the City, has been aware of the issue for some time and posted about the problem on Instagram as recently as last Friday. This summer, he had 15 smart digital rat traps installed in the pedestrian zone, following successful trials near the Atomium.
These traps are high-tech devices that not only attract and trap the rats but also record real-time data on how often the rats visit. This provides an insight into the size of the local rat population. The digital rat traps, an innovation produced by the Belgian company Strygoo, come in addition to the usual everyday pest control efforts.
‘Burgerisation’
As well as stepping up rat control measures, a more structural solution would, of course, be to make the pedestrian zone less attractive to rats looking for food.
Here, fast-food reigns supreme, one snack bar follows the next other. The city council is asking restaurant owners to take extra care to secure their rubbish bags. Consumers must also do their bit. Councillor Ben Abdelmoumen is calling on the public not to leave food scraps on the street.
“Some people dump whole loaves of bread or pizzas, others the leftovers from their fast-food meals. For rats, all of this is a feast,” explains his spokesperson, Andreas De Kerpel.
This includes both members of the public who, with good intentions, want to leave food out for the birds but give too little thought to the consequences, and thoughtless passers-by who, out of sheer laziness, throw their food scraps onto the street.
The City of Brussels hopes to curb the rat infestation through a combination of education and deterrent fines.

‘I Can’t Mislead People’: Ukraine’s Spy Chief Warns Russia Can Fight Through 2028
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
13:04:30 UTC
22:04:30 KST

Russia may have enough resources to continue its war against Ukraine through 2027 and 2028, while preparing intensified attacks on the country’s energy infrastructure during the coming autumn and winter, Ukraine’s military intelligence chief said.
Oleg Ivashchenko, head of Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence Directorate (HUR) made the assessment in an interview with the state-run Ukrinform news agency.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We do not rule out that Russia will have enough resources to wage war against Ukraine in 2027 and 2028,” he said.
Ivashchenko said Ukraine and its international partners must work together to restrict Russia’s access to the equipment and materials needed to sustain its military production.
Ivashchenko said sanctions must be effectively enforced, adding that Ukrainian intelligence knows which countries supply Russia with electronic components, machine tools, and specialized chemicals. He said numerous intermediary companies have emerged to deliver goods that are later used by Russia’s war machine.
The intelligence chief also said public dissatisfaction with the war was growing inside Russia, although it remained unclear whether it could develop into a significant protest movement.
According to Ivashchenko, more than 60% of Russians now oppose the war, a trend he attributed to worsening economic conditions and heavy battlefield losses. Russia’s contract recruitment model had largely exhausted itself, with regional governments increasingly unable to finance the payments offered to new recruits.
China Asks Ukraine Not to Strike Vladivostok During Forum
Ivashchenko has estimated that Russian forces lose an average of 1,200 to 1,400 personnel a day, with the figure sometimes rising to 1,500, including soldiers killed or seriously wounded.
Russia preparing combined winter attacks
Ivashchenko also warned that Russia was preparing combined attacks involving ballistic and cruise missiles, jet-powered Shahed drones, and new loitering munitions.
He said Ukrainian intelligence had information about the facilities Russia intended to target, the weapons it planned to use, and the approximate timing of potential strikes.
“I can’t please you and I can’t mislead people. As the head of intelligence, I have to speak objectively. People have to understand this, and our country has to prepare for this.”
According to him, Russia’s primary objective is to reduce Ukraine’s military potential and long-range strike capabilities. Russian forces are targeting ammunition storage sites and attempting to destroy Ukrainian defense production facilities, he said.
Energy facilities and thermal power plants are expected to become increasingly frequent targets as colder weather approaches, Ivashchenko said.
He also reported a significant increase in the use of jet-powered Shahed-type drones. Russia could deploy groups numbering 120, 300, or even 500 drones in a single day, while simultaneously launching ballistic and cruise missiles.
Ivashchenko said Russia was also introducing new loitering munitions that combine features of jet-powered drones and cruise missiles. He identified the weapons as the Banderol and Dan-T, saying they could travel at speeds of 500 to 700 kilometers per hour (about 310 to 435 mph), and be launched from either air or ground platforms.
The weapons use artificial intelligence and machine vision to improve accuracy and operate with greater autonomy, making them less dependent on external guidance and more difficult to counter.
He said their warheads weigh more than 130 kilograms (286 pounds), significantly heavier than those carried by Shahed or Geran-type drones, which he put at between 50 and 90 kilograms (110 and 198 pounds).
Ballistic missiles, particularly Iskander and Zircon missiles, remain among the most difficult targets for Ukrainian air defenses to intercept, Ivashchenko said. Countering them requires advanced missile defense systems and an adequate supply of interceptor missiles.
“The enemy is adapting. And our task is to adapt faster.”
Ivashchenko said military intelligence was working directly with Ukraine’s Air Force by providing information about potential threats. He added that securing sufficient numbers of PAC-3 interceptor missiles for Patriot air defense systems remained a priority for President Volodymyr Zelensky, his office, Ukrainian diplomats, and intelligence officials.

22:04:29 KST

Latvia has become the first European country to ban imports of Russian consumer goods including books and print media, framing the move as a defense against Kremlin disinformation and hybrid warfare.
Latvia has banned the import of books, newspapers and other printed materials from Russia and Belarus, citing "disinformation and war propaganda," its foreign ministry told AFP on Monday — a move with implications for how EU and NATO members handle information warfare from Moscow.
"The import ban is intended to protect Latvia's security interests and further reduce economic ties with Russia and Belarus, which continue to wage and support (the) war of aggression against Ukraine," the ministry said.
Latvia, a NATO and EU member bordering both Russia and Belarus, has positioned itself firmly behind Kyiv since the 2022 invasion. Riga says it has faced sustained "hybrid attacks" from Moscow since the war began — a term covering cyberattacks, drone incursions and disinformation campaigns — and has invested heavily in security, believing it could become one of the Kremlin's next targets.
The country also has a significant Russian-speaking population, with around a quarter of Latvians identifying as ethnic Russian, according to official statistics.
The ban, in effect since 1 September, is the first of its kind imposed on Russian consumer goods anywhere in Europe. It also covers other goods including clothing, toys and sports equipment. Latvia's government said the aim was "strengthening the resilience of society and reducing vulnerabilities in the information space."
Overall imports from Russia and Belarus have fallen roughly 91% since the war began, the foreign ministry said — but books and printed materials remained one of the largest consumer import categories still flowing from Russia, as the ministry put it, having "constituted one of the largest remaining consumer goods import categories from Russia."
Latvia has already scrapped VAT incentives for Russian-language publishing domestically and moved to reduce Russian-language instruction in schools, citing the need to counter Kremlin interference and better integrate Russian-speaking residents.
The move comes against a backdrop of rising friction between Moscow and the Baltic states. In May, Russia signalled plans to take Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia to the International Court of Justice over alleged rights violations against Russian speakers — claims the three countries reject, instead accusing Moscow of exploiting an ethnic Russian minority that grew substantially during decades of Soviet occupation to stoke regional tensions.

The metro and city institutions will operate, while mass events will be restricted — how life in Kyiv will change after September 10
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:02:54 EEST
22:02:54 KST

The metro and city institutions will operate, while mass events will be restricted — how life in Kyiv will change after September 10
Kyiv • UNN
From September 10, Kyiv will shorten the curfew and extend public transport operating hours. Metro operations will also change, bridge traffic will be altered, and mass events will be restricted.
In Kyiv, starting September 10, the curfew will be shortened by one hour, public transport operating hours will be extended, the operating rules for the metro and bridges during air-raid alerts will be changed, and the holding of mass events will be temporarily restricted in places without shelters. On September 7, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko wrote about this on his official Telegram channel, reports UNN.
According to him, the relevant decisions were adopted by the Kyiv Defense Council amid the deteriorating security situation in the capital.
Details
The changes will affect several areas at once:
-  the duration of the curfew; 
-  the public transport schedule;: metro service on open sections; 
-  travel across bridges over the Dnipro during air-raid alerts;  
-  the holding of mass events;  
-  the operation of municipal services; 
-  and alerts about various threat levels. 
All the new rules will come into effect at 00:00 on September 10.
Public transport operations
Given that Kyiv's curfew will be shortened, the operating hours of the capital's public transport will also be extended by one hour. This should allow Kyiv residents and city visitors to use the metro, buses, trolleybuses, and other municipal transport for longer before the curfew begins.
At the same time, the operating schedules of food-service establishments, entertainment venues, and shopping and entertainment centers will not be revised due to the change in the curfew. They will operate under the current rules.
Vitali Klitschko also recalled that, since September 3, by decision of the Kyiv Defense Council, transit heavy vehicles have been allowed to travel through the capital during curfew hours.
A separate decision was adopted regarding passengers arriving in Kyiv by rail at night. Since some trains arrive in the capital late and passengers may find themselves at the Central Railway Station during curfew hours, the city plans to organize four special bus routes to transport them.
Thus, visitors to the capital arriving in Kyiv late at night because of rail-service delays will be able to get from the station to other districts of the capital.
How the metro will operate during different threat levels
A separate set of decisions concerns the operation of open sections of the Kyiv Metro during air threats.
The service pattern will depend on the level of danger. During the yellow threat level, the Syretsko-Pecherska metro line, or the green line, will operate without restrictions. Train service will continue, including through the open section on the Southern Bridge. Passengers will be transported both from the left bank to the right bank and in the opposite direction. The "green line" will continue to operate as the only uninterrupted route between the two banks.
However, under the red threat level, the arrangement will be different. In that case, service on the "green line" will be possible only on separate sections: from "Syrets" station to "Vydubychi" station on the right bank and from "Slavutych" station to "Chervonyi Khutir" station on the left bank.
The metro will not transport passengers across the Southern Bridge during the red threat level.
The Sviatoshynsko-Brovarska, or "red," metro line will continue to operate according to the pattern used previously. During an air threat, passengers will be transported only along the underground section from "Akademmistechko" station to "Arsenalna". In this mode, passenger service on the above-ground section of the "red line" will be suspended.
At the same time, according to the mayor, surface public transport in the capital will continue to operate without restrictions. In addition, the city has already organized an additional bus route that partially duplicates the metro's "red line."
Buses are already operating regularly from "Palats Sportu" metro station via "Arsenalna" station to "Lisova" metro station. This route provides an alternative connection between the central part of the city and the left bank during periods when the above-ground section of the metro's "red line" does not carry passengers.
How traffic across bridges over the Dnipro will change
The Kyiv Defense Council also established a separate procedure for traffic across bridge crossings over the Dnipro during air-raid alerts.
The Southern Bridge will generally remain open to traffic during an air raid alert. At the same time, a technical closure of the bridge is planned for half an hour after an air raid alert is announced and for another half an hour after it is called off. In addition, the entrances to the Southern Bridge from Saperne-Slobidska Street and Mykhailo Boichuk Street will be closed directly during an air raid alert.
The other key bridge crossings over the Dnipro — the Darnytskyi Bridge, Paton Bridge, Metro Bridge and Northern Bridge — will operate without changes.
A separate regime has been provided for the Podilskyi-Voskresenskyi bridge crossing. There, as on the Southern Bridge, a technical closure will be introduced for half an hour after an air raid alert is announced and for half an hour after it is called off.
In addition, traffic management at the bridge crossing will be changed and reversible traffic will be introduced.
Mass events restricted in Kyiv
Due to the deteriorating security situation in the capital, temporary restrictions on mass events are also being introduced. According to Klychko, all entertainment and physical education and sports events held in open areas will be banned in the city.
The restrictions will also apply to events in buildings and structures without shelters.
Notifications about different threat levels
Against the backdrop of introducing different transport operating regimes depending on the level of danger, the city is also changing its system for informing citizens.
Klychko said that notifications about different threat levels are already available in the city's mobile application "Kyiv Digital". There residents and visitors to the capital will receive information about the relevant danger level during an air raid alert, which, among other things, will determine the operation of the open sections of the metro.
Operation of businesses and municipal institutions
Business entities of various ownership types will be able to continue operating in accordance with government decisions and established security rules.
At the yellow danger level, municipal institutions will also continue providing Kyiv residents with essential services. In particular, Administrative Services Centers will operate, as will institutions providing social services.
Educational institutions and medical facilities in Kyiv will operate in accordance with the security protocols established earlier. These decisions did not introduce new separate rules for schools, kindergartens, hospitals or other medical facilities.
Klychko emphasized that the city authorities are already taking the necessary organizational measures so that the capital's new operating regime can begin on the designated date.
"All these changes are being introduced in Kyiv from 00:00 on September 10. The city is taking the necessary organizational measures to implement the decisions adopted," the capital's mayor said.
Context
The Cabinet of Ministers adopted changes that adapt the operation of the state, economy and infrastructure to Russia's new tactics of terror. In particular, air raid alert signals are being divided by danger level into yellow and red, while in Kyiv it is proposed to revise the hours of the curfew and metro operation.
We remind you
In Kyiv, the curfew will be shortened and transport operation will be extended from September 10

Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) Chairman V Narayanan addresses a press conference
BENGALURU: Isro chairman V Narayanan Monday said genuine concerns of his colleagues would be clarified. “...If one or two people give you a letter, one cannot give a written communication immediately. Please understand, we are 20,000 employees. But we will address the employees,” he said on the sidelines of Bengaluru Space Expo 2026 here.Narayanan said that Isro had a system to regularly talk to employees. “...For example, when the space sector reforms were rolled out, from the Chairman onwards, we have regularly engaged with our employees,” he added.
Earlier at the inaugural, Isro chairman and IN-SPACe chairman Pawan Goenka made a strong case for greater participation by industry, startups and academia in India’s space programme, arguing that the country’s expanding ambitions cannot be met by the national space agency alone.Their remarks came a day after Isro and Goenka had released separate statements about the role of Isro, IN-SPACe and the private sector, which followed a letter by nine employees’ associations raising concerns over the future role of Isro.Narayanan said Monday that India’s requirements were set to rise sharply: “Our space programme is 64-65 years old. Right now, we have 56 space assets in serving the common man of the country.
But the [future] need is huge. I think you all know that,” he said, adding that industry would need to play a greater role in meeting that.He said industry had, in any case, long been an integral part of India's space programme. “Whenever an LVM3 is lifting off or a GSLV is lifting off, please do not think that everything is done in Isro. Almost 80% of the budget is invested in Indian industry. About 450 industries are working for us now,” he said.Narayanan said the growth of private companies and startups had to be welcomed if India was to meet its future requirements. From only one or two space startups around the time of the 2020 reforms, the country now has more than 450, he said.But he stressed that greater private-sector participation did not mean a reduced role for Isro. The agency's role was evolving as it took on an expanding range of programmes, including Chandrayaan-4 and Chandrayaan-5, the Venus Orbiter Mission, the Indian Space Station, a next-generation launch vehicle and the expansion of the Navic constellation.India's current capability to launch around 8,500-9,000 kg would also have to be raised to about 30,000 kg, he said. “Isro's role is in no way reduced. But we also have to handhold startup companies and the private sector.”Goenka, meanwhile, said India was building a “full-spectrum space economy” in which Isro, IN-SPACe, Nsil, private industry, MSMEs, academia and investors would play reinforcing roles.
From a single space startup in 2014, India now has more than 450, with over $160 million of private investment coming into the sector this year, he said. He urged established suppliers and MSMEs to move beyond supplying components and enter higher-value segments.“You are the quiet backbone of this story today,” Goenka told industry representatives, noting that a substantial share of what Isro builds already comes from its industrial suppliers. He urged them to move “from components to subsystems to full solutions” and serve global supply chains as well.

Struggling to find “the one”? A new psychology study says the problem might be your underlying motivation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
13:00:25 UTC
22:00:25 KST

A new study finds that the reasons single people want a relationship shape both the type of partnership they seek and whether they achieve their dating goals. Individuals driven by a genuine desire for connection tend to focus on relationship quality, while those driven by social pressure or a need for validation often prioritize simply finding a partner, which can hinder their progress. The research was published in Social Psychological and Personality Science.
Self-determination theory is a psychological framework for understanding human motivation. It suggests that our reasons for doing things exist on a spectrum, ranging from actions we take for pure enjoyment to actions we take because we feel forced or pressured. Historically, psychological research has shown that the internal drive behind our actions matters just as much as the actions themselves. For instance, a 2004 study demonstrated that why someone chases an objective and what that objective actually is are two distinct forces that shape their overall well-being.
Building on this idea, a 2008 study found that people tend to make far more headway on goals they truly care about than on goals driven by guilt or social pressure. Recently, scientists began applying this concept specifically to single people and dating. In fact, a 2025 study introduced a framework to measure internal versus external motivations for dating, noting that a person’s inner drive makes them more likely to find a partner. This framework aligns with a study covered by PsyPost in 2026, which found that emotional fulfillment strongly motivates the pursuit of long-term relationships.
The new study builds on this lineage to see how singles’ core motivations dictate the exact goals they set and whether they achieve them over time. “Previous work suggests that the average single person desires to partner, but it was unclear to us what exactly it is that single people desire from these relationships, if they desire one at all,” said study author Laura Hawkins, a second-year PhD student in psychology at the University of Toronto.
“In other words, what are their goals for romantic partnership?” The research uses this motivational framework to categorize why single people might want a relationship.
These categories include intrinsic motivation, which means enjoying relationships for what they are, and identified motivation, which means personally valuing partnership. They also include introjected motivation, which involves acting to avoid guilt or to boost self-worth, and external motivation, which involves acting due to social pressure. Finally, the researchers measured amotivation, which refers to a complete lack of desire or intention to seek a partner.
To understand how these motivations operate in the real world, the researchers recruited 4,019 single adults between the ages of 18 and 39. Participants completed a baseline survey that measured their motivations for wanting a romantic relationship. They were also asked to write out up to three personal relationship goals for the upcoming six months.
The research team read through the roughly 12,000 written goals and categorized them into 41 distinct themes. These themes included things like going on dates, improving finances, remaining single, or building intimacy. Six months later, 3,176 of the original participants returned for a follow-up survey. They reviewed the goals they had written down previously and rated their progress on a scale from zero to 100 percent. On average, participants reported a 41.7 percent completion rate across their goals.
The results indicate that singles who were intrinsically motivated or had identified motivation set goals focused on high-quality connections. Intrinsically motivated singles had a higher likelihood of setting goals to have fun, build emotional intimacy, and enter a healthy relationship. Identified motivation was linked to seeking committed, long-term partnerships. Both of these groups were far less likely to say their main goal was to remain single.
People driven by a need for self-affirmation or a fear of failure displayed a very different pattern. Singles with this introjected motivation focused more on securing a relationship than on the quality of that connection. They were more likely to set goals to go on dates, have sex, socialize, or improve their physical attractiveness and self-confidence.
At the same time, introjected singles were less likely to prioritize building intimacy, sharing a home, or having a healthy relationship. Interestingly, introjected motivation was also linked to making less progress on relationship goals over the six-month period.
“You would think that entering a relationship is easier than entering a quality relationship,” Hawkins said. “But one finding that surprised me was that singles who simply wanted to enter a relationship (irrespective of quality) actually made less progress on this goal.”
“Although we can’t be sure, we think part of the reason this may be is because these singles are fundamentally pursuing partnership to improve their self-image, which may hinder their ability to build a romantic connection,” she continued. “So, in an ironic twist of fate, the reason they want a relationship may actually be driving potential partners away.”
External motivation, or dating to appease others, was mainly linked to the goal of going on dates. Amotivation was strongly associated with a desire to remain single or setting no relationship goals at all. When evaluating their success six months later, amotivated singles reported the highest amount of progress among all the groups.
“Not every single wants to partner!” Hawkins pointed out. “In fact, our data suggests singles who did not want to partner were not necessarily relationally avoidant, but rather, actively pursuing singlehood.”
These findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost last year. That earlier study, which looked at whether singles actually entered a relationship rather than the specific goals they set, similarly found that autonomous motives support positive romantic outcomes while introjected motives and a lack of motivation do not.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The researchers did not test whether these patterns look different depending on a person’s age, gender, sexual orientation, or cultural background, which could change how people approach dating. The measurement of goal progress also relied entirely on self-reports, which might contain subjective biases.
Additionally, the structural nature of the goals varied wildly from person to person. For example, staying single is an objective a person can accomplish all on their own. Finding a healthy, long-term romantic relationship requires the cooperation of another person. Because of this, the high reported success rate of amotivated singles might simply reflect that it is easier to achieve the goal of staying single than the goal of finding a compatible partner.
“As a singlehood researcher I often get asked ‘how do I find “the one”?'” Hawkins noted. “Our data suggests that answer might lie inwards. Simply put, why you want to become partnered shapes the quality (or lack thereof) of the romantic relationship you seek.”
The study, “Does Why You Want Partnership Shape What You Want? A Self-Determination Perspective on Singles’ Relationship Goals,” was authored by Laura Hawkins, Serena Thapar, Will Ryan, and Geoff MacDonald.

Ukraine's PM and European Commissioner for Economy and Productivity discuss three issues concerning EU financial aid for Ukraine
Following a video conference between European Commissioner for Economy and Productivity Valdis Dombrovskis and Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi on 7 September, the European Commission said it was too early to name a specific amount for Ukraine's financial needs in 2026-2027, and that work to determine it would continue at the technical level.
Source: European Commission spokesperson Balázs Ujvári following the meeting, as reported by European Pravda from Brussels
Details: The European Commission has not yet finalised its assessment of Ukraine's financial needs for 2026 and 2027.
Ujvári said that Dombrovskis and Koretskyi discussed three main issues.
"So they discussed the financing needs of Ukraine for 2026 and 2027. That's one. Second, they looked at the implementation of the reforms which are needed in order to unlock the funding under the €90 billion loan programme. And thirdly, they looked at the preparations for Ukraine's 2027 financing strategy," Ujvári said.
He recalled that to gain access to the funds under the €90 billion loan, Ukraine must prepare financial strategies for both 2026, which has already been prepared and approved, and 2027.
According to Ujvári, "the two sides also agreed that it is important for other international partners to step up to the plate and put forward assistance, be it in the budgetary field or in the field of defence, on top of what the EU has committed".
Ujvári cited Norway as an example, noting that it had recently committed to providing Ukraine with US$9 billion in 2027.
"So this is a good example. This is the path. And we expect other partners as well to step up to the plate," he said.
Meanwhile, the European Commission stressed that the specific scale of Ukraine's financial needs still needs to be determined.
"I think what you need to do first is to get a clear picture of what the budgetary or financial situation is. That is step number one. And then as a potential step number two, you can look at ways of addressing it," Balázs Ujvári explained.
He said that Dombrovskis and Koretskyi's conversation focused specifically on the first stage – assessing the situation and obtaining information from the Ukrainian side.
"So before we can establish a concrete figure, more discussions will be needed. And that's exactly what we'll be doing in the coming days and weeks," he said.
On 8 September, Dombrovskis is also due to meet with Kristalina Georgieva, Managing Director of the International Monetary Fund. According to the spokesperson, the sides will discuss the results of the IMF mission that worked in Ukraine last week.
"The macro financial assistance programme of the EU is highly linked to the IMF programme, which is being rolled out in the country. The common goal there is to get Ukraine to advance reforms which strengthen the country's economic resilience," Balázs Ujvári stressed.
Background:
- The EU previously recalled that the €90 billion in assistance would cover only two-thirds of Ukraine's needs in 2026-2027.
- The EU recently said that Ukraine had not submitted a formal request to the European Commission asking for part of the €90 billion loan planned for 2027 to be disbursed ahead of schedule in 2026 in order to cover Ukraine's €27 billion defence budget shortfall this year.
- On 24 August, the European Commission approved €6.1 billion in defence procurement for Ukraine as part of the EU's €90 billion loan.
- The EU is expected to disburse around €20 billion to Ukraine by the end of 2026, with new tranches potentially arriving in the coming weeks.

Taiz again emerges as battlefield of choice in Yemen renewed war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
12:58:59 UTC
21:58:59 KST

Breadcrumb
Taiz again emerges as battlefield of choice in Yemen renewed war
The latest fighting around Taiz has revived fears of another major battle for one of Yemen's biggest cities.
But military analysts say the Houthis may have little interest in actually storming it.
Instead, they argue, the group's more achievable objective is to cut the roads keeping Taiz connected to the rest of government-held Yemen - and gradually make the city harder to sustain.
"The real danger does not lie in a direct attack, but in the Houthis succeeding in cutting the supply arteries and turning the siege into a permanent reality," military and security affairs researcher Assem al-Mujahid told The New Arab.
"Accordingly, the western front remains the key to the battle for Taiz: if the supply routes remain open and the forces retain the ability to manoeuvre, the strangulation project will remain obstructed, while cutting this corridor would mean subjugating the city without the need for a comprehensive assault."
That helps explain the pattern of the latest escalation.
The Houthis have launched intense attacks west of Taiz, using ballistic missiles and drones and temporarily breaking through government lines. But around the city itself, their strategy has largely involved pressure on roads and supply routes rather than an attempt to seize its densely populated neighbourhoods.
Al-Mujahid said: "The forces defending the city have accumulated extensive field experience in urban and mountain warfare, which has pushed the Houthis to favour a strategy of strangulation and attrition rather than entering a direct battle to storm the city."
Why Taiz matters
Taiz is Yemen's most populous governorate, with close to four million inhabitants.
Its importance is also strategic. To the west lie the port of Mocha and the approaches to the Bab al-Mandab Strait, one of the world's most important shipping routes.
Control of the governorate is divided among several anti-Houthi forces as well as the Houthis.
The internationally recognised government controls much of Taiz city and large parts of the governorate. On the western coast, the National Resistance forces of Tariq Saleh - an anti-Houthi commander who sits on Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council - control Mocha and other coastal districts.
The Houthis control much of the north and east, including the economically important al-Hawban area north-east of the city.
Al-Hawban contains major factories, trading companies and markets, giving the Houthis access to substantial revenues while most of densely populated Taiz city remains under their opponents' administration.
That makes the current division of the city economically useful to the group: it can extract revenue without assuming the full cost of governing Taiz.
The battle for the roads
The latest offensive began early last Thursday after the Houthis fired 14 ballistic missiles as well as drones, followed by fighting that lasted around 15 hours.
They temporarily reached strategic positions including Jabal Nu'man in Jabal Habashi district, before government and allied forces counter-attacked and recovered many of them.
At al-Kadha, an important link between Taiz and the western coast, anti-Houthi forces also repelled the attack.
Reinforcements have since arrived from the Giants Brigades, a powerful southern anti-Houthi force, and Nation's Shield, another military force aligned with Yemen's internationally recognised authorities.
The significance of the fighting lies in two crucial roads.
One connects Taiz with Mocha and the western coast. Another runs south-west towards Aden, the interim seat of Yemen's government.
For residents, they are not simply military supply routes. They are among the main arteries carrying civilians, food and commercial goods into and out of the city.
The Houthis have also targeted al-Wazi'iyah bridge, an important route between Taiz and the western coast.
"The Houthis understand that controlling the supply routes would give them the ability to gradually strangle the city and recreate the siege model of the early years of the war," al-Mujahid said.
"The Houthi objective at the current stage is focused on exhausting Taiz until it reaches a point where it loses its ability to withstand pressure, with the aim of draining the government and blackmailing it politically and militarily."
The consequences of cutting those routes could include higher prices, disruption to trade and further displacement among a population that has already endured years of war.
It could also give the Houthis greater leverage in future political negotiations.
Why not simply capture the city?
Taking Taiz would be extremely difficult.
The city consists of densely packed neighbourhoods surrounded by mountainous terrain, including Jabal Sabir, which provides defenders with a powerful natural position.
Government forces and local fighters have also accumulated more than a decade of experience in urban and mountain warfare.
Al-Mujahid said: "Taiz's rugged geography, the high ground surrounding it, and the complex nature of fighting inside residential areas make any large-scale attack a military adventure with uncertain results."
Military analyst Colonel Sarhan al-Muhaya argues that years of fortification have made the city's defences significantly stronger.
"The positions of the National Army inside Taiz have become literally impregnable, thanks to strong engineering fortifications combined with the rugged geography and innovative obstacles, alongside the precise implementation of concealment and camouflage principles. All of this has created a firm conviction among the Houthis that achieving any breakthrough is impossible, regardless of how long the war lasts or the intensity of firepower, meaning that the attacks result in human and material losses for them."
Even a successful assault would carry substantial costs.
The Houthis would have to fight through a hostile and heavily damaged city, then take responsibility for services and infrastructure serving a large civilian population.
By contrast, their current position around Taiz allows them to retain economic influence and military pressure without bearing those costs.
"The Houthis' dreams of controlling the al-Dhabab road and the Taiz-Mocha road, and closing the remaining corridors under the control of government forces, are unattainable, and Houthi forces will not be able to achieve them."
He added: "It has been proven theoretically and practically that the Houthi forces are unable to retake any territory they have lost in Taiz governorate despite their repeated attempts."
Fakhr al-Azb is a Yemeni journalist based in Taiz. Writes for Al-Araby Al-Jadeed, The New Arab's Arabic-language sister edition.

Oxford University museum to return human remains to Naga people

Oxford University museum to return human remains to Naga people in India
- Oxford University’s Pitt Rivers Museum will return 39 human remains to the Naga community in north-east India, collected during Britain’s colonial era.
- The repatriation is part of a wider movement to return artefacts and remains taken by Western institutions during colonial times.
- The museum is coordinating with the Naga community for a handover ceremony, highlighting the importance of memory and heritage restoration.
AI generated
LONDON – Oxford University’s Pitt Rivers Museum will return the remains of 39 people taken during Britain’s colonial era to the Naga community in north-east India, the museum said on Sept 7.
The museum, which holds the world’s largest collection of Naga artefacts, confirmed it was preparing the repatriation after the university approved a restitution request by the Forum for Naga Reconciliation (FNR).
The remains “have been away from their homeland for far too long”, museum director Laura Van Broekhoven said in a statement.
The human remains were collected in the early 20th century by British colonial administrators, and some remained on public display until 2020.
“Repatriation, for the Nagas, is not simply about bones and ancestral remains finding their way back to the land but importantly about memory returning to where it belongs,” the FNR and other Naga organisations said in a statement, welcoming the agreement.
The request covered 40 sets of human remains, Pitt Rivers Museum said.
Oxford University approved the return of 39 of them on July 13, concluding that one specimen “does not have a clear provenance as Naga”.
The museum said it was “working closely” with the Naga community to agree on a date for a handover ceremony, which has not been set yet.
The agreement forms part of a wider international movement to repatriate artefacts and human remains acquired by Western institutions during the colonial era.
In 2022, London’s Horniman Museum returned 72 artefacts to Nigeria, including 12 Benin bronze artefacts, and earlier in 2026 the University of Edinburgh returned the skulls of six people to a Native American group.
Greece has for decades demanded the return from Britain of the Parthenon Marbles, saying they were looted in the early 19th century by Lord Elgin, British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire.
London insists they were legally acquired and successive British governments have noted that the decision rests with the British Museum, where they are kept. AFP

The curfew in Kyiv will be shortened to 1 a.m. to 5 a.m. amid intensified Russian aerial attacks on the Ukrainian capital, the city's mayor, Vitali Klitschko, announced on Sept. 7.
The changes will take effect at midnight on Sept. 10, and the public transportation services in Kyiv will also be extended by an hour, according to Klitschko. He said that the working hours of restaurants, cafes, shopping malls, and other venues would remain unaffected.
The curfew reduction comes as the security situation in Kyiv deteriorates, with air raid alerts going off regularly and restricting movements within the city. Round-the-clock Russian drone attacks have targeted Kyiv for over a week, from the end of August to the beginning of September, leaving the city's residents to worry about what awaits them in the upcoming winter.
At the same time, all entertainment and sports events in open air locations or facilities without shelters will be temporarily prohibited in Kyiv, said Klitschko.
Facing a severe shortage of air defense missiles, Ukraine is increasingly strained in its efforts to protect cities, including Kyiv, from heavy Russian missile and drone attacks.
With trains often arriving in the city late, the city will organize four bus routes during curfew so people can get home from Kyiv's central railway station, Klitschko said.
Most restaurants and bars work until 11 p.m. in Kyiv, and the metro currently operates from around 5:30 a.m. to 11 p.m.
Earlier in September, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine will change how air raid alerts operate and introduce red and yellow levels, a change from the previous single air raid alert.
The yellow level corresponds to incoming drones, whereas the red level indicates threats from missiles, including ballistic missiles, and massive combined attacks, according to Zelensky.

John Healey backs growth but says Labour must be honest on spending
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
12:54:05 UTC
21:54:05 KST

John Healey has said boosting economic growth will be his defining mission as chancellor as he warned Labour had to “be honest” about the need to control public spending at next month’s budget.
In his first big speech since taking the job in July, Healey said the top priority for his 28 October budget would be to support stronger growth across the UK while sticking firmly to the government’s fiscal rules.
“I want to be the chancellor that gets things done and I want to see growth driven from more places across the UK,” he said.
Against a backdrop of jittery global financial markets, the chancellor said he and Andy Burnham were “in lockstep” in their commitment to meeting the government’s self-imposed target to balance day-to-day spending with tax receipts by 2029-30.
With the public finances under pressure from soaring long-term bond yields, which hit an 18-year high last week, Healey argued that stronger growth was the most sustainable way to balance the books. However, he also signalled that his budget would require Labour “being honest about the need to control government spending”.
Economists have warned the chancellor could be forced to increase taxes or cut spending in response to rising spending pressures and the economic fallout from the war in Iran triggering turmoil in global bond markets.
The UK’s 10-year borrowing costs rose slightly on Monday amid pressure on governments worldwide, as fears over the impact of the war pushed the price of oil closer to $100 a barrel.
Aiming to soothe concerns in a speech to business leaders at a manufacturing centre in Coventry, Healey said Britain was continuing to pay a “Truss penalty” almost four years since the former Conservative prime minister’s ill-fated mini-budget triggered a meltdown in the UK government bond market.
With Labour under pressure amid questions over Burnham’s tax and spending priorities and as the UK carmaker Jaguar Land Rover – headquartered down the road from the venue for his speech – announced plans to cut 4,000 jobs, Healey said maintaining fiscal discipline was important in an uncertain and volatile world.
“It makes our task in government harder. It makes the task of every business looking to invest much harder, too,” he added.
Business groups said they welcomed the chancellor’s pro-growth message, including pledges to devolve tax and spending powers to regional mayors and also his promise to “take an axe” to regulations he said were holding back business investment.
Louise Hellem, the chief economist at the Confederation of British Industry, said: “Firms will welcome the positive signals of intent from the chancellor and will now be looking ahead to the budget to see whether the government can match its ambition with decisive action to cut business costs and give firms the headroom they need to invest.”
The chancellor’s critics said his speech was light on detail despite the mounting pressure on the economy.
Andrew Griffith, the Conservative shadow chancellor, said: “John Healey sounds increasingly like continuity Rachel Reeves. Warm words about growth will not make growth a reality, or cover up the enormous damage Labour have done to businesses and family finances.”
Robert Jenrick, Reform UK’s Treasury spokesperson, said: “On the day 4,000 people are losing their jobs, Healey gave a dire and dreary speech that will change absolutely nothing.”
Refusing to be drawn on the details of his tax and spending plans less than two months before the budget, Healey promised to stick to Labour’s manifesto commitments not to raise taxes on working people. However, he signalled the government could look at finding savings from the welfare bill by tackling youth unemployment.
“As the prime minister has said, there is a need to bring down welfare costs. And most importantly for me we have to get more of Britain working again,” he said.
The chancellor ducked questions on whether taxes would need to rise and also a suggestion from the British Chambers of Commerce that the government should scrap the pensions triple lock to fund a cut in employer national insurance contributions to help support youth jobs.
The government is awaiting the findings of a highly anticipated review into youth worklessness by the former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn, which Healey said would “address this scar of youth unemployment”.
Healey said there was a “moral duty” and a “fiscal duty” to supporting young people to find work.
“A person coming off benefits and into work saves the taxpayer money. And that becomes a win-win when those people start paying tax themselves,” he said.

25 years after 9/11, Taliban rules Afghanistan again, but with U.S. firepower
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
12:54:03 UTC
21:54:03 KST

25 years after Sept. 11 attacks, Taliban rules Afghanistan again, but now with $7 billion in U.S. firepower
Kabul — As Americans reflect this week on the 25 years that have passed since the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, CBS News has returned to Afghanistan, where the war those attacks triggered ended five years ago with the Taliban's stunning return to power.
When the last U.S. and allied soldiers left after a brutal two-decade war, the Taliban's fighters seized billions of dollars worth of American-purchased military hardware. President Trump, whose first administration negotiated the deal to end the war with the Taliban, has accused the Biden administration of "totally botching" the withdrawal.
Five years later, the hardware of America's longest-ever war is still easy to spot on the streets of Kabul. Taliban fighters patrol in armored vehicles once supplied to Afghan forces, wearing American tactical gear and carrying American weapons.
CBS News saw one Humvee in the Afghan capital still adorned with a faded Green Bay Packers decal — a remnant from its past operators.
President Trump has been fiercely critical of the former Biden administration, accusing his predecessor of allowing the U.S. military to abandon billions of dollars in military hardware. Mr. Trump has demanded that the Taliban hand it back.
But the Taliban has proudly shown off its American-funded arsenal, even staging military parades through Kabul's streets.
Pentagon figures released last year show some $7 billion in hardware and weaponry fell into the group's hands when the Afghan National Army collapsed.
Shortly after the 2021 withdrawal, CBS News filmed as "Badri 313," an elite Taliban special forces battalion, patrolled in their American vehicles, American commando gear and with their American weapons.
Asked about President Trump's determination to reclaim the equipment, Taliban Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Abdul Qahar Balkhi told CBS News the hardware now belongs to "the state of Afghanistan, and we are not in the business of doing transactions and deals on the assets of the state of Afghanistan."
When it was pointed out that American taxpayers purchased the equipment, Balkhi said: "The Americans did a lot of things. Americans killed a lot of people, destroyed the majority of the country. Should they not be paying for that first?"
The Taliban waged a vicious insurgency during a war that killed more than 2,400 U.S. service members and tens of thousands of innocent Afghans.
But critics of the Biden administration's handling of the U.S. withdrawal say it's allowed the Taliban to transform from insurgents into a state military force armed with billions of dollars in American-funded firepower.
They have used those weapons to impose a draconian interpretation of Islamic rule on Afghanistan's people, almost completely depriving women and girls of the right to work and study, and restricting life for everyone in the country in ways that some analysts say are even harsher than during the group's previous reign.
Biden has offered little public commentary on the Afghanistan withdrawal, but he said in September 2021, a month after the Taliban took back control, that he "was not going to extend this 'forever war,' and I was not extending a 'forever exit.'"
"If anything, the developments of the past week reinforce that ending U.S. military involvement in Afghanistan now was the right decision," said the then-president in August 2021, as the Taliban reasserted their rule 20 years after being ousted by the U.S.-led military campaign. "American troops cannot and should not be fighting in a war and dying in a war that Afghan forces are not willing to fight for themselves."
In 2023, the Biden White House released a 12-page summary of a classified review of the Afghanistan exit that largely blamed the Trump administration for the deal it struck with the Taliban to withdraw U.S. forces from the country by May 2021.
The so-called Doha Agreement brokered by the first Trump administration laid out a series of conditions for the Taliban to fulfill in order for U.S. forces to leave. Another report partially declassified and released by the State Department in 2023 faulted both the Trump and Biden administrations for "insufficient" planning surrounding the withdrawal.

Qom: A province of ancient beacons along historic routes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
12:53:46 UTC
21:53:46 KST

Qom: A province of ancient beacons along historic routes
TEHRAN - Scattered across the mountains, plains and historic routes of Qom province, a group of ancient Meels, standalone beacon towers once used to guide travelers and caravans, offers a distinctive glimpse into the history of travel and communication in central Iran.
Often standing on elevated ground overlooking old roads and passes, the structures are among the lesser-known heritage sites of Qom. Their locations, architecture and relationship with ancient routes could make them compelling destinations for travelers, historians, architects and enthusiasts of Iran’s cultural heritage.
Speaking to ISNA, historian and researcher Hossein Sadeqi says Qom is unusual in having a relatively large concentration of historic Meels, with the structures spread across different parts of the province. Based on existing roads, the distance between some of them is estimated at around 50 kilometers.
The term Meel historically referred to a standalone beacon or light-bearing structure. Such towers were built beside important roads and routes, particularly in periods before and during the Islamic era, to help travelers and caravans navigate difficult terrain. Fires were traditionally lit at their upper sections, allowing people to identify the route during darkness or in fog.
Unlike minarets attached to mosques or other religious buildings, these structures were originally independent ones. According to Sadeqi, their functions included guiding travelers as well as communication and signaling. Their elaborate architectural features in some cases, however, have led researchers to consider whether certain examples served additional purposes.
Most surviving historic Meels in Iran date from the fourth to sixth centuries AH, although examples attributed to earlier periods also exist. Many were equipped with stairways leading to their upper sections, with some featuring separate spiral staircases.
Aliabad Meel
The stone Meel of Aliabad stands about 50 kilometers along the Qom-Tehran road, beside the historic stone castle of Aliabad. Built on an elevated hill, it is believed to have served as a landmark for caravans.
The tower is about 11 meters high and has an arched entrance approximately 1.5 meters wide. Spiral stairs lead toward the upper section. Stone and sarooj, a traditional Iranian waterproof mortar, were used in its construction.
Several rows of what appear to be reed pipes can be seen in the structure at a height of about three meters. Sadeqi suggests that these may have been incorporated to reduce the effects of ground vibrations.
The cylindrical structure has a base diameter of about 4.33 meters. Its association with the nearby Seljuk-era caravanserai and its construction style have led researchers to attribute it to the Seljuk period.
Imamzadeh Abdullah Meel
Another historic beacon stands outside the city of Qom along the old Qom-Isfahan road, near Cheshmeh Ali village. Located on high ground, the structure has a conical form and was once accompanied by a protective enclosure, of which only walls remain.
The Meel rises about 6.4 meters and has a base diameter of approximately 5.5 meters. Its exterior is built of rubble stone and gypsum mortar. The structure stands around 200 meters above the surrounding plain.
Its form and construction suggest that it dates from the Seljuk period.
Babak Meel
Babak Meel occupies one of the highest peaks of the northern mountain range overlooking the valley. From the tower, the surrounding valleys can be seen clearly.
Only about 3.7 meters of the northern section of Babak Meel survives. Its exterior consists of rubble stone and gypsum and sarooj mortar.
Chahak Meel
Chahak Meel lies in the Khalajestan district, east of Chahak village and north of the Vezva River, on high ground overlooking the surrounding plain.
Pottery from both the Sasanian and Islamic periods has been found in the area. Its masonry and architectural form have been compared with a Sasanian-era Chahar-Taq, leading to an attribution to the Sasanian period.
The surviving structure is about 4.6 meters high at its highest point and has a base diameter of roughly 5.1 meters. Its exterior is circular, while its interior follows a cross-shaped plan, recalling the architecture of Sasanian Chahar-taqs, or four-arched structures.
Shahrestan Meel
Shahrestan Meel stands in central Qom province, and it is attributed to the Sasanian period and is thought to have stood within the ancient settlement known as Shahrestan.
The area, now called Mazraeh Shahrestan, is believed to have been a fortified site in antiquity and a village by the fourth century AH.
The tower has been heavily affected by erosion and now resembles a cone-shaped structure. It stands about 7.5 meters high and was built of mud brick.
Safarali Meel
Safarali Meel rises on a mountain opposite Mount Sepor-e Rostam, west of Kaj village. The site commands extensive views over the surrounding settlements and plains.
The structure is about 6.8 meters high, with a base diameter of approximately seven meters. Its exterior is made of rubble stone and sarooj, while the interior was constructed without mortar.
Much of its interior is filled with rubble stone, while a circular chamber survives above it. The chamber has a floor diameter of about 3.45 meters and walls approximately 1.7 meters thick.
An opening on the eastern side faces Kaj village. The tower's elevated position provides views toward Mohammadabad, Korgol, Aliabad, Bayer Kalhar, Malek Qaleh and surrounding seasonal settlements.
Pottery found around the site includes prehistoric material as well as pottery associated with the Seljuk period. The latter has contributed to the attribution of the surviving Meel to that era.
Maghbulabad Meel
In Khalajestan, southwest of Maghbulabad village, another Meel survives at an elevation of about 1,893 meters above sea level and approximately 65 meters above the surrounding plain.
Its architectural style is attributed to the Seljuk period. The tower was constructed from local rubble stone and gypsum mortar and originally had a cylindrical form.
Only about 2.7 meters of its height survives today. Its strategic position is particularly notable: the tower stands at a point from which it could have served travelers using the historic routes connecting Saveh, Tafresh and Qom.
Although it has little decorative ornamentation, the arrangement of its masonry remains of architectural interest.
Meem Meel
Meem Meel, located in the village of Meem in Kahak district, resembles Safarali Meel but is smaller.
The structure stands roughly 85 to 90 meters above the surrounding plain and is about nine meters high. Its base diameter is approximately 4.62 meters.
Built of rubble stone and gypsum mortar, it has a conical exterior and an enclosed chamber inside. Its architectural similarities with other Qom beacons have led researchers to attribute it to the Seljuk period.
Rahjerd Meel
The stone Meel of Rahjerd stands near Dizijan village on the heights of Mount Zanbureh, overlooking a gorge and the Zavvarian passage in the Rahjerd area.
Approximately 4.25 meters of the structure survives. Its base diameter is about 6.3 meters, and it rises roughly 60 meters above the surrounding plain.
Its rubble-stone construction and gypsum mortar are similar to those used in other Seljuk-period Meels in Qom province.
Taken together, these structures form a scattered network of architectural landmarks that reflects the importance of movement across central Iran long before modern roads transformed the landscape. Their locations on high ground, near passes and along historic routes reveal a practical relationship between architecture and travel.
For modern visitors, the appeal of Qom's Meels lies partly in their isolation. Unlike major monuments located in urban centers, many of these towers survive amid mountains, plains and old travel corridors. Reaching them can therefore offer not only an encounter with historic architecture but also a sense of the landscapes through which merchants, pilgrims and caravans once moved.
