Chris Horton launches Taiwan edition of ‘Ghost Nation’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
12:53:07 UTC
21:53:07 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — On Saturday night in Taipei, down a quiet alley in the city’s Wanhua District, just a couple of blocks from the glowing screen-lit concourses of Ximending, a small bookshop rooted in the Xi-era Hong Kong and China diasporas hosted a capacity crowd for an event with an American writer.
Chris Horton, a journalist based in Taiwan for over a decade, had come to Nowhere Books to give a talk for the release of the Mandarin edition of his book “Ghost Nation: The Story of Taiwan and Its Struggle for Survival” (幽影之國：台灣的故事與其奮鬥求生的400年). Over the past year, he has traveled around Asia, Europe, and North America promoting it.
Horton has written on Taiwan for a long list of international publications, including The New York Times, The Atlantic, Nikkei Asia, and Bloomberg, where he was a staff writer. Before moving to Taiwan, he lived for many years in China followed by a stint in Hong Kong.
Although long known to people who follow English-language news about Taiwan, Horton’s profile has risen with the book’s publication, with the likes of Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim (蕭美琴) even photographed handing out copies to visiting lawmakers.
The following draws on Horton’s talk and written responses to questions from Taiwan News.
On the relevance of the Mandarin edition of Ghost Nation
“I have been very lucky to have interviewed a lot of the people who have shaped modern Taiwan,” Horton wrote to Taiwan News. “That includes the last interviews given by both Lee Teng-hui and Su Beng, as well as the first interview with Tsai Ing-wen after she stepped down as president.”
“I also had the good fortune to interview Lin Fei-fan shortly before he was appointed to the National Security Council — he really opened up about his political journey, starting with when his father would take him to protests as a kid. I think Kolas Yotaka's words describing the subtle and less-subtle types of discrimination faced by Indigenous Taiwanese might offer food for thought for non-Indigenous Taiwanese.”
“I also know how difficult it can be to explain Taiwan to foreigners. I hope the book can be useful to Taiwanese people who want their foreign partners, family, and friends to better understand their homeland so that they can have more substantial discussions of Taiwan's past, present, and future.”
On Chinese namefare over Taiwan
“Taiwan isn’t seen even when it is seen,” Horton told the audience at his event. “When you win a gold medal in the Olympics, you have this ridiculous flag, this Olympic flag with the plum blossom and the KMT emblem in the center, and nobody in the world knows what that is.”
“Actually, that KMT emblem is very appropriate because it was the KMT who negotiated the whole Zhonghua Taibei (中華台北, Chinese Taipei) silliness in 1981,” he explained.
He went on to note that Beijing has pressured journalists to refer to Tibet by the Chinese name Xizang (西藏), while East Turkestan becomes Xinjiang (新疆), meaning “new frontier” or “new territory”; Inner Mongolia becomes Beijiang (北疆), or “northern frontier”; and even Manchuria, homeland of the Manchus whose loose and overextended Qing Empire provides the historical basis for many of China’s expansive territorial claims, is simply Dongbei (東北), or “the northeast,” in contemporary CCP parlance.
“That’s what awaits Taiwan if it becomes part of China,” he said.
On historical misconceptions about Taiwan
“I lived in China for 13 years and Hong Kong for two before ever visiting Taiwan,” Horton wrote in an email. “I'd absorbed much more of the CCP line on Taiwan than I thought I had.”
“I didn't realize the Dutch were the first outsiders to colonize Taiwan. I didn't realize just how big Japan's influence on modern Taiwanese identity was and still is. I had no idea about 228 — not only the atrocities committed by the KMT, but also how the United States provided material support and political cover for the massacres of March 1947.”
“When I first arrived in Taiwan, most international coverage of Taiwan was done by China-based reporters who wrote about Taiwan from a Chinese perspective, often only including Chinese and KMT commentators. I didn't know at the time that the four years between 1945 and 1949 were the only four years in all of human history that a Chinese-identifying government based in China controlled all of Taiwan. Perhaps the biggest surprise was that Taiwan controlled territory across the strait in Kinmen and Matsu.”
On whether Taiwan has become less of a ghost in recent years
“I started writing the book in 2022. In the four-plus years since then, I would say the world sees and understands Taiwan much better than before. While there is much room for improvement of international media coverage of Taiwan, it is being covered with more breadth and depth than ever before, although starting from a relatively low bar,” he wrote.
“Regarding Taiwan's global visibility, it is worth noting that China does not control this; it is the rest of the world's countries who actually control how visible Taiwan is, and most of them tend to pretend Taiwan and their relations with Taiwan don't exist in order to avoid offending Beijing. The CCP knows this, which is why it attempts to disrupt or suppress any display of Taiwan's sovereignty or international solidarity with Taiwan anywhere on the planet.”
“It is the complicity of the world's largest and most powerful democracies in Taiwan's international isolation that I find most hypocritical. That said, as with international journalism, I would say that this has improved noticeably in recent years, and the diplomatic corps in Taipei is bigger than it's ever been since Taiwan's democratization in the 1990s, and Taipei-based diplomats have been more vocal than ever in speaking up for Taiwan, both here on the ground and when reporting back to their capitals.”
On whether he is more concerned about Taiwan than before
“Certainly more,” Horton wrote. “While I don't think an attack by China is likely this year or the next, I do see the next presidential election being likely to precipitate a crisis.”
“Should Lai win, then Xi may abandon hope of the KMT ever returning to power and decide to increase pressure. Should the KMT win, the government would in all likelihood move closer to Beijing, leading to social unrest.”
“Meanwhile as the PLA continues to upgrade its capabilities, especially in drones and robots, I worry that Taiwan's ability to deter is being weakened by the KMT-TPP coalition that currently controls the Legislative Yuan. With the PLA leadership whittled down by Xi's ongoing purge, Taiwan has a golden opportunity right now to build up its domestic defense industry, especially drones.”
“But for Taiwanese companies to make large long-term investments, there must be signalling from the government that it is committed to procurement going forward. The KMT and TPP stripped that signalling from Lai's special defense budget, resulting in the stunting of the drone industry's development here, and just as crucially, wasted time as Xi works to get his military in order.”
Green shoots and room to maneuver
“Taiwan’s visibility is not determined by Taiwan, and it’s not determined by China; it’s determined by the outside world,” Horton said to the crowd as the evening wore on. Regarding the Gwangju Biennale in South Korea, where China recently failed to pressure organizers to keep Taiwanese artists out of a major art world event, he said, “That was Taiwan winning one. China took its ball and went home. And that doesn’t happen very often.”
“What was the key?” he said. “Local solidarity. The communists aren’t good at what they do. They’re just relentless.”
He reminded the largely Taiwanese audience that Taiwan has leverage too: last year, a threat to restrict semiconductor exports to South Africa after the country downgraded Taiwan’s representative offices and sought to force its Pretoria office to relocate to Johannesburg marked a more assertive turn in Taiwanese diplomacy.
Toward the close of the event, Horton asked, “If everyone starts calling Taiwan a country, what’s Beijing going to do? Blow up the whole world?”
The line drew a burst of uneasy laughter from the audience. Soon afterward, attendees began lining up for the book signing.

Taiwan Chemicals Administration warns cat owners over insecticides
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
12:52:43 UTC
21:52:43 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Chemicals Administration urged cat owners on Monday to keep their pets away from areas where insecticides are being used, according to a press release.
The agency said some bug sprays contain pyrethrins, which are more toxic to cats than to humans and most other mammals. It issued a public reminder telling owners to protect their cats from direct and second-hand exposure.
The agency said cats are less able to metabolize the chemicals and are therefore more likely to develop severe symptoms after exposure. It warned owners not to spray insecticides directly on their cats and instead use approved veterinary flea treatments according to a veterinarian’s instructions.
The agency decided with experts and vendors to add warning labels. Existing products will not be subject to a mandatory recall, though retailers are encouraged to provide additional warnings at points of sale.
The agency recommended that owners keep cats away after spraying and sufficiently ventilate treated areas until the chemicals have dried to minimize exposure.
According to the Ministry of Agriculture, Taiwan had an estimated 1.74 million pet cats in 2025, a 32.8% increase from 1.31 million in 2023. The number of households owning two or more cats has also increased.

Saudi Arabia preparing to grant IAEA more intrusive powers, Grossi says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
12:51:59 UTC
21:51:59 KST

Saudi Arabia preparing to grant IAEA more intrusive powers, Grossi says
VIENNA, Sept 7 - A planned U.S.-Saudi atomic deal does not include Riyadh signing the Additional Protocol that gives the U.N. nuclear watchdog sweeping inspection powers, but something close to it on some points is in the works, the agency's chief said on Monday.
The U.S. and Saudi Arabia reached an agreement on civil nuclear power cooperation in July that would let Riyadh enrich uranium and build nuclear reactors using U.S. technology.
Non-proliferation groups, such as the Arms Control Association, have criticised the planned "123 agreement" for not including the Additional Protocol, which grants the International Atomic Energy Agency extra powers such as the ability to carry out snap inspections at undeclared locations.
Iran implemented the Additional Protocol from 2016 to 2021 under a nuclear deal with major powers that unravelled after the U.S. pulled out in 2018.
IAEA chief Rafael Grossi said while the Additional Protocol would be the "ideal setup", Riyadh was preparing to go beyond its core obligations under its Comprehensive Safeguards Agreement governing relations with the IAEA.
"What is important is that in the consultations, in the preparation process, it has been possible to introduce a number of provisions to the bilateral agreement that will give the agency additional verification and monitoring authorisations," he told a press conference.
Those would be in relation to activities such as uranium enrichment and the step preceding it known as uranium conversion, as well as reprocessing, which can separate plutonium from spent reactor fuel.
"These are sensitive activities, as we all know. So for those we are going to have authorisations and capacities which are very, very similar to those that you may find in an Additional Protocol," he said, without elaborating.
Once the details are finalised, the bilateral agreement between the IAEA and Saudi Arabia will be presented to the IAEA's 35-nation Board of Governors, Grossi said. REUTERS

Francesca Albanese, the United Nations special rapporteur on the Palestinian territories, warned in a statement Monday that the implications of Israel's "ongoing removal, crushing and relocation of rubble in Gaza" risked erasing traces of "atrocity crimes", and preventing the recovery and identification of human remains.
"Gaza's rubble contains human remains and physical evidence relevant to the investigation of alleged international crimes, including genocide," she said, pointing to estimates from Palestinian authorities that more than 10,000 people remain buried under the debris in the war-ravaged Palestinian enclave.

The Italian-born independent expert has faced harsh criticism from Israel and some of its allies over her long-standing accusations that Israel is committing genocide and other war crimes against Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
Albanese, who was appointed by the UN Human Rights Council in 2022 but who does not speak on behalf of the United Nations, said she had received credible information from multiple sources last month of "deliberate and widespread removal, crushing and transport of rubble".
In the devastated, Israeli-occupied Palestinian territory, "rubble is not just construction waste", the expert insisted.

China releases 5-year development plan for information, communications sector
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
20:50:10 CST
21:50:10 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology has issued a development plan for the information and communications industry during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030) to promote the high-quality development of this sector.
By 2030, a new-generation communications network with comprehensive coverage and leading performance is expected to be fully established, according to the plan, which has called for efforts to accelerate the development of a technologically advanced, secure and controllable information and communications industrial system.
Meanwhile, an agile and efficient governance system integrating technology and management is expected to be effectively established, and network and data security capabilities featuring all-domain coordination and practical application will be significantly enhanced, the plan said.
The industry's empowerment level and degree of globalization will be further improved, laying a solid foundation for basically achieving modernization of the information and communications sector by 2035, the plan added.
The plan also outlines 13 key indicators, including achieving information and communications industry revenue of 4.1 trillion yuan (about 604.8 billion U.S. dollars) by 2030, cumulative investment of 3.8 trillion yuan in information infrastructure, and an average annual growth rate of 7 percent in total telecommunications business volume.
By 2030, there will be 50 5G (including 5G-A) base stations per 10,000 people, intelligent computing power will reach 9,800 EFLOPS, and the 5G user penetration rate will reach 95 percent, the ministry said.
EFLOPS, or ExaFLOPS, is a unit of computing performance, with each unit representing 1 quintillion floating-point operations per second.
The plan lays out 26 key tasks across six major areas including information infrastructure construction as well as network and data security assurance. Among these, it specifically highlights the need to initiate 6G commercial services at an appropriate time and to accelerate the establishment of a nationwide integrated computing power network.
Specific measures also include building an industry anti‑fraud laboratory and supporting enterprises to deeply promote the integration of artificial intelligence and manufacturing, the plan said.
China has established the world's largest information infrastructure. Gigabit optical network access is available in every county, while 5G networks covers all towns and more than 95 percent of administrative villages.
The country is pushing ahead with its Digital China initiative, aiming to raise the added value of the core industries of the digital economy to 12.5 percent of GDP by 2030, according to the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030). ■

FREETOWN, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- Former Sierra Leonean president Ernest Bai Koroma returned to Freetown, the country's capital, on Sunday after criminal proceedings against him over an alleged coup attempt were dropped.
Koroma, 72, arrived from Nigeria accompanied by former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo and was received by Sierra Leone's Foreign Affairs Minister Mohamed Rahman Swaray.
The Sierra Leonean government dropped the criminal proceedings against the former president in July, ending a legal case that had followed a failed coup attempt in November 2023.
Koroma was charged with treason and placed under house arrest after gunmen attacked a military barracks and two prisons in Freetown, freeing more than 2,200 inmates. At least 21 people, including 14 soldiers, were killed in clashes during the incident.
The government had alleged that the attackers were backed by the former president, an accusation Koroma has denied.
The former president, who ruled Sierra Leone from 2007 to 2018, was later granted bail on medical grounds and permitted to travel to Nigeria in January 2024. ■

Economic Watch: From VR dinosaurs to beer index, China's tourism offers novel experience
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
20:49:45 CST
21:49:45 KST

TIANJIN, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- At an exhibition booth, visitors used game consoles to control cartoon dinosaurs racing across prehistoric landscapes in an immersive virtual world.
This was one of China Dinosaur Park's programs displayed at the 2026 China Culture & Tourism Industries Expo in north China's Tianjin last week.
The interactive experience was one example of how tourist attractions in China are turning to technology to reinvent the visitor experience.
The dinosaur park, one of the world's largest, sits in eastern China's Changzhou city. It has in recent years introduced virtual reality (VR) and mixed reality (MR) headsets, allowing guests to enter digital prehistoric worlds and interact with lifelike dinosaurs.
Traditional culture is also presented in an innovative way to appeal to modern consumers.
At the booth for Dong'e Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) Culture and Tourism Area, shelves were filled with ejiao (donkey-hide gelatin) products, incense, accessories and souvenirs.
In Dong'e County, east China's Shandong Province, attractions have been built around the centuries-old craft of making ejiao, which has been recognized as a national intangible cultural heritage item. This culture and tourism area now boasts museums, an experience factory, TCM study tours, wellness programs and heritage workshops.
"Visitors can tour the museums, learn how ejiao is made, and experience blended Chinese incense-making," said Chen Xiaoming, a booth staff member.
In 2025, the Dong'e TCM-themed tourist attractions recorded 1.07 million visits and more than 100 million yuan (about 14.8 million U.S. dollars) in operating revenue.
According to China's Ministry of Culture and Tourism, Chinese residents made 3.46 billion domestic trips in the first half of 2026, up 5.4 percent year on year, while their domestic tourism spending rose 2 percent to 3.21 trillion yuan.
Cross-industry integration is reshaping the tourism sector and blurring boundaries between tourism and other forms of consumption.
Experts at the Tianjin exhibition, which attracted over 2,500 culture and tourism enterprises from 20 countries and regions, noted that demand for high-quality cultural and tourism products, immersive experiences and diversified consumption scenarios continues to rise.
The Chinese government approved a five-year consumption promotion plan in July, calling for fostering new forms, models and scenarios of consumption.
At the expo, Beijing-based recreational vehicle (RV) firm Xingchengyao displayed Class C motorhomes, pickup campers and camper vans.
"We want the vehicles themselves to become part of the travel experience," said Wang Li, the company's operations director. "We have vehicles that can provide mobile stages for performances in scenic areas, and pickup campers that can be paired with camping or desert tours."
In 2025, Xingchengyao signed agreements with automotive and tourism partners to develop a new RV-tourism ecosystem, with plans to procure 20,000 vehicles over the next three years at a contract value of 2.2 billion yuan.
Another attraction at the expo was a beer exhibition featuring a giant screen displaying a stock market scenario, where beer prices fluctuated in real time based on sales. At the "beer exchange," visitors could buy beer as if trading shares.
On the expo's opening day, a total of 1,200 half-liter cups and 220 1.5-liter bottles were sold.
The combination of beer and tourism has already gained traction in Qingdao, a coastal city in Shandong known for its brewing heritage. A similar beer exchange opened there in May 2025, attracting an average of more than 10,000 visitors daily, with single-day sales this summer vacation exceeding 1,200 liters.
"Competition among tourism products has entered a new stage," said Ge Lei, secretary-general of the China Tourism Association. "It is now centered on content, experience and creativity." ■

Interview: Long-term thinking key to building global brand, says CUKTECH executive
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
20:49:39 CST
21:49:39 KST

BERLIN, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) - As technological change reshapes the global consumer-electronics landscape, competition is increasingly moving beyond raw specifications toward more sophisticated engineering, more intuitive interaction and new applications of existing technologies. At IFA Berlin 2026, this evolution is visible in the growing emphasis on how technological advances can translate into better products and new possibilities for everyday use.
For Eric Wang, chief marketing officer of Chinese charging-technology firm CUKTECH and head of its design center, good product design should combine performance with visual restraint. The company's devices, he said in a recent interview with Xinhua, should look "cool" while conveying a sense of quality and performance, yet should not become "the loudest voice in the environment."
Wang also believes a strong design language should carry across generations of products. His aim is to create devices that remain relevant over time, with each iteration retaining enough common details to make the brand immediately recognizable. Such continuity, he said, comes from deliberate refinement rather than change for its own sake.
Underlying this philosophy is CUKTECH's long-term focus on R&D in charging and portable power. Wang sees sustained investment in engineering as essential to improving efficiency, power density and the overall user experience. As Chinese technology companies build on strong engineering and manufacturing capabilities, he believes that building a global brand also requires trust built over time.
This technological base is also allowing CUKTECH to explore new areas. At IFA, the company unveiled a prototype lower-limb exoskeleton powered by its portable power banks, applying its accumulated expertise in battery systems and power management to wearable robotics.
Wang said the use of portable, swappable power banks gives the prototype greater flexibility across different scenarios and showcases how the company's existing expertise can provide a competitive edge. The company is still exploring where the concept may lead, with the aim of seeing whether technologies built up over years in power management can translate into real value in a new field.
As technology matures, Wang also sees room for products to respond to needs beyond pure functionality. Some CUKTECH products combine visible charging information with interactive elements designed to add what he calls "sentimental value," reflecting his view that advanced technology can also have warmth and personality.
CUKTECH products are now sold in more than 40 countries and regions, and the company is making its first appearance at IFA this year as it seeks to expand further in Europe. Wang described Germany as an important market, citing strong demand for premium charging products and consumers' close attention to engineering and product performance.
Looking ahead, Wang believes that CUKTECH will continue to build on its core technologies while exploring where those capabilities can be applied next. Whether in established charging products or emerging areas such as wearable robotics, sustained R&D, enduring design and trust built over time, in his view, form part of the same long-term process of building a global technology brand. ■

How rules operate differently for foreign, Indian MBBS graduates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
12:49:21 UTC
21:49:21 KST

NEET-PG aspirants arrive at an examination centre to appear for the medical entrance exam on August 30
NEW DELHI: The National Board of Examinations (NBE) has ruled out lowering the pass percentage for foreign medical graduates (FMGs), saying that “qualifying standards cannot be diluted”.However, when it comes to NEET-PG, the centralised entrance exam taken by almost all Indian medical graduates, the qualifying cut-off has been significantly reduced over the past five years.In NEET PG, percentile cut-off is used, whereas to qualify in FMGE,candidates have to score 50%.The initial cut-off for NEET PG in each of these years has been 50th percentile for the general category, which has been equivalent to roughly 35% marks, and 40th percentile for reserved category, equivalent to about 30%.However, for the sake of filling vacant seats, the cut-off percentile has been reduced every year.It was dropped to zero percentile in 2023 for all categories, which meant that everyone who wrote the exam was deemed qualified including those with negative marks.In 2024, it was dropped to 5th percentile for all, but the equivalent percentage score cannot be calculated because the data on marks was not made public that year.
If 50% marks was the cut off for NEET PG, only about 25% of those who appeared would have qualified in the last five years.The proposed single licensing-cum-entrance exam for post graduate seats in India, which would be common for FMGs and for Indian medical graduates, called National Exit Test or NExT, has been postponed indefinitely.NEET PG results raise the question: What share of Indian graduates would be able to qualify in such an exam with 50% and not 50th percentile as the qualifying cut off ?NBE points out that the difference between the FMG screening test and NEET PG is that one is for qualifying to get a licence to practise while NEET PG exam is to rank Indian medical graduates, who have already passed final year MBBS exams, for getting post-graduate seats.Final year MBBS exams are held in the medical colleges where the students have been taught and trained with the inherent vulnerability of institutional bias to boost pass percentages.FMGE was introduced in 2002 by the erstwhile Medical Council of India ostensibly to ensure that doctors trained abroad meet the same standards as those trained in India.
NEET-PG cut-offs and the share of candidates qualifying after revised cut-offs from 2020 to 2025
The 2002 regulation also made it mandatory for FMGs to complete one-year internship from an institution approved by the MCI after clearing FMGE to get a licence to practise.From Nov 2021, the National Medical Commission, which succeeded the MCI, has mandated that all FMGs, after passing the final year MBBS exam in whichever country have they trained in, have to obtain a licence to practise in that country before they appear for FMGE.While the criteria for an FMG to get a licence to practice in India has been progressively tightened, the opposite has been happening to medical education in India.The infrastructure and faculty norms, and the regulatory oversight for starting new medical colleges in India has been progressively relaxed or diluted to help rapid expansion of MBBS seats.Between 2014 and 2026, the number of medical colleges has jumped from 387 to 818 and the number of MBBS seats from over 51,300 to about 1.3 lakh with complaints piling up of colleges being run without adequate faculty, infrastructure or patient load.
Though every candidate appearing for NEET PG is supposed to have passed MBBS with minimum 40% in each subject and 50% overall, candidates scoring single digit, zero or even negative marks in NEET PG puts a question mark over the quality of graduates being churned out from medical colleges in India.It also raises the question, can India have different criteria/double standards for screening FMGs and its own medical graduates given the highly uneven standards of medical education here.

Iran head to Nagoya with a strong delegation
TEHRAN - Nagoya is preparing to host one of Asia’s biggest sporting events, with millions of sports fans across the continent turning their attention to the 20th Asian Games.
Iran will travel to Japan with a large delegation featuring a combination of experienced champions, established medal contenders and promising young athletes, all aiming to make a strong impact on the Asian sporting stage.
 
 Iran’s final delegation consists of 522 members, including 312 athletes.
 
 The size of the team has generated considerable discussion in recent months. While Iranian officials initially emphasized a “quality-based” approach focused on athletes with genuine medal prospects, the delegation was gradually expanded following the addition of new quotas.
 
 At one phase, 26 additional quotas were added to the initial lineup, raising questions over whether quantity had ultimately taken precedence over quality.
 
 However, a large delegation does not necessarily mean a lack of quality. Iran remains a serious medal contender in several major disciplines, with wrestling, taekwondo, weightlifting and shooting expected to form the backbone of its medal campaign.
 
 Shooting is among Iran’s strongest medal hopes, with 14 Iranian shooters set to compete in Japan.
 
 Weightlifting will also attract significant attention. The Iranian lineup includes established names such as Mostafa Javadi, Ali Aalipour and Ali Davoudi, alongside two female lifters. Yet the competition will be fierce, with Asia’s traditional weightlifting powers leaving little room for error.
 
 Athletics is another discipline carrying high expectations. A target of 10 medals has been discussed, although achieving that figure will be challenging given the gap between some Iranian athletes and the continent’s leading performances.
 
 In canoeing, nine Iranian athletes will compete, with hopes of ending a 16-year wait for an Asian Games gold medal.
 
 In team sports, Iran’s volleyball team remain one of the continent’s leading contenders. Basketball, football and several other teams, however, face tougher challenges. Iran’s U23 football team, in particular, have been drawn alongside China, North Korea and the United Arab Emirates, while limited preparation and a lack of sufficient friendly matches remain concerns.
 
 Beyond the established medal hopefuls, Nagoya 2026 could also provide a valuable platform for Iran’s younger generation. For some, this may be their first major international experience, potentially marking the beginning of a journey toward future success.
 
 With a blend of proven champions and emerging talent, Iran head to Japan with genuine hopes of producing a strong medal haul. From wrestling and taekwondo to shooting, weightlifting, volleyball, athletics and canoeing, the expectation is clear: Iran want to make their presence felt across Asia.
 
 The 20th Asian Games will be held from Sept. 19 to Oct. 4, 2026, in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan. As the continent’s best athletes gather for two weeks of competition, millions of Iranians will be watching their national delegation with hope and pride, dreaming of gold, silver and bronze medals and the sight of the Iranian flag rising above the podium in Nagoya.

Overcoming financial, logistical hurdles: path to Iran-Vietnam trade expansion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Overcoming financial, logistical hurdles: path to Iran-Vietnam trade expansion
TEHRAN- Despite significant potential in petrochemicals, agriculture, and industry, Iran and Vietnam have yet to reach their desired trade levels. Overcoming financial, logistical, and intermediary obstacles is essential for a leap in bilateral exchanges, reports Mehr News correspondent.
Vietnam has emerged as a major production and trade hub in Southeast Asia, while Iran—with its strong petrochemical, mineral, agricultural, and chemical sectors—can supply many of this export-driven economy's needs. Yet sanctions, payment transfer issues, reliance on third countries, logistics costs, and limited Iranian business awareness of the Vietnamese market have left much of this potential untapped.
UN Comtrade data shows Iran's exports to Vietnam at about $67.84 million in 2022, with imports around $38.64 million—totaling roughly $106.5 million, well below targets. However, signs of renewed momentum are emerging. In March 2026, Vietnam's ambassador reported bilateral trade reached about $109 million over eight months, with goods like rubber, coffee, and tea flowing to Iran, while petrochemicals, IT products, and construction materials moved to Vietnam. He projected 7–10% annual growth and hoped for a 50% increase over five years.
Vietnam's total foreign trade hit a record $930.05 billion in 2025, with exports of $475.04 billion and 8.02% GDP growth—making it a far larger market than current Iran-Vietnam figures suggest.
Mostafa Mousavi, head of the Iran-Vietnam Joint Chamber, reports fresh Vietnamese requests for petrochemical and agricultural purchases, with barter deals under consideration. In some cases, Vietnam has shown readiness to buy directly and even offered to send its own ships for cargo pickup.
A key challenge has been the indirect nature of much trade, often routed through third countries like the UAE. This inflates costs, lengthens transit times, and raises sanctions-related risks. Direct trade is seen as a crucial competitiveness booster. Barter and alternative financial channels are being explored, alongside leveraging Vietnam's 2015 preferential trade agreement with the Eurasian Economic Union—which Iran joined in 2023—as a complementary access route.
Direct air links are also improving. The Tehran–Ho Chi Minh City route launched on August 31, 2026, with Tehran–Hanoi to follow soon. Trade attaché Mohsen Rezaeipour called this a game-changer for business travel, investment, and high-value, time-sensitive cargo, complementing sea freight.
In agriculture, a Vietnamese delegation recently toured apple production and packaging facilities in West Azarbaijan, with quarantine hurdles largely resolved—opening a new market beyond traditional destinations. Beyond apples, Iran can export dried fruits, processed foods, and horticultural products, while Vietnam offers coffee, rice, tea, seafood, and consumer goods.
Petrochemicals remain Iran's strongest export advantage, with some non-official estimates placing chemical exports to Vietnam in the hundreds of millions for 2025, though data discrepancies exist. Meanwhile, Iran could import electronics, machinery, and rubber products, suggesting a balanced, diversified trade basket is achievable.
Vietnam's $930 billion foreign trade landscape means Iran's $109 million share is still marginal. Yet recent steps—direct flights, quarantine progress, and interest in barter—signal a shift from "potential" to "practical pathways." If stable financial mechanisms, reduced intermediation, and better logistics take root, Vietnam could become a key Iranian market in Southeast Asia, offering not only off-take for petrochemicals and agriculture but also a gateway to broader ASEAN supply chains.

Indian IT firm to build $7.4 bn data center campus for AI training
Indian IT services company Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) plans to build a $7.4 billion data center campus, exploiting the opportunities offered by the white-hot global demand for artificial intelligence as it seeks to move away from the traditional outsourcing model. 
The 1-gigawatt (GW) facility will cater to AI companies and large cloud providers, known as hyperscalers, offering support for AI training, inference, and other advanced workloads, TCS said on Saturday. 
TCS unit HyperVault will build the campus – expected to be among the country’s biggest – in the southern city of Hyderabad. The buildout will happen in phases, based on customer demand and technology requirements, the Mumbai-based company said in a statement.  
TCS CEO K. Krithivasan said the project is part of the company’s “infrastructure-to-intelligence” strategy. 
“AI demand is increasingly becoming infrastructure demand,” Sohom Banerjee, a technology analyst at the think tank CUTS International, told RT. He said TCS’s move should be viewed as some IT companies “moving vertically down the AI stack.” 
TCS, which reported about $30 billion in revenue in the financial year ended March, last month signed a $1.5 billion deal with German luxury carmaker Porsche to ride the AI-led transformation in the auto industry. 
The data center investment comes as AI rapidly reshapes India’s labor-intensive, billing hours-based IT services industry – whose boom drove the country’s economic growth in the last two decades. The IT and business process management industry in India is currently valued at more than $300 billion by revenue.
Banerjee noted that while AI is putting pressure on parts of the IT consultants’ traditional business model, it is also simultaneously creating demand for a new layer of services around data centers, computing capacity, cloud platforms, AI models, and enterprise applications.
Large domestic AI data center investments move India from “being primarily a user and integrator of AI toward becoming an important location for AI compute,” he said.
Demand for such capacity is already rising. Property consultancy JLL estimates India’s data center capacity will grow from around 1.6 GW in mid-2026 to 6 GW by 2029. Hyderabad is emerging as one of the hubs for gigawatt-scale investment.
Local officials have said the project could generate up to 7,000 direct and indirect jobs across technology, construction, engineering, and operations.

Estonian tennis player Mark Lajal gets death threats after tournament loss
Estonia's top tennis player Mark Lajal received abusive messages and death threats, some to his own phone, following a tournament defeat Delfi reported.
The messages came following his semifinals loss at the ATP Challenger 75 tournament in Manacor, Spain, held at the Rafa Nadal Academy on Mallorca, and the player said they were from sports bettors unhappy about losing money.
Lajal, currently ranked 152nd in the world, shared screenshots of messages he had received aftermath of his semi-final defeat, including from those who had obtained his personal phone number.
The screenshots were in English and included the message:"I really but really hope you will get cancer including your family as well. I hope you will see then [sic] suffer."
Another screenshot Lajal posted read "Look, you son of a b*tch, you're a f*cking loser. I hate you and you must die. You must die, you f*cking son of a b*tch. You and your family must die. You b*stard. I want to kill you."
"Know, we are going to talk, you know what you are doing and you are not dumb as you want people to know you, that's why I'm going to kill all your family," a third message stated.
Lajal, 23, said the abusive and threatening messages had come primarily from disgruntled sports bettors who had lost money on the outcome, and added while he would not normally post on the topic, the messages had gone too far.
"Sometimes these days happen, you lose, but then you get on your phone and somehow people have gotten your number and are calling and texting death threats," he explained, noting the threats and abuse had been directed against his family as well as personally against him after losing.
The player noted abuse like this is the lot of many top players, but questioned the trade-off between this and the big money that sports betting involves: "At the end of the day, ATP keeps accepting all this money from betting platforms, but at what cost?" he noted.
"Gambling addiction is a real issue and I hope these people find and get the help they need," Lajal concluded.
Lajal went through qualifying at the Mallorca event, and defeated Nicolai Budkov Kjaer, a Norwegian player with Estonian roots, 6-3, 6-1 The next round, the quarterfinals, saw him defeat Spanish player Alejo Sanchez Quileze again in straight sets, 6-2, 6-3.
The winning streak came to an end however with a 7-6 (7), 5-7 defeat to France's Felix Balshaw (ATP 252) in the semi final, despite the Estonian initially leading the second set 4-1.
The entire encounter lasted two hours and 10 minutes and Balshaw, 20, will face Spanish player Inaki Montes-De La Torre (ATP 274) in the final.
Other top tennis players who have recently reported receiving death threats and abusive messages include Italy's Matteo Berettini and Panna Udvardy of Hungary.

Next overturns equal pay ruling that raised basic wages for shop staff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
12:45:59 UTC
21:45:59 KST

The UK retailer Next has overturned a 2024 court ruling forcing it to pay its shop staff the same higher basic pay rates as its warehouse workers under equal pay rules.
The chain, led by the Conservative peer Simon Wolfson, said it had “won a landmark victory in its ongoing equal pay litigation”. It has succeeded in its appeal to the employment appeal tribunal “on the key issue of basic pay”, it said.
It comes two years after 3,540 claimants won a six-year legal fight for equal pay, which the fashion and homeware retailer then appealed against. Shop workers accused Next of paying its retail sales staff – who are predominantly female – lower hourly wages than its warehouse workers, the majority of whom are male.
Since that employment tribunal ruling in Leeds, several thousand more Next staff have brought equal pay claims, bringing the total number of claimants involved in the litigation to more than 6,400. Next employs more than 20,000 store staff across 458 stores in the UK and Ireland.
Next said the appeal judgment endorsed its position that it “should not have to pay shop assistants and warehouse operatives the same amount of basic pay, in circumstances where the market and working conditions are very different”.
The retailer argued that it had to pay a higher market rate to warehouse staff because of recruitment and retention pressures, which it said did not apply to the workforce in its stores. It added: “Next believes this element of the judgment is not only correct in law, but also a victory for common sense.”
The retailer said the judgment affirmed: “Employers must be able to pay what is necessary to recruit the people they need; and that doing so does not oblige them to raise the pay of other employees where there is no reason to do so.”
The law firm Leigh Day, which represents Next store workers, described it as a “mixed ruling” as it rejected Next’s challenge to the tribunal’s findings that it had failed to justify lower rates of night-time pay, overtime pay and the failure to provide paid rest breaks to store workers.
Next also failed to persuade the employment appeal tribunal that lower Sunday premium payments to store workers were justified. The appeal tribunal held that the issue remains to be determined and should return to the employment tribunal.
The Next case, which covered the period from 2012 and 2023, explained women made up almost 78% of retail sales jobs, while men made up about 53% of warehouse staff. During that time, some warehouse staff were able to earn between 38p and £3.13 more an hour than retail sales workers, according to Leigh Day.
Elizabeth George, a partner at Leigh Day representing the claimants, said: “I am pleased that the employment appeal tribunal rejected Next’s arguments that its pay practices do not disadvantage women. They plainly do and the appeal tribunal firmly recognised that. I am also pleased that the tribunal upheld the findings on night-time premiums, overtime premiums and paid rest breaks.
“The appeal tribunal’s conclusion on basic pay is disappointing. Next pays market rates in both its stores and its warehouses in order to recruit and retain staff. The market rate is higher in the predominantly male warehouse labour market, even though the work carried out in stores has already been found to be equal work.
“While the store staff and their legal team welcome many aspects of this appeal judgment, we respectfully disagree with this approach to justification. We remain confident in our clients’ position and intend to appeal.”
Next had argued that the equal pay ruling created a threat to the viability of many of its stores, and that it put retailers operating their own warehouses at a “material disadvantage” to rivals that contract out their warehouse operations.
The original employment tribunal and the appeal tribunal found that there was no direct discrimination. The employment tribunal found: “It was all about cost. Gender did not enter into the equation” when Next set pay rates.
Next said it had won the vast majority of the terms challenged in the equal pay litigation, including bonus pay to warehouse staff previously, and now basic pay. It intends to seek permission to appeal in relation to other terms.
“This judgment has come at the right time, the UK economy desperately needs jobs and the loss of this appeal would have represented a hammer blow to retail employment in the UK,” the company said.

Poland urges EU to deny asylum to migrants who violently cross its borders
Unknown

2026-09-07

Poland wants the European Union to deny the right to asylum for migrants who cross EU borders in organised, aggressive groups, just as Poland has itself done on its border with Belarus.
“This is about depriving people who illegally cross the border in organised groups, using violence or destroying border security measures, of the right to international protection,” Maciej Duszczyk, the deputy interior minister who oversees migration policy, told broadcaster RMF.
Polska zabiega o to, by Unia Europejska przyjęła jej interpretację przepisów dotyczących ochrony międzynarodowej. „Chodzi o pozbawienie prawa do ochrony międzynarodowej osób, które nielegalnie przekraczają granicę w zorganizowanych grupach, z użyciem przemocy albo niszcząc…
— Fakty RMF FM (@RMF24pl) September 6, 2026
The station reports that, at a meeting of the European Council next month, Poland will propose expanding the interpretation of article 33 of the United Nations’ Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees.
That section outlines the principle of “refoulement”, under which states are barred from expelling or returning refugees to places where their life or freedom would be threatened.
The article includes a clause saying that the principle does not apply if “there are reasonable grounds for regarding [a refugee] as a danger to the security of the country” in which they have arrived, or if they have a criminal conviction that makes them “a danger to the community of that country”.
Poland wants that clause to be applied in situations where someone applies for asylum after being part of an organised and aggressive border crossing.
Since last year, Poland has itself banned asylum claims from people who illegally cross the border from Belarus. Since 2021, the Belarusian authorities have encouraged and assisted tens of thousands of migrants, mainly from Asia and Africa, to try to irregularly – and often aggressively – enter the EU.
Poland’s asylum ban, which has exceptions for certain vulnerable categories of people, was introduced as a temporary measure in March 2025 but has been repeatedly renewed since then. Warsaw now wants a similar interpretation of international refugee law to be applied across the EU
Its proposals come in the wake of July’s incident in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta, where tens of thousands of migrants irregularly entered from Morocco. Soon afterwards, Poland urged the EU to adopt tougher measures, including making migrants who enter the bloc illegally ineligible for obtaining residence rights.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk was also one of 22 EU leaders who signed a letter expressing “serious concern” at the situation in Ceuta and warning that the EU “cannot allow uncontrolled mass border crossings, the instrumentalisation of migration, or other hybrid threats to create the impression that illegal entry…is possible”.
After last week's migration crisis in Ceuta, Poland has called for tougher EU measures, including an automatic ban on residence for anyone who enters illegally.
It pointed to its own experience of dealing with "weaponised" migration from Belarus https://t.co/2VHn5ZUJx7
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 5, 2026
Poland has long argued that the situation on the Belarus border is an example of how migration has been “weaponised” by Russia and its allies to sow social discord in EU countries.
In response, Poland has invested billions in strengthening physical and electronic barriers along the border, has deployed thousands of additional officers there (and granted them expanded rights to use firearms), and has banned asylum claims.
In 2021, Poland recorded almost 40,000 attempted illegal crossings from Belarus, and the figure remained as high as 30,000 in 2025. However, in the first half of this year, only 235 attempted crossings were recorded, which the Polish government has hailed as evidence of the success of its tough measures.
However, Poland’s human rights commission recently raised concern at how long the technically “temporary” asylum ban has been in place. Some Polish courts have also ruled that Polish border guards acted unlawfully when forcing migrants back into Belarus.
The number of attempted illegal crossings by migrants from Belarus to Poland fell from 15,500 in the first half of 2025 to 235 this year – a drop of over 98%
Poland also now claims a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally https://t.co/RFZkd7CeIk

Swiss union analyses AI impact on telecoms staff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
12:44:17 UTC
21:44:17 KST

Swiss union analyses AI impact on telecoms staff
Artificial intelligence (AI) is widely used in the Swiss information and communications technology (ICT) sector, but its impact on work is mixed.
Whilst employees do report an increase in efficiency, they also cite higher demands, a growing workload, uncertainty and ever-increasing pressure.
This has been revealed by a study carried out by the consultancy firm Ecoplan on behalf of the trade union Syndicom. The research was presented in Bern, with representatives from Swisscom, Sunrise and Microsoft in attendance.
More
How artificial intelligence is shaping the Swiss job market
According to the survey, AI is significantly altering the day-to-day tasks of workers in the sector. At present, this transformation mainly affects individual tasks rather than entire professions.
But the trend is clear: skills, judgement and continuous professional development remain crucial factors in coping with change.
Among the demands put forward by the employees interviewed are greater opportunities for professional development, transparent information on the opportunities and risks of AI, and active involvement in the design of innovation processes.
+ Read about how the future of work will change
Based on these findings, Syndicom has drawn up a package of demands: strong rights to participate in the introduction of AI, job security, reduced working hours, binding data protection standards, a clear allocation of responsibility in the event of algorithmic errors, and workers’ share in the productivity gains generated by digitalisation.
“The use of AI must be socially sustainable and prioritise the interests of workers,” said Carol Ghiggi, central secretary for the ICT sector at Syndicom.
More
Will AI secure or shake Swiss prosperity?
Anne-Thérèse Morel of Swisscom emphasised that the group uses AI in accordance with clear principles on data protection, ethics and governance, whilst investing in training, reskilling and socially sustainable transition.
Andreas Gertsch of Sunrise, for his part, highlighted the importance of giving employees the freedom to experiment with new technologies, whilst developing a critical mindset to assess the results and apply them responsibly.
All participants agreed that, in the absence of specific legislation, constructive dialogue between the social partners is essential for defining shared corporate rules and ensuring transparency within organisations.
The aim is to ensure that innovation does not benefit businesses alone, but actively involves those who, through their work, contribute to the digital transformation every day.

Russia has enough resources to wage war through 2028, Ukraine's military intelligence says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07

Russia has enough resources to wage war through 2028, Ukraine's military intelligence says
Russia is economically much weaker than it was at the start of the full-scale war, but likely has resources to fight for two more years, Ukrainian military intelligence (HUR) chief Oleh Ivashchenko told Ukrinform in an interview published on Sept. 7.
"The main problems facing the Russian economy are a shortage of labor resources, a growing federal budget deficit, and a deteriorating situation in the banking system," Ivashchenko told the Ukrainian news agency.
"At the same time, it still has enough resources to wage war against Ukraine. We do not rule out that these resources will last through 2027 and 2028."
Kyiv's wartime strategy has increasingly centered around long-range drone strikes against Russian refineries, oil depots, factories, and tankers, aiming to undercut the Kremlin's revenues and increase economic pressure.
About 40% of Russia's oil-refining infrastructure has been disabled amid Ukrainian strikes, leading to fuel shortages and prompting the country to ban exports of diesel and gasoline.
Ukraine has recently expanded its list of targets in Russia, systematically striking warehouses of online retailers like Ozon and Wildberries.
At the same time, Russia has been facing fiscal difficulties, as record military spending has driven Russia's budget deficit, which soared by 40% in the first half of the year — even as Russian President Vladimir Putin claimed the situation is not "critical."
Ivashchenko said that Ukrainian strikes are contributing to this deficit, "which today stands at $82 billion."
The intelligence chief also underscored the impact of Ukrainian strikes against Russian logistics in the Black Sea, forcing Moscow to seek more expensive routes for its grain exports.
"Russia produces about 130 million tons of grain (per year)," Ivashchenko commented.
"About 80 million are for domestic needs; the rest goes to foreign markets. And this is blocked today," he said, adding that Kyiv views Russia's grain exports as a resource sustaining the Russian economy and therefore its war against Ukraine.

Threatening letters revive fears among Kashmiri Pandits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
12:41:00 UTC
21:41:00 KST

Threatening letters revive fears among Kashmiri Pandits
September 7, 2026
A new wave of threatening letters targeting Kashmiri Pandits has deepened fears among those who have returned to the region as civil servants under an Indian government federal rehabilitation scheme. Kashmiri Pandits are members of the Hindu minority community who fled the Muslim-majority Kashmir Valley during a militant uprising in the 1990s.
The latest letters, which surfaced in the last week of August, named several employees. The letters also included their addresses, vehicle registration numbers and phone numbers.
Personal details exposed
"Similar threat letters surfaced in early August, but the latest contains our Jammu residential address, vehicle and phone numbers, which have also been shared on social media," Anil Koul, a government employee, told DW, urging authorities to investigate the source of the leak.
The letters have been attributed to a little-known group calling itself the United Liberation Council, which security officials suspect could be a front for the Pakistan-based Islamist militant outfit Lashkar-e-Taiba.
The group reportedly first surfaced in July, when it released a poster marking the death anniversary of a former militant commander. Authorities have yet to confirm the letters' authenticity or the existence of the group behind them.
The latest letters also distinguish between Pandits who never left the Valley — and are therefore "safe" — and those recruited under New Delhi's rehabilitation program, who are accused of working for "masters" outside Kashmir.
The fresh threats have also triggered a political row.
Jammu and Kashmir National Conference (JKNC) president and former Jammu and Kashmir chief minister, Farooq Abdullah, called them a "conspiracy" aimed at delaying the restoration of statehood, which the region lost in 2019.
Abdullah also questioned why Hindu officers from outside the region were not facing similar threats.
His remarks drew sharp criticism from Kashmiri Pandit groups and the ruling Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which accused him of being insensitive to the community's fears.
Familiar fears
Government records show 44,167 Kashmiri migrant families registered as having left since 1990 citing security concerns, of which 39,782 were Hindu.
For Pandit community representatives, however, the latest threats are part of a much longer security problem.
Sanjay Tickoo, president of the Kashmiri Pandit Struggle Committee (KPSS), said the threats should be viewed against the backdrop of targeted killings and repeated security concerns faced by Pandit government employees in the Valley. He blames security lapses and says repeated meetings with officials since a wave of killings in 2022 have failed to resolve their concerns.
"Since 2022, meetings have resulted in nothing," Tickoo told DW.
He also wondered how those making the threats have access to employees' personal details.
"How are these details being posted on social media?" Tickoo asked.
Targeted killings have occurred sporadically in the years since. At least seven Kashmiri Pandits were killed by militants during a spike in violence between 2020 and 2022.
One of the starkest cases was that of Rahul Bhat, a Pandit revenue official who was shot dead inside his government office in Budgam in May 2022.
The last confirmed targeted killing of a Kashmiri Pandit was in October 2022, when Puran Krishan Bhat, an orchard farmer, was shot dead in Shopian district.
Former Jammu and Kashmir police chief S P Vaid described the latest threats as part of a familiar militant playbook.
"There is nothing new in this," Vaid told DW, calling it "a ploy by Pakistan to Islamize society."
He said similar tactics had been used against migrant workers in the Valley.
The difference, this time, is the precision of the threats. Personal data that should not have been easily accessible has been made public, and no clear explanation of how it was leaked has been provided.
The return dilemma
The KPSS estimates roughly 6,500 Pandits who never left the Valley, along with another 4,000 who have returned as government employees under a federal rehabilitation scheme, live in India-administered Kashmir.
But the reintegration of those who fled decades ago has proved challenging.
Rahul Pandita, a journalist and author of "Our Moon Has Blood Clots: A Memoir of a Lost Home in Kashmir," said the government's record on rehabilitation was inadequate.
"The BJP has had no rehabilitation policy for Kashmiri Hindus," Pandita told DW, arguing that the government employees in the Valley had returned under a policy introduced during the previous government of former Prime Minister Manmohan Singh.
Some land has been returned and cases of killings have been investigated, he said, but "it is too little and too late."
Pandita said the bigger problem was that no government could guarantee a completely secure environment for a mass return.
"No matter what the government does, the situation will never be conducive enough for the Pandits to return," he said, arguing that as long as Islamist militancy exists in the region, Kashmiri Hindus would still be targeted.
"It's for them then to decide if they are willing to take such a risk," he said.
Beyond government employees, some Pandits who have returned and established businesses in the Valley are already living there quietly, Pandita said.
"That is the best-case scenario for Kashmiri Pandits in Kashmir Valley," he said.
Security beyond protection
Sushobha Barve, executive secretary of the Center for Dialogue and Reconciliation, said the latest threats expose a wider security paradox.
"Despite claims of normalcy, a tiny group of active militants has successfully disrupted the lives of migrant families. Breaking the cycle of panic is essential," Barve told DW.
She said there was also growing political frustration over the delay in restoring Jammu and Kashmir's statehood, arguing that this grievance cut across the region.
Amitabh Mattoo, an academic and professor of international relations at Jawaharlal Nehru University who has written extensively on Kashmir, said any return of Kashmiri Pandits had to be both secure and dignified.
"The state has an essential role in ensuring their physical security and in protecting their property, cultural and other legitimate rights. But security measures alone will not suffice," Mattoo told DW.
"A sustainable return will also require patient reconciliation, engagement with local civil society, and the gradual rebuilding of inter-community trust and social and economic ties."

‘Economic blockade is difficult in a multipolar world’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
12:39:56 UTC
21:39:56 KST

‘Economic blockade is difficult in a multipolar world’
TEHRAN- The head of the Iran-Russia Joint Chamber of Commerce, stating that the aim of US sanctions is to increase the costs of Iran's economic transactions, said: "In today's multipolar world, an absolute economic blockade against Iran is difficult, and shared economic interests are an important strategy for countering these oppressive measures."
Hadi Tizhoush Taban, in an exclusive interview with IRNA, referred to the US Treasury Secretary's announcement of intensifying sanctions and a naval blockade against Iran, and stated: "An economic blockade should not be understood merely as restrictions on trade routes, because at the same time, pressure is also applied to foreign exchange earnings from oil sales, transportation, insurance, banks, and payment networks in order to place Iran in a situation where the cost of trade for the country increases."
He added: "One of the goals of US economic pressure is to reduce the Iranian government's accessible resources, especially oil revenues, increase the costs of circumventing sanctions, and limit the country's financial capacity. Sanctions have also increased Iran's transaction costs by targeting shipping networks, intermediary companies, shadow banking, and even some cryptocurrency exchanges."
Tizhoush Taban, emphasizing that the main issue is not just the sanctions themselves, clarified: "The most important issue is the cost that sanctions impose on Iran's economy; higher discounts on oil sales, increased transportation and insurance costs, reduced investment, inefficient transfer of resources, and increased opportunities for corruption are among the consequences of this situation."
The head of the Iran-Russia Joint Chamber of Commerce, referring to the multi-polarization of the global economy, said: "Although the US can increase the cost of Iran's trade, imposing an absolute economic blockade against Iran is difficult, because today's global economy is multipolar and countries such as China, India, Russia, and the Persian Gulf states have independent economic interests."
He continued: "Iran also possesses diverse capacities and must use these capacities to reduce the economy's vulnerability. Geographic diversity, numerous neighbors in Central Asia, the Caucasus, and South and East Asia, as well as diversity in goods and services, are opportunities that can be utilized to develop foreign trade."
Tizhoush Taban emphasized: "Crude oil should not be the country's only source of foreign currency, and the share of petrochemicals, petroleum products, industrial goods, technical services, agriculture, and technology in foreign trade must increase."
Developing alternative trade routes is essential
Referring to the importance of diversifying trade routes, he stated: "Iran should not be heavily dependent on one or two trade routes, and multiple land, sea, and combined routes must be established for trade; the development of regional corridors is of great importance in this regard."
The head of the Iran-Russia Joint Chamber of Commerce added: "Sanctions are not just a banking issue, but also a logistics issue. If Iran can reduce the cost and time of goods transit, it will effectively neutralize part of the effects of sanctions."
Referring to the capacity of the country's northern routes, he said: "Northern trade routes can play a role in reducing dependence on southern ports, but none alone can fully replace southern routes, and a set of reliable and competitive routes must be established."
Tizhoush Tab?n emphasized: "Developing corridors is not just a construction project; it is part of the country's economic security infrastructure. Of course, these routes will only be effective if they can compete with alternative routes in terms of cost and time."
Financial Transactions Must Be Streamlined
Stating that one of the most important weaknesses of Iran's foreign trade is the method of transferring and receiving money, he said: "Iran may be able to sell goods, but if the exporter cannot receive and utilize export revenues at a reasonable cost, exports will be conducted through multiple intermediaries and with heavy costs, and such a model is not sustainable."
The head of the Iran-Russia Joint Chamber of Commerce identified the establishment of reciprocal accounts, the use of joint and regional banks, and the development of regional and digital payment systems as solutions to mitigate this problem, and added: "Eliminating the dollar alone will not solve the problem, because the dollar is not just a currency, but a financial and banking network. If a transaction is conducted in another currency but the bank or insurance company is still connected to a network that fears US sanctions, the risk of sanctions will still exist."
Tizhoush Taban, also referring to the possibility of developing trade in local currencies, said: "A portion of Iran's trade with Russia can be conducted in the national currencies of the two countries, but one important problem is the cost of currency conversion for economic actors."
He added: "In the current situation, an economic actor may face a significant loss in value when converting currency, and in some cases this reduction reaches about 20 to 25 percent. This imposes a heavy cost on the exporter."
He emphasized: "The government should not create a mechanism that increases the exporter's cost for supplying currency to the importer; rather, the exporter's currency should be converted at a fair rate with a very small margin compared to the real market rate."
The head of the Iran-Russia Joint Chamber of Commerce concluded: "By reducing currency conversion costs, developing trade in national currencies, and establishing regional payment mechanisms, some of the problems of Iran's foreign trade can be alleviated, and the groundwork can be laid for developing economic relations with neighboring countries and trading partners."

Kyiv Prepares Emergency Food and Water Supplies Ahead of Russian Winter Attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Kyiv Prepares Emergency Food and Water Supplies Ahead of Russian Winter Attacks
The Kyiv City Administration is stockpiling essential food and drinking water reserves to prepare for potential prolonged power outages and other emergencies ahead of the 2026–2027 autumn-winter period, the Kyiv City State Administration (KCSA) reported on September 7.
The initiative is primarily designed to ensure immediate assistance for low-income residents and individuals facing difficult life circumstances if the capital’s energy system is compromised.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The city’s preparations follow severe utility disruptions during the previous winter, when Russian strikes on critical energy infrastructure repeatedly left large parts of the capital without electricity, water, or heating.
Attacks on power substations in January 2026 plunged over one million Kyiv residents into darkness in subzero temperatures, leaving thousands of apartment buildings without heat and forcing the city to heavily rely on emergency response measures.
Accumulated supplies will serve multiple critical functions across the city during severe crises, according to Oleh Kuyavskyi, Deputy Head of the Kyiv City State Administration.
In addition to supporting vulnerable populations, the reserves will be deployed to supply Points of Invincibility during extended blackouts, aid victims of emergencies, and sustain emergency rescue crews engaged in urgent response operations, the Kyiv City State Administration reported.
“The capital’s food security is not only the availability of necessary reserves, but also a clear system for their distribution and delivery to those who need help the most,” Kuyavskyi stated. “We are preparing in advance for possible challenges of the autumn-winter period, strengthening reserves, and continuing to hold food fairs in all districts of the city.”
Supported by charitable and public organizations, the city currently maintains the logistical capacity to provide hot meals for up to 25,000 people, according to the Kyiv City State Administration.
To further strengthen these capabilities, the KCSA’s Department of Industry and Entrepreneurship Development plans to purchase an additional 20,000 emergency food kits, as confirmed by the Kyiv City State Administration.
The city’s emergency preparations are being coordinated through the Kyiv Humanitarian Headquarters, an entity established in February 2022 to unify the efforts of KCSA departments, district administrations, municipal enterprises, charities, and donors. According to the Kyiv City State Administration, this centralized headquarters manages accounting and resource distribution, ensuring the rapid deployment of aid if the security situation deteriorates.
“Thanks to our joint work, the city can quickly respond to emergency situations and provide assistance to low-income Kyiv residents,” Kuyavskyi noted, emphasizing that the situation in Kyiv’s consumer market “remains controlled and predictable.”
The stockpiling measures coincide with continued Russian strikes across the region. Recent Russian attacks on the Kyiv region and Odesa injured 19 people, including three children. According to the Kyiv Regional Military Administration, strikes on the Boryspil and Obukhiv districts wounded two civilians and damaged warehouses, administrative buildings, and private property.

Russia Launches 32 Rassvet Satellites but System Remains Inefficient, Ukraine’s HUR Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
12:38:28 UTC
21:38:28 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Launches 32 Rassvet Satellites but System Remains Inefficient, Ukraine’s HUR Says
Russia has placed 32 Rassvet satellites into orbit, but the system remains inefficient and lacks enough satellites to provide stable communications, Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) chief Oleh Ivashchenko said in an interview with Ukrinform on September 7.
Ivashchenko said Russia is continuing efforts to expand its satellite capabilities, but the current constellation remains limited in both size and effectiveness.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“We know that today the Russians are trying to put satellites into orbit. But so far, there are not enough of them, and their effectiveness is low. We are aware of this problem… To date, the Russian Federation has launched 32 satellites. We will not go into details about which orbits they are in, how frequently they operate, or which regions of Ukraine they cover,” Ivashchenko said.
The HUR chief noted that Russia’s satellite network remains significantly smaller than Starlink. More than 12,000 Starlink satellites are currently in orbit, he said, while Elon Musk’s company continues to expand the constellation by approximately 200 satellites each month.
The difference in scale leaves Russia’s Rassvet system unable to provide the same level of stable satellite communications, according to Ivashchenko.
“We are working on this. Russia’s ‘Rassvet ’ must turn into a ‘zakat ,’” Ivashchenko added.
Russia has been developing Rassvet as a domestic alternative to Starlink, allocating 102.8 billion rubles, approximately $1.3 billion, in state funding to the program. Commercial operations are scheduled to begin in 2027, with plans to expand the constellation from 250 satellites to 900 by 2035.
Following the introduction of restrictions by Ukraine and SpaceX in February 2026 that disabled unauthorized Starlink terminals used by Russian forces, Rassvet is expected to serve a similar communications function, potentially including military applications.
If deployed on a large scale, the satellite network could provide Russia with more resilient command-and-control capabilities for drones, enabling operators to maintain communications and potentially redirect unmanned systems beyond the reach of conventional radio links.
However, the project has encountered significant technical and logistical challenges. Satellites already deployed in orbit have been losing altitude, while newly launched spacecraft have struggled to reach their intended positions.
Deploying the planned constellation would also require at least 18 Soyuz-2.1b rocket launches, while Russia currently conducts only six to eight such launches annually.
The technical difficulties have already resulted in satellite losses. Defense Express reported on August 25 that one Rassvet-3 communications satellite had been lost, while two others were potentially at risk of reentering Earth’s atmosphere.

Tallinn Airport sees record passenger traffic in August
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
12:38:14 UTC
21:38:14 KST

Tallinn Airport handled nearly 390,000 passengers in August, the best monthly figure in the airport’s history, and 16% more than in August last year, writes ERR News.
In the first eight months of 2026, the airport handled 2.54 million passengers, or 11% more than in the same period last year. The increase in passenger traffic was mainly driven by the entry of low-cost airline Wizz Air. In August, Wizz Air handled 18% of the total number of passengers and offered nine destinations. The Latvian airline airBaltic maintained its position, carrying 29% of Tallinn Airport’s passengers. In total, 19 airlines offer flights from Tallinn to more than 50 destinations.
Tallinn Airport Board Member Eero Pärgmäe said that the record set in August shows that demand for flights is still high. He said that in the winter season (from the end of October), the number of routes will decrease compared to the summer, as usual, but it will still be possible to reach 39 destinations with direct flights and conveniently reach Europe’s largest airports to continue their journey.
The majority (94%) of passengers in August used regular routes, while the remaining six percent were charter flights – mainly to Antalya, but also to Greek resorts, Montenegro and Bulgaria.
The most popular flights were to Warsaw, followed by Helsinki, Riga, Frankfurt and Stockholm.
Compared to August 2025, the number of flights in August this year has increased by 5%. A total of 4,047 flights were performed.
Meanwhile, 6,787 passengers used Estonia’s regional airports in August, compared to 8,575 passengers in August last year. The decrease is due to the closure of Kuressaare Airport for reconstruction from the 10th to the 31st of August.

The Marmolada glacier, the largest in
the Dolomites, suffered a record loss of mass this summer, in
which Italy has been hit by a series of intense heatwaves,
according to data presented on Monday by several bodies,
including the University of Padua, the Veneto environmental
protection agency and the Italian Glaciological Foundation.
                                    
                                       
				This summer the  Marmolada shrank by around 23 metres on average
and its surface area dropped from 92 hectares to 83, the bodies
said
Experts said the only time the glacier suffered a similar loss
of mass was in 2022, when a serac collapsed following a heatwave
in which abnormally high temperatures were registered, killing
11 people.
                                    
                                       
				The world's glaciers, an important source of fresh water, have
been shrinking rapidly in recent years due to global heating
caused by human greenhouse gas emissions.
                                    
                                       
				"The data collected this year shows the trend already evident in
recent decades has gotten worse," said Mauro Varotto of the
University of Padua.
                                    
                                       
				"There has been a new record for the reduction of the glacier's
surface area, which has lost nine hectares in one year
"If summers like the one just passed repeat themselves, the
glacier may only have about 10 years left."
