Lower Saxony, Rafael and Aurelius to build Iron Dome components at former VW factory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:41:57 UTC
18:41:57 KST

The German state of Lower Saxony, Rafael Advanced Defense Systems and Aurelius Capital have signed a letter of intent to purchase Volkswagen’s Osnabrück plant, allowing the Israeli defense company to establish production of Iron Dome components in Germany.
The agreement, signed at the factory on Monday, will see the Volkswagen site in Osnabrück developed into a center of excellence for innovative security and defense solutions. It will combine German engineering expertise, industrial capital and quality standards.
First reported by the German publication WirtschaftsWoche and confirmed to D&T, is a change in direction from the original plan, which initially called for the German car-maker to cooperate with Rafael to produce the parts. Qatar, Volkswagen’s largest foreign shareholder, blocked that plan. D&T understands that while Qatar also opposed to this deal, the German government was able to move forward with it.
Following the statement of intent, the consortium will hold detailed negotiations, assessments of regulatory requirements, and the necessary internal decision-making processes by all parties involved. D&T understands that this is the first step towards Berlin procuring the missile defense system, marking the second time the system has been sold to a European country.
The Osnabruck plant currently employs 2,300 people and produces the T-Roc Cabriolet, Porsche Cayman and Porsche Boxster. According to reports, Volkswagen will leave the site in the second half of 2027, and while the Iron Dome’s Tamir interceptor itself will not be manufactured there, military vehicles, launchers, generators, and other equipment will be.
Initially designed to shoot down short-range rockets, the Iron Dome has become an integral component of Israel's multi-layered defense array.
The system’s modular architecture enables seamless integration with additional defense layers, and it can operate independently or as part of a broader air defense network that includes the the Arrow (Arrow 2 and Arrow 3) system, which intercepts ballistic missiles outside of the Earth’s atmosphere, and the David’s Sling missile defense system which is designed to intercept tactical ballistic missiles, medium- to long-range rockets, as well as cruise missiles fired at ranges between 40 to 300 kilometers. Rafael has also manufactured the Iron Beam laser defense system which has been operational along Israel’s northern border.
'Defense of today, tomorrow and well beyond'
Olaf Lies, Minister-President of Lower Saxony said that “this partnership creates realistic opportunities for long-term, highly skilled employment at a location that has stood for industrial excellence for 125 years.”
Lies added that the country’s “security environment has changed fundamentally. Germany and Europe must strengthen their capabilities in the security and defense industry and become more independent. This is both a responsibility and an economic opportunity. Osnabrück can play an important role in this effort. The workforce has repeatedly demonstrated its ability to achieve outstanding results. We are building on that strength.”
Rafael has been active in Germany for over 20 years and has established a strong presence in the country with various subsidiaries including Dynamit Nobel Defence, EuroSpike and EuroTrophy Gmbh.
Yoav Tourgeman, President and CEO, Rafael Advanced Defense Systems said that the partnership with Germany is part of a long-term relationship with the country “with the idea that the technology will be fully produced in Germany, to protect Germany and Europe.”
“The technology at the heart of this partnership is built for the defense of today, tomorrow, and well beyond. Our outstanding combat proven technology evolves constantly in order to be ahead of the threats, so that highly reliable defense will always be provided,” he added.
Aurelius Capital was co-founded by Alon Lifshitz and Tomer Jacob, alongside former NSA director Michael Rogers and former IAF commander Maj.-Gen. (res.) Amir Eshel and former Mossad deputy director Udi Lavi.
“At Aurelius, we are very proud to partner with Rafael and transform an advanced automotive manufacturing facility in Osnabrück into a leading defense production center. This initiative is made possible by Rafael’s groundbreaking technology, the highly important partnership with the Government of Lower Saxony, and the close cooperation with Volkswagen. Its goal is to strengthen the security of both Germany and Israel while creating significant value for all parties involved. This is only the first step in a strategic partnership that will continue to grow and deepen over time," Jacob said in a statement.
Aurelius, which is understood to have played a key role in the negotiations, is expected to take over the site together with Lower Saxony and develop new business there.
German defenses
Germany has also purchased Israel’s Arrow 3 as a response to Russia’s war against Ukraine and the growing proliferation of advanced missile systems.
Germany signed the $3.5 billion Arrow 3 contract in November 2023, the largest defense deal in Israel’s history at the time. In December, the two countries signed a $3.1 billion follow-up contract to expand interceptor and launcher stocks.
The Bundeswehr announced on June 30 that the second Arrow air defense battery site would be in the greater Kaufbeuren area of Bavaria and would house the ELM-2080 Green Pine Block C radar to detect and track threats. The second location would complement the initial battery at Fliegerhorst Holzdorf/Schönewalde, south of Berlin, the capital. That battery was the first time the system had been deployed outside of Israel.
Arrow 3, developed by Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI) is a highly maneuverable system designed to provide ultimate air defense by intercepting ballistic missiles when they are still outside the Earth’s atmosphere.

Turkey plans 229% defense spending boost over three years to advance domestic military tech
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:41:33 UTC
18:41:33 KST

Turkey plans to increase defense spending by 229% over the next three years as part of a push to develop its own technologies and produce higher-value products in the defense industry, Turkish Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz announced on Sunday, according to Turkish media reports.
“In the defense industry, we aim for a Turkey that develops its own technology and produces high added value,” Yilmaz said. “We are increasing defense spending by 229%.”
The plan was announced during a presentation of the country’s new Medium-Term Program (MTP), which sets out its economic roadmap for 2027-2029.
The increase in defense spending is the largest among the seven priority areas outlined in the program.
Spending on social housing is set to increase by 150%, mining exploration by 139%, industrial infrastructure by 54%, railways by 49%, health by 43%, and food supply security by 42%.
Envanter Medya, a Turkey-based news site that tracks developments in military technology, noted that the additional funding would support major defense projects, such as mass production of the TF-Kaan fighter jet, the first deliveries of the Bayraktar Kızılelma unmanned fighter aircraft, and the delivery of more than 10 Altay (tanks) to the Turkish Land Forces.
Turkey one of world's largest military spenders
“The global economy has recently been going through a new period in which economic, technological, and geopolitical developments are intertwined, predictability has decreased, and risks have risen to historically high levels,” Yilmaz said.
“The Turkish economy is, of course, not independent of the developments taking place in the world and in our region.”
Yilmaz said that the war with Iran had created both direct and indirect consequences in many areas, including energy and commodity prices, global trade, inflation outlook, and growth expectations.
Turkey’s military spending already reached $30 billion in 2025, making it the world’s 18th-largest military spender, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute. Turkish military spending rose 7.2% from the previous year, with SIPRI saying the increase was driven by ongoing military operations in Iraq, Somalia and Syria, but most of all by investment in Turkey’s domestic arms industry.

UN rights chief urges halt to arms transfers to Israel, business supporting illegal settlements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:39:07 UTC
18:39:07 KST

- Turk calls for global AI ‘red lines,’ warns advanced systems could pose ‘existential risk to humanity’
UN human rights chief Volker Turk on Monday urged states to end transfers of arms to Israel that risk being used to violate international law, and called on companies to stop business practices supporting illegal settlements.
Speaking at the opening of the 63rd session of the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva, Turk said Israel’s annexation of the occupied West Bank was “unfolding, unobstructed,” despite a clear ruling by the International Court of Justice.
“What more will it take for states to take action to prevent the entrenchment of occupation across land earmarked for Palestinians under the two-state solution?” he said.
“They (states) need to end the transfer to Israel of arms that risk being used to violate international law. Companies also need to end business practices that support illegal settlements,” he added.
The rights chief said words of condemnation “ring hollow in the face of deliberate violations and suffering,” calling for greater international efforts toward sustainable peace.
On Gaza, he said Israel has killed more than 1,300 Palestinians in daily strikes despite the ceasefire announced almost a year ago and continues to restrict humanitarian aid.
He said he is appalled by Israeli proposals for the forced expulsion of all Palestinians from the Gaza Strip, as well as executions and torture of Palestinians suspected of collaboration by armed groups affiliated with Hamas.
Turk calls for AI ‘red lines’
Turning to artificial intelligence, Turk called for an “all-out effort” to establish “cast iron guarantees” around AI safety and security, warning advanced AI could pose an “existential risk to humanity.”
"At a minimum, we need countries hosting AI and those involved in its supply chains to come together around agreed red lines," he said.
According to Turk, he would write to AI companies in the coming days, urging them to take immediate steps to reduce risks.
He warned that “a handful of men” wield “almost unlimited power over AI” and argued that delays in establishing effective governance benefit major technology companies, their owners and enablers.
Pointing to concerns about increasingly powerful systems, Turk said AI that can escape its testing environment or blackmail developers to prevent itself from being switched off is “AI that is too powerful.”
He also called for greater attention to AI’s human rights implications, including its effects on employment practices, fundamental principles of democracy and the environment.
Turk acknowledged recent international progress, including the establishment of the Global Dialogue on AI and the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, but said governments and companies need to listen to growing public concerns about the technology.
Resumption of US-Iran attacks 'alarming,' immediate return to talks needed
Turk also voiced alarm over the resumption of attacks between the US and Iran and their impact across the Gulf region, citing reports of civilian deaths and injuries, including at a wedding in Iran's Hormozgan province.
He called the crisis “entirely avoidable” and appealed for an immediate return to negotiations.
Turning to Ukraine, Turk warned that Russia's full-scale war was on a “menacing trajectory,” with rising civilian casualties and intensified attacks on energy infrastructure.
He said he was “horrified” by reports that fully autonomous drones launched by Russia killed three Ukrainians last month, while Ukraine has also reportedly field-tested such weapons.
“I join calls for the urgent prohibition of weapons that can take lives without human involvement,” he said.
Turk also urged the US to halt returns of people to countries where they could face “irreparable harm,” including Haiti, and ensure due process for removals to third countries.
He said four more people had died in US immigration custody since his last update to the Human Rights Council, bringing the total to 23 deaths in 2026, and called for accountability.
"Hard-won gains for people of African descent are deliberately being undermined in some countries, including cuts to anti-discrimination programs and attempts to distort history," the human rights chief said. “Politicians, traditional and social media amplify isolated incidents to portray migrants, refugees, Muslims, marginalized racial and ethnic groups, and minorities as a collective threat.”
Turk also expressed concern over renewed hostilities in South Sudan and escalating tensions in Yemen, urging restraint and greater international efforts to prevent a return to “all-out war.”
On Yemen, he renewed his demand for the Houthis to immediately release 73 UN and NGO personnel being held by the group.
The rights chief also reiterated concerns over China's Xinjiang Uighur Autonomous Region, including detention facilities, urging Beijing to investigate allegations of human rights violations, including torture.

Finland's largest sex crimes case opens with teacher accused of luring victims on Snapchat
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
12:39:00 EEST
18:39:00 KST

Pirkanmaa District Court has begun proceedings in what is believed to be the largest-ever sexual crimes case in Finnish legal history.
The hearings are expected to last until at least the end of this year, with the court sitting on 45 separate days throughout the coming autumn and into the winter.
The schedule, announced in court as the first hearing began on Monday morning, reflects the vast number of victims in the case — 361. Police said there may be many more, even as high as 900, as some 530 potential victims have yet to be identified.
The known victims are all boys aged between 9 and 15 years old, and they live in many different parts of Finland. Some legal representatives will participate in the session in court in Tampere, while others will join remotely from several different district courts.
The defendant, a 28-year-old man, will appear before the court remotely from Kanta-Häme District Court. He is charged with aggravated sexual abuse of a child, sexual abuse of a child, and aggravated distribution of images depicting a child in an offensive manner.
Man posed as a woman in Snapchat messages
The crimes are alleged to have occurred on the Snapchat messaging app between 2019 and 2022.
According to police, the defendant posed as a woman on Snapchat and sent messages to the children asking them for photos and videos. He then used screen recording software to capture the images without the knowledge of each sender.
The number and content of the images and videos vary by victim, but one boy sent about 160 videos to the defendant.
Police do not believe that the man met any of the children in person, meaning all the crimes occurred online.
They do however suspect that he knew some of the victims beforehand, either through sports or while working as a substitute teacher.
Attorney Jyri Kilpi, who is representing 77 victims, told the court in his opening statement on Monday that the defendant used the rosters of underage sports teams to select his victims and to understand more about their interests and hobbies.
He described the shame and regret his clients, and their parents, feel as a result of the defendant's actions — noting that many could not bring themselves to tell their parents what had happened.
"All responsibility lies entirely with the adult perpetrator, not the victim," Kilpi said.
Prior conviction
According to Yle's information, the defendant in this case was sentenced to three years in prison in 2023 after being found guilty by Kanta-Häme District Court of the aggravated sexual abuse of a child.
The court heard that the then-20-year-old defendant had sexual intercourse with his 14-year-old male student, while he was working as a substitute teacher at a primary school in the region. He also sent the boy hundreds of sexually suggestive messages, images, and videos.
The investigation of this case led the police to confiscate the suspect's phone, where they subsequently found thousands of sexualised images and videos of children.

Dining celebrates Samos' agricultural and maritime heritage through a sea-view à la carte restaurant, a mixology-focused pool bar and an intimate wine cellar located close to the Samos Wine Museum.

Ukrainian special services eliminated Oleg Shutov in occupied Donetsk. He was allegedly involved in the assassination of Major General Maksym Shapoval of Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence.
LB.ua reported the information, citing sources in the security services.
The operation took place on July 27, 2026, in Donetsk’s Leninskyi district.
Explosives were used to kill him and had been planted in advance on his Subaru. The explosion occurred after Shutov arrived at the Dynamo sports facility.
To avoid publicizing Shutov’s death, local Telegram channels started publishing reports claiming that the incident was allegedly caused by a drone attack.
Oleg Shutov worked for the so-called “Ministry of State Security of the DPR”. Ukrainian law enforcement officials consider him one of the perpetrators of the assassination of Major General Maksym Shapoval of Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence.

On June 27, 2017, a car carrying Major General Maksym Shapoval of the Defense Intelligence of Ukraine was blown up in Kyiv. The explosion occurred in the morning on Solomianska Street.

Investigators determined that an explosive device had been planted under the car in advance. Ukrainian law enforcement classified the explosion as a terrorist attack.

Israeli air strikes on southern Lebanon killed at least 11 people in Kfar Remman early on Monday, according to Lebanese state media, as a new wave of attacks hit residential areas and medical workers near territory illegally occupied by Israeli forces. The attacks followed days of fighting that has placed fresh pressure on a US-backed ceasefire framework.
Lebanon’s National News Agency said nine people, including two children, died when an Israeli strike hit a three-storey residential building in Kfar Remman in the Nabatieh district. Five others were wounded.
A separate drone strike hit a vehicle in the same town and killed two medics, according to the agency.
Lebanon’s Health Ministry gave an earlier toll of nine deaths. It said eight people died in the residential building and one paramedic died in the vehicle strike.
The Israeli military said it was examining reports of the deaths.
Israeli forces also struck Deir al-Zahrani in southern Lebanon after issuing a forced evacuation order. The Israeli military claimed it targeted a building near a Hezbollah facility that had been used to launch an explosive drone.
The attacks followed Israeli strikes across southern Lebanon on Sunday that killed seven people and wounded at least 20, according to Lebanese authorities.
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun said the escalation threatened the ceasefire framework agreed in June and called for international pressure on Israel to halt its attacks.
The agreement calls for Hezbollah to disarm, Israeli forces to withdraw from southern Lebanon in stages and the Lebanese army to deploy across the area.
Israel says Hezbollah has continued launching drones and rebuilding military infrastructure in the south. Hezbollah has accused Israel of breaching the agreement through strikes and continued illegal occupation.
The renewed fighting has forced residents to leave areas close to what Israel calls its “security zone”.
The pressure on Lebanon’s health system has also increased.
Israeli strikes destroyed Ghandour Hospital in Nabatieh al-Fawqa on Sunday, according to Lebanon’s Health Ministry. The hospital had stopped operating about two months earlier as fighting intensified, but had previously treated local residents and sheltered displaced people.
The ministry said 17 hospitals across Lebanon have sustained damage since March 2 and three hospitals in the south have been put out of service.
The Lebanese Health Ministry said in a report published on Sunday that 4,362 people have been killed and over 12,300 wounded since the conflict escalated in March. The Health Ministry says hundreds of women and children are among the dead.
The ministry also reported 180 attacks on ambulance crews since March 2, with 135 healthcare workers killed.
Israeli authorities say 40 soldiers and four civilians have died on both sides of the border during the same period.
According to UNHCR, around 360,000 people remained displaced by Israeli attacks in August, including at least 22,000 staying in collective shelters.
Israel has continued illegally occupying areas in southern Lebanon despite the June framework. Lebanese officials say that has stalled the withdrawal process and prevented displaced residents from returning to their villages.

French EDF Energy in talks to buy British So Energy as UK supply market consolidates

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:37:59 UTC
18:37:59 KST

France's EDF Energy is reportedly in discussions to buy So Energy, the smaller British supplier whose Irish parent company has put it up for sale, in a deal that would add to a renewed wave of consolidation among UK gas and electricity retailers.
French-owned EDF Energy is one of a handful of parties negotiating with British So Energy's owners, Sky News reported, and faces at least one rival bidder whose identity has not been established.
If EDF prevails in the auction, industry insiders expect the transaction to cover So Energy's customer base rather than the company as a whole.
So Energy has roughly 300,000 household electricity customers and was founded back in 2015.
Ireland's Electricity Supply Board took a controlling stake in 2021 and put the business under review this summer, appointing PwC to run the sale.
ESB, the Irish parent company of So Energy, has been open about the process.
"Our parent company, ESB, has initiated a process to evaluate potential divestment options for So Energy," a spokesperson for So Energy said in July adding that this followed a strategic review and that "ESB plans to focus on its core business."
For EDF, the appeal is scale in a market where it has been losing ground.
The company is among the big six suppliers that once dominated British energy, with three million customers and five million accounts, but now trails well behind Octopus Energy and Centrica-owned British Gas. Scottish Power finds itself in a similar position.
Buying a customer book rather than a company outright is the cheaper route to that scale, adding accounts directly while avoiding the operational complexity of absorbing an entire business.
The talks also come at an uncomfortable time for British households.
Ofgem lifted the price cap by 4% to £1,723 per year for the autumn, meaning bills will climb just as the industry reshuffles itself.
Meanwhile, government policy is pulling the other way as Andy Burnham used his first week as prime minister to announce that VAT would be scrapped from domestic energy bills, part of a broader push to tackle cost of living.
No agreement has yet been reached between the parties.

Jaguar Land Rover confirms plan to cut 4,000 jobs over two years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:37:31 UTC
18:37:31 KST

Jaguar Land Rover has announced thousands of job cuts in a “body blow for workers” as it grapples with tough trading conditions, Donald Trump’s tariff wars and the fallout from a cyber-attack.
Britain’s largest carmaker, which is owned by the Indian conglomerate Tata, confirmed the anticipated cuts on Monday, saying it wants to reduce its global workforce by about 4,000 over two years, as part of an effort to save £1.7bn.
JLR’s employs 44,000 people globally and 34,000 in the UK. The cuts will mainly affect the 26,000 UK employees who are salaried and management workers. The company has plants in Solihull, Warwickshire and Merseyside, and is headquartered in Coventry.
Its proposal threatens to provide an early reality check for the new prime minister, Andy Burnham, and his promise to “reindustrialise” Britain.
JLR’s profits have tumbled as it wrestles with strong competition in the global car market, Trump’s US tariffs and last year’s hack, which led to the shutdown of its factories.
The JLR chief executive, PB Balaji, said: “The automotive industry faces significant challenges, with technological change amidst intense competition and ongoing geopolitical uncertainty. Through our Growth Reimagined strategy, JLR is moving decisively to strengthen our competitiveness and position the business for long-term success …
“As part of this transformation, we will reduce our global workforce by around 4,000 roles over the next two years. We recognise this will be difficult news for colleagues affected, and are committed to supporting everyone with care, fairness and respect.”
The Guardian understands that factory workers who are paid hourly – the vast majority of those on the shop floor – will be unaffected by the cuts, which will instead fall on salaried employees in divisions such as management, marketing, and research and development.
The business minister, Jonathan Reynolds, has ruled out using taxpayers’ money to deter the company from pursuing the redundancies.
Reynolds will hold talks with Balaji and Sharon Graham, the general secretary of the Unite union, on Tuesday. Graham is expected to push for JLR to favour retraining and redeployment over compulsory job losses, if it cannot achieve enough redundancies voluntarily.
The cuts will be weighted towards more senior roles in management and research and development rather than shopfloor production workers.
Graham said: “While the cuts planned are not expected to impact the UK manufacturing footprint or its supply chain, we need to ensure that no stone is left unturned to mitigate these jobs losses in the highly skilled ‘white collar workforce.”
JLR announced the job cuts as the chancellor, John Healey, made an economic speech at the Manufacturing Technology Centre in Coventry, just a few miles from the carmaker’s offices. Healey said he wanted to “draw the line” under rising business costs.
A No 10 spokesperson said it was an “uncertain and concerning time for affected workers, their families and the wider communities and we know that current market conditions are challenging for the automotive sector globally”.
Liam Byrne, the chair of the Commons business and trade committee, said the news was a “body blow for workers, families and communities across the West Midlands”.
He added: “We now need urgent assurances that maximum support will be deployed to help everyone affected find new work.
“But the troubles at JLR underline the challenge facing the government’s reindustrialisation drive. Britain is preparing to spend billions more on defence, infrastructure and new technology. But British business needs cheaper energy and government orders, not at some distant point in the future, but now, now, now.”
Last year’s hack eventually cost the company about £200m and contributed to its pre-tax profit falling to just £14m, from £2.5bn a year earlier.
The government last year agreed to underwrite a £1.5bn loan to JLR to help it recover from the hack but the carmaker has not tapped the facility.
JLR has also suffered the fallout from Trump’s trade tariffs, which hit sales of models such as the Range Rover and the Defender as the company seeks to expand further in the US market.
JLR is in the midst of a large-scale overhaul of its products, including the launch of its first fully electric Range Rover this month, which will come with a starting price of £154,070, and a new electric Jaguar. It is also considering a deal with Stellantis to make some of its cars in the US to help ease the effect of trade tariffs.
Balaji said the cuts were aimed at “reducing organisational complexity” and would mean the company could break even on sales of about 300,000 vehicles a year.
European carmakers have faced tough trading conditions as Chinese manufacturers’ sales have surged across the UK and Europe, giving companies such as Chery and BYD a manufacturing foothold in the regions.
In July, Chery, which also owns the Omoda and Jaecoo brands, accounted for nearly 8% of UK market share, up from 3% last year, according to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders.
The West Midlands mayor, Richard Parker, said the job cuts were “deeply worrying” and said he will launch a £500,000 support package to help JLR workers taking voluntary redundancy find new jobs.
JLR follows Volkswagen in announcing large-scale job cuts, after the German carmaker said last week that it intended to make 50,000 more people redundant as part of a turnaround plan.

Popular Egyptian TV presenter Sarah Khalifa faces appeal battle after death sentence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:36:28 UTC
18:36:28 KST

Khalifa and 11 others face death sentences in a major synthetic drug trafficking case, with appeals and further legal challenges expected.
An Egyptian television presenter faces execution after a Cairo court sentenced her to death for financing and coordinating a synthetic drug network, but her lawyer says they will appeal, and legal experts say the case is far from over.
Sarah Khalifa, known for hosting the crime programme Mission Impossible on private channel Al-Mehwar and for her events business, was sentenced on Saturday alongside 11 others in a major synthetic drug manufacturing and trafficking case.
Nine defendants received life sentences and seven were acquitted. Those sentenced to death were also fined 500,000 Egyptian pounds (€8,000).
Khalifa's brother Mohamed was among those sentenced to death, on charges of manufacturing and testing drugs.
Khalifa's lawyer Mohamed El-Gendy said the defence would appeal and pursue all available legal avenues.
A higher criminal court can reconsider the evidence and each defendant's role, upholding, reducing, or overturning sentences. A further challenge before Egypt's Court of Cassation is also possible.
Before Saturday's ruling, the court had referred Khalifa and 12 other defendants to Egypt's Grand Mufti — a procedural requirement before a criminal court can impose the death penalty. The Mufti's opinion is advisory and not binding.
Twelve of those 13 defendants ultimately received death sentences.
More than ordinary hashish
Egyptian media initially described the case as involving synthetic hashish, but forensic evidence presented during the trial identified the substances as synthetic cannabinoids, laboratory-made chemicals that mimic some of the effects of cannabis on the brain but can be significantly more potent and unpredictable.
The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime describes MDMB-4en-PINACA as a potent synthetic cannabinoid placed under international control in 2021 following a World Health Organization recommendation citing severe adverse effects and deaths.
Synthetic cannabinoids can cause psychosis, seizures, heart and kidney problems, and in severe cases, death.
The committee said the substance was not specifically listed on Egypt's controlled narcotics schedule, but concluded it fell under Egyptian law because its chemical structure and effects were similar to already-listed substances.
The defence challenged that interpretation and the court accepted the committee's findings.
The case began in April 2025 when Egypt's anti-narcotics authorities said they had uncovered a network importing raw materials used to manufacture synthetic drugs.
Police initially raided two Cairo apartments and recovered around 200 kilograms of drugs, raw materials and equipment.
As the investigation widened, prosecutors said the total seized exceeded 750 kilograms. The investigation lasted some 40 days before prosecutors obtained arrest warrants.
Al-Masry Al-Youm newspaper, citing judicial and security sources, reported that investigators alleged raw materials were sourced abroad, concealed inside cosmetics containers and luggage on flights.
The prosecution said members had specialised roles covering procurement, manufacturing, storage and distribution. The case against 28 defendants relied on testimony from 20 witnesses and digital evidence including messages, photographs and videos.
Khalifa's alleged role
Prosecutors said Khalifa financed parts of the operation, travelled abroad to meet senior members of the network and acted as a link between them and other members inside Egypt.
According to investigation records reported by the Egyptian press, two defendants living outside Egypt bought batches of materials used to manufacture the drugs from China and obtained instructions on how to produce them.
Investigators said other members mixed the chemicals according to formulas supplied by senior figures in the network before testing newly manufactured batches on drug users to assess their effects, and then weighing, packaging and distributing them.
Khalifa's brother, Mohamed Khalifa, was identified by prosecutors as one of those involved in manufacturing and testing the drugs and was also among those sentenced to death.
Prosecutors also relied on digital evidence recovered from Khalifa's phone.
According to prosecution documents shared with domestic media, investigators found WhatsApp exchanges containing videos of substances resembling those seized in the case, as well as communications with other alleged members of the network.
A handwriting examination also concluded that Khalifa had written entries in a seized notebook containing names, figures and amounts that prosecutors said related to spending on the drug operation.
Khalifa consistently denied involvement in the network.
Saturday also brought a second conviction against Khalifa in a separate case.
A Cairo court sentenced her to three years in prison for assault after investigators found video footage on her phone showing a young man identified as her driver being stripped, assaulted and filmed naked inside her home.
Two other defendants in that case received seven years each and a fourth received five years.
Egypt retains the death penalty for serious drug trafficking offences. Amnesty International recorded 23 executions in Egypt in 2025, up from 13 the year before, and has criticised the country's use of capital punishment for offences that do not involve intentional killing.

Türkiye, Danish firm sign thorium technology agreement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:36:00 UTC
18:36:00 KST

Türkiye’s Energy, Nuclear and Mineral Research Agency (TENMAK) has signed a memorandum of understanding with Denmark-based Copenhagen Atomics to cooperate on the use of thorium in next-generation nuclear technologies.
The agreement aims to expand research and development capacity in advanced nuclear systems and examine the domestic production of thorium compounds that meet nuclear fuel standards for molten salt reactors, the Energy and Natural Resources Ministry said on Sept. 7.
The memorandum was signed at a TENMAK campus in Istanbul in the presence of Energy and Natural Resources Minister Alparslan Bayraktar.
“We hope this cooperation will deliver results and eventually lead to a commercial product,” Bayraktar said, adding that the focus on thorium gave the partnership particular importance.
Bayraktar said Türkiye was pursuing several small modular reactor projects in parallel with the involvement of public institutions and private investors.
It would become clearer over the next few years which technologies could progress toward commercialization, he added.
The agreement will involve Turkish industry, researchers and engineers in efforts to use the country’s thorium resources in higher-value nuclear technologies.
The initial work will focus on research and project development for producing thorium compounds in Türkiye that are suitable for use in molten salt reactors.
Copenhagen Atomics is developing thorium molten salt reactor technology and is working on a modular design called Onion Core.
Under the agreement, the company will assess its technology against Türkiye’s research infrastructure, workforce and industrial capabilities.
The ministry said the longer-term aim was to establish domestic production of nuclear-grade thorium compounds and develop Türkiye as an international supplier in the field.

Nauru opens embassy in Jerusalem, becoming ninth country with mission in Israeli capital
"You have recognized what we all know to be the truth- Jerusalem is the capital of Israel”
Nauru officially inaugurated its embassy in Jerusalem on Monday, becoming the ninth country to establish an embassy in the Israeli capital.
The opening ceremony was attended by Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar and Nauru’s vice president and foreign minister, Lionel Aingimea. Israel’s Foreign Ministry said the move reflected the close relationship between the two countries and Nauru’s commitment to expanding bilateral ties.
“Nauru is one of Israel’s most loyal and steadfast friends in the international community,” Sa’ar said. “You have recognized what we all know to be the truth — Jerusalem is the capital of Israel.”
Sa’ar also praised Nauru for consistently supporting Israel at the United Nations and for backing it during proceedings at the International Court of Justice.
Aingimea said the decision followed a conversation with Sa’ar when the two met in Fiji. He described support for Israel as deeply rooted in Nauru’s religious values and pledged that his country would align itself more closely with Israel in future UN votes.
“Our motto is ‘God first,’ and Israel has always held a special place in our hearts,” Aingimea said. “We believe with all our hearts that supporting Israel brings us God’s blessing.”
According to Aingimea, Nauru has voted with Israel at the UN 71% of the time. “Mark my words: That 71% will rise in the very near future,” he said.
The opening is part of an Israeli diplomatic campaign to increase international recognition of Jerusalem as its capital and encourage more countries to establish missions in the city. Most foreign embassies remain in the Tel Aviv area because Jerusalem’s status is among the most contentious issues in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.
Israel’s Foreign Ministry said the United States, Guatemala, Honduras, Kosovo, Paraguay, Somaliland, Papua New Guinea and Fiji also maintain embassies in Jerusalem. It added that more countries are expected to follow.
Israel and Nauru plan to expand cooperation in areas including health, agriculture, water management, innovation and climate resilience, the ministry said.

Who needs unity? The collapse of the Third Bloc parties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:33:59 UTC
18:33:59 KST

The three parties of the “Third Bloc”, the group of small right-leaning and centrist political factions in Israel trying to push for a broad unity government which launched with great fanfare at the start of the election campaign, are reaching the final stretch before candidate lists are submitted with a resounding political failure. It sounded promising, looked intriguing, and familiar, experienced politicians took the reins, recruited high-profile names and promised to offer the public exactly what it was supposedly looking for: an alternative that did not clearly belong to either political camp. But when the moment of truth arrived, it became clear there were almost no buyers for that product.
Ayelet Shaked, whose name was mentioned throughout the campaign as one of the figures who might fit into that political space, ultimately announced that she would stay out. In a Facebook post Sunday evening, she effectively also offered an explanation for the broader failure of the “third bloc.”
“I had hoped that after October 7, the political reality in Israel would change,” she wrote. But, according to her, this time too “the political system is converging around the same patterns of camps and boycotts, two blocs that in my view are tearing the country apart.”
Shaked explained that she still believes in a “broad cross-bloc government,” but acknowledged that she does not see a realistic way to establish such a government under the current political circumstances.
“I did not see a realistic way to represent you properly. If there had been one, I would have said: Here I am,” she wrote to supporters who had urged her to return to politics.
In that sense, her decision to remain outside may be the sharpest expression of the state of that political niche: It seemed there was demand for a party that would refuse to choose absolutely between the two camps, but as the deadline for submitting candidate lists approached, it became clear that the desire for “unity” was very difficult to translate into seats. Shaked, at least, chose not to take the gamble and join one of the parties now fighting for its political survival.
It began with Gilad Erdan and Yuli Edelstein’s Unity party, continued with Hili Tropper and Yoaz Hendel’s Zionist Home-Reservists party, and may now end with Benny Gantz’s Blue and White. Gantz, who removed himself from the anti-Netanyahu bloc and sought to create an independent political space, was in many ways one of the founders of that “third bloc.” But the other two parties have already collapsed and disappeared from the map, while Blue and White itself is now fighting for survival.
After Shaked’s decision to stay out, Gantz’s options narrowed further. There is currently no natural partner with whom he could merge or join forces, and discomfort is growing even among the few remaining lawmakers in his faction. They do not want to be dragged into a race that could end below the electoral threshold and cost the entire camp votes. Knesset lawmaker Michael Biton, one of Gantz’s closest associates for years, is expected to announce his retirement. Despite everything, Gantz is insisting for now on going all the way.
Erdan discovered how hard it is to build a party
Gilad Erdan entered the race with the ambition of leading a new political line, one that would try to leave behind the division of recent election campaigns into “only Bibi” and “anything but Bibi.” He presented the idea of “unity” as a particularly sought-after product after the October 7 massacre and the wars that followed, but failed to translate the slogan into real political power.
The way the party was managed also raised quite a few questions. Precisely during the critical days before the candidate lists closed, Erdan was abroad, and even before that the campaign seemed to be operating at limited intensity. On August 29, ynet obtained information that Erdan had decided to dismantle his campaign headquarters and that, without a significant merger, he would not continue in the race.
“That is a total and unparalleled lie,” one of his associates responded at the time. “Everything is working as usual. Not one person has moved.”
But as the days passed, it became clear that the information had been correct. In a sense, Erdan himself had already anticipated the difficulty before setting out.
“Building a party is much more complicated and difficult than I thought,” he said before deciding to run independently.
Yoaz Hendel’s reservists party also sought to position itself as part of that same politically unaffiliated space. To Hendel’s credit, he was among the few politicians who actually served hundreds of reserve-duty days since October 7. He seemingly had a clear political story to tell, but after three years of ongoing war even that sentiment was no longer enough on its own to sweep voters along.
The main problem was the message. Hendel, Tropper and their people struggled to provide a simple answer to the voter’s most basic question: What exactly will you do the day after the election? Will they join a government led by Netanyahu? Will they give Gadi Eisenkot the 61 seats he needs? Or will they try to force a unity government — and if so, how exactly?
As the questions multiplied, the message became blurred. In the end, the public was not convinced.
The person who may have benefited most from the collapse of the “third bloc” is Gadi Eisenkot. Not necessarily because he actively worked to dismantle it, but because developments worked in his favor. Erdan’s party evaporated, and he managed to draw Hili Tropper into his own slate. In doing so, he reduced the risks.
Now one major task remains for him: move Gantz out of the way. But here, the story is no longer only political. The relationship between the two is burdened by accumulated grievances, personal tensions and considerable frustration built up over the years.
After they parted ways, and after Eisenkot built himself a new political home, the possibility that Gantz will insist on running to the end could turn the battle between them from an electoral threat into a personal and public confrontation.
Thus, within just a few weeks, the promise of a meaningful “third bloc” has almost completely evaporated. What initially looked like a political space that could reshape the balance of power has, as candidate lists are about to be submitted, turned into a graveyard of new parties — and another reminder that in Israeli politics, there is often a vast distance between an idea that sounds good and actually crossing the electoral threshold.

Türkiye posts fastest growth in electricity demand among IEA members
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:32:11 UTC
18:32:11 KST

Türkiye’s electricity demand grew by an average of nearly 5 percent annually between 2005 and 2024, marking the fastest increase among member countries of the International Energy Agency (IEA), according to the agency’s Türkiye 2026 Energy Policy Review.
Türkiye’s strong economic and population growth is reshaping the country’s energy needs.
With electricity demand expected to continue rising in the coming years, Türkiye’s National Energy Plan projects electricity consumption to reach 510 terawatt-hours by 2035.
The report noted that the rapid growth in electricity demand, coupled with the expansion of renewable energy capacity, highlights that grid infrastructure, storage, flexibility and demand-side management, rather than generation capacity alone, will be among the most critical issues facing Türkiye’s energy system in the years ahead.
The IEA report also noted that growth in electricity demand has been driven primarily by economic activity, particularly in the industrial and services sectors.
Rising demand and expanding renewable energy capacity are expected to place additional pressure on the country’s power grid.
Renewable energy sources are expected to play an increasingly important role in meeting growing electricity demand.
Renewables accounted for 43 percent of Turkey’s total electricity generation in 2025, and the share is targeted to rise to 55 percent by 2035.

AI could pose ‘existential’ risk to humanity, UN rights chief warns
- UN rights chief Volker Turk warns that advanced AI could pose an existential threat to humanity and calls for urgent safety guarantees.
- Turk highlights that a few men hold nearly unlimited power over AI, urging countries and supply chains to agree on strict limits.
- The UN supports harmonised global rules and held its first governance meeting in July to reduce AI risks amid similar concerns from AI leaders.
AI generated
Geneva – UN rights chief Volker Turk warned on Sept 7 that artificial intelligence could become powerful enough to threaten humanity, and said he would urge companies in the coming days to reduce the risks.
“I share the concerns of industry insiders that advanced AI could pose an existential risk to humanity,” Turk told the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva in a sweeping speech ahead of the start of his second term in October.
“I am calling here, today, for an all-out effort to put cast iron guarantees in place around the safety and security of AI, before it is too late.”
Without naming them, Turk warned that just a handful of men held “almost unlimited power over AI”. Top AI companies include Meta, Anthropic, OpenAI and Google.
“At a minimum, we need countries hosting AI and those involved in its supply chains to come together around agreed red lines,” he said.
Turk’s remarks echoed previous warnings from top artificial intelligence executives themselves about extinction risks from AI, including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.
The United Nations has called for harmonised rules to reduce the risks and held its first global meeting on governance in July. REUTERS

BEIJING, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology has issued a development plan for the information and communications industry during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030) to promote high-quality development of this sector.
By 2030, a new-generation communications network with comprehensive coverage and leading performance is expected to be fully established, according to the plan, while adding that efforts will be made to accelerate the development of a technologically advanced, secure and controllable information and communications industrial system.
Meanwhile, an agile and efficient governance system integrating technology and management is expected to be effectively established, and network and data security capabilities featuring all-domain coordination and practical application will be significantly enhanced, the plan said.
The industry's empowerment level and degree of globalization will be further improved, laying a solid foundation for basically achieving modernization of the information and communications sector by 2035, the plan added.
The plan also outlines 13 key indicators, including achieving information and communications industry revenue of 4.1 trillion yuan (about 604.8 billion U.S. dollars) by 2030, cumulative investment of 3.8 trillion yuan in information infrastructure, and an average annual growth rate of 7 percent in total telecommunications business volume.
By 2030, there will be 50 5G (including 5G-A) base stations per 10,000 people, intelligent computing power will reach 9,800 EFLOPS, and the 5G user penetration rate will reach 95 percent, the ministry said.
EFLOPS, or ExaFLOPS, is a unit of computing performance, with each unit representing 1 quintillion floating-point operations per second. ■

Iran war: How US consumers spent an additional $100bn on fuel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:30:44 UTC
18:30:44 KST

Iran war: How US consumers spent an additional $100bn on fuel
The average US household has spent $763 extra on fuel in six months, as the US-Israel war on Iran pushes up fuel costs across all 50 states.
US consumers have paid an additional $100bn for petrol and diesel in the six months since the US-Israel war on Iran began on February 28, according to a tracker from Brown University’s Watson Institute for International and Public Affairs.
Across the country, the added cost works out to roughly $763 per household, based on an estimated 131 million households nationwide.
The war on Iran has been unpopular in the United States, with a majority of Americans blaming President Donald Trump for the rise in fuel prices. Trump has dismissed concerns about rising fuel prices in an interview with Reuters news agency, saying: “If they rise, they rise.” He has instead tried to shift the blame by accusing oil companies of “price gouging”.
Trump claimed that the war would last four to five weeks, but it has entered its sixth month, with no diplomatic breakthrough in sight.
Petrol accounts for the larger share of the cost because Americans use far more of it than diesel. The price of petrol has climbed 39 percent, from about $2.98 to $4.15 a gallon ($0.79 to $1.09 per litre). Diesel has jumped even more sharply, rising more than 60 percent from $3.67 to $5.90 per gallon ($0.97 to $1.56 per litre).
Where are fuel prices highest in the US?
Fuel prices vary significantly by state. Prices are highest on the West Coast, especially in California, where high fuel taxes and carbon pricing programmes were already pushing costs up before the war even started.
According to the American Automobile Association, California has the nation’s highest average petrol price at $5.85 per gallon ($1.55 per litre), followed by Washington state ($5.51), Hawaii ($5.39), Alaska ($5.03) and Oregon ($5.01).
Indiana has the country’s lowest petrol price at an average of $3.43 per gallon ($0.91 per litre).
The map below shows a state-by-state breakdown of petrol prices. Hover over each state to see the percentage increase from before the war to now.
How higher fuel costs drive up the price of food
Oil and gas touch nearly every stage of the food chain, from fertiliser and tractor fuel on farms to refrigeration and insulation in cold storage to plastic packaging and truck fuel for transport.
As oil prices rise, these added costs accumulate at each step: production, storage, packaging and delivery.
By the time food reaches supermarket shelves, those additional costs are passed on to consumers as higher prices.
In lower-income countries, where populations spend a far greater share of their earnings on food and import large quantities of grain and fertiliser, rising oil prices could rapidly translate into food shortages.

Anti-migrant protests are 'wake-up call' for UK government, says police commissioner
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:29:54 UTC
18:29:54 KST

A weekend of protests in Portsmouth and Dover has exposed deepening tensions over Britain's Channel crossings, even as the government insists arrival numbers are falling.
The UK government branded hundreds of demonstrators as "thuggish" after they blocked roads in an attempt to prevent asylum seekers leaving Portsmouth on Sunday.
The protest came after around 140 migrants arrived by small boat, as tensions over Channel crossings continue to mount.
"We condemn the intimidating and thuggish behaviour we saw in Portsmouth last night," a spokesperson for the UK's Home Office, said in a statement.
"The right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy but it must never cross a line into disorder."
Footage showed demonstrators, many dressed in black with their faces covered, confronting police officers holding riot shields as they formed a cordon around buses carrying the migrants to a processing centre.
Officials said the transfer was ultimately completed successfully.
Hampshire Police and Crime Commissioner Donna Jones told the BBC it was a "wake up call" for the UK government.
Jones said that "people have a right to peaceful protest" and that was "largely" the case last night but "there were crimes committed and they will now be investigated and I would not be surprised if there are arrests that come off the back of the footage that was captured as evidence".
The Conservative MP said "hundreds" were acting lawfully and warned it was a "wake-up call to the government... that the British people are fed up with the lack of control of our borders".
Sunday's protest followed a similar demonstration on Saturday, when masked crowds blocked access to the Port of Dover.
French authorities said the vessel carrying the 140 migrants had departed from the Baie de Seine in Normandy — an unusually long and riskier route compared with the boats that typically depart from closer to Calais and land near Dover.
Arrivals in the county of Hampshire, where Portsmouth is located, remain extremely rare.
Another local Conservative MP Joe Robertson called the development "extremely concerning," questioning whether smugglers were opening new routes for larger vessels.
The unrest comes despite recent data suggesting crossings are slowing. The Home Office said Channel arrivals in August fell to their lowest level since records began in 2018, with migrant numbers at their lowest since 2020.
The average number of passengers per boat has been rising in recent months. Some 16,513 migrants have crossed the Channel by small boat so far this year.
It is a small fraction of overall arrivals in Britain which total over 800,000 - most of which come through legal routes on student or work visas.
The issue continues to fuel support for the Reform UK party, underscoring how migration remains one of the most volatile political issues across Europe.

EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas has scrapped the launch of a new High-Level Group on Defense, which was to include former political and military leaders, after pressure from EU member states, Politico reports.
The group was meant to develop proposals for closing gaps in EU defense. Kallas had described it as bringing together "the brightest minds" to propose solutions "in the shortest possible time and in the most effective way."
The launch was scrapped due to resistance from some capitals, an EU official told the outlet.
"Some member states felt this wasn't the right way to go right now. After some discussion with ministers, we decided not to proceed with this initiative — we're looking for new ways to engage with member states," the official said.

Kallas's office kept the group's membership confidential. As previously reported, it was announced on September 1 that the EU would unveil a High-Level Group on Defense involving EU member states, Ukraine and the United Kingdom, aimed at developing recommendations for Europe's defense.

DNA Business: A Gene Gold Rush | Storyteller
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:25:14 UTC
18:25:14 KST

[NOTE: DNA Business: A Gene Gold Rush available until October 5, 2026.]
What if the most intimate information about who we are had become a commodity?
Once the exclusive preserve of elite scientists and medical laboratories, DNA can now be decoded by anyone — with a simple home testing kit. A handful of tech start-ups, including Ancestry, 23andMe and MyHeritage, have turned our desire to know where we come from, who we are related to and what diseases we might be vulnerable to into a global, highly lucrative business.
But how reliable are the answers these companies provide? Behind the seductive promise of discovering our origins or predicting our health risks lie methods whose scientific validity is questioned by leading geneticists. And there is an even bigger issue: what happens to our DNA once we have handed it over?
In 2019, an estimated 26 million people worldwide had taken a direct-to-consumer DNA test. By the end of 2026, that figure is expected to have nearly doubled, reaching close to 50 million. Many believe they are simply buying information about themselves. Few realize that their genetic data can become a valuable asset — collected, stored and potentially sold to pharmaceutical companies to fuel medical research and drug development. Regulation is struggling to keep pace. In some countries, certain insurers can already consider genetic-test results when deciding whom to cover—and at what price. Could other financial institutions one day seek access to the same extraordinarily sensitive information?
Through compelling personal stories, undercover investigation and interviews with leading geneticists, researchers and lawyers, this film exposes the hidden economy growing around our DNA.
This is no longer simply a story about science. It is a story about privacy, identity, money and power — and about the extraordinary possibility that, in the future, our genes could determine not only who we are, but how the world treats us.

Ebola burial teams endure exhaustion, hostility from communities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:25:00 UTC
18:25:00 KST

Yuma Adolphe and his team have one of the most difficult jobs in the fight against Ebola in Congo's Ituri province, the epicenter of the country's deadliest outbreak of the disease. They are responsible for ensuring that those who die from Ebola receive safe and dignified burials, a task that requires them to dig graves, prepare bodies and handle coffins almost every day.
But as authorities struggle to contain the outbreak, which has killed nearly 3,200 people among more than 6,600 confirmed cases, the burial teams say they are reaching their limits. Their workload is growing, while hostility and fear in affected communities make an already dangerous job even harder.
"It is difficult, but we try to push ourselves beyond our limits," Adolphe told The Associated Press (AP).
Since the outbreak began in mid-May, authorities have deployed small burial teams like Adolphe's to Ebola hotspots, where they work on the front lines of efforts to contain the rapidly spreading disease. The workers are paid $20 a day for handling some of the most dangerous and emotionally difficult tasks in the response.
Despite the exhaustion and risks, members of the burial teams say they remain committed to protecting their communities, knowing that safe burials are essential to preventing further transmission of the virus.
For Adolphe and his colleagues, the work is grueling, but they see it as a necessary sacrifice to help keep their communities safe.
"We have to look at our own mental well-being, and physically the fatigue mounts, but we keep going to ensure the community is protected."
But their work is in the crosshairs of locals' frustration with the outbreak, which has not only taken their loved ones but also prevented them from observing traditional burial rites.
Health workers exclusively handle the bodies because Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood or bodily fluids of infected people.
Experts say the bodies of victims still contain considerable amounts of active virus and can spread infections further.
Since May, health workers and burial teams such as Adolphe's have been attacked by bereaved families across the front line of the outbreak.
"Usually, the body is handed over to the family, who can handle it however they wish, in accordance with our African customs," Adolphe said. "But in this situation, it's difficult to let the family handle the body as they please. They are deprived of certain rituals, and that's what leads to misunderstandings."
Jeanne Alasha, adviser to the military governor of Ituri on health and humanitarian affairs, said that "as for those who continue to assault the teams, they are committing offenses punishable by law."
Ituri province, where the outbreak is concentrated, is also at the center of the rebel conflict in eastern Congo. The province is under a military government appointed by national civilian authorities in Kinshasa.
Shortly before noon last Friday, Justine Abineno, a chorister, was buried in Ituri. Abineno had died of Ebola. She had complained only of slight headaches before going to a hospital, where she was diagnosed with Ebola, her mother said.
A catechist presided over the ceremony, which was attended by dozens of people, as a team of burial specialists in scrubs and boots stood by.
Abineno's mother, Sofia Wanito, said doctors only allowed her to see the body through the window of the hospital ward, and she was not allowed to touch the coffin.
"In the past, we didn't die like this. I could not even cover her with the sheets myself and pay a final tribute," Wanito said.
The Ebola outbreak is spreading across six provinces in eastern Congo under some of the most difficult conditions imaginable, fueled by rebel violence, displacement and intense population movements. A weak health care and surveillance system also challenges responders, as do insufficient contact tracing and laboratory testing.
Efforts to contain the outbreak have also been complicated by the lack of an approved vaccine or treatment for the rare Bundibugyo virus causing it. Authorities have started vaccinating frontline health workers with the Ervebo vaccine, which the World Health Organization (WHO) says could offer some protection against Ebola, but there is no conclusive evidence that it would work against the current virus.
Health authorities say the true scale of the crisis is likely three times as high as official statistics suggest as the disease continues to outpace efforts to contain it. WHO has said the outbreak is projected to surpass the deadliest in history, West Africa's 2014-16 outbreak, which killed more than 11,000 people.
Frontline health workers in eastern Congo have gone on multiple strikes to demand pay for their work, complicating efforts to stop the outbreak.
Benjamin Muhindo, another burial team member, said his family worries that he might bring the virus home. For him, though, a bigger priority is ensuring the proper burial of victims, he said.
"Burials during this Ebola epidemic are very complicated, as we are working under pressure and constantly racing against the clock," Muhindo said.
Trauma experts say the high number of cases and deaths are only one side of the outbreak's impact at the personal and communal levels.
"The trauma of this outbreak doesn't stop with the case count," said Rose Tchwenko, Mercy Corps country director in Congo. The chain of transmission will only be broken by "an integrated holistic response," which includes a social response to bereaved families and frontline workers, she added.
After the burial on Friday, Adolphe said he was very tired but more worried about the community than anything else.
"We have no choice," he said. "We are here to safeguard our community."

China injects over €45 billion into state banks and insurers as growth slows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:24:28 UTC
18:24:28 KST

China's finance ministry is leading a combined 360 billion yuan (€46.1bn) capital injection into eight state-owned banks and insurers, a coordinated effort to strengthen balance sheets strained by weak lending, low interest rates and government instructions to prop up the stock market.
Beijing has reached for its chequebook.
The Chinese finance ministry is advancing a 360 billion yuan (€46.1bn) package to businesses, announced on Sunday through statements from the companies involved and reported by state news agency Xinhua, making it one of the larger interventions in China's financial system this year as growth slows.
The Chinese banks take the bulk of it, roughly 290 billion yuan (€37.2bn), intended to preserve their capacity to keep lending as Beijing presses them to increase support for economic activity.
Xinhua reported the injection would strengthen the institutions' "sound operating capabilities, risk resistance capabilities and ability to serve the real economy."
The Agricultural Bank of China is pursuing a private placement of A-shares worth up to 160 billion yuan (€20.5bn) and the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China up to 100 billion yuan (€12.8bn), with the finance ministry among the investors.
Unusually, so is the China National Tobacco Corporation, which operates the state tobacco monopoly and the Export-Import Bank of China which will receive 30 billion yuan (€3.85bn).
Insurers account for the remaining 70 billion yuan (€9bn).
China Life Insurance Group, the country's largest life insurer, gets 35 billion yuan (€4.5bn) and China Taiping Insurance Group 7 billion yuan (€900mn).
The People's Insurance Company of China plans to raise up to 15 billion yuan (€1.9bn) through a private placement to the ministry, China Export and Credit Insurance Corporation receives 10 billion yuan (€1.28bn), and China Reinsurance Group is raising 3 billion yuan (€385mn).
Insurers have been squeezed from two directions as years of low interest rates have eroded investment returns, while the government has directed them to put money into Chinese equities.
The currency has been moving in the same direction.
The Chinese yuan reached its strongest level against the US dollar since January 2023 on Monday, trading at around $0.149, a firmer exchange rate that also happens to blunt a long-standing American complaint about Chinese currency management, weeks before talks in Washington.
Beijing's busy month
The capital injection is not the only move Beijing is making this month.
Chinese President Xi Jinping is reportedly preparing to bring a large delegation of business executives to his Washington visit on 24 September, according to sources cited by news agencies.
It would be a notable departure from customary practice.
Xi rarely travels with corporate leaders, many of whom lost standing after the regulatory crackdowns on technology, education and property that began in 2020, and the last comparable delegation accompanied him to the US more than a decade ago, in 2015.
Washington's response has also been curious.
"The White House is not tracking a Chinese CEO delegation," a US official said, without explaining what tracking meant in this context, leaving the statement short of either confirmation or denial.
The gesture would be reciprocal in any case.
When US President Donald Trump visited Beijing in May, he brought a roster of American CEOs including Elon Musk, Tim Cook and Jensen Huang. Bringing Chinese counterparts to Washington would signal a willingness to invest and trade with the US, while handing the White House potential economic wins before November's midterm elections.
Expectations for the summit itself remain modest, with the two sides still divided over which products should count as non-sensitive under trade arrangements.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng are due to meet in early September to work on deliverables.

New high-speed train service links Antwerp, Brussels Airport and Leuven with Cologne
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:24:16 UTC
18:24:16 KST

Antwerp, Leuven and Brussels Airport are now directly connected to Germany via a new ICE high-speed train service. The first train arrived at Antwerp Central this morning, following stops at Brussels Airport and Leuven. The trains will now run twice a day in both directions between Antwerp and Cologne.
New high-speed train service links Antwerp, Brussels Airport and Leuven with Cologne
The first ICE train was given a warm welcome at the three Belgian stations on Monday morning. The train arrived at its final destination, Antwerp Central, at around 9.30 am, half an hour behind schedule. The ICE trains operated by the German railway company Deutsche Bahn can accommodate over 400 passengers.
Route and timetables: In Germany, the trains depart from Cologne, with a stop in Aachen. In Belgium, they stop at Liège, Leuven, Brussels Airport and Antwerp. Passengers travelling from Antwerp can reach Cologne by ICE in approximately 2 hours and 20 minutes. From Brussels Airport, the journey takes less than 2 hours; from Leuven, approximately one and a half hours. The trains arrive in Cologne at around 1.30 pm and 9.30 pm.
Tickets for journeys between Antwerp and Cologne are available from 29.99 euros. For Leuven and Antwerp, this is the first permanent direct high-speed rail link to Germany. Brussels Airport is once again connected to the high-speed network for the first time since 2015. Passengers travelling with Belgian flag carrier Brussels Airlines can combine train and flight on a single ticket.
Partnership with Belgian Rail NMBS
Deutsche Bahn is partnering with Belgium’s state-owned rail company NMBS to realise this ICE service. The NMBS will operate half the services. The Cologne–Antwerp route is the second ICE service between Belgium and Germany. Eight ICE train services already run daily between Germany (Frankfurt, Cologne, Aachen) and Belgium, stopping in Liège, and terminating at Brussels South.
Eurostar high-speed trains also run between Belgium and Germany.

Penghu tests drone deliveries to remote islands

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Penghu County Government said Monday it was testing the use of drones to deliver supplies to remote communities.
The county and National Penghu University of Science and Technology launched test flights from Magong City to Jibei Islet. The program is intended to provide residents with a reliable supply of daily necessities in the future.
The pilot flight took off from the university campus, with Earthbook CEO Hsu Wei-cheng (徐偉城) demonstrating the drone’s setup. NPU President Lee Wen-hsi (李文熙) and local officials attended the event.
Lee said the drone was designed to withstand strong winds and followed a route mapped using weather forecasting data. He said additional wind-resistance tests were scheduled for February.
Hsu said the drone can travel up to 120 kilometers and is controlled from an operations center on campus. He said the farthest of Penghu’s 19 inhabited islands is 40 km away.
The drone has a carrying capacity of 3.5 kilograms and can reach Jibei in 15 minutes while traveling at 100 kph, Hsu said.
The university said the test flight was successful. It plans future flights to Hua, Tongpan, and Hujing islets.
Deputy Magistrate Lin Chieh-hsing (林皆興) said only 19 of the county’s islands have permanent residents and transportation to many can be disrupted by poor weather. He said drones and unmanned vessels were necessary to provide access to medical care and daily necessities.

Gongwin canine cancer drug set to enter Taiwan market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:23:40 UTC
18:23:40 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Gongwin Biopharm Holdings Co.’s new animal cancer drug has received marketing approval from the Ministry of Agriculture to treat melanoma in dogs, Liberty Times reported Saturday.
Melanoma develops from pigment-producing cells and is one of the most common cancers in dogs. It can occur on the skin, toes, and in the mouth, with oral melanoma accounting for more than 80% of cases and being particularly aggressive, according to SBM.
Gongwin’s Gwa103 uses a mechanism called intratumoral drug ablation to destroy cancer cells. The drug selectively enters malignant cells, helping reduce damage to surrounding healthy tissue, according to Anue.
Current treatment relies mainly on surgery and chemotherapy. Because canine melanoma often develops in the mouth and limbs and can affect large areas, surgery may require the removal of additional tissue.
Gongwin has signed letters of intent to collaborate on the drug with more than 100 animal hospitals across Taiwan. The drug can be used as a standalone treatment or in combination with other cancer therapies, according to UDN Money.
After completing labeling, supply chain arrangements, and hospital onboarding, the company plans to begin supplying the drug in stages in accordance with regulatory requirements. It will also provide clinical training for veterinary teams.
Gwa103 is also eligible for conditional marketing approval in the US, where Gongwin has obtained authorization to conduct clinical trials. The company also plans to expand into other major pet markets, including Australia, Japan, China, and Hong Kong.
Fortune Business Insights said the global veterinary oncology market was worth NT$91.9 billion (US$2.9 billion) in 2025. It estimates the market will grow at a compound annual growth rate of 10.7% from 2026 to reach NT$225 billion by 2034.

Chi Mei to feature 8 rare string instruments in Kaohsiung concert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:23:35 UTC
18:23:35 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — This year’s Chi Mei Music Festival will culminate Nov. 14 with a concert featuring eight rare string instruments from the Chi Mei Museum collection at the National Kaohsiung Center for the Arts, also known as Weiwuying, per a press release.
The concert, titled “Mountains and Waters, Rain and Storms: A Feast of Masterpieces by Brahms and Dvorak,” will feature pianist Liu Meng-chieh (劉孟捷), French conductor Victorien Vanoosten, music director of the Toulon Opera, and the National Taiwan Symphony Orchestra (NTSO).
Liu, who specializes in the works of Brahms and received an Avery Fisher Career Grant, will perform Brahms’ Piano Concerto No. 1 in D minor. Vanoosten will conduct Dvorak’s Symphony No. 8 in G major with the NTSO, according to the museum.
One of the most notable instruments will be a 1674 viola by Austrian luthier Jacob Stainer featuring a lion-head design. The museum described it as one of only four surviving Stainer lion-head violas in the world. The NTSO’s principal players will use the eight instruments during the concert, adding depth to the orchestra’s middle and lower registers.
This year’s festival is centered on Johannes Brahms (1833–1897). Brahms was a major figure of the Romantic era who combined the formal structures of the Classical period with the emotional language of 19th-century Romantic music, per the press release.
The festival program covers different periods of Brahms’ musical career and places his works alongside those of composers who influenced him or were his contemporaries, including Beethoven, Schubert, Robert Schumann, Liszt, and Wagner, as well as Dvorak.
The festival is curated by Chiao Yuan-pu (焦元溥), a writer and producer who holds a doctorate in musicology from King’s College London. The museum said this year’s festival features 13 instruments from the Chi Mei collection across its concerts, including works by Stradivari and Guadagnini and examples from the German and Austrian violin-making traditions.
