U.N. nuclear agency chief says Iran engagement is key to resuming inspections
International Atomic Energy Agency Director-General Rafael Grossi said renewed engagement between Iran and the U.N. nuclear watchdog is essential to resuming inspections of Iranian nuclear facilities. At a briefing Monday, Grossi told reporters that access, security and confidentiality concerns can be addressed through dialogue.
Grossi said, at this point, "there's no engagement" with Iran, adding that it has indicated it will not cooperate until a broader political agreement is reached.
"We do not subscribe to this logic," he said, stressing that Iran's obligations as a member of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty "do not disappear."
Grossi said Iran has yet to provide information required under its safeguards agreement about the status and condition of safeguarded nuclear material following attacks on its facilities, which he said "should never take place."
Asked about the prospects for renewed inspections, Grossi gave a clear answer: "The best, shortest way for a positive outcome is for Iran to engage with us."
Traffic through Strait of Hormuz reportedly hits lowest level since May
Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz dipped to its lowest level since May, according to shipping data quoted by the Reuters news agency.
Data from analytics firm Kpler recorded on Sunday an average of 10 ships per day transiting the vital waterway. The 10-day average measured Saturday was 13. It was more than 15 on Friday.
Only two vessels passed through the strait on Saturday, and six on Sunday, using mostly the Iranian route, according to Reuters.
The dip in traffic comes amid a flare-up in the conflict, with the U.S. announcing on Saturday it had struck and disabled three Iranian oil tankers in retaliation for previous attacks. Tehran responded by announcing it had targeted more ships traveling in what it calls unauthorized routes.
Traffic through the strait has been volatile since a period of relative calm in the fighting between the U.S. and Iran, but it is still well below pre-war levels of 130 per day.
Lebanese President says Israeli strikes undermine efforts to stop escalation in region
Lebanon's president on Monday condemned Israeli airstrikes in the country's south, which local media said killed 11 people.
During a meeting with the visiting French justice minister, Lebanese President Joseph Aoun said Israel's attacks undermine "all the efforts made to stop the escalation in the south and the region as a whole."
"What Israel is doing through successive attacks, killing innocent people, children and women, destroying and burning homes, and bulldozing properties are condemned, rejected and unjustifiable crimes," Aoun said
Qatar says Gulf countries cannot rely on the U.S. alone for security
Qatar's foreign ministry spokesman Majed Al Ansari said Monday the war with Iran had shown that Persian Gulf countries should not rely solely on their strategic partnership with the United States to maintain their security.
"We need to recognize in the Gulf region that the presence of international forces in the region and the establishment of a strategic partnership with the United States are extremely important, but they are not sufficient," Al Ansari said during a panel discussion at the Hili Forum in Abu Dhabi. "Self-reliance in the field of security is the only way forward."
"We need our partners and allies, but we cannot rely on them alone for our security," he said.
Qatar was one of the countries targeted on a regular basis by Iran in retaliation for U.S. strikes at the height of the war.
Tehran says Iran-Oman talks on Strait of Hormuz in "final stages"
Iran's foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said Monday that negotiations with Oman regarding the future of the Strait of Hormuz had reached the "final stage."
The two countries sit on opposite sides of the strategic waterway and have been engaged in talks for months with the goal of reaching an understanding on how to manage commercial traffic through the strait in the future.
"Within the coming days, the understanding between Iran and Oman for a temporary route safe in the Strait of Hormuz will be registered with the International Maritime Organization."
Throughout the talks, both sides have suggested the possibility of charging fees for ships to transit the waterway, a notion the U.S. government has bristled at.
Emirati diplomat says restoring trust with Iran will be difficult but necessary
A top Emirati official appeared to extend an olive branch to Iran on Monday, saying that restoring trust with Tehran would be difficult, but necessary.
Anwar Gargash, a diplomatic adviser to the United Arab Emirates president, also said Persian Gulf countries had failed to respond in a united fashion to Iran's attacks and threats during the U.S.-Iran war, with each country defending itself but not embracing a shared strategy.
Gulf countries bore the brunt of Tehran's retaliation for American strikes, with missiles and drone strikes hitting military targets as well as civilian areas on a regular basis at the height of the fighting.
"Geography leaves us no alternative to engagement, but we must distinguish clearly between rebuilding a necessary and functional relationship with Iran and rebuilding the trust that has been broken. The first is necessary. The second will be far more difficult," Gargash said at the Hili Forum in Abu Dhabi.
CBS/AFP
Iran warns South Korea against military deployment alongside the U.S.
Iran's foreign ministry on Monday warned South Korea against deploying military assets or getting involved in any other way with U.S. operations in and around the Strait of Hormuz, saying such a move would have "serious consequences."
On Friday, the South Korean government said it would consider taking part in naval operations, provided that its own military readiness was not compromised, but added that no decision had been made.
On Monday, Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei warned Seoul against succumbing to what he called "U.S. pressure and intimidation."
"Any military deployment or participation in operations by other countries in the Persian Gulf or the Strait of Hormuz can only be regarded as direct support for the party responsible for that aggression and will have serious consequences," he said in a post on X.
Tehran says it will announce new Strait of Hormuz "exclusion zone"
The new head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council said Tehran plans to announce an "exclusion zone" outside the Strait of Hormuz aimed at vessels it believes are attempting to transit the waterway.
Mohsen Rezaei's comments to Iran's state broadcaster came with few details, a day after the U.S. struck three Iranian oil tankers in response to Tehran launching ballistic missiles at U.S. warships.
The new zone should be announced in the coming days and weeks and "will begin from the line of the U.S. naval blockade, extend toward the Strait of Hormuz, and from this side continue into the Persian Gulf," Rezaei said without providing more details.
CBS/AP
Price of oil climbs, as regular gas averages nearly a dollar higher than last year's Labor Day
The price of Brent crude, the international standard for oil, added another 67 cents, reaching $96.95 per barrel.
The average price of regular gas was $4.14 a gallon heading into the holiday, nearly a dollar higher than last year and well above the Labor Day weekend record of $3.82 from 2012, according to AAA motor club.
Prices shot up after the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in February and have not settled down since. Crude oil traffic through the key Strait of Hormuz has plunged, and Iran has refused to reopen the waterway.
Iran threatens "intense" and "painful" response to U.S. strikes on oil tankers
The speaker of Iran's Parliament, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, threatened on Sunday to launch swifter and more forceful responses to U.S. attacks, after Tehran targeted American warships in retaliation for U.S. attacks on tankers.
"The Americans must have understood that the era of proportionate responses has come to an end," said Ghalibaf in a speech carried by state media, adding that "any aggression against Iran's interests and security will receive a faster, more intense and more painful response."
U.S. Central Command said Saturday it had "permanently disabled" three Iranian oil tankers in the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman.
"Let the message to the IRGC be clear: If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost — taking out three of yours," Adm. Brad Cooper, CENTCOM commander, said in a statement. "We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran's limited and exposed oil fleet."

Interior Minister Quintin labels Leipzig drone incident “full-blown Russian attack”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
07:37:38 UTC
16:37:38 KST

The foiled drone attack at Leipzig Airport was a full-blown attack rather than a “hybrid threat” says Belgian Interior Minister Bernard Quintin (Francophone liberal MR). “We are in a kind of war,” he said, although, according to him, there are no precise indications of a similar attack on Belgium.
Interior Minister Quintin labels Leipzig drone incident “full-blown Russian attack”
“Findings from our services and partners point to Russian involvement in planning and execution of the foiled hybrid operation,” Mr Quintin’s German colleague said earlier last week, following a failed drone attack on a Ukrainian cargo aircraft at Leipzig Airport. Among other things, investigators found a drone carrying a powerful explosive. It failed to detonate due to a fault with the detonator.
In response, Germany closed a Russian consulate and a cultural centre. Russia described the allegations as “baseless and absurd”.
In a statement, Belgian Interior Minister Bernard Quintin said that there are “no concrete indications” of a similar threat in Belgium.
“That does not alter the fact that we have also had problems here. A few months ago, there were also drones here, but they were not loaded with explosives.”
“Our security services are, in any case, monitoring the situation closely. And they will continue to do so, in close cooperation with the security services of our neighbours.”
“This is not a hybrid threat, but an attack”
According to Quintin, the term “hybrid” threat does not do justice to the situation.
“I hate that word,” he says. “What happened in Leipzig was an attack. Full stop. We are in a kind of war.”
“We face cyberattacks every day. Cables are being cut in the Gulf of Finland, and it is clear that the Russians are behind it. These are attacks. They are waging a war against us.”
“We must have the courage to state the facts. That does not mean we should start a war with Russia ourselves, but our German partners have made it very clear that this was a Russian attack.”
According to Quintin, there is no cause for concern for the time being. “We must, however, be aware that we are living in a new geopolitical reality. That is why we must take measures.”
“First and foremost, we must ensure our security services function effectively, in close consultation with all our allies: our neighbours in Europe, but also the Americans. That way, we will certainly have the intelligence we need to protect ourselves.”
In addition, we must once again invest more in defence, Quintin concludes. “Over the past 10 to 15 years, this has not been done to a sufficient extent. Investment in the armed forces also strengthens our intelligence capabilities. Military intelligence services play a crucial role in gathering information.”

Hackers breached the Bitcoin platform company Liquid Network and stole approximately $320 million worth of bitcoin from its wallet. Reuters reports, as cited by UNN.
Details
According to Liquid Network, approximately 4,000 bitcoins may have been withdrawn from the wallet. The total amount of the stolen funds is estimated at approximately $320 million

It is noted that the funds were withdrawn through SideSwap, a settlement platform authorized to process withdrawals from the network, although the key used in the process was not compromised, Liquid Network added.

Israeli resident charged over ISIS ties, marking fourth in under two weeks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
07:36:16 UTC
16:36:16 KST

A 19-year-old resident of northern Israel was charged with membership in a terrorist organization on Monday, becoming the fourth person from the region indicted over alleged ties to ISIS in less than two weeks.
The concentrated run of cases included two alleged plots to attack Israeli security forces and a former IDF soldier accused of training to join ISIS abroad.
Yaqoub Shibli, a resident of the northern village of Shibli, was arrested on August 16 in a joint operation by the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) and the Israel Police Northern District’s central investigative unit.
Investigators allege that Shibli expressed support for ISIS, watched material about the terrorist organization and pledged allegiance to it.
The prosecution filed the indictment at the Nof Hagalil-Nazareth Magistrate’s Court. The indictment follows three others filed against northern residents since August 28.
Various other cases of ISIS-affiliated arrests in Israel
In the first case, Haifa district prosecutors indicted a 16-year-old from the Galilee and Ibrahim Kaabia, 19, of Haifa after authorities alleged that both had pledged allegiance to ISIS and developed separate plans to attack security forces.
According to police and the Shin Bet, the minor searched online for instructions on making an explosive belt and intended to attack police officers and soldiers at the Temple Mount. Kaabia allegedly planned an attack against an IDF base in northern Israel.
Kaabia’s attorney, Suhad Aga-Dahla, denied that he had planned an attack. She said his exposure to ISIS material stemmed from curiosity and described him as a loyal citizen.
Five days later, prosecutors charged Khamis Su’ad, 30, of Huseiniya in the Galilee, with training or receiving instruction for terrorist purposes.
According to that indictment, Su’ad, who served in the IDF from 2017 to 2019, developed a growing identification with ISIS beginning in 2023. Prosecutors allege that he later decided to travel to Syria or Africa to join the organization, saved money for the journey, and viewed training material on combat, weapons, and the production of missiles and drones.
The four cases involve substantially different levels of alleged conduct, ranging from viewing ISIS material and pledging allegiance to preparing for attacks or training to fight abroad.
Police and the Shin Bet said they would continue acting against Israeli citizens seeking to operate on behalf of terrorist organizations.

Firefighters extinguished a blaze that spread to a nearby power substation in central Berlin early Monday, as police separately investigated a possible break-in at another substation in western Germany, according to local media.
The fire broke out overnight at a construction site on Bissingzeile in Berlin’s Tiergarten area and spread to a nearby substation, a fire department spokesman told public broadcaster RBB. About 50 firefighters fought the flames. Police sealed off a wide area, and the criminal investigation department is examining whether the fire was a crime or caused by a technical fault.
Hours earlier, on Sunday evening at around 10 pm local time (2000GMT), police mounted a major operation at the Niederrhein substation in Wesel, North Rhine-Westphalia, operated by energy company RWE, the daily Bild reported.
Officers found a hole cut in the security fence, indicating unknown people had entered the grounds. A police helicopter circled the sprawling site as officers searched the complex. Police did not immediately say whether technical infrastructure had been damaged or tampered with.
The two incidents come as authorities hunt a 48-year-old man from North Rhine-Westphalia suspected of a series of attempted sabotage attacks on Germany’s power network since last week. Investigators published a wanted notice with photos on Saturday and asked the public for tips.
A large search at the Hambach Forest west of Cologne was called off Sunday without finding the suspect, public broadcaster WDR reported.
Letters signed with the man’s name and sent to several newsrooms last week claimed responsibility for attempted attacks on power infrastructure near the Jaenschwalde and Schwarze Pumpe brown coal plants in Brandenburg, as well as at sites including Gohr, Bergheim-Rheidt, Dormagen and Weisweiler in North Rhine-Westphalia, ARD reported. The sender linked the acts to opposition to fossil-fuel power generation.

“It’s just words, but turns into harassment, physical violence, discrimination”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
07:24:53 UTC
16:24:53 KST

The song ‘Praat Nederlands’ (Speak Dutch) by the Antwerp-based rapper FabioW has sparked a great deal of outrage online. On Instagram, the Belgian-Chinese Julia Zhu (27) spoke out about it in a widely shared video. For her and other Belgians of Asian descent, this isn’t just about one song: “It’s an accumulation of comments and stereotypes that we have to deal with our whole lives.”
“It’s just words, but turns into harassment, physical violence, discrimination”
In the track ‘Praat Nederlands’ Sebastiaan Van Thilborgh, better known as FabioW, sings about a trip he took to Vietnam. There, he meets a girl who he could not understand due to the language barrier. She sounded like “ching chang chong”, he raps.
The song has earned him a great deal of criticism online. Unia, the Interfederal Centre for Equal Opportunities, has also received several complaints regarding the matter. On Monday night, singer FabioW took his promotional videos for the song offline for the second time. The song’s title was again changed to ‘Praat Nederlands’.
“Otherwise, I could lose everything I’ve built up,” the singer wrote on Instagram.
“Strangers have been shouting ‘ching chang chong’ at me my whole life”
Julia Zhu (27) posted a video on Instagram explaining why the phrase upsets her. The reel was shared thousands of times and reignited the debate about FabioW’s song.
“Growing up, people would constantly shout ‘ching chang chong’ at me in the street,” she says. “By complete strangers. Can you imagine what that does to your nerves?”
“When you experience that every day, your body actually triggers a sort of panic response every time you hear it. Why does the way I look give someone the right to shout at me, making me feel unsafe?”
“Whenever I walk past a group of children, I’m already bracing myself for what they might say to me. I hear this from other friends with Asian roots too. Because it just happens every single time.”
According to Zhu, the impact of a song like FabioW’s should not be underestimated. “It starts with small remarks such as ‘ching chang chong’, ‘dirty Chinese’ or ‘go back to your own country’. But by normalising this, you create an environment in which people feel they have the right to treat an entire group of people differently, based on their appearance or ethnicity.
“The next step is discrimination, exclusion – for example, when looking for a place to live or a job – or even violence.”
To address this, Zhu contacted FabioW herself. She says his initial response did not reassure her. “That conversation was completely pointless,” she says. “He mainly defended himself but didn’t offer me an apology.”
“I’m not saying he’s a racist, but people can do or say things that are unintentionally racist. If people point this out to you, you can still change and learn,” concludes Zhu.

NEW YORK, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- Reigning Olympic champion Zheng Qinwen of China overcame a 5-0 deficit in the opening set to beat six-time Grand Slam champion Iga Swiatek of Poland 7-5, 6-3 on Monday and reach the US Open quarterfinals.
Men's top seed Alexander Zverev of Germany also advanced, defeating Italy's Luciano Darderi 6-2, 6-2, 7-6 (3).
Zheng, 23, recovered from a slow start to win 12 of the next 13 games against Swiatek. It was her second remarkable comeback in as many matches after she rallied from 5-0 down in the deciding set to eliminate American Madison Keys in the previous round Saturday.
Zheng said the consecutive turnarounds were no accident and credited a more aggressive approach against Swiatek.
"I think in the baseline, I tried to play more flat against her, because she has really good top spin that makes me feel uncomfortable. I also tried to play more aggressive and stay with her as long as I can," Zheng said.
Zheng, who underwent elbow surgery in July 2025, said she was delighted to be back on the US Open's biggest stage after recovering this season.
"People often ask me if I am tired. When I arrived here, I'm not tired at all. I just feel really pumped for my next match, trying to reach a better level here, show my tennis and enjoy this fantastic stadium," she said.
Zheng will next face second seed Elena Rybakina of Kazakhstan, who beat Japan's Naomi Osaka 6-1, 6-4.
Zverev struck 13 aces and held off a third-set fightback from Darderi to secure his place in the last eight.
"I felt my level was very consistent. It was just that he started playing incredibly well in the third set. I barely saw anyone hit the ball as hard as he did. So credit to him, he made it very difficult for me," Zverev said.
Women's fourth seed Coco Gauff of the United States eased past compatriot Iva Jovic 6-1, 6-4, while Russia's Karen Khachanov rallied to upset men's 14th seed Learner Tien of the United States 7-5, 4-6, 6-7 (6), 6-1, 6-4 in three hours and 50 minutes.
In women's doubles, China's Jiang Xinyu and Zhang Shuai reached the quarterfinals with a 6-4, 7-6 (6) victory over Japan's Miyu Kato and Wu Fang-hsien of Chinese Taipei. ■

Asia-Pacific Community: Chinese meteorological technology supports post-mudslide rescue efforts in Nepal
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
15:41:28 CST
16:41:28 KST

KATHMANDU, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- Following the catastrophic mudslide that struck Nepal's border regions, Chinese meteorological authorities swiftly established contact with their Nepali counterparts, sharing monitoring information and conducting joint consultations.
During a video consultation on weather conditions following the mudslide, Nepali experts requested precipitation and observation data, as well as satellite monitoring products, from the Chinese side.
China has since stepped up meteorological support for Nepal, providing satellite data and meteorological services to assist cross-border disaster monitoring and emergency response, according to the China Meteorological Administration (CMA).
Through MAZU, China's AI-powered meteorological early-warning solution, the CMA has provided Nepal with a range of meteorological products, including multi-source satellite data and products from the Fengyun-3 and Fengyun-4 meteorological satellite series.
China's National Satellite Meteorological Center has continued to monitor precipitation and weather changes in the disaster-affected areas. High-resolution satellite data have also been used to track upstream ice-rock avalanche areas and river channels, providing support for disaster assessment, rescue operations and meteorological services.
In response to Nepal's needs, the CMA has also developed customized services for the country and connected them with China's Fengyun meteorological satellite products in real time.
Nepal's Department of Hydrology and Meteorology recently expressed appreciation for the timely support provided by the China Meteorological Administration during the disaster.
"The support and rapid response provided by the Chinese side following the disaster were very important and highly appreciable," said Bikash Nepal, a senior divisional meteorologist with the department.
He said support from China has strengthened Nepal's capacity for monitoring meteorological disasters and providing early warnings.
Jagdishor Panday, press advisor to Nepal's foreign minister, said China has extensive experience and advanced technologies in disaster management and emergency response, adding that timely information sharing and technical cooperation are of great significance to disaster response.
"Nepal deeply appreciates the solidarity and support demonstrated by China following this devastating disaster," Panday said. "Effective communication and coordination between Nepal and China are particularly important."
"Weather knows no borders," Nepal said, expressing hope for further sharing of meteorological observations as well as satellite and radar information with China, and for stronger cooperation in the application of early-warning systems to enhance Nepal's capacity to monitor, forecast and issue warnings for severe weather. ■

Nationwide 24-hour transport strike to go ahead as unions rally
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
07:34:27 UTC
16:34:27 KST

Nationwide 24-hour transport strike to go ahead as unions rally
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Thousands of public sector workers are expected to rally in The Hague on Tuesday against the cabinet’s social security cuts, a day before a 24-hour strike halts all trains, buses, trams and metros across the country.
Staff from councils, provinces, ministries, water boards and universities will march to the finance ministry behind a mock golden coach, a week before the real one carries the king on Prinsjesdag.
Union federation FNV said the coach carries a briefcase of alternative plans for the cabinet. Home care and nursing home staff are also taking part, and The Hague’s street cleaners are on strike.
“This cabinet keeps putting the bill on ordinary people,” FNV chairman Hans Spekman said in a statement. “The social safety net we have all paid into for years is being dismantled.”
No trains on Wednesday
 The rally is the second of three days of action this week. Dockers in Rotterdam, Amsterdam and Zeeland walked out on Friday, and on Wednesday public transport stops for 24 hours.
NS is running no regular trains at all. The only exception is the airport sprinter between Amsterdam Centraal, Schiphol and Hoofddorp, which will run four times an hour.
International services, including Eurostar, ICE, Eurocity and the NightJet, will not run within the Netherlands, nor will the regional trains to Antwerp and Aachen. It is the first nationwide 24-hour public transport strike since May 2019, when unions walked out over the state pension age.
Back to normal on Thursday
 NS expects to run its normal timetable on Thursday but is advising passengers to check the NS app shortly before departure. Its refund scheme for delays applies on strike days, although a separate allowance for alternative transport was scrapped earlier this year.
FNV called the strike in July as part of its campaign against plans to shorten unemployment benefit and cut payments for the long-term sick and disabled.
Social affairs minister Hans Vijlbrief has since dropped a plan to raise the state pension age faster in line with life expectancy, and the cabinet has scrapped part of the remaining cuts and delayed others, according to the Telegraaf. The unions say most of the savings are still on the table.

UK pledges winter air defence package to boost Ukraine's defences
The UK will supply air defence interceptors, large-calibre artillery rounds and drones to help Ukraine defend itself against barbaric Russian attacks this winter, as part of Britain’s commitment to help Ukraine defend its freedom and sovereignty.
- 
    The UK commits £100 million to air defence package including Patriot missiles to help Ukraine defend against Putin’s attacks.
- 
    Defence Secretary chairs his first Ukraine Defence Contact Group, the 50-nation strong group providing military kit for Ukraine.
- 
    Builds on recent UK backing of Ukraine’s domestic production of long-range missiles and landmark AI deal to boost military capabilities.
The UK will supply air defence interceptors, large-calibre artillery rounds and drones to help Ukraine defend itself against barbaric Russian attacks this winter, as part of Britain’s commitment to help Ukraine defend its freedom and sovereignty.
Through a £100 million contribution to NATO’s Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) the UK will support Ukraine with Patriot missiles and other air defence equipment that will be delivered before the winter, helping Ukraine defend its critical national infrastructure, innocent civilians and armed forces from Russian attacks. This follows the Prime Minister and Defence Secretary’s visits to Kyiv, where they heard from President Zelenskyy on the importance of additional support going into the winter.
Britain’s commitment to provide over 120,000 drones to Ukraine this year continues, with 25,000 delivered to date, a figure set to ramp up ahead of the winter. These include interceptors that take out Russian drones, reconnaissance drones that enable the Armed Forces of Ukraine to see what is happening on the battlefield and behind enemy lines, as well as attack drones that help Ukraine take the fight to Russia.
This comes as military support for Ukraine reaches another milestone, with the UK recently delivering its millionth round of large-calibre artillery ammunition to Ukraine, vital to its defence against Putin’s war. Building on this, the UK will deliver tens of thousands of long-range artillery rounds in the coming months with funding from Britain, Germany, Denmark, Lithuania, Netherlands, Norway and Sweden.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting MP said:
  Both the Prime Minister and I heard loud and clear on our first visits to Kyiv the importance of supporting Ukraine through this winter, as Putin prepares to use winter as a weapon by continuing barbaric attacks against civilian and energy targets.
We promised to mobilise allies and provide more support wherever we can. Today, we are delivering on that, strengthening Ukraine’s defences and, alongside 50 allies, converting commitment into capability.
We will stand shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine until they win. Ukraine’s frontline is the frontline for freedom everywhere and our support will not waver.
This military support follows the Prime Minister’s announcement that the UK has agreed that defence firm MBDA can release classified information on UK components for the long-range missile, SCALP, also known as Storm Shadow, to establish local assembly lines in Ukraine.
The Prime Minister recently travelled to Kyiv to meet President Zelenskyy and sign a landmark AI deal that will see the two countries join forces to develop new military capabilities and the technology of the future.
Today’s Ukraine Defence Contact Group co-chaired by the Defence Secretary and his German counterpart Boris Pistorius, brings together nearly 50 nations. Taking place for the 36th time, it focuses on Ukraine’s urgent battlefield requirements and helps to sustain long-term military support for Ukraine.

Opening of first road bridge with Russia a sign of tighter ties, North Korea says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
07:35:25 UTC
16:35:25 KST

The opening on Monday came as Russia and North Korea have heavily boosted military and economic ties since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
North Korea called the first road bridge across its narrow border with Russia a concrete sign of tightening bonds, state media reported on Tuesday, as Pyongyang gains advantages from its powerful neighbours Moscow and Beijing.
The bridge over the Tumen river into Russia and an under-construction span to China are part of a shift that offers Western-sanctioned Pyongyang economic and strategic options it has long sought, experts said.
North Korea "will simultaneously secure two major overland routes linking it with Russia and China, allowing it to encourage competition between the two countries and maximise its gains," said Lim Eul-chul, a professor at Kyungnam University.
He noted the bridges also "can be a message to the United States that North Korea has no reason to beg Washington for sanctions relief or make concessions on denuclearisation in order to negotiate," Lim added.
Russia noted the bridge is designed to accommodate expanded growth in freight with the capacity for up to 300 vehicles daily, which adds to the rail and air links already between the neighbours.
Ukrainian rights group Truth Hounds, however, previously warned that the new bridge could become "a direct artery for moving North Korean troops, construction brigades and military officials into Russia, with Russian technology and resources flowing in the opposite direction."
The ceremony on Monday marking the new bridge's opening came as Russia and North Korea have heavily boosted military and economic ties since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
North Korea dispatched thousands of troops to Russia in 2024 to help ward off a Ukrainian incursion into the Kursk region, while Kyiv has accused Moscow of using North Korean missiles in its regular barrages.
South Korea's central bank estimated in July that North Korea's economy grew more than 3% for a third straight year in 2025, citing it's expansion of economic cooperation with Russia as a "major drive."
The bank's official said North Korea's gross national income also "received a boost from a sharp rise in foreign currency earnings" linked to the deployment of its troops to Russia.
Beijing-Moscow-Pyongyang bloc
"The completion of the bridge is a significant event adding a new dynamic movement to the overall bilateral cooperation," North Korean official Pak Thae-song said in comments carried by the official KCNA news agency.
North Korea and China are already connected by the Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge, which is regularly used by passenger trains, but its capacity is limited.
After a long halt, the bridge partly reopened and restored daily passenger train services with China earlier this year, but has not yet resumed issuing tourism visas to Chinese citizens, who once made up the bulk of its overseas visitors.
North Korea has long kept tight control over foreign visitors and effectively sealed its borders at the start of the COVID-19 pandemic six years ago.
The New Yalu River Bridge, intended as an alternative and eventual replacement of the Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge, is expected by experts to be completed this year.
The completion of the bridge "sends a political and geopolitical message demonstrating the formation of a "North Korea-China-Russia continental triangular bloc," said Lim.

Suspected migrant smugglers go on trial in Paris over mass drowning in Channel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
07:27:09 UTC
16:27:09 KST

Suspected migrant smugglers go on trial in Paris over mass drowning in Channel
PARIS, Sept 8 - Fourteen men face trial in Paris on Tuesday on smuggling charges related to the drowning of more than 30 people in the Channel five years ago, the worst disaster on record involving migrants in the narrow seaway separating France and Britain.
The migrants perished after their overloaded dinghy deflated as they made the perilous crossing across one of the world's busiest shipping lanes.
Investigators allege that Afghan and Iraqi-Kurdish smuggling networks organised the migrants' passage to Britain from camps near Grande-Synthe and Calais in northern France. The defendants face charges including involuntary manslaughter, facilitating illegal immigration as part of an organised gang and criminal conspiracy.
A French fishing vessel alerted emergency services after spotting bodies floating in the waters off the French coast near Calais in November 2021, according to the court referral order. Twenty-seven victims were recovered, while at least four others were never found. Only two men survived.
The victims were mainly Iraqi Kurds, but also included Afghans, Ethiopians, an Egyptian, a Somali national, an Iranian Kurd and a Vietnamese national. The youngest known victim was a 7-year-old girl.
The migrants had been packed on to a flimsy dinghy that was non-certified and unfit for open-sea navigation, and was not equipped with enough life jackets, the court document showed. Experts concluded its occupants had "no chance" of effectively dealing with an emergency at sea.
Among the defendants facing involuntary manslaughter charges are alleged organisers, transporters and logistics coordinators connected to the smuggling groups. Prosecutors argue their actions helped create the conditions that led to the disaster, even if some were not physically present when the boat launched.
Two of the defendants have eluded French authorities and will be tried in absentia.
Investigators cited evidence including mobile-phone data, intercepted communications, surveillance operations and testimony from survivors and relatives of victims.
A British inquiry into the disaster found the deaths were avoidable. It concluded that a French naval vessel failed to respond to a call for help from the British coastguard, which in turn made "a number of flawed decisions", including ending a search for survivors too early.
Families of some of the victims would travel from Erbil in Iraqi Kurdistan to attend part of the trial, their lawyers said.
"Justice must hold to account everyone who played a role in this tragedy," the statement read.
The trial was due to last until September 30. REUTERS

It called on the public to help safeguard clean elections, the financial system, and Taiwan’s national security.

Taiwan moves ahead with floating offshore wind demonstration projects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
07:45:47 UTC
16:45:47 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of Economic Affairs Energy Administration held a briefing Tuesday on a planned floating offshore wind demonstration program, with two to three projects expected to connect to Taiwan’s power grid in 2032 and 2033, per a press release.
Energy Administration Deputy Director Chen Chung-hsien (陳崇憲) said selection results could be announced as early as the third quarter of next year, with draft selection regulations expected by the end of this year.
A major concern for the industry is the renewable energy feed-in tariff, with a draft expected by the end of this year. Industry representatives have said a rate of at least NT$10 (US$0.32) per kilowatt-hour may be needed to make floating offshore wind projects competitive, per CNA.
At the briefing, the agency said the three key evaluation criteria for floating wind farms are technology, financial strength, and sustainability. Initially, two demonstration projects will be selected, with an additional project allowed depending on circumstances.
Each project should have six to 12 floating platforms, with a capacity of 100 to 200 MW. Total installed capacity for the demonstration program would therefore range from 200 MW to 600 MW, per IEK.
Regarding the selection timeline, Chen said draft regulations are expected to be announced in the fourth quarter of this year, followed by a six-month bidding period. Applications could be received by the second quarter of 2027, with selection results announced in the third quarter.
Projects are expected to be completed and connected to the grid by the end of 2032. Those that have installed all floating platforms or connected at least half their capacity by then may complete grid connection in 2033.
Chen said the draft renewable energy feed-in tariff would be announced by the end of the year, “giving the industry a basis for pricing.” He said operators should also provide detailed cost calculations to help determine the appropriate tariff.
Simply presenting a tariff figure without supporting cost information would not be sufficient, Chen said.
Chen said the cost of generating electricity from floating wind farms in countries including South Korea is above NT$10 per kilowatt-hour, per UDN. He cautioned that South Korea uses an inflation-adjustment mechanism, meaning the figures cannot be directly compared with Taiwan.
The Energy Administration had previously considered providing a one-time subsidy but has now returned to a feed-in tariff incentive mechanism, which it says provides developers with clearer financial calculations. There are therefore no current plans for one-time subsidies specifically for equipment or hardware.
Regarding reports that Orsted will not participate in the floating wind selection process, Chen said each company has its own considerations, with some prioritizing fixed-bottom wind farms while others are more optimistic about floating technology.
Chen said at least six potential sites have already passed relevant environmental assessment planning, and the government is not concerned about a lack of potential bidders.
He said the purpose of the demonstration projects is to identify technologies suitable for Taiwan’s unique environmental and climatic conditions. Regarding the water depth and distance from shore of floating wind farms, Chen said there will be no rigid requirements.
He explained that shallower waters are generally more suitable for fixed-bottom wind farms, while floating technology can allow development in deeper waters. Because water depth varies in different areas around Taiwan, the government will not set specific requirements for offshore distance or installation depth at this stage.
The Energy Administration said the demonstration program is intended to test the feasibility of technologies and infrastructure needed for development in deeper waters, including floating platform designs, power-generation performance, port facilities, financing models, and other aspects of commercial development.
